The team applies conformal analysis, a method that attaches honest error bars to each call. Those bars can be compared across sex, age, and ethnic groups. A sampling trick during training steadied the class balance first. The study checks how that trick changes the uncertainty picture. The method gives both group-level guarantees and per-patient scores. Such scores could help clinics judge when to trust the model.
arxiv-2504-00219:
Han Zhou, Wei Dong, and Jun Chen offered LITA-GS in 2025 for building 3D scenes from badly lit photographs. The popular Gaussian splatting method struggles in harsh or dim lighting: the initial point cloud recovered from such images misses detail, and noise, lost information. And color warping block a clean, usually exposed rebuild. Simply brightening each photo first also fails, because separate enhancement makes varied viewpoints disagree about lighting.

Their method needs no reference well-lit images. A first workflow extracts an actual prior that does not change with illumination, catching the scene's dependable spatial form. A form rendering plan built on that prior then renders views every time regardless of the first lighting. The design aims at faithful novel views of scenes photographed under adverse illumination, a common real-world condition.
arxiv-2504-03419:
Anthony Couthures and four co-authors study a model where views in a social web move with the state of the world round them. Trust in that world's signal is the key dial. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

By a guard rule, they show the long-run tale can be cut down to the case where all views move as one. They then map how the joint system splits as trust shifts. They give the terms for two kinds of split: a fork, where one path parts in two, and a loop-born swing. Worked runs with numbers round out the proof. The work shows how trust in a shared signal can tip a whole web.
arxiv-2504-07719:
Pegah Nokhiz, Aravinda Kanchana Ruwanpathirana, Aditya Bhaskara, and Suresh Venkatasubramanian wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies how erratic work schedules harm the money security of hourly and part-time staff in food service and retail.

When hours swing with little notice, pay swings too, and plans for saving and spending fall apart. The authors build a simulation in which a worker picks spending rules as news about the schedule comes in, while steering clear of ruin. Both theory and tests show that the more a worker can foresee shifts, the better the long-run outcome. Not knowing what comes next deepens the harm. The frame also lets fixes be tried and graded.
arxiv-2504-13419:
Wenyu Li and co-authors wrote this computer vision paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on rebuilding 3D scenes from photos. New foundation models do this well by matching points across views, but they falter where matching cues run thin, like blank walls or dim rooms.

Their method, Mono3R, adds help from single-image depth reading, which stays steady in those weak spots. A refinement module blends those one-view clues into the multi-view rebuild. The result is a fast, feed-forward system that needs no slow per-scene tuning. Tests across several standard benchmarks show clear gains in camera position accuracy and in the quality of the rebuilt point clouds. The authors present the blend as a fix for a known blind spot. Matching alone, they argue, is not enough for hard scenes.
arxiv-2504-13619:
Rohan Singh, Mitsuharu Morisawa, Mehdi Benallegue, Zhaoming Xie, and Fumio Kanehiro train a humanoid to walk on soft and uneven ground with deep reinforcement learning. Their paper from twenty twenty-five seeks robust bipedal control for real settings, where floors sag and bumps hide. Training runs in simulation with randomized terrain. The policy then moves to a real HRP-5P robot with body-sense feedback alone.

A simple curriculum of varied fake ground proves enough for the transfer. Demo walks cross hard floors inside and outside the lab. The team also argues that fixed-step gaits cap robustness. A new policy bends the clock signal, so step pace adapts to terrain and speed orders. Simulation tests back that gain on rough ground. Code for training and scoring is posted online.
arxiv-2504-14419:
Utkarsh Kumar, Abhijith Ajith, and Amresh Verma test whether dark matter is truly cold in this two thousand twenty-five cosmology paper. Their evidence comes from the latest baryon acoustic oscillation measurements by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, known as DESI. They fit a dark matter equation of state parameter that equals zero for ordinary cold dark matter. DESI data alone mildly preferred a slightly negative value.

Combined datasets sharpened the picture but disagreed with each other. DESI plus a supernova compilation excluded cold dark matter at notable significance, while Planck plus DESI stayed near zero yet still off the standard value. Low-redshift measurements drove the preference for non-cold dark matter; higher-redshift data remained consistent with the standard model. The authors argue every combination improves on the standard paradigm, though the internal tension demands explanation.
arxiv-2504-17219:
Hyomin Lee and four co-authors strengthen the autoencoders that sit inside image generators like Stable Diffusion. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Variational autoencoders compress images into a latent code and rebuild them. Their robustness has been little studied. Adversarial training boosts robustness in classifiers, but builders feared it would dull generation quality. The team challenges that worry.

Their SRL-VAE framework attacks the latent code with crafted perturbations during training. That pressure smooths the latent space itself. Smoother codes generalize better to odd inputs. A regularizer keeps the code faithful to the original image. The result improves both generation quality and robustness at once. The trade-off the field assumed turns out to be avoidable.
arxiv-2504-19319:
Francesco Mele and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a new gauge for non-Gaussian quantum states. Such states are a key resource for quantum edge in light based, or bosonic, setups. Their gauge, the symplectic rank, counts how many modes of a state's spread top the vacuum mark. It has a set of prized traits.

The gauge is cheap to work out. It marks the least modes the state's non-Gaussian core can be squeezed into by Gaussian steps. It caps the gate cost of making the state and the sample cost of mapping it. It never grows under Gaussian steps, even lucky ones. That yields hard no-go rules and shows the resource trade is one way.
arxiv-2505-00119:
Graham and Weigel show how to compute, in a 2025 preprint, the quantum part of the pull that a domain wall exerts. In field theory, a domain wall is a sheet-like structure built from a field kink stretched across extra dimensions. At the classical level, the kink's mass simply becomes energy per unit area, called tension. The quantum part is harder, because quantum jiggling around the wall in every direction must be counted.

The authors use spectral methods, which feed on data about how waves scatter off the wall. With that data they compute the leading quantum correction to the tension. The method also makes it easy to switch between renormalization schemes, the bookkeeping rules that keep such sums finite. They present the approach as an efficient route for a class of problems that is often messy. The work is aimed at theorists who study defects in fields.
arxiv-2505-04219:
Matias Alvarado wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It counts algebraic points of set degree on a smooth projective curve over a number field, sorted by a map that gives the curve's gonality.

The set in view holds points whose field grows by a set degree over the base, with that growth coming from the gonality map itself. Heights are capped, and the paper studies how fast the count grows as the cap lifts. Such counts sit in Diophantine geometry, where the shape of a curve rules how many low-degree points it can hold. The work is pure number theory.
arxiv-2505-04619:
Abdulaziz Almuzairee, Rohan Patil, Dwait Bhatt, and Henrik Christensen wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It improves how robots learn manipulation from sight when several cameras watch the scene at once.

Joining views gives richer input and faster learning, but the learned skill breaks if a camera fails and is heavy to deploy. Their method, called MAD, merges the views for learning while also training on single views mixed in. That yields skills that stay sound when a view drops and that can run light in the field. Tests on the Meta-World and ManiSkill3 suites show gains in both learning speed and sturdiness.
arxiv-2505-04819:
Tristan Aurégan and Luc Deike gauged how long face bubbles survive in turbulent air in a 2025 paper. Ocean bubbles mediate gas and heat exchange between sea and sky. Their lifetime is set by how fast their thin caps drain and burst. The tests blow turbulent air, standing in for wind, over bubbles floating on surfactant and salt answers. Carefully renewing the face layer so its traits stay constant, a control the authors show is essential for that can be rerun lifetimes.

Drainage follows a model combining outward viscous flow with convective evaporation. Without salt, evaporation alone sets the lifetime, whatever the surfactant level. With salt, low surfactant lets impurities trigger an early thick bursting, shortening life regardless of wind. The probability spread of lifetimes is also characterized.
arxiv-2505-05819:
Beretta studies how to learn junta distributions, where a probability rule depends on only a few of many variables. Such a rule over binary strings uses at most k of the n inputs. His first result ties this task to a famous hard problem. Learning these distributions is exactly as hard, in compute terms, as learning noisy parity functions. That problem, LPN, is a landmark in learning theory.

His second result is an algorithm whose sample use is best possible, up to log factors. Its compute cost matches earlier, less frugal methods. Together, the results say the algorithm cannot be much improved. Any big gain would need a breakthrough on LPN itself.
arxiv-2505-06319:
Zijian An and Lifeng Zhou wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It trains reinforcement learning agents to fight over nodes on a graph, in a multi-step game based on the Colonel Blotto setup.

Two players spread forces across rounds to hold prized nodes, and the best plan is hard to find since moves shift with the graph. The authors cast the game as a Markov decision process and run two learners, Deep Q-Network and Proximal Policy Optimization. A matrix trick builds the legal move set at each step from the graph's links. On varied graphs, both learners beat random and greedy rivals and held even against a trained foe. On lopsided graphs they learned to use shape as an edge.
arxiv-2505-07019:
Khang Nguyen Quoc, Lan Le Thi Thu, and Luyl-Da Quach present SCOLD, a vision language model for leaf disease in two thousand twenty-five. Leaf disease checks are core to smart farming. Past tools fuse image and text poorly, or pretrain on generic sets. Such sets lack the fine facts of plant health.

SCOLD pretrains on a large corpus of leaf images with symptom prose. Soft targets in its contrastive loss curb overconfidence. That shift lifts broad skill and strength on fine grained classes. Tests beat known rivals on zero shot, few shot, retrieval, and class tasks. It does so at a modest model size.
arxiv-2505-12019:
Jianyi Zhang, Ziyin Zhou, Yilong Li, and Qichao Jin propose FL-PLAS, a federated learning defense against backdoor attacks, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Federated averaging is vulnerable when malicious clients poison their updates, and attacks keep getting stealthier.

Most defenses fail once half or more of the clients are malicious, or they need an auxiliary server dataset. FL-PLAS instead splits each local model into a feature extractor and a classifier. Clients upload only extractor parameters for aggregation and keep their classifiers private, so poisoned labels cannot spread. Tests on three image datasets kept main-task accuracy high even with ninety percent malicious clients.
arxiv-2505-12119:
Yukalov and Yukalova describe a method to squeeze answers one can trust out of short perturbation series in nonlinear problems. Asymptotic expansions in a small parameter most often fail just where answers are wanted, at moderate or large values. Their self-similar approximants borrow from renormalization group thinking and optimal control to bridge that gap.

The approach extrapolates a series to finite values of the variable, and even to infinite ones. The team prove the procedure is regular. Worked examples show good agreement with direct numerical calculations. In good cases the method reconstructs the exact solution from a short series. The work surveys recent developments of the technique for physicists and applied mathematicians.
arxiv-2505-12719:
Chenxuan Zhang and eight colleagues explain the odd light of little red dots, a new class of far-off objects found by the Webb telescope. The dots are compact, very red, and show broad glowing lines. Their spectra bend into a V shape, with a break at one shared frequency. What powers that shape has been a puzzle.

The team built spectra for twenty-eight dots with known distances. They propose a two-part disk around a black hole. The inner disk is a standard hot disk, while the outer disk sits at the edge of collapse. That cool outer part shines mostly in infrared and visible light. Together the parts make the V shape with no need for thick dust. Most dots, they argue, feed modestly and shine weaker than they look.
arxiv-2505-16019:
Shaobo Li and Ben Sherwood predict the equity premium with penalized quantile regression in two thousand twenty-five. Mean regression can mislead here, since errors spread unevenly and have heavy tails. Quantile methods study the full spread of returns, not just the mean. Their method picks one shared set of predictors for all quantiles.

A group penalty forces the same sparse pattern at each quantile. That stops quantile lines from crossing and eases reading. Theory lets the predictor count grow with sample size. Tests on fake and real data beat rival methods. Some key predictors flip sign from low to high quantiles.
arxiv-2505-16719:
Olcay Coskun and Deniz Yilmaz introduce a new class of functors in a twenty twenty-five paper on algebra. Functors are maps between categories that keep structure intact. The new class, p-bifree biset functors, is fixed by a prime p and built from bisets whose left and right stabilizers avoid p in a set way.

The class sits between two known ones and acts as a bridge. The pair sorts all its simple members over a field of characteristic zero: each is tagged by a finite group plus a simple module. They then work out the makeup of key examples, like the Burnside ring functor and the character ring functors.
arxiv-2505-17019:
Chenhao Zhang and Yazhe Niu built a framework in 2025 for understanding what images imply, not just what they show. A picture's metaphorical meaning depends on culture, emotion, and context, and today's multimodal models, strong at plain question answering, often miss the unstated relationships between visual elements. The authors model their system, Let Androids Dream, on the human process of working out an implication.

It runs in three stages. Perception turns the image into rich, layered text descriptions. A search stage then repeatedly pulls in knowledge from other domains to close the contextual gaps and resolve ambiguity. Finally, a reasoning stage assembles the implication through explicit, checkable steps. Paired with a lightweight commercial model, the framework outperformed more than fifteen multimodal systems on an English benchmark for image implication, a sizable margin by the authors' report.
arxiv-2505-23819:
Keren Zhou and ten co-authors introduced Linear Layouts in twenty twenty-five, a mathematical framework for the unglamorous problem that governs deep learning speed: how tensors map onto hardware. Layout choices — which thread or register holds which element — were traditionally handled case by case, and converting between layouts exploded combinatorially as hardware grew more complex.

Their idea represents a layout as a binary matrix over the field with two elements, acting on the bits of hardware coordinates. Layouts then compose and convert by generic linear algebra, eliminating the quadratic blowup. Integrated into the Triton compiler, linear layouts optimized individual operators and full kernels, reduced backend engineering effort, and even fixed several bugs lurking in Triton's legacy layout system. The paper gives compiler writers a systematic language for a formerly artisanal problem.
arxiv-2505-24019:
Kaiyuan Zhang and five co-authors argue that AI agents should be built on classic security principles. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Agents that use large language models can do complex tasks, but talks between agents open new holes. Trick prompts and warped context can leak private data or hijack the system.

Old design rules from information security can help: defence in depth, least privilege, full checks on each act, and ease for users. They set out a frame, AgentSandbox, that weaves these rules through an agent's whole life. Tests with top models show high use value in calm and hostile runs, with far less privacy risk. The frame aims to ground trust in agent systems.
arxiv-2505-24719:
Amanda Dias Falqueto and Farid Tari studied the shapes of holomorphic curves and complex faces through singularity theory in a 2025 paper. Singularity theory classifies shapes by how they touch model objects, lines, planes, spheres. In the complex setting the measuring functions are usually only real-valued, blocking the theory's holomorphic tools. The authors show that with a well-chosen complex bilinear even form. The groups measuring contact between curves or faces and their models become holomorphic themselves.

That single move imports the tool set, yielding complex analogues of old-style real results. New invariants appear: C-bend and C-torsion for curves, C-main and C-Gaussian bend for faces. The building also gives geometric meaning to complexifying the contact groups of real analytic faces, tying two literatures jointly.
arxiv-2506-02619:
Yanbei Liu and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on learning from graphs whose nodes and links come in many types. Such mixed graphs model real nets like paper and author webs. Self taught methods learn from the graph with no labels. Most need hand made tweaks of the graph and hand picked pairs to match or split.

Their method, HGOT, skips the tweaks and the pair picks. It builds a core view by merging the views from each path type in the graph. An optimal transport plan then links each path view to the core view. That link nudges the encoder to learn rich node traits. Tests on four real data sets beat top rivals on tasks like node class calls.
arxiv-2506-03419:
Pablo Groisman, Cecilia De Vita, Julian Fernandez Bonder, and Yuanzhao Zhang solve a long-held guess about linked oscillators. The work came out in 2025. The guess asks how often the units fall into each stable state. Their setup is a ring of the same Kuramoto oscillators, the base model for things that tick in sync.

On a ring, the sole stable end states are twisted states. In those states, phases step at an even pace round the ring. Each state has its own winding number. A 2006 guess said the share of starts that land in each state drops like a bell curve in that number. The team backs the guess with both math and screen tests. The winding number locks in fast, in log time, before wide order can form. That early lock lets them work out the number from near-free parts.
arxiv-2506-04019:
Neeva Oza and co-authors wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on whether language models can tell if two programs do the same thing. Judging code equivalence matters for rewriting and translating software safely.

Their benchmark, CETBench, builds pairs of programs from a shared pool, then applies random chains of small code transformations. Some pairs stay equivalent; others quietly stop being so. Even top models stumble badly after these simple edits, the team finds. Comparing programs across languages makes the drop worse. A light fine-tuning pass on transformed pairs recovers much of the loss. Their generator can vary difficulty, transformation mix, and language pairs. The authors conclude that today's models lean on surface patterns more than true code meaning.
arxiv-2506-04819:
Jun-Jie Wei and Fulvio Melia used glowing gas galaxies as cosmic mileposts in a 2025 paper. Ionized hydrogen galaxies and giant star-forming regions obey a brightness relation that makes them standard candles, reaching far deeper in redshift than supernovae. Above all with fresh James Webb discoveries pushing the sample past two hundred sources covering most of cosmic history. Such reach can arbitrate between rival expansion models.

Fitting the Hubble diagram, the authors report their preferred nonstandard model strongly favored over the standard flat model and a dark-energy variant by an information criterion. They flag a caveat themselves: an unknown intrinsic scatter in the candle relation. Fitted freely, erases the gap and strains the inferred matter density against satellite values. The claim is presented with its weakness attached.
arxiv-2506-08719:
Yongpeng Zhao, Maik Pfefferkorn, Maximilian Templer, and Rolf Findeisen tune vehicle controllers with far fewer road tests. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses multi-fidelity Bayesian optimisation. Tuning by real driving alone is slow and expensive. Simulations are cheaper but never match the road perfectly.

The method learns from many simulations and very few real runs. A layered statistical model carries knowledge between the two settings. No extra simulations are needed once road testing starts. The workflow still matches the two-stage process industry already uses. Tests in simulation and on real vehicles both succeeded. Controller quality stayed high despite the tiny road sample. Car makers could cut tuning cost without losing performance.
arxiv-2506-11019:
Vincent Koc and three co-authors set out design patterns for AI coding tools that learn from live metrics. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Code tools now sit in platforms that track prompt traces, test scores, and run logs as work goes on. The Model Context Protocol links a code editor to those streams.

They give patterns for local prompt tweaks, for checks run in a build pipeline, and for agents that adapt from metrics on their own. Their frame fits tools such as DSPy and PromptWizard. They show it through Opik, an open server for model metrics. The work lays ground for study of prompt tuning and agent tools in rich metric settings.
arxiv-2506-12419:
Yuan Li, Zhong Zheng, Chang Liu, and Zesong Fei identify wireless channel types with a generative diffusion model. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Knowing the channel scenario guides modeling, positioning, and transceiver design. Classic methods read off statistics like path loss and delay spread. Similar scenarios fool those statistics. Moving scatterers leave hidden marks that numbers miss.

The team casts identification as a maximum a posteriori estimation task. They recast it as maximum likelihood and solve it with a conditional diffusion model. A transformer network extracts hidden channel features across latent layers. The generative route separates look-alike scenarios better. Radio fingerprint positioning stands to gain. The work brings modern generative tools into channel science.
arxiv-2506-13119:
Kamilia Zaripova, Ege Özsoy, Nassir Navab, and Azade Farshad find disease genes from symptoms alone, guided by a knowledge graph. Matching a patient's phenotypes to one causative gene is a precision medicine bottleneck. Their model, PhenoKG, fuses graph neural networks with transformers over a rare disease knowledge graph. It works with a candidate gene list when one exists, and without when none does.

On a real-world patient data set, the method's ranking quality clearly beat the strongest baseline across both reported measures. Ablations confirm each component earns its place. Generalization to phenotype-only cases matters most for the clinic, where genomic data are often incomplete. Decision support for rare disease diagnosis is the prize. The paper argues structured medical knowledge, not just bigger models, is what gene hunting was missing.
arxiv-2506-13519:
Petros Stefanou, Arthur Suvorov, and José Pons model the pull zones of magnetars in full three dims, with the rules of Einstein in play. Bursts from magnetars draw strength from streams in the pull zone. But past work on still forms with no pull took in most cases the same form round an axis. With neural nets bound by physics, the team builds three dim forms for stars of not the same tight pack.

Face stream trends modeled on hot spots seen in views serve as edge terms. The low strength fixes let just near thirty per cent more free strength than starved states in the axis same cases. That share drops to near five per cent with spots in three dims in set tracts. That short fall makes burst strength hard to clear up, sole if the field has traits past two poles.
arxiv-2506-14019:
Zhou and Wodtke give a sim way to read cause paths with more than one mid step. Cause path work oft meets more than one mid part at once. It also meets parts the first cause bends in its wake. Hands aim to guess more than one mark from such webs. Marks span straight, bent, and path-tied ends in the set. Their way sims end worlds from a chain of spread forms.

One form sits per mid part and one for the end in the chain. Past work for one mid part seeds the chain way in the text. Form-built runs can hold straight and bent ties in the sums. They hold more than one end type in the same frame too. The risk is wrong form picks for each sim in the chain. A no-form run with deep nets gives a twin path there.
arxiv-2506-14419: Cheng Yeaw Ku and Leyou Xu prove a conjecture about the eigenvalues of the transposition graph. That graph is the Cayley graph of the symmetric group generated by all transpositions, a central object in algebraic combinatorics. They show that every integer in an explicit symmetric interval, determined by a binomial coefficient, occurs as an eigenvalue. The interval's endpoint involves choosing two from a quantity near two-thirds of n. The result settles a recent conjecture by Kravchuk and adds exact spectral information about a much-studied family of graphs.
arxiv-2506-15919:
Juan Garcés, Florian Goertz, Manfred Lindner, and Álvaro Pastor-Gutiérrez reframe the Higgs hierarchy problem as a question about criticality. Naturalness has long asked why the Higgs mass stays so far below the Planck scale despite quantum corrections. The team runs the full Standard Model through the Wilsonian functional renormalization group, a first in this context. That machinery captures logarithmic and quadratic running together, as honest tuning estimates require.

Fine-tuning is then read as near-critical behavior of the Higgs sector's phase structure. Scheme-independent facts about the infrared Higgs phases and their quantum phase transition are extracted. An enhanced fine-tuning, usually omitted from estimates, gets its due. Coupling new physics to the Higgs can soften the high-scale sensitivity, and the framework recovers the known large-anomalous-dimension escape. Critical phenomena language, they argue, clarifies what tuning really means.
arxiv-2506-19219:
Guangqi Zhao improved the energy barrier bound in twenty twenty-five for higher-dimensional hypergraph product quantum error-correcting codes. Single-shot correction — fixing errors with one measurement round, even when measurements themselves are noisy — hinges on a confinement property that guarantees an energy barrier. Earlier work derived such a barrier for these codes from confinement alone.

By analyzing the structure of logical operators directly, Zhao proves a stronger bound for the low-density versions of the codes. Notably, these higher-dimensional codes can hold macroscopic barriers even when their classical ingredients cannot. The barrier is at least the distance of the underlying classical codes, and the bound is tight for cases like three- and four-dimensional toric codes. Macroscopic barriers mean memory that protects itself.
arxiv-2506-20219:
Xuening Cao, Hao Yang, and Min Wang lead a team of twelve on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It builds an ultrasound sensor on a chip that hears pressures down to a few hundred nanopascals.

The sensor pairs a thin suspended glass membrane with a silicon nitride ring that traps light. Sound bends the membrane, light reads the bend, and dual resonance sharpens both. In air the noise floor sets a record low at its test tone. In water it drops lower still. The team shows off two uses: sniffing a trace gas by its sound after light hits it, and imaging under water at fine detail. The chip fits standard CMOS lines. Such ears could serve clinics, field checks, and undersea links.
arxiv-2506-23419:
Barnard builds BenchMake, a tool that turns raw science sets in set test banks. Test banks let new learn ways prove they are firm and apt. In lab science, such banks stay rare for two plain facts. Each task set is one of a kind, and fields shift at pace. That lack makes fresh lab tools hard to grade fair. BenchMake hunts hard edge cases in a set by a set split rule.

A sign-free split finds the hull, the least bent shell of all points. A share of matched points then forms the test set by plan. That share pumps spread and score force to their peaks. The split spans flat, graph, shot, wave, and word sets alike. Ten known banks from wide science zones test BenchMake's splits. Its splits face stock splits and chance splits in the grade runs.
arxiv-2506-23719:
Alex Egg and five colleagues introduce DABstep, a benchmark for AI data agents, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Real data analysis mixes coding with reading documentation and reasoning across sources. Many benchmarks test only fragments of that workflow.

DABstep holds over 450 challenges drawn from a real financial analytics platform. Each task needs iterative, multi-step problem solving. Answers come in a factoid format that software can grade automatically. Leading language-model agents performed poorly in the authors' tests. The best reached only about fifteen percent accuracy on the hardest tasks. The paper details the benchmark's design and analyzes how agents fail. A public leaderboard accompanies the release.
arxiv-2507-00519:
Ruize Cui, Jiaan Zhang, Jialun Pei, and three co-authors build a vision system for liver surgery in this two thousand twenty-five paper. In laparoscopic operations, landmarks guide the surgeon and cut risk. To spot the landmarks is hard: they are tube-like forms, and the liver shifts shape as surgery goes on. Their frame, TopoNet, is built round keeping topology. That is how the landmarks link up and hold as one.

A dual-path encoder with snake-like convolutions takes in color texture and depth form. A boundary-aware fusion module joins both streams, sharpening edges while keeping the topology. The training loss adds center-line and topological persistence constraints, forcing the calls to match how the labels link up. Tests on the L3D and P2ILF sets showed strong marks at compute cost. The team says the system has promise for use in laparoscopic liver surgery.
arxiv-2507-02819:
Luke Guerdan, Devansh Saxena, and co-authors study how data scientists turn fuzzy ideas into a target for a model. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. A target may be a proxy for a soft notion, such as true health need or real student work. How that proxy gets built is not well known.

They speak with data scientists in schools and health care. The picture that emerges is one of bricolage: people make do with the data at hand, in a craft-like way. They weigh truth, ease, forecast power, port across sites, and cost. They swap or merge outcomes when one fails. The authors point to ways tools and study can back this craft.
arxiv-2507-03719:
Barnali Chakrabarti and colleagues simulated what happens when a cold quantum gas is suddenly made repulsive in 2025. The gas holds either bosons, which can crowd together, or fermions, which cannot. Starting calm in a trap, the system gets a sudden jolt in interaction strength, and the team solves the full quantum motion on a computer.

Several entropy measures track how disorder grows and whether the system settles down. A weak jolt leaves both kinds unsettled and alike. A strong jolt splits them: bosons settle toward the pattern random matrix theory predicts, while fermions do not. The contrast shows how particle type alone can decide whether a closed system relaxes.
arxiv-2507-08319:
Kentaro Seki, Shinnosuke Takamichi, Takaaki Saeki, and Hiroshi Saruwatari build speech corpora by collecting only the samples that teach a model the most. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works on text-to-speech synthesis. Fine corpora are the base of fine systems, but data growth strains storage. Their method grows the corpus through active learning rounds.

Each round swaps between gathering new samples and training the model. The model's gaps steer what gets recorded next. This stands apart from feed-forward builds that take data blind. Tests show a corpus built this way yields better speech than a same-size corpus built the old way. The gain is data efficiency: fewer hours of audio for the same quality. The approach suits labs that must cap storage or recording budgets.
arxiv-2507-08919:
Emanuele Viola gives a short new proof of a lower bound for a classic problem in communication complexity. Two players each hold an array of pointers and must follow a chain of them together. Each sees only one array, so they must message to advance. The question is how much they must say in the worst case.

Older proofs of the strong bound were long or only sketched, and a textbook omits the proof as too technical. Viola's proof, built on a fixed-set lemma, reaches a clean bound with far less machinery. The bound holds no matter how many rounds the players use. Even when the chain is as long as the bound itself, cheap protocols cannot exist. The result tidies a corner of theory that students often meet first through the gap it fills.
arxiv-2507-13719:
Daniele Pannone leads a team bringing museum artworks into augmented reality from a single photo. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A flat image hides the depth of a carved or textured work. Good 3D models usually need many views or costly scans. Museums want a cheaper path to rich visitor displays.

The pipeline pairs two pretrained depth models with split strengths. One reads the broad layout of a scene, and the other recovers fine local detail. Their outputs merge into refined depth maps. Those maps become point clouds and meshes ready for augmented reality. Odd outlines and varied textures, common in art, are handled along the way. Tests show clear gains in model quality. The work suits galleries with small budgets and large collections.
arxiv-2507-14019:
Mengran Li and Daniela Castro-Camilo warn that the math chosen for the far tail of weather distributions can swing climate attribution verdicts. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Attribution science asks how much human influence raised the odds of an extreme event. Extremes live in the tail, where data are thin and models differ.

Working inside a causal counterfactual frame, they compare three models of joint extremes. One locks the tail dependence in place, one bends flexibly, and one blends between regimes. Simulations with planted misspecification show the choice can mislead badly. Real cases cover European winter peaks and United States rainfall. Tail assumptions, they conclude, are not a technical footnote. Careful model choice and checking are essential before blaming or clearing the climate.
arxiv-2507-15519:
Nechyporenko, Ashwin, and Tsaneva-Atanasova identify a geometric pattern that organizes how brain networks switch states. Neurons alternate between busy up states and quiet down states. Rhythms overlay those modes, and together they serve perception and memory. The rules that govern switching were poorly understood. The team derives when a structure called a heteroclinic cycle can exist. They show it appears across standard models of neuron groups.

Near that structure, the balance of excitation and inhibition steers the network. It can tip the system among rhythms, two-state behavior, and up-down switching. Balance, then, does not just tune activity levels. It draws the map from which activity patterns arise.
arxiv-2507-16119:
An Le and colleagues segmented retinal layers in three-dimensional eye scans with tunable wavelet units in 2025. Optical coherence tomography gives doctors stacked images of the retina, and outlining each layer guides diagnosis. Standard networks shrink images with max pooling, which discards fine detail that thin layers need, hurting both accuracy and consistency across slices.

Three wavelet-based downsampling modules, each built from learnable filter banks, replace pooling inside a motion-corrected segmentation network. Wavelets keep both broad shapes and sharp edges as the image shrinks. On a university retina center dataset, scores and overlap measures rose clearly, with the most flexible wavelet variant performing best. Preserving frequency detail pays off in volumetric medical imaging.
arxiv-2507-17319:
Mengying Gao, Yuhua Sun, Tongjiang Yan, and Chun'e Zhao build classic codes that hold a rare self-dual trait, then turn them into quantum codes. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The classic codes are of a near-cyclic kind, built from a set count of sources. The team gives tests for when such codes are self-orthogonal, under three kinds of inner product. They then study the duals of a two-source class to find when those codes hold their own duals. That class covers many known codes. From these tests they build quantum stabilizer codes and quantum codes that can sync, some with marks that match the best known.
arxiv-2507-19919:
Subhadip Chakraborti and Vasily Zaburdaev derive large-scale flow laws for clumping bacteria in a 2025 physics study. Colonies of motile cells pull into dense clumps through active contractile forces. The colony's motion can be described as a fluid with transport coefficients. Those coefficients depend on density, which changes as clumping proceeds.

Starting from the small-scale dynamics of a model bacterium known for such clumping, the authors build a 2D fluctuating hydrodynamics theory. Large-scale equations then carry the fingerprints of the single-cell rules. The bridge from cell behavior to colony flow helps read experiments on living active matter.
arxiv-2507-22219:
Dongyub Jude Lee, Zhenyi Ye, and Pengcheng He propose a training method for machine translation that learns from a teacher's small edits. Preference methods like DPO need large, carefully built datasets and often fail outside their tuning domains. Their alternative avoids fixed preference lists entirely.

In their scheme, the student drafts translations, and a frozen teacher makes a minimal local edit to each draft. The student is rewarded for closing the gap, using edit distance plus a semantic quality score. Tested on FLORES-200 across five target languages, the method beat supervised, preference, and fixed-reference baselines. It also preserved named entities better and scored higher under model-based judging.
arxiv-2508-00319:
Sunghyun Park, Seokeon Choi, Hyoungwoo Park, and Sungrack Yun wrote this computer vision paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on steering a personalized image model at sampling time. Fine-tuning a generator on a few photos of a subject trades off against the model's grasp of text: push too hard and prompts stop working.

Standard guidance tricks cannot find the middle ground, the authors argue. Their personalization guidance uses a deliberately unlearned weak model, conditioned on an empty prompt, as a counterweight. Sliding a mix between the base and fine-tuned weights during sampling sets how strong the unlearning pull is. That steers outputs toward a balanced space where the subject looks right and the text still lands. The method adds no compute cost and plugs into many fine-tuning schemes. Experiments show gains on both fidelity and text alignment.
arxiv-2508-04019:
Salvador Ochoa-Oregon and four co-authors automate a quantum algorithm that reads causal structure in particle physics diagrams. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Multiloop Feynman diagrams hide which propagators can be on shell together. Loop-Tree Duality turns that into a querying task. Propagators map naturally onto qubits. The graph behind the diagrams is a directed acyclic structure.

Their Minimum Clique-optimised Algorithm borrows a graph partition trick. Grouping propagators into cliques trims the quantum circuit. Both acyclic and multiloop cases are handled. Evaluation counts transpiled circuit depth and area. Smaller circuits mean nearer-term hardware can run them. High-energy theory gains an automated causal detective.
arxiv-2508-05719:
Luciano Rota, Raffaele Argiento, and Michela Cameletti model how obesity rates evolved across Italian regions from two thousand ten to two thousand twenty-two, in a two thousand twenty-five statistics paper. Regional patterns over time can guide public health policy.

A Bayesian hierarchical beta regression handles the rates, with spatial and temporal random effects plus gender and outside predictors. Stochastic search variable selection identifies which predictors the data actually support. Structured spatial and temporal effects, together with gender, emerge as the main drivers of regional prevalence. Socioeconomic and lifestyle covariates add little at the regional level, however important they are individually. The authors stress that space-time structure is essential for macro-level obesity analysis.
arxiv-2508-10119:
Matthew Belyakov and Konstantin Batygin study the scattered disk, a swarm of small bodies far from the Sun. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with objects on stretched orbits whose closest pass sits near Neptune. Neptune's gravity keeps stirring them, and their motion can turn chaotic.

A past model showed that a chain of resonances, where orbit periods lock in ratios, drives this chaos. Belyakov and Batygin extend the math to higher order, which brings in new resonance families. They find no single new family sets the edge of stability. Instead, as orbits creep closer to Neptune, higher and higher resonance chains take over, and their overlaps shape the whole population.
arxiv-2508-12419:
Fabien Le Floc'h takes a fresh look at a math tool used to price options, in a solo paper from two thousand twenty-five. The tool is stochastic collocation, and here it uses the exponential of a quadratic spline. His aim is a way to fill in option prices that does not allow free-money gaps.

He checks two ways to build the spline in close detail. One way fixes the height points and tunes the place points. The other fixes the place points and tunes the terms of a B-spline form. By weighing which choice works best, the paper helps users pick a sound setup for this price task.
arxiv-2508-17219:
Bingyang Wu and six co-authors build TokenLake, a shared pool for the stored text starts that speed up long chats with large language models. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

When many requests share the same start, a cache of that start saves much work. In a cluster of machines, tying the cache tight to task plans leads to uneven loads, waste, and split-up memory. TokenLake pools the cache in small segments, apart from the plan of tasks. It gives a clean face that shows each request's needs and cache acts. The aim is a shared store with low lag, fine control, and room to stretch as long texts grow.
arxiv-2508-17619:
Nur Amirah Abd Hamid and four co-authors predict Alzheimer's test scores by learning the whole score and its parts at once. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses the ADAS-Cog scale, a standard gauge of cognitive decline. Past work chased the global score alone. Its items, though, track distinct skills and may carry the real signal.

Their multi-task model forecasts the global score and all items two years out. Inputs mix a baseline MRI with clinical scores from baseline and month six. Vision and Swin transformers read the scans. Joint learning lifted global accuracy. Three recall items drove most of the forecast. Some of those items were themselves hard to predict, which flags instability. Clinical inputs also swamped the scan data. The authors urge fusion and loss fixes for balance.
arxiv-2509-00119:
Jake Robbennolt, Sirajum Munira, and Stephen D. Boyles compare thirteen ways to rebuild bus and vehicle paths from location pings in Austin, Texas, in 2025. Automatic vehicle location data log where transit vehicles are, but pings arrive at uneven rates. Rebuilding the full path between pings is thus needed to read transit dynamics well.

High-resolution Austin data test both known and novel methods. Four factors are weighed jointly: speed, position, smoothing, and data density. Sparse and dense sets are both checked, which exposes the trade-off between accuracy and resource use. Scores blend math error with physical sense, such as matching speed to stopped states. The guide helps agencies pick a method that fits their ping rate.
arxiv-2509-00419:
Lianyu Hu, Fanhua Shang, Wei Feng, and Liang Wan present LightVLM in 2025, a training-free method to accelerate large vision-language models. Such models answer questions about images, but slow inference limits their use. Inference splits into an encoding stage, which reads the image and prompt, and a decoding stage, which writes the answer token by token.

Pyramid token merging cuts image tokens layer by layer in encoding, keeping only a few dominant ones at the end. KV cache compression in decoding drops needless stored values to raise throughput. Tests retain full performance while keeping only thirty-five percent of image tokens. The method deploys on existing models with no retraining.
arxiv-2509-00619: Antun Domic and one co-author, Luis H Gallardo, give new sufficient conditions under which Ryser's conjecture holds. A sufficient condition is a test that, when met, guarantees the claim, even if the claim might also hold in other cases. The record presents the work at this level, as a contribution to settling a named open problem in combinatorics, the study of counting and arrangements.
arxiv-2509-00719:
Radoslav Harman and one co-author, Samuel Rosa, speed up exact D-optimal design, a statistical problem of choosing experimental runs to maximize information. Approximate designs can be computed efficiently with convex methods, but exact finite-sample designs require hard integer optimization on large candidate sets.

Harman and Rosa derive necessary conditions, based on approximate designs, that every support point of an exact D-optimal design must satisfy. These conditions rapidly eliminate redundant candidates without losing optimality, cutting memory and runtime. They also prove that for large samples, exact design supports lie inside a typically small maximum-variance set. Benchmarks with candidate sets up to one hundred million points shrink by several orders of magnitude, enabling exact solutions with guarantees.
arxiv-2509-00919:
Xiuning Zhang, with three co-authors, Alexei Poliakov, Henrikki Tenkanen, and Elsa Arcaute, tests the 15-Minute City vision, a planning idea that daily needs should lie within a fifteen minute reach. The vision assumes local amenity provision translates into local use, yet behavioral evidence on recurrent visitation remains limited.

Their K-Visitation framework compares recurrent destinations with nearest options for each person, using eighteen months of mobile phone data from hundreds of thousands of users in Finland. People repeatedly bypass nearby options that already cover needed amenity categories, incurring measurable travel time costs. Divergence is sharpest in amenity-rich urban cores. Routine anchors follow proximity more closely, while specialized functions depend on wider catchments and connectivity.
arxiv-2509-01119:
Sending only the parts of a message that a task truly needs can save bandwidth and power. Senura Hansaja Wanasekara, with five co-authors, proposes SC-GIR, a system for sending images in that goal-driven way. Earlier systems often needed joint training at both ends and labeled data, which limited their use across new tasks.

SC-GIR learns on its own to extract a stable core representation, a compact summary that keeps the key content of an image. A contrast method based on covariance, a measure of how features move together, helps make that summary dense with meaning. The team tests the scheme on image data sets for machine tasks, aiming for lean transmission that still lets the receiver do its job.
arxiv-2509-01219:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a hunt for new heavy particles that decay into two jets of hadrons at the Large Hadron Collider. The search used proton collision data at thirteen teraelectronvolts, gathered by the ATLAS detector. To catch lighter resonances that normal triggers would discard for lack of bandwidth, the team used jets recorded inside the trigger itself.

Events with two energetic jets, close in direction, were scanned for bumps in mass between three hundred seventy-five and eighteen hundred gigaelectronvolts. A data-driven estimate modeled the background from ordinary multijet events. No clear excess appeared. The collaboration therefore set upper limits, at ninety-five percent confidence, on the strength of a sample new particle model and on how often such a resonance could be produced.
arxiv-2509-01319:
Forecasting vital signs such as heart rate and blood pressure could warn clinicians early, but a forecast without a trust range is hard to act on. Li Rong Wang, with four co-authors, builds prediction intervals for such forecasts, ranges that show how sure the model is. Their base is an uncertainty measure that reacts to shifts in the data and needs no labels to calibrate.

One method assumes errors and uncertainty follow a joint Gaussian copula form, giving intervals by a direct formula. The other is non-parametric, estimating intervals from nearest neighbors in the data. Wang and the team aim for intervals that are well calibrated, so a flagged change is more likely a real warning than model noise. Trustworthy ranges could help deep learning forecasts enter daily clinical care.
arxiv-2509-01519:
Stochastic delay equations model systems whose random future depends on their past, and irreducibility asks whether the system can reach any region of its state space. Hao Yang and Jian Wang study weak irreducibility for such equations driven by pure jump noise, randomness that arrives in sudden leaps. Their main contribution is a concise new proof.

The proof drops a condition that earlier work required, widening the result's reach. As an application, the pair derives weak irreducibility for delay equations with weakly dissipative coefficients, systems that slowly lose energy. A further novelty is that the driving noise may be degenerate, acting in fewer directions than the system has. Yang and Wang state that this closes the gap on irreducibility for delay equations under jump noise, a basic trait needed for later results on long-run behavior.
arxiv-2509-01619:
AI web agents browse at speeds and scales no human matches, and hostile or buggy agents could overload sites, scrape content, or flood login systems with fake accounts. Abhinav Kumar, with four co-authors, designs Web Agent Throttling, a framework that charges agents a tunable cost before granting access to resources. The challenges used as gates must be asymmetric, scalable, robust, and workable for any agent.

The team focuses on the language model inside most agents and asks it to solve reasoning puzzles, burning token generation as the cost. Existing puzzles from coding or math fail their stated properties, so they introduce rebus-based reasoning gates, puzzles built from pictures and wordplay. Kumar and the co-authors aim to protect services without locking out legitimate agent traffic, shifting defense from detection toward priced access.
arxiv-2509-01919:
Seohyun Kim leads five co-authors with DiTTO, a diffusion based tool that forges realistic storage traces for many devices at once. Storage traces log reads and writes over time and guide system design. Real traces are hard to share and hard to tune to a test need. Diffusion models build data by refining noise, and here they capture time patterns and cross device links.

Users can set precise configs to steer the forged traces. Tests show high fidelity, meaning close match to real traces, plus strong diversity across runs. Alignment with the guiding configs lands within a small error margin. The tool could supply shareable test data where real logs stay private or scarce. It also lets designers stress edge cases on demand.
arxiv-2509-02119:
Chanakya Varude, Jay Chaudhary, Siddharth Kaushik, and Prasanna Chaporkar study threshold based arm selection in monotonic bandits. Multi-armed bandits formalize choosing among options with unknown rewards over time. Here the goal is not the top arm but one placed relative to a prescribed threshold. Variants seek the first arm above threshold, a ranked arm above or below, or the closest arm.

Arm means follow a monotonic order, which the algorithms exploit. Asymptotic regret lower bounds depend only on arms adjacent to the threshold. Proposed algorithms meet those bounds and are validated by Monte Carlo simulations. Uses span channel allocation, clinical dosing, energy control, and recommendation. The work extends classic bandit theory with threshold constraints for sharper decisions.
arxiv-2509-02619:
Guangzheng Zhong, Yang Liu, and Jiming Liu present a 2025 game theory paper on decision-dependent games, where the data distribution itself shifts as players act. Market pricing is one example: prices change the demand data that firms learn from.

The goal is a performatively stable equilibrium, where every player's choice stays optimal under the distribution their joint choices create. Earlier theory needed a smoothness constant that cannot be measured when the distribution map is unknown. The authors replace it with a sensitivity measure built from gradients, directly tracking how decisions shift the distribution. Under strong monotonicity, they prove convergence and build a repeated retraining algorithm adjusted by that measure. Tests on prediction, Cournot competition, and revenue games beat leading baselines in loss and speed.
arxiv-2509-02719:
Luis F. Alday, Rodrigo S. Pitombo, and Aurélie Strömholm Sangaré wrote a 2025 string theory paper. It studies scattering in anti-de Sitter space. That curved spacetime is central to holography. Their case is the AdS Veneziano amplitude for four gluons in type IIB string theory.

The authors propose monodromy relations. The relations link amplitudes with distinct colour orderings. They follow from an emergent worldsheet picture of open string scattering. In the flat space limit, they reduce to the classic Veneziano monodromy relations. They also hold order by order in the small-curvature expansion. All known results obey them. That spans scattering of any Kaluza-Klein modes. The relations constrain future work on amplitudes.
arxiv-2509-02819:
Sameer Mathad, Taejoon Kim, and David J. Love present a 2025 wireless communications paper on opening new frequency bands beside legacy systems without harming the older users. Many legacy devices serve critical infrastructure and were designed under outdated interference assumptions.

Instead of geographic exclusion zones, the authors build protection into the signal design. Massive antenna arrays use precoding shaped by region constraints, caps on received power inside the geographic areas where legacy users sit. Capacity analysis covers a single-user system, and sum-rate analysis covers the multi-user case, both under transmit power and region limits. The proposed precoding lets new systems share nearby spectrum while respecting those caps. The approach replaces blanket distance rules with targeted interference control.
arxiv-2509-02919:
Silvia Mantovanini and 5 co-authors searched a low-frequency radio survey in 2025 for pulsars hiding in sky images. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radio waves past Earth. At low frequencies their signals can blur, so picture-based searches offer a useful backup to timing searches.

The team checked known pulsar positions in data from an Australian telescope array covering the galactic plane. They measured radio spectra, meaning brightness across frequencies, for nearly two hundred known pulsars. Over half were seen below a key frequency range for the first time. Cross-matching leftover radio sources with gamma-ray data then turned up a fresh list of possible new pulsars for follow-up.
arxiv-2509-03119:
Yash Vyas and Matteo Bottin built and tested a 2025 robot arm family called Forbal. The design starts from a five bar linkage, a closed chain of rigid bars that forms the arm's core. Force balancing means arranging masses so gravity and motion loads largely cancel, easing the strain on joints and mounts.

Two versions appear: a flat two-direction model and a spatial five-direction extension. The authors work through shape, motion, and dynamics choices that keep balance while leaving a large workspace. They derive the inverse motion math, which tells joint settings for a desired hand position. Bench tests against counterweight and unbalanced setups cut reaction moments and joint torques by large margins. Position error also fell on the smaller model.
arxiv-2509-03519:
Ronan Hix and three co-authors ask how cosmic rays move through the gas between stars in a 2025 research paper. Cosmic rays here are energetic particles near gigaelectronvolt energies. Their simulations use the TIGRESS framework, which models star-forming patches of a galactic disk in fine detail.

Three transport routes are tracked: drifting with the background gas, streaming along magnetic field lines, and diffusion relative to moving waves. Above the disk, drifting and streaming do almost all the work. Inside the disk's mostly neutral gas, diffusion takes over. Transport efficiency rises as star formation increases, and the team fits a simple formula for the resulting cosmic ray pressure. A compact subgrid recipe also captures how the varied gas phases affect scattering, without full simulation costs.
arxiv-2509-03919:
A 2025 mathematics paper from Sudip Bera and one co-author examines the difference graph of a finite group, built by comparing two of its classic graphs. The power graph joins group elements when one is a power of the other. The intersection power graph uses a related but different rule, and subtracting one graph's edges from the other's, then deleting isolated vertices, gives the difference graph.

Several questions organise the study. When do the two starting graphs coincide exactly, so the difference graph vanishes? What do isolated vertices in difference graphs look like before removal? Connectedness and perfectness of the difference graph are tied back to properties of the underlying group. A technique called twin reduction, which merges vertices with identical neighbourhoods, yields smaller graphs that are easier to analyse. The results map how sensitive this comparison graph is to group structure, giving new invariants for finite group theory.
arxiv-2509-04119:
Ke Wu and four co-authors model soft robots that bend like octopus arms in a 2025 research paper. Cable-driven continuum robots move by pulling cables along a flexible spine, which suits tight and messy spaces. Their ever-changing shape makes motion and force calculations heavy, though. The team's framework, LASEM, writes the energy stored by the pulling cables directly in terms of the cable inputs. Beam and rod theory then yields a forward model on paper.

One formulation accepts either pulling force or cable travel as input, covering both shape and load questions. It handles uneven bodies, varied cable paths, and stretch along the spine. Simulations confirm accuracy, and a companion method works backward from a wanted pose to the needed cable settings.
arxiv-2509-04219:
Leandro Márcio Bertholdo and four co-authors document what thirty days of flooding did to internet and technology systems in southern Brazil in a 2025 research paper. Heavy rain in May 2024 damaged infrastructure across Rio Grande do Sul, affecting hundreds of cities and millions of people. The team assembled data sets covering internet measurements, reports of cut fiber cables, and routing records from an internet exchange during the disaster.

Matching network failures against water levels and operations revealed weak points in fiber lines and data centers. Restoration followed clear patterns, and user behavior shifted as connections failed. The open data should help planners design disaster recovery steps and hardier networks before the next extreme event.
arxiv-2509-04419:
Xingtai Lv and ten co-authors argue that the two main ways of finishing a language model's training are really one process in a 2025 research paper. Post-training feeds models either their own generated attempts, used by reinforcement learning, or outside demonstrations, used by supervised fine-tuning. The authors derive one estimator, a unified policy gradient formula whose versions reproduce a wide spectrum of known methods under different data assumptions and bias-variance trade-offs.

Four interchangeable parts structure the estimator: a stabilization mask, a reference policy term, an advantage estimate, and a likelihood gradient. A hybrid algorithm then picks training signals dynamically, exploiting demonstrations while exploring stably. Across six mathematics benchmarks plus two out-of-distribution suites, the hybrid beat strong baselines at several model scales.
arxiv-2509-04619:
Learning-based controllers can perform well yet behave in hard-to-predict ways when conditions shift. Aditya Gahlawat, lead author with two co-authors, present a control method meant to keep guarantees in a 2025 paper. Their method, called distributionally robust adaptive control within an L1 framework, targets uncertain stochastic processes.

The design uses an ambiguity set around a nominal distribution, measured with Wasserstein distance, to bound how far reality may drift. The authors aim for robustness certificates covering finite-time and maximal distributional deviation. Their goal is to combine data-driven flexibility with the predictable performance that safety-aware applications require, without relying on learning models that are too simple.
arxiv-2509-05019:
Reading handwritten Arabic characters is hard for computers, especially on mobile devices with limited power. Mohsine El Khayati, lead author with five co-authors, combine transfer learning with lightweight convolutional networks for that task in a 2025 paper. They compare full fine-tuning, partial fine-tuning, and training from scratch across four mobile network designs.

Experiments use three benchmark datasets with differing difficulty. MobileNet performs best overall in their tests, balancing accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. Full fine-tuning gives the strongest results, while partial fine-tuning underperforms across metrics. One dataset proves hardest because of its variability, a challenge the authors highlight for future work.
arxiv-2509-05619:
Spray painting with a phone as the can is the experience built by Ruiqi Chen and four co-authors in a 2025 human-computer interaction paper on graffiti. Street art records the culture of city spaces, but spreading regulation limits where artists may legally work.

Their prototype, GestoBrush, turns a smartphone into a virtual spray can inside augmented reality, so creation uses the body and the surrounding space. A co-design workshop stressed how physical engagement shapes graffiti practice. Six graffiti artists evaluated the tool and reported stronger feelings of intuitiveness, immersion, and expressiveness in their augmented works. The study argues embodied tools can honour street art's ethos while opening digital room.
arxiv-2509-05719:
Farsi language technology for feelings and abuse lags far behind its speaker base, Donya Rooein and three co-authors document in a 2025 survey paper. Farsi has well over a hundred million speakers and a large web presence, yet it counts only as a middle-resource language, and closer inspection makes that label look generous.

Focusing on sentiment analysis, emotion analysis, and toxicity detection, the authors review more than a hundred publications. Public datasets are scarce, and existing ones often omit age and gender, factors that shape subjective language. Model results swing wildly across the few datasets available. More data volume alone, they argue, will not fix Farsi's position without better data.
arxiv-2509-05819:
Nearly complete rotation of a light wave's polarization by a sheet of electrons is reported in a 2025 paper led by Vishnunarayanan Suresh with seven co-authors. The sheet is a two-dimensional electron gas, a thin layer where electrons move freely in a plane. The rotation, called the Faraday effect, grows with magnetic field strength.

Working at microwave frequencies in a hollow waveguide, the team reached a rotation close to the ideal quarter-turn limit on a single pass. Weak coupling between the wave and the electron layer, set by a metal iris, lets the classical Hall effect drive the rotation far from the lossy resonance peak. The strength per field and thickness far exceeds earlier materials, suggesting one-way signal devices built on this effect.
arxiv-2509-05919:
Image recognition that copies the brain's glance-first strategy is proposed in a 2025 paper led by Chenghua Duan with eight co-authors. People grasp a scene's gist before its details, a pattern the authors call forest before trees. Their Brain-Inspired Quantum Classifier splits the job: a classical network reads the broad picture, and a quantum circuit inspects the detail-rich spots it flags.

The classical pathway analyzes global low-frequency information and steers the quantum pathway toward critical high-frequency regions. Simulations on varied datasets, including high-resolution images, show better accuracy and scalability than existing methods. The authors present the hybrid design as evidence that brain-inspired quantum-classical systems could power a next generation of visual tools.
arxiv-2509-06019:
Electrons moving in a strong magnetic field are described from their Landau levels upward in a 2025 paper by Kitinan Pongsangangan. A magnetic field squeezes electron energies into discrete Landau levels, whose states solve the Schrödinger equation exactly in that setting. Most transport theories relax collisions into a simple time constant; this one goes beyond that approximation.

Starting from the Keldysh formalism, a framework for nonequilibrium quantum systems, Pongsangangan derives a quantum kinetic equation directly in the Landau-level basis, valid for fields of arbitrary strength. As a test case, the equation is applied to the electrical conductivity of a two-dimensional electron gas in a perpendicular field. The basis choice suits strong-field phenomena above all.
arxiv-2509-06219:
Learning new classes on a graph without keeping old examples is the setting of MCIGLE, a 2025 framework from Haochen You and Baojing Liu. Multimodal graph data keep growing, and incremental learners face catastrophic forgetting, distribution bias, and tight memory. MCIGLE extracts and aligns features across data types, then retains knowledge through concatenated recursive least squares.

Multi-channel processing balances fresh accuracy against preserved memory. Tests on public datasets back up how well it works, by the authors' report. The framework targets systems, from recommendation to monitoring, where graph classes arrive over time and storing the past is not an option.
arxiv-2509-06619:
Setting one price with only sketchy knowledge of buyers is analyzed by Tim S. G. van Eck and two co-authors in a 2025 economics paper. A monopoly seller may know only summary facts about what buyers will pay: the average, a measure of spread, and the highest value. Pricing must then be robust against the worst market consistent with those facts.

Using distributionally robust optimization and max-min analysis, the authors judge prices by their competitive ratio, the share of the best possible revenue they still guarantee. They characterize the worst-case market and fully solve for the price that minimizes the ratio. Several spread measures are covered, including variance and fractional moments. Curiously, the worst market for the ratio is the same one that minimizes expected revenue. The results give practical guidance for pricing when market information is thin.
arxiv-2509-07219:
Yanxin Chen and 3 co-authors examine density waves in a high-pressure nickel compound in a 2025 paper. The compound, La3Ni2O7, turns superconducting near 80 kelvin under pressure, meaning it carries current with no resistance. Density waves are ordered patterns in spin or charge, and many think they hold the key to why this material superconducts, though their exact form is disputed.

The team uses variational Monte Carlo, a sampling method that tests trial states and keeps the best, on a bilayer two-orbital model of the pressurized phase. They map spin and charge correlations across a wide range of repulsion and exchange strengths. The result is a phase diagram that separates the different density-wave ground states. The map gives theorists firmer ground for debating the superconducting mechanism in this nickelate family.
arxiv-2509-07619:
Emir Sezik and 2 co-authors study how fluctuating interactions control the glass transition in a 2025 paper. In dense biological systems, pairwise interactions flicker on and off. That flickering can keep tissues fluid, guide growth, and form aggregates with strong mechanical response. A tractable model of that microscopic flickering was missing. The team studies a p-spin model with fluctuating couplings instead.

Each coupling has a strength and a persistence time. Stronger fluctuations suppress the glass transition, so the system stays fluid. More persistent fluctuations have the opposite effect. A fluctuation-dissipation relation emerges at long times. The critical temperature is drawn from the computer by a scaling relation near the transition. It is given as a function of both fluctuation settings. The result shows, in miniature, how living matter might tune its own solidity.
arxiv-2509-07819:
How are large language models changing who writes Wikipedia, and how? Moyan Zhou and 2 co-authors investigate that question in a 2025 study of online knowledge communities. Editors increasingly use these models in their writing workflow, yet the encyclopedia has no settled rules for the practice, leaving individuals to experiment alone.

Participation in such communities is social, not just a matter of producing text. The authors examine how model use affects contribution and community life, a gap that matters for writing future norms. Their findings can help communities decide where automated help supports volunteers and where it may weaken the human ties that keep a shared knowledge project alive and trustworthy.
arxiv-2509-07919:
Patrick Kreidl models how a computer system should respond while an attack is under way, in a solo 2025 cybersecurity paper. Intrusion tolerance assumes attacks sometimes succeed, so the goal is to keep operating and recover. His Markov decision process model keeps things deliberately simple: attacks advance in steps, defences only sometimes stop them, and resets may fail.

Analysis of the model yields a surprise. Even with perfect detectors, fighting back during an attack can be the worse long-run choice, depending on attack dynamics and response effectiveness. The overhead of constant defence can outweigh its benefit. A clear toy model like this helps security designers test intuitions before trusting them in real incident-response policies.
arxiv-2509-08119:
Taya Govreen-Segal and 2 co-authors model how X-rays fight through the gas surrounding their own source in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Bright sources photoionise nearby gas, changing how much radiation the gas absorbs. The team covers a broad range of column densities, from gas thin to X-rays up to gas thick enough that scattering dominates.

For the thin regime, a simple criterion based on luminosity, spectrum, radius, and column separates three cases. Sometimes neutral-gas models suffice, sometimes radiation ionises its way clear and no absorption is expected, and sometimes only a detailed model works. Misreading absorption distorts inferred source power and gas properties, so a quick diagnostic for which regime applies has everyday value for X-ray astronomers.
arxiv-2509-08219:
Senders who cooperate quantum mechanically can push more total data through shared channels, and Seung-Hyun Nam with 5 co-authors characterise when in a 2025 information theory paper. Earlier examples tied the gain to channels built from pseudo-telepathy games, where quantum players win games no classical players can. A full description of which channels benefit stayed open.

A broader class of game-induced channels is proposed, where each input is a question-answer pair from a nonlocal game. Classical, quantum, and no-signaling cooperation are compared on interference and multiple access channels without feedback. Knowing where cooperation helps separates genuine quantum advantage from curiosities, and it informs how future quantum networks might squeeze capacity from crowded spectrum.
arxiv-2509-09219:
A decision policy that only works for one warehouse layout is a parlor trick; real problems change size. Jakob Nyberg and Pontus Johnson present Vejde in a 2025 research paper. Vejde builds policies that generalize across problem instances with rich structure. It represents states as databases of facts about objects and their relations.

Each state becomes a bipartite graph, which a graph neural network maps into a latent state. Factored states and actions let one policy handle problems of varying size and shape. The team trained agents on eight problem domains, holding out instances purely for testing. Vejde policies generalized to the unseen instances with little loss. Their scores approached agents trained separately for each instance, and a strong online planner. Inductive policies like these could let one trained agent run a whole family of logistics or planning problems.
arxiv-2509-09419:
Olzhas Mukazhanov's 2025 astrophysics paper asks whether spin changes how entropy disturbances travel inward inside a collapsing massive star. Such stars churn with convection in their deep shells, and that motion matters once a supernova begins. Material falling toward the shock can add turbulence and feed the blast.

Mukazhanov models the disturbances as small waves on a steady background flow, using linear perturbation theory. Falling entropy variations create both swirling motion and sound as they go. His results suggest rotation barely alters their path before they meet the shock. That finding matches his earlier work on spinning convective eddies being swept inward.
arxiv-2509-09519:
Petru A. Cioica-Licht and 2 co-authors prove analytic estimates for the Dirichlet Laplacian on cone-shaped regions in a 2025 paper. Cones and wedges have tips and edges where smooth-domain theory breaks down, yet such shapes arise naturally in equations with noise and in degenerate heat problems. The authors work in weighted spaces that measure distance both to the boundary and to the tip or edge.

Their main result bounds the H-infinity calculus for the Laplacian in that weighted setting. As a payoff, the Poisson equation gains maximal regularity in matching weighted Sobolev spaces. For researchers studying stochastic partial differential equations on rough domains, results of this kind supply the backbone estimates that later well-posedness arguments rely on.
arxiv-2509-09619:
Roshan Balaji and 2 co-authors argue that chemistry's own functional groups make the best language for teaching machines about molecules in a 2025 paper. Deep models now predict molecular properties quickly, helping drug and materials searches, but chemists distrust tools whose reasoning they cannot read. Functional groups are familiar building blocks with known behaviour, so a representation built from them speaks the user's language.

Their framework mixes hand-curated groups with extra groups mined from a large molecule collection by pattern search. Pretraining on unlabelled molecules compresses each one into a compact code, and standard two-dimensional descriptors can be added. Across thirty-three varied benchmarks the method matched the best known scores while staying open to chemical inspection.
arxiv-2509-09719:
Hemanth Chandravamsi and 5 co-authors diagnose a failure mode in networks that use sine activations in a 2025 machine learning paper. Such networks, called SIRENs, fit signals by frequency content, yet their error swings wildly with the target's frequencies and with how weights start. In the worst cases the output collapses to zero, a breakdown the authors name a spectral bottleneck.

Tracking activation spectra and the neural tangent kernel during training shows energy spread badly across frequency modes before failure strikes. Adding Gaussian noise to a uniform starting point reshapes those spectra in helpful ways. Their proposed starting scheme, nicknamed WINNER, lifts fitting accuracy markedly. The broader lesson is that starts should adapt to the target as fine detail grows.
arxiv-2509-09919:
Franklin Yiu and 7 co-authors recast a popular level-building algorithm as a decision process in a 2025 game generation paper. WaveFunctionCollapse assembles tiled environments by propagating local fitting rules, but designers also chase global goals such as beauty or difficulty. Optimising tiles and goals together tangles the two jobs, and the authors propose splitting them cleanly apart.

Inside their Markov framing, the collapse machinery alone enforces every adjacency rule, while an outside optimiser pursues only the designer's objective. Across several domains of rising difficulty, joint evolutionary search struggled more and more, and the split version beat it consistently. Letting each mechanism do the job it is good at, the study argues, is what unlocks harder generation tasks.
arxiv-2509-10019:
Tatsuo Kobayashi and 2 co-authors study which couplings string theory allows on non-Abelian orbifolds in a 2025 theoretical paper.
