Orbifolds fold space through a symmetry group, and when that group is non-Abelian the boundary conditions sort into conjugacy classes of the space group. Couplings among twisted sectors, and between twisted and untwisted ones, then obey selection rules of an unfamiliar kind.

The rules that emerge are non-invertible, meaning they cannot be undone by a matching partner rule in the usual group sense. That novelty is not just bookkeeping: the authors show it stamps characteristic patterns onto Yukawa matrices, the tables that set particle masses and mixing. Orbifold model builders gain a sharper filter for which interactions a compactification can ever produce.
arxiv-2509-10319:
Lorenzo Ennoggi and 5 co-authors simulate two supermassive black holes crashing together in this 2025 paper. Such pairs likely swallow large amounts of gas as they spiral in, so they should shine in light as well as in gravitational waves. The run covers the late spiral, the merger itself, and the first moments after, with both holes equal in mass and spin.

The simulation couples general relativity with magnetized gas physics in three dimensions. Heat light came mainly from strong shocks, not from smooth disk friction as around single holes. Light and jet power faded slowly before merger, then jumped to a noisy plateau at the crash. The authors say that distinct pattern could help telescopes spot such mergers.
arxiv-2509-10619:
Michelle Kunimoto and nine co-authors release LEO-Vetter, a fully automated system for vetting exoplanet candidates from the TESS satellite, in this 2025 astronomy paper. TESS has flagged thousands of candidate planets, but human inspection of transit-like dips is slow and subjective, which blocks the demographic studies that measure how common each kind of planet really is.

Modeled on Kepler's Robovetter, the system applies flux-level and pixel-level tests against noise, instrument quirks, and astrophysical impostors. On simulated data it keeps ninety-one percent of real signals while rejecting ninety-seven percent of false alarms. As a demonstration, it sifted about two hundred thousand dwarf-star light curves, shrinking twenty thousand detections to one hundred seventy-two uniformly vetted candidates. The public tool lets anyone build a TESS catalog with known completeness.
arxiv-2509-10719:
Mohammed Humaid Siddiqui and three co-authors coordinate memory prefetching across processor cores in this 2025 paper. Prefetchers guess which data a program will need next. They fetch it early, hiding slow memory. On multicore chips, independent prefetchers waste effort. Up to a fifth of requests duplicate another core's. Strong single-core designs like Pythia lose about a tenth of their speed at four cores.

Their design, CRL-Pythia, changes the social contract between cores. Cores share what they learn. They make cooperative decisions together. Duplicates fall, and the reinforcement learning converges better. In experiments, CRL-Pythia beat single Pythia setups in every case. Bandwidth-starved workloads gained about twelve percent in instructions per cycle. The hardware cost stayed moderate. Sensitivity checks showed the gains hold up as conditions vary. Coordinated prefetching looks practical for contemporary multicore systems.
arxiv-2509-10919:
Earth observation satellites produce more imagery than labels, and Mohanad Albughdadi proposes a deliberately small foundation model for it in this solo-authored 2025 remote sensing paper. Giant models dominate the field but cost too much for many users. His Metadata-aware Mixture-of-Experts Masked Autoencoder has only two and a half million parameters.

Sparse expert routing keeps the model cheap, while geo-temporal conditioning feeds it latitude, longitude, and cyclic encodings of season and day alongside the imagery. Pretrained on the BigEarthNet-Landsat dataset, its frozen embeddings, probed with simple linear classifiers, competed with architectures hundreds of times larger. On EuroSAT-Landsat, which lacks metadata entirely, it stayed competitive. The claim: knowing where and when a picture was taken is worth a great deal of raw size.
arxiv-2509-11019:
Facundo Fainstein and 2 co-authors show that birdsong rides a mechanical resonance in this 2025 paper. Quiet breathing in birds already works at a natural resonance of the breathing apparatus. Song is different: it demands far faster breathing, and it is shaped by strong sexual selection, so it might have escaped such physical limits.

Recording canaries while modeling their respiratory mechanics, the team found that song pushes the system into a nonlinear regime. That regime widens the band of frequencies the apparatus amplifies, covering the full span of syllable rates the birds actually use, at close to the theoretical best amplification. The authors conclude that even a display under strong selection still leans on the same optimization as plain breathing.
arxiv-2509-11119:
Huagui Duan and three co-authors wrote this 2025 mathematics note. It concerns the common index jump theorem. That result deals with symplectic paths. It has become a standard tool for periodic solutions of Hamiltonian systems.

A 2024 paper introduced a similar statement. Its authors named it the index recurrence theorem. Duan and colleagues give detailed proofs about that theorem. Its main claims match an enhanced version of the older theorem. The same holds for an earlier 2020 paper. The matching version dates to 2016. The note records that two lines of work describe one theorem. Researchers can stop treating the result as two separate ones.
arxiv-2509-11319:
Shahram Najafi, Ahmad Moussavi, and Peter Danchev study a new family of rings in this 2025 algebra paper. In a 2-UQ ring, the square of every unit splits in two. One part is idempotent. The other is quasi-nilpotent. The two parts commute with each other.

The authors map this family against better-known ones. The relatives include 2-UJ rings and 2-UU rings. Tripotent rings appear too. Group rings with the property get full characterizations. The underlying groups turn out to be 2-groups or 3-groups in certain cases. Morita context extensions preserve the property under stated conditions. Potent 2-UQ rings prove to be exactly the semi-tripotent rings. Examples and counterexamples mark the family's boundaries.
arxiv-2509-11419:
Mengyuan Ma and five co-authors use roadside sensors to keep millimeter-wave beams on moving users. This 2025 communications paper pairs cameras with beam choice. A camera on a pole can see where a user is heading. That visual past can pick the right beam now and for near-future slots.

The team first built a large neural network. It reads image features and their timing. Attention helps it weigh the past. Top-five accuracy passed ninety percent for current and six future slots. The network used far fewer parameters than rivals. A smaller student network learned from it by distillation. The student needs much shorter input sequences. It nearly matched the teacher at a small share of the cost.
arxiv-2509-11619:
Spandan Anaokar and eight co-authors build defenses against chatbots that invent facts, in this 2025 natural language processing paper set in consumer law. Their test bed is a grievance-handling chatbot built on a compact industry model, exactly the setting where a hallucinated rule or deadline can harm real people.

The team's detector, HalluDetect, uses a language model to flag fabricated content and beat baseline detectors by a wide margin on F1 score. They then benchmarked five mitigation architectures head to head. One design, AgentBot, produced the fewest hallucinations per conversation turn while also keeping the highest token accuracy, making it the most effective strategy of the five. The authors offer the pipeline as a scalable framework, arguing that smarter inference design, not just bigger models, is what improves factual reliability.
arxiv-2509-11819:
Mrinmay Sen, Sidhant Nair, and C Krishna Mohan improve federated domain adaptation in a 2025 paper called FedDAF. A new client joining a privacy-preserving federation, such as a hospital, often has little labeled data of its own, and its data distribution differs from the sources'.

FedDAF tackles both domain shift and label scarcity together. It aggregates source and target models by similarity, measured through a functional distance: the angle between their average gradient fields on target data, normalized by a smooth S-shaped function. The global source model itself weights source models by closeness to the target. Experiments on real-world datasets showed FedDAF beating federated learning, personalized, and domain adaptation baselines in test accuracy.
arxiv-2509-11919:
What happens to cosmic phase transitions if the entropy formula for the universe gets an exponential correction? Rodrigo Rivadeneira-Caro, with two co-authors, works through that question in 2025 for the standard expanding-universe model used in cosmology.

Adding exponential terms to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy changes the Friedmann equations that govern expansion, and the altered thermodynamics turns out to be rich. When a key parameter is negative, the model shows first-order phase transitions above a critical temperature; when positive, the system leaves a phase and later returns to it, a reentrant pattern. Because such corrections should matter most in the early universe, the authors also compare their framework against present-day measurements of the expansion rate, hunting for any leftover trace.
arxiv-2509-12019:
Shrinking a large language model to fit tight memory means choosing how many bits each layer keeps, and Sangjun Lee with four co-authors automate that choice in 2025. Their framework, AMQ, handles mixed-precision weight-only quantization, where different layers get different bit widths.

The search space is astronomical, more configurations than any black-box optimizer could sample, so AMQ attacks it from four sides. Prior knowledge prunes hopeless settings, a proxy skips expensive format conversions during the hunt, a learned predictor estimates quality cheaply, and an iterate-and-update loop settles the search quickly. Together these reach the practical frontier where models are both compact and accurate, instead of trading one away blindly. Code is available publicly.
arxiv-2509-12119:
Algorithms that hand out scarce public benefits must be fair across groups and explainable to boot, two demands that often fight. Nora Bearth and three co-authors combine them in 2025 through policy trees fed with scrubbed data.

Preprocessing first removes dependencies between sensitive attributes and the features a decision may use, then a tree-based search finds the best allocation policy. Because scrubbing would otherwise muddy the explanation, a second transformation maps the tree's parameters back into the original feature space. Allocations end up pairwise independent of sensitive attributes while staying readable. The test case is Swiss administrative data on assigning unemployed people to labor market programs, where fairness improved a lot while expected employment outcomes dipped only slightly.
arxiv-2509-12219:
Take a convex quadrilateral, pick a point inside it, and join that point to the four corners. Four triangles appear, and placing a chosen center in each one yields four new points that form another quadrilateral. Stanley Rabinowitz and one co-author map the shapes of these central quadrilaterals in 2025.

With computer help they sweep a thousand named triangle centers, many choices of the inner point, and many starting shapes. The hunt finds when the new quadrilateral turns out to be a rhombus, a cyclic shape, or another special form. One sample result pairs the centroid of an equidiagonal quadrilateral with one specific center to force an orthodiagonal outcome.
arxiv-2509-12819:
M. Braun studies in 2025 whether a toy model of high-energy scatter with both even and odd exchange parts can carry a fair chance picture. Without the odd parts a chance recipe was known, but it breaks once odd parts join.

Starting from fair chances leads to a field theory that breaks mirror parity. Starting from a sound theory leads to bad chances that break parity and let particles pop in or out of empty space. Braun offers a new recipe based on wave parts. In that picture the spread of counts in fast hits and its disorder match lab-like trends more closely.
arxiv-2509-12919:
Takanori Adachi builds a shape model in 2025 where the present is a blend of many pasts, not one line. Classic chance theory tracks facts along one time line. Adachi argues that line may be a flat shadow of a richer shape.

A new class extends the simplex class so each time point holds context. Filters become maps from that class to chance spaces. Chain groups built from mean steps gauge holes where context views clash. A Dirichlet case shows how learning rebuilds fit across contexts. The frame links chance, algebra, and Bayes thought in one tongue.
arxiv-2509-13019:
Frederic Fort, David Nowak and Vlad Rusu embed a command tongue inside a proof tool in 2025. Command code still runs kernels and low layers. Proofs in real tongues drown in admin detail due to loose rules.

GallinaC sits inside Gallina, the tongue of the Rocq proof tool. It is complete and has a true free while loop. Proofs can use the same moves as pure code proofs. A test proof checks list flip for lists of unknown size. Work now links the mid form to Cminor, the entry tongue of the CompCert back end. First results look strong.
arxiv-2509-13219:
Jiahao Xu, Zikai Zhang and Rui Hu launch an out-of-distribution backdoor attack on federated learning in 2025, then build its guard. Classic backdoors need seen triggers and object edits, which curb real use. Shared learning across sites widens the stakes.

Out data serves as both poison and trigger at once. A stealth tweak aligns bad local models with good ones in size and direction. Top guards are evaded while main scores hold. The guard BNGuard watches batch-norm drift from out data on the server. Bad updates are flagged and dropped. Broad tests back both attack and guard.
arxiv-2509-13519:
Devjyoti Tripathy, Juzar Thingna and Sebastian Deffner bound in 2025 the quantum speed limit for information scrambling via the out-of-time correlator from an open systems view. Scrambling spreads local data across a system. The correlator tracks that spread.

An entropy theorem for the correlator yields a lower rate bound. Closed scrambling reads as effective decoherence from an environment in the frame. Decay bounds use coupling strength and environment correlations. Numeric checks on a non-integrable Ising chain validate the bound. A universal, model-free frame for spreading limits spans many-body and engineered platforms.
arxiv-2509-13619:
Shashank Kumar and three co-authors propose a laser scheme in a 2025 atomic physics paper. The goal is exciting helium into a very narrow, long-lived state. Reaching that metastable state efficiently is hard. The usual routes are slow or lossy. The state's extremely sharp energy line makes it valuable for precision work.

The team shows that broadband femtosecond pulses in the vacuum ultraviolet can drive a direct two-photon jump. The transfer reaches roughly a quarter to a third of atoms. That figure already counts ionization losses. Short pulses help by opening several excitation paths. They also offset energy shifts during the pulse. A two-color version pairs extreme ultraviolet with near infrared light. It cuts losses further, reaching around seventy percent transfer in their calculations.
arxiv-2509-13919:
Yuanchen Wu and four co-authors fix a consistency problem in vision-language models in a 2025 paper. These models answer questions about images with a rationale and then a final answer. The reasoning and the answer often disagree. Correct-looking explanations can sit on top of wrong conclusions, or the reverse.

Their Self-Rationale Calibration framework works in rounds. A light fine-tuning step first teaches the model to state its rationale before answering. The model then generates diverse candidate responses. A dedicated scoring model, R-Scorer, grades them for rationale quality and factual consistency. Confidence-weighted preferences from those grades drive a preference fine-tuning stage. Across several benchmarks, perception, reasoning, and generalization all improved.
arxiv-2509-14319:
Dimitri A. Gadotti and Camila de Sá-Freitas summarise in 2025 what is known about nuclear discs, small discs of stars at the centres of barred disc galaxies. Such discs are established by structure and motion studies. Their basic traits and links to other central parts were still loose.

Drawing on structural fits and star formation histories for a galaxy sample, the authors chart how nuclear disc size and mass are spread. They compare two scaling relations with those for nuclear star clusters, a denser central component. At face value the relations differ, though error ranges leave them marginally compatible. That near match constrains stories in which discs and clusters form in a linked way. Formation models must respect both the difference and the overlap.
arxiv-2509-14419:
Paul Laubie, writing alone in 2025, states a conjecture on Hilbert series for a family of algebraic structures called operads. Koszul operads encode types of algebras, and their Hilbert series count operations by arity. The family here is generated by one binary operation.

Paul Laubie proves the conjecture for set based operads by classifying them all explicitly. Only a small finite list exists, and several entries are new to the literature. Classification turns a guess about counting series into verified cases. Operad theory underlies work from algebra to field theory, so exact lists help builders check that a proposed structure is genuinely new rather than a known operad in disguise.
arxiv-2509-14619:
Feng Ding and three co-authors put forward LSTC-MDA in 2025, a shared frame for telling acts apart from skeleton data, the joint tracks of a body over time. Skeleton input skips raw video, which helps privacy. Two snags persist: few labelled samples and hard short plus long range timing.

A new time based module runs short and long term branches side by side. Learned weights line up and fuse the branches, keeping long range cues that strided steps lose. A mixing augmentation, widened with an additive mixup step, spreads training samples more widely. Both changes hit data scarcity and timing at once. Strong skeleton tools serve fall alerts, rehab checks and gesture control where large labelled video sets are out of reach.
arxiv-2509-14719: Hiroshi Isozaki and Evgeny L. Korotyaev develop scattering theory for waves governed by Hamiltonians that repeat in time, set on discrete graphs, in a short 2025 mathematics paper. Their setting allows long-range potentials, provided the potential averages to zero over each time period. The central result is that wave operators for this system both exist and are complete. In plain terms, waves coming in from far away and waves going out can be matched up without loss. That completeness gives the time-periodic graph model a firm scattering foundation.
arxiv-2509-14919:
Xinru Mu, Omar M. Saad, Shaowen Wang, and Tariq Alkhalifah borrow an idea from machine learning to attack cycle skipping in seismic imaging, in a 2025 geophysics paper. Full waveform inversion builds underground velocity maps by fitting simulated waves to recorded ones. When the starting model is off and low frequencies are missing, simulated and real waves can misalign by more than half a cycle, trapping the fit in a wrong minimum.

Neural network training faces similar traps yet often escapes them with large learning rates that break local optimization rules. Mu and the team ask whether gradient-based seismic optimizers, given enough iterations and aggressive step sizes, can behave almost like global search. Their study tests that question directly, probing iteration count and learning rate as remedies for one of the oldest failure modes in waveform inversion.
arxiv-2509-15219:
Haichao Zhang, Yi Xu, and Yun Fu extend a tracking task for agents that cameras cannot currently see in a 2025 computer vision paper. Trajectory prediction feeds driving, robotics, and surveillance, yet most methods assume clean, complete observations. Real sensors lose people and vehicles behind occlusions and coverage gaps, and their raw tracks are noisy.

The Out-of-Sight Trajectory task asks for clean visual trajectories of hidden objects inferred from noisy sensing. This extended study enlarges the earlier benchmark from pedestrians alone to pedestrians and vehicles, matching the needs of autonomous driving more closely. Multimodal tracking, sensor fusion, and forecasting combine to guess where an unseen agent travels and when it reappears. Robust prediction for the invisible is framed as a safety feature, not a curiosity.
arxiv-2509-15619:
Masaru Shibata and Sho Fujibayashi model the collapse of huge spinning star cores. These cores weigh from a hundred to ten thousand Suns. They sit near the edge of a collapse driven by pair creation in hot matter. The pair assume the core is mostly oxygen with even heat spread.

They find that lighter cores in that range can leave a heavy disk around the black hole they form. The disk needs spin above a set share of the breakup rate, and it can hold over a tenth of the core's mass. Fast spinning heavy black holes, like one seen in a known wave event, fit this path. The disks can wobble off axis and shed gravitational waves that a future detector could catch.
arxiv-2509-15719:
Mariana Sánchez leads a team that tracks how giant planets drift in young disks. Planet drift is well mapped for thick, syrupy disks. Thin disks with heavy planets are less understood. The team study planets much heavier than their star's usual ratio, in a disk with very low thickness of flow. They run fluid simulations across star types, from Sun like stars to small red ones.

A flip point appears: lighter heavy planets drift inward, while heavier ones drift outward. Outward speed tracks the local gas density the planet meets. Mild oval orbits sustain the outward push through a positive torque. Some settings push orbits more oval, and drift then stalls. The rules help explain how giant planets end up where they are.
arxiv-2509-15819:
David Ellerman, writing alone, steps back from the math of quantum mechanics to its basic ideas. For a century, he notes, theorists have read deep meaning into the formulas, with little success. His paper takes a different path: name the plain intuitions at the core of the theory and explain each one. He does not show how those ideas mesh inside the full math.

What he offers instead is a feel for the quantum reality the math describes. The goal is anschaulich understanding, a grasp a reader can picture. The essay suits readers who know the theory's fame but not its guts. It is a work of interpretation, not new physics.
arxiv-2509-15919:
Marit Fiechter and Mark Kamper Svendsen question the base equation used in polaritonic chemistry. In that field, molecules sit in a mirrored cavity where light and matter couple strongly. Lab work shows reaction rates and balances can shift there. Why they shift is still not well understood, despite much theory.

Most theory rests on one Hamiltonian, an equation for the system's energy. The pair inspect a part of it called the dipole self energy. Its cross terms seem to link all molecules at any distance. They show those terms cancel with a usually dropped term, but only if all light modes are kept, not just one. Number tests hint the canceling may reach further. The base equation needs care.
arxiv-2509-16719:
E. Dondoglio and a large team trace the past of a famous star cluster in a 2025 astronomy paper. Omega Centauri is the oddest cluster in our galaxy, with rich chemical variety. The team merge light-based and spectrum-based catalogs to sort its stars into groups. They then map where each group sits and what it is made of.

Some groups point to more than one source of past enrichment. Giant aging stars and exploding white dwarfs likely both played a role. One stream of stars seems to mix pure and diluted material. The pattern hints at a staged birth in a deep past. The cluster may be the stripped core of a lost dwarf galaxy.
arxiv-2509-17319:
Niccolo Torri and Ran Wei study a polymer wandering through a random landscape in a 2025 arXiv paper. The polymer is a simple random walk on a lattice in two or more dimensions. The landscape is a field of random weights with tails that decay like a power law. A Gibbs weight tilts the walk toward sites it has visited, charged by a field term that scales with the walk's range.

By tuning the tilt and the field with the walk's length, the authors map the phase diagram of the system. They analyze how the walk fluctuates under the tilted law and find scaling limits for the partition function. The paper follows their earlier work on the same model, where the field stayed fixed as a centering term. Letting the field move adds range penalties, and that change drives the new phases the paper charts.
arxiv-2509-17419:
C. J. Butler, M. Naritsuka, and T. Hanaguri review a family of layered metals that might host an exotic quantum phase. Their 2025 arXiv topical review covers the 1T metal dichalcogenides, compounds such as 1T-TaS2. These materials settle into a charge density wave state that insulates. Many have read that state as a Mott insulator, with spins stuck on a frustrated lattice, ripe for a quantum spin liquid.

The authors urge caution from the view of scanning tunnelling microscopy. Evidence now shows that layers interact strongly in bulk 1T-TaS2, and those links drive some of its most striking traits and even distinct insulating phases. The review asks how far bulk and surface forms count as Mott insulators, and where spin liquid behavior might survive. Studies of isolated single layers help separate the bulk story from the surface one.
arxiv-2509-17519:
Ruqaya Hussein, Sergey Kryzhevich, and Khosro Tajbakhsh model a mosquito control method that can partly fail. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies the sterile insect technique, used against malaria, dengue, and yellow fever. Released sterile males mate with wild females, and the population should crash. In practice, some released insects keep residual fertility, and delays creep into the life cycle.

Their three-dimensional delayed model joins wild, sterile, and non-sterile insects with a saturated release rate. The authors find when the positive equilibrium stays stable and when a Hopf bifurcation sets the population oscillating. Below a critical delay, the system holds steady; past it, cycles can emerge. As residual fertility varies in a narrow band, the non-sterile population swings sharply, a sign of sensitive dependence. The warning for field programmes is that small leaks of fertility can flip outcomes.
arxiv-2509-18119:
Yifan Xu and 9 co-authors train phone-use agents with live feedback from phone tasks. Their 2025 frame, MobileRL, deals with agents that tap and swipe through app screens. Task hardness varies a lot, and sampling phone worlds at scale is slow, so plain training stalls.

A core method adapts to task hardness in two ways. It replays wins on hard tasks more, and filters failed tasks into a staged path. A shortest-path tweak shapes rewards for multi-step tasks. Two open base models were trained with the frame. The larger one set top success scores on two phone bench sets.
arxiv-2509-18319:
Offshore platforms must survive rare, brutal ocean weather, and engineers need the odds of failure. Matthew Speers, Jonathan Angus Tawn, and Philip Jonathan compare ways to estimate those odds in this 2025 paper. The core tool is a map of which long-term sea states can push a structure past its limit. Failure odds come from adding up that map over all sea states.

Two methods are tested. One pairs a sampling method called parallel tempering with importance sampling. The other pairs a fitted emulator with Bayesian quadrature, a way of adding up uncertain maps. Tests cover a fake simple structure and a real monopile with a ringing response. The first method proved reliable at lower cost than brute force. The emulator method can be cheaper still, but only when a key weight is known ahead of time. When it is not, the first method is the safer pick.
arxiv-2509-18719:
Payment fraud unfolds over several steps, so catching it means judging a chain, not a single charge. Bo Qu and six co-authors pair reinforcement learning with large language models for that job in this 2025 paper. The learning agent treats each payment stage as a step in a decision process. Its success depends on the reward function, which is hard to design by hand.

Language models refine the reward function in rounds, using their reasoning and coding skills. That loop lifts detection accuracy in the team's tests on real-world data. The system also shows zero-shot skill, handling new patterns without fresh training. Long-term evaluations back its robustness. The authors present the pairing as a template for industrial reinforcement learning. Language models, they argue, can shoulder the expert-heavy reward design step.
arxiv-2509-18919:
Finding flaws on metal surfaces is a key check in factories, but flaw photos are scarce. Chuni Liu and six co-authors tackle the gap between training data and real plant images. Models first trained on everyday photos learn features that fit metal poorly. Models trained only on plant images often miss faint flaws hidden in rough textures.

Their method, called anomaly-guided self-supervised pretraining, teaches the model from maps that mark likely flaw spots. First the backbone network learns to copy the knowledge in those maps. Next the detector trains on rough flaw boxes drawn from the same maps. The team built a dataset of about 120,000 plant images, plus two small sets with pixel-level labels. Tests show clear gains over models first trained on everyday photos.
arxiv-2509-19019:
Leandro Lyra Braga Dognini, writing alone, studies economies where generations overlap, each living briefly and trading with the young and old around them. In such economies the first welfare theorem can fail: a market balance may waste resources even with no friction. A classic test by Cass can judge a given balance, but it does not say whether a good balance exists at all. Older work even gives cases where none exists.

Dognini gives conditions under which optimal monetary equilibria do exist, in economies with no durable assets, cash rules, or transfer schemes. Roughly, the economy must be prone to saving. He also builds an algorithm that finds these equilibria as the limit of shrinking sets of candidates. The sets come from working backward through the balance equations, starting from well-behaved far-future versions of the economy.
arxiv-2509-19219:
Rating the quality of top speech systems is tricky: the most sensitive listening test does not scale, and the scalable one goes blind at high quality. Laura Lechler and Ivana Balic propose MUSHRA-1S, a variant of the sensitive MUSHRA test that judges each system on its own, scored against a fixed reference and anchor. Standard MUSHRA needs all systems side by side, which limits how many listeners and systems a study can handle.

In their experiments, the new variant tracked standard MUSHRA scores more closely than the scalable alternative, including in the high-quality range where that alternative saturates. Fixing the context also reduced a bias that comes from listeners stretching their scales to fit the set. The method still pinpoints specific artifacts in a system's output. The authors offer it as a robust way to benchmark the best speech systems at scale.
arxiv-2509-19319:
Gyubok Lee and seven co-authors benchmark AI agents on questions about electronic health records stored in the FHIR standard. FHIR organizes clinical data as interlinked resources, not flat tables, and hospitals increasingly adopt it. Agents must fetch the right resources and reason across them to answer. Older benchmarks, built on conventional structured data, miss that difficulty. Their benchmark grounds about 2,900 real-world clinical questions in the FHIR format.

The team compares ways agents retrieve data, directly through the FHIR interface versus through specialized tools. They also vary whether agents work in one turn or several, and whether they reason in words or in generated code. Results highlight how hard retrieval from intricate FHIR resources is, and how much reasoning strategy matters. The dataset and scoring suite are public, aiming at more reliable clinical agents.
arxiv-2509-20119:
Belal Shoer and Yova Kementchedjhieva wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on science questions with images. In one test format, the figure, question, and answer options all sit inside a single image. Even the best commercial models do poorly on this format without extra training. Training data in this style is scarce.

The authors create new training data by merging separate image and text pairs into single images. They then fine-tune a small multilingual vision-language model on a mix of this synthetic data and the original exam set. The tuned model gained clearly across thirteen languages. Gains also transferred to languages beyond the training mix. The recipe is simple, and it shows how data design can matter as much as model size.
arxiv-2509-20419:
War crowds out dissent in the news, argues Taaha Saleem Bajwa in a 2025 arXiv case study of Pakistani media. The study covers the May 2025 conflict between India and Pakistan. Emerging democracies often restrict speech, and conflict tightens the pressure. Bajwa asks what happened to coverage of political opposition during the fighting.

Using a large language model, the study analyzed about two thousand six hundred articles from three major newspapers. War reporting grew sharply during the conflict. Coverage of opposition and dissent was pushed to the margins by comparison. The findings suggest that regional conflict can hollow out democratic discourse even without formal censorship. Bajwa closes by urging stronger safeguards for press freedom in volatile regions. The study appeared as an extended abstract at a workshop on language technology and democracy.
arxiv-2509-20519:
The galaxy NGC 4258 hosts the gold-standard black hole mass measurement, and Dieu Nguyen and ten co-authors remeasure it with Webb telescope data in a 2025 arXiv paper. Water masers orbiting its center gave the benchmark value long ago. Stellar dynamics offers an independent check, if the starlight can be separated from the active nucleus glare. Archival infrared spectroscopy from the NIRSpec instrument supplied the data.

The team extracted two-dimensional stellar motions from carbon monoxide absorption features near the center. Jeans anisotropic models fit those motions across a grid of twelve variants, testing assumptions about blur, mass-to-light ratio, and orbit shapes. The ensemble median gives a black hole of about forty-one million solar masses. That is just five percent above the maser benchmark and consistent with it. The paper argues for reporting whole model ensembles rather than one preferred fit.
arxiv-2509-20719:
A molecule is only useful in drug work if chemists can actually make it. Alston Lo, Connor Coley, and Wojciech Matusik present SynGA in a 2025 paper written for ICLR 2026. SynGA is a genetic algorithm that searches directly over synthesis routes rather than raw structures.

Custom crossover and mutation steps keep every candidate inside synthesizable space by construction. Changing the fitness function adapts the search to different jobs. The authors test it on finding synthesizable analogs of known compounds and on optimizing properties with few evaluations. A machine learning filter that narrows the building block set lifts performance further. A model-based variant pairs the search with Bayesian optimization for property tasks.
arxiv-2509-20819:
Modern science runs mix simulations, model training, and inference on the same supercomputer. Andre Merzky and three co-authors study how to run such hybrid workloads in a 2025 paper on high-performance computing runtime systems. Standard launchers like Slurm's srun limit how many tasks can run at once.

The team integrates RADICAL-Pilot with two runtime systems, Flux and Dragon, which manage resources in layers. They test the combinations on the Frontier supercomputer with synthetic and real workloads. The layered setups sustain far higher task rates than the standard launcher and keep the machine highly utilized. The results guide centers that must serve mixed AI and simulation campaigns without wasting capacity.
arxiv-2509-20919:
Some games have astronomically many actions per player, yet their structure is simple underneath. Andreas Kontogiannis and four co-authors study learning in such polyhedral games in a 2025 paper accepted at NeurIPS 2025. Examples include the classic Colonel Blotto game and congestion games.

The goal is to learn coarse correlated equilibria efficiently, with regret and per-step cost growing only slowly in the action count. Kernelization achieved this under full information. The harder, realistic setting gives players only partial feedback about outcomes. The authors develop kernelized learning methods for that bandit-style setting. Their algorithms aim to keep the polylogarithmic efficiency of the full-information case. The results apply to large strategic systems, from traffic routing to resource contests.
arxiv-2509-21419:
How close are automated species identification systems to the best human experts? An overview paper by Herve Goeau, Pierre Bonnet, and Alexis Joly examines the ExpertLifeCLEF 2018 challenge, which was designed to answer that question. Even top experts sometimes disagree on visual or audio observations. A single picture often lacks the information for certain identification.

Nineteen deep learning systems from four research teams were evaluated in the challenge. Their results were compared with nine experts on the same observations. Quantifying expert uncertainty matters for both computer scientists and naturalists. The overview reports how far automated systems stood from expert performance at that time, and why the gap is hard to close.
arxiv-2509-21519:
Grokking is the odd training pattern where a network memorizes first and generalizes much later. Yuandong Tian proposes a framework for its learning dynamics in a 2025 paper. Which features emerge during grokking, and under what conditions, lacked a mathematical account. The framework, named Li squared, covers two layer nonlinear networks with structured inputs. Three key stages organize the process.

Lazy learning comes first: the top layer overfits to random hidden features, so the model appears to memorize. Backpropagated gradients already carry label information at that stage, Tian argues. Each hidden node can then learn its representation independently. Interactive feature learning follows as the third stage. Scaling laws for feature emergence are derived as provable results within the framework.
arxiv-2509-21619:
Full training of a vision transformer is expensive, yet most weight change happens early. Krishu Thapa and 4 co-authors exploit that pattern in a 2025 paper. As training progresses, updates stabilize and look low rank. Their method, PreLoRA, switches training mode partway through. A hybrid scheme keeps full training first, then hands over to low rank adapters.

User defined settings determine the switching point for each layer. Rank per module follows its level of convergence. Experiments used the ViT-Large model. Accuracy was preserved while trainable parameters fell to a tenth of the original count. Time, compute, and memory savings follow. The flexible approach adapts the switch to how fast each part of the model settles.
arxiv-2509-21719:
Rain streaks, blur, and noise degrade outdoor video, and camera motion makes frame alignment fragile. Shuning Sun and 7 co-authors propose a fast deraining method in a 2025 paper. Optical flow alignment is expensive and less robust, they note. Lie groups represent non stop geometric transformations in a principled way. Their method, DeLiVR, injects spatiotemporal Lie group differential biases directly into attention scores.

A rotation bounded Lie relative bias predicts the in plane angle of each frame with a compact module. Normalized coordinates are rotated and matched with base coordinates. Spatial and time based consistency is enforced through that bias rather than explicit flow. Slight camera pose changes otherwise amplify cross frame mismatches. Fast video deraining for wild footage is the goal.
arxiv-2509-22219:
Pavan Karjol, Vivek V Kashyap, Rohan Kashyap, and Prathosh A P present a framework that finds the symmetry in the data instead, in this 2025 paper. They focus on one-parameter subgroups, continuous families of transformations that come in three geometric flavors: elliptical, like rotations; hyperbolic, like boosts; and parabolic, like shears. The framework learns an unknown function and its governing subgroup at the same time.

For whichever flavor is assumed, a matching network is assembled from invariant and equivariant layers shaped by the subgroup's Lie algebra, the infinitesimal description of the transformations. The generator parameters are then learned end to end from data. Because the symmetry is built into the architecture, it holds by construction and can be traced to specific parts of the model, with formal proofs. Tests on synthetic and real systems, from double pendulums to quark tagging, recovered the subgroups accurately.
arxiv-2509-22319:
Hyunwoo Kim and four co-authors present Progressive Weight Loading, a way to start a large model quickly and let it grow stronger as it runs. Big models load slowly, and on phones and other tight devices that delay hurts, since models are loaded and unloaded often. Shrinking a model by distillation is the usual answer, but the small model stays weaker. Their 2025 method instead deploys a lightweight student model first, then swaps its layers, one by one, for the teacher's layers.

To make the swaps seamless, the training method aligns the middle representations of student and teacher layers, and it also improves the student's own output quality. Experiments on three well-known architecture families show the pattern working as intended. Accuracy climbs gradually as teacher layers arrive, ending at the full teacher's accuracy. The initial inference speed, though, stays at the small model's level.
arxiv-2509-22419:
Matteo Pais and 3 co-authors model jets that fail to escape a dying massive star. Such choked jets dump their energy into a hot cocoon inside the star's outer layers. That cocoon can expand and break out as a slower outflow. The team ran relativistic fluid simulations around blue and red supergiant stars.

The runs map when a jet stays choked and when it breaks free. They also measure how fast shocks in this setting can speed up charged particles. Early results show very fast shocks seconds after energy input starts. Such shocks could make high-energy neutrinos, a key test for this hidden source class.
arxiv-2509-22719:
Adithya Giri adds the built-in biases of convolutional networks to vision transformers, so they can learn from small data sets. Transformers scale well and stay explainable, but they lack those inductive biases, the built-in assumptions about images that convolutions carry. On large data the biases can be learned; on small data they cannot. Giri introduces the biases through learned masks inside the attention mechanism.

The resulting model, IBiT, keeps the transformer's explainability. On small data sets it proved significantly more accurate than plain vision transformers. It reached that gain without knowledge distillation from a teacher model. The work suggests attention can be made data-efficient by building image structure in, rather than hoping scale supplies it.
arxiv-2509-22919:
Missing values plague time series data, and most fill-in methods ignore the class label. Jake S Rhodes and 7 co-authors use that label to guide the fill-in. Their framework leans on strong supervised models built for time series classification. From each model, they pull a tree-based closeness score between series.

That closeness score decides which known values fill each gap. The filled data often led to higher classification accuracy in their tests. Oddly, the filled values could differ from the true values and still help. Richer information, not exact recovery, drove the gains. The method fits tasks where labels are known at training time.
arxiv-2509-23119:
A claimed proof settles a generalized connected wedge theorem in holography. Bowen Zhao works in the AdS/CFT setting, on two-to-two scattering processes. The original theorem ties bulk scattering to strong mutual information between boundary regions. Liu and Leutheusser later enlarged the bulk scattering region. They conjectured that its non-emptiness fully characterizes that strong information link.

Zhao provides a geometric, general-relativity proof of a slightly modified version of their claim. The decision regions on the boundary anchor the statement. Only the modified form is proven, not the conjecture as first stated. The result sharpens how bulk events map to boundary data.
arxiv-2509-23419:
Federated training over wireless links drowns in update traffic, so each round must carry more signal per byte. Asadullah Tariq and 5 co-authors attack that overhead on three fronts. One step drops weak features and keeps strong ones. A quantization step sets its precision from how new and error-prone each gradient is. A third step tunes how often devices talk at all.

Wide tests compare accuracy, loss, and convergence speed with baselines. The joint plan reached high traffic savings in their framework. Accuracy held while traffic fell. Resource-poor wireless settings are the target use. The three parts were designed to work as one system.
arxiv-2509-23519:
Search tools that feed web pages to a language model can be poisoned by hostile pages. Zeyu Shen and 5 co-authors defend such retrieval-augmented systems with ReliabilityRAG. Their method leans on trust cues the search setting already gives, such as document rank. A graph links documents that contradict each other, and the system seeks a consistent majority set that leaves hostile pages out.

One algorithm finds a maximum independent set on that graph, favoring higher-ranked documents, with proven safety bounds under limited corruption. A second, sampling-based version scales to large result sets while keeping part of the guarantee. Tests show stronger defense than prior methods, with clean accuracy kept high.
arxiv-2509-24119:
Kimball Martin studies the fields that hold the Fourier coefficients of special modular forms. He states a conjecture: only finitely many such rationality fields occur among newforms of bounded degree. For forms with complex multiplication, he proves the claim, assuming a generalized form of the Riemann hypothesis.

Martin then works out exactly which quadratic and cubic fields occur for weight two CM forms. That list ties to the classification of CM abelian varieties of GL(2) type. Several of the fields he finds do not appear in the current LMFDB tables of newforms. The gaps show that the standard tables are still incomplete for these forms.
arxiv-2509-24419:
When production code changes, its unit tests must change with it, and hand upkeep is slow and easy to miss. Yuanhe Zhang and 3 co-authors built TESTUPDATER, a language-model system that updates tests just in time. Past tools mostly repaired broken tests and ignored the chance to extend tests for new features. They also gathered context by fixed rules and never checked their output.

TESTUPDATER lets the model gather and filter context, then guides it step by step through change types and new dependencies. An error-aware loop runs the updated tests and repairs failures by type. On a new benchmark of real samples, it beat the leading rival on pass rates and coverage.
arxiv-2509-25819:
Soumya Bhattacharya and Chiranjeeb Singha study gravitational wave memory in twenty twenty-five. Memory is a permanent shift left in spacetime after a wave passes. Their setting adds a dark matter halo around the black hole. The halo follows a Hernquist-type density profile, with and without a central spike.

They first solve geodesic motion under a wave pulse in that spacetime. That shows how halo and pulse together bend particle paths. They then compute the memory signal at far distance using the Bondi-Sachs formalism. Flux balance laws tied to BMS symmetries quantify the memory contribution. Folding it into ringdown templates could let detectors read halo properties from the waveform. Readers get a bridge between dark matter structure and a subtle wave effect.
arxiv-2510-00119:
Alfredo Amador-Portes and five colleagues published this 2025 paper presenting AAP-Imfit, a tool for radio astronomy. Telescope networks called VLBI make the sharpest radio maps of distant jets and black holes. Fitting each bright blob in those maps by hand is slow and hard to repeat. The new tool automates that fitting inside the standard CASA software package.

The program sets a detection limit, fits two-dimensional Gaussian shapes, and cleans up artifacts. It then reports each component's position and brightness in a uniform way. The team tested it on maps of the blazars 3C 279 and 3C 454.3 against published hand fits. The automatic results matched the hand fits closely on standard quality measures. The authors note that faint or tangled features still need a human eye, but large surveys become far faster.
arxiv-2510-00219:
Houjun Liu and colleagues at Stanford University published this 2025 paper introducing Thoughtbubbles, a transformer that thinks in parallel. Standard models spend extra effort by writing out long chains of thought, one token at a time. That serial style cannot be learned during pretraining and wastes effort on easy tokens. Thoughtbubbles instead clones internal streams so hard spots get extra hidden computation.

The model learns when to fork a stream into a bubble and when to delete one. Remarkably, ordinary language modeling loss during pretraining teaches this behavior with no extra supervision. Across model sizes from 150 million to 772 million parameters, it beat standard models on text prediction. It also won on zero-shot tests such as HellaSwag and LAMBADA in the paper. One smaller Thoughtbubbles model even outperformed baselines at the largest scale tested.
arxiv-2510-00319:
Wei Shen, Han Wang, and Haoyu Li published this 2025 paper on a stealthy attack against language models. Senior co-author Huan Zhang works at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. People judge model answers by reading the chain-of-thought reasoning shown with them. That trust is fragile if the reasoning itself can be poisoned. The authors introduce DecepChain, a backdoor that makes models reason plausibly toward wrong answers.

The attack fine-tunes a model on its own naturally mistaken reasoning drafts. Reinforcement learning with a flipped reward then strengthens the flaw on triggered inputs. A plausibility term keeps the false reasoning fluent and ordinary-looking throughout. Across benchmarks and models, attack success ran high while normal performance barely dipped. Human raters in the study could hardly tell the rigged reasoning from honest reasoning. The authors warn this quiet failure mode could corrupt answers while eroding trust in shown reasoning.
arxiv-2510-00419:
Kairun Zhang and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on learning a better optimizer for fine-tuning language models. Zeroth-order methods tune models by probing outputs rather than computing gradients, which slashes memory use. Their sampling strategies, though, are hand-crafted and fixed for every model. The team's ZO Fine-tuner learns the perturbation strategy for a given model instead.

Because only a few foundation models dominate practice, training the optimizer once per model pays off. The learned optimizer then transfers across downstream tasks and even to fine-tuned derivatives. Experiments spanned four language models and seven datasets in the paper. The learned optimizer beat earlier zeroth-order baselines in most task and model combinations tested. Its design stays compact and adds minimal overhead during tuning. The authors frame it as a train-once, reuse-widely path to efficient fine-tuning.
arxiv-2510-00519:
Hadiza Yusuf and Khouloud Gaaloul published this 2025 paper on how artificial intelligence reshapes cyber-physical system design. Such systems fuse computation with physical processes, from vehicles to factory control. Adding AI controllers boosts adaptability, but the structural fallout is poorly mapped. The authors compare Simulink models built with classical controllers against twins driven by deep reinforcement learning.

Block by block, the AI versions look different: more logic, more discrete parts, denser wiring. Core functionality blocks rose by about twenty-six percent on average. Connectivity climbed by about twenty percent as well. Those gains buy flexibility, yet they strain computation and blur reliability. Standard verification methods, tuned for tidy classical designs, struggled on the AI models. The authors call for guided architecture rules and adaptive verification built for intelligent, interconnected systems.
arxiv-2510-00619:
Michiel Braat and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on knowing what a self-driving system has actually learned. A trajectory planner is only trustworthy where its training data reached. The authors turn driving datasets into knowledge graphs of entities and relationships. Any scene then decomposes into small configurations that can be counted in the data.

Their competence score weighs two things: how often each configuration appears, and how complex the full scene is. Complex scenes demand more coverage before competence is granted. Applied to the NuPlan dataset, the metric tracked a real planner's performance closely. Scenes scored competent were indeed where the planner behaved well. The graphs also describe datasets in plain terms humans can audit. The authors offer the method as a monitoring tool for safe deployment of driving AI.
arxiv-2510-00819:
Melo, Abate, and Gal tackle unstable policy gradient training for language model reasoning in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning gives large models much of their maths and coding skill, yet its updates can collapse without warning. Teams often pick timid settings for safety, which wastes training samples and raises cost. The authors model the training dynamics with second-order curvature information to spot trouble early.

Their algorithm, CAPO, tracks curvature during updates and masks out samples that push training toward instability. They prove monotonic improvement guarantees under realistic assumptions. On standard maths reasoning benchmarks, CAPO stayed stable under aggressive settings where the baseline GRPO method collapsed outright. By rejecting fewer than eight percent of tokens, it reached up to thirty times better sample efficiency in their experiments.
arxiv-2510-01119:
Luo, Ran, and Lu present Instant4D in this 2025 arXiv paper on dynamic scene reconstruction from ordinary video. Rebuilding a moving 3D scene from one uncalibrated camera is a prize for augmented and virtual reality, but earlier systems need hours of optimization per clip. Instant4D starts with deep visual SLAM to recover the scene geometry and camera path. It then prunes its grid representation to remove redundant primitives while keeping the geometry intact.

That pruning shrinks the model to under ten percent of its original size. A streamlined 4D Gaussian representation handles motion, giving roughly a thirty-fold speed-up in their experiments. A typical two-hundred-frame video is fully reconstructed within about ten minutes, with training itself under two minutes. Quality stayed competitive on standard benchmarks, and the system also handled casual in-the-wild footage well.
arxiv-2510-01219:
Wang builds a concept-learning test that exposes hidden biases in language models which ordinary question-and-answer checks miss. Models that ace standard bias benchmarks can still smuggle skewed assumptions into their reasoning. Teaching a model a rule from examples, then probing its guesses, reveals what it truly assumes.

The dataset wraps quantifier concepts in small stories about quantities and yes-or-no judgments. Models showed a pull toward upward monotonicity, reading rules as more permissive than the examples justified. Direct prompting without the learning setup barely hinted at the bias. Concept learning thus works as an X-ray for assumptions models never state. Upward monotonicity means assuming that more of a good thing stays good. Human concept learning supplied the experimental template. Hidden bias matters most in systems already deployed at scale. The test needs no access to model internals at all.
arxiv-2510-01319:
Huang and co-authors find a protected phase where fault-tolerant quantum gates can turn by any angle, not just fixed clicks. Transversal gates are naturally safe in error-correcting codes but provably cannot do everything alone. Magic-state factories fill the gap at heavy cost in overhead.

Working with the surface code, the team exhibits continuously tunable logical rotations from transversal operations plus decoding. Their error shrinks exponentially with code size compared with the rotation angle. A simple protocol built on the phase performs small-angle rotations cheaply. Quantum simulation, which lives on such tiny turns, stands to gain most. Dephasing noise is the adversary the phase withstands. Decoding after the transversal step completes the logical operation. More efficient code families may inherit the protocol directly. Experimental demonstration remains the acknowledged next challenge. Overhead drops most where rotations are smallest and frequent.
arxiv-2510-01719:
Chung and four co-authors ask what models that use pictures and text really learn in this 2025 machine learning paper. Such models now attempt hard tasks like olympiad-level geometry problems. A single accuracy score hides which subskill improved and which one lagged. The team built MathLens, a benchmark that separates perception, reasoning, and the integration of both.

MathLens uses textbook-style geometry problems with diagrams and matching text descriptions. Some questions test seeing alone, while others test reasoning with the picture taken away. Their analysis found that reinforcement learning mainly strengthened seeing, especially when text help was present. Reasoning improved only when perception improved alongside it. Joining the two stayed the weakest skill, and most remaining errors gathered there. The benchmark gives trainers a clearer map of where model skill actually grows.
arxiv-2510-02019:
Courtney, Galke, van Luijk, and Stottmeister loosen the rules for building operator systems from simpler pieces in this 2025 paper. Inductive limits assemble complex operator systems from basic building blocks. The classic construction demands strict coherence between the pieces at every step. Their soft version relaxes that demand to an asymptotic one and allows indexing over arbitrary nets.

Such soft systems arise naturally from completely positive approximations of nuclear systems. The authors then adapt an argument of Ding and Peterson to a classic question. They prove a separable operator system is nuclear exactly when it is an inductive limit of matrix algebras. That result extends a classic Lazar-Lindenstrauss theorem into noncommutative Choquet theory. Nuclearity is a central regularity property in the field. Characterizing it through matrix algebra limits gives researchers a concrete test. The flexible limits also serve quantum information, where operator systems model quantum channels.
arxiv-2510-02119:
Morisset, Hardy, and Durmus analyze when adding fake data helps estimate a precision matrix. Their 2025 statistics paper works in high dimensions. A precision matrix is the inverse of a covariance matrix. It reveals which variables link directly to each other. Data augmentation pads a dataset with artificial samples. Those samples may come from a generator or simple transformations. The authors compare augmentation against linear shrinkage estimators. Shrinkage pulls the estimate toward a scaled identity target. For both families, they derive error bounds with hard guarantees.

The bounds show how error concentrates around its typical size. Analysts can compare methods before running them. The bounds also guide tuning choices, like the share of fake samples. Random matrix theory supplies the technical engine. A new deterministic equivalent handles dependent samples with structure. Numerical experiments support the theory. More data helps only when the mix is right.
arxiv-2510-02219:
Tran, Li, Florian, and Sun find the few attention heads that actually retrieve in this 2025 machine learning paper. Attention-based re-rankers score documents from transformer attention weights. Most heads add noise and redundancy rather than signal, dragging accuracy down. The authors score heads contrastively, rewarding attention that lands on relevant documents and punishing attention that lands on irrelevant ones.

The winning set, called CoRe heads, makes up under one percent of all heads. Aggregating only their signals produced a state-of-the-art list-wise re-ranker across three language models. These heads concentrate in the model's middle layers. The finding prunes re-ranking computation drastically, since the useless heads can be ignored. It also sharpens interpretability: retrieval lives in a tiny, locatable circuit. Search systems built on frozen language models get a cheaper and stronger scoring core. Less than one head in a hundred carries the ranking signal.
arxiv-2510-02319:
Sai Teja and co-authors defend AI text detectors by measuring the attack itself. Their 2025 paper studies detectors that label text as human or machine made. Paraphrasing breaks many of those detectors. A rewritten machine text can look statistically human. Standard extra training helps only against shallow tricks. The team builds a framework called PIFE instead. PIFE first normalizes each text into a standard form. It then measures how much the text changed. Edit distance and meaning similarity become direct clues for the classifier.

Their tests used attacks at character, word, and sentence levels. A strong transformer baseline failed under meaning preserving attacks. Its true positive rate fell below half at a strict false alarm setting. PIFE stayed far more resilient across the same attacks. Modeling the tampering beats memorizing examples. Detector builders gain a sturdier design pattern.
arxiv-2510-02419:
van de Weygaert tests whether the walls of the cosmic web are real structures. His 2025 cosmology paper uses the caustic skeleton model. That model traces the web back to folds in the dark matter flow. Walls are thin sheets separating near empty voids. They form first in the collapse sequence. Filaments later grow inside those walls. The study derives where proto-wall centers should sit. Constrained simulations then follow their evolution over time. The team counts wall centers across scales in the runs. They also compute the early universe volume that walls occupy.

Halo distributions and density fields around walls get measured too. Results compare against older saddle point conditions. The walls emerge as genuine, organized features of the web. Their subtlety in surveys explains why they seemed doubtful. Survey maps may hide walls more than they reveal. Structure formation theory gains a firmer backbone.
arxiv-2510-03019:
Zhou and co-authors rebuild radio fields inside rail tunnels from thin data. High-speed trains need rock-solid wireless links in tunnels. Predicting the field there is slow with classic solvers. Trains can carry only a single sensor line in practice. The team asks a network to fill the whole cross-section from that line. Their model is an inception-enhanced generative adversarial network. Physics rules are baked into its training loss.

Multi-scale inception blocks let the generator read patterns at several sizes. A staged training plan steadies the learning process. Output fields matched the accuracy of a classic wave method. The classic method needs far richer input to run at all. The new route also runs much faster. Tests used both simulated fields and data from real train runs. Operators could thus tune tunnel networks from live runs.
arxiv-2510-03619:
Fang, Shentu, and Lu present a 2025 arXiv paper building a broadband source of quantum photon pairs in a lithium niobate waveguide. Photon pairs from down conversion power quantum imaging, tomography, and measurement, and wider bandwidth sharpens all of them. Their chip is a step chirped periodically poled waveguide, under seven millimeters long, on a lithium niobate on insulator platform. Varying the poling pattern along its length lets one device phase match across a span of wavelengths.

For second harmonic generation, the device averaged an efficiency of about fifty four percent per watt per square centimeter across a telecom band in the study. For pair generation, tuning the pump among three wavelengths produced bandwidths up to ninety nine terahertz. Brightness reached twenty gigahertz per milliwatt per nanometer. Broad pairs enable interference measurements with narrow features. The design is simple to fabricate, which helps labs adopt it for quantum metrology work.
arxiv-2510-04019:
Zhan presents this 2025 arXiv paper on teaching diffusion language models to reason better with reinforcement learning. Diffusion models write text by unmasking many tokens in parallel, unlike standard models that write one token at a time. They now match ordinary models at large scale, but the reinforcement learning methods that sharpen reasoning were built for the ordinary kind. 

Zhan's algorithm, AGRPO, adapts policy gradient methods faithfully to the diffusion setting. It uses Monte Carlo sampling to compute an unbiased estimate of the policy gradient, a first for this model family. On math and reasoning tasks, AGRPO improved the base LLaDA model by several points on the GSM8K benchmark. It also multiplied performance on the Countdown arithmetic task compared with the base model. The work shows online reinforcement learning can extend to diffusion models without giving up theoretical soundness.
arxiv-2510-04619:
Ivan Homoliak and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on protecting blockchain leaders from attack. Proof of stake chains elect a leader to propose each block, and designs name that leader in advance. An attacker who knows the name can flood the leader with traffic and stall the chain. The team built a consensus protocol with onion routing woven into its core. The routing hides the network identity of the proposer.

Leader choice stays weighted by stake and random, as in designs. The anonymization layer then wraps the path to the leader so rivals cannot aim at it. The team implemented the protocol and ran it on a six node test network. Throughput reached about one hundred ten transactions per second with the privacy layer on. That speed shows the shield costs only a modest share of performance. Chains gain denial of service resistance without giving up their single chain design.
arxiv-2510-04819:
Benlin Liu and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on what multimodal language models see inside. These models pair an image encoder with a language model, yet they fail at perception tasks. The authors trace how visual information moves through the language model layers. They probe image tokens stored inside with tests. Those tokens, it turns out, carry enough signal for hard tasks done cold.

Segmentation, matching points across images, and finding named objects worked from the internal tokens. The language model does add visual detail beyond the encoder output. Still, its tokens hold less visual information than the vision encoder that feeds it. Odd artifacts appear in image key tokens in the later layers and drag perception down. Adding a text prefix before the image improved the internal pictures. In one benchmark, a third of the style questions had the perception inside the model, unspoken. The output never used it.
arxiv-2510-04919:
Davood Rafiei and four co-authors study when fine-tuning actually helps a language model in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their task is text-to-SQL, turning plain questions into database queries. Fine-tuning on extra data sometimes lifts accuracy a lot. Other times it adds nothing, or even hurts.

The authors trace the difference to alignment between the training data and the target task. They measure alignment by comparing the structural features of SQL queries across datasets. Across three large benchmarks and several model families, alignment strongly predicted fine-tuning success. Well-matched data brought large gains in accuracy and query quality. Poorly matched data brought little or none. Their method lets teams check a dataset before spending on training.
arxiv-2510-05019:
Aziz Fall studies how crystal defects can reshape electronic behavior in this 2025 arXiv paper. Dislocations are line defects that thread through many real materials. Theory predicts that patterned dislocations create flat bands, where electrons barely move with momentum. Such bands can trigger exotic effects, including unusual superconductivity.

Fall builds a simpler one-dimensional model to explain where those bands come from. He averages the dislocation positions along one special direction into an effective potential. A single parameter in the model measures the strength of the strain modulation. Turning that dial shows how dislocation strain drives flat band formation. The framework gives researchers a transparent handle on a complex three-dimensional effect.
arxiv-2510-05219:
Ajit Bhand, Ashoke Sen, and Ranveer Kumar Singh isolate the fingerprint of single black holes in string theory in this 2025 arXiv paper. Black hole counting in heterotic string theory uses the inverse of the Igusa cusp form. Its Fourier coefficients mix single-centered and two-centered black hole states. Untangling the two contributions matters for precision counting.

The authors construct a manifestly duality-invariant generating function for the single-centered index alone. They subtract a two-centered generating function, built from the Dedekind eta function, from the inverse cusp form. Careful analysis in the Siegel upper half plane shows the definition is unambiguous. Apparent poles cancel exactly between the two pieces. Two different definitions of the single-centered index are proven to coincide.
arxiv-2510-05519:
Raman and colleagues propose judging AI systems by human rights, not just by lab fairness scores. International law already names rights that apply everywhere, such as equality, health, and security. Generative AI now touches all three, from hiring tools to asylum decisions. Their 2025 paper builds a framework for measuring the risk a model poses to specific rights.

The framework rests on the UN guiding principles for business and human rights. It has three stages, starting with tasks where rights risks are likely. Next, it designs measures of the scope, scale, and chance of harm in that setting. Last, it reads those measures against the named rights at stake. A case study applies the method to language models used in political news work. The results bear on rights to information access and free thought.
arxiv-2510-05619:
Anand and colleagues generate speech the way humans do, by moving a vocal tract. Modern speech synthesizers are huge transformers that work as black boxes. They offer little insight into how sounds are physically made. The team's 2025 framework treats speech as a motor control problem instead.

Reinforcement learning trains a policy that steers the tongue, lips, and jaw. An audio perceiver called Sylber grades each attempt against the target syllable. A pretrained decoder, SPARC, turns the learned movements into sound. Training covered six target syllables and converged successfully. Similarity scores between generated and target audio exceeded zero point eight five. Lightweight perceptrons, not transformers, choose each articulator movement. Listeners correctly transcribed syllables like please, loot, and cat. Every motor command stays traceable, which suits clinical speech applications. The setup also mirrors how infants learn speech through feedback.
arxiv-2510-05919:
Garreta Basora and Mulayim compare autoencoders for spotting anomalies in twelve-lead ECGs. Electrocardiograms reveal cardiovascular disease, but expert reading is slow and error-prone. Unsupervised models trained only on normal hearts can flag deviations automatically. Their 2025 study benchmarks three architectures on a public Chinese dataset.

A convolutional autoencoder is the simplest baseline. A variational autoencoder with bidirectional memory captures temporal structure better. Adding multi-head attention produces the strongest detector overall. The attention model is, to their knowledge, the first of its kind for ECGs. It recalls about eighty-five percent of anomalies in held-out tests. Its precision-recall area score also leads the comparison. Interpretability of the anomaly diagnosis is a stated qualitative strength. An interactive dashboard visualizes where anomalies localize for clinical triage. Early cardiac warnings can save lives and cut system costs.
arxiv-2510-06019:
Bozga, Iosif, and Zuleger study how graph-like structures can be joined together in a 2025 computer science paper. Standard composition glues structures only at marked interface points, so the whole stays determined by its parts. The authors instead study fusion, an operation that merges unmarked elements from two structures when their labels allow it.

Repeated fusion can produce structures whose tree-width, a measure of how tree-like a structure is, grows without bound. The team proves that, for families described by a finite grammar, one can always decide whether a bound on tree-width exists. When a bound does exist, they show the fused family can again be described by an effectively built grammar. That result lets automated checkers test logical properties across the whole fused family, which matters for verifying reconfigurable systems.
arxiv-2510-06419:
Kayaalp and six co-authors ask whether time series forecasting needs one giant model or a portfolio of small ones in a 2025 machine learning paper. Foundation models keep growing, but scale carries heavy training and deployment costs. A portfolio of smaller pretrained models offers an alternative.

The team assembles portfolios and combines members through ensembling or per-task selection. These portfolios matched large monolithic models on large-scale benchmarks. They used far fewer parameters overall. Design experiments revealed a clear pattern about composition. Specialist collections consistently beat portfolios of independently trained generalists. Post-training one base model proved a compute-effective way to make diverse specialists. The study compared test-time strategies directly. Ensembling and selection beat test-time fine-tuning on compute efficiency. The message is practical: curate a diverse bench of small models instead of betting on one giant.
arxiv-2510-07119:
Jung and colleagues present MoRe, a method that fixes 3D scenes built from single-camera views. Their 2025 paper starts from a known flaw. Each single view gives depth with its own unknown scale. Stacked together, the views clash and the scene warps. MoRe needs no new training, which makes it easy to add to existing tools.

The method first matches points that appear in more than one frame. It then adjusts the views so the matched points line up. A graph-based step refines both the points and the surface angles at once. Local flat patches guide that step and keep the scene shape intact. Tests showed cleaner 3D rebuilds from photo sets. The aligned scenes also rendered new views better when few photos were on hand. Better depth from plain cameras helps robots and phones alike.
arxiv-2510-07619:
Buyukdagli wrote this 2025 physics paper on electrolytes, the charged solutions found in batteries and living cells. Ions in these liquids attract or repel each other electrically. They also have real size, so they cannot overlap. Earlier theories often handled charge and size separately. Buyukdagli builds one framework that treats both effects together from the start.

The theory predicts how ion pairs are arranged at concentrations up to about two moles per liter. Its results match recent computer simulations with quantitative precision. It also reproduces the measured osmotic behavior of several water-based and non-water solutions. One clear finding is that strong ion pairing stays confined to dilute non-water solutions. At higher concentrations, crowding blocks pairs from forming. The work links solvent polarity and ion size to when pairing can occur. That boundary gives experimenters a clear, testable prediction.
arxiv-2510-07719:
Tian, Yousefijamarani, and Alameldeen wrote this 2025 computer architecture paper on processing-in-memory systems. Such systems place processors inside memory to avoid hauling data back and forth. The savings vanish when the needed data sits in a remote memory module. The authors show that remote transfers and queuing delays dominate the cost of memory requests. Their fix focuses on keeping data close to the processor that uses it.

Their design, DL-PIM, watches for movement overhead and moves hot data into a reserved local area. A hardware lookup table redirects requests to the data's current home. Because redirection itself costs time, an adaptive switch turns it off for workloads it would hurt. On two stacked memory designs, request latency fell by about half. Workloads with data reuse gained the most speed. The study gives memory architects a way to protect the promise of processing in memory.
arxiv-2510-08019:
Srivastava and Shukla wrote this 2025 nuclear theory paper on collectivity and long-lived excited states in lead isotopes. Lead nuclei sit at a famous shell closure, so their ground states stay spherical. Yet competing motions inside them produce coexisting shapes at low energy. The authors study even-even lead isotopes from mass 196 to 206. They run nuclear shell-model calculations with the KHH7B effective interaction across a fourteen-orbital model space.

The calculations report energy spectra for the isotope chain. They also give electromagnetic properties, which probe how charge and current are distributed and how states decay. Isomeric states, the long-lived excited configurations, receive dedicated results. The authors position the work as a reference for experiments still to come. Upcoming measurements can test these predictions directly. Reliable structure predictions also feed weak-interaction studies, where decay rates depend sensitively on the wave functions involved.
arxiv-2510-08219:
