Hoffmann, Laguna, Vandenhirtz, Palumbo, and Vogt wrote this 2025 machine learning paper upgrading interpretable concept bottleneck models after training, without touching their weights. These models predict through human-understandable concepts, letting users correct a wrong concept and fix the final answer. Modeling dependencies between concepts improves corrections, but existing methods retrain everything. The authors instead bolt on a small module predicting a covariance over concepts. Two training strategies for the module are proposed.

On real-world data, the upgraded models matched or beat standard bottleneck models in concept and target accuracy. Under interventions they adapted much faster than the originals, though not as fast as a fully retrained stochastic model. Disabling the module restores the original predictions exactly. That reversibility matters in regulated settings like healthcare, where an approved model cannot simply be retrained. Interpretability upgrades can be cheap add-ons rather than rebuilds.
arxiv-2510-08419:
Xi Huang, Lixing Zhang, and Di Luo design a protocol that learns quantum Hamiltonians at the best possible precision in a 2025 arXiv paper. A Hamiltonian encodes a system's energy and drives how it evolves over time. Continuous-variable systems, like light modes, live in infinite-dimensional spaces with unbounded operators. That makes learning their Hamiltonians hard, and past Heisenberg-limit protocols needed special structures or tough resources.

Their method, D-RUT, applies displacement steps mixed with random unitary transformations. It learns the coefficients of general bosonic Hamiltonians of any finite order. Total evolution time grows only in proportion to the inverse of the target error, the Heisenberg scaling. The scheme stays robust to state preparation and measurement errors, they show. For multi-mode systems, a hierarchical recovery strategy improves statistical efficiency further. An extension learns parameters of position-momentum Hamiltonians in first quantization.
arxiv-2510-08619:
Tennison Liu and co-authors set swarms of AI research agents loose to hunt hypotheses in large data sets in a 2025 arXiv paper. Modern biobanks, cell atlases, and Earth data sets invite open-ended exploration, unconstrained by preset questions. They call this hypothesis hunting: cumulative searching across vast hypothesis spaces. Their framework, AScience, models discovery as agents, networks, and evaluation norms interacting.

The implementation, ASCollab, is a distributed system of language-model research agents with heterogeneous behaviors. Agents self-organize into evolving networks, producing findings and peer-reviewing them against shared standards. Experiments showed these social dynamics accumulate expert-rated results along diversity, quality, and novelty fronts. Successes included rediscovering established biomarkers, extending known pathways, and proposing new therapeutic targets. Cancer cohort experiments demonstrated the approach, though wet-lab validation remains indispensable, they stress.
arxiv-2510-08719:
Debjyoti Biswas and Prabha Mandayam bring syndrome measurements to noise-adapted quantum error correction in a 2025 arXiv paper. Standard error correction reads syndromes that pinpoint error type and location cleanly. Approximate, noise-adapted schemes instead use tailored recovery maps like the Petz map, which are hard to implement in hardware. The authors propose an algorithm that identifies error syndromes for any code and any noise process.

With syndromes in hand, they build a syndrome-based variant of the Petz recovery map, implementable through ordinary syndrome measurements. They demonstrate the approach on amplitude-damping noise with the four-qubit code. Recovery circuits ran on IBM quantum hardware in their experiments. The protocol achieved break-even performance, a key practical threshold for error correction. Qubit lifetimes, measured by T1 times, improved up to threefold under the scheme.
arxiv-2510-09019:
Achasov and the SND collaboration report the most precise measurement yet of a rare particle decay channel, in this 2025 arXiv paper. At the VEPP-2000 collider in Russia, electrons and positrons annihilate at energies near the phi meson, a short-lived particle. Sometimes the outcome is an eta meson plus a photon. That channel tests theories of how quarks bind at low energy, but it is faint and hard to measure cleanly.

The team analyzed collisions recorded in 2018 and 2024, catching the eta through its decay into two photons. Their measured rate for the process is the most accurate to date and sits higher than earlier experiments found. Fitting the energy dependence with a standard model of meson dominance extracted a product of two branching fractions, the chances of the phi decaying to electrons and to the eta-photon pair. Such numbers feed tests of quark-model predictions and flavor symmetry.
arxiv-2510-09319:
Manisha Kumari and Dinesh Kumar write a 2025 arXiv paper in complex dynamics, the study of how repeated functions behave. They work with a transcendental semigroup, a family of very fast-growing functions combined under composition. For one such function, earlier work defined the bungee set and its companion, the filled Julia set, which sort starting points by how their paths wander, escape, or stay bounded.

The authors carry those ideas over to whole semigroups and generalise many single-function results. For semigroups without a certain wandering region, they give conditions that place the bungee set inside the Julia set. They also study the filled Julia set and the escaping set in this wider setting. Special cases include conjugate semigroups and abelian ones, where the order of applying functions does not matter. New features of the escaping set appear along the way.
arxiv-2510-09419:
María Hernández Ruiz, Christopher Kiehl, Vito Giovanni Lucivero, and Morgan Mitchell use a sensitive magnetometer to watch bacteria in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their instrument is a light-pumped magnetometer read out with the Pound-Drever-Hall technique, a laser method that tracks tiny magnetic changes. Magnetotactic bacteria are microbes that align with magnetic fields thanks to internal magnetic particles.

The team reports a noise floor set by photon shot noise, plus short-term and long-term stability figures. They then point it at a dense mixture of the bacterium Magnetospirillum gryphiswaldense. The bacteria's relaxation after a field change did not follow the simple smooth pattern on second timescales. Those breaks reveal the spread of magnetic moments and spin drag across the population, and both changed as drying and settling crowded the sample. The authors say such direct views of these uneven traits are new.
arxiv-2510-09519:
Veronica Rammouz and five co-authors, among them Anthony Rios, ask whether model rankings without labelled data can be trusted, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Practitioners often need to know how a language or classification model will perform in a new domain before paying for labels. Earlier estimation methods used dataset similarity or predicted correctness, but it was unclear when their rankings match reality.

The authors run a two-step evaluation: four base classifiers, plus several large language models acting as error predictors. Experiments on two datasets, GeoOLID and Amazon Reviews, spanning fifteen domains, show that error predictors built on large models give rank correlations with true accuracy that are stronger and more consistent. Two conditions govern reliability: rankings are safer when true performance gaps between domains are large. They also depend on whether the error model's predictions line up with the base model's real failure patterns.
arxiv-2510-09819:
Sar and co-authors review swarmalators in this 2025 arXiv paper on collective behavior. A swarmalator is an agent that both swarms, moving with a group, and oscillates, keeping an internal rhythm like a flashing firefly. The review gathers work on how spatial grouping and timing sync shape each other in such systems.

The authors survey models and results across the young field, tracing how order in space and order in time can boost or block each other. They cover the main theory and point to uses where swarming and syncing meet, such as groups of robots or networks of oscillators. The paper maps what is known so far and where the open questions lie.
arxiv-2510-10219:
Li, Lizy K. John, and Neeraja J. Yadwadkar present Exgen-Malloc in this 2025 arXiv paper on systems software. Memory allocators sit beneath nearly every program, handing out and reclaiming memory. Small inefficiencies in them ripple through caches and the memory hierarchy, a cost operators call the datacenter tax.

The authors optimize single-threaded applications with their allocator design. Even programs that use one thread pay allocator overhead on every allocation. Exgen-Malloc aims to cut that overhead where it is paid most often. The title's claim is that old, well-understood components still hide real wins: careful allocator engineering can speed up whole application stacks without changing any application code.
arxiv-2510-10319:
Ianconescu and co-authors question intermediate tracing in quantum interactions in this 2025 arXiv paper in quantum physics. When separately prepared quantum systems interact, standard practice tensors their density matrices together and applies Hamiltonians on the joint system. The paper asks whether a common shortcut in that computation is valid.

Intermediate tracing means summing over part of the system before the interaction finishes. The authors examine when that step gives the measurable results correctly and when it misleads. Getting this right matters for any experiment with many interacting quantum systems, from quantum optics to quantum computing. A wrong intermediate step can quietly corrupt predictions that experiments then test.
arxiv-2510-10619:
Maximos Kaliakatsos-Papakostas and five co-authors teach a machine learning system to turn MIDI files into guitar tablature, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Tablature tells the player which string and fret to use for each note. A good assignment stays playable across the whole track and keeps finger motion economical. Guitar styles have also developed standard fingerings for common chord shapes, which a transcription should respect. The team's method takes only the MIDI part, possibly with several polyphonic tracks, as input.

The system assumes a limit on how far fingers can stretch and covers standard six string tuning only. It also tackles pieces never meant for guitar, even orchestral parts, by augmenting the musical information and training on artificial data. Results show that training with augmented data improves performance even on simple monophonic cases. The authors also report the system's weaknesses and possible improvements.
arxiv-2510-10819:
Vivek Acharya surveys how generative AI is transforming software development practice, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Large language models now support new development styles. These include chat oriented programming, where developers converse with a model, and vibe coding, where they steer by feel. They also include agentic programming, where autonomous agents carry out tasks. These styles can accelerate work and broaden who can code. Acharya examines the techniques and the issues of trust, accountability, and shifting skills that come with them.

The survey covers iterative chat based development, multi agent systems, dynamic prompt orchestration, and integration through the Model Context Protocol, a standard for connecting models to tools. Drawing on case studies and industry data, he weighs opportunities such as faster cycles and democratized coding against challenges like reliability and cost. He also describes new roles and best practices for using AI responsibly in software teams.
arxiv-2510-10919:
Alice Ho and four co-authors derive universal limits for two resistances that increasingly bottleneck tiny electronic devices, in this 2025 arXiv paper. As devices shrink toward atomic scales, electrical contact resistance and thermal boundary resistance dominate energy loss. Future devices will mix materials with varied band structures, from parabolic to conical, in wires, sheets, and bulk forms. The team derives a single general expression for the quantum limit of electrical contact resistivity covering all these cases.

A corresponding result gives the quantum limit of thermal boundary resistance. These limits are the best any contact or interface could ever do, set by quantum mechanics rather than by engineering. The authors offer the formulas to co-design devices, benchmark real contacts against the ideal, and guide efforts to lower these resistances. Knowing the limit focuses research where gains remain.
arxiv-2510-11019:
Bingjie Tang and nine co-authors close the gap between robot assembly in simulation and industry grade reliability, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Policies learned in simulation reach about 80 percent success on precise, contact rich assembly, but performance swings wildly with initial conditions, and chaining such policies breaks down. Their Refinery framework attacks both problems. Bayesian optimization guides fine tuning of individual policies. At deployment, a Gaussian mixture model samples starting configurations that are likely to succeed.

The combined approach raised mean success rates by 10.98 percent over state of the art simulation learning methods for robotic assembly, reaching 91.51 percent in simulation with comparable performance on real hardware in the reported experiments. The team then chained the refined policies to assemble products of up to eight parts, without any explicit multi step training.
arxiv-2510-11219:
When hadrons collide, the number of particles produced varies from event to event, and part of that variation is quantum in origin rather than geometric. S. M. Troshin and N. E. Tyurin examine those quantum multiplicity fluctuations in this 2025 arXiv high-energy physics paper. They separate variation caused by the varying impact parameter from quantum fluctuations at fixed impact parameter.

At LHC energies the interaction region is turning from a black disk into a black ring with a reflective inner area, measurements at 13 TeV indicate. As scattering enters this reflective mode, the quantum fluctuations become the dominant source of event-by-event multiplicity variation. The range for impact parameter variation shrinks. The authors note that spotting these quantum fluctuations in experiments at finite energies is feasible, which would test the reflective scattering picture.
arxiv-2510-11619:
Materials that are both magnetic and electrically polarized are rare, because ferroelectricity and magnetism demand conflicting electronic structures. Y. Sun and co-authors create such a multiferroic by straining a helimagnet in this 2025 arXiv condensed matter paper. Their material is Cr1/3NbS2, whose spins form a spiral; the spiral alone is nonpolar, but strain can generate it in such hosts.

To detect the induced polarization they introduce magnetoelectric birefringence, an optical probe that images polar order with spatial resolution and little doubt. The probe reads it out by light, without electrical contacts. Combining that imaging with strain engineering, they confirm a polar vector switches on at the magnetic transition temperature. This establishes strained Cr1/3NbS2 as a type-II multiferroic. In such a material magnetism itself creates the polarization, and the two orders are strongly coupled. The route is general: strain can write polarity into many spiral magnets.
arxiv-2510-11919:
Armel Zebaze, Rachel Bawden, and Benoît Sagot test whether thinking out loud helps machines translate. Large reasoning models generate intermediate thought tokens before answering, which boosts their math and coding. Translation, though, might work differently. Their 2025 arXiv paper tries reasoning models on many language pairs, from well-resourced to scarce, in several configurations.

The headline result is negative: thinking tokens do not improve translation quality. Fine-tuning a model on synthetic step-by-step explanations, distilled from a teacher in the style of human translators, also fails to beat plain input-output training. One recipe does help: building the intermediate tokens from modular, translation-specific prompting strategies that contain actual translation attempts. The broader lesson follows. For translation, a teacher's effort is better spent refining target translations or expanding parallel corpora than on narrating its reasoning for students to imitate.
arxiv-2510-12019:
Lily Whitler and seven colleagues test whether a giant bubble of ionized gas existed when the universe was still mostly neutral. At redshift eight point seven, Lyman-alpha light should mostly be swallowed by neutral hydrogen. Galaxies shining through suggest ionized bubbles of their own making. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses deep JWST spectroscopy in the EGS field to measure one candidate bubble.

The field is genuinely crowded. Its galaxy density runs about three times the average, enough to carve a two-megaparsec bubble. Yet the measured Lyman-alpha transmission is modest, around a quarter. That matches the cosmic average at that epoch, not the high transmission a two-megaparsec bubble would allow. The team concludes such a large bubble is unlikely here. Smaller bubbles, half to one megaparsec across, fit both observations.
arxiv-2510-12219:
Khuong and co-authors propose DIANet, a network for recognizing micro expressions, in a 2025 arXiv computer vision paper presented at an IJCAI workshop. Micro expressions are brief involuntary facial movements, lasting under half a second, that can reveal genuine emotion. Reading them matters for psychology and security, but their subtlety and the scarcity of labeled data make recognition hard.

Dynamic images summarize the motion of a short clip in a single frame, yet earlier methods ignored that a micro expression has distinct phases. DIANet uses two streams, one encoding the movement from onset to apex and the other from apex to offset. Each stream has its own convolutional network, and a cross attention module merges their features according to context. On the CASME II, SAMM, and MMEW benchmark datasets, DIANet consistently beat conventional single phase dynamic image approaches.
arxiv-2510-12319:
Pérez surveys a three decade program, joint with Meeks and Ros, classifying minimal surfaces of finite genus, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics article following his ICM invited talk. Minimal surfaces are surfaces that locally minimize area, like soap films. The program studies complete, properly embedded examples in ordinary three dimensional space, where topology can be rich yet tame.

The article explains a four step classification of embedded minimal surfaces with genus zero and infinitely many ends. The steps cover the periodic case, quasi periodicity for two limit ends, and nonexistence of one limit end examples. It then reviews lamination techniques, which study surfaces through their limit leaves. A dynamics theorem, bounds linking topology and index, and a settlement of the embedded Calabi Yau problem for the finite genus case follow. Open problems close the survey.
arxiv-2510-13219:
Xiao and a large team survey prompt-based adaptation of vision models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Visual prompting and visual prompt tuning both adapt huge pretrained vision models cheaply, by adding small learned inputs rather than retraining everything. The literature uses the two terms interchangeably, though, and their boundaries have blurred. The survey aims to separate them cleanly.

Revisiting both designs from first principles, the authors unify them under one framework called prompt-based adaptation. Their taxonomy splits methods into learnable, generative, and non-learnable prompts, and further by injection granularity, pixel-level versus token-level. The survey then examines integrations across medical imaging, three-dimensional point clouds, and vision-language tasks, plus roles in test-time adaptation and trustworthy AI. Benchmarks, open challenges, and future directions are summarized, with a maintained repository listing methods for practitioners.
arxiv-2510-13519:
Marraffa and co-authors reduce large recurrent neural networks to small models that expose their core dynamics. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies networks used in neuroscience to mimic collective neuron activity. These networks live in huge parameter and activity spaces, which hides how they compute. The team turns to spectral submanifolds, low-dimensional surfaces that attract the network's motion.

By fitting these surfaces from data, they shrink each network's dynamics by orders of magnitude. The reduced models then give precise definitions of line and ring attractors. Neuroscientists use those attractor ideas loosely to explain decisions and working memory. Making them exact turns vague pictures into testable mathematical objects. The authors argue this clarity yields fresh predictions about the neural computations behind behaviour. Several contemporary neuroscience networks serve as their test cases.
arxiv-2510-13719:
Vijarnwannaluk and a large team measure the shapes and sizes of galaxies hosting active black holes, using JWST images. Their 2025 arXiv paper draws on the COSMOS-Web survey's sharp near-infrared views. The sample holds 690 moderate-luminosity active nuclei across redshifts zero to three. Host sizes and shapes test whether mergers trigger black hole growth.

The hosts' light spans effective radii of roughly one to five kiloparsecs. That range sits between star-forming and quiescent galaxies of the same mass. Hosts shrink toward higher redshift, as other galaxies do. Their size grows with mass more steeply than for star-forming galaxies, though. Shape measures reveal a strong spheroidal, bulge-like component in most hosts. Only about six percent show signs of merging, while disks, bars, and spiral arms appear in leftover light. That low merger share strains theories needing major mergers to light up black holes.
arxiv-2510-13819:
Stamatelis, Chen, Wymeersch, and Alexandropoulos localize a wireless user by jointly steering a smart surface and the user's transmit power. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses a reconfigurable intelligent surface, a wall of tunable reflectors aiding the base station. Real surfaces offer only discrete phase settings, making configuration a hard combinatorial problem. A feedback link lets the base station also coach the user's power level.

Their multi-agent algorithm mixes neuroevolution with supervised learning to run both controls. Neuroevolution evolves neural policies without gradients, suiting the non-smooth hardware constraints. Power control needs just single-bit feedback messages sent back to the user. Simulations show the scheme beating fingerprinting and deep reinforcement learning baselines. It also outperforms position estimators trained by plain backpropagation. Handling realistic discrete surface elements is a core design goal throughout.
arxiv-2510-13919:
Hrishikesh Jagtap and Moumanti Podder study a two-player game on directed graphs in this 2025 arXiv paper. In a Maker-Breaker game, one player claims unclaimed edges hoping to complete a target shape, while the other claims edges to block her. Here the board is a tournament, a complete directed graph, and the target shape is a directed triangle, meaning three edges forming a cycle.

On a special parity tournament, the authors find an exact threshold at seven vertices, with Breaker winning below that size and Maker winning from seven upward. For a biased version where Breaker claims extra edges each round, they bound the critical bias between two square-root growth rates. On random tournaments, Maker wins with probability approaching certainty as the board grows, and a new flip-budget variant has a threshold growing with the square of the board size.
arxiv-2510-14219:
Young and a large collaboration report the design and performance of the cryostat that cools the SPT-SLIM receiver, a millimeter-wavelength mapping instrument on the South Pole Telescope, in this 2025 arXiv paper. SPT-SLIM is a pathfinder experiment for on-chip spectrometer technology for line intensity mapping, a way to chart the universe's structure through faint spectral lines.

The receiver's focal plane of superconducting filterbank spectrometers must sit about a seventh of a degree above absolute zero, held there by an adiabatic demagnetization refrigerator, a magnetic cooling device. The team shows stable thermal performance of the focal plane module during the first season, matching thermal modeling. It enables a cryogenic efficiency above eighty percent. They also describe the receiver control system, built on the Observatory Control System platform, which handles cryogenic running at the remote polar site.
arxiv-2510-14319:
Xu Shen and co-authors present MASC, a metacognitive watchdog that catches and corrects errors inside multi-agent language-model systems before they cascade, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In these systems a faulty step can propagate across agents and derail the trajectory, yet the agents rarely notice.

MASC reframes detection as anomaly scoring conditioned on history. It predicts the embedding of the next step from the query and interaction history, so steps that break causal consistency stand out. It steadies those predictions with a prototype of what normal steps look like. That helps when context is sparse at the start. When a step is flagged, a correction agent revises the agent's output before the error flows downstream. On the Who&When benchmark of agent failures, MASC beat baselines at step-level error detection, and plugging it into multi-agent frameworks delivered end-to-end gains with low overhead.
arxiv-2510-14419:
Tapio Pahikkala and co-authors introduce the interaction concordance index, a measure for methods predicting how pairs of entities interact, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their example is drug-target affinity: two drugs and two targets interact when swapping the pairings changes the effect. Capturing those effects improves decisions such as allocating drug doses to their best targets.

Metrics score affinity values but not whether the model gets the direction of effects right. The index measures the share of predicted effect directions in the data, for both fixed predictors and learning algorithms. The authors show the index is invariant for predictors that cannot capture interactions. Such models cannot score unfairly well. They also develop the theory for learning effect directions from affinities. These can be used alone or together with side information such as chemical structures. The index complements the estimators by grading the skill that decisions depend on.
arxiv-2510-14519:
David Dougan and co-authors calculate how readily lead ions in several charge states absorb light, supplying atomic data needed to model the atmospheres of subdwarf stars, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Spectra of subdwarf stars show high lead abundances, but interpreting them requires photoionization cross sections, the probabilities that photons knock electrons off lead ions, which were missing.

The team developed four structures with a relativistic atomic structure package, checking that their energy levels, transition rates, and oscillator strengths agree with experimental and theoretical sources. Photoionization cross sections computed with Dirac atomic R-matrix codes are released in a database format and follow the trends across the ion series. As a test case, modeling the helium-rich hot subdwarf EC 22536-5304 shows differences in lead line profiles. The differences appear between the standard equilibrium assumption and the realistic non-equilibrium treatment the new data enable, in both ultraviolet and optical light.
arxiv-2510-14719:
Chen and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a compiler that writes expert-level graphics processor code automatically. Modern GPUs contain specialized units that reward a style called warp specialization, where different thread groups take producer and consumer roles in an asynchronous pipeline. Programming this way by hand means orchestrating low-level communication in detail. It is slow, error-prone work that few teams can sustain.

Their compiler, Tawa, starts from a high-level tile-based program. Its key abstraction, asynchronous references, expresses communication between warps without exposing hardware details. Tawa then splits the program into producer and consumer roles and manages the dataflow pipeline itself. On NVIDIA H100 hardware, Tawa reached up to 1.1 times the speed of the tuned cuBLAS library for matrix multiplication in the reported tests. For attention workloads it beat Triton and matched a hand-optimized kernel, with far less effort.
arxiv-2510-14919:
Montgomery and co-authors extend scaling laws, in a 2025 arXiv paper, so they predict not just training loss but actual task performance, which depends heavily on context. Classic scaling laws link cross-entropy loss to model size, data, and compute, yet they say little about downstream tasks, where the prompt and context matter enormously. The authors propose an interpretable formula that models performance jointly from training compute and context length.

They fit it on Llama-2-7B and Llama-2-13B with extended context, across sixty-five thousand instances spanning arithmetic, common sense, and translation tasks. The fitted law modeled in-distribution performance accurately. It generalized across three orders of magnitude in training compute, a thousandfold range. And it extrapolated how performance improves as more context is supplied. The authors offer the law as guidance: it clarifies how training compute and context use trade off, helping builders design long-context models efficiently.
arxiv-2510-15219:
Patricia Medina and Rasika Karkare continue their work on teaching computers to sort 3D LiDAR scans into object classes, in this 2025 arXiv paper, the second part of a series. LiDAR sensors map scenes as clouds of points, and classifiers must decide what each region is. The pair add product coefficients, mathematical descriptors drawn from measure theory, alongside the raw spatial features.

This follow-up pairs those coefficients with an autoencoder, a network that compresses data into a compact code, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier. The combination gave steady gains over baselines built on principal component analysis and over the authors' own earlier framework. Adding the coefficients level by level helped in a clear pattern: richer sets separated the classes better and lifted overall accuracy. Medina and Karkare present the trend as evidence that layered geometric descriptors and learned compression work well together.
arxiv-2510-15419:
Hrithik Barman studies tiny self-propelled particles that swim in circles while held inside a soft trap, in this solo 2025 arXiv paper. Such chiral active particles model bacteria and synthetic microswimmers that burn energy to move. The trap is harmonic, pulling the particle back toward the center like a spring, and the question is what steady behavior emerges from the two competing tendencies.

Barman finds that circling motion creates oscillating cross-correlations between the particle's position components, which vanish when the circling torque is switched off. The trap also produces a finite delay between the particle's orientation and its velocity, a fingerprint of broken time-reversal symmetry that differs from ordinary inertia effects. The long-run position distribution looks strongly non-Maxwellian. Weak confinement spreads it into broad rings, while strong confinement squeezes it into compact peaks. Trap strength and rotational noise set the delay's depth.
arxiv-2510-15819:
Rihui Lan and Jorge Reyes add a conservation-friendly formulation to a turbulence model to gain accuracy over long times. The Ladyzhenskaya model is a large-eddy simulation of incompressible flow, used where direct simulation is too costly. The EMAC formulation keeps energy and both momenta conserved even when incompressibility is enforced only weakly, and it has beaten the popular skew-symmetric form in direct and regularised settings.

Joining EMAC to the model also addresses the excess dissipation known from the classical Smagorinsky model. Lan and Reyes build a finite element scheme for the combined system, prove stability, and derive error estimates. Long-time behaviour improves over the standard model, largely because the growth constant no longer depends on the Reynolds number. Benchmark runs show sharper flow structures, above all at high Reynolds numbers.
arxiv-2510-15919:
Neil J. Calkin, Robert M. Corless, Laureano Gonzalez-Vega, J. Rafael Sendra, and Juana Sendra attack a conjecture about how far apart the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix can spread. The spread is the largest distance between any two eigenvalues. The conjecture, from Fallat and Xing, says the maximum spread over all symmetric matrices with entries in an interval is reached by a rank-two matrix using only the interval's endpoints.

Zhan had already proved the symmetric interval case. The five authors reinterpret the problem geometrically through polynomial resultants, which turns the conjecture into something computation can grip. With that view they prove the conjecture for several cases that were formerly open. The work links eigenvalue spread, a purely spectral quantity, to algebraic geometry tools that can certify extremal matrices.
arxiv-2510-16119:
Gauhar Abbas and Vartika Singh take a fresh run at a stubborn math problem in particle theory. The problem is a correction term for how tau particles, heavy cousins of the electron, break down into lighter debris. Theory writes this term as a long sum that grows less and less steady, so its true value stays fuzzy.

The pair use Levin-type sequence transforms, a trick that speeds up slow sums by smart guessing at their limit. Their method settles into a stable value near 0.209 for the key correction, in line with past work. It also predicts three higher terms of the sum that no one had pinned down. The result shows these transforms are a sharp tool for handling wild theory sums in general.
arxiv-2510-16319:
Rui Yang and four co-authors generate sketches that copy not just a picture's content but the hand of a reference artist. Faithful style transfer for drawing means carrying over stroke qualities like line thickness, wobble, and texture sparsity while keeping the subject intact, a finer demand than most style methods handle.

Stroke2Sketch needs no training. Its cross-image stroke attention, inserted into the self-attention layers of a generative model, builds fine-grained correspondences between content and reference so stroke attributes land in the right places. Adaptive contrast enhancement and semantic-focused attention reinforce the subject and foreground. The authors report sketches that look handcrafted, beating earlier methods on expressive stroke control and semantic coherence, and they release the code publicly.
arxiv-2510-16419:
Jiayi Guo, Haoxuan Li, Ye Tian, and Peng Wu take up a fair-test problem in their 2025 paper. Drugs and plans can help some people more than others. Tools that guess who gains most are hard to score, since true gains stay hidden. Their frame scores two such tools by the gap in their errors, not by raw error.

They work out when that gap score can be trusted. A neural net, a learned web of weights, then learns the side facts the score needs. Tests show the frame ranks tools in a sound way. The same net also trains a new tool that does well. Fair tests help doctors pick the right tool for care.
arxiv-2510-16619:
I. M. Moiseenko, D. A. Svintsov, and Zh. A. Devizorova study light drag in a thin electron sheet in 2025. Photon drag makes a current when light hits a sample. It can sense light very fast, but in bulk samples the effect is weak. A metal gate edge above the sheet bends the light field sharply. That bend should boost the drag a lot.

They solve the exact light scatter task for a half-gated sheet. Two scaled values rule the size of the drag reply. Gated plasmons, waves of charge under the gate, drive the reply. Plasmons are joint waves of charge and light in a sheet. The drag push under the gate runs one way at all sheet states. That way is the reverse of the push at a side contact.
arxiv-2510-16819:
Shantanu Agarwal, Joel Barry, Steven Fincke, and Scott Miller tackle a hard authorship puzzle in their 2025 study. Authorship attribution means naming who most likely wrote a text. Their case is harder because the test text comes from a different genre. A system must ignore topic clues and read writing style instead.

Their method works in two stages, first retrieving candidates and then reranking them. Ordinary reranking training, they show, teaches the wrong lessons for style. So they build training data that forces the model to learn author habits. On two tough benchmark sets, scores jump far past earlier systems. The gains matter for cases like disputed or anonymous writing.
arxiv-2510-16919:
Christian Baer and Lashi Bandara wrote a user's guide to boundary problems in a 2025 paper. The topic is first-order elliptic operators on spaces with edges. Such operators appear throughout geometry and topology. Boundary conditions say what solutions may do at the edge.

The guide explains existence, smoothness, and Fredholm behavior in plain sequence. Fredholm behavior means the problem has finitely many obstructions and free parameters. The authors cover a very general class of boundary conditions. One special family within it yields the relative index theorem. They also give a new description of one useful subclass. The aim is practical: researchers can pick up operator methods confidently. Worked structure replaces the usual scattered folklore about these problems.
arxiv-2510-17319:
Solving heat like equations on oddly shaped regions is hard, because the boundary itself resists neat maths. Yuejin Xu, writing alone, studies the diffuse domain method for a class of such problems with a boundary rule named after Neumann. The method blurs the sharp edge of the region into a thin layer, described by a smooth function that marks inside and outside.

With the blurred edge, the problem moves onto a larger rectangle that is far easier to handle. Xu proves that as the layer thickness shrinks toward zero, the computed solution moves toward the exact one. He also derives best possible error bounds and runs numerical tests that back the theory.
arxiv-2510-17419:
Jennifer Bartlett, with Alfie Myers Wilson and two co-authors, studies a flaw in quantum key sharing in a 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum key distribution lets two people build a secret key using light signals. In this design, sender and receiver use their own lasers, so their signals drift apart in phase, meaning wave timing.

A helper signal lets the receiver measure and correct that drift. The team found that uneven response in the light detector skews this measure. Skewed measures shorten the distance over which keys can be shared safely. The authors propose a fix for the uneven response. They also check the effect with a method that maps the full state of the light.
arxiv-2510-18119:
R Abbasi, with four hundred thirty-two co-authors from the IceCube effort, tests whether high-energy neutrinos line up with the nearby cosmic web. The South Pole observatory sees space neutrinos arriving almost evenly from all directions, and only a small share match known sources. Since such neutrinos are born in violent places fed by collapsing matter, their sources should trace large-scale structure.

Northern sky track events are cross-matched with an infrared galaxy catalog built from two sky surveys. No significant clustering signal appears. The null result still narrows where the mystery sources can hide in distance and in kind.
arxiv-2510-18519:
Md Arafat Hossain and his five co-authors improve tests for business software. Such software leans on outside services. When real services are out of reach, testers fake them. They build the fakes from recorded message exchanges. Most fakes ignore the service's inner state. Their replies drift from what the real service would say. The drift is worst when replies depend on past messages.

The new approach mines the recorded traffic for context. It finds which past messages a reply depends on. It maps how data values relate to each other. Models built this way respect the service's state. The team tested the method on real traces. The traces came from stateful and stateless services alike. Response accuracy rose in a clear way. So did the speed of response generation. The test setup became much more realistic.
arxiv-2510-18819:
Neel Patel, Alexander Wong, and Ashkan Ebadi build an explainable AI system for detecting tuberculosis on chest X-rays. Tuberculosis still burdens regions with few radiologists, so screening tools matter, but training them needs large labeled data sets that are expensive to gather. Their teacher-student framework combines two supervised heads with a self-supervised head to improve both disease detection and symptom detection at once.

The system distinguished COVID-19, tuberculosis, and normal cases with accuracy near ninety-nine percent, and it labeled multiple symptoms with a macro-averaged score near ninety percent, clearly beating baselines. Just as important for clinical trust, explainability checks showed the model's decisions rested on relevant anatomical features rather than on stray artifacts. The authors present the framework as promising for screening and triage in settings where specialist readers are scarce.
arxiv-2510-18919:
Wei Dai, Su Gao, and Víctor Hugo Yañez examine which isometry groups and countable groups have the Lévy property. A group has that property when a dense part of it can be built from a growing chain of compact subgroups that show a strong form of measure concentration.

The authors give several new classes with the stronger version, where the subgroups in the chain are finite. Their cases include isometry groups of certain Urysohn metric spaces and groups tied to Lipschitz maps. The work widens the known map of groups where this concentration behavior can be proved.
arxiv-2510-19119:
Ahmed Sayeed Faruk, Mohammad Shahverdikondori, and Elena Zheleva learn peer influence probabilities with linear contextual bandits, modeling how likely one person is to act on another's recommendation. Influence depends on who sends and who receives, their relationship, the item itself, and the setting, so a single average rate misleads.

Static data can confuse correlation with real influence, making the learning problem hard. A bandit approach gathers evidence through action, adapting estimates as context changes. Better influence estimates help explain how information spreads and make viral marketing spend its effort where recommendations actually change behavior.
arxiv-2510-19219:
Lei Xu and Ling Wang propose a symmetry-adapted solver for strongly correlated quantum systems that separates where a wave function is sampled from where it is defined. Parallel quantum circuits handle entanglement inside blocks of a lattice, while a matrix product backbone links the blocks and restores global correlations.

Configurations are drawn directly from the sampled amplitudes, block by block, with no Markov chain needed. The variational state itself lives in a symmetry-adapted basis, where each class of equivalent configurations gathers its total weight. Mixing quantum circuits, tensor networks, and symmetry in this way targets accurate energies for hard materials.
arxiv-2510-19419:
Yuan Gao and four co-authors introduce BLiSS, a benchmark for judging how small language models handle the language of bilingual learners. Standard tests reward raw performance, while teachers care whether a model tolerates natural learner errors more than artificial ones, a distinction the authors call selective tolerance.

Built from millions of natural learner sentences, the benchmark holds well over one hundred thousand controlled triplets: a corrected sentence, the learner's version, and a matched artificial error. Models cluster strongly by how they were trained, showing selective tolerance is a skill of its own, separate from plain grammaticality judgments.
arxiv-2510-19519:
O. O. Svystunov and four co-authors compare grating shapes for dielectric laser accelerators, tiny on-chip structures that use laser light to accelerate particles. The study covers transparent structures with a rectangular profile and triangular profiles at ridge base angles of thirty-six, thirty, and twenty degrees. Each triangular shape was tested facing both left and right.

For every shape, the team also tried a version coated with reflective gold. They measured the maximum energy gains and accelerating gradients for all variants, transparent and reflective alike. The comparison shows how profile geometry and coating choice affect the strength of these miniature accelerators.
arxiv-2510-19719:
I. Juanikorena Berasategi and three co-authors model how magnetic fields shape the polarization of calcium lines in the Sun's atmosphere. The Ca II H and K resonance lines and the infrared triplet are key tools for measuring chromospheric magnetism, but their polarized profiles depend on subtle atomic physics. Using a spectral synthesis code on a static model atmosphere, the team includes anisotropic radiation pumping, partial frequency redistribution, and interference between atomic levels.

Each effect matters in a different part of the line profile, from the core to the far wings. The resonant lines respond to horizontal fields from below one gauss to tens of gauss, while the triplet's scattering polarization senses far weaker fields. The results guide how observers should read these lines to infer the Sun's magnetic field.
arxiv-2510-19919:
Margot Leemker and six co-authors use heavy water to ask whether the water in planet-forming disks is inherited from interstellar space or destroyed and remade locally. Doubly deuterated water is the tracer: its abundance records the cold chemistry of a molecule's past. The team measured it in the disk around the outbursting young star V883 Orionis.

The ratio of heavy to ordinary water matches values in protostellar envelopes and in a comet, and sits about a hundred times above what local reprocessing would produce. A second ratio among the deuterated forms reinforces the conclusion. The water ice in disks, the authors argue, largely survives from the earliest phases of star formation, linking cold dark clouds chemically to comets and planets.
arxiv-2510-20819:
Nimrod Berman, Omkar Joglekar, Eitan Kosman, Dotan Di Castro, and Omri Azencot propose a general method for translating between data types such as images and audio without bespoke designs for each pair. Prior translation methods often demand matched sizes, bell shaped source priors, or a fresh architecture per modality.

Their Latent Denoising Diffusion Bridge Model works in a shared hidden space, learning a bridge between any two modalities without aligned dimensions. A contrastive loss keeps paired samples close in meaning, while a predictive loss steers training toward accurate cross domain results. A domain neutral encoder and decoder handle noise prediction in the hidden space, giving one framework for many translation jobs.
arxiv-2510-20919:
Christiaan Boersma and six co-authors study carbon dust in the Iris Nebula. The Iris Nebula is cataloged as NGC 7023. They focus on its northwest photo dissociation region. A photo dissociation region is where starlight breaks molecules apart. They combine new SPHEREx data with older Spitzer spectral maps.

They track aromatic and aliphatic compounds across the region. Aromatic and aliphatic are two broad classes of carbon compounds. They also track PAH size, using carbon rich molecules called PAHs. All measured PAH bands peaked at the region's edge zone. They split one band into two smaller features. Fits gave average PAH sizes and the share of small PAHs. Dense and diffuse zones showed clearly distinct trends. Some size measures tracked band ratios, but only loosely. More varied objects are needed to make these links firm. That would turn them into reliable tools for measuring PAH size.
arxiv-2510-21219:
Xiaoyuan Zhang and seven co-authors argue that world models, AI systems that learn how environments change so they can plan ahead, are split in two. Most models learn either physical dynamics or social behavior, and very rarely both together, even though real decisions need the pair.

Real settings mix the two, since physical surroundings shape social life and social choices reshape surroundings. The authors say joining both kinds of prediction, in both directions, is the next major step for the field. They list the main obstacles, propose guiding principles they call the ACE Principles. Sketch a framework plus a research road map toward models that treat physical laws and shifting social dynamics as one system.
arxiv-2510-21319:
Evgeny Feigin and Markus Reineke study a family of geometric spaces built from representations of quivers, which are diagrams of arrows between points. Their spaces, Grassmannians of sub-bimodules over path algebras, include earlier constructions known as brick manifolds and their generalizations by Labelle.

They give an explicit construction of these spaces, work through examples, and clarify how the spaces connect with the representation spaces of quivers. They also prove the spaces are smooth, build decompositions of them into cells, and realize them as framed moduli spaces, which describe families of objects with extra fixed data. That last realization leads to a recursive formula for their motives, an algebraic measure of the spaces.
arxiv-2510-21519:
Simone Manti and thirty-six co-authors lay out EXKALIBUR, a program to X-ray exotic atoms across the whole periodic table at an accelerator in Frascati, Italy. In a kaonic atom, a heavy negative kaon takes an electron's place, and its X-ray lines probe strong-force interactions and fundamental constants at low energy with unusual sharpness.

Different detectors cover different energy bands: silicon drift detectors for light targets such as lithium and oxygen, cadmium zinc telluride detectors for mid-weight atoms. A high-purity germanium detector for heavy ones up to lead, with a crystal spectrometer for the finest studies. The goals include shrinking the uncertainty on the charged kaon's mass, building a database of nuclear shifts and widths to test interaction models. Checking bound-state quantum electrodynamics in strong fields.
arxiv-2510-21719:
Kenji Saito and Rei Tadika turn thesis writing into a game, hoping to keep novice researchers motivated now that generative AI can out-write them. Their chatbot, GAMER PAT, casts the student as a player, with a co-author character who helps write and anonymous reviewer characters who hand out missions in place of plain criticism.

The team analyzed over twenty-six gameplay chat logs, from the author's own use and from supervised graduate students, coding them with a structured qualitative method. A four-phase scaffolding pattern emerged: posing the question, stepping back to a meta view, structuring the paper, and reflecting recursively. Players' writing structure improved alongside reflection and motivation, the authors report. They present the study as a descriptive account rather than proof of effect, and close by speculating on how curiosity and agency survive beside capable AI.
arxiv-2510-22119:
Lihuang Fang, Xiao Hu, Yuchen Zou, and Hong Zhang improve stereo depth estimation, the task of turning two camera views into a distance map. Learned stereo systems shine on the datasets they were tuned for but lack the easy generalization that foundation models show elsewhere. They fail predictably where matching is ambiguous: hidden surfaces and textureless walls.

Their framework, CogStereo, lends the matcher a sense of the whole scene. Depth features from a single-image model, which carry holistic layout understanding, are embedded into the refinement stage as a spatial cognition prior. A dual-conditional corrector weighs pixel-level uncertainty together with those cognition features to fix mismatches coherently. Across six benchmarks and real-world footage, the system reached leading accuracy and, notably, kept its quality when carried to scenes unlike its training data.
arxiv-2510-22319:
Jing Wang leads a thirteen-author team fixing a quiet failure in reinforcement learning for image generation. Flow-matching models tuned with the GRPO method chase a proxy reward upward while the actual pictures get worse, an over-optimization trap. The clipping that should restrain the updates turns out to be the broken part.

The diagnosis is statistical: the importance ratios that clipping polices drift systematically below one and swing differently at different timesteps. Updates carrying good news never reach the clipped zone and overconfident improvements sail through unchecked. Their enhancement, GRPO-Guard, regulates the clipping so the restraint bites again on both enthusiastic and negative updates. The result is training where rising proxy reward stops masking collapsing image quality and prompt alignment, keeping the learned policy usable in the real world.
arxiv-2510-22419:
Kaihua Chang presents a PyTorch framework that makes non crossing quantile regression practical at large scale. Fitting several quantiles separately can produce crossed lines, which imply impossible negative probability. A joint constrained method fixes that by construction, but its older linear programming form grows far too slow for big data.

Chang pairs an augmented Lagrangian method with a smooth pinball loss and a fast solver, cutting the cost to linear growth. On data sets past seventy thousand rows, crossing nearly vanishes within minutes. A school growth percentile example shows real use, with only a small loss of accuracy.
arxiv-2510-22519:
Grouping data points works better when experts can say some pairs must join or must stay apart. Pedro Chumpitaz-Flores, My Duong, Cristobal Heredia, and Kaixun Hua tackle that constrained clustering task in 2025, noting exact global search is normally far too hard at large scale.

Their algorithm merges must linked samples into shared centers and prunes cannot link pairs with geometric rules. Group based branching still guarantees a global optimum, meaning the best possible grouping. Tests reach hundreds of thousands or over a million samples depending on constraint type, far beyond earlier methods, while staying within a small gap from optimal.
arxiv-2510-22719:
A dilute gas of fermions can switch from nonmagnetic to magnetic order. Fermions are matter particles such as electrons. Oskar Grocholski and Piotr H Chankowski compute the free energy of such a gas in 2025. Free energy tracks the useful energy in a system. Their gas has spin up and spin down parts.

The pair work to third order in a small interaction measure. They also sum two endless sets of diagrams to all orders. One set covers paired particle paths. The other covers particle and hole paths. Adding the second set changes the result a lot. In that version, the Stoner phase switch simply vanishes.
arxiv-2510-23119:
Yi-Lin Wei and six co-authors present OmniDexGrasp, a framework that lets multi-finger robot hands grasp varied objects from human commands. Dexterous grasping is hard to generalize because data sets of skilled grasps with meaning are small. Foundation models know much about objects, but turning that knowledge into feasible hand motions remains a gap.

The framework bridges that gap and adds force feedback, so the hand can adjust its grip on contact. The authors aim for one system that handles many objects and tasks rather than one narrow setup. Such general grasping would bring service robots closer to useful work in homes and warehouses.
arxiv-2510-23419:
Fredrik Hasselgren, Max O Al-Hasso, Amy Searle, Joseph Tindall, and Marko von der Leyen use probabilistic computing to optimize complex spin-glass systems. Spin glasses are lattices of disordered magnets with random interactions, tied to magnetization theory and to hard combinatorial problems. Methods that are both accurate and efficient remain elusive.

Because these topologies are low-partite, they suit probabilistic bits in an Ising machine. The team solves complex spin-glass topologies on a simulated probabilistic computer. Success would give optimizers a fast, physics-based route to problems from logistics to materials design.
arxiv-2510-23519:
Scott Jones and Prakash Murali study how to scale trapped ion quantum computers using surface codes, a leading scheme for error correction. Today's trapped ion machines hold fewer than sixty qubits, far below what useful programs need. The modular Quantum Charge-Coupled Device design promises growth, but no one had mapped how its hardware choices affect running large error-corrected codes.

The authors build a topology-aware compiler that arranges operations to fit the hardware, beating existing compilers by about 3.8 times in logical clock speed on average. Using it, they test how trap size, wiring, and connections change performance. Surprisingly, tiny traps holding just two ions came out best for both speed and hardware cost, against the older guess that traps of twenty to thirty ions would win. The result could shape how the next machines get built.
arxiv-2510-24219:
Alexey Khartov studies a wide class of chance laws on the real line, working alone. The laws are called rational infinitely divisible laws. Each one is a ratio of two laws from the classic divisible class. They also have a form that uses signed weights in place of plain ones. The class is wide and has many good traits. For weak forms of closeness, it can match any law on the line.

Khartov asks if the class can also match any law in a much stricter sense. That sense is the total variation gap, which is hard to make small. He treats the question case by case. The split depends on where each law puts its mass. The results show how far this flexible class can go when closeness must be strict.
arxiv-2510-24319:
Mohamedou Ould Haye and Anne Philippe give a new test to tell if a data series is steady in time or not. Two cases are hard to split. A series can have long memory, with slow decay of links over time. Or it can be unsteady, with its traits shifting. Both give slow decay that looks the same at a glance. Past tests fail on long memory data or misjudge the rate of false alarms near the split.

Their test uses no fixed constants. It compares the frequency plots of the series across a few time blocks. They work out the limit laws for both the steady and the unsteady case. Those laws are sums of weighted chi square terms. In trials, the new test did well next to past tests, with sound behavior near the hard split cases.
arxiv-2510-24419:
Changjian Yu, Jinbin Li, and Kui-Tian Xi, three authors, study a cold quantum gas. The gas is a Bose-Einstein condensate, a cloud where atoms act as one wave. Its atoms have small magnetic poles, so each atom pulls and pushes on far ones. Such clouds can form striped states where density rises and falls in waves. The team asks how heat changes these striped states.

They solve a wave equation that adds a heat term to the usual model. Heat shifts the lines that mark where one state gives way to another. At zero heat, the jump in stripe strength is sharp and sudden. With heat, the same change turns smooth and slow in a trapped cloud. They also bound how much of the cloud can flow without friction. The work helps labs read real warm clouds, not just ideal cold ones.
arxiv-2510-24519:
Rinku Sebastian and two co-authors propose a speech feature that adds time information to the classic mel frequency representation. Mel frequency cepstral coefficients are the most widely used features in speech and speaker recognition because their filtering mimics the human ear. Their main drawback is that they show which frequencies are present but not when each frequency occurs.

The wavelet transform, with its flexible time frequency window, suits non stationary signals like speech. The authors combine mel filtering with wavelet analysis in the time domain, producing coefficients that carry both time and frequency detail. The feature aims to improve recognition where the timing of sounds matters.
arxiv-2510-24619:
Snegha A, Sayambhu Sen, Piyush Singh Pasi, Abhishek Singhania, and Preethi Jyothi test ways to teach a model a new task in English only. The goal is for the skill to carry to more than thirty five other tongues with no more training. They focus on soft prompt styles, which are less used than the more known low rank method.

With two large models, the prompt styles beat the low rank base lines by up to six points on one reading test. Gains held across tongue groups, scripts, and model sizes. One style used just over one million learned weights, yet still gave steady gains.
arxiv-2510-24919:
Hossein R Nowdeh, Jie Ji, Xiaolong Ma, and Fatemeh Afghah tame a snag in joint learning from more than one sense: one sense can drown the rest. Their frame, M-SAM, works with many sense types and with both early and late ways to join them. It acts in three steps in each pass of training.

First it finds the top sense by a fair share score of its part in the wins. Next it reshapes the loss to force sturdiness in that top sense first. Last it moves the weights with the reshaped slopes. That way the weak senses still add their own traits. On four sets, the frame beat the newest train and slope tricks.
arxiv-2510-25019:
Remy Mahfouf, the sole author, proves that spin links in the Ising model act the same at the brink on a wide class of grids. The grids repeat in two ways, like a tile floor. At the brink point, past work on the plain square grid showed the links take a smooth shape in the large view.

Mahfouf shows the same smooth limit holds on the tile grids, with no need for the exact solve tricks of the square case. Tools from discrete math and chance cluster ways fill the gap. The brink rule for such grids was known from past work, as was their smooth frame. This proof caps the shared shape tale for tile grids.
arxiv-2510-25419:
Johannes U Lange led sixty-three co-authors on redshift calibration. Diana Blanco, Alexie Leauthaud, and Angus Wright helped. Abigail Fisher, Joshua Ratajczak, and Jessica Nicole Aguilar followed. Many further collaborators from the DESI collaboration joined. Their 2025 paper calibrates photometric redshifts for lensing surveys. Weak gravitational lensing needs accurate galaxy redshift distributions.

They introduce a method using high-quality spectroscopic redshifts. Neural network importance weights shape the calibration. Three leading stage-III lensing surveys are unified here. Those are DES, HSC, and KiDS surveys together. Spectroscopic data come from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument. A new data-driven approach verifies their method. Statistical uncertainties reach about one hundredth or smaller. Their analysis is largely independent of previous calibrations. That provides an important cross-check amid cosmological tensions. Results agree excellently with DES and HSC findings. Some differences appear for KiDS mean redshifts. Cosmic structure growth estimates barely changed, however.
arxiv-2510-25619:
A C Ulibarri led five co-authors detecting single spins electrically. D J McCloskey, D Wang, and N Dontschuk helped. A M Martin and A A Wood complete six. Their 2025 physics paper uses diamond nitrogen-vacancy centers. Electrical finding methods attract quantum technology scholars. They are chip-scalable and avoid small photon budgets. Realizing high-fidelity electrical readout remains challenging, though.

Their scheme stores spin information as trapped charges. Spin-dependent photoionisation generates carriers from centers. Carriers store in long-lived traps at a Schottky junction. Illumination releases stored charge under bias. Photocurrent reflects the spin state stored. Spin readout after coherent control is showed. They call the protocol charge-capture detected magnetic resonance. Charge-based imaging identifies generation and trapping processes. The technique mixes electrical finding advantages with trap stability. Solid-state spin qubit readout gains a new option.
arxiv-2510-25719:
Nikolaos Koukoulekidis and Iman Marvian build a resource view of asymmetry in bosonic Gaussian systems. Their 2025 paper in quantum theory studies how symmetry and Gaussian shape play off each other. Free moves in their scheme are Gaussian moves that keep the symmetry. Closed and open motion are both in scope.

They prove each free move can be built from parts that keep the symmetry. A bath in a pure, symmetry-keeping Gaussian state is part of the build. They find a set of gauge scores for states in this scheme. Those scores never rise under free Gaussian moves. In closed systems they stay the same in full. Under non-Gaussian moves that keep symmetry, the scores can break. Side results cover a new route to the Stinespring result, and a growth of Williamson's result for shared mode splits of Gaussian systems with kept charges.
arxiv-2510-25819:
Tobin South leads twenty co-authors in a white paper on identity rules for AI agents. An AI agent is software that acts on its own to carry out tasks for a user. Such agents need clear rules for proving who they are, who may act, and what access they should get, and current protocols leave those rules unclear.

South and the team, writing for the OpenID Foundation audience, list tools already available to secure agents in use today. They then set an agenda for harder problems ahead, such as access control at scale, delegated authority, and telling AI workloads apart. The paper speaks to builders and policy makers alike.
arxiv-2510-25919:
Shivanshu Dwivedi and Kalum Palandage map how to engineer paired electrons in tiny clusters of quantum dots. A quantum dot is a small semiconductor trap that holds a few electrons, and a Hubbard cluster is a simple model of electrons that hop between sites and repel on site. They vary three levers: the shape of the cluster, mixing between orbitals, and an applied electric field.

Using Hartree Fock simulations, a standard approximate method, on clusters from a tetrahedron to a face centered cubic patch, Dwivedi and Palandage find three design rules. More neighbors make pairing resist repulsion, orbital mixing can aid pairing at moderate repulsion by reshaping site energies, and a field squeezes charge into pairing, most strongly in sparse clusters.
arxiv-2510-26319:
Mario Grossmann leads six co-authors in an experiment on the ultrafast birth of either a Rydberg gas or an ultracold plasma from a Bose Einstein condensate. A condensate is a cloud of atoms in a single quantum state, and a single femtosecond laser pulse can ionize it along competing paths. Tuning the laser wavelength across the two photon ionization threshold selects whether free electrons dominate, forming a plasma, or bound excited electrons dominate, forming a dense Rydberg gas.

The broad pulse bandwidth overcomes the Rydberg blockade, which normally limits excitation density. Grossmann and the team measure the kinetic energy of released electrons and compare the final mix of free, bound, and plasma electrons with molecular dynamics simulations that include collisional ionization and recombination. The match with the data is very good.
arxiv-2510-26719:
Gurvir Singh and Arvind link two quantum ideas that had seemed separate. Unextendible product bases are sets of product states, states with no entanglement between parts, that cannot be extended while staying product and orthogonal. They are central to telling quantum states apart locally. Quantum contextuality, where measurement outcomes depend on what else is measured alongside, had no clear tie to them.

Singh and Arvind build that tie with graph theory. They show a known contextuality test's vectors match a named product basis, then build a one-parameter family of bases that links contextuality strength to bound entanglement. The match extends to generalised versions on both sides. They also construct a new class of minimal bases in a stated dimension from graph representations, and show every minimal basis there is graph-equivalent to theirs.
arxiv-2510-26919:
Andrea Moscatello and four co-authors study dust noise for the Einstein Telescope in 2025. The telescope is a planned detector that hears gravitational waves, ripples in space from far events. Its arms are vacuum pipes, tubes with air removed, lined with plates inside. Baffles are plates that block stray light in a tube.

Dust grains on those plates can scatter light and add noise to readings. The team studies scatter by grain size, from far below to far above one wavelength. A wavelength is the length of one full wave of light. They also weigh grain traits and the light's polarization, the set path of its wave swings. For the telescope arms, they set the most dust allowed on each plate. They close with cleanliness rules for building the pipes and the work space.
arxiv-2510-27019:
Jingyao Zhu leads fourteen co-authors in cataloging small gas-rich galaxies that orbit larger ones nearby. The sample holds over a hundred dwarf satellite galaxies around dozens of host galaxies within a nearby volume. Radio data at the twenty-one centimeter line reveal their hydrogen gas, while optical surveys supply starlight properties for most of them.

The satellites span wide ranges in gas and stellar mass, with line widths much like dwarfs in our own Local Group. Tests with fake injected galaxies show how faint each survey can detect. Satellites per host stay few and rise with host mass, matching counts around the Milky Way. Low gas fractions and many quenched satellites point to gas stripping by Milky Way-mass hosts.
arxiv-2510-27119:
Qiyan Deng leads eleven co-authors in building UDA-Bench, a benchmark for systems that let users query messy documents like a database. Large language models can pull structured attributes from unstructured text, and many analysis systems now compete with different interfaces and strategies. Without a shared test, no one could tell which design works best where.

The team spent extensive effort curating five datasets across domains and hand-building relational database views as ground truth. Queries cover many operator types at varied selectivity and complexity. The study dissects query interfaces, optimization, operator design, and processing across existing systems with exhaustive experiments. For builders of document analytics, the benchmark finally gives a common yardstick and a map of which building blocks matter most.
arxiv-2510-27519:
Shinichi Nakagawa leads nine co-authors in SAFE bootstrap, a simulation recipe giving bias-corrected effect sizes and sampling variances for any statistic. Meta-analyses need both quantities from primary studies, yet variance formulas may not exist for a chosen effect size, and hand-derived delta method expansions challenge non-statisticians. Their single-fit parametric resampling replaces that algebra with four steps: fit, draw, transform, and summarise.

Drawing once from a simple sampling model and converting each replicate into the target effect size yields bias and sampling variance in one unified framework for continuous or discrete outcomes. Worked examples cover a simple case, common measures like the standardised mean difference and log odds ratio, and rarer ones, with extensions for zeros and small samples. R code supplements the tutorial.
arxiv-2511-00219: Pierre Bertrand and Wolfgang Stummer write a brief math note on distance measures between data patterns. They take smooth cases of a broad family called phi-divergences, plus a new family they name scaled shift divergences. For these cases they derive close approximations to the widely used L1 distance and L1 norm, which add up absolute gaps. The note is aimed at readers in statistics and probability who work with such measures.
arxiv-2511-00519:
Ariyan Hossain and six co-authors measure and reduce gender bias in encoder-based transformer models such as BERT and RoBERTa. These models inherit strong gender skews from training data, and the bias lives in their word embeddings. The team introduces MALoR, a new metric that scores bias from the model's own probabilities when filling masked words in sentences.

Their remedy continues pre-training on a gender-balanced dataset built by counterfactual data augmentation, swapping gendered terms to even the exposure. Bias scores fell sharply across pronoun pairs and model sizes, in some cases to a small fraction of the original value. Performance on downstream tasks held steady, showing the fix does not trade fairness for skill. The study gives practitioners both a yardstick and a practical debiasing recipe.
arxiv-2511-00819:
Yuxuan Hu and co-authors analyze Native Sparse Attention, a design that lets large language models handle long texts by attending to only part of the context at each step. They look for structural changes that help long range information move through the network.

Their main change alternates attention styles across layers: some layers use local sliding windows, while others use compressed or selective global views. They also add latent attention variants that shrink the memory cache by half compared with the original design. On models up to about a billion parameters, the revised system matches or beats full attention on reasoning and long text tasks, suggesting a practical route to cheaper long context models.
arxiv-2511-01019:
Bowen Chen and colleagues present OceanAI, a conversational platform for ocean data that is designed not to make things up. General chatbots often produce confident but unverified numbers, a serious flaw for science. OceanAI instead ties a language model to live data streams from NOAA, the United States ocean and atmosphere agency.

A question such as the highest water level in Boston Harbor in a given year triggers real API calls. The answer is built from the returned data with its source shown, plus visualizations. In a blind test against three popular chat products, only OceanAI gave NOAA sourced values with references. The platform connects to several NOAA products and supports hazard forecasting, ecosystem assessment, and water quality monitoring.
arxiv-2511-01619:
Nikola Ljubešić, Peter Rupnik, Ivan Porupski, and Taja Kuzman Pungeršek present ParlaSpeech 3.0, a set of spoken corpora built from debates in four parliaments: Croatian, Czech, Polish, and Serbian. All told, the corpora hold about 6,000 hours of speech. They were built by matching ParlaMint transcripts and metadata to each parliament's audio.

This release adds layers of markup to both text and speech. The texts gain language annotations and sentiment scores. The speech gains marked filled pauses, the most common slip in normal talk. For two of the four languages, the team also added word- and letter-level alignments and marked stress in longer words. A sample study links sound features to sentiment. The corpora can be downloaded as JSONL or TextGrid files, or searched with a concordancer.
arxiv-2511-01719:
Garrison Koch and Darren Narayan study graphs in which exactly one smallest dominating set exists. A dominating set is a group of vertices. Every vertex is in the group or next to one of its members. Fischermann and coauthors asked in 2003 how many edges a uniquely dominatable graph can have. They conjectured a bound and gave a construction meeting it.

Koch and Narayan ask how the answer changes when the graph must be bipartite, its vertices split into two camps with edges only across. They conjecture a bipartite bound and give constructions showing it is tight. They prove it for domination number two. They also prove it when the vertex count is three times the domination number. They also connect the constructions to perfect domination and exhibit graphs meeting both the general and bipartite bounds.
arxiv-2511-01819:
Hamed Fard, Mahsa Kholghi, Benedikt Groß, and Gerhard Wunder hunt jammers indoors with machine learning. Ultra-wideband positioning is accurate to centimeters but vulnerable to jamming, a real risk for asset tracking and intrusion detection in smart buildings. Finding the jammer, rather than the tags, inside a single room, and keeping the method working when the room's layout changes, was largely unexplored.

The authors collected two new datasets, in an original and a modified room layout, and set baselines across many methods. In the source room, random forest reached the best F1 score and XGBoost located jammers with a mean error of about 20 centimeters. Moved to the rearranged room, errors ballooned roughly tenfold, a stark domain shift. Their domain-adversarial autoencoder, using a gradient-reversal layer to align features across layouts, pulled the mean error back to about 35 centimeters, a 77 percent improvement over plain transfer learning.
arxiv-2511-01919:
Shashwat Sardesai, Gabriel Freedman, Sarah Vigeland, and Caitlin Witt tune the hunt for individual gravitational wave sources inside pulsar timing array data. Arrays of pulsars can sense the background hum of countless supermassive black hole binaries, and possibly single loud ones, continuous waves from individual pairs. The Fp-statistic is the standard frequentist detector for those continuous waves.

The authors study how two complications, each pulsar's own red noise and the background itself, affect the statistic's behavior. Handling the red noise by marginalizing over it versus plugging in its maximum-likelihood values made little difference, a useful simplification. They then ran the statistic on the NANOGrav 12.5-year dataset and found no evidence for continuous waves, agreeing with the previously published Bayesian analysis of the same data.
arxiv-2511-02119:
Ziheng Geng and five co-authors build a simulator for one stubborn policy puzzle: why so few Americans at risk of flooding buy flood insurance. Their system, InsurAgent, is an agent powered by a large language model, with modules for perception, retrieval, reasoning, action, and memory. A benchmark dataset the team constructed captures how purchase probability varies with different factors.

Tested directly, language models grasped the direction of those factors but misjudged the size of the effects. InsurAgent grounds its choices in real survey data through retrieval, reaching accurate estimates of single-factor and paired probabilities, then uses the model's common sense to extrapolate to new situations. Its memory module can trace how one simulated person's decisions evolve across a lifetime, which the authors offer as a tool for behavioural modelling and policy analysis.
arxiv-2511-02219:
Changjiang Jiang, Fengchang Yu, Haihua Chen, Wei Lu, and Jin Zeng help language models answer numerical questions about tables. On such tasks the models often stumble over tangled queries, dirty data, and weak arithmetic. Their framework, TabDSR, splits the work into three stages named in its title: decompose, sanitize, and reason. A decomposer breaks a complex question into parts, and a sanitizer cleans and filters the noisy table.
