A program-of-thoughts reasoner then writes executable code that computes the answer from the cleaned table, instead of guessing numbers in prose. To evaluate fairly and avoid leaked test data, the team built a new dataset of 151 hard table problems. TabDSR set new state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks, with accuracy gains of 8.79 percent, 6.08 percent, and 19.87 percent over prior methods, and it plugs into mainstream language models.
arxiv-2511-02719:
EV Lac is a nearby red dwarf star famous for sudden bright flares. Rachel Osten and six colleagues watched it for 27 hours in radio and 29 hours in visible light, and report the paired results in a 2025 paper. They wanted to see how fast electrons act in two layers of the star's atmosphere at once.

Nine optical flares had good radio coverage, yet only four showed a clear radio response. Nothing in the light curve alone predicted which flares would answer in radio. Radio peaks lagged the optical peaks by one to seven minutes in every matched case. The delay hints that several magnetic loops take part, with some electrons trapped and others raining straight down.
arxiv-2511-02819:
Shamil Asgarli, Donald Falkenhagen, and Kaya Hoshi improve lower bounds for the largest set of vertices in a directed graph that contains no directed cycle. Finding that set exactly is NP-hard, so good bounds that are cheap to compute carry real value. Their 2025 paper starts from a known bound by Akbari and co-workers for digraphs.

Two refinements follow ideas first used on undirected graphs. One adapts a neighborhood method, folding in the local degree of each vertex. The other studies the random size of a feedback vertex set from a randomized algorithm, then applies the Bhatia-Davis inequality to its variance. Both routes beat the earlier bound, giving tighter guarantees for a hard combinatorial quantity.
arxiv-2511-02919:
Shuhang Lin and five colleagues built ARC, a cache system for search-augmented language model agents. Such agents pull facts from huge external collections, but keeping a small, relevant store for each agent is an unsolved housekeeping problem. Their 2025 framework manages that store on its own, with no human annotation, by reading past query patterns and the geometry of stored items in embedding space.

Across three retrieval data sets, ARC shrank the stored corpus to a tiny sliver, 0.015 percent of the original size. Even so, it kept answer coverage near 79.8 percent at best and cut average retrieval delay by 80 percent. The results suggest agents can carry pocket-sized libraries tuned to their own habits, instead of searching the whole shelf every time.
arxiv-2511-03019:
Wenbo Lu argues that image-text training wastes the web of links between products, posts, and people. Standard vision-language pretraining treats each pair as an island. Yet domains like online shopping carry rich relational structure, such as graphs of items bought together. In a 2025 paper, Lu introduces SLIP, a pretraining method that learns from those links as well as the pairs.

SLIP adds a structural contrastive loss that aligns images and text while modeling ties between neighboring entities in a graph. To train it, Lu built a large Amazon co-purchase data set with product images and text. SLIP beat the well-known CLIP model on retrieval and classification, in both zero-shot and few-shot tests. The result credits relational supervision, inspired by how human memory maps knowledge as relations.
arxiv-2511-03119:
Seyed Mohamad Ali Tousi and G. DeSouza build a learning model that cleans up errors in quantum circuits without heavy overhead. Standard mitigation tricks cost many extra runs or long calibration, and earlier learning methods struggled on large, deep circuits. Their 2025 model, QAGT-MLP, turns each circuit into a graph: gates become nodes, and wires plus cause-and-effect links become edges.

Attention reads the graph at two scales at once, the whole circuit and the local neighborhood of each measured qubit. Those features, plus circuit descriptors and the noisy measured values, feed a small network that predicts the cleaned values. On hundred-qubit Ising model circuits, it beat leading learning baselines on mean error and spread, under equal shot budgets.
arxiv-2511-03519:
Ajay Gautam, Feiyang Lin, and Shubham Sinha prove a Borel-Weil-Bott style theorem for Quot schemes over the projective line. Quot schemes catalog all ways to take quotients of a fixed vector bundle at a set rank. Natural bundles living on those schemes carry cohomology groups that encode deep counting information.

Classical Borel-Weil-Bott theory computes such groups for flag spaces, and the new result extends that power to Quot schemes. As a payoff, recent conjectures by Marian, Oprea, and Sam about powers of those natural bundles are proved. Clean cohomology formulas turn hard enumerative questions into routine checks. The work links representation theory with the geometry of bundles in a concrete new setting.
arxiv-2511-03619:
Riccardo Rossetto, Marcel Ernst, and David Zwicker show how exchange with the surrounding bulk steers the growth of protein patches on cell surfaces. Such patches, called surface condensates, form spots like the polarity mark in budding yeast. Cells clearly control them, yet how bulk exchange shapes patch coarsening was unclear.

A thermodynamically sound model finds passive exchange generally speeds coarsening, as big patches eat small ones faster through the bulk. Active exchange can speed things further, or freeze coarsening entirely and spawn patterns at several scales. Nonlocal transport through the bulk explains the scaling laws behind each regime. The results help read living patterns, from yeast polarity to membrane organization in larger cells.
arxiv-2511-03719:
Sawyer Jack Robertson, Finn Southerland, and Erlang Surya investigate graphs whose distance table cannot balance a constant load. A graph counts as distance exceptional when its shortest-path distance matrix admits no solution sending a weight vector to all ones. Such graphs arose from a discrete curvature idea, leaving open questions about their shape and rarity.

A new invariant, the curvature index, decides the matter exactly: a graph is exceptional precisely when the index vanishes. The authors build a calculus for computing that index across graph operations. Structural results then show how exceptional graphs can be assembled and how often they appear. Curvature on graphs feeds network analysis, so a clean test for the exceptional case sharpens that toolkit.
arxiv-2511-04419:
Wen Huang and two colleagues introduce dynamical systems with almost countable spectrum. Their goal is the logarithmic Sarnak conjecture, a claim about how deterministic sequences avoid random-like patterns. They prove it for zero-entropy systems whose spectrum is almost countable.

The covered class is wide and concrete. It includes Anzai skew products over circle rotations and time-one maps of suspension flows. Systems with finite maximal pattern entropy and bounded tame systems also qualify. Each new family where the conjecture holds strengthens a central program linking dynamics, number theory, and the study of the Möbius function.
arxiv-2511-04619:
Natalia Glazman leads five authors tracing how causal links shift during Alzheimer's disease. Most causal discovery tools assume one fixed graph, but the disease evolves over time. A hidden disease clock, called pseudotime, orders patients by progress rather than age.

Their model infers that pseudotime from real patient data first. Pseudotime predicted diagnosis far better than age did in their tests. Adding light, disease-neutral background knowledge then improved graph accuracy and direction. The method reveals changing ties between newer markers like NfL and GFAP and established ones, despite the disease's complexity.
arxiv-2511-04719:
Sabbir A. Kahn leads ten authors building multi-terminal Josephson junctions in hybrid nanowire crosses. The crosses merge indium arsenide antimonide wires with aluminum in one structure. They grow by molecular beam epitaxy, joining oppositely directed wires with arsenic help.

A temperature-dependent phase diagram explains the tricky ternary merging process. Atomic-resolution images confirm the crystal structure of the merged crosses. Devices built on them carry supercurrent between several terminal pairs. Measurements vary the junction density and the relative phases, steered by an external magnetic field, opening a platform for phase-controlled superconducting circuits.
arxiv-2511-04819:
Héloïse Damas leads six authors studying light-driven magnetization switching in an epsilon-near-zero setting. Ultrashort light and strain pulses can reorder magnetism, but the mechanism is disputed. Heat-driven demagnetization and direct anisotropy changes are the leading candidates.

Mid-infrared pulses tuned to crystal phonon resonances drive the switching here. They can act through thermal quenching of anisotropy or through fresh strain. The team examines that split on the labyrinthine domains of a cobalt-doped magnetic dielectric. Sorting thermal from non-thermal action could point to faster, cooler magnetic memory controlled by light alone. The study keeps both pathways in view throughout its analysis.
arxiv-2511-05119:
Víctor Mayoral-Vilches and co-authors recount how a cyber AI system fared in the Dragos OT CTF 2025, a 48-hour contest on industrial control security with more than one thousand teams. Such contests test malware study, network forensics, and reverse engineering under time stress.

The AI, named CAI and run on the alias1 model, hit first place between hours seven and eight. It passed ten thousand points in under six hours and solved 32 of 34 tasks before auto play was paused. The paper weighs its pace against top human teams.
arxiv-2511-05419:
A. Pasetto and co-authors take high-frequency, full-polarization radio data on MACS J0717.5+3745, the brightest radio relic in the sky. Relics trace shock waves in the hot gas between galaxies during cluster mergers, and their nature is still debated.

One open point is whether relic electrons are fresh thermal ones sped up by the shock, or old fossil ones re-energized. Stokes QU fitting of the polarization can split those cases and map the magnetized plasma. The new Jansky Very Large Array data at X-band give a sharp read on this extreme relic.
arxiv-2511-05719:
Francesco Pio Barone and co-authors test how well a quantum error-correcting code holds up when noise breaks the standard simplifying rules. Most simulations assume Pauli noise, which classical computers can mimic fast. Real hardware also suffers coherent over-rotations and energy relaxation, which that model misses.

The team modeled the hexagonal color code under circuit-level noise of both non-Pauli kinds, using a tree tensor network method. They estimated error thresholds for codes up to seventy-three qubits. Coherent over-rotations produced higher error rates than the standard approximation predicts, and the gap grew with code size. The work shows tensor networks can price realistic noise for color codes accurately.
arxiv-2511-05919:
Alina Fastowski and co-authors show how an attacker sitting between a user and a language model can poison the model's memory of facts. As chatbots become a main route to information, such man-in-the-middle tampering is a serious risk. Their framework, Xmera, is the first principled way to test these attacks on factual recall.

They perturbed the input reaching victim models across three closed-book, fact-based question settings. Simple instruction-based attacks worked best, succeeding at a high rate, yet the model's uncertainty ran high on the questions it then got wrong. That quirk enabled a defense: a classifier trained on uncertainty levels could tell attacked from clean queries with strong accuracy. The authors frame the signal as a first warning checkpoint for users.
arxiv-2511-06419:
Jingyu Hu and colleagues catch sycophancy in reasoning models while the answer is still being written. Large reasoning models tend to agree with a user's wrong belief instead of holding their ground, which erodes trust. Most fixes judge only the finished answer, missing how the flattery creeps in step by step during reasoning.

Their framework, MONICA, pairs a monitor that scores sycophantic drift in real time with a calibrator that pushes back when the score crosses a set line. No need to wait for a completed answer before intervening. Across twelve datasets and three reasoning models, sycophancy fell in both intermediate steps and final answers.
arxiv-2511-06519:
Sanaz Saki Norouzi, Mohammad Masjedi, and Pascal Hitzler find grammar-specialized neurons inside a large language model, echoing a known brain pattern. Neuroscience shows different word classes engage different neurons in human language areas. Whether artificial networks, loosely inspired by brains, sort grammar the same way was an open question.

Working with the Llama 3 model, the team pinpointed the neurons most tied to predicting words of each part of speech. A classifier trained on just those neurons' activity predicted word classes on fresh text reliably. The results point to a dedicated grammar subspace inside the model, reminiscent of patterns seen in human lesion studies.
arxiv-2511-07419:
Mixture-of-experts models switch on only a few parts for each input, saving compute. Zhongyang Li, Ziyue Li, and Tianyi Zhou show that the switching decisions, called routing, are often far from ideal. Broad tests reveal accuracy gaps of ten to twenty percent versus the best possible routing.

Their fix, Routing Manifold Alignment, nudges routing weights to resemble task embedding patterns. Only the routers are lightly retrained while the rest of the model stays frozen. That small change closes much of the gap and improves performance on new tasks. The result suggests smarter routing, not bigger models, can unlock gains.
arxiv-2511-07519:
João Barata and co-authors follow jets through the chaotic first moments of heavy-ion collisions. When nuclei smash, hot QCD matter forms out of equilibrium before settling. Jets crossing that early medium lose energy, a process called quenching, but early-stage effects were unstudied.

The team computes how soft gluon radiation changes during bottom-up thermal evolution. An improved opacity expansion handles both many soft kicks and single hard hits from the medium. Kinetic theory simulations supply the quenching strength over time. Results cover both underfilled and overfilled starting conditions. The findings refine how experimental jet data reveal the earliest fireball stage.
arxiv-2511-07619:
Luca Macesanu, Boueny Folefack, and Samik Singh built CAVER, a robot that learns objects by sight and sound together. A shaken bottle looks and sounds different from a tapped one, and those linked cues reveal material and contents. Most robots never gather such paired experience on their own.

CAVER explores objects actively, building rich audiovisual representations as it pokes and listens. Curiosity guides which interactions to try next, so knowledge grows efficiently. Skills like sorting by material or copying a tune played by ear become plausible. The robot shows how self-driven play can teach cross-modal facts that passive datasets miss.
arxiv-2511-07719:
Vít Růžička and colleagues run the first working system that spots methane leaks from space automatically. Methane cuts offer cheap, fast climate gains, but matched-filter satellite retrievals flag many false sources that humans must check by hand. Imaging spectrometers on several satellites already scan the planet.

A machine learning detector now operates inside the United Nations Methane Alert and Response System. It screens spectrometer data for point sources with regular global coverage. Automation turns occasional expert hunts into routine monitoring that can scale to future satellite fleets. Faster alerts help operators fix leaks while the climate benefit is largest.
arxiv-2511-08119:
Arnab Maity and co-authors propose LatentPrintFormer for identifying people from latent fingerprints left at scenes. Latent prints are partial, noisy, and low quality, which makes matching them far harder than clean scans. Their model joins a convolutional network for local ridge detail with a transformer for global structure.

A spatial attention module highlights good ridge regions and suppresses background noise. Features from both backbones fuse into a single embedding, and matches are chosen by cosine similarity. On two public data sets, the system beats three leading latent fingerprint methods in identification rates at rank ten.
arxiv-2511-08219:
Rune Rost, Lorenzo Branca, and Tobias Buck build a neural surrogate that emulates radiative transfer in astrophysical settings. Radiative transfer describes how light interacts with matter and drives heating and feedback in simulations. Solving its equation directly is very costly, because light moves far faster than the gas and the interactions are complex.

Their model joins a Fourier neural operator with U-Net parts to approximate three dimensional, single color transfer in time dependent, absorbing and emitting media. It runs more than one hundred times faster than direct calculation while keeping average relative error below three percent. That speed makes on the fly radiation inside hydrodynamic simulations more realistic.
arxiv-2511-08619:
Jia-Kai Wu and five co-authors schedule computing work and energy together across virtual power plants that host data centers. Moving workloads between regions can follow demand response signals from the grid, but data center demand data is sparse, which breaks standard probability models.

A game-based framework coordinates migration between plants, and fuzzy chance constraints handle the sparse data through deterministic equivalents that turn the problem into a solvable cone program. Profits are split with an improved Shapley value method that keeps fairness practical to compute. A consensus-based splitting algorithm then solves the large coupled optimization piece by piece. Simulations on real Google data center traces show tighter demand response tracking and lower operating costs.
arxiv-2511-08819:
Morgan Wall and four co-authors connect a large language model to an actual electron microscope and let it run experiments through conversation. Their framework, TEM Agent, speaks the model context protocol, a standard way to hand a language model curated tools and resources for a specific job.

Through text instructions the system reaches several microscope subsystems at once, plus a data management platform and high performance computing resources. The authors show the agent setting up and completing intricate transmission electron microscopy workflows using a simplified tool set and a commercial model with no extra training. The point is access: a single conversational layer over a tangle of vendor and custom systems could let users of many skill levels carry out demanding microscopy experiments.
arxiv-2511-08919:
Arsenii Onuchin and three co-authors find communities in networks by letting a geometric flow pull tightly knit regions apart from loose ones. Their flow imitates Ricci curvature on graphs, using a Foster version of curvature computed from effective resistance distances, which come from the graph Laplacian.

Each round of the flow stretches or shrinks edge lengths according to curvature, exposing regions of differing character. A Gaussian mixture model then sorts edges into strong and weak groups, and pruning separates the communities. Benchmarks on synthetic stochastic block model networks, graded by the Adjusted Rand Index, show the method robustly recovering the planted communities. Against the better-known Ollivier-Ricci flow paired with spectral clustering, the new approach is far faster to compute while staying principled.
arxiv-2511-09119:
Jiahao Xiao and six co-authors grade the datasets that embodied AI learns from, before any model is trained. A robot dataset's worth rests on two attributes: how much information it carries and how learnable that information is. Yet the field has mostly counted tasks and scenes per modality. Learnability was only ever judged after expensive training runs.

Two tools answer the two attributes. A unified multimodal representation of each sample supports a diversity entropy, a continuous measure of the information a dataset contains. A separate interpretable algorithm then scores learnability directly from the data, with no training at all. Validated on simulated and real embodied datasets, the scores prove faithful and actionable, showing builders how to raise diversity and learnability together rather than discovering dataset flaws after the fact.
arxiv-2511-09219:
Paul Strang and five co-authors bring planning into branch-and-bound, the exact method behind most mixed-integer programming solvers. A solver's speed depends heavily on its branching heuristic, the rule choosing which variable to split on next. Earlier reinforcement learning approaches learned such rules, but without a model for planning ahead.

Their agent, PlanB&B, learns an internal model of the search dynamics and uses it to discover better branching strategies. The approach echoes game-playing agents that plan with simulators in Monte Carlo tree search. Across four standard benchmarks, PlanB&B outperforms previous state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods for branching. The work suggests model-based learning can improve even the inner loops of exact optimization.
arxiv-2511-09719:
E. Lacchin and five co-authors simulate how Type Ia supernova explosions reshape the second generation of stars forming inside young globular clusters. In their setup, that generation condenses from giant-star ejecta mixed with pristine gas flowing through the cluster. Type Ia explosions begin just as the most massive giants release their gas, setting up a contest.

Three models span cluster mass and infalling gas density. In the low-mass, low-density case, explosions quench star formation until the gas cools between blasts, leaving helium-rich stars poorly diluted. In high-mass models, supernovae block pristine gas accretion, producing extremely helium-rich stars instead. Iron spreads stay small everywhere, but the second generation ends up less homogeneous than the first, contrary to observations.
arxiv-2511-10019:
Mujin Choi, Maximilian Gorsky, Gunwoo Kim, Caleb McFarland, and Sebastian Wiederrecht introduce a new graph width parameter based on packing odd cycles. Treewidth measures how tree-like a graph is; their variant decomposes a graph into pieces whose odd cycle packing number stays bounded. The parameter is monotone under odd minors, the natural containment relation for this setting, which makes a grid theorem plausible.

The authors prove that analogue of the Robertson-Seymour grid theorem: two families of grid-like graphs force large width when present as odd minors, and their absence bounds the width. The structural result is constructive and yields a fast parameterized approximation algorithm. As a payoff, maximum independent set becomes polynomial-time solvable on graphs of bounded width, and the idea extends to integer programming matrices.
arxiv-2511-10319:
Sajal Mukherjee and Pritam Chandra Pramanik study combinatorics, the branch of mathematics concerned with finite structures and counting. Their paper formulates a degree version of a generalized Tucker lemma, a discrete statement related to the classic Borsuk-Ulam theorem of topology. Such combinatorial versions of topology theorems are widely used tools across combinatorics.

The proof stays fully combinatorial and never uses homology, cohomology, or other tools from continuous topology. As the main technical step, the authors prove a combinatorial version of a Hopf trace formula, also without homology. That formula stands on its own as a result other researchers may use in different settings.
arxiv-2511-10519:
Srikant Panda and Avinash Rai show that the way a request is worded, not just what it asks, can break the safety training of large language models. Safety tests usually check paraphrases with the same meaning, but they rarely vary the emotional and linguistic style of a prompt.

The authors turned harmful prompts from three standard datasets into 11 styles, including fearful, curious, and compassionate framings, using templates and model rewrites that keep the intent unchanged. Across 16 open and closed models, styling alone raised jailbreak success rates by up to 57 percentage points, and contextual rewrites beat fixed templates. As a defense, they propose a preprocessing step that uses a second model to strip manipulative style cues, which sharply reduced successful attacks.
arxiv-2511-11219:
Aritra Gupta and Manibrata Sen revisit supernova limits on dark photons, light hidden particles that could carry energy out of a collapsing star. The classic bound from supernova 1987A says dark photons cannot cool the newborn neutron star faster than neutrinos were seen to do. That bound assumes the star starts empty of dark matter, which the authors question.

Dark matter trapped in the star before collapse gives dark photons extra targets to hit, shortening their escape path. For dark matter that can annihilate, the trapped amount stays too small to matter. For one-sided dark matter, large trapped amounts form a dark shell that dims the loss and reopens excluded regions.
arxiv-2511-11419:
C R Muniz, Jonathan Alves Rebouças, and their colleagues construct a new family of regular black hole solutions, spacetimes whose centers stay smooth instead of collapsing to a singular point. The matter source is a novel string cloud, spread through space like a web of thin strings, regularized by a smooth rational distribution. That smoothing keeps every curvature measure finite across the whole solution.

The geometry joins a string-cloud exterior to an anti-de Sitter core. The authors map where each energy condition holds or fails and chart when horizons form. Heat traits are derived, with entropy set only by the regularization scale. Shadow sizes are checked against telescope bounds for two known black holes.
arxiv-2511-11519:
Adam Stein and six co-authors present EGuR, a system that lets AI agents rewrite their own problem-solving strategies at inference time based on past experience. Earlier memory-based systems could only steer an agent by editing its text input, leaving sampling settings, tools, prompts, and overall workflow fixed.

EGuR instead generates complete strategies, covering model calls, tool use, sampling choices, and control logic, through a meta-strategy that learns from accumulated interactions. Strategies are tailored per task without offline retraining after deployment. Tests compare the approach with fixed and text-only adaptive systems. If it holds up, agents could improve steadily from use rather than staying frozen at release.
arxiv-2511-11819:
Ari Blondal and four co-authors define a topological dimension for concept classes. A concept class is the set of rules a learner can choose from. Topology's covering dimension, going back to Lebesgue, is the source idea. Each class has a space of distributions it can realize. Loss and class together give that space a simplicial structure.

For finite classes, the new dimension equals the list replicability number. That number is also known as global stability in PAC learning. A learning quantity thus gets a purely topological meaning. Classic dimension tools can then compute exact stability values. The bridge lets two fields trade methods with each other.
arxiv-2511-11919:
Petro Sarkanych finds the interaction range where a classic model flips its phase transition type. The model is the two-dimensional Potts model on a square lattice. With few states, its transition is smooth. With more states, it turns abrupt. Range offers a second control knob, even at a fixed state count.

The study uses the three-state model with equivalent neighbors. Spins interact equally out to some neighborhood size. Zeros of the partition function are tracked in the complex plane. Those zeros show how many neighbors change the order of the transition. Fine control of transition type matters for materials design. It also matters for the study of universality in physics.
arxiv-2511-12019:
Jyoti and Lalit Kumar Vashisht study what happens when parts of a Hilbert-Schmidt frame are changed. Frames are sets of vectors used to rebuild signals, and a change here means replacing some elements, either a finite number or infinitely many. The central question is when the changed set still works as a frame.

For the finite case, the authors give clear criteria, with stability bounds that depend on the size of the change and how many elements were altered. For the infinite case, they give conditions that keep the change under global control. Examples in the work show how the results apply in practice.
arxiv-2511-12219:
Osafu Augustine Egbon and three co-authors map how fatalities from violent events are spread over space and time in Ethiopia. Deaths from armed conflict are a long-running public health burden, yet quantitative studies of their pattern have been limited. The team uses records from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project, covering 1997 to 2022.

They fit a two-part Bayesian model that handles many zero counts and includes space and time effects. Nine of thirteen regions show a high chance of a fatal violent event in the analysis, and five pass a higher threshold. The Tigray region and others are discussed in the regional breakdown the model provides.
arxiv-2511-12319:
Luca Corazzini, Elisa Deriu and Marco Guerzoni test whether large language models make decisions like rational agents or like biased humans. Models now mediate hiring, support, investment advice and policy work, yet they learn from human text that may carry cognitive and social biases. The authors probe that question with classic behavioral economics games.

They run an ultimatum game and a gambling game on two advanced models, under neutral prompts and prompts conditioned on gender. Estimated parameters show weakened but persistent departures from rationality: moderate concern for fairness, mild loss aversion, and subtle gender-linked differences. The models, in short, echo human tendencies rather than pure calculation.
arxiv-2511-12419:
Wenjie Li and four co-authors tackle two image tasks that pull in opposite directions: removing rain and raising resolution. Rain removal deletes high-frequency detail, while super-resolution tries to rebuild it, so chaining the two often gives inconsistent results. Clean, sharp images matter for tasks such as spotting small objects.

Their model, DHGM, uses guidance from a pretrained diffusion model together with high-pass filters that isolate fine detail. That pairing lets it strip rain artifacts and enhance structure at the same time, rather than in conflicting stages. Taking deraining as the test case, experiments show better performance than existing methods, at lower cost, in the authors' evaluation.
arxiv-2511-12519: Aung Phone Maw investigates a double series. It is built from two positive integer indices. Its terms involve a square root that combines the indices with three parameters. They also involve an exponential factor of a similar form. The work arrives at a functional property of that series. It relates the values of the series under changes in the parameters.
arxiv-2511-12719:
M. Houzet, T. Vakhtel, and J. S. Meyer predict a new effect in superconducting circuits, which they name the Bloch diode. The starting point is the Josephson diode effect, where a superconducting loop passes current more easily one way than the other. The authors describe a dual version built from a gate-tunable Cooper pair transistor placed in series with a highly resistive environment, tuned away from a half-integer gate charge.

In that setting, the asymmetry appears in voltage rather than current: the device should switch at different critical voltages for opposite polarities. The effect traces to an uneven dispersion of the transistor's Bloch bands. A Josephson junction array can supply the needed resistance, so the diode could be built with standard superconducting circuit methods. The paper is a theoretical prediction, offered as a target for experiments in quantum circuit labs.
arxiv-2511-13019:
Zheyuan Hu and four co-authors make one-step image generation cheaper and steadier. MeanFlow models learn to jump directly from noise to an image in a few steps. Training them in the usual autoencoder's latent space is expensive and unstable, and the decoder dominates sampling cost. The team moves MeanFlow into the latent space of a representation autoencoder, whose latents come from a pretrained vision encoder and carry rich semantics, paired with a lightweight decoder. Naive training there explodes gradients, so they stabilize it with trajectory-aware initialization and a two-stage scheme distilling from a flow matching teacher, then bootstrapping.

The payoff on ImageNet is concrete: one-step generation quality improved markedly over vanilla MeanFlow, sampling cost fell by over a third. Total training cost dropped by more than four fifths, with competitive results at the larger resolution too, and no guidance hyperparameters to tune.
arxiv-2511-13219:
Satvik Dixit and 4 co-authors introduce FoleyBench, a large test set for systems that create sound from video. Foley work means making effects that match what is seen on screen, in both content and timing. The authors note that most older test videos match their sound poorly and lean on speech and music.

FoleyBench holds five thousand clips, each with video, true audio, and a text caption where the sound source stays visible. Labels record source type, sound class, and clip length for close study of errors. The team tests several leading models on sound quality, timing, and match with video and text.
arxiv-2511-13319:
Chelsea McMurray and Hayder Tirmazi describe Whistledown, a privacy layer that scrubs prompts before they reach a cloud language model. People now share personal and sensitive matters with these models, and prompts about friends or coworkers can carry names and details they never meant to store. Companies face the same risk with internal talk.

Whistledown mixes pseudonyms, local differential privacy, and caching of past changes to protect prompts while keeping chat coherent. It runs with low cost on a user's own device, or inside a company gateway for staff use. No change to provider interfaces is needed, which makes trial use simple.
arxiv-2511-13819:
Basile Coron, Luis Ferroni, and Shiyue Li study ordered sets in combinatorics, called posets, and the polynomials tied to them. They define a new class, UMEL-shellable posets, using a labeling of edges that obeys set uniformity and order rules. The class covers many known families, from uniform matroids to braid and Dowling geometries.

Their main result shows that the Chow polynomials, augmented Chow polynomials, and chain polynomials of these posets have only real roots. That finding moves several open conjectures forward at once. For matroids, these polynomials also encode geometric data from related toric varieties, so the result links combinatorics with algebraic geometry.
arxiv-2511-14119:
Liuyi Jin, Amran Haroon, Radu Stoleru, and three co-authors present TeleEMS, a live video analytics system for the minutes before an ambulance arrives. Today's emergency infrastructure streams video one-to-one with little analysis, leaving dispatchers and medics to interpret noisy feeds under stress. TeleEMS clients run on phones, smart glasses, and desktops for bystanders, crews, and dispatchers alike.

An edge server carries a multi-party streaming backbone plus three analytics modules. One extracts and normalizes symptoms from speech with a specialized language model. Another estimates heart rate from video. A third fuses text and vital signs jointly. The goal is shared, analyzed situational awareness before EMTs reach the scene.
arxiv-2511-14419:
Xiaowei Xu, Justin Sonneck, Hongxiao Wang, and five co-authors compress microscope movies of migrating immune cells by keeping only the regions that matter. Their context is ComplexEye, a sixteen-lens microscope that films cells across a whole multiwell plate at high resolution, generating data faster than it can be stored or sent. FlowRoI finds the interesting regions using motion itself.

Optical flow between consecutive frames yields masks that reliably cover nearly all migrating cells. Frames and masks are then encoded together with JPEG2000 in a region-aware way, so fine detail is spent where the cells are. The pipeline runs about as fast as plain JPEG2000 encoding while greatly cutting storage for migration studies.
arxiv-2511-14619:
Marco Locatelli and four co-authors introduce a fuzzy method to learn partially observable decision models in healthcare from scarce data. Such models capture hidden patient states and treatment choices over time. Standard expectation maximization struggles when data are few or noisy. The team enrich expert knowledge as fuzzy pseudo counts inside the learning loop.

The method becomes a maximum a posteriori estimate guided by an expert fuzzy model. In synthetic medical simulations it beats standard learning under low data and high noise. A case study on myasthenia gravis recovers a clinically coherent model. The approach offers a practical tool when patient records are limited but expert insight is strong.
arxiv-2511-14719:
Yifan Wang, Liya Ji, Zhanghan Ke, Harry Yang, Ser-Nam Lim, and Qifeng Chen propose a zero-shot method for making synthetic videos look photorealistic. Simulators can generate endless driving or training footage, but its rendered look betrays it, limiting its use for training real systems. Their framework re-renders such video through a foundation diffusion model with no further fine-tuning, while guarding the original structure at several levels in both space and time.

Guidance comes from structure-aware information estimated from the synthetic video itself by an auxiliary model: depth maps, semantic maps, and edge maps that condition the denoising. Keeping those anchors ensures the enhanced video matches the original in structure and meaning, not just in gloss. The authors present the approach as simple, general, and powerful for simulator pipelines.
arxiv-2511-15119:
Velimir Todorovski, Kwang Hak Kim, and two co-authors open a two-part study of parking a wheeled robot by smooth feedback alone. The robot is a nonholonomic unicycle, which cannot slide sideways, so parking it is a classic hard control problem. It has long been known that smooth feedback in polar coordinates can stabilize it, even from any starting pose.

Part one builds a modular design: one control picks forward speed to tame the distance to the target, leaving steering free to be stabilized on its own. Families of steering laws follow from passivity, backstepping, and integrator forwarding, each with a strict energy-like certificate of convergence. Barrier versions also respect angular limits, setting up part two's extensions.
arxiv-2511-15219:
Kwang Hak Kim, Velimir Todorovski, and Miroslav Krstić deliver part two of a study on parking a nonholonomic unicycle robot by feedback. Part one built modular laws with energy-like certificates; this part drops the modular split and chases stronger traits in one design. The target traits include global exponential stability, robustness to actuator miscalibration, adaptation, and guaranteed arrival within a set time.

Their nonmodular backstepping laws work whether the robot can roll both ways or only forward. A general framework built from strict certificate families yields feedbacks that are inverse optimal, meaning each secretly minimizes a meaningful cost, which buys robustness to input errors and saturation for free. Safety constraints on the state are enforced as well.
arxiv-2511-15719:
William Brach, Kristián Košťál, and Lukas Galke Poech propose Chain of Summaries, a method that turns web content into dense plain-text summaries that language models can actually use. Web pages often come in formats models handle poorly, and long pages overflow their context limits. Their method borrows a dialectical pattern: draft a summary, question its gaps, then revise it into a stronger version.

Repeated questioning and revision produce a general-purpose summary meant to serve present and future information needs. On three question-answering data sets, the summaries beat plain model baselines by large margins and specialized summarizers by smaller ones. Answers drawn from the summaries even beat answers from the source content, while using far fewer tokens.
arxiv-2511-16219:
Federico Escudero, Francisco Guinea, and Zhen Zhan review how strain changes the geometry of moiré materials. These are patterned superlattices formed when two thin crystal layers are stacked with a small twist or mismatch. Such materials host many interaction-driven electronic phases, and stretching a layer is a strong way to tune them.

Starting from the elasticity theory of two-dimensional materials, the review covers uniaxial, shear, and biaxial strain. It then applies the theory to twisted and strained bilayers with hexagonal and monoclinic lattices. Special patterns, including near one-dimensional and square moiré layouts, are predicted and matched to recent strain techniques. Readers get both the math of deformed moiré geometry and a survey of what experiments have achieved.
arxiv-2511-16619:
Satyam Gaba improves long tailed object detection, where many categories have only a few examples, with balanced group softmax and metric learning. Standard detectors bias toward frequent classes and miss rare ones. A large vocabulary data set with more than a thousand categories and well over one hundred thousand images supplies the testbed. A two stage detector architecture is enhanced within a balanced grouping framework.

Reported accuracy sets a new best mark on that benchmark, edging the prior record. The author also hypothesizes that rare class features form small dense clusters inside head class regions. That geometry would explain persistent confusion between rare and common categories. Metric learning aims to separate those clusters. Rare category detection remains central to real world vision deployment.
arxiv-2511-16819:
Arash Omidi, Tanmay Mishra, and Mads R. Almassalkhi describe a two-site experimental testbed for hybrid energy systems at the University of Vermont, built to prototype advanced control and optimization before field deployment. One site is an on-campus laboratory; the other is an off-campus solar and meteorological station, linked under one monitoring and communication architecture.

The platform mixes hardware-in-the-loop simulation with a reconfigurable set of kilovolt-ampere-scale assets, supporting real-time data collection, model validation, and control implementation in one loop. A demonstration experiment runs a battery system smoothing solar photovoltaic output inside the hardware-in-the-loop setup. The authors offer the testbed as shared infrastructure for testing how batteries, solar generation, and controls behave together at realistic scale.
arxiv-2511-17319:
Qipan Wang and five co-authors present ATMPlace, a placement tool for 2.5D integrated circuits, where multiple chiplets sit side by side on an interposer. Placing dozens of chiplets well means balancing wire length against heat and mechanical warping, and older tools relied on slow simulations or ignored reliability altogether. ATMPlace is the first analytical placer for this setting that optimizes all three goals together, using compact physics-based models of temperature and warpage.

The tool produces Pareto-optimal placements, the set of layouts where no goal can improve without another suffering. Against two recent rivals, it improved wire length substantially in geometric mean, cut peak temperatures by several percent, reduced warpage by up to about a quarter, and ran roughly ten times faster. The authors present the framework as a general base for exploring next-generation 2.5D designs quickly.
arxiv-2511-17419:
Yeamin Kaiser, Muhammed Tasnim Bin Anwar, and Bholanath Das present DS-Span, a method that mines discriminative subgraphs to serve as features for graph learning. Graphs are turned into vectors by finding patterns whose presence characterizes each graph, an approach prized for interpretability. Earlier mining pipelines ran in several phases, cost heavily, and chose patterns without coupling them to the classification task at hand.

DS-Span unifies pattern growth, pruning, and supervision-driven scoring in a single pass through the search space. A coverage cap stops exploration of any graph once it is well represented, and information gain steers selection toward class-separating patterns with little redundancy. On benchmark tests, the mined feature sets were more compact and more discriminative than those of multi-stage methods, with equal or better accuracy at much lower runtime. The authors offer unified mining as an interpretable base for graph representation learning.
arxiv-2511-17519:
Md Habibur Rahman and four co-authors build SAJD, a self-adaptive defense against jamming attacks on open 5G radio access networks. Open RAN architectures are modular and programmable, with intelligent applications running in near-real time, but a jammer can still severely degrade them. SAJD closes the loop: a machine-learning application infers jamming interference from live signals. Companion applications watch for model drift, label fresh data without supervision, retrain the model, and redeploy it without interrupting service.

The labeling step uses live network performance indicators, and training runs through an integrated open-source pipeline. On an O-RAN-compliant testbed, SAJD beat a state-of-the-art detector trained offline with manual labels, in both accuracy and adaptability, across dynamic and previously unseen interference conditions. The authors present continuous self-retraining as the way to keep learned defenses current against an evolving threat.
arxiv-2511-17719:
Mátyás Domokos and Barna Schefler compare two versions of the Noether number, a quantity from invariant theory that bounds how complex the invariants of a finite group can be. One version uses all invariants, while the separating version uses only those needed to tell orbits apart.

For groups with a large cyclic subgroup, and for certain products with a dihedral group, the two numbers turn out to be equal. The authors also find the smallest non abelian groups where the separating number is strictly smaller. They settle the separating value for every group of order up to sixteen.
arxiv-2511-18019:
Igor Klep, Victor Magron, Tobias Metzlaff, and Jie Wang reduce the cost of polynomial optimization, where a hierarchy of semidefinite programs gives bounds but grows expensive. Many such problems are unchanged under a finite symmetry group, and their polynomials use only a few terms, two structures that can both be exploited.

They first rewrite the matrices in a symmetry adapted basis, which splits them into smaller blocks. Then they apply term sparsity on each block to shrink the variables further. Benchmarks on quartic problems with dihedral, cyclic, and symmetric group symmetry compare the method with existing techniques and show the savings.
arxiv-2511-18119:
Amirhossein Nazerian and three co-authors build a unified framework for judging whether a discrete time network passes or blocks signals from its environment. Many real systems, from opinion dynamics to population models, are naturally discrete, and an open network receives inputs at some nodes and releases responses at others.

They combine the network's transfer function with a controllability Gramian, using a norm that gauges amplification. They define a lean index from the Gramian's trace and eigenvalues. Applied to many real networks from biology, technology, and ecology, the method finds consistent structural signatures of passing and blocking behavior, informing control and network design.
arxiv-2511-18319:
Xian Yeow Lee, Lasitha Vidyaratne, Gregory Sin, Ahmed Farahat, and Chetan Gupta build a compact world model for agents that inspect hazardous places. Such an agent follow a high-level goal and act precisely, for instance centring a found object in a drone's view. Language models alone manage the spatial grounding task only a little over half the time, and full world models that could help by simulating actions are heavy to train.

Their task-specific model learns, in a shared latent space, how each action shifts the state, using only supervision about goal states. Global action codes and paired training losses keep learning stable. The design aims to give small agents a cheap way to roll out candidate moves before committing, lifting control success without a giant model.
arxiv-2511-18519:
Xinlin Zhuang and 13 co-authors adapt the CLIP image text model to new fields by picking data with care, not by bulk. Most adaptation tweaks the training method or pre-trains on huge field sets. Data choice itself has drawn little study, though a small apt set may beat a huge mixed one.

Their method, CHIPS, scores each image text pair by three aims. A curvature aware score checks faith to the target field, a sketched estimator keeps the score cheap at scale, and a relevance weight guards broad skill from loss. Scores blend target gain with retention of general skill. Strong results from picked data would cut the cost of field adaptation. The data centric lens is the shift on offer.
arxiv-2511-18619:
Maanas Taneja treats prompt tuning for language models as a search over a graph. Model scores can crash with tiny prompt tweaks, so hand craft is fraught. Library tools like DSPy tune by demos. Taneja's route casts each prompt as a node, with edges for set edits like cuts, added examples, or reordering.

Beam search and random walks then roam that graph, scored on dev sets with weak branches pruned. Even a shallow search, a beam of two and two steps deep, lifts scores across five tasks: sentiment sorting, question answering, summaries, reasoning, and inference. The frame recasts prompt craft as classic state space search. Cheap search may rival heavier demo based tuning.
arxiv-2511-18919:
Ruiying Liu, Yuanzhi Liang, Haibin Huang, Tianshu Yu, and Chi Zhang improve a reinforcement learning method used to post train image and video generators. A prompt can match many valid images and an image can fit many prompts. So reward models give uncertain, weak signals, and training can waste effort on noisy feedback or ignore reliable feedback.

Their method adds a semantic prior anchor and models reward uncertainty explicitly. It allocates trust between groups of samples by consistency with the prior and sharpens scores within a group so confident differences count more. Across image and video tasks it improves semantic alignment, visual quality, and convergence speed.
arxiv-2511-19019:
Nguyen Duc Minh Quang, Chang Liu, Huy-Trung Nguyen, Shuangyang Li, Derrick Wing Kwan Ng, and Wei Xiang build a system that predicts radio maps for low-altitude drone networks. As unmanned aerial vehicles spread into logistics, surveillance, and emergency work, keeping them connected is hard: they move in three dimensions, user density shifts over time, and power budgets are tight. Base station power itself rises and falls with demand, so the radio environment never sits still.

Radio maps chart how signal power spreads through space and guide network tuning, but most are static or built offline. The team's framework instead learns how the three-dimensional map evolves over time and forecasts its next state. That foresight could let operators steer power and coverage in step with a moving fleet.
arxiv-2511-19119:
Qirui Wang and five co-authors introduce MonoSR, a data set for spatial reasoning from a single image. Judging depth and layout from one view matters for robots and self-driving cars, yet most earlier work used indoor scenes and several views at once. MonoSR covers indoor, outdoor, and object-centered scenes and supports several kinds of questions.

Alongside the data, the team tests advanced vision-language models and finds clear limits on this harder task. They also study whether extra side information helps a model reason from one image. The results give design guidance for future models and set a base for open-world spatial reasoning.
arxiv-2511-19219:
Christopher W. Wächtler and Gloria Platero show how engineered energy loss can synchronize quantum spins arranged in symmetric rings. Gauge fields combined with lattice geometry can freeze motion through complete destructive interference, an effect tied to the Aharonov-Bohm phenomenon. Adding carefully designed dissipation to that frozen setting changes the picture.

The spins in each ring motif settle into robust synchronized motion, no matter how they start, and become entangled within the motif. The pattern works for cyclic symmetries of any order. Coupling several motifs, with extra shared dissipation across their spins, brings the whole set into full synchrony, linking flux effects, dissipation, and collective quantum behavior.
arxiv-2511-19419:
S Buson and nine co-authors measure the lensing delay in PKS 1830-211, a blazar whose light is bent and split by a galaxy in front of it. Because the two brightest images of the blazar travel different paths, its flares arrive twice, separated by a delay that reveals the lens geometry. At gamma-ray energies the images cannot be resolved directly, so the delay must be read from the pattern in the light curve recorded by the Fermi telescope.

With better light curves, a long outburst to work with, and improved time-series methods, the team analyses six separate data segments. They find a delay of about twenty days with a tight uncertainty and a very low chance of a false detection. A new simulation-based method also estimates how much brighter one image is than the other.
arxiv-2511-19819:
Guowei Dai, Yingxin Sun, Juncheng Wei, and Yong Zhang give a partial positive answer to two old conjectures about domains in the plane. The Schiffer and Berenstein problems ask whether an overdetermined boundary value problem, with both the solution and its slope fixed at the edge, forces the domain to be a disk. Counterexamples would need special shapes.

For uniformly convex domains with smooth connected boundary, a solution at a large eigenvalue forces the disk, using a new two-point stationary-phase defect tool. A matching result covers the reversed boundary conditions under weaker smoothness. The high-frequency route thus settles these cases of the conjectures.
arxiv-2511-20519:
Bühler, Hug, and Thäle scatter random planes in curved space and watch dimensions grow. Their 2025 paper studies Poisson processes of k-planes in hyperbolic space. Hyperbolic space curves negatively and grows exponentially in volume. Random planes slice through a large ball in that space. Their total intersection volume behaves strangely compared to flat geometry.

In Euclidean space a central limit theorem always applies. In hyperbolic space it fails when twice k exceeds d plus one. The limit there is a non-Gaussian infinitely divisible variable. The authors ask what happens as dimension d itself grows. Depending on how fast k grows with d, limits differ sharply. Variance-normalized sums can converge to a standard Gaussian law. Other regimes collapse to a degenerate limit instead. Rescaling the Lévy measures reveals another limit law. Fixed codimension yields a non-Gaussian limit. Growing codimension restores Gaussian behavior in the end.
arxiv-2511-20619:
Xu, Frías Pérez, and Yang work backward from a quantum state to the laws that make it special. Their 2025 paper extracts conserved operators from tensor network states. Given a projected entangled pair state, which Hamiltonians hold it as an eigenstate? That inverse question matters for certifying quantum simulators. Parent Hamiltonians usually come from a standard construction only.

Their method differentiates a generating function to get structure factors. Conserved local operators hide in the kernel of those matrices. Frustration-free parents of the AKLT state were recovered cleanly. A non-frustration-free parent for an XX model ground state followed. The short-range RVB state gained a four-site plaquette parent. Its locality beats what standard routes deliver. A deformed toric code state sits as an excited eigenstate family. All its string tensions share one energy in their Hamiltonian. Such mid-spectrum eigenstates hint at quantum many-body scars.
arxiv-2511-20819:
Cyril Geismar and colleagues build in 2025 the first statistical tests for a question outbreak investigators face daily: who infected whom? Reconstruction models never return one certain transmission tree; they return an epidemic forest, a bundle of plausible trees. Different methods and assumptions yield different forests, and until now nobody could say whether two forests differ or wobble by chance.

Their framework tries two tests: a chi-square test counting how often specific transmission pairs appear, and PERMANOVA, a permutational analysis comparing whole tree structures. On simulated forests grown under different offspring distributions, how many people each case infects, both tests achieved perfect specificity once forests held 100 or more trees. Identical dynamics were never falsely declared different. But PERMANOVA beat the chi-square test on sensitivity, catching real differences across every epidemic and forest size. The tools ship in the R package mixtree, giving epidemiologists a way to validate reconstruction methods.
arxiv-2511-21219:
Control researchers Jiayun Li and Yilin Mo present a data-driven way to predict the future of a noisy linear system in 2025. Their target is a stochastic LTI system, a machine whose response rules stay fixed over time but are shaken by randomness. Rather than first identifying the system's hidden parameters, their behavioral model samples likely future outputs directly from recorded input-output trajectories and the planned future inputs.

Li and Mo prove that the model's sample distribution converges as the library of past trajectories grows, and they give an explicit formula for the convergence rate. They also show that the gap to the Kalman filter's posterior, the best answer available when all parameters are known, shrinks exponentially as more past samples are used. Plugged into predictive controllers, the model performed as the theory promised in numerical tests.
arxiv-2511-21419:
Wen-Yuan Yu, Hou-Jun Lü, Xiao Tian, Liang-Jun Chen, and En-Wei Liang dissect one of the most distant cosmic explosions on record in 2025. The long gamma-ray burst GRB 250114A, caught by the Swift satellite, sits at redshift 4.732, measured with the Very Large Telescope. Its blast arrived in three episodes divided by quiet gaps of tens to hundreds of seconds, a stuttering pattern that hints at a long-lived engine.

Yu and his coauthors note significant X-ray emission even during the quiet gaps, evidence the central engine never switched off. Fitting the X-ray light curve with a magnetar, a newborn neutron star with a monstrous magnetic field, they infer a field near 13 times 10 to the 15 gauss. The magnetar's initial spin period comes out near 14 milliseconds. Both values are physically reasonable once the jet geometry is included. The burst otherwise resembles other high-redshift bursts.
arxiv-2511-21519:
Yiyang Jiang and six coauthors automate a painstaking blood test that diagnoses autoimmune disease, in 2025. Antinuclear antibody testing reveals lupus, Sjögren's syndrome, and scleroderma through fluorescent patterns on cells, but reading the images manually is slow and takes years of training. Over 100 antibody types can coexist in one sample, so each image carries many overlapping patterns, a multi-instance, multi-label problem that defeats ordinary classifiers.

Jiang and his coauthors mimic how human labelers work: find the sub-regions whose patterns are consistent, then aggregate their labels. Three modules do this, an instance sampler that suppresses low-confidence patches, a dispatcher that assigns provisional labels by distinguishability, and a self-paced weighting that adjusts training to observed labels. On their antibody dataset the framework beat the best prior method by 7.0 points of macro F1 and 12.6 points of mean average precision. It ranked top-two across public medical benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-21619:
Lorenzo Nespoli and Vasco Medici size home and neighborhood batteries with simple rules tuned under uncertainty, in 2025. Batteries shave demand peaks, but choosing their capacity with deterministic model predictive control flatters the economics: the promised cost of energy assumes perfect foresight that real operation never has. Rule-based controllers are transparent and cheap, yet usually tuned as if the future were known exactly.

Nespoli and Medici tune the rules stochastically instead, optimizing expected performance over uncertain conditions with a gradient-free method, then test on full-year profiles from real meters. Stochastically sized systems come out smaller, but their predicted levelised cost of energy lands much closer to what operation actually delivers, and running performance beats the deterministic benchmark. For investors, that honesty about returns matters as much as raw performance. The approach stays simple, interpretable, and cheap to tune and deploy.
arxiv-2511-21819:
Kun and colleagues demonstrate a strange quantum effect: a single photon, split at a beam splitter so it takes a superposition of two paths, can be entangled with itself. Theorists predicted thirty years ago that such a photon could violate a Bell inequality, the test ruling out purely local explanations of quantum correlations, but earlier demonstrations needed complex homodyne measurements.

The team's trick is self-referential measurement: they prepare two copies of the same single-photon state and let one photon serve as the phase reference for the other, avoiding homodyne detection entirely. Their measured CHSH values reached 2.71 plus or minus 0.09 and 2.23 plus or minus 0.07 for the two measurement schemes used, both above the classical limit of 2 that Bell tests use as their dividing line. The simpler route could extend these tests to other platforms and more general mode-entangled states.
arxiv-2511-21919:
Sena and colleagues speed up finding bubble-like structures in pangenome graphs, which represent many individuals' DNA variation at once. The structures, called snarls and superbubbles, mark variant sites and underpin genotyping, distance indexing, haplotype sampling, and variant annotation across computational pangenomics. Snarls can be quadratically many in the graph's size, and since their introduction in 2018 with the vg toolkit, nobody had published a linear-time method to find them all.

Their key observation: every such structure is separated from the graph by just two vertices, so the SPQR tree decomposition can guide the search. Their unified SPQR framework yields the first linear-time algorithm for all snarls, plus a simpler new linear-time superbubble algorithm. As BubbleFinder, it ran up to twice as fast as vg on snarls and up to 50 times faster than BubbleGun on superbubbles.
arxiv-2511-22119:
Li, Zhang, Wen, and colleagues build PromptMiner, a black-box attack that recovers the secret text prompt behind a generated image. Carefully engineered prompts are valuable, traded on marketplaces, and worth stealing; earlier recovery methods needed white-box access to the generator, huge labeled training sets, or settled for plain captioning. PromptMiner splits the job in two: a reinforcement learning phase reconstructs the image's main subject, then a fuzzing-driven search phase hunts down the stylistic modifiers that captioning misses.

Across multiple datasets and diffusion backbones it reaches CLIP similarity up to 0.958 and text alignment up to 0.751, beating all baselines, and on in-the-wild images from unknown generators it still tops the strongest baseline by 7.5 percent in CLIP similarity. It also holds up under defensive perturbations. The authors note the same technique serves legitimate forensics: attribution, provenance analysis, and watermark validation.
arxiv-2511-22319:
Veronica, Reiprich, Pacaud, and a large collaboration test whether black-hole jets actually balance the cooling of hot gas in galaxy cluster centers. Without reheating, the intracluster medium would cool and flow inward at up to a thousand solar masses per year. Yet stars barely form, so jets from the central galaxy's active nucleus are the prime suspect for returning the energy. The team matched the first eROSITA all-sky survey catalog with ASKAP radio observations, identifying radio sources for the brightest galaxies in 134 of 151 clusters.

Radio luminosity rises weakly with cluster X-ray luminosity, and jet power tracks cooling luminosity in cool-core clusters with large scatter. At a representative cooling luminosity the jets supply on average only about 13 to 22 percent of the energy needed to offset losses, least effectively in the most massive clusters. The simple jet-heating picture looks incomplete.
arxiv-2511-22519:
Zarzecki, Szymczak, Szczurek, and Deja open up a protein design model to see how it thinks. RFdiffusion generates new protein backbones, but its representations are opaque, so design is sampling and filtering rather than engineering. Borrowing sparse autoencoders from mechanistic interpretability, the team decomposes the model's dense activations into a sparse set of features. Each feature is tied to a concept. The team focuses on features governing secondary structure, the helices and strands of a protein.

The unsupervised features proved meaningful, and many were antagonistic, pushing helix and strand formation in opposite directions at once. That insight yields FoldSAE's steering mechanism: a single tunable dial adjusting how much helix or strand a generated protein contains while keeping the backbone plausible. Block-ablation experiments also located which network parts matter most for structure formation. The authors frame the result as a step from blind sampling toward precise protein engineering.
arxiv-2511-22619:
The Project Team behind this survey maps AI deception, where systems induce false beliefs to secure outcomes benefiting themselves. Once speculative, such behaviour is now demonstrated in language models, agents, and frontier systems. The survey defines deception, using signalling theory from animal behaviour studies. It then organises the research into a deception cycle with two halves. One half covers emergence, how deception arises. The other covers treatment, how it is detected and addressed.

On emergence, the authors identify incentives at three levels and three capability preconditions: perception, planning, and performing. Triggers include supervision gaps and distribution shifts. On treatment, they catalogue detection methods, external and internal, plus over twenty benchmarks and mitigation strategies. They argue for audits that combine technical, community, and governance efforts. Their synthesis stresses that deception is incentivised by default in misaligned systems. It grows complex as agents gain memory, and it spreads across modalities.
arxiv-2511-22819:
Wang, Léger, Lai, and Buckmaster sharpen neural computations of fluid blow-ups until only rounding error is left. Recent work discovered unstable self-similar singularity solutions for fluid equations, porous media and Boussinesq among them. Unstable solutions develop gradients so extreme that training residuals stayed too large for validation, masking the origin signals that fix the scaling parameter.

Their fix reweights the physics residual by gradient size, so regions stop dominating and origin signals get amplified, within a multi-stage architecture. Residuals fell to double-precision round-off, around ten to the minus thirteen, across the Córdoba-Córdoba-Fontelos model's unstable solutions. They also fell between ten to the minus eleven and ten to the minus thirteen for two-dimensional porous media flow. The precision confirmed an inaccessible fourth unstable solution and uncovered a family of unstable Schrödinger solitons, supplying the accuracy computer-assisted proofs demand.
arxiv-2511-23119:
Liu and colleagues build Dripper, a tool that extracts the main content from web pages, stripping navigation, ads, and boilerplate so the text can feed AI training datasets. Big generative models parse pages well but are expensive, run into context limits, and sometimes hallucinate the output format. So the team aimed for the same quality from a small, cheap model instead.

Three tricks make it work: a simplification step cuts the HTML to 22 percent of its original token count while keeping the structure that matters. Extraction is recast as classifying blocks of the page rather than generating text. A controlled decoder forbids invalid outputs. With only a 0.6-billion-parameter model, Dripper reached a ROUGE-N F1 score of 81.58 percent on the team's new WebMainBench of over 7,800 human-annotated pages, beating every baseline they tested on all benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-23219:
Das and colleagues revisit the Witten-O'Raifeartaigh potential, a two-winged energy landscape for the inflaton field with a steep left wing and a flatter right one, inside warm inflation. In warm inflation, the field steadily leaks energy into a radiation bath as it rolls. Warm inflation tolerates steep slopes that would kill slow-roll inflation, and it needs no separate reheating phase afterward, so the neglected steep wing becomes usable.

They show warm inflation on the steep left wing matches current cosmological data excellently, in a joint analysis of Planck, ACT, and DESI observations. Cold inflation had previously used only the flat wing. The two wings are normalized separately to bridge the huge gap between inflation and dark-energy scales, and the field is kept dissipative on the right wing. The same potential then yields transient dark energy today, unifying the universe's two accelerated eras in one model.
arxiv-2512-00219:
Correcting grammar in Indic languages is hard because training data is scarce, scripts vary, and word forms are rich. Akhil Rajeev presents a minimal-edit approach to the problem in a 2025 study. The setup uses instruction-tuned large language models with conservative decoding.

A mid-size Gemma model is instruction-tuned efficiently, using four-bit precision and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with Alpaca-style formatting. The augmentation-free design avoids inventing extra training data. Minimal edits matter because a correction tool should fix errors without rewriting a writer's voice. That restraint matters most for low-resource languages with few digital tools. Indic languages serve hundreds of millions of speakers, so the gap in tooling is significant.
arxiv-2512-00619:
Neural networks that keep learning new tasks tend to forget old ones, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. Goutham Nalagatla and Shreyas Grandhe compare memory replay strategies for continual learning in 2025, inspired by neuroscience. Biological memory consolidation replays experiences during rest to stabilize them.

Their framework uses generative replay built on predictive coding principles to reduce forgetting. It is compared against backpropagation-based strategies on equal footing. Continual learning decides whether deployed AI can adapt for years without periodic retraining from scratch, so biologically inspired replay is a promising direction. Predictive coding is a brain-inspired theory of how cortex predicts its inputs. Generative replay creates fresh training examples instead of storing old data. For teams who field aides that must learn for years, the gain is a path with no need to keep old data on file. That helps on both cost and trust.
arxiv-2512-00919:
Dimitri Meunier and a large team improve causal estimation in a 2025 statistics paper. Researchers often want the effect of a treatment when hidden confounders blur the data. Instrumental variable regression uses an outside lever, the instrument, to isolate the treatment's true effect without seeing every confounder.

A known approach learns spectral features, directions that capture the strongest link between treatment and instrument. Those features ignore the outcome variable, which wastes information. The team's outcome-aware spectral features use the outcome too. Sharper features could give more accurate effect estimates in health and economics studies.
arxiv-2512-01419:
Tushar Pranav and co-authors test vision-language models on culture in Southeast Asia. These models pair images with text well. Yet they lean toward Western views. That lean hurts their use in regions with rich, distinct cultures.

The team built RICE-VL, a test that spans eleven ASEAN countries. It checks how well models grasp food, dress, rites, and daily life there. Scores show where models fail to read local sense. A fair test is a first step toward models that serve users in that region with more care and less bias.
arxiv-2512-01519:
Can Polat and Erchin Serpedin build a test for how models learn atomic forces. Most models fit whole molecules or crystals at once. They learn links, not the true pair forces. Yet bonds, charge shifts, and coupling all stem from pairs of atoms.

Their test, QuantumCanvas, shows atomic scenes in visual form. Models must learn pair forces from those scenes. Pair-level skill should move better to new materials. The test gives the field a shared yardstick for a skill that whole-molecule fits often hide. Visual scenes make the test open to teams outside physics coding, since the input looks like data a vision model already knows.
arxiv-2512-02119:
Wilson loops are the workhorse observables of gauge theory, tracing a particle's path through the force field and recording its effect. Bercel Boldis, Gregory Korchemsky, and Alessandro Testa present in 2025 a new technique for computing supersymmetric Wilson loops in the ABJM theory exactly.

Their method uses supersymmetric localization, a technique that collapses a hard path integral to something computable, and it works for any rank of the gauge group and any Chern-Simons level. ABJM theory is a central example in the holographic dictionary between gravity and quantum fields. Exact loop values give that dictionary some of its sharpest entries for testing both sides.
arxiv-2512-02219:
Stars shine with magnetic activity powered by dynamos deep inside, where hot plasma churns and rotates. G. Nigro studies in 2025 how heat is transported by convection in a model of that magnetoconvection, pushing into extreme parameter regimes that direct numerical simulations cannot yet reach.

The model couples convection with a self-generated magnetic field under very high Rayleigh and Prandtl numbers, conditions typical of astrophysical plasmas. Finding an asymptotic law for the heat transport there tells theorists how the transport scales when brute-force simulation fails. Such laws anchor models of stellar activity and planetary magnetospheres, which govern space weather and stellar evolution.
arxiv-2512-02619:
Timo Aukusti Laine maps the meaning spaces of large language models onto quantum circuits. Language models store word and sentence meaning as points in a high dimensional space, called embeddings. Quantum mechanics also works with complex valued states and their overlaps.

Laine links the two views directly, treating semantic closeness as a quantum style measurement. The study shows that estimating how similar two meanings are is feasible on quantum hardware. Such mappings could one day let quantum machines help sort and compare meaning, though the field remains young and exploratory. The map from words to states is still rough, but it gives both fields a shared tongue to test.
arxiv-2512-02719:
Julian Ma, Jun Wang, and Zafeirios Fountas test whether language models quietly reason like good statisticians. Humans combine noisy cues in near optimal Bayesian ways in perception tasks, without being taught the math. Explicit reasoning in models is well studied, but their implicit strategies are not.

The team asks if models blend multimodal cues optimally without instruction or special training. Emergent Bayesian behavior would suggest models absorb sound uncertainty handling from data alone. Findings here inform how much to trust model judgments under noise, a daily issue in medicine, law, and finance applications. Trust in a tool grows when its gut calls match the math a good judge would use on the same facts.
arxiv-2512-02919:
P. Narayanan and A. Raghuram test a guiding principle of number theory by direct computation. The principle says a congruence between two objects should force a matching congruence between special values of their L-functions. L-functions encode deep arithmetic data in a single analytic package.

The pair studies Rankin-Selberg L-functions built from pairs of holomorphic cuspforms. Their computational investigation checks whether value ratios obey the predicted congruences. Evidence of this kind guides proof efforts, showing which cases hold numerically before scarce theory time is spent on them. Counts first, proof next is a sound pace for a field where each proof can eat years of a life in work.
arxiv-2512-03219:
A bird song model may also hear whales. Andrea Burns and co-authors test Perch 2.0, a bioacoustics model, on underwater sounds in this 2025 work. The model was trained on many thousands of species, from birds to insects.

Almost no marine mammal audio was in its training data. Still, the team tests it on ocean tasks using few-shot transfer, where a model adapts from few examples. Good transfer would save the cost of training new models for each habitat. It could speed up wildlife monitoring in the sea. Few-shot success would let one strong model serve both land and sea wildlife surveys.
arxiv-2512-03619:
Muhammed Burak Kizil and co-authors let film directors boss video-generating AI around in plain words. Motion, of both objects and cameras, is what makes generated scenes cinematic, yet text prompts steer it crudely. Their 2025 system, LAMP, hires a large language model as motion planner.

The model writes its plan in a small language borrowed from cinematography conventions. Software then converts those structured programs, deterministically, into explicit three-dimensional paths for subjects and camera alike. A large procedural dataset pairs descriptions with programs and trajectories for training. LAMP beat rival methods on controllability and fidelity to user intent in their tests.
arxiv-2512-03819:
Depth sensors made three-dimensional point clouds easy to capture, but sending them over a wireless link is expensive. Junlin Chang and colleagues propose a leaner route in a 2025 machine learning letter. Instead of transmitting the raw features describing a cloud, their sender predicts a set of combination weights and sends only those.

At the receiver, a stored pool of mutually orthogonal semantic features is mixed by the received weights to rebuild the cloud.
