Many news systems are black boxes, which gives editors little insight into why a story is pushed. Their system uses fuzzy neural networks that learn readable rules from reader behaviour.

By setting a threshold, users can trade rule length against clarity. The four authors test the system on two public news data sets, MIND and EB-NeRD. It predicts clicks about as well as several established baselines while still producing readable rules. Those rules also reveal patterns in how audiences consume news. Editors could use such patterns to match story choices to the habits of a target audience.
arxiv-2601-04119:
Martin Ehler and Karlheinz Gröchenig derive exact size limits for sampling measures on the unit sphere. Good sampling there means Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities hold, a pair of bounds that tie sums over samples to true integrals. Most past work left the constants hidden, which limits practical use.

Using sharp localisation estimates for Jacobi polynomials, Ehler and Gröchenig bound the measure of geodesic balls at the natural scale from above and below, with fully explicit constants. Those bounds then limit the Hausdorff volume of sampling sets in each dimension. For sampling curves they obtain best possible lower bounds on length. The fully measured form lets users check a concrete sampling design against the theory, rather than trusting that some constant exists.
arxiv-2601-04219:
Yuxin Liu, Zeqing Song, Jiong Lou, Chentao Wu, and Jie Li present AgentTutor, a teaching system built for many-turn, personalised lessons. Current smart education tools often answer one question at a time. They cannot gauge a learner's level, shift strategy from live feedback, or grow beyond one-off replies.

AgentTutor joins a multi-agent system powered by a large language model with a personal learning profile for each learner. The profile tracks status, goals, tastes, and study materials in varied forms, and teaching plans update as learning proceeds. Five modules handle splitting the curriculum, assessing the learner, choosing strategy, reflecting on teaching, and remembering knowledge and experience. Across benchmark data sets, the five authors report clear gains in learner performance and strong quality in multi-turn teaching against baselines.
arxiv-2601-04319:
Stavros Pastras, Panos A. Patsis, and E. Athanassoula study how gas moves through a barred galaxy whose underlying stellar orbits form unusually large loops near the bar's ends, in a 2026 arXiv paper. In that zone several orbit families overlap and chaos rules, so the gas shocks that trace spiral structure might be expected to bend with the loops toward the galaxy's corotation circle.

To test the flow they run the same model through two very different hydrodynamics codes, the mesh-free particle method SPH and the adaptive-mesh code RAMSES. Both agree that the big loops do not pull the shocks inward. The shocks bypass the loop regions at an angle, while dense gas tails stream from the loop zone toward the straight shock lines. The two codes, they conclude, give complementary views of the same machinery.
arxiv-2601-04719:
Maanas Taneja and Purab Shingvi squeeze the memory that chokes long language model conversations, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The key-value cache, which stores attention context so the model need not recompute it, grows linearly with sequence length and can outweigh the model itself. Their fix is to quantize the cache to eight-bit integers on the GPU, cutting its footprint fourfold — provided the compression is fast and the rounding does not corrupt attention.

They built four CUDA kernels — naive, tiled, coarsened, and vectorized — and benchmarked them up to a billion elements. The vectorized kernel runs dramatically faster than CPU baselines while keeping reconstruction error tiny and attention score error small even for very wide attention heads. The measured overhead sits in the tens of milliseconds, supporting their claim that integer quantization is a practical pressure valve for inference.
arxiv-2601-05219:
One labelled example is sometimes all a new task offers, and Maja Waldron's 2026 paper adds trustworthy uncertainty estimates to that setting. One-shot prediction adapts a pretrained foundation model using a single example, but it lacks principled uncertainty quantification. Conformal prediction gives finite-sample coverage guarantees, yet standard split conformal methods waste scarce data on splitting and lean on a single predictor, both costly when labels are precious.

Waldron proposes CAOS, which blends several one-shot predictors, weighting them adaptively, and calibrates with a leave-one-out scheme that uses every labelled point. Honest uncertainty from one example matters in fields like medicine and science, where a new category may have exactly one confirmed case. A bare prediction is not enough to act on.
arxiv-2601-05319:
Teo Muñoz-Darias and 4 co-authors review accretion disc winds in X-ray binaries in a 2026 paper. X-ray binaries pair a black hole or neutron star with a normal star whose gas it pulls in through an accretion disc. Theory long expected large, massive outflows from those discs, yet firm proof of them arrived only in the 2000s, when detections finally caught up with predictions.

The review summarizes two decades of observational progress, with wind phenomenology now seen across X-ray, ultraviolet, optical, and near-infrared regimes. Disc winds are now seen as a routine feature of these systems, perhaps a universal one. They matter because winds carry away mass and energy that would otherwise feed the compact object, reshaping how binaries evolve and shine.
arxiv-2601-05719:
Jun Usami and Hiroshi Fukuyama report, in a 2026 paper, evidence for a novel superfluid phase in the second layer of helium-4 on graphite. Superfluidity means flow without friction, here in an atom-thin film at temperatures near absolute zero. Earlier studies disagreed partly because different samples and substrates introduced uncertainty.

By running torsional-oscillator and heat-capacity tests on one and the same sample down to very low temperature, the authors removed that ambiguity. The new phase shows both friction-free flow and enhanced viscoelasticity across a finite density range. That combination supports a proposed superfluid liquid-crystal picture. A random Josephson network analysis suggests the reported way superfluid density changes with heat likely stems from substrate imperfections. Both tests ran on one and the same sample, so the two results describe the same thing, not two close copies.
arxiv-2601-05919:
Luca Ferrigno studies in 2026 unlikely intersections between a curve and special subvarieties inside a family of abelian varieties with complex multiplication. A 2020 theorem by Barroero and Capuano showed such intersections are finite unless the curve hides inside a proper subgroup scheme. Ferrigno extends that line of results to algebraic subgroups of the complex-multiplication fibers.

His work generalizes an earlier result by Barroero for fibered powers of elliptic schemes. A key ingredient is clear control of canonical heights, which measure arithmetic complexity of points, under endomorphisms. He bounds how height changes when an endomorphism is applied, by determining exactly when certain divisor differences remain ample, tying the geometric finiteness result to concrete height estimates.
arxiv-2601-06119:
AI that complements a specific person's strengths must handle people it has never met. Dileepa Pitawela and 2 co-authors present L2CU in a 2026 paper on human-AI cooperative classification, where a person and a model label items together. Earlier methods assumed one global user model, ignoring individual differences.

L2CU works from sparse, noisy annotations to find representative annotator profiles, each capturing a distinct labeling pattern. A new user is matched to a profile, and a profile-specific model then complements that user's judgments. The combined accuracy improves over treating everyone alike. Tests across image and text datasets, including medical and news data, showed the framework works as a model-agnostic way to lift joint human-AI performance.
arxiv-2601-06319:
Brandon Iritani and 5 co-authors create and precisely measure fragile strontium molecules in a 2026 atomic physics paper. The molecules pair two strontium-86 atoms in a halo state, a huge, weakly bound arrangement where the atoms spend much time far apart. Neighboring weakly bound states were also produced.

Production used one-photon photoassociation, joining free atoms with light, which needs good overlap between excited and ground vibrational wavefunctions. Autler-Townes spectroscopy measured transition strengths to find optimal production paths. Splittings among the three least-bound vibrational states were measured with uncertainties below 100 hertz. From those, absolute binding energies followed. The precision prepares the way for a molecular isotope shift measurement, a sensitive probe of nuclear and atomic structure.
arxiv-2601-06519:
A med answer built from source texts can still hold one claim with no ground. Yuelyu Ji and 5 co-authors built a check tool for that risk in a 2026 paper. In care work, one false claim can harm a sick man or woman. Their tool works claim by claim, not on the whole text at once.

It splits an answer into lone claims. Each claim is tried two ways: does the source text back it, and does it fit a bank of med facts? The scores roll up into a map of what went wrong: a fetch fault or a write fault, thin proof, a clash, or a grave slip. A small, fast twin of the tool does the same checks at scale. On four med quiz sets, it flagged bad claims with care and showed how risk shifts by which tool wrote the text.
arxiv-2601-06719:
Adithya Murali and three co-authors build proof tools for heap-based code in a 2026 paper. Heap logics help prove that code which links chunks of memory is right. They build the first two heap logics with chunks left implicit, they report.

Those logics give a strong pledge on proof: all true claims get proved in time. The pledge treats terms that call on themselves in a broad fixpoint sense. Proofs that once stalled can now be sure to close in the end. Left-implicit chunks make proof specs much less of a chore to write. Those who prove code right gain a tool of a new class. The work pushes heap proof toward full self-run in thought, if not yet in fact. Pointer code is where proof help is most in need today.
arxiv-2601-06819: Feihu Liu and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with unimodular equivalence of integral simplices. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. China, Testing the unimodular equivalence of two full-dimensional integral simplices can be reduced to testing unimodular permutation (UP) equivalence of two nonsingular matrices. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06919:
Meng-Dong Zhu and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with high-capacity dual degrees of freedom quantum secret sharing protocol beyond the linear rate-distance. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Quantum secret sharing (QSS) is the multipartite cryptographic primitive.

Most of existing QSS protocols are limited by the linear rate-distance bound, and cannot realize the long-distance and high-capacity multipartite key distribution. The work proposes a polarization (Pol) and phase (Ph) dual degrees of freedom (dual-DOF) QSS protocol based on the weak coherent pulse (WCP) sources. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07219:
Thanh-Nhan Vo and three co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to edit a photo by text. Their tool is called VENUS. Top tools in this field face a trade-off as they edit. They must keep the parts of the scene that should not change. They must also make the new parts fit the sense of the scene.

When a tool fails, it can build a whole new photo and lose the old scene, or miss the edit the user asked for. VENUS takes a new route based on a scene graph. A scene graph lists each thing in the scene and how the things relate. VENUS also flips noise in the photo back and forth as it works. That route gives the user more control over each edit. The graph keeps the edit tied to the things it should touch.
arxiv-2601-07419:
Niklas Kormann and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers position. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Over-smoothing and over-squashing have been extensively studied in the literature on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) over the past years.

We challenge this prevailing focus in GNN research, arguing that these phenomena are less critical for practical applications than assumed. We suggest that performance decreases often stem from uninformative receptive fields rather than over-smoothing. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07519:
Margherita Firenze and colleagues take on slice-to-volume reconstruction, a core task in medical imaging. The problem: turn misaligned two-dimensional slices into one three-dimensional view of anatomy. Scans of moving patients, especially fetal imaging, rarely line up neatly. The method must estimate both the 3D anatomy and each slice's pose. Their 2026 preprint uses modern neural networks.

Fully convolutional networks excel at learning features across scales and making fast predictions. Yet their use for slice-to-volume reconstruction remains little explored, the authors note. The team proposes a fast approach built on multi-scale unrolled optimization. Unrolling turns an iterative solver into network layers. Readers in medical imaging get a method aimed at speed without giving up the joint estimation task.
arxiv-2601-07619:
Luisa Estrada, Sasha Glendinning, and Andrew Nugent review how scholars model the manipulation of opinion. Their 2026 review covers mathematical and computer science approaches to opinion formation. Manipulation means deliberate efforts to shift what a population believes. The authors introduce the main tools and compare them side by side.

Those tools include ordinary and partial differential equations, chance-based models, control theory, and rules for how views spread. Each tool makes different assumptions about how people influence each other. A side by side look helps readers pick the right model for a set case, such as a vote or a web site. The review also clarifies where models disagree. It serves newcomers entering the field and experts who want shared words across their fields.
arxiv-2601-07819:
Robert Petersen and colleagues argue that thyroid treatment should use two hormone measures, not one. Standard practice adjusts thyroid replacement dose using only TSH. The authors say adding free thyroxine, FT4, may benefit patients with hypothyroidism. Their 2026 preprint uses nonlinear programming solvers to generate hypothalamus-pituitary curves for individual patients. Those curves describe how the gland system responds to hormone levels.

A curve per patient could guide dosing more personally than a single lab value. Nonlinear programming finds the curve that best fits a patient's measurements. The hypothalamus-pituitary axis controls TSH release, so its shape matters. Clinicians treating stubborn hypothyroidism cases are the readers. The paper blends endocrinology with optimization methods. It proposes a tool, not just a critique of current practice.
arxiv-2601-07919:
Aishwarya Linesh Thakur and colleagues probe the dense gas around long gamma-ray bursts using the burst's own light. The region within one to one hundred parsecs of these bursts was unexplored. Extreme ionization by the burst blocks optical absorption spectroscopy at those distances. The authors show the burst's ionizing flux stamps a unique time- and space-dependent pattern on the gas. X-ray absorption can read that pattern. Their 2026 preprint develops the method.

The gas near a burst traces the star-forming region that produced its progenitor star. Reading its density and structure tests where massive stars die. A time-dependent pattern is a gift: it encodes distance as well as composition. The method turns a problem, blinding ionization, into the measuring tool itself. The paper serves high-energy astrophysicists and interstellar medium scholars. It opens a scale around bursts that was previously dark.
arxiv-2601-08119: Kisun Lee computes new bounds on the asymptotic rank of tensors. The 2026 arXiv paper applies numerical implicitization across all computationally feasible cases. It uses the geometric framework of Kaski and Michalek, which studies secant varieties of tensor spaces. By showing that low-degree vanishing polynomials are absent on these varieties, Lee obtains sharper bounds. The new bounds improve on generic border rank bounds. Tensor rank matters in algebraic complexity, where it measures how hard matrix multiplication and related tasks truly are.
arxiv-2601-08219:
Paimon Goulart and Evangelos Papalexakis ask whether a small agent team can take a matrix apart. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes an agentic approach to matrix deflation. A solver language model builds rank-1 singular value updates, one slice at a time.

A vision language model then accepts or rejects each update and decides when to stop. That removes the need for fixed norm thresholds to end the process. In-context learning and row or column permutations improve solver stability. Permutations expose visually coherent structure the vision model can judge. The work tests whether paired models can handle a classic numerical task with judgment instead of rigid rules.
arxiv-2601-08519:
Kexin Bao and five co-authors present CD2, a constrained dataset distillation method for incremental learning. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets few-shot class-incremental learning, where classes arrive with few training samples. Catastrophic forgetting is the key problem: new learning erases old classes.

Many methods store previous knowledge in external memory and treat it equally with new classes. The authors argue that habit fails to preserve what is essential. Constrained distillation instead compresses past knowledge into a small distilled dataset with safeguards. A compact memory that keeps the right examples could let field-deployed classifiers grow without bloating storage or losing early classes.
arxiv-2601-08719:
Vikas Dwivedi, Monica Sigovan, and Bruno Sixou work on hard math problems that come from physics. Such problems can change fast in one place and slow in a next place. Old tools that learn from physics rules often fail on them. They need much time to train, and they need hand set wave sizes to work well.

The team builds a new tool with the short name KAPI-ELM. It splits the space into soft parts that can shift and grow. Those parts set both the test points and the width of small bell shaped curves. In this way the tool can move from a wide view to a fine view in one smooth step. It needs no fixed wave parts and no hard walls in the space.
arxiv-2601-08819:
Roshni Kaushik and Reid Simmons ask how old users like a coach robot to speak and move. The robot guides users through safe moves for health. Some users like much talk and praise. Some like brief cues. A wrong pace can bore a user or rush them, and they may quit the plan.

The team tests paces of speech and body cues with old users. They watch how users react and what pace they pick. The goal is a coach that fits each user, not one pace for all. A reader who builds health bots gets user facts, not guesses. The facts can guide how oft a bot should speak, nod, or stay still.
arxiv-2601-08919:
Sourav Saha and Mandar Mitra grade chat models that act as judges of text and image work. Labs now use such judges in place of paid human marks. A judge score is cheap and fast. But a coarse score can hide where a judge is weak, such as on close calls or on one class of task.

The pair call for fine grade checks. A judge should be tested by task type, by gap size, and by type of flaw in the work it marks. Fine checks show if a judge can tell a near miss from a true hit. A reader who uses AI judges gets a stricter scale. It can stop a lab from trust in a judge that fails where it counts.
arxiv-2601-09219:
Guy Kortsarz gives a fast near best plan for a tree link task with a strong ratio. The task starts with a tree, a net with no loops. Add links so the net stays whole if any one link fails. Use as few new links as one can. That task is called the Tree Augmentation Problem, and it is hard to solve in full.

His plan gets at most four thirds of the best count, a tight ratio for this task. It climbs by rungs, a step view of links, and it holds off some picks to later steps. A reader in net design gets a plan with a proof of its ratio. It fits backup link buys for real nets.
arxiv-2601-09719:
Hoyoon Byun and four co-authors propose a steadier building block for large language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper offers a bounded hyperbolic tangent as an alternative to pre-layer normalization. Pre-layer normalization is the default choice in current models and is key to stable pretraining.

The default has costs: it repeats statistical calculations and suffers a curse of depth. As layers pile up, hidden states grow in size and spread, which destabilizes training. A bounded activation could cap that growth by design. A cheaper, calmer block would ease the training of deeper models.
arxiv-2601-10019:
Mykola Pinchuk adds time sums as inputs for a boost tree model. The model type is XGBoost. The task is to guess if a user will click an ad. The data set is the Avazu click set. Time sums pool past clicks by hour spans.

A strict rule guards the build. Sums for one hour can use only prior hours. No data from the same hour or later may leak in. That rule keeps the test fair, as in real use. The paper asks which spans help most. It also checks if the gains hold on a later time split, not just in the build span.
arxiv-2601-10219:
M. J. Everitt and co authors rebuilt a physics degree from the ground up. The degree is at Loughborough University. Past fixes tend to tweak one course at a time. The team took a new path. They treat the whole degree as one rig.

The rig view comes from systems design. Each part has a job that can be checked. The lead rule is real world truth. Tasks should act like work in labs and firms. The paper lays out how the new degree was built. It gives a case for how a degree can be planned as a whole.
arxiv-2601-10319:
G. V. Voloshin, K. A. Barantsev, and A. N. Litvinov track a light shift in an atomic trap. The trap holds atoms in a dark state by two light beams. It is named coherent population trapping. Its tone is used in clocks and sensors, so shifts in it count.

Light from the beams can shift that tone. The team model the shift with a three level atom in a Lambda form. They add one more level at the top. Both weak and strong links to off tone beams are in the model. The paper gives a fresh term for the shift.
arxiv-2601-10419:
J. Dhamothiran and Saudamini Nayak build simple Lie superalgebras from their root sets. Superalgebras mix two kinds of parts, even and odd. Their root sets grade how those parts link. Serganova set rules for such root sets and sorted the base kinds.

Those root sets match the base superalgebras one to one. Dhamothiran and Nayak give one joint build for all of them. They start from the root set as a pure form. They pick a base with the least count of null roots. The build then yields the full algebra. One path thus spans the whole class.
arxiv-2601-10519:
Andrea Melis, Andrea Piroddi, and Roberto Girau use Transformer models to run cognitive radios. A cognitive radio scans the air waves and adapts. It picks a band, a code, and a rate to fit the scene. That skill can lift how well the scarce air waves are used.

Transformers are strong at sequence tasks. The team set them to pick how the radio should send. The picks adapt as the scene shifts. The work claims gains in how full the band is used. It also claims gains in how firm and safe the link is. Such radios may serve dense nets of the next era.
arxiv-2601-10619:
Karol I. Wysokiński and Marcin M. Wysokiński look past the standard Hubbard model of electrons in solids. That model treats electrons that repel each other on the same site. Real materials may also show correlated hopping, where an electron's jump depends on its neighbors. The authors test what this extra effect does in two settings.

First, they study the superconducting transition near the Mott metal-insulator transition, where a metal turns into an insulator. Second, they study transport through tiny quantum dot devices linked to electrodes. Both settings are places where strong interactions rule the behavior. The results help show when the simple Hubbard picture is not enough for real devices.
arxiv-2601-10919:
Michael T. Gorczyca writes a note on a quiet flaw in log-normal trigonometric regression: harmonics that the fit leaves vague. Scientists who study rhythms fit responses that rise and fall over time. The standard fit models the response as a sum of sine waves. When the response does not follow a bell curve, analysts either transform it or move to a GLM.

Gorczyca looks at the log-normal case, where the response is logged before fitting. The note flags how harmonics can be left out or set too loosely in that setup. Missing a harmonic can bias estimates of a rhythm's phase and strength. Day-night and seasonal studies lean on such fits, so the warning has real bite for rhythm research.
arxiv-2601-11019:
Xinwei Wu and co-authors hunt for the translation switch inside large language models. Models often translate well with no task-specific fine-tuning. The inner mechanism behind that ready skill is largely opaque. The team uses sparse autoencoders, tools that pull apart a model's activity into readable features. They build a framework to find task-specific features.

Their target is the set of features that initiate translation, the switch that tells the model to switch languages. Finding such features would show how one model routes itself among skills. It could also give engineers a dial: turn the feature on or off to control behavior. The work advances the craft of reading models from the inside.
arxiv-2601-11119:
Petr Kolman and Hans Raj Tiwary study the bond polytope of a graph. A cut splits a graph into two parts. A cut is a bond when both parts stay connected. The bond polytope is the convex hull of all bonds, a geometric object that encodes them. Computing the maximum weight bond is NP-hard, even for planar graphs.

The authors examine how the polytope behaves under vertex-sums and edge-sums, ways of gluing graphs together. If the polytope of a glued graph can be built from its parts, hard problems may split too. Polyhedral views turn discrete problems into geometry, where facets hint at algorithms. The work serves combinatorial optimization, where bonds model reliable network partitions.
arxiv-2601-11719:
Ho Fung Tsoi and Dylan Rankin, at the University of Pennsylvania, study how to group jets in high energy physics. Jets are sprays of parts made when quarks and gluons fly out of a crash. Their method, called jBOT in the work, learns from data with no labels.

They use self-distillation, where a model trains a copy of itself. The learned traits can then be tuned for later tasks. The title states that clear groups with real sense emerge from this training. Such traits could help sort jets by type with less hand made code.
arxiv-2601-11819: Shirlene Rose Bandela, Sanjeev Parthasarathy, and Vaibhav Garg share a data set of hard life stories from Reddit. The posts come mostly from women. They deal with loss of a pregnancy, abortion, and sexual violence, and the text warns that some may find the content hard to read. People post such stories to share pain and seek support. A clean data set lets teams study how support is given online. It can also help build tools that treat such posts with care.
arxiv-2601-11919:
Nam Nguyen, Thinh Nguyen, and Bella Bose study lossy compression built for a task. The source is a Bernoulli stream. The error gauge is Hamming distance. The class to keep is tied to the source by a symmetric noisy link.

They derive closed forms for the trade. That trade links rate, error, and class skill. They treat both the one-shot case with shared randomness and its dual form. Task-first compression can save bits when full detail is not needed. The forms give exact limits for this clean case.  Closed forms give exact limits for this clean task.
arxiv-2601-12319:
A team with Narendra Sahu propose a testable frame for light fermion dark matter aided by a first-order phase transition. The dark matter mass sits in the MeV to GeV range. It is charged under a dark U(1) gauge group.

A scalar field breaks that group and gives mass to the dark gauge boson. Forbidden dark matter needs aid to form at the right rate in the early universe. A phase transition can give that aid, and can also make gravitational waves. Those waves give a test path for the frame.
arxiv-2601-12419:
Mahammad Namazov, Tomas Koref, and Ivan Habernal study how to explain the calls of legal AI. Their test case is outcome classification for cases at the European Court of Human Rights. Trust in such tools needs clear reasons, not just a bare verdict. Some teams build task specific ways to pull out the key text.

Other ways read the model weights to judge which words drove the call. The open question is which style of rationale matches what legal experts would pick. The title gives the thrust of the result: legal experts disagree with what these tools extract. That gap matters for any court facing use of AI. A rationale that lawyers reject may fail the trust test even if the verdict is right.
arxiv-2601-12519:
Abdullah Umut Hamzaogullari and Arkadas Ozakin teach neural networks the paths of relativistic particles. Their tool is a Lagrangian neural network, which learns a Lagrangian from trajectory data. From that learned law, geodesics and dynamics can be derived. Such networks promise physics aware learning, but their odd training objective makes them unstable.

That instability has limited their use on complex systems so far. The team present a stabilized form of the network for harder cases. Their test ground is relativistic geodesics and chaotic dynamics, both stiff tests. Chaotic systems punish small errors fast, so stability really matters there. A stable learner could help model black hole orbits and other extreme paths.
arxiv-2601-12719:
Lin Zhao and a large team, from Snap Inc. and Northeastern University, bring video generation to mobile phones. Diffusion transformers have raised the quality of generated video in recent years. Their heavy compute cost makes real time or on device generation infeasible, though. Phones lack the power and cooling of data center hardware.

Their model, S2DiT, is a streaming sandwich diffusion transformer. It is designed for efficient, high fidelity, streaming generation on mobile hardware. Streaming means frames flow out as they are made, not after a long wait. Sandwich refers to its layered design, detailed in the work. Mobile generation would put video creation tools in every pocket.
arxiv-2601-12819:
G. H. Yu validates a detector encapsulation for a dark matter search upgrade called COSINE-100U. The upgrade boosts sensitivity by immersing the detector array in liquid scintillator. The array must run cold, at minus thirty degrees Celsius. Crystals of sodium iodide with thallium serve as the sensing material.

Yu built a module with the new encapsulation design. A dedicated long term stability study checked it under the planned conditions. Encapsulation must keep the crystals dry and intact while cold and submerged. A failed seal could ruin a rare event search that runs for years. Validation of this kind is the quiet groundwork of dark matter science.
arxiv-2601-13119:
Satyam Sahu and a large team tune the sound like waves of a layered crystal. The crystal is CrSBr with part of its bromine swapped for chlorine. Swaps of one atom for a kin atom give a clean knob to tune how a crystal shakes.

The team pairs two tools. They use Raman light scatter, split by the angle of the light, to read the shakes. They also run first principles sums to match what they see. They track how the shakes shift as the chlorine share grows to about half. Their care with low symmetry helps staff who want to set shake traits by design in flat matter.
arxiv-2601-13219:
Dirk Wulferding and a large team show how a small swap can wake hid waves in a linked crystal. In such stuff, spin and orbit forces vie with field from the crystal plan. That vie can make joint spin orbit waves, called magnons. Such waves bend fast when the plan or charge state shifts.

The team uses a dopant, a small swap of one atom for a kin, to break the plan's symmetry. That break lets hid magnons show in their probes. The trick gives a knob to tune wave acts past spin only rules. For staff who dream of wave based tools, hid modes that can be switched are a prize.
arxiv-2601-13419:
Lorenzo Mauri and co-authors read gene data through the pathways genes serve, not just one gene at a time. Gene marks make sense in groups. A pathway is a set of genes that run one cell job. Old tools cut data dims with no tie to such groups, so their parts can lack a clear life sense.

Pathway led tools do exist, but they oft bind with stiff terms or need huge hand work. The team builds Bayes factor models that take pathway notes in a flex way. Latent parts then map to real cell jobs. For bio teams, parts with a life sense beat parts that just fit sums.
arxiv-2601-13819:
Balma Duch, Pere Masjuan, and Hubert Spiesberger compute a small quantum correction to electron-quark scattering in 2026. The term is the gamma-Z box graph at one loop, at low energy. Low momentum transfer means the particles graze, not smash. Both electron and quark masses are kept non-zero in the work.

From the result, they extract coupling constants for a low-energy effective theory. That theory includes parity-violating four-fermion interaction terms. Such constants feed tests of the Standard Model at low energy. Precise values help experiments spot any crack in the theory.
arxiv-2601-13919:
Yuezhe Yang and co-authors build a diagnosis system that links patient records with X-rays in 2026. Automated clinical diagnosis must integrate multi-modal data and reason over complex contexts. Medical vision-language models have advanced report generation and visual question answering. Most methods still treat each case in isolation.

That isolated style ignores longitudinal health records and related patient examples. Their HyperWalker uses dynamic hypergraph-based deep diagnosis for multi-hop modeling. Links across records let the model reason over a patient's history. Richer context could raise the quality of AI help in clinics.
arxiv-2601-14019:
Frederik Walter and co-authors build a security frame for chemical systems that act like locks in 2026. They introduce chemical functions, which model chemical systems as noisy challenge-response primitives. A challenge is an input, and the response depends on the chemical makeup. The idea builds on the theory of physical functions.

They define robustness, unclonability, and unpredictability for such functions. Both finite and asymptotic regimes get rigorous treatment. Security games capture the adversary's power and the goals at stake. Chemical functions could one day tag drugs or goods against counterfeits.
arxiv-2601-14119:
Nikita Titov and Andrea Trombettoni compare two quantum models on graphs in the large limit in 2026. One is the O(n) quantum rotor model, defined on a general graph. The other is the quantum spherical model on the same graph. They take the limit as n grows without bound.

They show the large n limit of the rotor model has the same critical behavior. Critical behavior means how the system acts near a phase change. The critical exponents depend solely on the spectral dimension of the graph. That single number captures how waves spread on the graph's structure.
arxiv-2601-14319:
Fabian Veider, Georg Jäger, and Bao Quoc Tang model opinion spread on social media in this 2026 paper. The rise of platforms and their recommendation algorithms has raised fears of polarization and echo chambers. The team studies those fears with an adaptive voter model. In such a model, people hold opinions and rewire their links over time.

They compare two ways links can change. Free global rewiring lets a person connect with anyone who shares their opinion. Friend-of-a-friend local rewiring copies how platforms suggest links, as on Facebook or LinkedIn. By setting the two side by side, the study shows how the rewiring rule itself shapes the social network.
arxiv-2601-15419:
Yashuai Yan and Dongheui Lee teach one control space to serve many robot bodies. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with cross-embodiment humanoid control. Humans and humanoid robots come in many shapes: single-arm, dual-arm, and legged forms among them.

The framework learns a shared latent representation of motion. It works in two stages. First, a decoupled latent space captures local motion patterns body part by body part, using contrastive learning. That structure allows accurate, flexible retargeting of motion. One person's movement can then drive robots of very different size and body builds.
arxiv-2601-15619:
Jie Lin and five co-authors report a nearby binary star system in a 2026 arXiv paper. The system pairs a compact object with a K-type star companion. It is a wide post-common envelope binary. That means the pair once shared an envelope of gas, then shed it. A white dwarf is the candidate for the compact partner. Such binaries test theories of how the shared-envelope stage works.

Most known systems of this kind have tight orbits. Their periods run from hours to a few days. Wide systems like this one are harder to explain. Standard accounts assume the envelope is expelled with low efficiency. A wide survivor challenges or refines that picture. Finding one in the solar neighborhood is a bonus. Nearby systems allow close, detailed study.
arxiv-2601-15819:
Yanfeng Zhang and seven co-authors improve short-packet wireless links in a 2026 arXiv paper. Ultra-reliable low-latency communication, or URLLC, serves tasks that cannot wait or fail. Sparse vector coding is a promising method for such short packets. Their scheme is dual-mapping sparse vector coding, or DM-SVC. Dual mapping is the twist they add to the base method. The aim is better transmission performance for short packets.

Short packets carry control signals, alarms, and machine commands. Reliability there matters more than raw speed. Next-generation networks promise URLLC for factories and vehicles. Each coding gain makes those promises more credible. The paper speaks to wireless engineers designing for the strictest latency budgets.
arxiv-2601-16019:
L. Scholz-Díaz, A. R. Gallazzi, S. Zibetti, and D. Mattolini relate galaxy mass to dark halos in a 2026 arXiv paper. In the standard cosmological model, galaxies grow inside dark matter halos. Halos supply the gravitational framework for complex baryonic processes. How far halo properties shape what we observe stays unclear. The authors study the stellar-to-total dynamical mass relation. They resolve it spatially, looking inside galaxies rather than at whole-galaxy sums.

Spatial resolution shows where stars dominate and where dark matter takes over. That pattern tests how baryons settle into halos. Galaxy evolution is the joint story of both components. A resolved mass relation gives modelers a sharper target than global ratios. Surveys with integral-field data make such studies possible at scale.
arxiv-2601-16119:
Erkao Bao, Robi Huq and Shengzhen Ning study a Morse view of group acts on shapes. Their 2026 preprint deals with shapes moved by a Lie group. A Morse tool reads shape traits from high and low points of a map. The team use a fix trick to make the map work with group acts. Small shifts of the map then give firm Morse Bott maps.

With firm maps, they build the group linked form of shape counts. They also gain the cross term rules the build needs. The build stems from the Austin and Braam path in the field. Firm maps close a gap in that path. The work adds rigour to group shape counts.
arxiv-2601-16719:
Martina Alutto, Fabrizio Dabbene, Angela Fontan, Karl Johansson, and Chiara Ravazzi model a race of two new tech goods. Folks in a crowd sway each other by talk. Use of one good feeds views of that good. Views then feed fresh use in a loop. Their 2026 preprint builds a two-layer frame for this race.

Once folks adopt one good, some grow sour on it. They may switch to the rival good. The frame tracks such switches over time. It can show when a lead is safe or frail. Firms and towns could use it to time launches. It may also flag where ads or rules tip a race.
arxiv-2601-16919:
Thomas Tram builds a light tool to teach the early cosmos in class. The cosmic microwave glow is a faint light from the young cosmos. Its wave spread shifts with each cosmic dial. Those shifts are a core theme in space class. But live play with the dials oft costs too much compute. His 2026 preprint shares CosmoSlider, a tool for that play.

Sliders let class users turn many dials at once. The glow's curve then shifts in real time. Light code keeps the tool fast on plain laptops. Such play helps class users feel how dials shape the glow. It turns a hard chart into a hands-on lab.
arxiv-2601-17119:
Babette Döbrich, Jan Jerhot, Karim Massri, Jonathan Schubert, and Tommaso Spadaro weigh a new hunt for faint bits at CERN. Faint bits may hide in the MeV to GeV mass range. Beam-dump hunts are a strong way to seek them. A proton beam hits a block, and faint bits slip through. Their 2026 preprint sets an old hunt next to a new-site plan.

The old hunt is NA62, run in dump mode at CERN. The new plan reuses its eyes at a fresh hall, ECN3. Same eyes, new hall, more beam time and reach. Such hunts could crack the dark stuff case. Cost-wise reuse makes the case more strong.
arxiv-2601-17319:
Hien Duy Nguyen and Dan Wang study process control through p-values. Factories and labs chart key values to catch drift early. The authors chart p-values instead of raw measures. When a process is in control, a valid p-value stream is super-uniform. That trait holds with no model of the process itself. It works in nonparametric and two-phase designs.

A chart with no model demand is a strong draw. Teams can watch complex processes they cannot fully describe. False alarms stay in check if the p-values are valid. The work gives quality teams a flexible watch tool. It shifts focus from the measure to the proof of change.
arxiv-2601-17519:
Aida Abiad and five co-authors bound the edge-isoperimetric number of graphs. That number measures how well a graph's sets connect to the rest. It is tied to edge expansion, a core trait for networks. The team gives sharp spectral bounds, approximations, and exact values. Their focus is graph powers and rich families. Distance-regular graphs and finite geometry graphs are among them.

Expansion governs how fast data spreads in a network. It also sets the strength of codes and designs. Exact values for key families save later guesswork. Spectral bounds let users test big graphs fast. The work serves network science and pure graph theory. It links shape, spectrum, and spread in one frame.
arxiv-2601-17819:
Mi Zou and co-authors report a lab test of a quantum key method for groups. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantum cryptographic conferencing. The method lets many parties build one shared secret key over a quantum network. Its safety rests on the laws of physics, not on hard math. So far, though, tests have reached only across city-scale links.

The team runs a phase-matching protocol with three light levels. They count the finite-size effects that real runs must face, since keys are built from limited data. Longer safe links would help quantum networks grow past one metro area. Each lab step of this kind tests gear and theory at once. The work pushes group key sharing toward wider use.
arxiv-2601-17919:
Arnulf J. Snedker-Nielsen and co-authors explore making color centers in silicon for quantum devices. Their 2026 preprint deals with silicon-on-insulator, a wafer type built for chips. Color centers are tiny defects that can emit one photon at a time. Some, like the T center, also hold spins that link to light. Those links can tie photons and spins into networks for quantum tech.

The team studies how several kinds of centers form in this material. They stress forms that could be made in bulk with chip-style methods. A source that fits the chip industry could speed quantum hardware a great deal. The paper maps routes toward that goal and the trade-offs in each.
arxiv-2601-18019: S. Carolina García-Martínez, Pascual Lucas, and H. Fabián Ramírez-Ospina study a class of surfaces in de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spaces. Their 2026 preprint treats orientable surfaces immersed in these three-dimensional spacetimes. The surfaces are of L1-2-type, a class defined through the shape operator and its traces. The paper works out the properties that such surfaces must have in each of the two spaces.
arxiv-2601-18519:
Andrei Bengus-Lasnier and Mikhail Shkolnikov study a way to shrink hard shape tasks into a plane of counts. The shrink turns curves on a shape into points on a flat chart, where they are much less hard to count. A phase tag rides with each point and holds key facts the shrink would lose. The trick has roots in a way to build real curves from flat parts.

It also sits at the heart of a famed proof that tied counts in the shrunk world to counts in the full world. The pair ask what the set of points for one phase looks like as a whole. Those sets, called fibers, chart how much the phase tag pins down. A clear chart helps staff use the shrink with trust. It may also spark new ways to count curves.
arxiv-2601-18619:
Jorge Quesada and Ghassan AlRegib teach vision tools to mark small, sparse things in shots with few hand marks to learn from. Self-taught tools learn form from raw shots with no tags. That path works well for big, plain zones of a shot. It works far less well when the thing to mark is small, thin, or spread in specks.

A speck can wash out when the tool shrinks the shot to learn its broad form. Their plan makes the tool scale-aware, so fine specks stay in view while it learns. That care should lift marks on roads, crops, and scans where the key zone is tiny. Good marks with few hand tags could cut cost in fields from health to maps. The work names a blind spot in self-taught vision and sets out to fix it.
arxiv-2601-19219:
Shota Ono and Ryotaro Ohse ask where each kind of atom sits in a mixed layered crystal. The crystals swap sulfur, selenium, and tellurium in a structure that can flip between an insulating and a metallic phase. That flip, from the 2H form to a skewed form, has been seen in tungsten based mixes.

Tellurium atoms, reports say, favor one specific site in the skewed structure. Ono and Ohse work out the site preference across the family, for molybdenum and tungsten alike. Where atoms sit decides the phase and the traits, so the map guides the design of switchable thin materials.
arxiv-2601-19319:
Efthymios Sofos counts how often a polynomial takes square free values, and pins down the error in that count. A square free number has no square factor past one. A folk conjecture says the count of such values for an integer polynomial grows like a constant times the range, with a small error.

Sofos proves that the average error is the fourth root of the main term, a precise rate. Average results cover the typical polynomial even when each single case stays out of reach. Square free values feed number theory questions about equations and the shape of integer sequences.
arxiv-2601-19519:
Ofir Abramovich, Ariel Shamir, and Andreas Aristidou build motion capture that works outside the studio. Standard systems film a performer with many cameras and track markers on the body. That setup fails outdoors or in cluttered spaces where cameras cannot see every point. The team instead uses small sensors worn on the body that measure distances between each other.

Their system rebuilds full-body three-dimensional motion from those sparse distance readings alone. The sensors use time-of-flight ranging, timing tiny radio signals between wireless nodes. With no cameras in the loop, the method keeps working in open or messy places. Animators and sports scientists could record natural movement in the wild. The work moves motion capture from a fixed stage to almost anywhere.
arxiv-2601-20519:
Paige Ramsden, Sean L. McGee, and Matt Nicholl use tidal disruption events to uncover quenched galaxies whose central black holes are smaller than expected. A tidal disruption event flares when a star wanders too close to a black hole and is torn apart. Because very massive black holes swallow stars whole without a flare, these events reveal otherwise hidden low-mass black holes.

The authors find an unexpected population of galaxies that have stopped forming stars yet host under-massive black holes. That pairing tests the standard story in which black hole growth and star formation shut down together.
arxiv-2601-20619:
Jhoan Eusse, Esteban Vasquez, Tom Rivlin, and Elizabeth Agudelo write lecture notes on the foundations of quantum optics for quantum information. Nonclassical states of light and their correlations are core resources: they underpin both the exploration of quantum phenomena and the working of quantum information protocols.

The notes offer an accessible yet rigorous introduction, stressing relevance to quantum information science and technology. Students entering the field need exactly this bridge, from the physics of light to the logic of quantum devices. The crash-course format suits a first pass before deeper study.
arxiv-2601-20719:
Shubhadeep Sadhukhan and nine co-authors study how immune cells swallow soft targets. Their 2026 paper is about phagocytosis, the process by which a cell engulfs a particle. It is a basic tool of the innate immune system. The team asks what physical rules govern the act when the target is soft. Real targets bend and deform during contact.

Older theory mostly treats targets as rigid balls. That choice skips a key fact: both the cell and its target change shape as they meet. The authors study how membrane curvature and actin, the cell's inner scaffold, work together. Their focus runs from the first bite to full engulfment. The work helps explain how immune cells handle soft prey that gives way under pressure.
arxiv-2601-21019:
Markus Holzleitner and four co-authors study learning when training and test data come from different worlds. Their 2026 paper builds a regularization framework for unsupervised domain adaptation. The setting is vector-valued regression under covariate shift. Covariate shift means the input distributions differ between training and test. The outputs may be vectors, not single numbers. Such shift poses significant challenges for reliable learning.

The framework uses vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. These spaces give a rich, structured way to fit functions. Regularization keeps the fit from chasing noise in the source data. No labels from the target domain are assumed. The paper develops the theory for this general case. It serves fields like medicine and sensing, where labeled data sit in one setting and use happens in another.
arxiv-2601-21219:
Daniel Bernstein, Luca Di Carlo, and David Schwab compress neural networks by letting their weights attract each other. Their 2026 paper presents soft quantization. The method adds short-range attractive couplings between weights during training. Those couplings pull weights toward shared values. The weight distribution then discretizes on its own. Remarkably, it does so in a mixed-precision manner. Only two additional hyperparameters control the effect.

Standard quantization forces weights onto a grid after training. Soft quantization grows the grid during training instead. The model adapts to its own compression as it learns. Mixed precision emerges rather than being assigned by hand. Smaller models run cheaper on phones and edge devices. The paper offers a physically inspired route to that goal. It treats a network's weights like particles that cluster.
arxiv-2601-21319:
Vade Shah and Jason R. Marden compare ways of forming alliances in a simple contest game. In the game, two players each fight a shared adversary across several contests. Each side splits a limited budget among the contests, and the higher spend wins each one.

Alliances change who pools resources and how the pooled budget is split. The authors analyze several alliance rules inside this coalitional game. The comparison shows which setups help the allies and which mostly help the adversary. Such toy models give clean insight into real coalition politics, where partners must share limited strength.
arxiv-2601-21719: Yaxi Hu, Johanna Düngler, Bernhard Schölkopf, and Amartya Sanyal study privacy in LoRA. LoRA is a widely used way to fine-tune large models with small added parts. Their 2026 preprint asks when random projections help protect the data used in training, and when they do not. The tool they build for the job is a randomized method they call the Wishart projection mechanism.
arxiv-2601-21919:
Yiqun Chen and co-authors try to make reasoning models briefer without making them dumber. Large reasoning models write long chains of thought, and the redundant parts slow responses and bottleneck deployment. Earlier reinforcement learning fixes coupled a length penalty with rewards for correct outcomes.

That simple weighting struggles to balance brevity against accuracy, since forcing short answers can damage critical reasoning steps. The team's 2026 preprint instead compresses chains of thought through multi-agent reinforcement learning, where several agents shape the training signal. If models can learn to skip only the waste, users get faster answers at lower cost. And long reasoning stays affordable for everyday use rather than special occasions only.
arxiv-2601-22019:
Neelanjan Chakraborti, Snehasish Nandy, and Sudeep Kumar Ghosh probe a faint effect in some solids. Some fields pull like a magnet and swing back and forth in time. A solid can respond in ways that are not in step with that pull. The size of that response can reveal the hidden shape of the states inside the solid.

Some of that shape comes from how spins turn as states change. The team studies an effect where this spin shape drives the response. The effect is built into the solid, not forced by flaws in it. Work like this gives lab teams new ways to probe odd solids. Those solids may one day be used in fast, low-power parts for chips.
arxiv-2601-22119:
Han Yang and co-authors search for trade rules that work. In stock trade, a rule is a math form that aims to pick stocks that will do well. To find good rules by machine is a prized task. But most search tools roam free, with no check on form. They coin rules that break the rules of trade or mean naught at all.

The team sets a strict grammar for the search. Each rule the tool may coin must fit that grammar. It must be well formed and make sense in trade terms. Their tool is called AlphaCFG. Rules found this way can be read by men and checked by hand. They can also be used with more trust in live trade.
arxiv-2601-22219:
Aurora Ireland and Vincent Vennin ask whether the seeds of galaxies ever lost their quantum traits. Their 2026 preprint studies the tiny ripples born in the fast growth of the early cosmos. Most work treats those ripples as plain chance fields, like tossed dice.

The pair look for a sign that the ripples stayed truly quantum. They focus on phase links between branches of the state, which can leave marks of quantum clash. They also weigh how odd, non-bell-shaped spread in the ripples shapes that sign. The work tests a deep claim about cosmic birth.
arxiv-2601-22419:
Nicholas Lopez, Francisco Marmolejo-Cossío, Jose Roberto Tello Ayala, and David Parkes design group testing that does the most social good. Pooled testing checks many samples with one test, saving scarce kits. Their 2026 preprint notes the cost: a pooled result says less about each person.

Their method shapes pools over time to lift total welfare, not just cut kit use. Code and test scripts come with the work. Such plans matter when disease spreads fast and labs are swamped. They help officials spend each test where it helps most. The work ties math to public health aims.
arxiv-2601-22719:
Ivan Krasionov and a team take single-shot films of vortex birth in a room-temperature quantum fluid. Quantized vortices are the swirls that mark a quantum fluid. Their 2026 preprint uses interferometry on an organic exciton-polariton condensate, a hybrid of light and matter.

Across hundreds of runs, vortex cores land at random spots, with no favored spin. That pattern fits a stochastic, unseeded birth, as Kibble-Zurek theory would suggest. The team also read how the pattern scales. Such films test a deep claim about how order forms. Few setups can catch it live.
arxiv-2601-22819:
Yaxing Ma, Lijuan Wang, and Huaiqiang Yu study how fast a delayed control system can be steadied. Their systems are infinite-dimensional, like heat or fluid flow, and include a fixed time delay in the control loop. Delays often make control harder, so the effect on rapid stabilization is a real question.

They prove two results: the delay does not harm rapid stabilization, and feedback needs no past history to work. Those findings simplify controller design for systems with lag. They apply where models are described by partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-22919:
Fabian Bally, Michael Schötz, and Thomas Limbrunner design a data pipeline for training self-driving cars. Data both enables and bottlenecks that training, since cars record far more than teams can process. Rare but safety-critical events matter most, yet finding them takes long hours of driving.

Their serverless, edge-native design processes data near where it is gathered, scaling up only when needed. Smart selection can surface the rare events that teach cars to handle danger. The goal is training sets that are balanced, not just big. Balanced coverage is the stated goal, since a fleet can drive safely for months yet still miss the one dangerous case.
arxiv-2601-23219:
Shuai Shao, Yixiang Liu, Bingwei Lu, and Weinan Zhang scale multi-agent systems while keeping performance rising. These systems use a router to split tasks among specialized agents. Adding new agents seems an easy way to grow capability, but naive expansion can collapse performance.

The problem is the router cold-starting on new, mixed-quality agents it cannot yet judge. MonoScale aims for monotonic improvement, so each addition helps rather than hurts. Steady growth rules matter as agent pools become large marketplaces of tools. Cold-starting routers are the failure to avoid, since a router cannot route well to agents it has never evaluated.
arxiv-2602-00219: Saeid Jamshidi and coauthors build a federated intrusion detection system for zero shot, open set attacks in cyber physical and Internet of Things networks. Their semantics driven frame adds language derived supervision to federated tuning, enabling detection of unseen attack behaviors. Attack prototypes come from a Tri-LLM ensemble of GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and LLaMA-3-8B, aligning clients around shared meaning rather than shared raw data. The design thus aims at new attacks without pooling private traffic in one place.
arxiv-2602-00319: Siyuan Shen and Kai Wang detect AI generated content in academic peer reviews over time. Detection stays minimal before 2022, then rises substantially through 2025, with about 20 percent of ICLR reviews and 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews counted as AI generated in 2025. Growth in Nature Communications peaks between the third and fourth quarter of 2024. The findings suggest a rapidly increasing AI assisted presence in peer review, warranting further study of effects on scholarly evaluation.
arxiv-2602-00819: Wojciech Florkowski and colleagues give one account covering both spin-1/2 and spin-1 particles through perfect spin hydrodynamics. They clarify how the parts of the spin-1 density matrix connect to observables found in heavy-ion collisions. They stress the advantage of the adjoint representation for spin matrices, then present the equilibrium spin density matrix and its Wigner function. With suitable definitions for energy-momentum and spin tensors, the framework yields perfect spin flow just as for spin-1/2 systems.
arxiv-2602-01119: Konstantin Chernyshev and co-authors run Tendem, a work plan where AI does set, repeat jobs and people step in when models fail or checks are due. Each job gets a full quality look before it reaches the client. In-house tests on 94 real jobs pitted Tendem against AI-only teams and people-only crews hired online. Tendem gave better work faster, at costs near people-only work, while its lone AI arm neared top scores on web and tool tests.
arxiv-2602-01219: Qishuai Wen and co-authors build MiTA, a fast-weight focus plan scaling attention to long contexts. Plain attention acts like a two-layer fast-weight net as wide as context length, so power grows with context but stalls at huge lengths. Their plan sorts focus into a five-way route-or-squeeze taxonomy, then uses landmark queries to grab top-k pairs as bendy routed experts, plus a narrow shared expert. Vision tests show top scores and speed, with token-prune effects and easy shifts from plain attention.
arxiv-2602-01519: Shiju Zhao and co-authors propose native position-independent caching for language models, needing an encoder. Prefix-based Key-Value caches handle arbitrary-order retrieved contexts poorly. Position-independent caching promises KV reuse without positional constraints, yet methods degrade accuracy badly. The team reintroduces the encoder into decoder-only models, training it for position-independent caching. Their COMB system integrates with existing inference frameworks, cutting time-to-first-token by 51-94% and tripling throughput with similar accuracy. DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat gains show COMB applies elsewhere.
arxiv-2602-01819: Davide Carolillo and colleagues revisit term algebras after Maltsev. Extensions are set by how many indecomposable elements. For k from one to omega, the free term algebra on k generators serves as the standard model, complete via Ehrenfeucht-Fraïssé games without quantifier elimination. Those models are rigid and atomic, and their theories lack the finite cover property. The theories are stable, not superstable, with trivial forking, so no infinite group is interpretable. T0 is the model companion of locally free algebras, while higher k theories are not model complete.
arxiv-2602-01919: Hend Al-Khalifa introduces Vibe Coding, using language models as coding assistants for concepts and critical thinking. In a senior NLP course, students did seven labs generating code with language models, graded via reflection questions. Feedback from 19 students showed satisfaction, with mean scores near four point five out of five across engagement, learning and fairness. Students valued less debugging load and deeper focus, though time limits, verification and task specs remained challenges. Prompt logging and reflection assessment can shift learning from syntax fluency to concept mastery for AI augmented work.
arxiv-2602-02019: Fucai Li and colleagues study the compressible Navier-Stokes-Transport system in Besov spaces, coupling density and momentum with a temperature transport equation. Unlike the Fourier system, where a parabolic equation supplies dissipation, their transport equation removes it for density. They establish global well-posedness for d at least two. Introducing a Mach number, they prove the low limit, showing solutions converge to the incompressible inhomogeneous system globally, even for ill-prepared data. A refined energy analysis yields optimal decay rates in dimensions at least three, with bounded density.
arxiv-2602-02119: Elio Vinciguerra and colleagues present CHAOS, a modular, open-source, configurable fault frame built for the gem5 simulator. Fault injectors test system reliability and resilience. They let teams mimic hardware and software faults to study behavior under errors and judge whether it keeps working. Such testing is vital for spotting weak points. CHAOS supports precise, systematic fault injection across architectural levels, backing broad tolerance and resilience tests. Its configurability and smooth fit with gem5 let researchers roam fault models and scenarios. That makes CHAOS a prized tool for dependable computing.
arxiv-2602-02219: Yuzheng Xu and others reveal position bias in rubric-based tests of language models as judges. Prior work examined pointwise or pairwise protocols, while rubric tests attracts focus where verification is difficult. The team shows rubric tests implicitly resembles several choice, so models prefer score options at given positions in the rubric list. Controlled tests confirm steady bias with model-given direction: some judges favor the first option, others the last. Ordering criteria also shifts scores, and permuting rubric options attenuates bias, mainly helping strongly biased models.
arxiv-2602-02319: Behzad Aalipur and Rachel Kilby study uncertainty quantification in graphon models, where gauging guarantees lack tractable theory for edge probabilities. They present a leave-one-out neighborhood smoother building neighborhoods without target-column edges, so averaged notes become independent Bernoulli variables with differing probabilities. That separation yields concentration bounds and a Berry-Esseen-type normal-approximation bound for every fixed target pair, with a pair-independent numeric constant. That leave-one-out structure gives an edge-wise no-leakage checks identity, since the held-out edge never builds its predictor.
arxiv-2602-02619:
Mohan Jiang and 10 co-authors mine sequences of software pull requests to teach language models long-horizon agency, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models excel at short tasks but struggle with workflows that unfold over many dependent stages. Training data capturing authentic long dependencies is scarce, and human annotation is prohibitively expensive.

Pull requests, the authors argue, already embody the needed supervision. A chain of pull requests decomposes a complex objective into verifiable submission units, keeps functional coherence across iterations, and encodes real refinement through bug-fix histories. Their system, daVinci-Agency, extracts that structure through progressive decomposition, consistency enforcement, and verifiable refinement. The resulting trajectories average eighty-five thousand tokens and over a hundred tool calls. Fine-tuning on only two hundred thirty-nine samples produced broad benchmark gains, including a large relative jump on an agent benchmark.
arxiv-2602-02719:
Yu-Chen Guo's 2026 paper, with 3 co-authors, uses quantum tomography to read the spin state of fermion pairs made in electron-positron collisions. Beam polarization, usually treated as a luminosity knob, becomes a control dial for quantum resources. Three cases anchor the study: top-quark pairs, muon pairs, and Bhabha scattering, across threshold, resonance, and channel-interplay regimes.

Three quantities are tracked: entanglement through concurrence, Bell nonlocality through an optimized CHSH setting, and magic, the non-stabilizerness resource, through a Rényi entropy. In single-channel cases, polarization reshapes each spin polarization while correlations stay robust, though magic varies strongly. Bhabha scattering behaves differently because polarization shifts the balance between channels, moving all three readouts. All remain visible beyond five sigma including systematics. Tuned polarization turns future colliders into tunable laboratories for quantum information in particle interactions.
arxiv-2602-02819:
Mathieu Even and 5 co-authors rebuild the evaluation of membership inference attacks on causal foundations, in research posted to arXiv in 2026. These attacks test whether a specific record was in a model's training set, quantifying memorization and privacy risk. Standard evaluation needs repeated retraining, which is prohibitively costly for large models, so cheaper one-run and zero-run protocols are common but statistically shaky.

The authors define memorization as the causal effect of including a data point in training. That framing exposes the biases: one-run methods suffer interference between jointly included points, and zero-run evaluations add distribution shift between member and non-member data. Causal analogues of standard attack metrics follow, with practical estimators for all three regimes and non-asymptotic consistency guarantees. Validation spans pretrained and fine-tuned language models, enabling reliable privacy measurement without retraining.
arxiv-2602-02919:
Automated science discovery drives a 2026 paper by Jiachen Jiang and 2 co-authors. Language-model evolutionary systems propose and improve candidate programs over many rounds. Earlier systems fed the full code history back as context. That wastes space and buries the key ideas behind routine implementation details.

Their framework, DeltaEvolve, stores structured semantic deltas instead. A delta records how and why a change between versions affected performance. Deltas are organized in a multi-level database with progressive disclosure, cutting input tokens further. The authors frame evolution as an expectation-maximization process. Tests across scientific domains followed. DeltaEvolve found better solutions than full-code systems while using fewer tokens for context.
arxiv-2602-03019:
Fine-tuning large models across many private devices is made cheaper by Guohao Yang and 4 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Federated learning trains collaboratively without centralizing data, keeping privacy. Full fine-tuning, though, costs too much communication and memory for resource-constrained clients, while lighter setting-efficient methods often lose results compared with the full version.

Their method, FedKRSO, updates models inside shared random low-part subspaces made by the server. Clients send only compact accumulators along those subspaces, not full settings. The server aggregates and redistributes the global model efficiently. Convergence is analyzed rigorously for general federated settings. Tests on the GLUE benchmark across scenarios showed strong results with low overhead, approaching full federated fine-tuning quality.
arxiv-2602-03619:
Judging a long research report needs a rubric, but generic rubrics are coarse and hand-written ones do not scale. Changze Lv and 16 co-authors train generators that write query-specific rubrics in a 2026 paper. The rubrics are grounded in human preferences over paired DeepResearch-style reports, collected into a dedicated dataset.

Reinforcement learning trains the generators with a hybrid reward mixing preference consistency, format validity, and model-based rubric scoring. On held-out human preferences, the learned rubrics separate favored from rejected reports better than generic, prompted, or supervised alternatives. Used as reward signals, they then train report-generation systems to substantial gains on DeepResearch Bench, under both a single-agent and a multi-agent workflow.
arxiv-2602-03719:
Training an agent over long horizons founders on sparse rewards: one final outcome must grade dozens of decisions. Yubao Zhao and 6 co-authors propose BranPO in a 2026 paper, a value-free method that manufactures localized supervision. The difficulty is non-monotonic correctness, where early mistakes get rescued later and promising states still fail.

BranPO cuts trajectories at intermediate points and resamples their continuations, forming contrastive branches that share a start but end differently. Those pairs isolate the decisions that drove success or failure. Difficulty-aware sampling and redundant step masking keep the process efficient. Across multi-hop question answering benchmarks, BranPO beats diverse baselines without extra training cost, and it generalizes to broader long-horizon agent tasks.
arxiv-2602-03919:
Airton Deppman derives a famous nonstandard entropy from first principles in a 2026 paper. Tsallis entropy describes systems with long-range correlations, where ordinary entropy fails to add up. Deppman starts instead from algorithmic information theory, which measures a string's complexity by its shortest description.

By imposing grammar-like rules on how strings form, he shows the cost of description grows as a power law rather than linearly. Tsallis entropy then emerges naturally as the measure of information growth. Consequences include reduced heat dissipation bounds for correlated systems and a fresh reading of Zipf's law. Numerical simulations support the derivation.
arxiv-2602-04319:
Phosphorus atoms in silicon can be tickled in step between split energy states. Adam Gindl and 6 co-authors show that excitation with mid-infrared pulses in a 2026 paper. The transition links the ground split states of the donor electron, a system eyed for quantum devices.

A pump-probe method tracked the wavepacket's dynamics through polarization changes in the probe. Pre-excited carriers changed both the wavepacket's amplitude and coherence time. Under some conditions the excitation switched character entirely, reaching even a Raman-forbidden transition. Steering donor states with light, including how background carriers spoil coherence, is groundwork for silicon-based quantum technology.
arxiv-2602-04819:
Aqsa Sultana and 7 co-authors build a very small model to flag precancerous colon polyps in a 2026 medical imaging study. Sorting low-grade tubular adenomas by later cancer risk is hard because pathologists judge subtle patterns subjectively in whole-slide images.

Their model, XtraLight-MedMamba, blends a shallow convolutional feature extractor with parallel state-space blocks that model local texture within global context. An attention bridge module sharpens multi-scale features, and a special fixed classifier cuts parameters while improving generalization. The dataset grouped patients by whether colorectal cancer later developed. With only tens of thousands of parameters, the model reached high accuracy and beat larger transformer and Mamba rivals, suiting it to resource-constrained settings.
arxiv-2602-04919:
Large language models reason well but cost a lot to run, and the usual remedy, pruning parameters in one pass, often wrecks the reasoning it meant to keep. The paper comes from Yiran Zhao and 9 co-authors. The usual fix, pruning away parameters in one pass, often wrecks reasoning skill and then needs heavy retraining to recover.

Their method compresses gradually, in many small rounds. Each round prunes a little, then fine-tunes to restore performance, like the slow warming in the boiling frog story. With only light retraining, models shrank to nearly half their size while keeping reasoning scores close to the original. The loop works with different pruning styles, from removing neurons to removing whole layers, and with different retraining styles. Tests beyond math, including code generation, also held up.
arxiv-2602-05019:
Learning algorithms that must respect a budget face a harder problem when the situations they meet are chosen adversarially. Dhruv Sarkar and Abhishek Sinha study that problem, called constrained contextual bandits, in this 2026 learning theory paper. Each action brings a random reward and a random cost, and the algorithm must keep both regret and total budget violation low.

Earlier work mostly assumed friendly, random contexts. Building on a known framework called SquareCB, the authors give a simple reduction: solve the constrained problem by calling ordinary online regression tools on cleverly reshaped rewards. The scheme keeps working even after the budget runs out, which matches real deployments. Their guarantees improve on prior results for the adversarial setting, and the analysis is compact enough to teach from.
arxiv-2602-05119:
Combinatorial problems can be softened into probability problems, where each yes-no choice becomes a coin's bias. Thanawat Sornwanee, writing alone, studies how to compute gradients in that softened form in this 2026 machine learning paper. Exact gradients seem to demand many evaluations of the underlying combinatorial function, which can be expensive.

Sornwanee proposes a stochastic gradient that is unbiased yet needs only a single query of the function per step. One known method, REINFORCE, falls out of the framework through importance sampling, which suggests the construction is natural. Around it sits a whole class of new stochastic gradients with the same one-query property. The paper runs to 23 pages and develops the theory carefully. Cheap unbiased gradients matter because they let standard optimization machinery attack problems that are otherwise all-or-nothing.
arxiv-2602-05219:
Private prediction asks a hard question: can one labeled dataset answer a long stream of questions without leaking its contents? Chao Yan, writing alone, improves the known limits in this 2026 learning theory paper. The setup, introduced by Dwork and Feldman in 2018, requires every answer together to stay differentially private with respect to the original sample.

Standard accounting makes the needed sample grow like the square root of the number of queries. Yan cuts that dependence to polylogarithmic in streaming settings. Against an oblivious online adversary, the sample size for any concept class depends on its VC dimension and only logarithmically on the query count. Against an adaptive adversary, the result covers halfspaces in any dimension, again with logarithmic dependence on queries. Answering vastly more questions from the same private data is the practical upshot.
arxiv-2602-05319:
Forecasting from a stream of observations usually means resampling a generative model from scratch at every step, which is slow. Yinan Huang and 4 co-authors recast sequential flow matching as Bayesian filtering in this 2026 machine learning paper. The Bayesian view suggests a neater recursion: carry yesterday's posterior forward instead of starting over.

Their framework learns a probability flow that transports the posterior from one time step to the next, conditioned on the new observation, mimicking how Bayesian beliefs update. Starting each sample from the previous belief, an informative distribution, slashes the number of sampling steps needed. Across accelerator beam dynamics, fluid dynamics, and weather forecasting tasks, plus decision-making benchmarks, the method matched full-step diffusion on distributional quality while running with far fewer steps and much lower latency. Code is available.
arxiv-2602-05519:
Grokipedia, a generative encyclopedia, now sits beside the human-edited Wikipedia, and Ortal Hadad, Edoardo Loru, and 4 co-authors compare the two. They ask how machine mediation changes which pages exist, how text is rewritten, and how stories are framed.
