Inclusion in Grokipedia is modeled as a function of a Wikipedia page's popularity, reference density, and recent editing activity.

Pages with more views and more editorial conflict were likelier to appear in Grokipedia. Among shared pages, heavy reference use and recent controversy made full rewriting more likely, while the most popular pages were often copied unchanged. Actor-relation networks built from the texts show that narrative structure stayed mostly alike across domains such as United States politics and geopolitics. Generative systems seem to keep the skeleton of the content while reshaping selection, wording, and tone.
arxiv-2602-05619:
Some neural network layers behave one way during training and another during evaluation, and that split can quietly destabilize reinforcement learning. Mohamad Mohamad, Francesco Ponzio, and Xavier Descombes show that in Proximal Policy Optimization, a widely used training method, batch normalization creates exactly this problem. The mismatch between modes leads to policy drift and, in bad cases, reward collapse.

Their fix, Mode-Dependent Rectification, is a lightweight two-phase training procedure that needs no change to the network architecture. It stabilizes training under batch normalization and, the authors note, extends naturally to other mode-dependent layers such as dropout. Experiments cover procedurally generated games and a real-world patch-localization task. In both settings the method improved stability and performance over standard training. The paper should interest practitioners who train vision-based agents with on-policy methods.
arxiv-2602-05719:
Quantum systems of many particles in a time periodic field raise a basic question: do the particles eventually scatter freely, and which states take part? Erik Skibsted studies N body Schrödinger operators with time periodic short range pair potentials. Using a time dependent commutator method, he shows that all channel wave operators exist, meaning each breakup pattern has a well defined scattering description.

For two particles he proves asymptotic completeness with a simplified version of the method, recovering a result Yajima proved by a stationary approach. The paper proposes a finite energy subspace, the states with finite asymptotic energy, and shows it coincides with the wave operator subspace. For three or more particles, completeness under time periodic potentials stays open, and the author offers the result as a possible stepping stone. A sharp minimal velocity bound for states outside the pure point subspace is another key ingredient.
arxiv-2602-05819:
Writing with a language model is a partnership, and Yeon Su Park, Nadia Arvi, Seoyoung Kim, and Juho Kim ask how that partnership changes a writer sense of authorship. They tracked two inner states during collaboration: self efficacy, the belief in one own writing ability, and trust in the model. A study with over three hundred participants logged every interaction and collected turn by turn ratings of both states.

Collaboration generally lowered self efficacy while raising trust. Writers who lost self efficacy were more likely to ask the model to edit their text directly. Those who recovered it asked instead for review and feedback. Participants with stable self efficacy reported, and showed, higher authorship of the final text. The authors draw design lessons for writing tools that protect authorship rather than erode it. The study was conditionally accepted at a leading human computer interaction conference.
arxiv-2602-06219:
Robots learning by reinforcement usually practice inside simulators, but simulators falter on contact, soft materials, and rich camera input. Joseph Amigo and 3 co-authors instead train policies inside world models learned from real robot experience. World models are costly to run, which blocks the gradient methods that train policies efficiently.

Their fix couples two models. A large diffusion world model unrolls accurate futures, while a small latent surrogate mimics its local behavior for cheap gradients. On a pushing task, the method beat a standard baseline by a wide margin in sample efficiency. A second test had a four-legged robot manipulate objects from its own camera view.
arxiv-2602-06319:
Graph problems make a stern test for large reasoning models: they need long careful chains, their difficulty tunes cleanly, and answers check by program. Qifan Zhang and 6 co-authors built GrAlgoBench, a benchmark of nine graph algorithm tasks for exactly those reasons. Math and code benchmarks, they argue, miss these strengths.

Two weaknesses stood out. Accuracy fell steeply as graphs grew, dropping below half once graphs passed a modest size, driven by execution slips, weak memory, and redundant steps. Models also over-thought: long self-checking traces added bulk without adding correctness. The benchmark gives researchers a sharp tool for studying how reasoning models fail and improve.
arxiv-2602-06419:
Where people look on a three-dimensional object mixes shape cues with meaning: a plain patch can draw the eye because it signifies something. Soham Pahari and Sandeep C Kumain present SemGeo-AttentionNet, a model of human visual attention on 3D surfaces that keeps those two streams separate, then fuses them.

One stream processes geometry from point clouds. The other draws semantic priors from diffusion models over rendered views. Cross-attention lets geometric features query the semantic content, so bottom-up distinctiveness guides top-down retrieval. The framework extends to generating scanpaths over time with reinforcement learning that respects mesh structure and avoids revisiting spots. Tests on three data sets showed substantial gains.
arxiv-2602-06819:
Ahsan Mehmood, Naveed Ul Hassan, and Ghassan M. Kraidy ask whether large language models can handle the physical-layer optimization tasks of future 6G Internet of Things networks. Their framework, PE-RTFV, avoids retraining entirely. It uses the natural feedback loop already present in wireless communication to steer an optimizer model that writes structured prompts for an agent model, which then produces solutions.

Working iteratively, the optimizer model refines its prompts from real-time feedback, guiding the agent toward better answers in a process resembling gradient descent. In a case study on a wireless-powered IoT testbed, the task was to design signal constellations balancing data rate against harvested energy. The framework reached near the performance of a genetic algorithm within only a few iterations, suggesting a practical route for resource-limited networks.
arxiv-2602-07219:
Finding the middle value of many numbers sounds easy, but neural networks struggle to do it accurately without growing very deep.  Abhigyan Dutta and two co-authors study how ReLU networks approximate the median of many inputs, and their construction beats expectations.

They build a constant-depth, linear-width network whose error shrinks exponentially over the unit hypercube, using stages that discard non-central values while guarding a candidate set around the median.  A reduction from the maximum to the median breaks a barrier suggested by earlier work on the maximum, which implied depth must grow.  Approximation theorists get a stronger result for the median than was known even for the maximum.
arxiv-2602-07319:
When language models answer medical questions for patients, a hallucination is not just wrong: it can be dangerous if it tells someone what to do.  Savan Doshi argues that testing should measure risk, not only factual accuracy, since current metrics treat all errors as equally severe.

The proposed method scores hallucinations by risk-bearing language, including treatment directives, contraindications, urgency cues. High-risk medication mentions, and combines that score with a grounding measure to flag high-risk, low-grounding failures.  Applied to three instruction-tuned models, it surfaces failure modes accuracy alone hides.  Clinicians and model evaluators get a safety lens for patient-facing medical AI.
arxiv-2602-07419:
If a newborn magnetar powers a gamma-ray burst, its spin-down should leave gravitational wave fingerprints in the X-ray afterglow.  Shu-Jin Hou and five co-authors hunt for those fingerprints, finding a promising case in GRB 130603B.

Fitting that burst's X-ray light curve with a model where spin-down is driven in turn by r-mode instability and magnetic deformation yields an initial spin period near half a millisecond. The fit also gives a dipole field around 5 x 10^14 gauss and a small ellipticity.  The result shows how afterglow decay can encode gravitational wave physics even before direct detection.  Space experts get a rare case study linking magnetar physics to observable afterglows.
arxiv-2602-07619:
The Kronecker sum is the unique matrix operation that exponentiates to the Kronecker product, and quotients give an algebraic view of product breakdowns. Keegan Doig Anderson and two co-authors explore Kronecker differences, a kind of inverse for sums.

They map the correspondence between them and quotients, and they characterize a class of differences through families of matrices that are themselves products. The approach offers a nonlinear perspective on tensor breakdown, distinct from standard linear treatments. Matrix theorists get a new family of tools with a clean characterization. The work also shows how these tools give a fresh view of tensor breakdown.
arxiv-2602-07919:
Text-to-image models can be abused to generate harmful content, and unlearning a concept usually means expensive full fine-tuning. Mansi and three co-authors propose TRUST, a method for targeted, robust, selective fine-tuning that dynamically locates the neurons responsible for a concept and retrains only those, stabilized by Hessian-based regularization.

Unlike static localization methods, TRUST adapts as training proceeds, and it handles concept combinations more realistically than single-concept approaches. Experiments against strong baselines show robustness to adversarial prompts, largely preserved generation quality, and much faster unlearning. The paper gives model providers a cheaper, more surgical way to remove harmful capabilities without degrading the model as a whole.
arxiv-2602-08219:
Designing hand-object interaction in virtual reality still means manual trial and error over how objects are grasped and manipulated for other users. Dohui Lee and two co-authors present HOICraft, a vision-language-model-based authoring tool that works inside VR to design part-level interactions.

The tool recommends interactable parts of 3D objects, customizes interaction properties, and maps hand movement to object behavior, building on a formative study with expert designers and preference data from twenty participants. In a study with twelve VR interaction designers, HOICraft's mapping cut trial-and-error iterations significantly versus manual authoring. VR designers gain an in-situ assistant that turns interaction design from guesswork into guided iteration.
arxiv-2602-08319:
When two neutron stars merge inside the crowded disk around a supermassive black hole, the short gamma-ray burst jet must push through a thin cavity carved by earlier outflows. Hao-Yu Yuan and three co-authors model the high-energy neutrinos such a jet would emit. They use three light sources to seed the process: the burst itself, the disk's heat glow, and scattered disk light.

Proton collisions with light dominate the neutrino output, and disk photons shift the spectrum toward lower energies. That shift grows for lighter black holes and bursts closer in. For a million-solar-mass black hole with the burst ten horizon radii out, IceCube could reach about 180 megaparsecs and its successor about 400. Readers get a concrete case for pairing neutrino alerts with light-based follow-up in active galaxies.
arxiv-2602-08419:
Fields that spike like one over distance, or blow up at crack tips, defeat ordinary neural networks that split coordinates apart. Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan and Bum Jun Kim first prove the obstacle: any smooth radial function that also separates additively must be quadratic. Their arXiv paper then offers Radial Müntz-Szász Networks as the way around it.

These networks mix learnable radial powers, including negative exponents, with a stable logarithmic term for exact log behavior. Closed-form gradients and Laplacians support physics-informed training on punctured domains. Across ten benchmarks the method cuts error by 1.5 to 51 times against standard networks, using just 27 parameters versus tens of thousands. Readers get a tiny, sharp tool for singular fields, with its limits honestly reported.
arxiv-2602-08619:
Timetabling is a classic hard scheduling problem, and hybrid methods promise to combine the strengths of different search styles. Laura-Maria Cornei and Mihaela-Elena Breabăn pair an evolutionary search method with a graph-based neural model for staff rostering. Their arXiv paper uses the network to encode general domain knowledge as an enhancement operator guiding the genetic search.

Both components were first optimized independently, then combined and tested against each standalone version. The hybrid brings statistically significant gains in both time efficiency and solution quality. To the authors' knowledge, it is the first such hybridization for timetabling. Readers get evidence that learned guidance and evolutionary search complement each other well.
arxiv-2602-08819:
Reward models grade language-model answers so training can steer them toward what people prefer. Jiwoo Hong and two co-authors point out a limit: once trained, these graders stay fixed, even when the goals change. Their 2026 paper offers a grader that can be steered on the fly with a few example preferences.

The method, called ICRM, treats a preference as an unknown chance that can be updated from examples, using Bayesian math. More examples lift its RM-Bench score from 60.5 to 70.8 and widen the range of trade-offs it can handle. It also beats a standard grader at math reasoning, showing it can carry checkable rewards into training.
arxiv-2602-09319:
Retrieval-augmented generation pairs a language model with an outside store of documents, a setup now common in business chatbots, health assistants, and agent memory. A 2026 benchmark paper led by Zhisheng Qi, with eleven co-authors, warns that cleverly phrased questions can draw private store contents out through the model, threatening trade secrets and privacy. Until now, attacks and defenses had been tested in scattered ways that made fair comparison hard.

The paper gathers the field into one systematic benchmark covering many attack and defense strategies, several retrieval embeddings, open and closed generators, and both graph-based and plain indexing. All entries are judged under shared rules across datasets in several languages. By making results reproducible and directly comparable, the benchmark aims to give builders a firm basis for designing retrieval systems that keep their knowledge stores closed to extraction attempts.
arxiv-2602-09619:
Dario Gasbarra and five co-authors study discrete-time, discrete-state multi-state Markov models through algebra stats in their 2026 paper. Widely used in event history work, these models are defined by a state space, a starting spread, and move odds, with finite paths as runs of states at finite times. The paper bridges event history work and algebra stats.

Joint path odds admit a natural monomial formula from starting and move odds. Setting aside stat limits on settings, varying models of any order appear as slices of split layered models. That yields a full account of their zero ideals as toric ideals made by stated two-term sets. Steady models behave apart, adding extra poly links and strictly larger ideals, with their own two-term sets derived. Fit guessing agrees between classic and algebra rules for varying models but grows more complex for steady ones.
arxiv-2602-09719:
Test-time adaptation updates model parameters at inference time using signals at hand at deployment. Longhuan Xu and two co-authors focus on one common yet underexplored regime in their 2026 paper. The model adapts alone per prompt, using only the prompt itself, with no gold answers or outside supervision. Naive adaptation with a handcrafted learning rate proves unstable. Updates overfit prompt stats, drift from the wanted answer spread, and harm generation quality.

The failure mode is unsurprising: adaptation must fit a single prompt within a few gradient steps, unlike standard training averaging updates over large sets. The authors offer layer-wise dynamic test-time adaptation, tuning adaptation strength by prompt picture, model structure, and adaptation step. Only low-rank adapter parameters change, with a light hypernetwork predicting per-layer, per-step learning-rate multipliers. Tests across sets and models show stronger adaptation with better stability and performance.
arxiv-2602-10019:
Training reasoning models with reinforcement learning hinges on estimating advantage, the credit each action deserves. A 2026 paper led by Qingnan Ren, with six co-authors, argues that static advantage estimates waste that credit, since a sample's usefulness shifts as training proceeds. The result is slower convergence and shakier learning.

The team introduces ADORA, which reweights advantage dynamically by sorting training samples into temporarily helpful and unhelpful groups during online rollouts. The scheme plugs into existing policy optimization methods without major surgery. Across model families and data scales, ADORA improved long reasoning in geometry and mathematics tasks without fussy hyperparameter tuning.
arxiv-2602-10419:
For machine learning interatomic potentials in molecular dynamics, gauging doubt matters. It flags extrapolation regimes and enables doubt-aware workflows like active learning. A 2026 paper led by Zhongyao Wang, with seven co-authors, notes current methods are often costly or weak. Evidential deep learning offers a grounded single-model option yielding both aleatoric and epistemic doubt in one forward pass. Pushing evidential methods from scalars to atomic forces raises hard problems, above all staying true when rotated.

The authors answer with Equivariant Evidential Deep Learning for Interatomic Potentials, a backbone-agnostic framework for forces and doubt jointly. Doubt becomes a full symmetric covariance tensor that turns with rotations. On diverse benchmarks it beats a plain rival and the ensemble method on accuracy, efficiency, and reliability. It gains better data efficiency through full equivariance while keeping single-model inference speed.
arxiv-2602-10519:
Victor Ostrik and Alexandra Utiralova describe new groups of braided finite tensor categories in a 2026 math paper. Tensor categories sort the algebra forms behind quantum symmetries and spatial phases, and the Witt group sorts them into equivalence classes. Whether every class contains a well-behaved semisimple member was an open question.

The paper answers it with stated endless groups. Its simplest example is a non-degenerate braided tensor category that is not Witt equivalent to any semisimple category. That single example shows a non-semisimple Witt class, showing the Witt sorting reaches beyond the semisimple world and widens the landscape of quantum algebra structures.
arxiv-2602-10719:
Sining Ang and ten co-authors compare language-grounded and vision-only backbones for end-to-end driving in a 2026 paper. Vision-language-action driving adds language-enabled vision to planning. But how those models differ from vision-only encoders after policy learning, and whether the difference matters, remains unclear.

Under a unified paradigm, a vision-language hidden state pairs with a spread policy. The team compares several vision-language families against standard vision-only encoders with the planner fixed. Policy learning enlarges a shared decision subspace, yet both branches keep non-shared residual factors. The shared-plus-unique pattern replicates on a standard planning benchmark, and latent interventions plus scenario analysis show the residuals shape conduct. The paper maps what language adds to driving perception.
arxiv-2602-10919:
Guang-Yao Xiao and six co-authors report a second giant planet around HD 164604 in a 2026 paper. The new planet orbits a K-type dwarf, with results from combined high-sharpness radial velocities and Hipparcos and Gaia astrometry. Its mass runs about nine and a half times Jupiter's mass under one orientation assumption, or about seven and a half under another.

The authors also refine the inner planet's orbit, finding a much eccentric path and a mass above Jupiter's by an order of magnitude. Depending on the outer planet's orientation, the mutual inclination between the two planets varies. It is small for a prograde configuration or very large for a retrograde one. Long-term dynamical integrations show most retrograde shapes remain stable, constraining the system's history.
arxiv-2602-11019:
Insider attacks hide in long stretches of quiet audit logs. Hayden Beadles and Jericho Cain split each time window into two parts. A mask says whether activity happened, and values say how strong it was. A two-channel autoencoder rebuilds both, with value loss counted only where activity exists.

Tests on the CERT r5.2 set show short attacks surface mainly through presence, while longer ones add a magnitude signal. Noise weakens magnitude and pushes finding back to presence. At campaign scale, signal piles into a few odd windows, so simple pooling of extreme scores recovers long attacks without sequence models. The lesson is that matching the model to sparse time structure matters more than adding hardness.
arxiv-2602-11219:
Doubt is often split into reducible and irreducible parts, yet both splits come from one spread and stay correlated. Tanmoy Mukherjee and three co-authors propose structural separation instead: knowledge and aleatoric doubt get disjoint setting paths and distinct supervision targets.

They build the idea into a credal concept bottleneck model and a credal self-explaining network, and prove that the two doubt heads avoid coupling through shared gradients. Across five ambiguity-aware benchmarks, separation cuts knowledge-aleatoric link while keeping predictive results. Aleatoric scores track annotator ambiguity, while knowledge scores track error and data scarcity. The result is doubt that is operationally distinct, not just decorrelated.
arxiv-2602-11419:
Reconstructing an outbreak from partial confirmed cases is a public health staple. Ritwick Mishra and two co-authors extend it to group surveillance, where pooled samples from wastewater or aerosol monitoring test many people at once. A negative pool clears all members, but a positive pool hides who is infected.

They formalize POOLCASCADEMLE: find a most likely cascade subgraph steady with pooled outcomes, choosing at least one node per positive pool. Under independent cascade spread, even a one-hop version proves NP-hard. Approximation recipes follow from group Steiner tree reduction and from straight programming relaxation with rounding. Tests on real and built contact networks beat rivals based on individual testing, improving missing-infection recovery and prevalence values.
arxiv-2602-11519:
Milnor numbers measure singularity hardness for curves, but rings need their own analogue. Yotam Svoray, writing alone, presents an analogue for 1D local rings inspired by Milnor's formula. It satisfies analogues of the classic Milnor number's properties for curves over a field.

Two analogues of the value semigroup are also studied, showing how they relate to the new Milnor number. Those tools then classify 1D rings of finite Cohen-Macaulay type by their semigroups, relating them to the semigroups of classic ADE singularities. The paper extends a curve invariant into ring theory with classification power.
arxiv-2602-11619:
Ask the same AI agent the same question ten times and you may get several different action sequences, a wobble most evaluations ignore. Aman Mehta turns that wobble into a tool: tasks where the agent behaves consistently prove far more accurate than tasks where it diverges, a gap that survives controls for difficulty. Across 8000 runs on 200 questions, steady tasks score roughly 82 to 87 percent while unstable ones fall to roughly 41 to 65 percent.

Divergence clusters early, at step two in about half of one model tasks, and consistency scores detect failures with moderate success. Answering only when three runs agree lifts accuracy to about 87 to 88 percent at roughly 54 to 62 percent coverage, matching a conformal baseline that needs held-out calibration data. Single-run rankings, the study warns, misorder models nearly 29 percent of the time.
arxiv-2602-11919:
Most tests of robotic hand motion use still objects, leaving moving targets and split-second timing largely unexamined. BoCheng Hu and four co-authors close that gap with DynaHOI-Gym, a unified online closed-loop platform with motion generators that can be tuned and rollout-based scores for dynamic capture tests. Built on that platform, they release DynaHOI-10M, a large-scale benchmark with 10 million frames and 180 thousand hand capture paths, whose target motions fall into 8 major groups and 22 finer subgroups.

The authors also offer a simple observe-before-act baseline called ObAct. It blends short-term observations with the current frame through spatiotemporal attention to predict actions, lifting location success by about 8 percent. Together, the platform, benchmark, and baseline give researchers a shared way to test hand motion against targets that move, rather than targets that sit still.
arxiv-2602-12419:
Smart factories need a bridge between a human's high-level intent and a machine's exact actions, and that bridge is still hard to build. Takoua Jradi led this work with six co-authors, joining instruction-tuned language models to ontology-aligned knowledge graphs for Manufacturing-as-a-Service. The goal is intent-driven interaction, where plain wishes become executable manufacturing steps.

Mistral-7B-Instruct-V02 is fine-tuned on domain data to turn natural language intents into structured JSON requirement models. Those models map onto a Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in the ISA-95 standard, aligning processes, resources, and constraints. Tests beat zero-shot and three-shot baselines, reaching 89.33 percent exact match and 97.27 percent overall accuracy, laying groundwork for scalable, explainable, adaptive human-machine manufacturing.
arxiv-2602-12519:
Poisson algebras and their Novikov variants appear in many algebraic settings, and transposed versions add a new twist. Jiarou Jin led this work with one co-author, Yanyong Hong. They define transposed Novikov-Poisson algebras, whose affinisation gives transposed Poisson algebras.

A natural transposed Poisson structure also appears on tensor products with right differential Novikov-Poisson algebras. It also arises from a transposed Novikov-Poisson algebra by taking the commutator Lie algebra of its Novikov algebra. Tensor products of two such algebras stay in the class, and several constructions are presented. These algebras relate closely to half-derivations of associated Novikov algebras. Using those derivations, the team shows non-trivial structures exist on solvable Novikov algebras under some conditions. If a non-trivial case is simple, its Novikov algebra is simple too. So over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, any simple case has dimension 1.
arxiv-2602-12619:
Mullins' model of thermal grooving describes surface diffusion flow with contact angle and no-flux boundary conditions, a classic problem in materials science. Yoshikazu Giga led this work with one co-author, Sho Katayama, studying that model in a multi-dimensional half space. If initial slope is close to that consistent with the contact angle, a unique global-in-time solution exists.

In particular, a self-similar solution exists for a given behaviour at space infinity. The global solution converges to a self-similar solution as time tends to infinity, if initial data are asymptotically homogeneous at space infinity. No assumption on contact angle size is imposed. Readers get a rigorous global existence and asymptotic profile for thermal grooving in multiple dimensions, with self-similarity as the long-time attractor.
arxiv-2602-12719:
Top quarks and their antimatter partners are not produced in exactly equal patterns at the Large Hadron Collider, and those small asymmetries test the standard model of particle physics. Nils Faltermann, reporting work from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations, sums up the latest experimental results on these asymmetries.

Asymmetries matter because they probe subtle differences in how matter and antimatter versions of the heaviest known particle emerge in collisions. By gathering the newest ATLAS and CMS findings in one place, the summary lets readers see where the two large experiments agree and where questions remain. It is a short status report rather than a new measurement on its own.
arxiv-2602-13219:
Extensions of Riemann shape since general relativity aim at a quantum, dynamic space-time reconciling gravity with quantum mechanics. Kareem Mubaidin and six co-authors go beyond earlier approximations by incorporating a phase-space metric tensor into general relativity. A canonical shape quantisation approach, presenting free-falling quantum particle kinematics in a tangent bundle, expands quantum mechanics to fast-motion gravitational fields and generalises the four-D Riemann surface to eight dimensions.

Finsler and Hamilton metrics follow straight from the Hessian matrix, and the quantised four-D metric tensor can be deduced through approximations in earlier work. This research instead derives a quantised eight-D metric tensor without those approximations and examines its upshots and the matching relative space-time. The derivation offers a concrete shape route toward reconciling relativity and quantum theory in a single space-time picture.
arxiv-2602-13319:
Personal agents need to model what a user wants, feels, and is facing, not just what they clicked. That inner state is rarely labeled, and raw digital traces are private, which creates a data bottleneck for perspective-aware AI. Situation Graph Prediction reframes the task as inverse inference: rebuild a structured, ontology-aligned picture of a user's perspective from observable multimodal traces, meant to serve as long-term memory for personal agents.

Since real labels are scarce, the authors generate synthetic data structure-first, aligning hidden labels with visible traces by design. A diagnostic study across three frontier models found latent perspective inference consistently harder than surface extraction, confirming the task is non-trivial. Jisung Shin leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13419:
Retrosynthesis asks how to build a target molecule, and language models can propose routes yet lack fine control over chemically sensitive sites they must avoid. Protect* grounds generation in chemical logic through a neuro-symbolic design: rule-based reasoning over more than 55 SMARTS patterns and 40 protecting groups identifies and guards reactive sites, while neural intuition proposes pathways.

Two modes operate: an automatic mode where symbolic logic deterministically guards sites, and a human-in-the-loop mode that folds in expert strategy. Active state tracking injects hard constraints into inference via a protection state tied to canonical atom maps. Case studies on complex natural products include a novel route to Erythromycin B. Shreyas Vinaya Sathyanarayana leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13619:
Finding when a data sequence changes is a core task, and privacy rules complicate it: local differential privacy means each observation is privatized before analysis. This paper studies offline pinpointing of a single change point among independent observations under that constraint. In the non-private setting, improved finite-sample accuracy bounds are derived for a generalized likelihood-ratio estimator using martingale methods.

Minimax lower bounds in both private and non-private settings show pinpointing accuracy is capped by Chernoff information between pre- and post-change distributions. Private algorithms based on pooled randomized response and binary tools push that information up in low- and high-privacy regimes. That measures the statistical cost of privacy, with tests on made-up data backing the theory. Anuj Kumar Yadav leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13819:
The axiom of choice implies every preorder can be extended to a total preorder keeping the strict relation, an extension called a prelinearization. This paper asks how much choice is really needed to build them. It isolates funicular preorders and shows they have prelinearizations in models of ZF plus dependent choice holding no nonprincipal ultrafilters over the natural numbers. Funicular preorders include coordinatewise domination on real sequences, Turing reducibility, and various preorders from social choice theory.

The relevant models are first built with tools from the geometric set theory of Larson and Zapletal, which requires an inaccessible cardinal. Then the inaccessible cardinal is removed using amalgamation methods for Cohen reals. The result separates prelinearization for this class from the strong choice principles it might seem to need. Azul Fatalini leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-14019:
Fei Hou and two co-authors tackle a 2026 arXiv problem on wave formulas outside an obstacle. For three-dimensional waves with a square non-linear term, long-time results for small data were known. But the two-dimensional Neumann case stayed open. The paper studies small-data answers with homogeneous Neumann boundary values.

New point-wise space-time decay bounds for waves in split form carry the proof. A set of good unknowns for energy bounds also helps. The result gives long-time life for small data. It applies at once to two-dimensional Euler flow for two gas types. It also applies to membrane formulas with Neumann data. All cases live outside an obstacle with sealed walls.
arxiv-2602-14119:
Ahmet Burak Yildirim and three co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv method for rebuilding 3D shapes from a single image. Large reconstruction models have advanced fast, but their outputs often show geometric flaws and misaligned details. The paper adds a self-correction loop that uses the model's own depth and normal predictions.

GeoFusionLRM feeds those geometric cues back through a dedicated transformer and fusion module, letting the model fix errors and stay consistent with the input view. No extra supervision or outside signals are needed. Tests show crisper shape, steadier normals, and truer detail than top large reconstruction baselines, with tighter fit between mesh and input views.
arxiv-2602-14419:
Kiyotaka Kasubuchi and one co-author recast a 2026 arXiv view of transformer focus through measure theory and frequency analysis. The paper argues falsehood is a built-in shape limit: the code space acts as a conditional mean over a sigma-algebra, and its failure to match the meaning truth set breaks logic calm.

The offered WavePhaseNet builds a Meaning Idea Rank Form using the discrete Fourier transform along the run size. Low-rate bands grasp global meaning and intent, while high-rate bands grasp local syntax and wording. That staged split enables precise meaning steering in diagonalized space. GPT-4's 24,576-size code space, with a 1/f spectrum from language self-likeness and Zipf's law, is studied through summed energy to back the build.
arxiv-2602-14519:
Chaosheng Dong and three co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv open-source setup for deep multi-task learning to rank. DeepMTL2R tunes many fit rules at once, joining mixed fit signals into one joined, context-aware model via transformer self-focus. That design handles varied and at times clashing goals in new ranking systems.

The setup holds 21 top multi-task learning methods and backs multi-goal tuning to find Pareto-best ranking models. By grasping tangled ties and long-range links among items and labels, it offers a scalable, rich answer and enables fair weighs across multi-task plans. Tests on a public set show matching scores, with trade-offs among goals drawn out, and the code is public.
arxiv-2602-14619:
Functions of several complex variables can share values in ways that force them to match. Abhijit Banerjee, with Sujoy Majumder and Jhilik Banerjee as co-authors, studies shifts and difference operators on such functions. The tools come from Nevanlinna theory in several variables.

A key section builds results on Borel exceptional values, which then drive the main uniqueness theorems. The theorems cover sharing with and without counting repeats, extending one-variable classics. Applications give conditions for a shift equation and growth bounds for partial differential-difference equations. The authors present it as the first systematic study of its kind.
arxiv-2602-14819:
Matteo Rinaldi, Rossella Varvara, and Viviana Patti present Testimole-Conversational, a corpus of more than thirty billion word-tokens of Italian discussion board messages from 1996 to 2024. Its sheer size suits pretraining native Italian language models, while its span captures informal written Italian, discourse dynamics, and online social interaction across nearly three decades.

Beyond language modelling, domain adaptation, and conversational analysis, the corpus supports studies of language variation and social change in computer-mediated Italian. A nation's online talk, archived at scale, becomes both training data and sociolinguistic record. Italian language technology gains a native-scale foundation.
arxiv-2602-14919:
Tianyi Ma and others give BHyGNN+, a no-label learning plan for mixed hypergraphs, where nodes that share a link tend to be unlike in sense or kind. Past hypergraph nets, with the team's own BHyGNN midst them, tame mixed nets but lean on marked data, a lean that bars use where marks are few or dear.

The new plan learns from the data alone, with no ground-truth marks in play, so mixed nets can be read where marks are thin. Hypergraph lore thus gains a no-label road into messy, unlike groups.
arxiv-2602-15019:
Vinogradov and colleagues argue that drug asset scouting must now hunt globally. Many new drug assets arise outside the United States and surface first through regional, non-English channels. More than 85 percent of patent filings originate abroad, China holds nearly half the global total, and China accounts for about 30 percent of drug development across more than 1200 novel candidates. Missing quiet assets can cost investors billions.

Yet current deep research agents still trail human experts at high-recall discovery across mixed multilingual sources without hallucination. The team builds a completeness benchmark from expert screening queries and a tuned tree-based Bioptic Agent. On that benchmark Bioptic scores about 80 percent F1, ahead of six rival systems that range from about 27 to 59 percent, with performance still rising steeply with added compute.
arxiv-2602-15119:
Martínez-Miravé and colleagues assess whether the neutrino burst from a stellar helium flash could be detected. Low-mass stars ignite helium under degenerate conditions, ending in a nuclear runaway known as the helium flash. Alpha capture on nitrogen makes large amounts of fluorine, whose decay spawns an intense burst lasting about a day. Electron capture on fluorine adds a strong neutrino line.

Detection faces large backgrounds in current observatories such as JUNO. Next-generation facilities such as the Jinping experiment would stretch the detection horizon considerably for a locally significant signal. Yet helium flashes occur only a few times per year in the Galaxy, and no stellar candidate nears the tip of the red giant branch within range. For now, the authors conclude, asteroseismology remains the most promising probe of the most energetic thermonuclear event in a low-mass star's life.
arxiv-2602-15319:
Aich and colleagues offer a copula-based setup to measure tail risks from twin markers. After turning marker edge to rank pseudo-values, they model link with Archimedean copulas, covering lower-tail, upper-tail, and given lower-tail risk. Doubt is gauged via a narrow Jeffreys guess on the copula value and later guess, giving a later for each tail-risk.

In tests from Clayton and Gumbel copulas across link levels, later ranges hit fit for three risks. They then study NHANES 2017 to 2018 fasting sugar and HbA1c data from 2887 people at alpha five hundredths, getting narrow later ranges for link and tail risks. Results show high edge swing versus chance; under Gumbel, the later mean joint upper-tail risk is about twenty-nine thousandths, about eleven and a half times benchmark. The method gives a sound, link-aware way for joint and given edge notes with Bayes doubt.
arxiv-2602-15619:
Kasri and colleagues design nonlinear phase gates for trapped ion quantum processors, a key ingredient for universal continuous-variable quantum computing. Their protocol is deterministic and uses simultaneous two-tone sideband drives beyond the Lamb-Dicke regime. Rather than suppressing higher-order interaction terms, the method harnesses them to build the gates.

That choice pays off in engineering terms: high-fidelity gate design comes with a near three-fold cut in control pulses compared with leading theoretical proposals. Fewer pulses mean less room for error to pile up and simpler control sequences. The paper will interest builders of trapped ion systems who need nonlinear gates that are both faithful and economical to run.
arxiv-2602-15819:
Ren and colleagues treat sketching as inherently ordered. People draw strokes in sequence to explore and sharpen ideas. Most ways of making them handle sketches as still pictures, leaving out the time-based process behind creative play. Earlier methods lean on big human-drawn sets or language-model instructions, and visual quality often suffers. Their VideoSketcher method reshapes pretrained text-to-video diffusion models around how sketches form, sparsely and continuously.

Language models and video diffusion models offer complementary strengths. Language models act as semantic planners decomposing concepts into step-by-step instructions. Video diffusion models serve as renderers translating them into time-ordered sketch sequences. A two-stage fine-tuning strategy decouples temporal structure from visual appearance. The order of strokes comes from made-up shape collections, while style comes from just seven hand-drawn examples. Despite minimal training, the method generates diverse ordered sketches following specified orders.
arxiv-2602-16019:
Elallaf and colleagues make chest X ray retrieval more trustworthy by replacing point embeddings with distributions. Vision language models learn strong image and text encodings, but their fixed vectors give no sense of doubt. That is a flaw in high stakes medical retrieval, where one report can match many images and vice versa.

MedProbCLIP models each image and report as a Gaussian cloud, trained to match pairs while penalizing overconfident scores. Multi view images and multi section reports supervise training, yet inference needs only one radiograph and one report. On MIMIC chest X ray data it beats fixed vector and prior probabilistic baselines on retrieval and zero shot classification. Calibration is better, selective retrieval is safer, and behaviour under realistic clinical corruption is sturdier.
arxiv-2602-16219:
Jaume Gine asks whether quantum gravity might emerge from geometry rather than from a fundamental postulate. The question is whether the generalized uncertainty principle can arise as a real manifestation of space shape, specifically from the statistical fine structure of local horizons. Under suitable assumptions about the multifractal structure of microscopic edges, the author argues that a real generalized uncertainty rule can indeed be induced by shape.

That perspective recasts quantum doubt not as a basic ingredient of nature but as an emergent consequence of how spacetime organizes statistically at the Planck scale. The framework does not claim to be a complete theory of quantum gravity. It offers a proof of concept for a geometric origin of generalized uncertainty relations. It also gives a thermodynamic route linking horizon fine structure, entropy corrections, and real quantum behavior. That route is compatible with several modern approaches through scale-dependent shape.
arxiv-2602-16419:
Ivan Emelyanenkov and Eduard Emelyanov prove results on relative uniform convergence and the Archimedean property in pre-ordered vector spaces and Abelian groups. For a pre-ordered vector space, they show that a certain quotient space, built from the closure of the positive wedge in the relative uniform topology, is an Archimedeanization of the space. A construction of an almost Archimedeanization is also given.

Analogous results are presented for pre-ordered groups. The paper further gives an explicit example of a family of vector lattices. In that family, a chain of spaces of infinitely small elements stabilizes first at any chosen ordinal up to and including the first uncountable ordinal. The work thus ties the Archimedean property to concrete quotient constructions in both vector spaces and groups.
arxiv-2602-16519:
Marco Leon Scheiter and Sebastian Wolf study radiative torques in the molecular cloud core L43. Polarized emission from dust grains is widely used to infer fields from the diffuse medium to cloud cores, so understanding dust alignment matters for reading field properties.

L43 holds an embedded yet optically visible star that lights its surroundings unevenly, letting the authors test torque alignment. From polarization maps at three wavelengths, they use differential measure analysis to infer field strengths and study the global spectrum. They find plane-of-sky field strengths from about thirteen to sixty microgauss, varying with wavelength, and a negative polarization slope. That favors radiative torques as the main mechanism, with polarization tracking temperature and local radiation strength.
arxiv-2602-16819:
Yiqing Xie and co-authors present Hybrid-Gym, a training environment that teaches coding agents to generalize across tasks. Most coding agent benchmarks test single GitHub issues, as in SWE-Bench, yet real use demands varied skills: exploring codebases, testing software, and designing architecture. The paper first names transferable skills shared across diverse tasks by splitting trajectories into fine-grained parts, then derives principles for auxiliary training tasks.

Hybrid-Gym offers scalable synthetic tasks such as function localization and dependency search, built on those principles. Agents trained on its synthetic tasks generalize to real-world tasks absent from training, lifting a base model by large margins on SWE-Bench Verified, SWT-Bench Verified, and Commit-0 Lite. It also complements downstream-task datasets, giving agent builders a practical generalization curriculum.
arxiv-2602-16919:
Nivasini Ananthakrishnan, Alireza Fallah, and Michael Jordan study signaling in data markets via free samples. A buyer seeks to gauge an unknown parameter by purchasing samples from one of several sellers. Each seller privately knows data quality and a private per-sample cost. The game has two stages: a free-trial stage where sellers may signal quality by offering a few samples free, and a procurement auction stage.

Buyers update beliefs from the sample variance of free data, then run the auction. For the auction, the paper characterizes a near-optimal Bayesian incentive compatible mechanism. The buyer picks one seller by minimizing a belief-adjusted virtual cost. For the free-trial stage, equilibrium is characterized with that mechanism as continuation. Free trials may fail to emerge. But under strong competition, a unique equilibrium exists where sellers reveal the maximum allowable samples.
arxiv-2602-17119:
Zhenyu Bai led a seven-author team designing a processor architecture that refuses to choose between specialization and flexibility. Domain-specific accelerators excel on their target workloads but falter on new kernels or ragged inputs, while programmable chips like FPGAs and GPUs stay flexible yet lose efficiency on irregular, sparse data. The paper introduces Canon, a parallel architecture meant to match specialist efficiency without giving up general-purpose agility.

Canon runs on dynamic, data-driven control: programmable finite state machines, set at compile time, turn incoming metadata such as sparse coordinates into control instructions on the fly. A time-lapsed SIMD scheme staggers instructions across processing units over several cycles, spreading control cost thin. Tests across varied kernels showed high performance with specialist-like efficiency, keeping the flexibility that programmable hardware promises.
arxiv-2602-17319:
Rik Versendaal, writing alone, proves a large deviation principle for weighted geodesic random walks on a complete Riemannian manifold. For almost all weight sequences under a suitable measure, these walks, suitably scaled, satisfy the principle with a universal rate function. The result extends earlier work that handled only the real-valued case.

The argument also works for general vector spaces, the author shows. That generality lets the paper import methodology in which large deviations for geodesic random walks follow from large deviation estimates for associated random walks in tangent spaces. The work thus lifts a real-valued result to manifolds and vector spaces alike, with a single universal rate function.
arxiv-2602-17619:
A team led by Jothi Prasanna Shanmuga Sundaram improves data spread for grid-powered Internet of Things networks. Many hops separate senders from receivers in such nets. An earlier contention-based protocol, DRP, cut control-packet overhead with delay timers tied to link quality. But field tests showed real link swings still caused overlapping sends and costly back-offs.

Their enhanced protocol, EDRP, adds two parts. Link-quality aware CSMA narrows back-off ranges from live link estimates, so well-linked nodes wait less. A machine-learning block-size selector for rateless codes predicts link conditions and trims overhead. Field tests show average goodput gains of nearly two fifths over rival protocols, a practical win for dense multi-hop deployments.
arxiv-2602-17819:
Eric Lindström and Larisa Beilina present a variational optimization approach for a coefficient inverse problem. The goal is to rebuild dielectric permittivity and conductivity functions at once in time-dependent Maxwell's system, using limited edge readings of the electric field. Such joint rebuilding from partial data is hard.

The approach builds a weak form of a Lagrangian, enabling finite element based rebuilding methods. Rules for the Lagrangian and an error bound for the adjoint problem are derived. Smoothness of the Lagrangian and of the tamed Tikhonov goal is also shown. Flat and solid sim runs confirm the theory, giving readers a tested route from edge data to material traits.
arxiv-2602-18019:
Yujie Jin and colleagues push security-oriented video understanding beyond threat spotting. Earlier work mostly detects and locates threats such as shootings and robberies in video, but cannot explain or judge what caused them. Their new chat-paradigm task, DeepSVU, asks systems to identify and locate threats and also attribute and evaluate the causes behind threatening segments.

Two challenges shape the task: modeling coarse-to-fine physical-world information, from human behavior and object interactions to background context, and balancing those factors adaptively. Their Unified Physical-world Regularized MoE approach pairs two parts: a Unified Physical-world Enhanced MoE block that models that information, and a Physical-world Trade-off Regularizer that balances it. Tests on two DeepSVU instruction datasets show the approach beating advanced video language models and non-vision-language approaches, confirming the value of coarse-to-fine physical-world information.
arxiv-2602-18319:
Nam Hee Kim and five co-authors built Robo-Saber, a system that generates player motion for playtesting virtual reality games, the first of its kind. Their 2026 paper trains a player model on the large BOXRR-23 dataset to generate headset and controller movements from in-game object layouts. Style exemplars guide it, and it is tuned to maximize simulated game score. The test game is the popular Beat Saber.

The resulting model plays skillfully and mirrors the skill levels and movement patterns of its style inputs, capturing diverse player behaviors. That matters for game makers: synthetic play data can feed predictive applications, and a physics-based whole-body agent can playtest VR games without recruiting human testers for every build. The paper opens a practical path to automated VR playtesting.
arxiv-2602-18719:
How few sample points are enough to pin down a function, and how well can least squares do with them? Abdellah Chkifa, with three co-authors, generalises a sparsification algorithm of Batson, Spielman, and Srivastava in 2026, making one part of its result independent of dimension.

The payoff is discretisation inequalities in both average and worst-case norms on finite-dimensional spaces, plus a suitable infinite-dimensional version, with direct implications for the error of sample-based least squares. The argument gives a more constructive route to several recent approximation bounds that had relied on a stronger, less constructive result. It also improves the constants and oversampling factors involved.
arxiv-2602-18819:
Most simulations of how suspensions flow assume a uniform material, yet real suspensions often contain coexisting phases that change everything. Raul Molina-Prados Lallena, with five co-authors, reports in 2026 on the rheology of a two-dimensional Lennard-Jones suspension across its gas-liquid and gas-solid coexistence lines.

Comparing the heterogeneous system with homogeneous references shows that the presence of multiple coexisting states strongly affects mechanical behaviour. The result is an extended map for navigating these materials, in which density and temperature alone do not decide the story. Phase coexistence itself helps dictate the shift from viscous to elastic-dominated behaviour under shear. That map offers a benchmark for future work on heterogeneous fluids where complex coexisting states are common.
arxiv-2602-19019:
Generative models can copy artistic styles and concepts without credit, and marking often fails when several concepts combine in one image. Li Zhang, with four co-authors, introduces TokenTrace in 2026, a proactive marking frame for robust, multi-concept credit.

Signatures are embedded in the semantic domain by perturbing both the text prompt embedding plus the initial latent noise guiding diffusion generation. For retrieval, a query-based module takes a generated image plus a textual query naming which concepts to retrieve, such as a specific object or style. That mechanism disentangles concepts and verifies each independently from a single image. Experiments show state-of-the-art performance on single-concept and multi-concept credit tasks, beating existing baselines while keeping high visual quality and robustness against common transformations.
arxiv-2602-19119:
Poisson's equation for Markov chains gains new ground here. Julian Hofstadler, writing alone in 2026, studies general state-space chains under a Wasserstein shrinking assumption. Answers exist for Lipschitz functions. Their smoothness traits are studied in detail. The setting is general. State spaces need not be finite. Chains may live on rich spaces.

More follows. With a reversible kernel, answers for Lebesgue-integrable functions also exist. Combined with Doob's martingale inequalities, maximal bounds follow for shrinking chains. Examples demonstrate the results, especially for Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. Contractive chains thus gain a fuller analytical toolkit.
arxiv-2602-19319:
Health records live in scattered systems, and patients rarely control them. Sujaya Maiyya and two co-authors present Health+, a vision paper for a user-centered, multimodal health data system. It would let individuals, including those with little technical experience, upload, query, and share their own data across forms such as text, images, and reports. It avoids waiting for institutions to overhaul their systems.

At the system level, Health+ tackles storing, integrating, and securing varied health records, aiming for both efficiency and privacy. Intuitive interfaces and smart recommendations would guide decisions about access and sharing. The paper lays a foundation for a more connected and interpretable health information ecosystem, one where the patient, not the institution, steers the data.
arxiv-2602-19519:
Chain-of-thought reasoning helps language models, but it wastes tokens on simple requests, a problem in cost- and latency-sensitive settings. Yirou Ge and ten co-authors study selective thinking for tool-using language models and introduce Ada-RS, Adaptive Rejection Sampling, an algorithm-agnostic sample filtering framework. For each context, it scores multiple sampled completions with a reward that penalizes length adaptively.

Stochastic rejection sampling then keeps high-reward candidates only, or preference pairs, for later optimization. Ada-RS plugs into both preference-pair methods such as DPO and grouped policy methods such as DAPO. On a synthetic tool-call e-commerce benchmark with Qwen3-8B and LoRA, it improves the accuracy-efficiency frontier, cutting average output tokens by up to 80 percent.
arxiv-2602-19619:
Discrete diffusion language models offer a fast, flexible rival to autoregressive models by denoising in parallel steps. Luhan Tang and three co-authors ask a pointed question: is the sampler itself correct, or do scores mix up denoiser error with sampler error? They build a sampler-centered oracle setup that swaps learned denoisers for an exact Hidden Markov Model posterior from a known Markov chain.

Few-step samplers turn out not to be distributionally correct even with an oracle denoiser, where transition-level mismatch fades only as step counts near the sequence length. Better negative log-likelihood, generative perplexity, or MAUVE scores do not prove correct sampling. Readers get a clean test rig for sampler error, plus public code.
arxiv-2602-19719:
Guessing the full three-dimensional pose of an object from images is hard when the object looks the same from several angles, or when it lacks distinctive local marks. A 2026 arXiv paper by Amir Hamza and four co-authors recasts the task as conditional flow matching, a generative approach that denoises a pose estimate step by step.

Their method, Flose, conditions that denoising on both geometry and appearance-based semantic features, so symmetry ambiguities are eased, and it adds a robust registration step to handle outliers. Tested on five data sets from the established BOP benchmark, Flose beats prior methods on average recall. The paper thus offers a generative route to pose estimation that copes better with symmetric and feature-poor objects.
arxiv-2602-19819:
Learning parity with noise is a hard problem that underpins the security of several post-quantum cryptosystems, and the best classical attacks scale exponentially. A 2026 arXiv paper by Daniel Shiu, working alone, asks whether quantum methods might open a different route.

Inspired by Regev's link between lattice problems and the hidden dihedral subgroup problem, Shiu uses neighbourhoods of binary fields to build a function close to satisfying Simon's promise. Its difference equals the secret parity vector. Running Simon's algorithm is unlikely to recover that vector directly, but it essentially produces fresh problem samples. Those samples might let one ignore variables one by one and shrink the problem. The author claims no competitive edge, only that the idea merits deeper study.
arxiv-2602-20019:
Spotting anomalies in dynamic graphs matters for fraud, security, and monitoring, but labelled anomalies are scarce. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yuxing Tian and five co-authors proposes a framework that learns a sharp boundary mainly from normal and unlabeled data, using scarce labels without overfitting to them.

Unsupervised methods avoid labels but draw fuzzy boundaries, while semi-supervised methods can overfit the few labels and fail on new anomalies. The new framework has three parts. First, residual encoding captures gaps between current interactions and their history. Second, a restriction loss keeps normal vectors inside an interval set by two co-centred hyperspheres. Third, a bi-boundary tuning step learns a robust boundary from a normalizing-flow model of log-likelihood. Tests across diverse settings show the framework beating rivals while staying model-agnostic and widely usable.
arxiv-2602-20119:
Long robotic tasks need joint reasoning about task structure and physical contact. Zero-shot planning from vision-language models plus video generation tends to fail. Hallucinated physics and geometric errors compound over time. A 2026 arXiv paper by Jiahui Fu and nine co-authors introduces NovaPlan, a layered framework for robust zero-shot long-horizon handling. It proposes, verifies, and repairs visual plans.

At the high level, a vision-language planner breaks tasks down. It filters out futures that violate dynamics by checking multiple candidate video rollouts. Imagined futures become reliable physical actions through a hybrid spatial representation. That representation switches as needed between flow centred on objects and flow from human hands. NovaPlan then closes the loop. It monitors the run throughout, checks outcomes, and creates local non-prehensile fixes such as fingertip poking when the run drifts.
arxiv-2602-20519:
Fractionally charged particles are predicted by theories beyond the standard model, yet most searches assume heavy lepton-like particles, leaving light-mass candidates little studied. The DAMPE Collaboration, led by F. Alemanno, searches for light-mass fractionally charged particles in primary high-energy cosmic rays using ten years of on-orbit data from the Dark Matter Particle Explorer satellite. It targets particles with charge two-thirds that of the electron.

No candidate was observed. The team sets an upper flux limit for particles near half a megaelectronvolt in mass at ninety percent confidence. The null result constrains the light-mass window that underground and space-based searches had largely left open, showing what a decade of DAMPE data can rule out.
arxiv-2602-21019:
String-to-string functions with polynomial growth form a robust class called polyregular functions. Thomas Colcombet, Nathan Lhote, and Pierre Ohlmann propose an exponential-growth analogue in this 2026 arXiv paper: expregular functions. Three models describe the class: MSO set interpretations, yield-Hennie machines, and a new model called Ariadne transducers.

The main contribution translates MSO set interpretations into yield-Hennie machines, which are known to reflect regularity. That step shows MSO set interpretations reflect regularity too, settling a major conjecture: every automatic omega-word has a decidable MSO theory. A second translation runs from Ariadne transducers back to MSO set interpretations, proving all three models equivalent. Readers get a robust new class with three interchangeable descriptions.
arxiv-2602-21619:
Muku Akasaka and one co-author test whether adding information helps visual spatial reasoning in vision-language models. Visual spatial reasoning stays hard for modern vision-language models despite multimodal gains. A common fix injects extra data at run time, such as spatial cues, commonsense knowledge, or chain-of-thought instructions. But it is unclear when such data helps and when it adds noise.

The team runs a hypothesis-driven study across three models and two public benchmarks. They vary spatial context type and count, commonsense amount and relevance, and the interplay of spatial grounding with chain-of-thought prompting. Results show a steady pattern: more data does not always mean better reasoning. Targeted single spatial cues beat multi-context aggregation, excess or weakly relevant commonsense harms scores, and chain-of-thought helps only when spatial grounding is precise enough. The lesson favors selective, task-aligned data injection.
arxiv-2602-21719:
Jouni J. Takalo studies a prime-weighted oscillatory model inspired by structural aspects of the Euler product of the Riemann zeta function. The model builds finite superpositions of prime-frequency modes and shows zero-like crossings from destructive interference. He analyzes how the weight exponent controls amplitude growth, slope scaling, and crossing stability.

A heuristic asymptotic argument singles out one half as the balance regime separating high-energy from over-damped behavior. The results concern the defined model itself, not the zeta function directly, and map how the exponent shapes the model's crossings.
arxiv-2602-21919:
Cuong Anh Pham, Praneeth Vepakomma, and Samuel Horváth tackle a classic headache in machine learning: teaching a model new tasks without wiping out what it learned before. Their 2026 arXiv paper revisits methods that keep new learning at right angles to old learning. They note that directions tied to small singular values sit nearly at right angles to the inputs of past tasks.

From that insight they build NESS, a method that works straight in the model's weights and trains only one small matrix per task, held inside an estimated null space. Tests on three standard task sets show strong results, low forgetting, and steady accuracy across tasks. The paper argues that these small values deserve a central place in continual learning design.
arxiv-2602-22219:
Retrieval-augmented generation shines on plain text, but e-commerce assistants must query structured knowledge graphs, where scaling retrieval and preserving relationships is harder. Teri Rumble and three co-authors compare retriever-reranker pipelines for natural-language queries over knowledge graphs in online retail. Cross-encoders sharpen precision, yet their fit to structured data is little studied.

The study designs and compares multiple pipelines, tracking how retrieval and reranking choices shape answer quality over graph data. It gives production teams evidence for which combinations hold up at scale in a live assistant setting. For builders of domain-specific shopping help, the paper maps a practical route from graph queries to grounded answers.
arxiv-2602-22419:
CLIP models learn from image-text pairs, but their training captions are usually short, biasing them toward simple descriptions of salient objects. Marc-Antoine Lavoie and four co-authors identify a subtler bias in long captions. They typically open with a one-sentence summary, which becomes a shortcut that concentrates attention on early tokens and weakens alignment over the rest. Both human- and machine-written captions share the pattern.

The team introduces DeBias-CLIP, which removes the summary sentence during training, forcing attention across the full caption. The fix targets coarse alignment on complex scenes and dense descriptions, where CLIP currently falters. Multimodal builders gain a simple training change that teaches models to read the whole caption, not just its opening line.
arxiv-2602-22719:
Vamshi Sunku Mohan and three co-authors learn to steer state-space models by squeezing their bottlenecks. State-space models offer a lean alternative to attention-heavy transformers, yet how to interpret or steer modern versions remains little explored. Using mechanistic interpretability tools, the team locates activation subspace bottlenecks in the Mamba family.

Their test-time fix is strikingly simple: multiply the bottleneck activations by a scalar. Across seven state-space models and six benchmarks, that tweak lifted performance by about eight percent on average, with no task-specific tuning. The team then rebuilt the bottleneck itself into Stable-Mamba, which gained on long-context tasks when retrained from scratch, confirming the bottleneck was truly holding performance back.
arxiv-2602-23019:
Nikolai Kaschewski and two co-authors build a general theory of spin-tied density-density links for two-state Fermi gases. It holds at any heat, push-pull, size, and mass or headcount gap. Gauge sameness and the Pauli principle yield constraints in line with the wobble-loss theorem and Wick's theorem, giving the links a firm formal footing.

As an example, the team studies the BCS to Bose crossover in two dimensions at zero temperature, inspired by lithium-6 experiments. Two-particle irreducible contributions from collective excitations, many-particle scattering, and vertex corrections prove essential, producing the experimentally observed minimum in opposite-spin density-density correlations that simpler treatments miss.
arxiv-2602-23219:
Hiroki Naganuma and five co-authors test whether a classical statistics tool, Takeuchi's information criterion, can measure how well deep neural networks generalize. Reliable generalization measures are hard to build for singular models such as deep networks, whose complex structure resists standard theory. The authors develop theory showing the criterion applies near the neural tangent kernel regime, where wide networks behave almost linearly.

The experiments are large: over 5,000 trained networks across 12 architectures, including VGG-16, on four data sets, with several feasible approximation methods for the criterion. Estimated criterion values track the generalization gap well near the neural tangent kernel regime, but the link vanishes outside it, as theory predicts. The criterion also beats existing methods at pruning trials in hyperparameter search.
arxiv-2602-23319:
Youssef Trifa and three co-authors extend quantum gravity probes from single probes to many-body atom groups. Clocks using the mass-energy link and beam tests using spread-out states share an account in terms of a working qubit-qubit link. The paper extends that account to atom groups treated as linked joint qudits.

Many-body boosts raise the signal-to-noise ratio and the working link rate, making it easier to see gravity-made entanglement and its fading, checked by spin-squeezing tests done locally and jointly. Trapped two-mode Bose-Einstein clouds with long-range links, including dipolar links, emerge as a tunable test bed for copying gravity-driven quantum motion at lab-scale time and energy scales. Adding a sensor network widens the spotting window further.
arxiv-2602-23419:
Alloni studies whether RES-NOVA, a novel cryogenic experiment using crystals grown from archaeological lead, can probe neutrino non-standard interactions. Dark matter detectors can already observe solar neutrinos through coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, opening a window on new neutrino physics. RES-NOVA uses lead tungstate crystals grown from ancient lead, chosen for its low intrinsic radioactivity.

The sensitivity study assumes a nominal one keV energy threshold and one ton-year exposure, under both a conservative heat-only readout and an ideal heat-plus-scintillation background rejection scenario. In its nominal setup, RES-NOVA is not sensitive to Standard Model solar neutrino interactions, yet it reaches non-standard interaction sensitivities matching current global fits. Lowering the threshold to 0.5 or 0.2 keV, or raising exposure to ten ton-years, would push beyond global fits and test new parameter space in the electron and tau sectors.
arxiv-2602-23519:
L. G. Barbosa and two co-authors study scalar bosons with Coulomb potentials in a spacetime holding both a cosmic string and a global monopole, within Rainbow Gravity. An effective metric describes the combined topological defects together with the energy-dependent deformation of spacetime.

The Klein-Gordon equation is set up in this background with scalar, vector, and nonminimal couplings, and solved by separation of variables. Generalized Coulomb-type interactions allow a unified treatment of scattering and bound states, with the bound-state spectrum read from poles of the S-matrix. Two choices of rainbow functions are examined numerically and, in suitable limits, analytically. The results show how defects plus rainbow corrections shape the spectrum, while known results return in appropriate limits.
arxiv-2602-23919:
Matteo Faini proves global regularity results and Schauder estimates for a class of stationary operators that do not sit in divergence form. The 2026 solo paper treats operators built from homogeneous Hörmander vector fields, a family of directions that can generate full space through their commutators. This holds even when fewer directions than the ambient dimension are given.

The coefficients form a symmetric, uniformly positive-definite matrix whose entries vary in a Hölder-continuous way, measured with the control distance set by the vector fields. The fields need not be left-invariant, which widens the setting beyond group cases. Schauder estimates of this kind control how smooth solutions must be, given smooth coefficients and data, and they underpin existence and regularity theory for degenerate elliptic equations modeled on such vector fields.
arxiv-2602-24019:
Lorens F. Niehof and three co-authors extend the analogy between freezing lakes and cosmological expansion by adding buoyancy-driven heat transport. The 2026 paper reformulates the Stefan problem for ice growth with both conductive and convective heat fluxes, yielding an ice-thickness equation structurally analogous to the Friedmann equations for the universe's scale factor.

Beyond reproducing radiation-like, matter-like, and curvature-like behaviors, a reduced description of convection, modeled as a power law in liquid-layer thickness, adds two effective contributions. One is a constant term, analogous to a cosmological constant, arising from persistent buoyancy transport under confinement. The other falls inversely with thickness and, in Friedmann form, implies a fluid with negative energy density, possibly an effective description of a domain-wall network. The authors stress that the second term reflects their reduced flux assumption, not a universal prediction.
arxiv-2603-00319: Pradeep and Welikala build a model predicting battery charge depletion over time and motor-drive duty cycle for a simulated four-wheel Arduino robot. A forward-motion simulation, including motor electrical traits and mechanical dynamics, generates charge time series across duty cycles from 1 to 100 percent. Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics plus regression then yields one unified nonlinear model of charge over time and duty cycle. The framework supports planning that saves energy for similar robots and can extend to other starting charges and environments.
arxiv-2603-00419: Shaldehi and Salkuyeh build inexact block splitting preconditioners for three by three block systems from a special class of indefinite least squares problems. They first pin down when the matching stationary iterations converge, then show preconditioned eigenvalues cluster inside a unit circle centred at one. That clustering speeds the GMRES solver, and a detailed eigenpair study yields a theoretical cap on GMRES iteration counts. Numerical tests confirm the new preconditioners work well in practice.
arxiv-2603-00519: Chen and four colleagues speed diffusion generation with Jano, a training free method that notices image regions settle at uneven rates during denoising. An early stage check reads regional convergence needs from the first denoising steps, then a scheduler spends compute where it is still needed. Tests on leading models average twice the speed, reaching up to 2.4 times, while holding quality. Uniform rules thus waste effort that region aware timing saves.
arxiv-2603-01119: Bhattacharya, Ocelli, and Westling set out causal triangulation, mixing figures from rival models with varied ID rules instead of picking one model. Their mix weights each model's found figure by data-driven trust scores, with a bound on distance from the true effect and terms for that gap to vanish. Valid inference follows, and tests plus a real case show strength under a many-model view without needing models to agree.
arxiv-2603-01319: Kieserman and six colleagues study how users explore close roleplay with chatbots on Character.AI, joining platform study with analysis of Reddit posts from its users. Against popular stories, they find users want close role-play with young adult, male-looking figures placing users in inferior power spots within well-defined scenes, plus diving in boundless fantasy settings. Users also flag both too much and too little sexual content in such chats, a finding calling for novel digital-safety tools.
arxiv-2603-01419: Fang and four colleagues apply deep learning models to spot carbon-14 pile-up events in the JUNO testbed, where leftover carbon-14 in glow fluid hurts positron sharpness. Gauging neutrino mass order needs high-quality positron sharpness, with JUNO aiming to settle the order at 3-sigma trust within 6 years from late 2024. Carbon-14 signals are far smaller than positron signals, and close event time and vertex compound the challenge. The paper tests a range of deep learning models for pile-up spotting.
arxiv-2603-01519:
Takashi Maruyama, Tatsuki Seto, Viktor Zaverkin, and Henrik Christiansen recast a key rule of statistical physics in this 2026 work. The hyperforce sum rule links forces in a fluid at rest to how its parts are arranged. It extends a classic chain of equations that tie each level of particle groups to the next.

Their new form rests on a Leibniz rule for how derivatives act on paired test functions and distributions. From that one rule, both the sum rule and the classic chain at any level follow in flat space. The same step also gives the sum rule for boxes with periodic edges, a common setup in simulations. A cleaner base can make later proofs shorter and show where the rule truly comes from.
arxiv-2603-02219:
Junfeng Fang, Nachuan Chen, Houcheng Jiang, and colleagues build a live safety filter for language models in this 2026 paper. Text arrives token by token, so a filter must act mid-stream, not after the fact. Filters trained per token need costly labels and tend to overfit. The team argues that ready-made filters already hold token-level risk clues inside them.

Their filter, NExT-Guard, reads those clues with sparse autoencoders, tools that split inner signals into clear features. It needs no new training and uses autoencoders from public base models. In tests it beat both late filters and trained live filters. Gains held across models, autoencoder types, and risk types. The approach offers a cheap, flexible path to real-time safety.
arxiv-2603-02519:
Wei Jiang, Tong Chen, Wei Yuan, and colleagues detect mixed-source misinformation with agent teams in this 2026 paper. False content can hide in lying text, forged images, or a mismatch between them.
