Medicine, finance, and science often face this shortage, and image style tricks do not transfer well to tables. Their method, called SeBA, splits each table into two matching views and aligns what the model learns from each view.

No artificial changes to the data are needed, which keeps table meaning intact. Theory supports the approach, and tests across several benchmark tables place SeBA at or near the top in most cases. Table based learning with scarce labels gains a fresh route that respects the data as it is.
arxiv-2605-08819:
Felix Krones asks whether pretraining medical image models on medical data actually pays off downstream. Deep learning has transformed medical imaging, yet the link between pretraining choices and final performance stays murky. Krones systematically compares convolutional networks and transformers across supervised and self supervised pretraining, varied starting points, and data types, then tests them on natural photos, chest X-rays, chest scans, and retinal images.

Only pretraining closely matching the target modality reliably improves results. Self supervised learning can beat supervised approaches, but its edge shifts with context. The study gives developers concrete guidance: match the pretraining diet to the clinical target instead of assuming any large scale start transfers equally well to patient care.
arxiv-2605-09119:
Enoch Hyunwook Kang, writing alone, studies personalized alignment, the task of adapting a language model to users whose preferences differ. His 2026 paper in learning theory asks exactly when such adaptation can be statistically efficient, in the sense of very low regret during online use and few samples needed offline. The answer turns on a single user-diversity condition about the spread of user-specific preference directions.

Kang proves that condition is both necessary and sufficient. When the population of user heads spans every reward direction that could change the best response, simple greedy methods reach the benchmark rates. When the span fails, every learner in a natural class pays at least a growing regret cost. The result names user diversity as the basic driver of whether personal preferences can be identified at all, giving designers a sharp test for when personalization promises are realistic.
arxiv-2605-09319:
Duong and two colleagues defend semantic watermarks for diffusion models against removal and forgery attacks that exploit diffusion inversion. Their analysis shows both attacks shift latents across a line: watermarked latents are pushed out of the watermarked region, and unwatermarked latents are guided into it.

They propose Progressive Guided Inversion and Denoising, a plug-and-play noise extraction method that needs no training, the first built to defend against both attack strategies. PGID sends changed latents back to the region where they belong, clearing mid-course latent deflections and softening hostile tweaks through progressive inversion-denoising cycles. Across many watermarking schemes, PGID restores reliable detection, getting back removed watermarks and flagging forged cases. The defence needs no retraining and fits existing detection setups, making watermark checks harder to fool.
arxiv-2605-09719:
Asfour and four colleagues shrank a large AI system that reasons about three-dimensional space into a much smaller one. Their student model has 2.29 billion settings against a teacher model's 7 billion, yet keeps much of the teacher's skill at spatial tasks. The work targets vision-language models, AI that links pictures with words, for devices that cannot run huge models.

Instead of training the small model on worked step-by-step answers, the team gave it a fixed set of learnable thinking tokens. These tokens act as a private scratchpad before it answers. The student also learned to describe scenes, judge depth, and spot objects within one shared design. It ran about 8.7 times faster than the teacher while holding 54 to 72 percent of its performance on focused spatial tests.
arxiv-2605-10019:
Wang and two colleagues studied when and how generative models learn rules, tracing two training time points called clocks. The first clock, tau-rule, marks when outputs first turn rule-valid. The second clock, tau-mem, marks when models start copying training data. Generative models trained on finite data face a tension: their training goal settles on the seen data spread, not the true spread they seek to learn.

Starting with parity and other binary rules and puzzles, the paper maps how the clocks depend on the learning setup. Tau-rule rises with rule hardness and falls with model size. Tau-mem stays nearly the same across rules and scales nearly with dataset size. The innovation window between the clocks widens with dataset size, narrows with hardness, and can vanish when tau-rule catches tau-mem. The same structure appears in DiT and GPT models, with design-dependent offsets.
arxiv-2605-10119:
Fernández-Hernández and four colleagues argue that balanced Adam's remaining parameter is a memory scale, not a fixed constant. Recent evidence shows Adam works robustly when its two momentum parameters are tied, leaving a single parameter, but how to set it is poorly understood. In balanced Adam, it defines a memory horizon, the inverse of one minus beta. The paper studies the refresh count: how often Adam renews its inner stats during useful training.

Across eleven vision and language experiments, choosing beta for a refresh count near one thousand picks different beta values per training scale. Yet it beats the best fixed-beta baseline. Against the strongest fixed choice, beta equals 0.944, the refresh rule cuts the worst-case validation-loss gap by 33.4 percent and brings all eleven runs within one percent of their validation oracle. The result offers a budget-aware view of optimiser scaling.
arxiv-2605-10719:
Leander Thiele gives a teaching account of run-based guessing for star physics and cosmos study. Run-based guessing trains neural networks on forward runs to estimate model settings, serving hard odds and time-constrained after-the-fact sampling. After showing where the approach helps, the paper describes the basic after-the-fact, likelihood, and ratio methods. Other paths, in-order versions, and learned recaps are covered briefly, with a short guide to choosing among methods.

Because failures can be subtle yet invalidate results, run-based guessing needs testing, and the paper explains common check methods. Recent uses in the cosmos study and star physics literature are listed, and current method hurdles are covered. Training with limited run budgets is the key problem for cosmos and star-physics applications, where forward runs are costly and after-the-fact closeness rests on few runs.
arxiv-2605-11319: Michael Salins and Yuyang Zhang study when solutions of the stochastic heat equation blow up in finite time. The equation adds a superlinear reaction term and polynomially growing noise, driven by space-time white noise on a periodic interval. They refine prior results in a less understood regime. They show mild solutions can explode with positive probability when the reaction exponent lies between one and three with matching noise, or above one with weaker noise.
arxiv-2605-11419: Bustos-Espinoza and nine colleagues explore stellar streams and satellites around Malin 1. Malin 1 is a giant low surface brightness galaxy with a disc exceeding one hundred kiloparsecs. They build gravitational potentials from optical and hydrogen data, testing NFW and ISO dark-matter halos. The ISO halo favours bound satellite orbits more than NFW. Giant streams look like substructures of satellites along leading and trailing paths. The most distant satellite may have passed pericenter about 1 point 6 billion years ago, supporting interaction-driven shaping of Malin 1.
arxiv-2605-11519: Tennenholtz and colleagues treat controllable user simulation as a causal inference problem for testing conversational agents. Offline datasets miss rare cases and cannot test new policies, driving interest in prompted or fine-tuned simulators. They show that training simulators on post-hoc trajectory labels yields a biased model, since labels link to the generating policy and inject look-ahead bias. Under policy shift, metric variance grows geometrically: controllability collapse. Their causal simulators use a-priori controls, stepwise dynamic controls and direct policy learning to restore consistency.
arxiv-2605-11819: In 2026, Kenji Kurosaki and Masahiko Arakawa simulate how shattered, differentiated asteroids reassemble into rubble piles. Their smoothed particle hydrodynamics impacts show catastrophic disruption stretching core and mantle into a sheet that fragments under its own gravity, yielding fragments with nearly identical iron-rock ratios. The largest remnant is thus an iron-rich rubble pile, and such piles arise only if the core is molten. The results frame metal-rich bodies such as Psyche and Kalliope for NASA's Psyche mission to test.
arxiv-2605-12019: Aleksandr Bredikhin, Philippe Lalanda, and German Vega reuse frozen large language models as time cores for sensor-based human motion tracking. A shaped convolution step maps motion and spin signals into the language model's latent space, and lean LoRA tuning keeps training cheap. Tests showed fast settling, strong data thrift, and robust cross-dataset transfer, above all with little data. Local patterns sit at the signal level while long-range links ride the ready-made core.
arxiv-2605-12119: Haofeng Liu and eight colleagues build MoCam, which makes views of a scene from old ones. Shape cues line things up but thin out and go wrong as views shift, while look cues keep detail but lack space links; mixing both creates clashes. MoCam leans on shape cues first for rough form, then switches to look cues to fix shape flaws and polish detail. Splitting the two jobs in time unites still and moving view work, beating past systems when point clouds have big holes or warps.
arxiv-2605-12319: Kikot, Shulgin and Xu tackle a practical step in turning plain questions into database queries. When several candidate queries are on offer, their method picks between them using small data examples that separate the candidates, plus records of where each result came from. Tested on part of the BIRD-DEV set, it beats three simple rivals most clearly when only two or three candidates exist and no agreement score is available.
arxiv-2605-12519: Kim and nine colleagues train language models to get answers right and reason soundly at the same time. Rewarding only final outcomes can raise scores while harming thought traces, leaving them wrong, partial or at odds with each other. Their verifiable process supervision first fine-tunes models into a structured thought format, so mid-way claims can be pulled out and checked. Adaptive weighting then focuses on subtasks with the largest errors left, forming a hidden curriculum. Chess serves as a testbed where steps can be checked against engine signals.
arxiv-2605-13019: Zhu describes quantum graphs as left ideals in the extended Haagerup tensor product of an algebra with itself, dodging representation issues. From these ideals plus operator space theory she derives a new representation-free account of quantum graph morphisms, compatible with earlier representation-dependent versions. A notion of categorical limits and colimits for quantum graphs follows. She also explores one other quantisation of graphs as bimodules over C-star algebras, noting that its morphisms differ from C-star correspondences.
arxiv-2605-13219: Wang and colleagues compare ways to fill gaps in survey photometry before estimating galaxy distances. Missing colour bands can badly damage photometric redshift estimates, which cosmology studies rely on. A nearest neighbour method wins when gaps are random and training data are complete. An attention based model called SAITS proves tougher when training data are incomplete or gaps follow mixed patterns, while flux limit gaps defeat both approaches.
arxiv-2605-13419: Bogdan Djordjevic fully characterises when the Sylvester equation ax minus xb equals c has a solution in Banach modules. The setting uses two unital complex Banach algebras and a Banach module acting between them, with given elements a, b and c whose spectra overlap. He states checkable rules that are both sufficient and necessary for a solution to exist. He also gives formulas for particular solutions when the equation can be solved. Finally, he characterises when solutions are unique.
arxiv-2605-13719: Hao Wang and six colleagues argue the very late-time glow of GW170817 favours a wobbling jet over a narrow shaped jet. The slow decay of the very late-time glow defies narrow jet guesses. A tilted ring-shaped jet thus explains the multi-signal data without extra parts. Bayes study favours a ring-shaped jet over a narrow jet at 4.8 sigma, giving a wobbling angle near 27 degrees. Such a large angle points to big disk tilt, maybe from disk-falling gas mixing or uneven angular spin loss.
arxiv-2605-13819: The ATLAS Collaboration searches for weak chargino pair production and chargino-neutralino associated production. Each breaks through a B-L R-parity-breaking coupling to a lepton plus a W, Z or Higgs boson. Data from 140 inverse units at 13 TeV and 56 inverse units at 13.6 TeV, collected between 2015 and 2023, are matching with Standard Model guesses. Results give limits at 95 percent confidence level on model-free cross sections for events beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2605-14019: Aldridge gives a closed-form account of regret in stochastic optimization. The usual route re-solves the problem across many simulated scenarios, at a cost that scales with scenario count and solve cost. Instead, regret can be read from the joint moments of the cost vector and the optimal decision. Regret splits into minus the covariance of cost and optimal decision, less a residual term. That residual vanishes when the optimal decision is affine in cost, which covers unconstrained and equality-constrained quadratic programs and many linear programs.
arxiv-2605-14319: Nicola and Campbell work out an approximation for the evolution of the population rate or flux in coupled integrate-and-fire networks, as a function of the initial voltage spread. Firing rate fluctuations show up at several time scales, in single neurons, across trials, and across populations. Unlike earlier mean field approaches using steady states, this approach uses the transport solution to the advection equation, assuming slow inputs and driven neurons. The transport mean field system shows how firing rate fluctuations arise from interaction between inputs, initial densities, and coupling.
arxiv-2605-14419: Jain and colleagues introduce zSort, an adaptive z-score distribution sorting algorithm. It guarantees stability with key-width-independent pass counts. Analysis finds lower bad-speculation overhead than stable baselines and fast unstable algorithms, with an instructions-per-cycle figure of 1.44. Across inputs up to ten million elements, zSort runs three to four and a half times faster than stable comparison sorters. Gains over LSD Radix are largest on duplicate-heavy and partly ordered inputs. It matches unstable sorters on throughput and shows no extreme worst case.
arxiv-2605-14619: Chen, Nian, Cao and Jiang map how multi-run chain-of-thought reasoning splits and rejoins, instead of collapsing runs to final answers. Their SliceGraph links reasoning slices by sparse activation-key similarity into a problem-model-cell graph. Across math and science runs from three models, most cells split correct chains with the same answer into several process families, dubbed process isomers. Success-linked regions also split into separate high-value cores, with route families specialising over them.
arxiv-2605-14719: Mauerer and Schonberger present a toolbox for studying quantum annealing applied to data management problems. The link between device physics and problem difficulty is poorly understood in this area. The toolbox analyses spectral and dynamical traits, such as energy gaps and eigenstate structure. Hardware tests cannot reach these traits directly, yet they govern hardness and scaling. Derived quantities and plots support reading optimisation dynamics, spotting links to standard physical models, and building reduced effective descriptions.
arxiv-2605-14819: Li and team identify a Velocity Deficit in flow matching. The mean squared error objective tends to lower velocity size. Samples thus fail to reach the data manifold, an effect termed Integration Lag. Two fixes are proposed. Magnitude-Aware Flow Matching trains with size awareness. The Scale Schedule Corrector needs no retraining. Contraction is shown to harm the trajectory start yet help denoising at its end. On ImageNet, the corrector is claimed to improve FID by about forty-five percent with five times faster generation.
arxiv-2605-15119: Hayato Tagawa studies staggered diff-in-diff designs. Treated and control units can face each other's adoption. With a researcher-chosen exposure map, he splits the total effect into a switch effect of one's own adoption and a spillover effect without it. Trend matching identifies both by matching treated cohorts to never-takers in matching exposure states, and the difference gives the spillover. Outcome-regression and doubly robust estimators follow, with an application to Community Health Centers showing falling mortality.
arxiv-2605-15219: Salman Avestimehr, Ken Duffy, and Muriel Médard ask whether AI can find new knowledge through iterative self-improvement. Their NOVA model treats the generate-verify-accumulate-retrain loop as a live sampling process over knowledge space. Loose feedback can trap generation on early accepted artifacts and leave reachable valid items unfound with positive probability. Tying updates to a fixed base distribution prevents wild warp, guaranteeing continued exposure. Under flawed verification, small false-positive rates can admit invalid items faster than genuine finds once easy knowledge runs out.
arxiv-2605-15319: Jonah Berggren and Clément Chenevière present a wider abstract for two papers in drafting on framing lattices, which generalize Tamari lattices and weak orders. They model irreducible elements and canonical join representations in all framing grids through bricks and brick cliques, extending non-crossing arc diagrams for the symmetric group's weak order. The model captures the join-meet bijection and duality under flips, proved one-to-one with a direct two-step reconstruction. Corner cliques then define cubical coordinates extending Tamari bracket vectors.
arxiv-2605-15719: Wei Shao and five colleagues build a light, repeatable sleep tracker from raw accelerometer signals. It turns signals into epoch activity traits, smooths them, scores them, and sorts sleep from wake with a tuned threshold. Tuned on MMASH, it misses total sleep time by 41.6 minutes, with start slip 6.3 minutes and end slip 7.4 minutes in the test set. On WeBe data from three people, it misses total sleep time by 27.4 minutes, with start slip 13.9 minutes and end slip 8.0 minutes in field sessions. A commercial ActiGraph line shows wider gaps.
arxiv-2605-16019: D'Enterria and four colleagues compute inclusive charm and bottom quark pair production cross sections at next-to-next-to-leading order accuracy. Covering collision energies from about 10 GeV to 400 TeV, they compare the new MaunaKea code against all existing data up to 14 TeV. Second-order results run up to twice the first-order values, with smaller scale uncertainties, and match data across the full range. Charm data at multi-TeV energies can further constrain the gluon density at very small x.
arxiv-2605-16219: Mansouri prices the privacy cost of tail-risk learning under differential privacy. For tail mass tau, the privacy sample size is not n but n times tau, so the effective private tail size is epsilon times n times tau. Private CVaR excess risk splits into ordinary tail error plus a privacy price. Complete rates cover scalar estimation and finite classes under pure differential privacy, with lower bounds extending to approximate privacy in small-delta regimes. The canonical hard case is ordinary private learning on the tail records.
arxiv-2605-16619: Bragagnolo and Kumar track the interior of an evaporating black hole in a simple Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity model with an end-of-the-world brane. They read complexity from a boundary-to-brane geodesic length, including wormhole effects. Unlike a non-evaporating hole, whose complexity rises then plateaus, here it rises early, peaks shortly before the Page-time crossover, then decays exponentially. Fluctuations stay small before that crossover, then grow large, signaling a loss of self-averaging.
arxiv-2605-16919: Lu's team studies forecasting for distribution-valued time series, where observations are shares or mixtures that live on the probability simplex. Their method, CAST, retrieves past successors from causal context, steadies them with a persistence anchor, and applies bounded local transport on ordered supports, keeping every stage on the simplex. They expose a failure mode, latent transition-kernel aliasing, where similar distributions evolve differently by regime, and prove summary-only forecasters carry an irreducible error floor. On eleven benchmarks, CAST ranks best on average for one-step and rollout scores.
arxiv-2605-17319: Choi, Singh and colleagues model pulsed jets through passively flexible nozzles with three-dimensional fluid-structure simulations. Softer nozzles slow deformation waves, stretch the expansion phase and store elastic energy, then release it to boost jet acceleration and vortex strength. For the most flexible nozzle, vortex circulation rises 52 percent and total impulse 62 percent over a rigid nozzle. A lumped oscillator model predicts those outcomes within a few percent.
arxiv-2605-17419: Ren Ozeki, Rizk and Yamaguchi build a landslide early-warning system robust to displaced rainfall forecasts, which shift rain fields and corrupt local accumulation estimates. Their model learns latent representations from rain and terrain data that stay stable under field motion, trained with rainfall-motion-aware contrastive learning that mimics forecast displacement. Tests on two years of Japanese data across 19 landslide regions beat leading baselines in precision by up to 37 percent.
arxiv-2605-17619: Singh and colleagues study dynamic shear banding in a grain aggregate using defect mechanics and experiments. The model uses a length scale tied to hardening from dislocation density, plus crystal plasticity with Voce-law strength. Simulations capture finite-width shear bands and low-angle subgrain boundaries even without heat conduction, plus size-dependent strengthening for grains from 1 to 20 micrometers. Large 3D runs with one million elements track strength, stress and temperature through large strains. Dislocation density piles up at grain edges and pattern interiors, showing change before failure.
arxiv-2605-17719: Diego Adame and nine colleagues propose Patch-MoE Mamba, a design for outlining structures in medical scans. It keeps nearby pixels together while reading at several scales. Standard convolutional nets miss long-range links, and transformers grow costly with image size. So the team scans patches in order and fuses scan directions through expert modules that adapt to object size and shape. Tests on five polyp benchmarks and two skin-lesion sets show the approach works broadly.
arxiv-2605-18319: Johanna Marie Gegenfurtner, Moritz Grillo, and Guido Montúfar sort out which different weight settings of a deep ReLU network actually do the same thing. For three layer bottleneck nets, they pin down every typical family of equivalent settings in full. Their account writes each family out in explicit semi algebraic form and turns the sameness question into a test that runs in polynomial time. Some symmetries create local conserved quantities along gradient flow, while the rest leave no such law behind.
arxiv-2605-18419: Franciskus Xaverius Erick, Johanna Paula Müller, and Bernhard Kainz present GAUC, a 2026 training-free method for picking demo examples. The target is vision-language models in histopathology, where fine-tuning is costly and example choice swings results. GAUC works in the pretrained multimodal embedding space, balancing three goals: distributional fidelity, robustness to prompt paraphrases, and a penalty on shaky outputs. On CRC-100K and MHIST it matches the strongest baselines on accuracy while lifting calibration and prompt robustness.
arxiv-2605-18519: V. Martínez-Fernández and three co-authors provide, in a 2026 paper, the first tomography of a light nucleus, helium-4, from elastic form factors and deeply virtual Compton scattering. Constraining generalized parton distributions at next-to-leading order, with kinematic twist corrections and full evolution, they reach theoretical precision unprecedented even in proton studies. The tomography reveals distinct transverse spatial distributions of quarks and gluons inside the nucleus.
arxiv-2605-18719: Komal Kumar and five co-authors propose SafeDiffusion-R1, a 2026 online method for safe diffusion training. Older methods need costly supervised data, and offline training suffers catastrophic forgetting. Their method trains with Group Relative Policy Optimization on mixed prompts, needing no specialized reward models. A steering reward pushes text representations toward safe directions and away from unsafe ones in CLIP space. Inappropriate content falls to about eighteen percent, from about forty-nine percent for SD. Nudity detections fall from 646 to 15, while GenEval quality rises to about forty-eight percent.
arxiv-2605-18819: Kumbha Nagaswetha and Rabi Pathak explain why pseudo-observation batch methods work in Bayesian optimization, and when they fail. Constant Liar, Kriging Believer, and fantasy models all pick batches by filling in guessed values, yet no unified theory had tied them together. The authors identify efficient conditioning. It means predictions update in closed form when data grows. They prove Gaussian processes meet it, unify the three methods as one mechanism with different guess distributions, and link the idea to local penalization.
arxiv-2605-19219: Han Li and 19 colleagues present SimGym, a tool for A/B test simulation on e-commerce storefronts with vision-language model agents in a browser. It combines persona generation from clickstream data, a browser agent with perception, memory, and guardrails, and a protocol comparing simulated shifts with real buyer shifts. Validated on UI theme tests, SimGym agents reach 77 percent directional alignment with add-to-cart shifts in real traffic. It shrinks test cycles to under an hour, from weeks before, enabling rapid tests without exposing real buyers to candidate variants.
arxiv-2605-19819: Areces, Barceló, Cassano, Castro, Demri and Fervari show satisfiability for knowing-how logic over linear plans is NP-complete, tightening previously known complexity bounds. Knowing-how assertions capture an agent's ability to reach a goal under linear-plan semantics. The proof translates the logic into modal logic S5, a tool with broad uses in knowledge representation. The result sharpens the complexity picture for a logic of ability, placing its satisfiability problem exactly at NP-complete.
arxiv-2605-20019: Andreas Fring and Marta Reboiro study a time-dependent non-Hermitian spin-boson model with complex couplings. Its Dyson map links the model to a Hermitian counterpart and sets a positive physical metric. They prove a no-go result for a Gaussian number-squeeze-number class: with a nonvanishing linear interaction, Hermiticity plus bounded invertibility force the map's bosonic part to be unitary. A separately driven single-mode cavity then breaks the matching symmetry while preserving parity, coupling dressed sectors two bosonic quanta apart and enabling genuine transitions.
arxiv-2605-20119: Emaad Khwaja and twelve co-workers show time-series foundation models scale, releasing Toto 2.0. One training recipe yields steady forecast gains from four million to two point five billion parameters. The family of five open-weights models leads three benchmarks: BOOM for observability, GIFT-Eval for general forecasting, and the contamination-resistant TIME benchmark. The report details architecture, training recipe, training data and a hyperparameter-transfer pipeline, with all five base checkpoints released under Apache 2.0.
arxiv-2605-20619: Liuyuan Jiang, Chentong Huang, and Lisha Chen propose SURF, a way to sample uniformly along the Pareto front in multi-objective optimization. Evenly spaced scalarization weights usually give uneven front coverage, since solutions traverse the front at nonuniform speed as weights vary. Integrating that speed gives cumulative arc length, and normalizing it yields a distribution function on weights. Its inverse picks points at equal arc-length gaps, and the authors derive closed forms for structured cases like bi-objective bandits.
arxiv-2605-20919: Emma Leonhart presents Sutra, a typed, fully functional programming language whose built forward pass is a PyTorch neural net. The compiler beta-shrinks the whole program, primitives, control flow, and string input-output, to one merged tensor-op graph over a fixed embedding substrate. Rotation binding, unbind, pack, polynomial Kleene three-valued rules, and tail-recursive loops all drop to tensor operations. Validation is one fact tested two ways, with the same program running on four frozen embeddings spanning two modalities.
arxiv-2605-21219: Ningxin Kong, Matteo G. A. Paris, and Qiongyi He propose criticality-assisted noncommutative preparation, a framework for quantum-enhanced metrology. Direct use of criticality in encoding limits which parameters can be sensed and narrows the useful range. Their approach instead uses critical evolution to prepare states, so noncommutativity between preparation and encoding boosts quantum Fisher information. The gain can arrive at fixed total sensing time and energy cost, and Wigner-Yanase skew information tracks the same critical scaling.
arxiv-2605-21319: Matthew A. McCartney and co-authors seek the best time window and frequency band for subject-specific motor imagery EEG classification. Such EEG is often classified with linear discriminant analysis on common spatial pattern features, yet scores vary across studies using varied windows and bands. They train and test subject-specific models across combos for one hundred nine subjects, comparing scores with repeated measures ANOVA. Results show clear gaps between specific windows and specific bands, guiding per-subject choice.
arxiv-2605-21419: Jingtao You and co-authors study cosmic collider signals from right-handed neutrino loops in inflation with the seesaw mechanism. Its interaction with right-handed neutrinos goes through a unique dimension-five operator with shift symmetry. This creates a chemical potential during slow roll, yielding helicity-based output and stronger signals. The work links early-universe physics to particle physics. It treats that field as the driver of the effect.
arxiv-2605-21519: Joshua Dennis Booth and Vishvam Patel present neural acceleration for graph partitioning. Graph partitioning matters in social networks, VLSI design, and other domains. Spectral methods give quality partitions with small edge cuts. But computing the Fiedler vector is a bottleneck. Their approach replaces eigenvalue calculation with a neural network approximating the Fiedler vector.
arxiv-2605-21719: Silva and Ayanian design a way for robot teams to cover unknown territory by chasing information rather than a preset map. Their method builds a target distribution from environmental models that update live from sensor feedback, then steers each robot so its time spent across regions matches that distribution. Simulations show the teams concentrate on high-interest areas and use their resources more efficiently than fixed ergodic search.
arxiv-2605-22019: Sachin Bhalekar studies pantograph delay differential equations, in which the delay is a fraction of the present time. He derives exact rules that split the plane into unstable, long-run stable, and delay-based stable regions. Tests back the theory and show how sharp the boundaries are. The paper also builds a scaled-delay analogue of the Mackey-Glass chaotic delay equation and studies the behavior that results.
arxiv-2605-22119: Papatsaroucha and co-authors review human weakness assessment in cybersecurity, on methods, models, and instruments. Checks usually target digital assets and digital systems, yet the human factor is increasingly targeted and manipulated by adversaries, and technical checks alone fall short. Human flaws extend beyond individual susceptibility to threats. The review covers literature through 2025, asking whether any methods address the full range of human flaws dynamically. It finds gaps in current solutions and calls for holistic checks spanning both unintentional and intentional dimensions.
arxiv-2605-22519: Rankin offers algebroid desingularizable Poisson manifolds from a symplectic Lie algebroid. The class equals E-symplectic manifolds. A tiny block: at a zero, its isotropy must contain an abelian ideal of at least half its size, so semisimple ones fail. In the linear case, the dual of a real n-sized Lie algebra with KKS structure passes iff it has an abelian ideal of size n-r. Here 2r is the max orbit dimension. One is built.
arxiv-2605-22619: Jiang and team propose GLeVE, a graph lesion grounding framework with anatomical checks. Grounding radiology reports to 3D CT volumes is hard due to the notes-body gap. Older tools rely on phrase-level or dense pixel training, with weak links and weak localization. GLeVE treats each lesion note as one. It encodes organ links, traits, and lesion links through graph logic for picks. Body picks with checks enforce direct matches, while octree tuning sharpens. Tests on AbdomenAtlas 3.0 show gains over mixed models and report rivals in segmentation.
arxiv-2605-22819: Yang and eight colleagues build Cambrian-P, a video model that tracks camera position and direction across frames instead of treating each frame alone. Camera pose gives every view a shared spatial frame, yet most video models ignore it. Their model adds learnable camera tokens and a pose prediction head, gaining several percent on spatial reasoning tests and reaching top streaming pose scores on ScanNet.
arxiv-2605-22919: Argüelles and four coauthors build a full theory of open quantum systems tied to scale-invariant settings. Such settings are described by unparticle baths with one scaling dimension. From a uniqueness result they derive memory kernels, exact noise kernels, and a fractional Caldeira-Leggett equation. That dimension drives a thermalization shift at 3/2, an Ohmic edge at 2, and a decoherence shift at 5/2. Uses span critical Ising models, inflation, and high-energy neutrinos.
arxiv-2605-23019: Ling and six coauthors present PACE, a two-timescale framework for small language model agents that evolve themselves without weight updates or frontier-model teachers. PACE refines prompts under fixed control logic until gains level off, then considers constrained control-logic updates accepted only through held-out validation. Across three frozen backbones from 4B to 14B parameters and four benchmarks, it won all twelve combinations, improving over vanilla agents by up to 9.2 percent and over single-mode evolution by up to 5.4 percent.
arxiv-2605-23119: Guo and Li extend the stabilizer rules for linked quantum error codes with noisy ebits. They move it from binary to general q-ary cases, where q is a prime power. Using the general Pauli group and symplectic geometry over finite fields, they build a unified framework for qudit systems. Matching forms use geometry and additive codes. They construct several groups of q-ary codes with noisy ebits. Under certain noise cases these can beat standard codes with equal error power.
arxiv-2605-23319: Holtgrefe and Schestag make budgeted phylogenetic diversity tractable on networks, where picking taxa to protect must weigh both evolutionary distinctness and uneven costs. Diversity over trees is easy, but networks and budgets together turn hard. Through node scanwidth, a measure of how tree-like a network is, they optimize two variants in time exponential only in that width and quadratic in budget. A harder third variant gets scored on a similar basis. Tests on simulated networks with hundreds of taxa run in fractions of a second.
arxiv-2605-23819: Jorge Chang Ortega and colleagues ask whether human-like vision comes from telling categories apart or from modeling how images form. Holding architecture, scale and data fixed, they slide one mixing knob on joint energy models between the two training styles and test six human alignment benchmarks. Alignment peaks in the middle, not at either end, because hybrids keep both crisp category structure and sensitivity to input detail. Balance, they argue, beats picking a side.
arxiv-2605-23919: Mayr, Meddah, and Tubikanec model tax compliance and evasion as a random process in which audits push cheats toward compliance while imitation pulls taxpayers toward cheating. Each force alone drives the population to an extreme: full compliance under audits only, full evasion under imitation only. Both forces keep population and total income conserved. Combined, they stop the system settling at either extreme, instead producing swings around the deterministic path and hinting at a stable long-run distribution. The result pictures compliance better than fixed-behaviour models.
arxiv-2605-24019: Wang and three co-authors compress vision-language models with MGVQ, a quantization method mixing sensitivity-aware precision and gradient-Hessian fusion. One module assigns bit-widths by channel sensitivity, using global and local analysis; a second folds first-order gradients into second-order error correction, using Kronecker and Block-LDL decomposition to keep cost low. It answers two flaws: one codebook cannot fit visual and textual weight patterns, and second-order correction drifts from pretrained optima. At 2 bits, it beat quantization rivals by up to 4.9 points on InternVL2-26B.
arxiv-2605-24119: Kumar and six co-authors make and study ZnCrGaO4, a tangled pyrochlore-like magnet with mess from cation sorting. Response gives a large below-zero Curie-Weiss heat near minus 205 kelvin, showing strong opposing exchange between chromium moments. Despite that strength, no long-range order appears down to 125 mK, and no spin freezing shows in cooled response or in flat AC response. Broad low-heat maxima plus power-law heat below 1 kelvin point to short-range links and odd jitters, evidence for a ground state and spin-liquid ways.
arxiv-2605-24219: Badave and eight co-authors present Trajel, a dataset and frame for auditing trajectory-level hallucinations in multi-agent industrial workflows. Most hallucination benchmarks grade only the final output, missing failures born in intermediate steps. Trajel sorts expert-annotated traces from AssetOpsBench into five hallucination types: factual, referential, logical, procedural, and scope-based. Benchmarks at subtask, trajectory, and long-context levels show nearly half of hallucinated trajectories mix several types, and detectors with strong accuracy still miss the subtlest types. Trajectory-aware detection beats standard post-hoc checks.
arxiv-2605-24319: Wingate and fifteen co-authors ask whether language models invoke religion for everyday ethical questions, a gap they term omissive bias. Their AllFaith benchmark pairs 150 ethically salient questions from chat transcripts and faith contributors with a judge rubric that credits any mention of a religion, practice, or leader fully. The questions cover grief, forgiveness, relationships, purpose, and honesty, not religion itself. Across 27 models, LLMs underrepresent religion versus human expectations, invoking it more for abstract existential questions than for practical situations like grief, marriage, family conflict, and addiction.
arxiv-2605-24419: Dey and four co-authors tackle time-scale making from mixed cesium and hydrogen clocks. The Kalman filter struggles because error spread blows up. The team builds a Kalman filter on observable split form with no wild terms, then uses it for group syncing. The method syncs each clock's drift from ideal pace to the hidden group mean of phases, with chosen weights. By tuning free-running motion through the weight vector, the rate stays calm over shorter or longer spans. A case shows the method's value.
arxiv-2605-24819: Pierre-Louis Poirion leads random-subspace Frank-Wolfe, a fix for Frank-Wolfe methods over curved regions. Full-space linear minimization can become the bottleneck there. RSFW swaps the ambient oracle for exact oracles over random low-dimensional affine sections, while keeping every step feasible. For smooth convex problems over compact strongly convex sets, the team proves a dimension-explicit oracle inequality and recovers the standard rate. Short steps plus a gradient floor give linear convergence, and random sections can even sharpen the local curvature model.
arxiv-2605-24919: Riasad Alvi leads MultiHaluDet, a detector for hallucinations in large language models working across languages without language-specific tuning. Output-confidence tricks and single-layer probes often miss deep factual slips. The problem bites hardest outside English. The method probes the full hidden-state path of a frozen model, pulling cross-layer features through multi-scale and self-attention pooling. It feeds out-of-fold embeddings to a tuned ensemble of classifiers. It tops prior English hallucination results and carries its skill to French, Bangla, and Amharic.
arxiv-2605-25519: Kim studies choices that happen in layers, where people first decide whether to take part and then sort into ordered or unordered groups. He shows this sorting layer reshapes what can be learned: single-stage selection bias fits one summary control function, but layered sorting generally needs several. The number needed sets how much continuous variation the data must supply. Kim proves matching cases where identification fails and where it succeeds, and offers two-step sieve estimators. He uses it on gender wage gaps among Korean graduates.
arxiv-2605-25619: Li and Altafini show an analogy between one transformer layer, ignoring its feedforward network, and one step of the power method. Passing through a layer tilts tokens toward the principal eigenvector of a matrix formed by multiplying that layer's output and value weight matrices. When all layers share weights, this alignment grows especially clear in experiments and admits an analytic proof. The analogy further suggests steering transformer output toward any chosen direction in token space.
arxiv-2605-25819: Jälkö, Pradhan, Räisä and Honkela examine whether fast membership inference vulnerability review can be trusted. Vulnerability is usually judged by a model guessing whether a sample was in training data, using shadow models on random splits. Aggregates hide sample-level problems. Two weaknesses emerge: sampling shadow datasets from a fixed superset inflates estimates, and concatenating scores across individuals skews true hit rates at very low false alarm rates. For both they propose fixes, the simplest adding no computation, with costlier options improving reliability further.
arxiv-2605-26419: Joohwan Ko and Justin Domke ask whether one inference network can serve many Bayesian models without retraining per family. Their Amortized Factor Inference Networks portray a model as typed prior and likelihood factors, then map that portrayal plus observations to a Gaussian posterior estimate via an encode-merge-decode network. Learned weights stay independent of latent size and observation count. Synthetic and real benchmarks show one trained network rivaling per-task variational inference and NUTS sampling at far lower test-time cost. Optional importance sampling sharpens accuracy further.
arxiv-2605-26619: Shailendra Dabral rebuilds chaotic trajectories from sparse, noisy peeks with a physics-guided diffusion model called PIDM-DP. A fifth-order Dormand-Prince solver sits inside the denoising loop, so each generated path must obey the governing equations. A ramped physics weight stops gradient blowups on stiff systems. Across five benchmarks at ten percent observation density, it improves reconstruction error up to 15.4-fold over plain diffusion and beats an ensemble Kalman filter on stiff cases, while preserving chaotic invariants.
arxiv-2605-26819: Granata and four colleagues build RAGEAR, a recommender that suggests university courses from full lecture transcripts plus a knowledge graph of courses, lessons, credits, and prerequisites. Unlike metadata-only tools, it matches transcript passages to a student's query and rolls passage-level evidence up to course-level scores. Tests on 152 student-like queries show transcripts beat metadata alone, and RAGEAR beats a transcript-only baseline, most clearly at the top ranks.
arxiv-2605-27319: Elsa Jochl and colleagues test whether graphene Landau polaritons in a terahertz cavity undergo a superradiant phase transition. Tuning carrier density drives coupling to about 40 percent, near the critical point, yet the expected polariton softening never appears. A Hopfield model with a near-field cavity account reproduces the full dispersion instead.
arxiv-2605-27419: Quan Zheng and colleagues scale LLM-agent population simulation with Adaptive Prototype Simulation. The framework queries core prototypes, singleton tails, and shadow-audit agents instead of every agent each round, correcting bias from audit residuals. In a 10 million-agent opinion run it cuts online calls more than 380-fold while closely matching the full-LLM reference.
arxiv-2605-27519: Debasish Borah and colleagues probe the inverse seesaw with low-frequency gravitational waves. A low-scale first-order phase transition from the seesaw's dynamical origin could register in pulsar timing arrays. Gravitational wave searches stay sensitive where active-sterile mixing is small, complementing heavy neutral lepton searches that cannot reach that space.
arxiv-2605-27619: Sai-Aakash Ramesh, Archit Sood, Andrew Corbett, and Tim Dodwell propose Supervised Distributional Reduction, learning codes that track the target, with optimal transport and a dependence boost. The method aligns input link structure with sample points through a fused Gromov-Wasserstein objective plus a direct dependence term. The resulting compact representations feed adaptive kernels for Gaussian process modeling under shifting geometry.
arxiv-2605-27819: Poduval and colleagues rethink sparse autoencoders, tools that split a model's inner activations into interpretable features, for work spanning several layers at once. Ordinary layer-by-layer versions waste capacity re-encoding information already carried forward, so ReSAE trains each later layer only on what earlier layers fail to explain. On two open models the approach cut decoder overlap and improved probing and targeted edits.
arxiv-2605-27919: Junlin Wang tackles a flaw in robots taught by copying people: human demos are jerky and noisy, and copycat learners pick up the jerks. His Frequency Guidance Operator guides the making of actions through bands of ever wider pitch, smoothing motion while keeping fine detail. Across fifteen robot tasks it gave smoother, steadier action with no loss of success.
arxiv-2605-28319: Gernot Akemann, Sung-Soo Byun, and Seungjoon Oh chart the dissipative spectral form factor of the complex elliptic Ginibre ensemble across non-Hermiticity regimes. They derive precise asymptotics for disconnected and connected parts, characterizing the dip-ramp-plateau shape with dip and Heisenberg times. A mesoscopic regime interpolates between non-Hermitian and Hermitian spectral behavior, with ramp shape varying by scaling.
arxiv-2605-28719: Xian-Yu Wang, Songhu Wang, and Konstantin Batygin refit 256 Rossiter-McLaughlin systems with one method, joining spectral energy curves, transit light curves, transit times, and radial speeds. Using 146 single-star systems with solid planet masses, they find eccentricity-tilt patterns that depend on planet mass. Sub-Saturns can be both eccentric and misaligned, Jupiters are misaligned only on circular orbits, and super-Jupiters and brown dwarfs stay aligned across all orbits. A 2D Kolmogorov-Smirnov test confirms three mass regimes differ clearly, showing obliquity alone does not trace past history.
arxiv-2605-29019: A. C. S. Costa and colleagues show quantum crossovers can be pinned down through local measurements only. They link local quantum Fisher information to the onset of crossover shifts. Quantum obesity, by contrast, does not extend the quantum steering ellipsoid volume as a crossover indicator. In some cases the ellipsoid volume misses the transition, while the key signs live in the local Bloch vector, showing a geometric split between local and global signs.
arxiv-2605-30019: Natalie Maman, Florian Hettstedt, Andreas Erbslöh, and Gregor Schiele present elasticAI.explorer, a Python frame for hardware-aware architecture search on Optuna. Older frames weld search spaces, model code, and deployment together, blocking moves to new hardware or custom operators. Their frame states search spaces in YAML that turn into runnable networks during sampling, covering layer-wise, cell-based, and hierarchical spaces. It adds hardware code generation, Docker cross-compilation, and auto-built benchmarking binaries. Built-in evaluators score FLOPs, parameter counts, and latency.
arxiv-2605-30119: Thalea Schlender, Peter A. N. Bosman and Tanja Alderliesten compare two genetic-programming routes to interpretable survival analysis, predicting time until an event from censored data. Survival trees stay readable but must grow large for complex patterns, while greedy building can miss the best splits. The authors evolve inspectable feature sets for tree builders, and also evolve whole trees with their split logic. Evolutionary feature construction lifts accuracy across builders, depths and two datasets. Whole-tree evolution looks most promising for its speed and presentation, the authors judge.
arxiv-2605-30419: Aaditya Datar, Arun M. Thalapillil and Palak Thareja bring a quantum view to axion-photon mixing. They study the sector of axion-photon oscillations, showing how coupled dynamics make axion-photon entanglement. They link peak axion-photon entanglement with resonant or strong-mixing conversion, with distinct thresholds for peak values of the quantum measures. They study Mandelstam-Tamm and Margolus-Levitin speed limits for both axion-photon and neutrino systems. Orthogonalisation happens only at axion-photon resonance, or at peak neutrino mixing, where the two bounds meet.
arxiv-2605-30619: Pukdee, Balcan, and Ravikumar analyze Best-of-N preference data: N candidates drawn, the best paired with a rejected response. For independent-reference variants, reward targets follow from N and the base distribution, preserving reward ranking. For best-versus-random and best-versus-worst variants, shared candidate sets break Bradley-Terry representability, though minimizers approach the targets as N grows. Design rules: larger N widens margins but cuts connectivity, so use larger N when labels bottleneck, smaller N when generation bottlenecks, and weight the base distribution toward test-time comparisons.
arxiv-2605-30719: Hatgis-Kessell and Brunskill ask when language models can serve as black-box policy optimizers for reinforcement learning. Their Prompted Policy Optimization prompts a model with Python descriptions of state, action, and reward, then has it generate and refine policies from feedback. Across exploration environments, Meta-World robotics tasks, and real-world problems, it often matches or beats baselines while using far fewer interactions. Output policies range from tuned controllers and rule-based plans to value iteration, but the method underperforms in MuJoCo domains where fine continuous control is required.
arxiv-2605-30819: Wang and colleagues present Function2Scene, making 3D layouts from use-based briefs. Most methods make rooms from object-centric prompts. Yet layouts are judged by how well they support users. Given a brief, the system parses profiles and tasks, then derives constraints from 17 criteria. They span spatial, comfort, task, and setting factors. Rather than relying on a language model to produce a scene, Function2Scene iterates evaluation and refinement. It combines geometric measurements, contextual reasoning, and assessment. Experiments on 30 cases show Function2Scene produces layouts that better satisfy requirements.
arxiv-2605-30919: Lu and colleagues reframe language-model unlearning as removing data credit rather than tuning loss functions. Standard methods that raise loss on forgotten data often over-forget and damage model utility. Their DareU framework uses reinforcement learning to lower the credit score of responses to the owners of those data, thus de-attributing those data. Tests using a language-model judge as a credit proxy show DareU beats existing baselines, achieving effective forgetting while balancing forget quality and model utility well.
arxiv-2605-31119: Ravie and colleagues propose a continual method for a mobile agent learning from shocks in unseen places. Dangers vary, and not all can be foreseen. Recent models guessing common-sense dangers struggle to capture contact-driven harms. Their method, Don't Fool Me Twice, first sees shocks and their effects. Boosted with visual context, this note queries a model to predict causes. Kernel fit maps the local shock for glitch models. Voxel model gauges doubt, giving bounce-back by treating shocks as spatial acts. They present four guesses, tested in sim.
arxiv-2605-31519: Lien and Quintino show that entanglement, usually a boon for telling quantum channels apart, can sometimes hurt. They exhibit a pair of unitary channels perfectly distinguishable with no entanglement at all. Yet any strategy using maximally entangled inputs lands near blind uniform guessing. To systematize this, they define maximal-entanglement worst-case and best-case channel pairs and give conditions for each class. For worst-case pairs, the best input states must be separable. They also give measurement channels where entanglement necessarily lowers the best discrimination chance.
arxiv-2606-00419:
Bharti and co-authors build a tune-free tool for live range calls that hold fair across groups. Range calls must stay sound when data shift with time. Group-wise sound calls guard fair play for each set of points. Past live tools gave up group guards or needed a set learn rate.

Their tool holds group guards with no dial to set at all. Proof gives it the best group-wise marks in its class. Tests span fake and real data runs. It beats past tune-free tools on how sound its calls stay. Its range widths tie well-tuned group tools in size. The work lays a base for fair, firm range calls in shift-prone fields.
arxiv-2606-00619:
Liu and co-authors treat an agent's whole memory pipe as code that can evolve, not a fixed frame. Long-run agents need memory past the span of one chat. Most memory tools build a bank, then fetch from it by a set pipe. That pipe stays fixed while the bank grows and shifts shape.

Their frame, MemPro, keeps a tree of full pipe builds that can run. An evolve agent picks bright builds from that tree. It reads where those builds fail in a loop of runs. Fresh child builds are made by edits led by those fail modes. Tests span long chat, ask, and tale sets. MemPro beats fixed and prompt-led kin tools in few rounds. Gains keep up as rounds grow, at a fair cost.
arxiv-2606-00719:
Xia and co-authors study a class of graphs at the edge of a strength limit in this 2026 maths paper. A graph's strength is the best edge-connectivity found in any of its subgraphs. A graph is k-edge-maximal when its strength stays at or below k. Yet adding any missing edge pushes some subgraph past k.

The team defines two new tools, the kernel and the closure of a graph, and works out how closure behaves. With those tools they give an exact test for when a graph is k-edge-maximal. Their test sharpens a known result from 1990. They also pin down which edge counts can occur for such graphs on n nodes. The count must match a set formula tied to a small whole-number parameter. Last, they describe the full shape of these graphs for each set edge count.
arxiv-2606-01019:
Su and co-authors speed up language model output by guessing when a cheap draft is worth checking in this 2026 paper. Models write one token at a time, which costs a full run per token. Speculative decoding drafts many tokens at once and verifies them in one pass. The gain turns on how many drafts get accepted.

Cheap draft sources, like caches, can propose long runs in structured and agent work. A cache hit that looks good now may pay off poorly next step. Their method, Hybrid Verified Decoding, predicts the accepted length of a cache draft before the check. That payoff estimate picks between cache verification and a model based drafter. Across three models and sixteen datasets, the method shines on agent workflows. It beats EAGLE3 in every such setting, with a mean speedup near two and three quarter times, they report.
arxiv-2606-01319: Huang and Li prove a short result on the Bergman metric. They work on a pseudoconvex domain in complex space of dimension at least three. Its Bergman metric may have constant scalar curvature. This is the csc case named in the title. Huang and Li show what that condition forces on the boundary. Every strongly pseudoconvex boundary point must be spherical. The note is brief and technical. It suits specialists who study how curvature constrains domain shape.
arxiv-2606-01419:
Rawat builds DENSER, a system for new views of soccer matches. Broadcast footage gives few camera angles of a play. Novel view synthesis fills in the missing angles. DENSER extends the EFA-GS method with three additions. A camera-height loss weighting favors ground-level broadcast views. Monocular depth from Depth-Anything-V2 guides geometry in flat regions. Textureless zones gain structure from that depth signal.

A three-model ensemble averages pixels for the final image. Its members diverge from one shared base checkpoint. They vary training length and Gaussian scale clamping. On five held-out challenge scenes, scores are strong. Mean PSNR reaches 29 point 89 dB. SSIM and LPIPS scores support the result as well.
arxiv-2606-01619:
He and co-authors reconcile skill creation with policy learning in agent RL. RL lets LLM agents improve from environment rewards over time. The resulting policies rarely accumulate reusable strategies, though. Modular skills could supply those strategies across tasks. Past skill-augmented RL splits skill creation from policy optimization. Adopted skills can then conflict with the evolving policy. ReSkill is an RL-in-the-loop skill creation framework. It exploits the group-wise structure of GRPO for its design.

An assertion-driven creator diagnoses failures and proposes skill revisions. Within-group sampling compares skill versions in a controlled way. Thompson Sampling with adaptive discounting picks versions over time. Skills get created, tested, refined, and pruned automatically. Gains are largest on unseen tasks in their tests.
arxiv-2606-01719:
Naidu shows that fair fine-tuning can block distribution inference attacks. Models trained on sensitive data can leak population-level facts. An attacker with black-box access infers demographic properties of the training set. No training data is observed directly in that attack. Defenses like differential privacy exist, but the fairness link was unexplored. Fair Fine-tuning fine-tunes a model on the complementary distribution. An Equalized Odds constraint governs that fine-tuning pass. He proves a tight bound on adversarial advantage.

The bound is the EO disparity times a distinguishability factor W. A necessary condition for the method to help is also proved. Six datasets span tabular, image, and NLP data. Rehearsal-based fine-tuning drops the accuracy gap below detection thresholds. On ACS Income it falls from about 15 percent to under 4 percent.
arxiv-2606-02119:
Chen and co-authors make machine unlearning aware of how hard each case is. Unlearning removes the influence of specific training data. Privacy, copyright, and bias concerns motivate that removal. Retain data performance must be preserved meanwhile. Past methods mix forget and retain losses by weight. They cannot promise set gains for all data points.

The team take a constrained optimization view instead. Hardness is quantified by forget-retain similarity. Similar data are harder to reconcile across the objectives. Their HAMU algorithm derives from that insight. It carries theoretical grounding for its updates. Forget quality and retain utility are targeted jointly. Specified extents of improvement become achievable goals. The method addresses a clear limit of prior work.
arxiv-2606-02419:
Li and co-authors present DPA4, a machine-learning model for forces between atoms. Such interatomic potentials now near quantum-level accuracy. The most expressive designs cost a lot to run. Some also lean on extra pre-training tricks. DPA4 aims to break that trade-off.

The design is equivariant under 3D rotations and reflections. Six size classes span 0.48 to 25 million parameters. Its convolution mixes edge and node features across all angular degrees. Training uses only the energy-gradient path. A compiled build makes that path three times faster. On Matbench Discovery, DPA4 leads every ranked metric. Each variant sits on the accuracy-throughput frontier. The Pro variant posts the lowest energy error on OMat24. The authors frame DPA4 as leaderboard-grade accuracy at routine cost.
arxiv-2606-02619:
Kerker and co-authors probe polaritons at the diamond carbon K-edge with X-rays. X-ray parametric down-conversion gives access to high-energy polaritons. These arise when down-converted photons hybridize with electronic excitations. The team studies the effect with spectral resolution. The setting is the K-shell absorption edge in diamond.

Clear signatures of polaritonic hybridization appear. A polariton spectral map visualizes them. Theoretical modeling supports the analysis. Coupling at this edge is much stronger than in a prior non-resonant case. It reaches well into the strong-coupling regime. The measurements also yield the refractive index of bulk diamond. It is extracted at high spectral resolution around the carbon K-edge. The work opens a spectroscopic window on light-matter hybrids at X-ray energies.
arxiv-2606-02719:
Ettori reconciles X-ray scaling relations for galaxy clusters and groups with two physical ingredients. Scaling relations link the thermodynamic traits of hot cluster gas. Data depart from self-similar predictions, above all at low masses. Ettori models the departures with power laws in two quantities. The gas mass fraction is one. The temperature variation across the system is the other.

An MCMC meta-analysis uses a wide set of published scaling relations. It constrains how both quantities depend on temperature and redshift. Gas fraction shows no significant evolution with cosmic time. It falls steeply as halo mass decreases. Temperature variation rises mildly with mass and redshift. Tension among relations collapses under the model. Relations in strong tension drop from 49 percent to 11 percent. The generalized form predicts slopes and evolution for several scaling laws. A new volume proxy links directly to mass with no redshift evolution.
arxiv-2606-02919:
Zhang and co-authors present Pixel Cube, a diffusion method for relighting portrait videos. The goal is new lighting that looks real and stays steady over time. Training rests on a hybrid dataset. It mixes real captured video with rendered video, across varied faces, motions, poses, and known lighting.

The team built an LED lighting rig to capture high-speed relighting data with realistic light. Their model starts from a pretrained video diffusion model. A per-frame high dynamic range environment map controls the new lighting. A synthesized background image adds control over exposure and color tone. The output keeps the subject's identity, expression, and fine features such as wrinkles and facial hair. Tests on in-the-wild videos with many environment maps show strong results. The authors report state-of-the-art scores for realism, lighting harmony, and temporal consistency. They also show uses in portrait photography.
arxiv-2606-03019:
Hatta argues that reproducible builds, not copyleft licenses, are the right safeguard for the age of advanced AI. Copyleft used copyright to tie source code to every distribution. Its force rested on a quiet premise: source and object code stand in a clear, auditable, reproducible relation.

Language models and future AGI break that premise. Code, data, weights, and toolchains each face separate legal and technical limits. Capable AI can also rewrite licensed source into equivalent code stripped of its obligations. Hatta proposes bit-exact reconstructability from declared inputs as the new guarantee. The paper reviews copyleft's logic and critiques the claim that AI fulfills free software's dream. Drawing on several openness frameworks, Hatta defines seven requirements for AGI-oriented reproducible builds. The Model Context Protocol is treated as a new linking layer where copyleft fits poorly. A protocols-not-platforms approach is offered as a better governance template.
arxiv-2606-03219:
Tiwari and co-authors test how much labeled data African languages need for a language task. African languages have very little labeled data. It is not clear that more labels always help. The team runs a scaling study on natural language inference, using the AfriXNLI benchmark across 16 African languages.

Two multilingual transformer models of about 0.6 billion parameters are tested. Sample sizes run from 50 to 500 labeled cases. Results are averaged over repeat random draws. The trend is not a steady rise. Some languages level off early, and some get worse as data grows. Low-resource settings also show high variance from run to run. The authors conclude that data volume alone does not promise stable gains for African language inference. They call for language-aware dataset building and stronger multilingual models.
arxiv-2606-03519:
Hoffmann and co-authors present SIGMA, a streaming partitioner for distributed graph neural network training. How a graph is split across machines drives training cost. Older partitioners pick one side only, vertex or edge. They also chase one goal, like edge cut, under one balance rule. SIGMA handles both split styles in one frame.

Vertex and edge balance are tracked at the same time as cut quality. A clustering step adds global structure before the streaming pass. That step lifts quality while keeping the speed of streaming methods. Six benchmark graphs test the system across domains and scales. Two training systems run the trials, one edge-partitioned and one vertex-partitioned. SIGMA performs strongly in both settings. It often beats rival streaming tools and rivals in-memory partitioners. Gains are largest for edge-partitioned training. Teams get one tool for very different training setups.
arxiv-2606-03619:
Smith gives a unified account of the chiral anomaly in all its forms. The anomaly appears as abelian and singlet versions, and as consistent and covariant versions. A novel master expression covers the fully generic case. It works with massive or massless fermions. It includes triangle, box, and pentagon diagrams alike.

From that master form, each traditional version follows in a transparent way. The topological side of each form is described without differential language. Stokes' theorem is the one exception allowed. A FeynCalc implementation lets readers reproduce every calculation in reasonable time. The unified view serves two goals at once. It clarifies the physics behind the many forms. It also gives a practical tool for phenomenology. Students and researchers get one source for a topic usually scattered across many papers.
arxiv-2606-03819:
Rheinboldt, Berdoz, and Wattenhofer speed up speculative decoding with TreeFlash. One-shot block drafters write a whole draft in one pass. They are fast, but each token is conditioned only on the prefix. Draft tokens ignore the tokens drafted just before them. The draft thus drifts from the verifier's true distribution as depth grows. Tree drafting worsens the gap across branches.

TreeFlash adds an MLP layer fed by the drafter's hidden state and the prior token. It approximates the true autoregressive distribution for each draft step. A two-stage mechanism keeps decoding time constant, like one-shot drafters. Across tasks and models, TreeFlash sets the state of the art. Block efficiency rises 12 percent over marginal tree drafting. Speedup rises 9 percent as well. Inference teams get faster decoding without giving up draft quality.
arxiv-2606-03919:
Maillart and co-authors forecast how scientific concepts spread, testing the method on quantum computing. Models of science must split two forces. Concepts firm up from inside a field, or spread in from outside. The OpenAlex quantum subtree supplies a time-based network of concept pairs. Each pair is tracked through its citation past and downstream spread.

LightGBM models predict inside growth, outside spread, their ratio, and spread entropy. Inside growth proves largely unpredictable in the main test. Outside spread and entropy are strongly predictable. Upstream variety and citation breadth drive those calls, as SHAP checks show. Repeats in robotics, advanced materials, and neuro implants keep outside spread on top. Sharp entropy jumps mark new frontiers. Entropy drops signal convergence or paradigm shifts. Foresight teams get early signs of cross-domain uptake.
arxiv-2606-04119:
Ushangi Goginava studies in 2026 when double Fourier series, the two-dimensional version of representing a signal as a sum of waves, can fail to converge. Summing such series over rectangles is notoriously wild: some well-behaved functions diverge everywhere under that scheme.

Restricting the sum to a narrowing cone around the diagonal can restore convergence, and a theorem by Antonov pinned down how fast the cone must shrink. Goginava proves that condition is exactly sharp in the square-integrable setting. For any slower shrinkage, he constructs a function whose symmetric rectangular sums fail to converge almost everywhere along the cone. The construction mixes a Fefferman-style analytic block with random shifts to spread the bad behavior.
arxiv-2606-04319:
Pedro Figueiredo and co-authors propose PureLight in 2026, a neural method for rendering complex light fixtures. Such fixtures are hard to simulate: small emitters sit inside several reflective layers.

Ordinary path tracing wastes nearly all its samples on them. PureLight instead traces rays once, from the emitter to the fixture's exit surface. A large normalizing flow network then learns the full pattern of outgoing light. That learned look is distilled into a small, fast network for rendering. Companion networks handle direct lighting and place the fixture into a scene. The result renders stubborn fixtures accurately with very few samples, in arbitrary scenes.
arxiv-2606-04719:
Eom and colleagues make Mamba-based vision-language models both better and faster with a smarter bridge between image and language, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Connecting vision to Mamba still requires turning image features into a sequence, and earlier designs needed a hand-crafted 2D scan order. Their query-based cross-modal projector instead compresses visual tokens through cross-attention, selecting what the query needs.

The projector also removes the need to design the scan order manually. Across various vision-language understanding benchmarks, models equipped with the projector improved both performance and throughput over Mamba-based multimodal baselines. The gains matter because multimodal inputs are long: images inflate token counts, exactly where quadratic attention hurts most and where a selective, query-driven compression can save the most computation. The authors present the design as a general way to bolster Mamba multimodal models rather than a task-specific trick.
arxiv-2606-04819:
Basu measures a blockchain that claims its mining does useful AI work, and finds none, in a 2026 arXiv empirical study. Pearl, a layer-1 blockchain, markets its proof-of-useful-work protocol as securing the network and performing AI inference. Basu's measurements of the deployed system tell another story: the network's enormous hash rate, roughly 320,000 GPU-equivalents consuming an estimated 112 megawatts, produces zero useful AI computation.

The evidence spans five dimensions. All 8,012 analyzed workers run inference-capable hardware, yet the dominant mining software contains no inference code. The verification protocol accepts random matrices by design, and its checks fall to adversarial Gaussian sampling. Mining economics are near breakeven at current prices. Meanwhile budget GPU rental prices rose 38 percent and utilization surged after the mining software's release, displacing research workloads. The study quantifies the verifiability-usefulness tension for proof-of-useful-work systems.
arxiv-2606-05419:
Andrew Charbonneau, K. Deck, and T. Schneider build a machine-learned snow albedo parameterization for climate models in this 2026 arXiv paper. The scheme predicts how albedo changes, its tendency, from snow and weather inputs that a climate model has available.

The parameterization is a constrained neural differential equation, a learned equation whose form is restricted to stay sensible. It was trained on years of ground-based and satellite observations from many locations. It reproduced albedo evolution across climate zones with a median error under 7.5 percent, an improvement of 10 to 30 percent over established models. It generalized to sites never seen in training and scaled from model grids down to point locations. Because the framework can absorb new variables as observation networks grow, the authors offer it as an adaptive component for next-generation land and climate models. It replaces hand-built albedo formulas with one that keeps learning from data.
arxiv-2606-05619:
Engelgardt and Ryzhikov hunt for a one-sided measure of disorder in a 2026 arXiv paper on ergodic theory. The field studies actions that shuffle a space while keeping total measure fixed. Classic entropy scores such shuffling the same forward and backward. The authors work with a family of finer scores, the Kirillov-Kushnirenko entropies. Each score reads the action along a chosen sequence of group steps.

For grid-like groups of dimension at least two, typical mixing actions behave unevenly across mirrored step sequences. The main theorem finds a subsequence where the entropy along one sequence is zero. Along the mirrored sequence the same action's entropy stays fully positive. The inverse action flips the pattern exactly. Both full entropies remain infinite, so the asymmetry hides inside the finer scores. The result gives a new way to tell apart actions that classic entropy scores rate as identical.
arxiv-2606-05719:
Yamanaka and colleagues dissect five quantum circuit designs for a toy gauge theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. The designs, Hamiltonian variational ansatzes, shape a quantum state to mimic a target system's ground state. Each respects the local and global symmetries of a two-dimensional lattice gauge theory. That respect splits the state space into fine invariant blocks. The team measures how rich each circuit's motion is inside those blocks.

Two gauges of richness agree: the size of the motion algebra and the rank of a quantum information matrix. All five circuits build their generators from weight-three Pauli terms, a barely explored choice. In solver runs, adding parameters past a threshold erased the local minima that trap optimization. Loss then fell at a rate that grew in direct proportion to parameter count. The findings sharpen design rules for circuits that must scale without stalling.
arxiv-2606-05919:
Konrad and Kuschnig make an impossible search cheap: finding the handful of data points that sway a result most in a 2026 arXiv paper. Removing a well-chosen set can swing a regression coefficient or treatment effect. But testing every subset explodes combinatorially. For effects with a linear-fractional form, the authors show the hunt collapses to a one-parameter chain of top-k ranking problems.

Dinkelbach's method then solves it at linear cost per iteration, with guaranteed finite termination. For fixed prepared inputs, the returned set is globally optimal for the ratio objective. That covers the partial linear model used across applied econometrics. With estimated nuisance parts, stability conditions keep the answer near the oracle objective. A separation condition upgrades approximation to exact recovery. Simulations and applications recovered exact influential sets that brute force could never reach. Influence auditing becomes a routine check rather than a supercomputer job.
arxiv-2606-06019:
Siebersma, Seibert, Shuman, and Craig explore quantum mechanics rebuilt on a discrete stage in a 2026 arXiv paper. Polymer quantization, inspired by loop quantum gravity, gives position a discrete topology. Its commutation relations differ genuinely from the textbook Schrödinger representation. The paper summarizes the scheme, then quantizes systems whose classical spaces are compact: a particle on a ring and one in a box.

The polymer construction yields states living on a finite graph of points. On those lattices the authors solve both example systems exactly. Energy eigenvalues and eigenfunctions come out in closed form. Comparisons show where the discrete version echoes and where it departs. The continuum limit is then taken carefully. Exact polymer eigenfunctions approach their familiar continuum counterparts in detail. The work gives loop-inspired quantization a fully worked finite laboratory. Compact spaces, it shows, make the polymer world's strangeness exactly computable.
arxiv-2606-06319:
W Urban and co-authors map excited states in neodymium nuclei in this 2026 arXiv paper on nuclear physics. Around mass one hundred fifty, nuclei change character, moving from spherical shapes toward deformed, collectively rotating ones. The team studied four neodymium isotopes, from mass one hundred forty six to one hundred fifty two, fed by praseodymium decay or californium 252 fission.

Using the Gammasphere array, they charted the gamma rays each nucleus emits as it sheds energy. The haul was large: one hundred fifty nine new levels, including two new isomers, three hundred five new gamma transitions, and eighty three new spin parity assignments. Special attention went to zero plus and two plus excitations tied to emerging quadrupole collectivity, and to one neutron orbital, the eleven halves extruder state.
