They conclude that single particle excitations dominate these transitional nuclei, with collective modes only mixed in.
arxiv-2606-06619:
Some seven dimensional spaces carry a special geometric structure named after the group G2, and its solitons are shapes that flow into themselves. Li, Ma, and Zheng study families of those solitons in this 2026 arXiv paper. A soliton here is a complete, endless space equipped with a gradient field, a direction of steepest change, whose potential function drives the shape's self similar motion.

The authors prove compactness theorems, results saying that whole families of these solitons cannot scatter into chaos but must gather near well behaved limits. They assume a floor under the scalar curvature, a measure of bending, plus a broad growth condition on the potential. First they establish convergence in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense, a rough notion of shapes drawing close. Then fine regularity estimates sharpen that to smooth convergence when a uniform energy bound holds at half the dimension.
arxiv-2606-06919:
Quantum computers need excellent starting states before they can simulate hard materials. Byungmin Kang, Kwon, Scarola, and Park prepare one famous family in this 2026 arXiv paper. The states are Gutzwiller projected BCS states, standard models for strongly correlated electrons. The projection step is the hard part to build as a circuit.

Their algorithm combines a general BCS circuit with amplitude amplification. Amplification boosts the projection's success chance directly. It replaces slow postselection, which throws away failed runs. The improvement is quadratic in the number of projection queries. Projected weight shrinks fast as systems grow, which sounds fatal. Even so, the savings stay decisive at realistic sizes. On a one hundred site benchmark, queries fell by about seven orders of magnitude. The authors present this as an enabling step for quantum simulation of lattice models.
arxiv-2606-07119:
Companies are buying AI agents faster than they are building ways to govern them. Sergio Alvarez-Teleña and Marta Diez-Fernandez propose a governing architecture in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their Three-Ring Architecture stacks the enterprise in layers. Ring one is today's production systems. Ring three is frontier language model intelligence.

Ring two, the middle, is their central claim. It is a federation layer of strategy based agents with deterministic behavior. The authors call it the operating system of the agentic enterprise. It abstracts resources, coordinates processes, enforces permissions, and hosts compounding intelligence. The two outer rings carry opposite risk profiles. Deterministic agents leave traceable, recoverable deviations. Language model agents can deviate without a retrospective trail. So the governance layer is not optional decoration. Every gain in model capability, they argue, raises the stakes of skipping it.
arxiv-2606-07219:
Fake social media accounts powered by large language models can now imitate real users closely enough to fool many detectors. Trokhymovych and co-authors fight back in this 2026 arXiv paper by building the kind of data such attackers would create. Their adversarial approach generates posts in the voice of specific real users, using each person's history, stance, and writing style. The result is a paired dataset of genuine and machine-written messages across languages and platforms.

Detectors trained on generic synthetic text often fail on short, stylistically varied social posts. Training instead on this realistic impersonation data produced classifiers that spotted AI-generated content far more accurately. The gains held on real-world data outside the training distribution, where earlier content-based bot detectors typically collapse. That out-of-distribution strength is the central finding, suggesting detection improves most when training data mirrors how actual manipulation campaigns write.
arxiv-2606-07519:
Valenzuela-Escárcega and co-authors define a search task linking the sentences of papers to the code fragments implementing them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ordinary code search matches files or functions. Understanding a published method instead needs snippets in both directions: a phrase finding its code, or a code fragment finding its explanation. Their dataset trains on descriptions of code generated automatically by GPT-4, then tests on 3 splits, one in-domain and two out-of-domain with hand-annotated material from other fields.

Their system shares one encoder across 4 subtasks that locate answer spans in both directions. It achieved in-domain results and out-of-domain performance. The gap between the two settings is the headline: automatically generated training data can bootstrap the task, but cross-domain generalization remains open work. The authors argue fine-grained code-text linking would help scientists verify, reuse, and teach computational methods.
arxiv-2606-07919:
Mondal and Ghosh dissect the polarised radio glow of one distant galaxy in fine spectral detail, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The galaxy was catalogued by the SPICE-RACS survey, taken with the ASKAP telescope across thirty-six channels from about eight hundred to one thousand eighty megahertz. Polarised radio waves rotate as they cross magnetised plasma, an effect called Faraday rotation. Untangling it reveals the magnetic environments along the line of sight.

The galaxy's rotation measure is about three hundred forty-six radians per square metre, with an excess of roughly one hundred seventy-one over the Milky Way foreground. Its Faraday spectrum is complex: the dispersion ratio reaches about eight point six. The best model combines one Burn slab, a uniformly mixed emitting and rotating layer, with two external dispersion components. A secondary component carries strong depolarisation, evidence of turbulent magneto-ionic gas around the galaxy.
arxiv-2606-08119:
Masaki Hashimoto and co-authors design a language for writing access-control policies fine-grained enough for layered defence, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Defence in depth stacks security layers, and each layer needs authorisation decisions at proper granularity. Existing policy languages, the authors argue, cannot express the leading access-control models faithfully, particularly conditions about a running process's dynamic status.

Their language treats such conditions as first-class decision data alongside subjects, objects, and actions. It is implemented in Datalog, the logic programming language of deductive databases, so policies are rule sets that a logic engine can evaluate and audit. As a test, they compose the policy of SELinux, a major mandatory access control system, in the new language, and evaluate it for validity and expressiveness. The language captures a real, complex policy without flattening its distinctions. The text is an English translation of the authors' earlier Japanese journal paper.
arxiv-2606-08219:
Wang proves that two classic control problems coincide for systems driven by randomness, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The systems are stochastic differential equations, equations of motion that include a random noise term modeled by Brownian motion. One problem asks for the fastest way to steer the system to a target. The other asks for the gentlest control, measured by a norm, that reaches the target within a fixed time. Showing these are equivalent requires proving that the minimal norm varies continuously with the time allowed.

In deterministic problems a time-shifting trick gives that continuity, but it fails here because admissible controls must be adapted, meaning they cannot use future information about the noise. Wang instead constructs the minimal norm control explicitly, and continuity follows from the construction. Beyond the theoretical equivalence, the explicit form helps design numerical schemes for computing both kinds of optimal controls.
arxiv-2606-08319:
Busko offers a test for whether brief flashes seen on old astronomical photographs are real, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Searches of photographic plates from the Palomar sky surveys of the nineteen fifties have reported fast transients, sources that appear and vanish quickly. Critics objected that such images could be plate artifacts, defects of the material. Busko examines the shapes of the transient images for a signature that genuine starlight should carry and defects should not.

Real point sources recorded off the telescope's axis show coma, an aberration that smears a point into a comet-like shape in a predictable pattern. Busko shows the transient images exhibit exactly this coma pattern, which plate artifacts cannot naturally reproduce. The author is careful about the conclusion: the data do not by themselves establish what physical source produced the light. They do support hypotheses explaining the transients without instrumental effects.
arxiv-2606-08419:
Jiawei Chen, Nguyen, and Shum overturn a famous piece of auction wisdom in this 2026 arXiv paper. In a common-value auction, where the object is worth the same to everyone but that worth is uncertain, winning usually brings bad news. Everyone else bid less, suggesting the value is low. This is the winner's curse. The authors study auctions where bidders have horizontally differentiated preferences. They value different features of the object, so their private information does not line up along a single scale of optimism.

In their two-bidder parameterization, winning conveys good news about the object's value to the winner, a phenomenon they name the winner's bliss. Other implications flip as well. When preferences are horizontally differentiated, seller revenue decreases as more information is disclosed, reversing the standard prescription that transparency helps sellers. Advantageous selection can also sustain trade where standard reasoning predicts breakdown.
arxiv-2606-08519:
Voloshina and Tarasenkov report new brightness measurements of two erupting binary star systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The systems are SU UMa-type dwarf novae. A white dwarf orbits a low-mass companion star that spills matter onto it through an accretion disk. Such systems show ordinary outbursts and rarer, brighter superoutbursts. During a superoutburst the light curve carries superhumps, periodic brightness modulations slightly offset from the orbital rhythm. The authors present photometric observations of the systems RZ LMi and KV Dra during their superoutbursts.

Superhumps were detected in both light curves, and their periods and amplitudes determined. The measurements clarified each object's subclass. RZ LMi belongs to the ER UMa subclass, whose members erupt unusually frequently. KV Dra belongs to the WZ Sge subclass, known for rare, dramatic superoutbursts. For KV Dra the authors also determined an orbital period of just under an hour and a half.
arxiv-2606-08619:
Fako and Schwaller rethink how chemistry describes molecules binding to surfaces, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Catalysis theory treats chemical affinity as an attribute of discrete geometric sites on a surface. Three long-standing puzzles follow from that choice. Which site is the active site is ambiguous. Brønsted-Evans-Polanyi relations are purely empirical. And breakdowns of linear scaling relations are unpredictable. The authors show all three symptoms resolve when affinity is represented as a continuous property of the interface, which they call the covalent field.

In their Covalent Field Theory, active sites emerge as regions where the field sustains a bias toward bond formation. Linear scaling relations become correlation structure in the field. Their breakdown is a topological bifurcation with a clear signature. The Brønsted-Evans-Polanyi correlations arise from the field's split, giving an empirical regularity a theoretical basis.
arxiv-2606-08819:
Feser and Evangelou give SLOPE models a Bayesian way to choose their tuning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. SLOPE is a regression method selecting variables or groups while controlling the false discovery rate, the share of false alarms. That control is guaranteed only in orthogonal settings with known noise, which data rarely supply. The fallback, cross-validation, optimizes prediction rather than discovery control. The authors embed SLOPE in a spike-and-slab Bayesian framework.

Their Bayesian Group SLOPE handles group selection, and a sparse-group version handles selection at both. A trick called Two-step Orthogonal makes a general problem orthogonal so the guarantees apply again. Across synthetic and real-data studies, the Bayesian models held the false discovery rate at its target. They achieved higher power, finding more true variables, and predicted better than competing methods. The paper argues model choice for SLOPE should target discovery control.
arxiv-2606-08919:
Turan argues that oversight of AI agents has a capacity limit, and that more approvals can make a system less safe, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The usual safety pattern makes risky agent actions wait for a human click. Turan questions two assumptions behind it: that risky has one correct answer, and that the reviewer is a tireless, perfect judge.

Reviewers rating his one hundred twenty-five hand-labeled actions agreed only moderately on what is risky, with a Fleiss kappa of 0.52, so no ground truth exists. Modeling the reviewer as tiring while the approval queue grows, Turan finds safety follows an inverted U in the escalation rate. The safest guard escalates a middle share of actions, not everything. A load-aware policy resists a flooding attack, where one malicious action hides among routine approvals for a fatigued reviewer. Oversight, he concludes, is a resource-allocation problem, not just classification.
arxiv-2606-09119:
Chatterjee, Sen, and Gangopadhyay check whether a tabletop test for quantum gravity survives realistic physics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The test uses a Bose-Einstein condensate in a trap as a detector. Earlier work showed that only quantum gravity generates non-Gaussian behavior in such a system, because only quantum gravity produces non-quadratic terms in the Hamiltonian. That makes non-Gaussianity a clean signature, if it survives.

The authors add leading-order post-Newtonian terms to the same model. The condensate platform is attractive because Feshbach resonances let teams tune electromagnetic interactions toward zero, isolating gravity. With corrections included, the signal persists, but its signal-to-noise ratio is slightly damped. The verdict is positive for the experimental program: the signature is robust to the first layer of realism, though weaker than promised, which matters for detector planning.
arxiv-2606-09819:
José Nogales, Karen-Luz Burgoa Rosso, and Marcelo Alvarenga probe a subtle gap between two writings of the same gravity twist in this 2026 arXiv paper. Rastall-type gravity bends Einstein's rules by tying the field to the trace of the matter source. Two parameter forms of that bend can be mapped into each other exactly, if the source coupling is rescaled in step.

The catch is what a lab means by the source. If the stress tensor is fixed by an operational recipe, its scale is not free to float. Under that fixed-source rule, the map stops being a mere relabeling. The pair of forms then agree only at the Einstein point, where the bend vanishes. If the two couplings are instead bare knobs, each set from the same measured Newton constant, the clash fades. The result marks the extra convention a claim of sameness needs.
arxiv-2606-09919:
Michal Podolinsky and colleagues present a system that helps mixed robot teams see past blocked views, in a 2026 arXiv paper on robot perception. Their teams combine air and ground robots working outdoors, where no single viewpoint shows the whole scene. Occlusions, where objects hide what sits behind them, create uncertainty that varies by viewpoint. Large vision-language models reason well here but run too slowly on board.

Their system, Co-GLANCE, distills that reasoning into a smaller onboard model. It segments occluded areas and assigns the best-placed robot to gather a clearer view. Conformal prediction, a method giving statistical coverage guarantees, tells it when to abstain and send help instead. In real-world trials, Co-GLANCE beat cloud-based vision-language baselines on occlusion segmentation by twenty-five percent and on robot allocation by thirty-six percent, while cutting per-frame latency roughly three hundred fifty fold.
arxiv-2606-10219:
Han and Li show that a systems programming language can make a classic learning method fast enough for live financial data, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning systems. Exact nearest-neighbor learning is simple and predictable, but searching large historical datasets is slow, while trading and risk systems face strict latency limits.

They prove that under standard assumptions the design asymptotically dominates both brute-force search and the widely used scikit-learn k-d tree in the fixed-stock, large-sample, moderate-dimension regime. Across eight financial datasets on two processor architectures, speedups reached roughly eighteen to twenty-two fold over scikit-learn's tree on x86 while preserving exact outputs. The tests used up to about two hundred seventy-seven thousand training samples. Compiled execution also let an Extra Trees volatility pricing model train on ten times more options data, cutting its pricing error measurably.
arxiv-2606-10419:
Pal and his team study the magnetic behavior of a lightly lithium-poor cobalt oxide, in a 2026 arXiv paper on condensed matter physics. The compound, with lithium content near nine tenths, is related to battery cathode materials and to systems where doped holes form magnetic polarons, carriers dressed by local magnetic twisting. Using bulk magnetization, specific heat, nuclear magnetic resonance, and electron paramagnetic resonance tests, they probe both bulk response and local spin conduct.

The bulk probes show the material undergoes in part an antiferromagnetic transition below about ten kelvin, where neighboring spins align oppositely. A weak ferromagnetic response also appears. It causes history effects in low-field readings and lasts above room temperature, which they blame on ferromagnetic clusters formed by magnetic polarons. In the resonance readings, only a fraction of spins take part, showing Curie-like behavior, and the spectra's temperature change fits spreading of magnetic polarons.
arxiv-2606-11119:
Heming Zou and a large team present TRACE in a 2026 arXiv paper on training language model agents with reinforcement learning. In RL with verifiable rewards, agents learn from rollouts, sampled attempts scored at the end. Learning stalls when rewards lack contrast: easy or hard prompts return uniform feedback, and outcome-only rewards grade every turn identically.

Earlier methods allocated rollout budget across prompts only. TRACE goes finer. It treats each thought-action-observation turn of a ReAct-style rollout as a tree node. Budget goes to prompt roots and intermediate prefixes most likely to yield mixed terminal rewards, some successes and some failures. A shared predictor estimates success probability at each anchor from its history, guiding the spending. The adaptive tree enriches feedback and amplifies the update signal. On multi-hop question answering, TRACE improved Qwen3-14B accuracy by 2.8 points over competitive baselines at equal sampling cost.
arxiv-2606-11219:
Okocha and Grant benchmark semantic reasoning in audio language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such models answer questions about spoken audio, but most evaluations reward plausible answers, even when the response leans on priors rather than evidence in the recording. They test reasoning grounded in the audio itself, under accent variation and domain shift.

Their benchmark, built with large-scale hypothesis generation and human verification, spans five tasks: entailment, consistency, plausibility, accent drift, and accent restraint. It asks whether predictions stay stable when accents change. Next-token prediction models, notably Qwen2-based variants and AudioFlamingo, substantially outperformed contrastive baselines on most tasks. Still, models showed over-entailment, concluding more than the audio supports, and commonsense bias. Gaps appeared under domain shift and accent variation across the curated African-accent datasets. The resources aim at audio models that ground inferences in acoustic evidence.
arxiv-2606-11319:
Tahmassebpur, Bhuiyan, Kim, and Lesser study how neural networks learn from corrupted inputs in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is attribute noise: inputs corrupted, labels intact, a case with far less attention than label noise. They consider additive noise and replacement noise. Experiments with perceptrons on corrupted datasets show networks stay robust, keeping well-above-chance accuracy even with inputs over ninety percent corrupted, beyond human recognition.

To explain it, they analyze infinite-width networks in the heavy-corruption regime. They derive a leading-order decision rule: the network implements a prototype rule, the nearest class mean, assigning each test point to the class whose training average it most closely resembles. The rule is universal across perceptron architectures of any depth, and wide classes of activation functions and noise distributions. The same centroid mechanism matches finite-width behavior in experiments, explaining why learning succeeds when examples carry almost no signal.
arxiv-2606-11419:
Seyed Hojat Mirtajadini and five co-authors present a drone inspection pipeline in a 2026 arXiv paper. Most drone inspection systems must fly dangerously close to a target or follow complex paths for small details, and disturbances can make a narrow-view drone lose its target. Their pipeline, aerial_micro_inspection, assumes a PX4 drone with two cameras: a zoomed, gimbal-mounted inspection camera, and a wide-field stereo navigation camera.

The wide camera acquires the target surface on site, estimates range, and partitions it into smaller regions. A vision-based feedback loop corrects for drone motion during each visit. It is open-source in ROS 2 and adapts by swapping segmentation and detection checkpoints. Simulations show improved coverage robustness under disturbances. Real-world experiments cover tree inspection for oak processionary caterpillars and their eggs, and greenhouse sticky traps for whiteflies, with effective detection and high-detail insect imaging.
arxiv-2606-11519:
Saif combines two flexible antenna technologies in a 2026 arXiv paper on downlink wireless communications. A base station with two sub-arrays of movable antennas transmits to users via a reconfigurable intelligent surface, a panel whose elements can be selected and tuned. Exploiting antenna positioning and element selection together adds degrees of freedom to boost desired signals and suppress interference, maximizing sum-rate.

Saif formulates the joint problem over antenna positions, beamforming, and element selection, under minimum separation and power constraints. The problem is highly non-convex, so an alternating scheme splits it into three tractable subproblems. Zero-forcing beamforming handles the transmit design, a one-dimensional search selects surface elements, and block coordinate descent with convex tools places them. Simulations show the joint design clearly improves sum-rate over fixed antennas and random benchmarks. Spatial notches suppress interferers while strong directional beams serve the intended users.
arxiv-2606-11619:
Zongwu Xie and five co-authors estimate spacecraft poses from single camera images in this 2026 arXiv paper. A 6D pose gives a craft's position and orientation, needed for docking and servicing. Glare, harsh shadows and weak surface texture make local image evidence unreliable, so pose guesses can wobble badly.

Their model, PAID-ViT, is a vision transformer, an image network built on attention, with three added ideas. It separates tokens carrying pose structure from tokens carrying lighting appearance. It scores each patch's reliability before combining them. And it trains with a foreground mask so the craft's silhouette stays informative. A geometry module then converts the results into rotation and translation. On the SPEED+ V2 benchmark, translation errors roughly halve against a strong baseline. In the harsh sunlamp test the error falls from forty centimetres to about fifteen, a cut of nearly two thirds.
arxiv-2606-11719:
Enhan Zhao leads a team teaching vision-language models spatial reasoning with far less data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial reasoning means judging where objects are and how scenes are laid out. Standard training uses huge fixed datasets, wasting effort on examples a model already finds trivial and on ones still far too hard.

Their framework, Ouroboros-Spatial, closes the loop between data and model. One frozen copy proposes questions from scene records and video frames, with code that computes trustworthy answers. A second, learning copy trains on accepted questions, and its confidence becomes a difficulty signal. That signal guides the next round of questions toward the learner's current level. On VSI-Bench, the method lifts two Qwen vision models by roughly ten and seven points, using about twenty-six thousand examples, ten to one hundred times fewer than curated rivals.
arxiv-2606-12419:
Pal Chowdhury and co-authors record real geometry tutoring where teachers point at diagrams as they talk, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most tutoring datasets are text-only, yet human geometry teaching is deeply visual. GeoDial collects over 1.3 thousand dialogs between experienced math teachers and students. Instructional turns are explicitly grounded in diagram highlights: the exact lines or regions a teacher marks while explaining. An annotation protocol layers dialog acts, visual highlighting, and feedback onto each exchange.

The dataset enables fine-grained supervision of both what a tutor says and what it shows. The authors fine-tune several vision-language models on GeoDial and test both skills. Supervised training substantially improves the quality of generated tutoring dialog. Producing accurate diagram highlights, however, remains hard for current models. Fluent pedagogical language, the authors warn, has outrun visual grounding. Human-like tutors need visual reasoning integrated with interaction, not just better text.
arxiv-2606-12619:
Reygers and co-authors sharpen the background subtraction behind direct-photon measurements in heavy-ion collisions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Smashing lead nuclei creates a quark-gluon plasma whose temperature photons can reveal. But direct photons hide under decay photons, from neutral pions, with the eta meson contributing ten to fifteen percent. The eta-to-pion ratio at low momentum is poorly measured, yet it sets that background.

The team predicts the ratio below three GeV/c using the measured kaon-to-pion ratio plus a blast-wave model of the flowing source. The fit handles radial flow and feeddown from particles. The framework also yields an uncertainty for the extrapolation. For central lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV, the eta-related decay-photon uncertainty near one GeV/c comes to ten percent of the direct-photon signal. That is an error bar where previously there was guesswork.
arxiv-2606-12819:
Sasaki analyses the strong deflection of light by a charged black hole in Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton theory using Picard-Fuchs equations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. When light passes very close to a black hole, its deflection angle grows logarithmically, a regime captured by a log-formula with 2 constants that depend on the black hole's parameters. For specific dilaton coupling values, the deflection angle can be written with elliptic integrals, which makes a differential-equation approach possible.

Sasaki shows the deflection angle, viewed as a function of 2 dimensionless variables tied to the background charge and the impact parameter, satisfies a system of 2nd-order linear partial differential equations. These are the Picard-Fuchs equations. These reduce to 1st-order ordinary differential equations for the 2 constants in the strong-deflection log-formula. Requiring agreement with the Schwarzschild case when the charge vanishes then fixes the charged results uniquely.
arxiv-2606-13119:
Peng and colleagues develop MP3, a multi-period pattern pre-training plugin that helps spatio-temporal graph neural networks tell temporal mirages apart, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Urban spatio-temporal data shows this mirage phenomenon: similar short-window inputs can have divergent future trends, and unlike windows can converge. Current forecasting networks, fed short windows, cannot identify mirages because those windows observe the underlying periods only partly, spatial links are heterogeneous, and causality is superposed across periods.

Its temporal component uses edge convolution to spot period patterns. Its spatial component uses a bottleneck projection and a global memory bank to capture heterogeneous global spatial relations. A causality-enhanced Transformer models links across period patterns. Tests on 5 baselines across 5 real-world data sets verify consistent gains: on average MP3 reduces mean absolute error by 4.7 percent and root-mean-square error by 5.0 percent.
arxiv-2606-13319:
Aritomi and a large collaboration report a control demonstration for gravitational-wave detectors in this 2026 arXiv paper. Detectors such as LIGO use squeezed vacuum light, light whose quantum noise is redistributed, to sharpen their hearing. A filter cavity, an optical resonator the light passes through, makes the squeezing frequency-dependent, which broadens the benefit across the detector's range. The cavity's length and alignment must be held precisely against the squeezed field, or the advantage is lost.

The team demonstrates length control using coherent control sidebands, reference tones already used to steer the squeezing angle in existing sources. Their scheme extends that established technique to the filter cavity itself. Success matters because frequency-dependent squeezing is planned for the fourth observing run of the advanced detectors. The paper documents the scheme working in practice, a needed step before observatories can rely on it during science runs.
arxiv-2606-13619:
Pohoata disproves a conjecture in additive combinatorics in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Elekes-Rónyai problem asks whether a polynomial in two variables that is neither additive nor multiplicative must expand sets a lot, producing many distinct values. Such expansion results underpin sum-product theory. Pohoata constructs very large finite sets of real numbers where one polynomial, combining a sum with a squared difference, produces noticeably fewer values than expected. The saving is a power in the exponent. That polynomial is neither additive nor multiplicative, so the construction is a genuine counter-case.

The proof grows one local defect in two directions at once. Horizontal amplification spreads it over squarefree products of rational primes, while the vertical step runs through towers where those primes split fully. A fixed local density defect thereby becomes global. Pohoata suggests the mechanism is broader, potentially producing similar extreme constructions elsewhere.
arxiv-2606-14019:
Vila and Nakano give one framework for the moments of any random variable. Moments are averages of powers of a variable; they summarize spread, shape, and tail weight. Classical tail-integral formulas connect moments to survival probabilities, but mainly for nonnegative variables. Their 2026 arXiv paper extends the picture to the whole real line, covering continuous, discrete, and mixed cases, including fractional and negative moments.

For discrete cases, series formulas in tail sums yield simple tests for whether a moment exists. Worked cases on the zeta and Skellam laws show how tail behavior decides finiteness. A final section treats log moments, linking log means, Laplace transforms, and the Frullani identity. The paper connects tail chances, distribution functions, and moment existence in one view.
arxiv-2606-14119:
Pulse and colleagues build a safe testbed for asking language models to diagnose factory faults from piles of manuals. In smart factories machines interconnect, so one failure cascades, and facts scatter across manuals written in different terms. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents FactoryLLM, an open-source playground for evaluating retrieval-augmented models over multi-machine documentation. Scoring runs through RAGAS metrics and an LLM-as-a-judge setup. Safety comes from local or open-source models: sensitive data never leaves the site.

The demonstration involved an Autonomous Intelligent Vehicle and its Mobile Planner software. Three models answered thirty maintenance queries from roughly six hundred pages of cross-machine documentation. Every model achieved a groundedness score above zero point eight eight, answers staying tied to retrieved sources. Retrieval precision was limited, yet grounded generation held up. Full code is released for others to test their own scenarios.
arxiv-2606-14319:
Loukaki and Spyridakis prove a 2026 arXiv result in group theory. This branch of math studies symmetry and structure. They study abelian groups, where the order of steps does not matter. Their question is when three subgroups of equal size can share one common transversal. A transversal is a set that meets each coset, or shifted copy, exactly once.

The pair give a full rule for when such a shared transversal exists. The same rule settles a lattice question as well. It asks when three lattices of equal volume can share one basic tile. That question had been open since nineteen ninety-seven for the case of three lattices. The proof closes it in full. It also covers the group case in one joint statement.
arxiv-2606-14919:
Tasnim and Zhao formalize a game-engine design in a 2026 arXiv paper, presented at the ACM Symposium on Applied Computing. The design is the Entity Component System, or ECS. It splits data from behavior: entities are bare identities, components hold data, systems hold logic. Engines like Unity DOTS, Bevy, and Flecs use it. But the popular archetype variant was never pinned down formally.

The authors give archetype ECS a formal model. Creating entities, composing parts, running systems, and moving between archetypes become state transitions with clear rules. They then test it in a Tower Defense game. Under identical conditions, the archetype design beat rival designs. It reached a higher frame rate with better frame stability. Better cache use and steady entity access explain the edge. The work gives ECS users a firm basis for reasoning about correctness and side-by-side execution.
arxiv-2606-15019:
Tran and coauthors build a deep learning screener for cervical cancer that works across countries in a 2026 study. Screening cuts deaths sharply, but expert colposcopists and biopsy services are scarce in poorer nations. Most earlier algorithms trained and tested on private data from a single country. The team frames lesion detection as a joint task of image classification and lesion segmentation.

Their model trains on acid-stain colposcopy images with hand-drawn lesion masks and pathology results. In local validation it beats medical experts at separating low-grade cases from grade two or higher lesions. External tests on datasets from four countries beat baseline methods, though accuracy varies widely between sites. A failure analysis shows comorbidities hurt performance most, far more than age or visibility of the transformation zone. The authors argue robustness across settings is the key gap for global deployment.
arxiv-2606-15219:
Chen and coauthors ask whether gradient-trained neural networks can hit the optimal tradeoff between samples and computation, in a 2026 theory paper. The testbed is the Gaussian single-index model, where the label depends on data only through one hidden direction. Query-based theory sets a floor on the samples any efficient method needs, governed by a difficulty exponent of the label rule. Whether plain network training reaches that floor was open.

The authors give a unified gradient procedure for a two-layer network that learns a representation aligned with the hidden direction. Its sample count matches the lower bound, up to log factors, at every difficulty level. For sparse hidden directions they add a weight perturbation trick exploiting the sparsity, again matching a new lower bound they prove. Feature learning, the results say, can be provably optimal, and exploration noise should match the geometry of the target.
arxiv-2606-15519:
Tanji and colleagues study the adjoint problem for ideal magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium in 2026, the equations that describe a steady magnetically confined plasma. Adjoint methods let engineers compute how an equilibrium responds to many parameter changes, which supports sensitivity analysis and design work. The team derives the adjoint of the three-dimensional equations under fixed-boundary conditions, then reduces it to the axisymmetric case used for tokamaks.

The central result is that the reduced operator coincides with the perturbed Grad-Shafranov operator, the equation for axisymmetric plasma equilibrium. The reduced scalar variable is the adjoint field read along the equilibrium flux gradient. Because the 3D system assumes no flux surfaces or symmetry, one framework covers both tokamak-style and fully 3D devices. That match means axisymmetric sensitivity tools rest on the same math as the general case. Designers can also check 3D adjoint codes against the known axisymmetric answer.
arxiv-2606-15619:
Tang and colleagues predict how excited hidden-charm pentaquark molecules should decay in 2026, extending the molecular picture of the Pc states from LHCb. The observed Pc(4312), Pc(4440), and Pc(4457) are read as bound states of a charmed baryon and an anti-charmed meson. The team studies the excited partners, with a radially excited meson, and asks how they fall apart by emitting a pion.

In a chiral quark model, they compute pion-emission decays from the excited molecules to the known Pc molecules. The widths are sensitive to spin structure and to interference between coupled channels, which can switch a decay from strong to forbidden. One mixed state decays to Pc(4440) with a width of several MeV, while its width to Pc(4457) is suppressed below 0.3 MeV by destructive interference. Such patterns give LHCb and PANDA decisive signatures to hunt for, since a seen or missing line tests the molecular assignment.
arxiv-2606-15819:
Yang and colleagues present SACE in 2026, the first concept-erasure method built for visual autoregressive image models rather than diffusion models. Erasure techniques transplanted from diffusion cause catastrophic semantic collapse in these models, which generate scale by scale rather than by denoising steps. The team's starting point is a claim about where concepts live in that process.

Their Semantic Singularity Axiom holds that any target concept is locked in at the very first scale, Scale-0, before finer scales add detail. A saliency analysis called ISSA validates the axiom and exposes the coarse-to-fine injection of semantics. SACE intervenes only at the first scale, pairing an entropy-regularised erasure objective that prevents degenerate sampling with a preservation loss anchoring benign concepts. Experiments show surgical erasure across domains with minimal training overhead, while generative capacity survives. Erasing at the moment of commitment, not everywhere at once, makes the surgery clean.
arxiv-2606-15919:
Stamatakis and colleagues test whether LLM chatbots are good enough to support computer science students on multiple-choice exercises in 2026. They wrote 70 multiple-choice questions for a university lecture on interactive visual data analysis, ran several chatbots under different prompt designs, and compared scores with students'. A user study in two lectures then measured how seeing ChatGPT answers with explanations changes student performance.

The chatbots split sharply by size: smaller models struggle to answer in a zero-shot setting, while GPT-4o and GPT-5 score best, though errors remain. Prompt design cuts both ways: extra context helps the GPT models and hurts the smaller ones, with inconsistent persona effects. Most sobering, showing students ChatGPT answers with explanations does not improve their performance in general; chatbot output can help or hinder learning. Course-specific fine-tuning and careful integration, not raw chatbot access, are what education needs.
arxiv-2606-16619:
Hager and Kreher expand the rough Heston model in a 2026 mathematical finance paper. The Heston model prices options using a random volatility, and its rough version lets volatility move more jaggedly than Brownian motion. Roughness is set by the Hurst parameter, and option prices depend on a fractional Riccati equation that is costly to solve again for every new value.

The authors derive a Taylor expansion of that Riccati solution in the Hurst parameter around any chosen expansion point. Each coefficient comes from a linear Volterra equation with a fractional-logarithmic kernel, solved one after another. They prove the series converges locally and uniformly, so the solution is analytic in the parameter. Starting from the classical Heston case or a Padé approximation at zero, low expansion orders already give accurate implied volatilities for European call options. One reference solution can then serve many nearby roughness values cheaply.
arxiv-2606-16719:
Kerner analyzes the structure of borosilicate glasses in a 2026 paper on glass physics. These glasses mix silica and boron oxide with soda and lime, and they are workhorses in laboratories and industry. The puzzle is predicting the glass transition temperature, the point where the frozen material softens, as the recipe changes.

The test bed is Stochastic Agglomeration Theory, a model first built for simpler covalent glasses. Its idea is that networks grow by joining stable clusters, and the transition temperature follows from average connectivity and rigidity. Kerner shows that once the local structural units are identified correctly, the model reproduces the measured transition curve for the studied glass family. Two key features of the curve match the model's energy assumptions about sodium-bearing clusters. The agreement extends a theory made for chalcogenide glasses to oxides, tying a practical engineering number to countable network features.
arxiv-2606-16819:
Ericson surveys forty years of parallel computer architecture in a 2026 historical paper on in-network computing. The story starts with the NYU Ultracomputer and IBM's RP3, machines that built a Fetch-and-Add operation directly into their interconnection networks. Many processors could then update shared counters at once without colliding.

Ericson contrasts that fine-grained shared-memory vision with the distributed-memory IBM SP line, then with today's in-network computation in products like NVIDIA SHARP and HPE Slingshot. The survey profiles how often real message-passing programs use each operation, and maps one-sided atomic operations onto modern hardware paths. It also examines the software boundary in deep learning, from translation layers to low-precision arithmetic on current chips. A case study asks whether combining switches could have been built from Transputer chips programmed in Occam. The survey closes by tracing a group lock idea into later work.
arxiv-2606-16919: A logic paper on how rational agents should revise their beliefs when faced with contradictions. The authors work with LTL, a formal language for reasoning about time, and show how to build preference relations, rankings of which beliefs to keep, even when some questions have no definite answer. The result is a practical guide for AI that reasons reliably about changing situations.
arxiv-2606-17519:
Gillespie and Perry present a 2026 arXiv paper on how routing accuracy falls as enterprise AI assistants grow their catalogues of specialised agents and tools. Their test bed is a deployed productivity assistant with over a hundred agents and hundreds of tools to choose among. Three frontier models were scored on single-step routing as the catalogue scaled from ten agents to the full set, with special attention to vague, under-specified user requests that dominate real traffic.

Routing quality dropped steeply with scale on under-specified requests, losing well over a dozen points of F1 score. An oracle analysis splits the loss into a retrieval gap and a confusion gap that persists even with perfect retrieval. Shortlisting candidate tools with embeddings recovered much of the loss at full scale for every model tested. A study of human-labelled production requests confirmed the recovery on real traffic.
arxiv-2606-17719:
Carmi and colleagues compute pieces of holographic theory in a 2026 physics paper on Witten diagrams in the presence of a defect. In holography, a conformal field theory in flat space pairs with gravity in anti-de Sitter space, and a defect in the theory becomes a probe brane in the curved bulk. The team studies diagrams that feed into correlation functions of scalar operators.

Using a split form for the propagators adapted to the brane setup, they decompose contact, tree-level exchange, and some one-loop two-point diagrams into conformal blocks. For tree-level cases they get explicit formulas for the expansion coefficients, plus recursion relations for the crossed channel and the seed values those relations need. The results supply concrete inputs for the analytic bootstrap program, which aims to pin down field theories from consistency alone.
arxiv-2606-17819:
Shaposhnikov and colleagues present a 2026 framework for testing agent skills, the reusable knowledge packs that extend what language model agents can do. Such skills spread fast in industry, but no standard method existed to judge whether one skill truly helps. Their approach lets a skill author build realistic tasks that probe the parts of the skill they care about most.

The team applied the method at scale to about five hundred real skills, making a thousand tasks drawn from their content, with scoring rubrics for instruction following and goal completion. They then ran nineteen agent and model setups on those tasks. Skills gave gains that varied widely by model, driven largely by how closely each model stuck to the instructions written inside the skill.
arxiv-2606-18119:
Abouzaid and colleagues report a stress test of AI systems on genuine research mathematics, in a 2026 document from the First Proof project. Ten problems were drawn from the contributors' own active research across a broad spread of fields, so none were textbook exercises with known answers in circulation. Several AI systems attempted proofs, and human referees graded the attempts with full logs published alongside.

The results expose how current systems fail at the frontier. One submission invented a quoted theorem, attributing to a published paper a result that paper does not contain, then deduced the target from its own fabrication. Referees caught the hallucination, and the editorial decision was rejection. The batch serves as a benchmark and a warning: fluent proof-shaped text is not proof, and research-level checking still demands expert readers.
arxiv-2606-18419:
Schiebelbein-Zwack and colleagues model how many compact object binaries released by torn-apart star clusters the Gaia mission should see, in a 2026 astronomy paper. Dense clusters are factories for pairing white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes with luminous stars, and many clusters have since dissolved into the Milky Way.

The team links cosmological simulations of cluster formation to Monte Carlo models of cluster dynamics, then runs the resulting binaries through a mock Gaia observation pipeline. Hundreds of thousands of binaries were released over the Galaxy's history, mostly with white dwarf companions, yet the predicted detectable yield is tiny. Only a couple appear in data, rising modestly in the next release, because most systems are too distant or their orbits too long. Black hole binaries hide especially well behind dim companions. The model also suggests observed neutron star systems probably did not come from disrupted clusters.
arxiv-2606-18619:
Luo and colleagues present a security-auditing agent that must write down its assumptions before declaring code safe, in a 2026 software security paper. Autonomous language-model agents are now finding critical vulnerabilities in foundational open-source software, but their reasoning is opaque. When an agent calls a function secure, the assumptions it made about that function's inputs stay tacit, and wrong assumptions mean missed bugs and misplaced trust.

Their system Code-Augur flips the workflow to specification-first. Whenever the agent judges a component secure, it commits the local invariants behind that judgment as assertions in the source, while a guided fuzzer works in parallel to falsify them. A triggered assertion exposes either a genuine vulnerability or a flawed specification to refine. On real projects Code-Augur found twenty-two new vulnerabilities, sixteen already fixed or confirmed by developers, outperforming comparable state-of-the-art agents.
arxiv-2606-18719:
Garmendia-Lazcano, Mínguez, and Minondo reassess how much of Spain's exports really run through independent intermediaries, in a 2026 international trade paper. Earlier studies sort firms by what they report doing, wholesaling or retailing, and conclude intermediaries account for a large share of exports. Trade theory also treats them as outside firms that buy from producers lacking the skill to export at a profit.

Using Spanish firm-level customs data, the authors show many so-called intermediaries are manufacturer-owned export arms, shipping only their parent firms' products. Others are vertically integrated firms, controlling design, production, and distribution under their brands. Excluding both groups, the count of true brokers falls by roughly forty-two percent, and their share of export value drops by about seventy percent. Pure brokers differ markedly from the excluded firms, suggesting export-promotion policy may gain more from helping producers.
arxiv-2606-19519:
Manuel Hernández and Eduardo Sánchez-Soto argue in 2026 that blockchain consensus needs a new mathematical language. Most formal models treat a blockchain as a finite state machine, step-by-step state changes with fixed rules. In that view, consensus, the hard part where split nodes agree on one truth, sits outside the model as messy code.

Hernández and Sánchez-Soto place consensus at the centre using topos theory, the study of sheaf categories. Sheaves join local data that agree on overlaps into one global picture, much as nodes join local ledgers. Smart contracts and ledger states then live inside a logic built for local consistency. The frame recasts agreement as a gluing problem with clear rules for when local views can merge. For system builders, the payoff is a model where the core promise of a chain is the object of study, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2606-19719:
Aditeya Baral, Radoslav Ralev, and Iliya Zhechev expose a calibration gap in semantic caching in 2026. Semantic caches serve stored answers to near-duplicate queries, cutting language model costs. Standard scoring uses PR-AUC, which grades ranking quality only.

Deployment, though, needs scores that work at one fixed threshold. Top-ranked models by PR-AUC often perform worst in operation, the team show. Two new metrics answer the mismatch: Precision-Cache Hit Ratio AUC and Calibration Retention Rate. The operational gap splits into a recoverable calibration part and a structural part set by the data's positive rate. Experiments tie the calibration gap to the training objective, not data scale. Post-hoc calibration closes only part of the gap. Model choice for caching is thus a calibration problem first, and measuring it starts the fix.
arxiv-2606-20019:
Hans Goedbloed and Rony Keppens revisit leaky waves in the Sun's coronal magnetic flux tubes in 2026. Leaky waves radiate energy away from the tube that guides them, and solar physicists hoped their spectra could reveal hidden coronal conditions, a programme called coronal seismology. The authors compare these magnetohydrodynamic waves in detail with leaky electromagnetic waves in dielectric media, where a similar idea works.

The electromagnetic modes can be regularized by a normalization that trims the outside region, earning them the name quasi-normal modes. Magnetic flux conservation forbids the same trick for the coronal waves. Leaky MHD wave spectra therefore cannot systematically support coronal seismology, however appealing the analogy. A negative result of this firmness saves observers from building diagnostics on sand.
arxiv-2606-20119:
Sin Kyu Kang, Ranjeet Kumar, and Hemant Kumar Prajapati build a minimal model explaining neutrino masses and supplying a dark matter candidate in one stroke. Their 2026 paper presents a Dirac scoto-seesaw framework based on a gauged B-L symmetry with an unusual charge assignment, minus four, minus four, and five, for right-handed neutrinos. That chiral assignment splits the two observed mass gaps by origin: the atmospheric gap arises at tree level, the solar gap radiatively, through loops.

After the symmetry breaks, a leftover Z6 symmetry keeps the lightest dark particle stable. The authors study two minimal versions. In one, both normal and inverted orderings work; in the other, only normal ordering survives, and each case leaves distinctive marks for experiments. The chiral charges also suppress the new Z-prime boson's dilepton signal, weakening ATLAS bounds versus the standard scenario. Both dark matter candidates find viable room.
arxiv-2606-20319:
Rodrigo Alonso, Francesca Chadha-Day, Despoina Dimakou, Yunji Ha, and Valentin Khoze map which electric and magnetic charges can coexist in the Standard Model. Their 2026 paper investigates the Witten effect, where a theta angle endows magnetic monopoles with electric charge, turning them into dyons. Working with a general global gauge group, the authors determine which values of the three theta parameters yield distinct families of allowed dyon spectra. They construct and classify the corresponding charge lattices.

The analysis re-derives the known dependence of theta periodicities on the global group, and finds all CP-invariant points in theta space. The electromagnetic subgroup emerges before electroweak symmetry breaking, once anomalous B+L transformations are factored out, shrinking the physical theta space from a three-torus to a two-torus. One striking consequence: discovering an electromagnetic monopole with nonzero electric charge would fix the Standard Model's last unknown parameter.
arxiv-2606-20419:
Karn Tiwari, Varnith Chordia, and Prathosh A P edit vision-language model weights directly to cut object hallucination. Their 2026 paper addresses models that fluently describe objects absent from the image. Their method, QK Product Steering, needs no training data, no fine-tuning, and adds no cost at inference time.

The edit targets the per-head query-key product, the operator behind the attention scores, suppressing a few dominant singular modes in middle layers. A closed-form update maps the edited product back onto the query weights while shared key weights stay fixed, so grouped-query attention still works. Across three GQA-based models, hallucination scores fall by about 4 percent on the CHAIR measure, while random-mode controls barely move. Splitting the product into symmetric and antisymmetric parts shows the signal lives mostly in the mutual-attention channel.
arxiv-2606-20519:
Emanuel-Cristian Boghiu and Kyrylo Simonov accelerate semidefinite programming for causal games with GPUs. Their 2026 paper works in the process matrix formalism, which describes quantum correlations between labs with no fixed causal order. Causal games turn those exotic correlations into win rates that experiments can chase.

In the Guess-Your-Neighbour's-Input game, any definite or mixed causal order caps the winning probability at one half. The best known process-matrix strategy reaches about 0.6218, while the strongest dimension-independent upper bound is 0.7592. The authors investigate whether the gap can be narrowed with GPU-accelerated semidefinite programs at larger local dimensions. Faster solvers decide how far indefinite causal order can be pushed as a resource.
arxiv-2606-20819:
Sriram Kalathoor and Joseph Oefelein examine how disturbances grow in a reacting mixing layer in 2026, using receptivity and biorthogonal decomposition. A temporal mixing layer forms where two streams meet. In a reacting layer, combustion changes the base flow. The study uses direct and adjoint eigenmodes of a linearized operator built from the mean reacting state. Focus falls on the Kelvin-Helmholtz branch, a classic shear instability.

Three questions guide the work. How does reaction modify the chosen instability? Where does localized forcing excite it most efficiently? How strongly does the modal family appear in simulation data? Receptivity maps cover mass, momentum, thermal, and mixture forcing channels. A decomposition then gives modal amplitudes and few-mode reconstructions. The results help explain how flames and turbulence interact, knowledge that feeds into models of engines where mixing and reaction must be controlled together.
arxiv-2606-20919:
Mojgan Forootan and four colleagues present GIM-ENDO in 2026, a multimodal dataset of endoscopic images and video for gastric intestinal metaplasia, a precursor to stomach cancer. Early detection can interrupt the path to cancer. AI could help during endoscopy in real time. Reliable models need public, validated data. Such data, with pathology confirmation and subtype labels, have been missing.

The dataset holds demographic data, endoscopy findings, pathology results, and infection status for twenty-four patients. Most are GIM-positive, with two normal controls. Imaging uses white light and enhanced methods, including narrow-band imaging. Annotations cover six endoscopic signs used to judge the condition. Images and video clips are both included. A shared dataset with ground truth from tissue tests could let AI teams compare models fairly, instead of each training on private cases that others cannot check.
arxiv-2606-21119:
Di Dai and eleven colleagues present MammoExpert in 2026, a data set of mammograms with step-by-step reasoning labels for breast cancer research. Mammography is a key tool for finding breast cancer early. Public data sets with rich labels are still scarce. Subtype coverage is thin, and records of how experts reason are rare. Their data set fills that gap across three phases of diagnosis.

Images cover many tissue subtypes in the WHO scheme. Nine senior radiologists label dozens of features per exam. Reasoning is recorded from first look, through fact checks, to final synthesis. Adding a public data set plus this one lifts accuracy by a clear margin. Training on the reasoning adds a further gain. Traces matter in clinics, because a right label reached by wrong reasoning may fail on the next hard case.
arxiv-2606-21219:
Junhui Cao and Alexey Kavokin built a band theory in 2026 for exciton-polaritons, hybrid particles of light and matter, inside a three-dimensional inverse-opal crystal doped with quantum dots. They start from a bright photonic branch near the gap edge and build an exciton-photon Hamiltonian, the energy rule book for the coupled system. The lower polariton band has its lowest point at the W point, with a crowded saddle at X nearby.

Their results show the W valleys set the threshold for Bose-Einstein condensation, where many particles share one state. The X saddle adds room for excited particles and shifts the critical temperature when the W-X gap is small enough for heat to bridge. A Boltzmann model of pumped, decaying particles then maps three regimes, from W-led condensation to an X-led coherent state.
arxiv-2606-21319:
Ovidiu Popescu defines new classes of mappings in 2026 and proves fixed point theorems for them, extending the century-old Banach contraction principle. A contraction shrinks distances between points, which guarantees one fixed point, a point the map leaves unchanged. His significant pointwise contractions widen that family: they still extend Banach contractions, yet they also include nonexpansive maps and may hold several fixed points while staying continuous.

Popescu shows every such map on a complete metric space has a fixed point reachable by Picard iteration, repeatedly applying the map. Companion classes follow: significant pointwise shrinkings, which have fixed points on compact spaces, and annular pointwise contractions, distinct from Suzuki mappings, with their own existence theorem. Examples separate the new classes from earlier piecewise contractions, marking out fresh territory in fixed point theory.
arxiv-2606-21519:
Shin'ichiro Ando extends a new dark matter probe in 2026: the wave-optics fingerprints that small dark matter subhalos leave on strongly lensed gravitational waves. A galaxy-scale lens splits a gravitational wave into macro images, and subhalos threading the lens distort each image's amplification in a frequency-dependent way. A companion paper treated the magnified minimum image; this study tackles the harder saddle-point image and asks whether the space-based detector LISA could see the effect.

A time-domain method handles the saddle calculation, where the signal is a small difference of large terms. Across simulated cold dark matter subhalo populations, subhalos imprint percent-level modulations on both image types. Matched filtering that projects out lens parameters detects the combined signal in sixty-two percent of cases for favorable sources, forecasting ten to twenty detections over the mission.
arxiv-2606-21619:
Matteo Biagiola, Jahrim Gabriele Cesario, Luca Di Grazia, George Zakhour, and Guido Salvaneschi name a hidden failure mode of constrained code generation in 2026. Forcing a language model's output to obey types or syntax during decoding should kill compile errors by construction. But the constrainer, the model, and the target language can be misaligned: an incomplete constrainer rejects valid programs, an unsound one admits invalid ones.

Across seven models, two languages, and two constrainers on three benchmarks, incompleteness backfires badly. It pushes generation into low-probability corners of program space, causing frequent timeouts and cutting functional correctness by up to 97 percent, so plain unconstrained decoding wins. The study quantifies how constrainers must be built if formal guarantees are to help rather than harm code generation.
arxiv-2606-21719:
Oluwatumininu E. Ayo-Ojo, Akpevweoghene Ogheneowho Ugono, and Nkosinathi Dlamini argue in 2026 that polymer simulations are won or lost before the first timestep. Sloppy starting structures, wrong bonds, overlapping atoms, inject fake stresses and energy spikes that poison everything downstream. Their Python framework builds star and cyclic polymers with exact ring closure and enforced spacing, using spatial hashing to catch overlaps.

It writes LAMMPS-ready data files with no third-party libraries. Against naive random placement, the starts are stable, energy spikes shrink, and behavior through equilibration stays consistent, with steadier results throughout. The pitch is conceptual: treat initialization as a controlled boundary condition, not a random chore, and soft-matter simulation gets more trustworthy.
arxiv-2606-21819:
Yang and colleagues built RAPID in 2026, a system that judges disaster damage by pairing satellite views with street-level photos. After hurricanes, floods, wildfires, or earthquakes, responders need fast and sound damage estimates, yet older trained methods cope poorly when conditions shift. RAPID instead splits the work among several software agents, each with one clear job.

One agent aligns the two views of a scene, one restores poor images, one reads damage in a structured way, and one reasons about place. The system needs no training for a new disaster and works in zero-shot mode, judging events it has never seen examples of. It reports damage levels and types, plus concrete next steps for response, repair, and recovery, written as reports tied to each site. Across several disaster types and input mixes, RAPID reached an overall accuracy of 0.92 in the authors' tests.
arxiv-2606-21919:
Jiang and colleagues introduce WALL-E in 2026, a framework that lets WebAssembly programs use libraries written in managed languages such as Python, Java, and JavaScript. WebAssembly runs compiled languages like C and Rust at near-native speed in a portable, secure format, but managed languages were largely shut out. The usual workaround nests one runtime inside another, which is slow and complex.

WALL-E instead links libraries externally through a client-server design: the WebAssembly module calls out to the library running in its own native runtime. Native speed and full language features survive because no second virtual machine sits in between. In evaluation, the framework supported ten managed languages with no changes to the framework itself. It ran hundreds of times faster than the runtime nesting solution, with low communication overhead. The authors position the approach for cloud and edge computing, where multi-language applications are common.
arxiv-2606-22019:
Madl studies subliminal learning in 2026, the phenomenon where a student model inherits a teacher's hidden trait from training data that never mentions the trait. His question is practical: when can such transfer be audited before training begins? The answer depends not on model identity or size but on channel location, the route through which the trait reaches the student.

Three regimes emerge from the experiments. In a controlled body channel tied to initialization, a pre-training screen works: one alignment measure predicted held-out transfer almost perfectly. In pretrained language models, single-token traits instead ride shared vocabulary geometry, which no initialization screen can catch. Removing a named entity from the loss still left its probability hugely elevated in the student, because neighbouring tokens carried the preference. Conditional behaviours such as sycophancy routed through the network body and evaded four audits across two model families.
arxiv-2606-22119:
Daouadi and Benkhedir use density functional theory calculations in 2026 to study how arsenic doping and vacancies change a monolayer of molybdenum disulfide, a 2D semiconductor used in electronics and optics. They compare the pristine material with sulfur and molybdenum vacancies, arsenic placed at each of the two sites, and arsenic placed between atoms. Each modification reshapes the electronic band structure differently, which is what the study maps.

Every defect introduced new states inside the band gap. In the vacancy systems and both substitution systems, the Fermi level shifted down toward the valence band, signalling p-type behaviour. Interstitial arsenic did the opposite, pushing the Fermi level toward the conduction band for n-type behaviour. The authors highlight arsenic at the molybdenum site for photocatalysis and solar cells. The interstitial system could enhance transistor performance, showing how defect choice steers one material toward different devices.
arxiv-2606-22219:
Jiang and colleagues introduce, in 2026, a diagnostic benchmark that asks not whether language models fail at maze navigation, but where they get lost. The benchmark decomposes navigation into three levels from human spatial cognition: fine local passability, meso junction topology, and macro goal direction. Three chat models are tested on 1,050 mazes from three-by-three up to thirty-by-thirty.

Structured coordinate text proves the most navigable input format, far ahead of rendered images. One-shot navigation collapses almost to zero by size ten for every model. Yet the same models answer isolated single-level probes at thirty to seventy-five percent well beyond that size. First errors concentrate at meso junction choices and fine perception, almost never at global direction. The barrier is thus aggregating separate competences over a long plan. A hierarchical walker lifts GPT-4o success by up to ninety-two points at mid sizes.
arxiv-2606-22319:
Zhang and colleagues propose EmbodiedUS-FS in 2026, a fast-slow two-level system for robotic ultrasound scanning in real clinical settings. Scanning demands both high-level planning and low-level control: physicians' spoken instructions hide implicit procedural logic, while patient motion, contact variation, and target drift disturb execution. A single-speed architecture handles neither side well.

The Slow Brain parses intent and plans stage by stage, augmenting its knowledge from an API and handbook corpus, then builds task graphs and verifies the resulting plans. The Fast Brain fuses multimodal feedback, refining local actions and carrying out recovery behaviours. A Safety Shield and an escalation policy constrain risk, triggering replanning or human confirmation on failure. Experiments on planning, closed-loop execution under disturbances, and safety checks show the design significantly improves task success while reducing safety violations.
arxiv-2606-22419:
Madhulatha Mandarapu and Sandeep Kunkunuru revisit a claim about medical AI in this 2026 study. A recent Nature Medicine paper reported that language models beat specialized retrieval tools on clinical benchmarks, and that retrieval can even hurt strong models. The authors ask whether grounding answers in a knowledge graph, a network of linked facts, changes that picture.

First, their reproduction shows the headline score near eighty-eight comes from a Consensus variant, not the full HealthBench test. On the full benchmark, frontier models score only in the mid-forties under a physician-calibrated grader. Second, neither simple graph retrieval nor an agentic query loop improved MedQA accuracy across models from weak to strong. On a synthetic graph of invented facts, though, the same pipeline lifted accuracy from chance to near perfect. Grounding, they conclude, pays only when the decisive fact lies outside the model's training data.
arxiv-2606-22619:
M. Wavasseur, N. Blagorodnova, M. A. Gómez-Muñoz, and O. R. Pols compare two luminous red novae in this 2026 astronomy paper. These transients come from binary stars in unstable mass transfer, often ending in a merger. The study targets the events AT2021biy and AT2021blu, to pin down their progenitors and ejected mass.

The team generated binary evolution grids with the MESA code, constrained by Hubble photometry for one event and ground-based data for the other. Mass-transfer instability criteria selected progenitors able to merge on the observed timescales. The donor stars were constrained to roughly eighteen to twenty-three solar masses for AT2021biy and about fourteen solar masses for AT2021blu. Envelope mass bounds from the available orbital energy were compared with light-curve estimates. NEOWISE infrared data then yielded dust masses up to three years after outburst.
arxiv-2606-22719:
Mao Guan and Qian Chen audit forecasting benchmarks for information leakage in this 2026 paper. Benchmarks often credit models with skill they could not have had: features stamped with a target's date were not observable when the decision was due. The authors rebuild the test so their forecaster sees only decision-time information.

Each month-end from 2023 to 2026, a retrieval-augmented seven-billion-parameter model received lagged Federal Reserve variables, recent event summaries, and the Cleveland Fed's inflation nowcast. A retrieval module picked similar past states; a critic model compressed them into one rule, and an actor scored seven equity factors. The pipeline's median rank correlation reached about fifteen hundredths, positive across three year-long windows. Yet the mean was underpowered, its confidence interval including zero. A nearest-neighbor baseline matched the median, so live data and retrieval explain most of the signal; the model's edge sat in extreme rankings.
arxiv-2606-22819:
Xiaxia Guan and Xian'an Jin study polymatroids in this 2026 mathematics note. A polymatroid generalizes a matroid, a structure capturing independence. For a connected matroid, deleting or contracting any single element leaves at least one minor that stays connected. For polymatroids, work by Hall in 2013 guaranteed only two such elements.

The authors look instead at slice-projections, a family of operations that includes deletion and contraction as special cases. They prove that for any element of a connected polymatroid, at least one of its two consecutive slice-projections stays connected. They also show that a slice-projection from the top of a polymatroid and one from the bottom of its dual have the same connectedness. Both results extend known theorems for graphs and matroids, and sharpen what is known about how these objects hold together.
arxiv-2606-22919:
Megha Sharma, Daniel J. Price, Alexander Heger, and Katie Auchettl ask whether most detected tidal disruption events are partial, in this 2026 paper. In such an event, a star passing a black hole loses mass to tidal forces. A partial event leaves a stellar remnant behind, and several dozen events have been detected.

Using the Phantom simulation code, the team modeled a Sun-like star orbiting a million-solar-mass black hole on zero-energy orbits, with impact parameters causing at most half the star's mass to be lost. For deeper encounters, the mass fallback rate could exceed the Eddington limit, letting debris form a reprocessing layer, as in full disruptions. The fallback decayed less steeply than the classic law, tracking a steeper alternative law more closely. Their temperatures and luminosities matched the detected optical and ultraviolet events, supporting the argument that some events classified as full disruptions are actually partial.
arxiv-2606-23919:
Rokon, Acharya, Desai, Yao, and Lee test how best to tell one shared model which of six relevance jobs it is doing. The setting is Walmart's e-commerce systems, in their 2026 paper on machine learning. One relevance model should judge query to product matches, product similarity, and four other relationships on one shared scale. Separate models waste knowledge and disagree with each other. The puzzle is routing: how task identity reaches the shared model, since encoder and decoder designs use that signal very differently.

They compare three routings across adapted language models and cross encoders. The private layer ensemble wins, reaching about ninety percent accuracy on four hundred fifty three thousand test cases. Removing text prefixes cripples decoder only models, one falling from about eighty seven to fifty six percent, while cross encoders barely notice. Training on many tasks together lifts low resource tasks by up to fourteen percent.
arxiv-2606-24119:
Verma and Yadav show that a borrowed warning signal for failing language-model training is, in their tests, useless. Masked diffusion language models are fine-tuned with cheap adapters called LoRA. Trainers watch top-1 concentration as a collapse alarm. It gauges how strongly the model favours its single likeliest token, and it comes from denoising diagnostics. Across hundreds of LoRA setups from three model families, the 2026 study finds the alarm firing everywhere.

Not one run actually collapsed at the checked horizon, so the alarm's precision is zero. The cause is pre-equilibrium saturation. Concentration starts high before training and soon stops responding to stability. A parameter-side signal works better: the maximum LoRA gradient norm, logged early. It flags the worst final-loss runs on a held-out split with solid precision. Verma and Yadav advise dropping the token alarm, logging gradients early, and calibrating thresholds per model family.
arxiv-2606-24519:
Antonio Lijoi, Igor Prünster and J. Zhang offer a 2026 review of Ferguson's 1973 Dirichlet process paper. The review covers its place in Bayesian nonparametrics, where the unknown is a probability distribution rather than a few numbers. Their subject is the prior Ferguson built on the space of probability measures. That prior was the first to combine wide support with calculations that stay workable after data arrive.

Ferguson's three constructions structure the review: one through finite-dimensional distributions, one by normalizing a gamma process, and one through predictive distributions. Each view also serves as a template for wider priors, including Gibbs-type priors and normalized random measures with independent increments. De Finetti had set out the wider framework in the 1930s without a usable prior. They argue Ferguson solved that decades-old problem and propose naming it the Ferguson–Dirichlet process.
arxiv-2606-24619:
Lippolis and colleagues study what makes competency questions hard to verify against an ontology. Such questions state, in natural language, what an ontology, a formal model of a domain, must be able to answer. CQ checking tests the model against them. The process is slow and error prone. Linguistic nuance must align precisely with formal constructs, and ambiguous or overcomplex questions poison the decisions downstream.

Nineteen people performed checking on twenty tasks inside OE-Assist. That is an engineering environment, with a language model assistant supporting evaluation. Analysing where they struggled identifies what makes a question challenging, and which supports improve performance. The headline result is about process. A tool to refine questions before they are published is necessary, scrubbing ambiguity before later engineering phases inherit them. Lippolis's 2026 study treats question quality as groundwork. Checking fails upstream, at the writing desk, more often than at the model.
arxiv-2606-24819:
Sarah Meiklejohn and seven colleagues introduce HelpBench, a benchmark for the advice language models give on digital privacy, safety, and security. People increasingly ask chatbots how to recover locked accounts, judge suspicious email, or choose between security keys and other two factor methods. Some questions carry personal stakes, such as whether an abuser could track someone through device accessories. Bad advice in this area can do real harm. HelpBench tests accuracy and tone together.

The benchmark holds 450 questions drawn from authentic user situations. Each question carries a rubric for scoring factual accuracy and tone. An automated rater graded responses from 18 leading language models. Average scores look strong, around 82 percent. The tail worries the authors, though. One response in ten scores below 65 percent, reflecting advice that is inaccurate or even harmful. Meiklejohn and colleagues argue that closing this tail is what trust in such help requires.
arxiv-2606-25519:
Shrinking a reasoning model to fewer bits per weight is supposed to make it cheaper to run, but the savings can leak away through longer answers.
