Xinyu Lian and colleagues document that hidden cost in 2026 across maths, code, science questions, and tool use tasks. Low bit quantised models often kept their accuracy while quietly writing much longer chains of thought. The team defines a token inflation ratio comparing reasoning length against the full precision original to make the effect measurable.

Closer reading of the traces found more intermediate steps and more repetition of the same ideas. Those extra tokens translate into real serving slowdowns despite faster per token decoding. Prompting tricks and sampling changes gave inconsistent relief. Quantisation aware training looked more promising, trimming both accuracy loss and inflation, and the authors urge reporting reasoning length beside accuracy in future evaluations.
arxiv-2606-25619:
Augmented reality needs a hand's true size and position in the room, not just its shape relative to the wrist, and most trackers deliver only the shape. Ruitao Jing and colleagues present ScaleHP in 2026, built on a simple bodily fact: the proportions among hand bones are stable across people and quietly encode the hand's overall metric size. A transformer decoder with a dedicated scale token fuses shape and appearance cues across resolutions, then a perspective constrained least squares step solves for coordinates in real camera space.

No separate depth module is needed, removing a fragile link in earlier pipelines. On standard benchmarks the system set new marks for metric error, including the best reported scores on two widely used hand datasets. The authors argue that built in anatomy, used as a prior, beats bolted on range sensing for everyday hand tracking.
arxiv-2606-26219:
Sumit Sarbadhicary tests a tool for reading a star's age from where it sits in a galaxy's history. Delay-time distributions extract progenitor ages and birth rates from star-formation history maps. Stellar evolution is full of uncertain knobs: mass loss, rotation, mixing, overshoot. Classical Cepheids in the Large Magellanic Cloud supply the check, since their ages are independently known.

Detections land where they should. Fundamental-mode Cepheids show strong signals at young ages across tens to two hundred million years. First-overtone Cepheids peak in a narrower old slice of that range. Peaks match period-age-colour relations best when those relations include overshoot and rotational mixing. One older outlier group appears for the fundamental-mode stars, but near-infrared maps do not confirm it. Upcoming Roman survey data could turn the method on Cepheids and RR Lyrae stars at scale.
arxiv-2606-26419:
Heng Zhang settles an open question in spectral geometry. That field studies how a shape's vibration patterns reveal its geometry. On a sphere-like surface, the first nonzero eigenfunction is the smoothest non-constant vibration pattern. Mathematicians asked how many separate peaks it can have. Peaks are called local maxima. The question assumed the surface curves positively everywhere, like a ball.

Zhang proves that any target count of two or more is possible. Some smooth, positively curved surface shaped like a sphere does the job. On that surface, the relevant vibration value is simple. Simple means it occurs only once. The pattern itself has at least that many distinct peaks. Each peak is a point where the surface is locally highest. The result answers Grossi and Provenzano in the negative. Positive curvature alone does not limit the number of peaks.
arxiv-2606-26519:
Zhiyuan Xu, Yueqing Dai, Junling Li, and Junwen Luo present NeuraDock Agent, an open-source system that keeps a language model inside safe bounds. The system supports a seven-channel EEG headset. EEG records electrical activity from the scalp. With few channels, coverage is sparse and signal quality varies. A general model can easily invent interpretations the hardware cannot support.

NeuraDock splits the work in two. A fixed local engine parses recordings, checks quality, and runs reviewed analysis steps. The language model sees only a short approved summary and a context pack. The pack states the hardware limits, the available workflows, and the scientific boundaries. Raw EEG never leaves the user's machine. Tests showed identical results across repeated runs. Capture and failure-injection tests confirmed that the data boundary held.
arxiv-2606-26719:
Jiale Cai and eight colleagues strengthen protected examples, a privacy defence for images. Such examples add invisible noise to training data. Models trained on them fail to extract usable features, protecting the data from exploitation. The authors found a critical weakness: simple a blurring filter, destroys the protection. The useful noise was hiding almost entirely in high frequencies.

Their method, FUSE, spreads protection across the full range of frequencies. During generator training, random bands of frequencies are masked out, forcing the remaining bands to carry the effect alone. A guidance step keeps high and low frequencies consistent with each other. That improves low-frequency protection while keeping images faithful. Tests across data sets, model designs, and filtering attacks showed strong protection where earlier methods collapsed.
arxiv-2606-26819:
Zhihang Xie, Marco Gaido, Sara Papi, Matteo Negri, and Luisa Bentivogli describe FBK's entry to a speech competition, the IWSLT 2026 instruction following shared task. Speech language models take spoken instructions and act on them. Tasks include transcription, translation, and spoken question answering. The team built systems for short and long speech under tight resource limits.

Short-form results were strong on the task's main benchmark. For long-form speech, three ways of cutting audio into segments were compared. A new score was introduced to handle unstable long outputs fairly. Fixed thirty-second segments proved most robust and earned the best long-form score. Error analysis showed the main failure mode: the model hallucinated by inserting repeated text. That flaw hurt transcription and summarisation scores. Short-form skill survived the long-form extension largely intact.
arxiv-2606-27019:
Sander Land introduces MinGram, a minimalist tokenizer that splits text into pieces for language models. Tokenizers decide the units a model reads. The Unigram family keeps an editable token list with elegant scoring, but its training is heavy, needing suffix arrays and repeated pruning passes. MinGram keeps the list and slashes the training machinery.

A seed vocabulary from the rival BPE method starts the process. Hard expectation-maximisation on a shortest-token path refines it. One flat pruning step finishes the job. Token count is the main objective; the Unigram score only breaks ties. Across six languages, MinGram compressed text better than both BPE and standard Unigram. Its alignment with word morphology stayed competitive. In controlled model training, Unigram-family tokenizers beat BPE on efficiency, with MinGram among the best.
arxiv-2606-27119:
Yan and colleagues attack a scaling bottleneck in quantum error correction decoding. Foundation decoders are large neural networks that read error clues, called syndromes, and guess what went wrong in a quantum chip. Their neural transfer unification framework aligns decoding tasks across code sizes. Shared algebraic structure inside scalable code families carries knowledge from small codes to large ones in this proposal from 2026.

A transformer version is built for planar surface codes alongside bivariate bicycle codes, two leading code families. On a mid-sized surface code under circuit-level noise, it beats correlation-aware matching. On a larger code, transfer adaptation again lifts it past standard matching. For a bicycle code case, it surpasses a leading belief-propagation rival where physical error rates are low. Training large decoders once, then adapting cheaply, becomes a realistic route to fault-tolerant machines.
arxiv-2606-27319:
Splittgerber, Seiler, and TaheriNejad design a full microcontroller that computes inside its own memory array. Ultra-low-power edge devices strain under the von Neumann bottleneck, where shuttling data between memory and processor burns energy. Memristive in-memory computing merges storage and computation in one non-volatile part. This thesis instead proposes a standalone, general-purpose architecture for the tiniest edge devices in 2026 work, with an instruction set drawn closely from the RV32I standard.

The design uses the IMPLY stateful logic paradigm inside a memristive crossbar array. A novel addressing scheme supports computation within the array itself. A complete implementation of the instruction set is provided. Simulations compare energy use and circuit metrics against traditional microcontrollers. An intelligent environmental sensor node serves as the proving application. Standalone in-memory microcontrollers emerge as a viable path for dormant, sip-power sensing.
arxiv-2606-28019:
Some radio galaxies shoot jets across five to seven megaparsecs. How such relativistic outflows survive that far is an open question. Gourab Giri and eleven colleagues run three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations in 2026 of two jet configurations. The jets inject continuously at different powers into low-density regions. Collimation versus disruption at extreme scales is the focus.

The stronger configuration reaches five megaparsecs in just fifteen million years. Higher thrust, better collimation, and magnetic stabilisation keep it confined. The weaker jet dissipates faster, forming lobe-like structures and reaching only about three megaparsecs in about thirty-five million years. Pinch and kink instabilities drive the transverse distortions. Suppressing them preserves a fast spine behind a slower head. Head speeds show two regimes, near half light speed and a slower band. A synchrotron proxy concentrates emission at the first recollimation shock and at the jet head.
arxiv-2606-28319:
Yu-Jie Feng, Qian Wang, and Qiang Zhao study how a proton and an Omega baryon, an exotic particle made of three strange quarks, interact when their relative energy is near zero. Whether the pair can bind into a new state is an open question that experiments are beginning to probe.

Feng and colleagues solve the Lippmann-Schwinger equation, the standard scattering framework, using two models of the force between the particles. Adding Pomeron exchange, a mechanism borrowed from high-energy physics, brought the computed binding energy, scattering length, and effective range closer to measurements. The Pomeron also supplies extra attraction that makes the state more compact. For a second spin channel they predict a weak quasi-bound state, giving future experiments a clear test of the mechanism.
arxiv-2606-28419:
Teerath Kumar, Raja Vavekanand, and Muhammad Turab augment scarce medical images without ruining the evidence doctors read. Ordinary augmentation can warp the very structures that carry a diagnosis, and free-running generative models may invent content that clashes with the labels. Their MedDiffuseMix framework mixes images under the guidance of saliency maps that mark what matters.

A classifier's saliency map splits each image into diagnostic foreground and background. Diffusion-guided mixing then acts mainly on the background, with adaptive strength, smooth blending at the boundary, and a preservation rule that rejects samples dragging the model's attention away from real evidence. Tested on four public benchmarks, from pneumonia chest images to breast tissue slides, and across CNN and transformer classifiers, the method improved accuracy and related scores over standard and generative rivals.
arxiv-2606-28619:
Axel Schulze-Halberg, writing alone, takes the derivative of a classic family of polynomials with respect to an odd variable: their order. Jacobi polynomials are workhorses of mathematical physics. They are orthogonal polynomials set by two parameters and an integer order. Taking that derivative is not basic calculus, and the result is not a basic function.

Schulze-Halberg works out the order derivative in explicit form, naming the basic special cases where it simplifies. The formula then does work: combined with a recently devised technique, it resolves a new class of indefinite integrals that contain Jacobi polynomials, integrals that were out of reach before. Short and classical in style, the paper adds a concrete tool to the special-functions repertoire, the kind of explicit derivative that later work in physics and applied math quietly depends on.
arxiv-2606-28719:
Guanglong Sun, Shuang Cui, Bo Lei, Liyuan Wang, Zihan Zhai, Hongwei Yan, Hang Su, Jun Zhu, and Yi Zhong give vision-language models a memory. The memory is modeled on the brain's own division of labor. Test-time adaptation tunes a deployed model on the data it meets, but most methods adapt locally and forget. Others work in one modality while the model's strength is precisely that it has two.

ComMem pairs a fast, detailed visual memory, cast as the hippocampus, caching high-confidence test images. It pairs that with a slow, abstract textual memory, cast as the neocortex, continually refining global text prototypes. Each new instance updates both jointly, enforcing agreement across modalities. Across fifteen benchmark datasets, under natural distribution shifts and cross-dataset tests alike, ComMem significantly outperformed state-of-the-art adaptation methods, a promising template for models that must keep learning after deployment.
arxiv-2606-28919:
Kang and Watt ask how letting welfare recipients top up a public benefit with private purchases changes the best way to design that benefit. In-kind transfers give goods rather than cash, and recipients may add their own money in a market to consume more. A social planner, meanwhile, offers a nonlinear price schedule, where the price per unit shifts with how much a person takes.

The answer turns on how demand lines up with need. When those who most deserve help also want the good most, topping up leaves the optimal design unchanged. When the link runs the other way, topping up weakens screening, the planner's tool for telling types apart, and cuts redistribution. Fewer settings justify stepping in at all. Where the planner does act, the free public option shrinks, fewer people are served, and aid shifts away from those with the highest claim to it.
arxiv-2606-29119:
Kumaresan offers a cheap screening rule for deciding whether an evolutionary outer loop is worth building for a neural network project. Such loops, which evolve network weights or structure over generations, cost hundreds of times more than the gradient training inside them. Whether they beat a simple single-shot method is usually learned only after paying.

His rule is computed before any implementation, at a phase-zero gate, and was pre-registered, its threshold fixed in advance. It forms a recovery ratio from the best single-shot gain and the best gain of any rival method. If the ratio reaches ninety percent, skip the outer loop. In two cases from a within-lab series, the gate fired and the loops were abandoned. In one, the apparent win came from a static substrate change, not evolution. On one project the gate cost tens of GPU-hours and screened out hundreds more.
arxiv-2606-29519:
Livi studies why recurrent neural networks struggle to learn long-range dependencies, links between inputs far apart in time. Under stochastic gradient descent, a past input's influence fades with the lag. If that fade is exponential, the data needed grows exponentially too. A power-law fade keeps the cost manageable.

Livi shows the fade's decay class is not fixed by the architecture. It emerges from how state and parameter dynamics couple during training. Two regimes appear: a collapsed regime with fast exponential forgetting, and an anti-collapsed regime with slow power-law forgetting. Training pulls time scales short, while rare heavy-tailed fluctuations push a few of them very long. The extended regime survives only when those pushes balance the pull. A single spectral exponent then governs the spread of time scales and, with it, the forgetting rate.
arxiv-2606-29719:
Liu Zewen warns that scores from proprietary language model evaluators can go invalid within weeks, and offers tools to catch that decay. Self-adapting agents increasingly rely on evaluator scores to shape their choices. His diagnostic framework, EPC, combines a preference collapse index, a coupling matrix, and a divergence measure.

Across eight test conditions, coupling values range from zero to above one, with wide variation. Four conditions show strong coupling and four collapse to near zero. The most telling case is drift in GPT-4o between May and June: a small re-replication inverts the study's conclusion. The instrument thus detects its own instability. Self-evaluation collapses almost completely. Liu releases EPC with all data, arguing that single-snapshot evaluator studies are unreliable.
arxiv-2606-29819:
Tuleganova and five colleagues study gravitational time advancement in Bumblebee gravity. This theory breaks Lorentz symmetry, the rule that physics looks the same to all observers moving at steady speeds. Time advancement is a negative time delay, the opposite of the well-known Shapiro delay that slows light near a mass.

The team uses a spinning black hole solution in this theory, worked out to high order. They compute signals between Earth and the Moon and Earth and a satellite. They show a critical distance above Earth exists where the Shapiro delay vanishes, and beyond it the delay turns negative. The measured distance to the Moon would come out shorter than plain geometry suggests. The size of the effect is bounded using data from the Cassini spacecraft.
arxiv-2606-30019:
Kaixing Yang and ten colleagues present a system generating dance videos from multimodal input. Music, text, or both can drive the generation. Earlier methods struggled to combine expressive motion with visual quality. No large, clean dataset existed for this task. The team built one from internet videos. They also designed their generator around a modern foundation model.

Their dataset, CIPE-Dance, holds about three hundred thousand high quality clips. The clips total over four hundred hours of dance. They span many dancers, settings, and genres. Text annotations are informed by choreography knowledge. The generator, OmniDance, treats text and music as complementary signals. Text carries slow, broad meaning, while music carries fast timing. A depth aware architecture and easy-to-hard curriculum support this design. Tests show top results across text, music, and combined tasks.
arxiv-2606-30119:
Iliana Fayolle and five colleagues test whether modern web agents can hide from website defenses. Since twenty twenty-three, language model based agents browse the web autonomously. They solve anti-bot challenges and mimic human behavior convincingly. Some 2026 agents even run on the user's own machine. Site operators struggle to tell them apart from people.

The team deployed honeysites guarded by standard anti-bot mechanisms. Defenses included robots files, CAPTCHAs, proof-of-work, and Cloudflare tools. Six language model based web agents were sent to visit. Fingerprinting covered network, HTTP, and browser layers at once. Some agents bypassed every anti-bot mechanism they faced. Yet every agent could be distinguished from humans by fingerprinting. Agents were also distinguishable from one another the same way. Stealth techniques often backfired, making agents easier to spot.
arxiv-2606-30719:
I. Lazar and nine colleagues chart how galaxy shape changes from the most massive galaxies down to dwarfs. Dwarf galaxies, below about three billion solar masses in stars, are poorly mapped, especially beyond our local neighbourhood. The team assembled a mass-complete sample of roughly one thousand galaxies spanning a huge mass range. They measured each one's concentration, asymmetry and clumpiness alongside visual classifications.

Several trends emerged. As stellar mass falls, galaxies grow less concentrated, more asymmetric and less clumpy. In both mass regimes, concentrated and symmetric galaxies were more likely to be red and quenched, meaning they had stopped forming stars. Because concentration fades at low mass, the standard shape parameters lose their power to separate early-type from late-type dwarfs. The fraction of barred galaxies also declined steadily with mass, reaching zero near one hundred million solar masses, hinting at a minimum mass for bar formation.
arxiv-2606-30919:
Wei Geng, Nitinder Mohan and Jörg Ott rethink how edge cameras decide which video frames deserve the cloud's strong detector. Standard pipelines run a weak local detector first and route based on its output, so the weak pass runs even on frames that get offloaded anyway. The team build a weak-skipping estimator that reads routing signals straight from raw pixels. At 0.153 GFLOPs it is about 29 times lighter than the weak detector itself, and it beats the usual after-weak placement. Yet neither placement wins everywhere along the offload-budget curve.

Their budget-adaptive router switches between the two placements using two offline-tuned thresholds, tracing the upper accuracy envelope of both on PASCAL VOC. It cut per-frame latency by up to 19.1 milliseconds, about 30% at the heaviest offload setting, and at some points even beat the strong model's peak accuracy by 1.7 points.
arxiv-2606-31619:
Jeet and two colleagues fuse topological data analysis with LSTM networks to catch intrusions in network traffic. Topological features describe the shape of traffic patterns over time, while long short-term memory networks read sequences. Either alone misses part of the signal: shape without order, or order without shape.

Their hybrid feeds Betti curves and persistence diagrams, the summaries topological analysis produces, into the deep model beside the sequence data. On the CIC-IDS2017 benchmark, with millions of labelled flows across fourteen attack types, the hybrid posts near-perfect detection scores in the reported tests. Ablations show the topological and temporal parts each add value, and the hybrid beats a topological random forest and an isolation forest baseline by clear margins on several measures.
arxiv-2606-31719:
Li, Gatt and Poesio ask whether vision-language models confuse seeing the same thing with agreeing on what it means. In collaborative dialogue, common ground is built turn by turn, not granted by shared perception. The team built an interpretation-matching task from 13,077 annotated reference expressions in HCRC MapTask dialogues, where partners navigate with deliberately different maps.

Giving models the authentic map images improves overall performance but shifts them toward over-predicting that partners' interpretations align, hurting accuracy exactly on the non-aligned cases. Text descriptions of the same maps reproduce the bias, while uninformative images suppress alignment predictions entirely, so the driver is map content rather than the visual channel. Calibration and reference-chain analyses suggest models lean on static map cues instead of tracking how grounding unfolds through the conversation.
arxiv-2606-32019:
Pandey and three others show the first laser-atomic oscillator built with cesium atoms. A laser-atomic oscillator works like an active mode-locked laser whose modulator is the atoms themselves, oscillating at a ground-state hyperfine frequency. The device can serve as a self-contained atomic clock or as a self-oscillating magnetometer, with optical and electrical outputs.

On the clock transition, short-term fractional frequency instability sits around the ten to the minus ten level in the reported setup. Run as a magnetometer, sensitivity reaches about 100 femtotesla per root hertz at 60 hertz. Cesium's 9.2 gigahertz hyperfine splitting allows a cavity under 1.63 centimetres long. Chip-scale clocks and magnetometers become realistic targets on this route.
arxiv-2608-00219:
Davis and Walther propose a changepoint method that controls the false discovery rate. The task is detecting and localizing a growing number of changepoints. Their data are a sequence of independent observations. The method is called Lean Bonferroni Detection, or LBD-FDR. It yields localized regions where a changepoint likely sits.

The method guarantees false discovery control across wide settings. Non-parametric and heavy-tailed data are included, a hard case. For Gaussian sequences, they derive when all strong changepoints are detected consistently. The method attains the optimal detection constant in certain regimes. It can beat the minimax Type I method in power in some settings. A feasible algorithm and simulations against five rivals round out the work.
augustine-confessions-watts-vol-1-1919:
William Watts gave Augustine's Confessions English dress in 1631. A 1919 print of that old dress fills this book. Book One holds Books One to Eight of the Confessions. Augustine was a north African bishop and a great mind of the Church.

A wild youth, a trade in fine speech, and a flight from his mother's faith fill the tale. The famed scene in the garden at Milan turns his life at last. Watts's dress keeps the tang of the age of King James. The book is the first great tale of a soul in the West.
aurobindo-human-cycle-1919:
Sri Aurobindo wrote The Human Cycle as essays in his journal Arya during the First World War, and the book appeared in 1919. Aurobindo had been a revolutionary against British rule in India before turning to yoga and philosophy. Here he offers a philosophy of history on the grand scale.

He traces societies through stages ruled in turn by symbol, custom, reason, and self-seeking trade. Beyond those stages he foresees a spiritual age, in which human unity grows from inner change rather than from force. The book states the hopeful core of Aurobindo's later teaching on the evolution of society.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-19:
Volume nineteen of Rodkinson's set steps outside the Talmud text itself: it is the first volume of his History of the Talmud. Rodkinson, a Russian-born scholar who settled in America, wrote the history to frame his twenty-volume translation. The 1918 edition gathers his long study of the work's making.

He traces the oral law from Moses through the Mishnah's writing under Rabbi Judah the Prince. Then he follows the centuries of debate in Babylon that grew into the Gemara. Lives of the great rabbis and schools fill the story. Readers who finish the translation here learn how the vast book itself came to be.
beaumont-fletcher-maids-tragedy-1619:
Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher were the most popular English playwrights of their generation, writing just after Shakespeare. Their tragedy The Maid's Tragedy was performed by the King's Men around 1610. It was first printed in 1619.

The plot turns on a wedding night secret. The king has forced the bride, Evadne, to remain his mistress, and her new husband learns the truth too late. Shame, loyalty, and revenge drive the court toward murder. The play's dark picture of a corrupt king made it the defining tragedy of court corruption in its era, and actors revived it often.
berzelius-essai-proportions-chimiques-18:
Berzelius sets out his essay on chemical proportions in French in 1819, laying ground for the modern table of atomic weights. He fixed the relative weights of the elements with new care. His letter symbols for the elements, H, O, and the rest, are the ones chemists still write today.

Measurement replaces recipe as the soul of chemistry in his hands. Long tables of trials back each number he dares to print. The work turned a craft of mixtures into a science of exact amounts. Few books did more to give chemistry its modern shape, and students still use his symbols daily without knowing his name.
blok-iambs-1919:
Alexander Blok gathered poems in iambic meter under the plain title Iambs, printed in Russian in 1919. He was Russia's leading Symbolist poet, famed for The Twelve and his verses to a beautiful lady. These late poems were shaped in the heat and fear of revolt.

Blok turns the steady beat of the iamb toward Russia's fate and the artist's place in a burning world. The tone is tense, grieving, and musical at once. Gone is the dreamy haze of his youth. In its place stands a poet speaking plainly while his old world collapses fast around him, line by ringing line, year by bitter year.
brendan-s-fabulous-voyage-a-lecture-deli:
John Crichton-Stuart, third Marquess of Bute, lectured on Brendan's Fabulous Voyage before the Scottish Society of Literature and Art in January 1893. Bute traces Brendan, son of Finnlogh, born at Tralee in Kerry about 481. The saint's restless temper drives the tale from the first page.

Fostered by the nun Ita and taught by Bishop Erc, Brendan takes to the sea. Bute reads the old voyage tale closely: a burning mountain fled at speed, seven days south, and wonders faced with dry care. Parallels with Rider Haggard's She show the tale's strange modern echoes. Bute treats the saint as a real man behind fabulous reports. Scholars of Celtic saints get a noble amateur's careful, fond reading.
burchard-corrector-decretum-19:
Burchard of Worms asks the flock hard asks in the Corrector, Book 19 of his Decretum, writ near 1012. Burchard was a bishop who built a vast book of church law. This book is a quiz for priests to put to folk who own their sins. Have you flown by night with Diana? Have you feasted with souls, or wrought harm by charms in the dark?

Each sin gets its price in fasts and prayer. The text shows what folk of that age held true in their hearts. It holds the famed canon Episcopi in full. Sages mine it still.
cabell-jurgen-1919:
James Branch Cabell sent a pawnbroker through myth in Jurgen, his comic novel of 1919. Jurgen wins back his youth and roams through hell, heaven, and old tales. He meets queens, gods, and his own past loves. Wit is his sword and shield.

Courts charged the book with lewd acts, and the case made it famed. The ban drew crowds of new fans. Back of the jokes lies a sad view of love and age. The book made sly, learned fun a mark of high class tale craft. Jurgen claims he seeks fair play, yet takes each boon life grants. That gap twixt word and deed is the joke at the book's heart.
chekhov-bishop-1919:
Constance Garnett's 1919 Chekhov volume takes its name from The Bishop, one of his last and finest stories. Bishop Pyotr, ill during Holy Week, feels the weight of office, ceremony, and distance from simple faith. Only his mother's visit brings him close to his younger, freer self.

The Letter turns on a message carried between an exiled bishop's circle and a proud dean. Easter Eve sets a monk's grief and joy against the river and fireworks of the feast night. Chekhov wrote these tales near the end of his life, and their tone is quiet and grave. The volume shows his late mastery at its most tender.
cia-0000010919:
Ferdinand Marcos had just taken office as president of the Philippines when the CIA weighed the country's prospects in January 1966. The paper covers internal security along with foreign and domestic problems. The Philippines was an American ally sending troops to Vietnam, yet it still faced unrest at home left over from the old Huk rebellion.

Analysts looked at Marcos's early grip on power and the restless politics of the islands. They weighed the fading Huk movement and the strains on the economy and government. Read later, the estimate stands near the start of a rule that would end in martial law and dictatorship.
cia-0000012419:
The fortieth debriefing: meeting number forty falls on October 10, 1961, in the Paris phase. The number itself testifies to the operation's scale and stamina over two seasons. Forty sessions in under six months, across three cities, with one source giving everything he knew. No Western intelligence operation had ever debriefed a source so thoroughly, and the file's plain numbering makes the record without any need for boasting.

The record marks the milestone in the series' usual plain form. Handlers by then could measure the colonel's whole knowledge in sittings. For readers, the page is the count made visible: forty, and still the questions came.
cia-0000013219:
Take them alive: Viet Cong instructions stressing the capture of American personnel fill a CIA item from April 1971. Living prisoners were worth more than dead enemies. They could be questioned, traded, and shown to the cameras. The take-alive guidance shaped how patrols acted on both sides. Men who knew the other side wanted prisoners fought with that knowledge in mind during every ambush.

The item preserves the other side's playbook in its own terms. Such instructions explained patterns American units had noticed the hard way. For readers, it is a tactical page with a human edge: the value set on a living enemy.
cia-0000014619: Travel to Mexico by the family of Morton Sobell is tracked in a CIA file dated June 2, 1958. Sobell was serving a long prison term for his part in the Rosenberg spy case. His family's trips abroad drew official watch for years after the trial. The file is one piece of the long tail of surveillance that followed that case.
cia-0000014719: Letters concerning Julius and Ethel Rosenberg fill a CIA file dated February 2, 1954. The file came months after the couple's execution in June 1953. Letters about them kept arriving at offices long after their deaths. Gathering them shows how the case lived on as a cause, argued in mailbags as much as in courts.
cia-0000015319: A letter to Donald Keyhoe from J. S. Harman fills a CIA file dated September 5, 1958. Harman thanks Keyhoe for his letter of September 22, dates again reversed in the title. Keyhoe's charges of a cover up never slowed. The agency's calm, short replies never changed either, year after year. This Keyhoe letter is now kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015419: Student papers on flying saucers, sent in by Dr. Thornton Page, reached the CIA in a file dated January 2, 1960. Page was an astronomer who had served on the government's early saucer panel. That students were writing class papers on the subject shows how far it had spread. The agency kept the papers, one more sign that saucers had entered campus life.
cia-0000022219: American casualties in Son La Province, North Vietnam, are recorded in a CIA item dated in 1974. Son La is a mountain province in the northwest of the country. By 1974 the last American combat troops had left Vietnam, yet the counting of the lost went on. A province level tally served the long work of accounting for every man.
cia-0000022319: Moscow would let two Virginia lawyers represent Gary Powers, a CIA record dated August 4, 1985, reports in its heading. The offer itself belonged to the 1960 trial, when Powers needed defense counsel in a Soviet court. The late file date likely marks a later handling of the old item. Even so, the heading keeps a real step in the famous case.
cia-0000022619: Three American prisoners of war were sighted in southern Laos in mid June 1971, a CIA record dated in 1972 reports. Southern Laos held the Ho Chi Minh Trail country, where many airmen fell. A mid June date fixes the sighting in the wet season of that year. The report joined the stack of leads checked against the missing lists.
cia-0000036519:
A special estimate dated September 3, 1965 weighs what would follow if Southern Rhodesia declared independence alone. The white-led government in Salisbury was moving toward breaking from Britain without agreement. American analysts were asked to game out the results before the break came.

The estimate looks at the likely fallout across Africa and beyond if the declaration went ahead. It weighs unrest, diplomacy, and the strain on Britain and its allies. Forecasts like this let readers see a crisis as officials saw it, before the outcome was known. Rhodesia did in fact declare independence alone later that same year, in November.
cia-0000045219:
The FMLN reportedly admitted responsibility in the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. Reportedly is the careful word in the title, and it matters. Admissions in wartime are often claimed before they are confirmed.

Inside, the reported admission is recorded as it reached the file. Owning the seizure changed the talks at a stroke if true. It told the government exactly whose terms it had to meet. Until then, even the authorship of the seizure had been part of what the talks had to settle. The record preserves the claim and its hedge together, which is honest history: the admission as reported, with the doubt of the first reporting still attached.
cia-0000049119: An excerpt tied to the name Santivanez survives in a CIA item from 1986, kept with the Truth Commission records. Roberto Santivanez was a Salvadoran officer who broke ranks and spoke about death squads, which made his words evidence. The excerpt preserves a fragment of that testimony's long life in the files.
cia-0000049319: Guerrilla use of mine warfare in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049319, dated May 5, 1987. The paper, noted for the Truth Commission, focuses on one tactic rather than the war as a whole. It survives as a short declassified record that names its topic plainly, useful for tracing what subjects the agency tracked during the conflict.
cia-0000098319: CIA comments on proposed handling of the recommendations of the Report to the President fill declassified CIA document 0000098319, dated January 5, 1957. The heading is cut short in the catalog. Readers get an early comments record in the long recommendation sequence, the agency responding to how a presidential board's advice should be handled.
cia-0000098719: Program Summary -- PAR 90-002 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000098719, dated September 1, 1992. The title gives a code, not a topic, so the program behind the code cannot be named from the heading alone. The brief record is a summary, filed under that code in the early post-Cold War years. Its catalog entry keeps the code exactly as released.
cia-0000102919: Construction activities of prisoners at Nizhanaya Tura and Sverdlovsk, with dates of information from the nineteen forties in cut-short form, fill declassified CIA document 0000102919, dated February 4, 1981. Two places are named. Readers get a short prisoner construction record spanning older information, filed beside the panel system item that opens this cluster.
cia-0000103319: Egypt-Iraq: Iraqi Treatment of Egyptian Workers Sours Ties is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000103319, dated October 3, 1989. The title links how Iraq treated Egyptian workers to a cooling between Baghdad and Cairo. It names an effect, souring ties, rather than any single incident. The brief record is a relations item, filed in the autumn of 1989.
cia-0000107419: Africa Review - South Africa: Igniting a Missile Race? is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000107419, dated November 5, 1989. The title poses a question, with its question mark intact, about South Africa and missiles. A question in a heading marks debate, not a settled finding. The brief record is a review item in the Africa series from 1989.
cia-0000112819: China Digest is the whole heading, with its date marked as an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000112819, dated January 1, 1945. The title is two words: a digest on China. A digest sums up reporting in short form, by its own name. The brief record preserves the estimate note with the short title as released in the files there.
cia-0000119719:
From September 1956, this CIA paper is a briefing outline for the National Security Council on Hungary and Poland. The Council, the president's top advisory body, received the distilled version of events. The outline keeps the shape of the argument as it was prepared for that room.

Briefing outlines show what officials chose to stress when time was short. Here the subject was two restless Soviet allies in the same tense autumn. The paper preserves the structure of the case laid before the president's advisers: the facts picked out, the order they came in, and the judgments attached. It is the crisis of 1956 reduced to the points Washington's leaders were meant to carry away.
cia-0000124319: A September 1951 CIA document covers United Nations prisoners of war held in Communist China. Troops from many nations fought under the UN flag in Korea, which made the prisoner question an international one. The paper records their treatment in Chinese hands as reported to the agency. The UN label in the heading covers men from many armies, a reminder that Korea was fought by a coalition whose prisoners shared camps and hardships together.
cia-0000132619: Pro-Castro demonstrations possibly coming within the week fill item 12 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 2, 1960. Its headline breaks off after the words a number o, plainly meaning a number of countries. Analysts were watching the region's streets for organized shows of support. The short item warns where the demonstrations were expected.
cia-0000135819: The record dated 4 March 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about a coup attempt, reported in a short cable from the Lincoln station in March 1954. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000135919: A declassified CIA letter dated 1 September 1979 is addressed to Thomas Farmer at the White House about the PBSUCCESS project. PBSUCCESS was the code name for the CIA effort to bring down President Jacobo Arbenz of Guatemala, which ended with his fall in June 1954. Read with the rest of the file, it shows the operation still drawing official letters twenty-five years later.
cia-0000136119: The open CIA files hold a cable dated 6 April 1954 that deals with the UDT mission, the frogman arm of the operation, in a cable addressed to CADICK. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136219: A cable in the declassified CIA files, dated 2 May 1954, covers Diaz, a single name standing as the whole subject of a cable from the Lincoln station. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136319: From 2300 on 25 June to 1700 on 26 June 1954, the radio operators summarized here kept stressing one need: air support. Messages relayed through LINCOLN report 300 men at Carpaja needing supplies, machine guns and mortars wanted in Chiquimula, and enemy troops mobilizing at Jutiapa. A border unit of 200 men was offered to relieve pressure at Jutiapa. The cable shows the rebel force's dependence on aircraft during the PBSUCCESS climax.
cia-0000136619: An estimated 1 January 1961 date is attached to this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade collection, and the catalog marks it as estimated. Brigade 2506 was the CIA's force of anti-Castro exiles. The record gives the document no subject. Preserved in Spanish, it belongs to the cluster of brigade items the reviewers placed at the start of 1961. Its contents, like its exact date, are matters the record leaves to the text.
cia-0000136919: Give the ambassador your information, a senior military man in Guatemala is told in April 1954. The order is quoted in this relayed message. It carries the backing of several headquarters offices. It is in the national interest, the order says. He should share what he learns of the military's attitude toward the regime. His normal contacts with Guatemalan officers are the source. He should also steer conversation toward that subject. Routine liaison thus becomes political reporting.
cia-0000137319: Cuba's agrarian reform law is the subject of this CIA briefing. It served the 405th National Security Council meeting on 21 May 1959. The cabinet proclaimed the long-expected law on 17 May. Official publication was held up for last-minute changes. Moderate cabinet members opposed the unofficial version. The agriculture minister was among them. Changes will probably be minor, though. Wide publicity has already been given the program. Land over 99 acres faces expropriation. Land in intensive sugar or rice cultivation is excepted.
cia-03436119:
Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 31 July 1955 carries three items, led by comment on Chou En-lai's speech on foreign affairs. The bulletin reads his 30 July address to the National People's Congress as a sign that Peiping would seek talks with the United States on larger issues at Geneva. It notes his call for a pact of collective peace among Pacific powers, including the United States.

Chou is reported restating Formosa and the offshore islands as the basic topics, and naming the blockade, embargo, and American air moves as linked issues. Southeast Asia items report that Vietnamese officials believed a French official was tied to bombings in Saigon. Premier Nu of Burma is also reported opposing his cabinet on an American aid question.
cia-06527519:
Memorandum for the record dated 5 February 1976, numbered ORD-0327-76, tracks work on a bird camera. The memo covers TCT activities from 5 January to 4 February 1976 and states the program was on schedule. The schedule itself had been set in a memo of 5 January 1976.

The first model of a new 16 mm camera arrived on 12 January and was tested. Its rate is given as about one frame per second, covering a ground strip 90 feet wide at 100 feet of altitude. Working from a bird speed near 50 feet per second, the memo figures about 140 linked pictures and 14.5 acres covered. Two cameras were test flown on live birds in California on 23 January. Later notes list faults found, including a timing circuit failure and underexposed film from a filter choice.
cia-06619119:
Secret memorandum from the Director of Security, sent to the Director of Central Intelligence, reviews the case of James Speyer Kronthal. The memo states that Kronthal, a deceased Agency employee, died by suicide at his Georgetown home on 31 March 1953. It was prompted by a Newsweek article of 15 May 1989 titled The Soviet's First CIA Mole.

The memo sets out Kronthal's service from the Coordinator of Information and OSS in 1942 through CIA posts ending in March 1953. It then reviews claims in the book Widows, which alleged he had been co-opted by the Soviets. Those claims, and statements from a man named Ford about an Agency test in 1951, are reported as allegations under review, not as findings. An FBI memo of 10 April 1953 on coroner testing is also cited.
cia-06675419:
Secret State Department cable dated 24 November 2001, sent through the Roger Channel with a burn after reading note, quotes a CIA information report. The quoted report, serial dated 21 November 2001, covers illegal drug use in Southwest Asia. Countries named are Bangladesh, Pakistan, India, and Nepal, and the report is marked not finally evaluated intelligence.

Its summary states all four countries had serious drug problems and took a hard line on trafficking and use. Rehab efforts were mostly token or run by charities, and wide corruption blunted enforcement, the report says. Heroin is named the major problem drug across the region. In Nepal, most people could afford only locally grown marijuana or hashish. A source in the report disputes United Nations figures for Pakistan, claiming no more than half a million real heroin addicts there.
cid-lay-rose-bacon-1919:
Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, the Cid, rides through Spain's oldest surviving epic, The Lay of the Cid, from about 1200. R. Selden Rose and Leonard Bacon rendered it in English verse in 1919. Exiled by his king, the Cid wins land, wealth, and honor by his sword, and takes Valencia as his prize.

The poem honors loyalty under insult: its hero serves the king who wronged him, and shames the coward sons-in-law who wrong his daughters. Its spare, direct style feels closer to history than to romance. Rose and Bacon's translation carried the national epic of Spain to English readers in ringing form.
conrad-arrow-of-gold-1919:
The Arrow of Gold, published in 1919, is Conrad's late romance of Marseilles in the 1870s. A young seaman, Blunt, is drawn into gun-running for the Carlist pretender to Spain's throne, and into the orbit of the mysterious Dona Rita.

Rita, an heiress of strange beauty and a wilder past, is fought over by smugglers, artists, and aristocrats. Conrad tells the tale at one remove, through an older man's memory, giving it a haze of legend. The novel divides readers: some find it tired, others a dreamlike farewell to his world of conspiracy and desire.
constitution-cuba-2019:
Cuba approved a new constitution by public vote in 2019, replacing the charter of 1976. Early chapters give the political and economic bases of the nation. Cuba is a socialist state, and the Communist Party is named the leading force of society and the state. Havana is the capital, and Spanish is the official language.

A National Assembly of People's Power is the top lawmaking body. The 2019 text restored a president of the republic as head of state and a prime minister to run the government, splitting roles the older text had joined. Later chapters cover rights and duties, the courts, elections, and local assemblies. For the first time, the charter plainly accepts some private property.
constitution-egypt-2019:
Egypt's constitution dates from 2014, after the upheaval that removed two presidents in three years, and the hosted text includes changes made in 2019. Early chapters found the state. Egypt is a republic, Islam is the state religion, and Arabic is the official language. The principles of Islamic law are named the main source of lawmaking, a clause kept from earlier charters.

A president holds strong executive power, and a prime minister runs the cabinet. The House of Representatives makes laws, and a Senate was restored by the 2019 changes as a second chamber. Later chapters cover the courts, the armed forces, the press, and local rule. The 2019 changes also lengthened the presidential term and widened the army's stated role.
constitution-greece-2019:
Greece adopted this constitution in 1975, after the fall of a military junta, and the hosted text carries revisions through 2019. Part one gives basic provisions. Greece is a parliamentary republic, and the text names the Orthodox Church the prevailing religion while still promising freedom of worship. Part two covers the rights of each person and of society, from equality to speech, work, and health.

A president serves as head of state with limited powers. Real rule sits with a prime minister and cabinet that must hold the trust of Parliament, a single chamber often called the Vouli. Later parts cover the courts, local rule, the monastic community of Mount Athos, and how laws are made and published.
constitution-ireland-2019:
Ireland's constitution, Bunreacht na hEireann, was approved by the people in 1937, and the hosted text includes changes through 2019. Early articles cover the nation and the state. Irish is named the national language and the first official language, with English a second official tongue. Later articles set out the president, the parliament, and the government in turn.

The Oireachtas, the parliament, joins a Dail chosen by the people with a Senate partly chosen by graduates and councils. A Taoiseach, the prime minister, leads the government. The president is head of state. Other articles protect personal rights, cover the family, education, and property, and guard the courts. Every change to the text must pass a public vote, which has made Ireland a land of famous referendums.
constitution-macedonia-2019:
North Macedonia adopted its constitution in 1991, as Yugoslavia broke apart, and the hosted text includes changes through 2019. The 2019 changes put the word North into the country's name, settling a long dispute with Greece. Early parts give basic provisions and the bases of the system. A long part protects human and citizens' rights and freedoms in detail.

A president serves as head of state, while a prime minister and government hold the real executive power. The Assembly, a single chamber, makes the laws. Later parts cover the courts, a Constitutional Court, local self-rule, and public finance. Macedonian is the official language, with the tongues of large communities guarded in local use. The charter has been changed many times to fit peace deals and European hopes.
constitution-ukraine-2019:
Ukraine adopted this constitution in 1996, five years after leaving the Soviet Union, and the hosted text includes changes through 2019. Section one gives general principles for a unitary, democratic republic. Ukrainian is the state language. Section two covers the rights, freedoms, and duties of the person and citizen in detail, from life and free speech to work, health, and schooling.

A president heads the state, while a prime minister runs the government with parliament's consent. The Verkhovna Rada is the single lawmaking chamber. Later sections cover the courts, a Constitutional Court, Crimea's self-rule inside Ukraine, and local self-government. Changes in 2019 wrote the course toward the European Union and NATO into the text itself. Russia's attacks since 2014 test the charter daily.
crowley-equinox-vol-3-no-1-1919:
The Blue Equinox broke the journal's silence in March 1919, as volume three, number one. Crowley recast The Equinox as the public charter of the O T O, his second order. The blue covers held a manifesto, not just a miscellany.

Its core is the Gnostic Mass, the central rite of the O T O, printed for all to read. The constitutions of the order and the word of the Law of Thelema stand beside it. The issue told the world what the order was and what it claimed. It is the most famed single number of the whole journal.
defoe-robinson-crusoe-1719:
Daniel Defoe published Robinson Crusoe in 1719, often called the first English novel in the modern sense. The book invented realist fiction, the castaway narrative, and the economic individual as hero for readers. Defoe wrote it at sixty, drawing on castaway tales like that of Alexander Selkirk in print.

Crusoe, a York sailor, is wrecked alone on an island near the Orinoco's mouth for years. He builds, plants, pots, and keeps a journal, turning despair into methodical daily work and prayer. A footprint in the sand terrifies him, then brings him Friday, his companion and convert in time. Rescue, mutineers, and a return to England close a tale of self-reliance and providence in balance. Its plain style and concrete detail made fiction feel true to common life.
doe-osti-2998337-completion-of-level-2-f:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory milestone memo LLNL-TR-2012381, by Tom Chapman, dated October 2025, records completion of a fiscal year 2025 Level 2 milestone, number 9193. Milestone memos are the laboratory's formal proof that a promised experiment series ran. This one concerns laser shots studying laser-plasma interaction, the instabilities that scatter laser light inside fusion targets.

During the year the laser pulse was stretched to 11 nanoseconds in a three-shot series. All three shots fired successfully and the key diagnostics collected good data. Drive energy fell short of plan, so the pulse was reshaped, dipping power at the peak and restoring full power later, to probe the interaction late in the pulse as intended. The memo closes the milestone with the workaround on record.
doe-osti-3376024-system-study-high-press:
Report INL/RPT-25-89613 from Idaho National Laboratory, by Zhegang Ma and dated February 2026, grades the high-pressure core spray system at eight U.S. boiling water reactors from 1998 to 2024. Core spray is a last-line system. It floods the core from above when pressure stays too high for low-pressure pumps. Only a small set of plants carry this system, so the fleet here is eight. The study was made for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

Fresh SPAR risk models supply the math. Demand, run hour, and failure counts come from the industry IRIS reporting base. The output is a year-by-year set of failure grades for the whole span. Tables break the record down by part: pumps, valves, and the plant generators that back the system. One long run of generator fail-to-start data shows years with zero failures in about one hundred forty demands.
doyle-vital-message-1919:
Arthur Conan Doyle presses his cause in The Vital Message, his next book of 1919. The Great War had left a land full of grief. Doyle holds that word from the dead is not a fad, but the most grave news of the age. He sums the proof, meets the foes, and calls the church to take the new light to heart with speed.

His tone is that of a man on a quest, not a sage at rest. The book is his flag in the post war push of the faith. It shows his zeal at full heat.
drayton-idea-1619:
Michael Drayton shaped his sonnet sequence Idea over some twenty-five years, and the final form appeared in 1619. The sixty-three sonnets address a beloved he calls Idea, linked in his life to Anne Goodyer. She is both a real woman and a figure for beauty itself in the poems.

The opening sonnets compare the poet to a sailor reporting a long and risky voyage. Later poems play with conceits about murder, counting griefs, and a heart that will not rest. Standing beside Sidney and Spenser, the sequence shows an Elizabethan poet polishing the same love poems across a whole working life.
dunsany-tales-of-three-hemispheres-1919:
A phrase that named a whole kind of story was born in Dunsany's book of 1919. Tales of Three Hemispheres gives us beyond the fields we know, the gate phrase of portal fantasy. Its tales cross from our world to lands that run on dream's laws.

Old gods walk in new cities, and travelers trade the known fields for stranger ground. The book mixes his myth tales with yarns of a more modern cut. That mix shows Dunsany at a turn in his long career. The phrase alone would earn the volume its place in letters.
entstehung-und-ausbreitung-der-alchemie-:
Edmund O. von Lippmann writes the great German history of alchemy in Entstehung und Ausbreitung der Alchemie, published by Julius Springer in Berlin in 1919, with an appendix on the early history of metals. Lippmann, director of the sugar refinery at Halle, opens with Kopp's verdict: the history of alchemy is the history of an error. Yet the error held for nearly two thousand years.

Early chapters work through the Leiden and Stockholm papyri, the remains of the oldest alchemical writing. Greek philosophy, oriental influences, and the Hellenistic melting pot follow. Indexes of Greek words, authors, places, and subjects run past page 683. The scan's Fraktur is spaced and scarred, but the text reads. Cultural history, not a recipe book, is the aim.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-19:
Experience closes Michel de Montaigne's Essays, and Volume 19 gives that final chapter a book of its own. Charles Cotton's translation keeps the voice direct and physical. Montaigne (1533-1592) wrote it while ill, aging, and wary of doctors. No chapter sums up his whole project more fully.

Laws multiply without settling disputes, Montaigne argues, since no two cases ever match exactly. Kidney pain teaches him more than medical books, and he describes diet, sleep, and bodily habits in plain detail. He urges readers to study themselves, accept limits, and enjoy small goods without shame. Quotations from Lucretius, Horace, and other Romans crowd the margins of his talk. Anyone finishing the Essays meets the payoff here: self-knowledge treated as a daily practice, not a school subject.
essays-on-phrenology-or-an-inquiry-into-:
George Combe defends the new science of the skull in Essays on Phrenology, an inquiry into the principles and utility of the system of Drs. Gall and Spurzheim, printed at Edinburgh in 1819. The essays answer objections in order: metaphysical, anatomical, and popular. An Edinburgh statuary's advertisement bound in front sells casts of the human head with the organs marked, in stucco at three shillings.

Combe holds that single faculties sit in single parts of the brain, observed case by case. The organ of locality, he writes, gives the sense of space and distance, inspires the traveller and geographer, and feeds the genius for landscape painting. The hosted volume's front pages are badly scarred in the scan, but the argument reads clean.
europmc-pmc10019719:
Pak and co-authors test whether AlphaFold can predict how single mutations change a protein's stability and function, in a 2023 study. AlphaFold predicts protein shapes from sequence with striking accuracy. Some had even claimed the protein folding problem was solved. The authors ask a harder question: can the tool sense small changes?

They compare AlphaFold predictions for normal and mutated proteins across known cases. Their checks show where the tool helps and where it stays blind to change. The study gives a sober guide for researchers who want to use AI shapes in mutation work.
europmc-pmc10316519:
Rusch, Layden, and Dugas wrote a 2023 review on how gut microbes may shape thought and memory. The gut holds vast numbers of microbes, with more genes than the human body itself. These microbes talk to the brain through nerves, hormones, and the immune system.

One key path runs through the stress system, which makes the hormone cortisol. The right level of cortisol helps the brain grow and helps learning. Rusch reports that microbes affect this stress system across the whole life span. Stress can also disturb the gut and brain link. Most proof so far comes from animal studies, and human trials are now under way.
europmc-pmc10355019:
Tu and Wang, with the Special Writing Group of China Stroke Surveillance Report, summed up stroke in China in 2021. Stroke has led deaths and disability in China since 2015. A stroke strikes when blood flow to the brain is blocked or a vessel bursts. The report draws on national screening and hospital data.

An estimated 17.8 million adults in China had had a stroke by 2020. About 3.4 million had their first stroke that year, and 2.3 million died that year. Most strokes, at 81.9 percent, came from blocked vessels. High blood pressure touched 24.7 percent of adults, yet just a quarter of cases were well controlled. Hospital care for stroke cost about 58 billion yuan in 2020.
europmc-pmc10356619:
Hickey and colleagues mapped the human gut at single-cell scale in 2023. The gut runs over nine metres and its jobs shift along its length. The team took samples from eight gut sites in nine donors. They used image scans and tests of gene activity in single cell cores.

Cell mixes differed a lot from site to site. Hickey found many subtypes among the surface cells that line the gut. The same cell types grouped into distinct zones, which formed immune niches, or local defence hubs. Gene control patterns hinted at a step-by-step path as cells mature. The team also linked gut disease risk genes to specific cell types.
europmc-pmc10550819:
Zhou led a team in 2023, with the UK Biobank Eye & Vision Consortium, to build a base AI model for eye scans. Most medical AI models learn from labelled scans, which take expert time to mark. Each model also fits just one task. Their model, RETFound, learned from raw scans with no labels at all.

Training used 1.6 million retinal images, the photos of the back of the eye. Zhou then tuned the model for set tasks with a small stock of labelled scans. It beat rival models at spotting eye diseases that threaten sight. It also foretold body-wide ills such as heart failure and heart attack. The shared base cuts the expert marking that clinics must fund.
europmc-pmc11324519:
Camargo and colleagues present a framework that finds mobile genetic elements in sequencing data in this 2024 paper. Mobile elements, such as plasmids and viruses, move genes between microbes. They shape ecology, biotechnology, and public health. Spotting them in vast sequence data is essential but hard.

Their tool, geNomad, blends gene content with a deep neural network to classify sequences. It draws on over 200,000 marker protein profiles to annotate genes and assign viral taxonomy. A statistical model detects proviruses, viral DNA woven into a host genome, with high precision. Benchmark scores reached 77.8 percent for plasmids and 95.3 percent for viruses, substantially beating rival tools. The team processed over 2.7 trillion base pairs and found millions of new viruses and plasmids, shared via public databases.
europmc-pmc1183519:
Grün and colleagues mapped tiny gene regulators in fruit flies in 2005. These regulators are called microRNAs, short bits that curb protein output. Each one binds to matching sites on gene messages. The team used a program named PicTar to predict targets.

Comparisons across seven fly species sharpened the search. On average, each microRNA was linked to about 54 target genes. Some clustered microRNAs seem to act as a team. Grün also compared fly targets with mammal targets. A few control links appear shared, while others seem unique to each group.
europmc-pmc1195719:
Liu and co-authors mapped chemical marks on yeast DNA packaging in 2005. DNA wraps around histone proteins in units called nucleosomes. Small chemical marks on histones affect gene use and repair. Many mark types exist, and their combined patterns were unclear.

A fine-scale chip read 12 mark types on thousands of units. Marks did not occur at random or alone. They fell into roughly two partner groups. One group left a distinct zone near gene start sites. Liu shows packaging marks form patterns, not noise. Those patterns may encode gene control rules.
europmc-pmc1253619:
Molyneux, Hotez, and Fenwick proposed bundled control of neglected tropical diseases in 2005. Seven infections in Africa anchor their plan. Such diseases deepen poverty and carry stigma in rural areas. Past campaigns had already cut several of them sharply.

Treating the seven together would cost about 40 cents per person yearly. Hundreds of millions could gain lasting benefit from that spend. Guinea worm may even face eradication soon, they note. Lymphatic filariasis, river blindness, leprosy, and trachoma had all receded. Molyneux argues joint delivery beats one-disease campaigns for the poor. These infections are ancient, noted in the Bible and other old texts. They have burdened people for ages.
europmc-pmc13324819:
Alexander and the Concise Guide team catalogued G protein-coupled receptors in 2023. The guide is the sixth biennial edition of a pharmacology reference. It summarizes about 1,800 drug targets in compact tables. Roughly 6,000 interactions with about 3,900 ligands are covered.

Receptors in this section form one of six major target classes. Entries stress selective pharmacology where it exists. Links point to the open Guide to Pharmacology database. The printed guide runs almost 500 pages yet condenses the website. Alexander provides a permanent, citable snapshot of receptor knowledge. Other sections cover ion channels, hormone receptors, enzymes, and more. Each edition freezes the fast-moving database at one set date.
europmc-pmc1391919:
Bentley and co-authors sequenced the capsule genes of all 90 pneumococcal serotypes in 2006. The pneumococcus wears a sugar capsule to survive in blood. That capsule also defines vaccine targets and serotypes. Each serotype makes a chemically distinct capsule.

Sequences were related to known sugar structures and typing serum reactions. The full set gives the most complete picture of capsule diversity origins. The complete gene repertoire enables a full analysis of one capsule system. It also lays foundations for molecular serotyping. Bentley lays groundwork for tracking vaccine escape types. It appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2006.
europmc-pmc1457019:
What drives year-to-year swings in Lyme disease risk? Ostfeld and co-authors spent 13 years on that question in 2006, in New York forests where the disease is common. Risk rests on how many young ticks carry the Lyme germ. They weighed weather, deer counts, rodent counts, and acorn crops as drivers.

Deer counts had no power to foretell risk. Rain and warmth had weak effects at best. The best clues were mice and chipmunk counts from the year before, plus acorn crops two years back. Ostfeld concludes that food for tick hosts, and the hosts themselves, set the risk people face.
europmc-pmc1852419:
Perkins and colleagues profiled microRNAs in 2007 in the brains of people with schizophrenia. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that block protein production from specific messages, tuning gene activity after transcription. Schizophrenia affects about one percent of people, and postmortem work had found altered message and protein levels without one faulty protein.

The team measured microRNA levels in the prefrontal cortex, a brain region central to thought and planning. Samples came from people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and from comparison subjects. The profiling pointed to an association between the illness and shifted microRNA expression. Such a shift could explain why many messages and their proteins drift out of step in the disorder. The authors present the link as possible rather than proven, calling for further work.
europmc-pmc1977719:
Newlands and co-workers reported a Phase I trial in 1992 of temozolomide, a cancer drug related to mitozolomide. Phase I trials test safety and dose in patients for the first time. The drug had shown wide action against mouse tumours. It also caused less suppression of bone marrow, called myelosuppression, than related drugs in early tests.

The team first gave single doses to 51 patients, by vein and then by mouth. Low blood cell counts set the dose limit. They then tested a five-day oral course in 42 patients. Four of 23 melanoma patients responded, and two patients with brain tumours also shrank. The authors recommended 150 mg per square metre daily for five days for later trials.
europmc-pmc2118019:
Edwin O. Jordan studied Bacillus pyocyaneus and the pigments it makes. The germ produces two pigments: a fluorescent one and pyocyanin. Jordan found the fluorescent pigment forms under the same conditions that govern it in other fluorescent bacteria. Pyocyanin, by contrast, needs no phosphate or sulfate in the medium. It can form in foods without protein.

Light and air slowly change both colors: the fluorescent pigment yellows as it oxidizes, and pyocyanin darkens toward black. In culture, the power to make pyocyanin fades sooner than the fluorescent power. Jordan sorts the germ into four varieties, from the common kind making both pigments to a rare kind making pyocyanin alone and one making neither. The varieties are fairly stable, not easily turned into one another. Readers get a neat piece of early bacteriology on how a germ's colors depend on its conditions.
europmc-pmc2124519:
F. H. Pike, C. C. Guthrie, and G. N. Stewart reported the first of their resuscitation studies in 1908, from the physiology laboratories of Western Reserve University and the University of Chicago. Working with animals, they asked what it takes to bring an apparently dead body back. Their summary is blunt. Defibrinated blood soon loses its power to sustain the higher nerve centers, and artificial fluids make a poor substitute for blood.

Oxygen, they insist, is indispensable. The heart often beats on for minutes after it stops registering on their gauge. Massage from outside the chest, with artificial respiration, sometimes revives it. Direct massage of the heart is the surest method they have. Proper blood pressure is required for the heart to keep working. Anesthetics, bleeding, and shocks to the heart make revival harder. Readers get the ground rules of resuscitation.
europmc-pmc2125219:
Joseph R. Losee and Albert H. Ebeling grew human connective tissue outside the body in 1914, from the New York Lying-In Hospital and the Rockefeller Institute. Their material was tissue taken from a fresh cadaver. The method was Carrel's, which had kept animal connective tissue alive in vitro for more than two years.

Their human strain stayed in active life for more than two months. Earlier tries by Carrel and Burrows in 1911 had mostly failed, the plasma liquefying around human fragments. The new work shows how unforgiving the routine is. Twenty-four hours after its thirty-third passage the same line had been growing excellently. The authors expect that a steadier medium will let human tissue live indefinitely. Readers get human cells granted a laboratory life, and lost by a long weekend.
europmc-pmc2126319:
Waro Nakahara traced where the surge of lymphocytes after heat treatment comes from, publishing alone in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1919. Heat first destroys lymphocytes and then provokes a strong rise in their numbers, a pattern called lymphocytosis. Nakahara examined the spleen and lymph glands during the rebuilding phase to find the source.

The germinal centers of those organs were crowded with dividing cells as the tissue regenerated, and the organs grew larger than before. That growth shows the new cell production more than replaced what heat had killed. The first drop in blood lymphocytes always came with heavy cell decay in the spleen and glands at the same moment. So the later surge flows at least in part from these centers working harder in answer to the damage. It is a repair response that overshoots its loss.
europmc-pmc2128219:
Peter K. Olitsky and I. J. Kligler separated the two poisons of the Shiga dysentery bacillus and tested each on rabbits. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1920. One poison leaves the germ and spreads freely, an exotoxin; the other stays in the germ's body, an endotoxin. The two had long been tangled in studies of dysentery.

The pair are distinct in body and in action. The exotoxin breaks down easily with heat, forms early in growth, and raises its own antitoxin serum. It attacks the rabbit's central nervous organs, causing bleeding and dead patches in the upper spinal cord and medulla. The endotoxin withstands heat, forms later, and is not neutralized by the exotoxin serum. It attacks the gut, causing swelling, bleeding, and ulcers, chiefly in the large intestine. The split explains dysentery's two faces, gut disease at home and nerve damage in severe epidemics.
europmc-pmc2128419:
Leslie T. Webster compared six strains of paratyphoid-enteritidis bacilli in white mice, weighing germ strength against host weakness. His paper is the second of a series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923. The strains came from man and animals, and he passed them repeatedly through mice by belly injection and by mouth.

The six strains differed markedly in virulence for mice. A strain's inborn strength did not change with repeated passage through mice, by either route. At the same time, individual mice differed in how open they were to each strain, and to graded doses of a chemical poison as well. Those host differences look non-specific: a mouse weak against one challenge tends to be weak in general, rather than weak against one germ only. Infection's outcome, Webster's design shows, is written by both parties, a fixed germ character and a varying host.
europmc-pmc2131119:
David Marine described a common, little-known disease of cats: lime deposits in the suprarenal glands. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1926, from Montefiore Hospital in New York.

Calcification of the cortex's fascicular zone was found in sixty-four of two hundred fifty-seven cats. It is always true calcification, never bone formation. It is commoner in young animals and, in Marine's experience, tied to distemper. Severe cases can be recognized in the living animal, with symptoms like those of cats surviving a few weeks after both glands are removed. The poison causing the cell death is oddly specific; several kinds of experimental injury failed to copy the lesion. The sequence runs from cell injury and death to calcium laid down first as fatty compounds, later as carbonate and phosphate. Experimenters using cats, Marine warns, should reckon with glands already quietly ruined.
europmc-pmc2131519:
Frederick Flinn and William VonGlahn, at Columbia University in New York, studied copper and the liver in a 1929 paper, with chemical and microscope methods. Copper taken in over long periods had been blamed for pigment deposits and scarring in the liver. They fed copper and its compounds to rabbits, guinea pigs, and rats and examined the organs.

Copper caused neither pigment deposition nor cirrhosis in any of the three animal kinds. Pigment turned up often in the livers of normal rabbits on the usual laboratory diet with no copper at all. A diet of carrots alone produced the same pigment in full. The pigment in rabbit liver, the authors conclude, most likely comes from outside the body, from the food itself.
europmc-pmc2131619:
Rivers, Haagen, and Muckenfuss, at the Hospital of The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, examined Maitland's medium for growing vaccine virus in 1929. Maitland had claimed to cultivate vaccinia virus in a simple mix of serum and Tyrode's solution, without tissue culture. That claim raised a sharp question: can the virus multiply with no living host cells at all?

The team checked the medium itself for surviving cells. Cells in the serum and Tyrode mix lived at least five days, and at times they multiplied. Living cells are therefore present in the medium that was said to need none. The observation undercuts the claim of cell-free growth, since the virus may have had living hosts all along.
europmc-pmc2140419:
Maxwell wrote part three of his labyrinth and equilibrium series in 1920, from Berkeley and Woods Hole. The labyrinth is the inner ear's balance organ. In the dogfish, removing the otolith organs does not destroy the static functions. The eyes and fins still take compensating positions when the fish is tilted. They hold them while it is held. Maxwell asks what mechanism drives those static responses.

The stimuli arise from the labyrinth itself, not from other senses, and vanish when the rest of the labyrinth is destroyed. He argues the same mechanism serves both static and dynamic functions. Changes of tension on the ampullae, the canal organs, do the work. The tension comes from the inertia of the fluid inside, not from currents flowing in the canals.
europmc-pmc2206519:
Zappitelli and co-workers tested a urine marker in 2007 to spot acute kidney injury early in critically ill children. The standard marker, serum creatinine, rises late after damage. The candidate protein, called NGAL, rises early when injury timing is known. Whether it predicts injury in general intensive care was unclear. The team followed 140 ventilated children, collecting urine daily and grading kidney injury by paediatric criteria.

Urine NGAL rose at least six-fold in children developing kidney injury. The rise came two days before and after the creatinine jump, while controls stayed flat.
