NGAL predicted new injury with an accuracy measure of 0.78, and persistent injury lasting 48 hours or more with 0.79 on the same measure. It rose step by step with worse final injury grade. That supports its use as an early warning test in this setting.
europmc-pmc2409519:
Michalaki, Syrigos, Charles, and Waxman measured two immune signal proteins in prostate cancer patients in 2004. The proteins, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, are cytokines, messengers that can help tumors grow and spread. The study covered 80 patients split by disease bulk, plus 38 healthy controls.

Blood IL-6 in patients with spread disease averaged 9.3 picograms per millilitre, versus 1.3 in patients with contained disease, a gap the tests rated highly significant. TNF-alpha showed the same pattern, at 6.3 versus 1.1 in the same units. Both rose in step with how far the cancer had spread. In 40 patients whose cancer returned, both signals climbed at the moment a standard marker, PSA, signalled progression. The authors suggested tracking the pair alongside other markers of disease activity.
europmc-pmc2697319:
Burton and colleagues modeled in 2009 what the remodeling of the mother's spiral arteries does to blood flow into the placenta. In a healthy pregnancy these arteries lose their muscle walls and flare open five to ten times wider at the mouth. When the widening fails, preeclampsia and stunted fetal growth follow.

Using measured dimensions, the team calculated that the flare slows incoming blood from a racing 2 to 3 meters per second down to about 10 centimeters per second. At that pace, blood takes roughly 25 seconds to cross the placenta's exchange space, matching what is observed. Without the flare, blood would jet in turbulently at full speed. Such a jet would tear the delicate exchange tree, rupture anchor points, and spasm shut, starving and stressing the tissue. The harm of failed remodeling, they argue, is mostly this violence of flow, not simple shortage.
europmc-pmc2757919:
Keller and co-authors profiled in 2009 microRNA expression in blood cells as a biomarker for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. That disease strips insulation from nerves in the brain and spinal cord. It is chronic and inflammatory in nature. The disease varies widely in course and treatment response, so objective markers are prized. They measured eight hundred sixty-six microRNAs in twenty patients and nineteen healthy controls.

One hundred sixty-five microRNAs differed significantly between patients and controls, and one hundred twenty-two of them had never been linked to any other disease. The best single marker separated groups with about ninety percent accuracy. A set of forty-eight microRNAs, judged by a machine-learning method with cross-validation, reached about ninety-six percent accuracy, which supports blood microRNA profiles as a diagnostic biomarker.
europmc-pmc2874019:
Thompson, Swan, Moore, and vom Saal introduced in 2009 a journal theme issue on what they call our plastic age. Humanity uses over two hundred sixty million tonnes of plastic a year, roughly eight percent of world oil output. The papers survey rising use and the real benefits plastics bring, from medicine to food safety.

Balanced against those gains are growing harms as waste piles up in landfills and oceans. Debris entangles and is swallowed by wildlife, and chemicals that soften or harden plastics raise health worries because some disrupt hormones. The editors weigh fixes, from better waste handling to safer additives and biodegradable materials, and set out the research and policy steps needed to act on them.
europmc-pmc2876119:
Blows and a huge collaborative group pooled in 2010 more than ten thousand early breast cancer cases from twelve studies to test whether tumor subtypes forecast survival. Subtypes are set with standard stains that detect hormone sensors and a growth protein on tumor cells. The groups differ in biology and behavior, yet how survival chances shift over time after diagnosis was unclear.

The analysis sized death rates for each major subtype across short and long follow-up. Tumors lacking hormone sensors carried the worst early outlook, while hormone-sensitive tumors did better early but kept a lingering risk for many years. That time pattern matters when doctors estimate a patient's future chances, since a subtype's danger can fade or persist as years pass since diagnosis.
europmc-pmc2878219:
Gurley and a large outbreak team reported in 2007 that Nipah virus, a bat-borne virus that inflames the brain, passed directly between people in a Bangladeshi village. In the first Malaysian outbreak a decade earlier, nearly all patients caught it from pigs, and spread between people was not found. Bangladesh saw repeated small outbreaks with a different pattern worth probing.

Careful tracing of cases and contacts showed patients infecting family caregivers and others in the community, often through close contact with saliva or breath during illness. The virus's presence in respiratory secretions fits that route. Household spread changes the control playbook, the team stresses, adding barrier nursing and caregiver protection to the animal-focused measures used before.
europmc-pmc2880419:
Wishart and co-authors built PREDICT in 2010, a model that estimates survival after surgery for early invasive breast cancer in British patients. It was fitted on nearly fifty-seven hundred women treated in East Anglia, with separate curves for tumors that carry the estrogen sensor and those that do not. Standard factors went in, including tumor size, grade, node spread, and whether screening found the cancer.

Checked against a second registry of nearly fifty-five hundred women from the West Midlands, the model's forecasts landed within about one percent of the real death rates at eight years. Its accuracy scores beat chance by a wide margin for both overall and breast cancer deaths. Good calibration means doctors can quote its percentages to patients with reasonable trust.
europmc-pmc2963619:
Gudmundsson and Thiele released fastFVA, a fast open-source tool for flux variability analysis, in a 2010 article. The method probes how much each reaction in a metabolic model can vary, but slow computing had limited its use.

Their implementation cuts run times so sharply that networks with thousands of reactions finish within seconds. That speed lets researchers ask harder questions about network flexibility and robustness under varied conditions. Because the code is open, modelling groups can adopt it directly. The authors frame the gain as widening what systems biology studies can realistically attempt.
europmc-pmc3009619:
Chakravarthy and co-authors pooled studies on what raises the risk of late age-related macular degeneration in a 2010 meta-analysis. The disease is the top cause of blindness in Western nations. Many candidate risks had been reported with uneven strength.

Across two dozen studies covering well over a hundred thousand people, four factors showed strong consistent links: older age, current smoking, past cataract surgery, and family history. Heavier weight, heart disease history, high blood pressure, and a clotting protein showed moderate links. Sex, ancestry, diabetes, and cholesterol measures looked weaker or inconsistent. The short list targets prevention advice.
europmc-pmc3073119:
Hooper, Killick, and Lovestone set out in 2008 their hypothesis that one overactive enzyme drives much of Alzheimer disease. The enzyme, called GSK3 in short, normally handles jobs from sugar storage to gene control and is unusual in being switched on by default. Its overactivity, they argue, could explain the disease's hallmarks at a single stroke.

Excess activity would impair memory and drive the tau protein into the tangles that clog patient neurons. It would also raise production of the amyloid that forms plaques, and stir local inflammation around those plaques. Familial and common forms of the disease would share this one mediator. If the hypothesis holds, blocking the enzyme becomes a prime drug strategy. The authors lay out the evidence chain and the open questions it must survive. The piece is a position paper meant to focus a crowded field.
europmc-pmc3082519:
Sun and colleagues used in 2011 a pairing of yeast genetics and protein chemistry to map how the FUS protein may drive Lou Gehrig disease, also called ALS. FUS is an RNA handling protein that clumps in the neurons of some patients, much like its better studied cousin TDP-43. Which parts of the protein cause clumping and toxicity, and how patient mutations change them, were open questions.

In yeast, human FUS formed clumps and poisoned the cells, copying key features of the human disease. Systematic trimming showed which regions are required for that behavior, and patient linked mutations made the protein clump more readily and harm cells more strongly. A gene screen then found modifiers that dial the toxicity up or down. The work gives the field a fast test bed for this protein and a map of its dangerous parts, guiding the search for protective drugs.
europmc-pmc3214619:
Robert Buck and colleagues set out to fix the confused naming of PFAS chemicals in this 2011 paper. These perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances are found in the environment, wildlife, and people, but inconsistent terminology hampered communication among scientists, regulators, and industry. The authors propose one clear, shared vocabulary.

They define the PFAS family, sort it into families and subfamilies, and recommend common names and acronyms, including terms for fluorinated polymers. They also explain the two main manufacturing routes and the byproducts each creates. Finally, they map how PFAS families transform into one another, stressing which ones can break down into the long-chain acids now targeted by regulation. A supplement lists hundreds of individual compounds.
europmc-pmc3320019:
Singh and Cuervo reviewed a cell process that eats the cell's own stored fat, in a 2012 article. Fat droplets inside cells were once dismissed as inert storage blobs, but they are now seen as active structures with many jobs. Cells must turn them over in a controlled way, and a cleanup process called autophagy handles part of that job.

The fat eating branch of that process, named lipophagy, breaks droplets down and releases their energy for the cell to burn. It also influences how much food an animal wants to eat, linking cell level cleanup to whole body balance. Faulty fat eating has been tied to fatty liver disease, obesity, and clogged arteries. The authors note that autophagy fades with age, which may help explain the metabolic problems that gather in later life.
europmc-pmc3374119:
Ma and colleagues pooled observational studies in 2012 to settle whether type 2 diabetes goes with stronger or weaker bones. Reports on bone mineral density in diabetes had disagreed for years. Their search covered studies published before May 2010 that measured density with standard X-ray absorptiometry scans.

Fifteen studies, with several thousand diabetic patients and far more controls, entered the pooled analysis. Density came out higher in diabetic patients at the hip, femoral neck, and spine, though not at the forearm. The pattern held for both men and women. Younger age, male sex, higher body weight, and higher blood sugar markers each tracked with higher density in the diabetic group.
europmc-pmc3468719:
Flacking and co-authors argued for keeping parents and preterm babies close in intensive care, in a 2012 paper in Acta Paediatrica. Babies born early often spend weeks in neonatal units, where machines and routines can keep parents at a distance. The authors weigh both physical closeness, such as skin-to-skin holding, and the emotional bond parents feel.

They review evidence that closeness aids the baby's brain growth, steadies parents' mental health, and strengthens the parent-child bond. Unit layout and culture can either help or hinder that closeness. Flacking's group urges longer visiting, family rooms, and early skin-to-skin contact as standard care. More study is needed, they say, on what helps families stay close in these settings.
europmc-pmc3505519:
Statisticians test correlations constantly, and Ruud Wetzels and Eric-Jan Wagenmakers propose a default Bayesian test for them in 2012. Their method applies Bayesian variable-selection ideas from regression to plain correlations and partial correlations, the kind that hold other variables fixed.

Standard tests can only reject a null hypothesis; they cannot support it. The Bayesian test can quantify evidence in favor of no correlation, a real practical gain. Researchers may also watch results as data accumulate instead of fixing sample size in advance. Three worked examples from psychology show the method in action, and the authors deposit computer code and example data in the journal archives for reuse.
europmc-pmc3538419:
Mosquitoes out-evolve insecticides partly through detox enzymes, and Jean-Philippe David, Hanafy Mahmoud Ismail, Alexia Chandor-Proust, and Mark John Ingraham Paine review the cytochrome P450 side of that arms race in 2013. Malaria and dengue control still lean on chemical insecticides, and resistance keeps eroding them.

Mosquitoes carry over a hundred P450 genes. New genomic and functional tools are finally pinning down which enzymes metabolize insecticides, and how the same enzymes answer pollutants. Knowing the culprits enables diagnostics that spot resistance early and insecticides designed to dodge or exploit the enzymes. The authors frame P450 profiling as a way to protect both disease control and the environment.
europmc-pmc3573019:
Kimberly Bloom-Feshbach and colleagues compared flu and RSV seasons around the world in PLoS ONE in 2013. Both viruses cause yearly epidemics, but their timing in the tropics was poorly charted, which hampers vaccine planning. The review assembled laboratory-confirmed season data from 137 locations, then modeled weekly reports from the World Health Organization system to measure peak timing, season length, and strength.

Temperate places peaked reliably in winter. Tropical patterns varied much more, with twice-yearly peaks fairly common in Southeast Asia for both viruses. Northern Europe showed two-year RSV cycles, and four-fifths of tropical sites still had clear RSV seasons lasting about six months. In both hemispheres, peaks fell later in the year as latitude rose. The global map gives health planners a firmer calendar for timing campaigns.
europmc-pmc3640019:
Guessing which drug will hit which cancer is the goal of a 2013 PLoS ONE study by Menden and six colleagues. Large screens had tested many drugs on cancer cell lines and logged which gene faults went with strong or weak effects. Past models used gene facts alone, or drug facts alone. This team fed a learning machine both kinds of fact at once.

The models foretold drug strength, scored as the dose that halves cell growth, for cell line and drug pairs. Scores for fit ran to 0.72 in cross-checks and 0.64 on a blind test set. They held up, at 0.61, even for cell lines from a tissue type left out of training. Such models could fill gaps in screen data and point to new uses for known drugs, the authors say.
europmc-pmc3664019:
Forest trees are locally tuned to their home climate, Alberto and ten colleagues review in a 2013 Global Change Biology article. That tuning is both hope and problem as the climate warms: populations must shift their traits. The review draws on 250 years of common garden trials, where trees from many homes are grown side by side. It covers 19 adaptive traits in 59 tree species, mostly northern ones.

Population differences in traits showed in 90 percent of cases, and smooth change along climate gradients in 78 percent. So most trees have evolved local fits that a warming world will unmatch. The authors sort what is known about the gene base of such traits and what must still be learned. Range edges get special care. The best shot at response, they say, lies with large populations rich in gene variety under strong selection.
europmc-pmc3672519:
Keep the random part of a mixed model as full as the design allows, Barr argues in a 2013 Frontiers in Psychology article. Mixed-effects models split effects into fixed parts and random parts tied to subjects and items. Many workers trim the random parts for ease, which can make false hits far more likely when interactions are tested. Simulations in the R language back the claim.

The proposed rule is plain: when a design repeats measures within units, include random slopes for the full within-unit mix under each interaction tested. Where each unit gives one measure per cell, slopes cannot be told from noise and may be skipped. The rule matches the error terms of older variance analysis.
europmc-pmc3702519:
Pulli and colleagues set out to standardize how myeloperoxidase activity is measured in tissue samples. The enzyme, released by immune cells, drives oxidative damage in many diseases, but common activity assays disagree with each other and with imaging results, partly because other substances in tissue extracts interfere.

Their fix is to capture the enzyme with an antibody first, then measure activity. They validated the method in mouse models of multiple sclerosis, fatty liver inflammation, and heart attack. Knockout animals lacking the enzyme served as controls. The protocol proved specific and reproducible, and the intracellular activity tracked how many neutrophils had entered the tissue. A step-by-step method is provided.
europmc-pmc3707819:
Jansen and Naci explain, in plain terms, when a network meta-analysis can be trusted as much as a standard pairwise one. Network methods compare treatments indirectly, through trials that share a common comparator, which lets many options be ranked without head-to-head studies. Their validity worries many readers.

The hinge, the authors argue, is effect modifiers: patient or study traits that change how well a treatment works. If those traits are distributed unevenly between the different kinds of direct comparisons feeding the network, the indirect conclusions are biased. If the distributions can be assumed balanced, the network result stands on the same footing as the pairwise one, whatever the network's shape.
europmc-pmc3750319:
Bastian Hoesel and Johannes Schmid wrote a review in Molecular Cancer in 2013 on the complexity of NF-kB signaling. NF-kB is a family of transcription factors, proteins that switch genes on. It is essential to inflammation and front-line immunity, and it is now seen as a key player in many steps of cancer growth.

The review maps how NF-kB talks with other signaling systems. Partner transcription factors such as STAT3 and p53 can bind its parts directly or act on the same target genes. Kinases such as GSK3-beta, p38, and PI3K tune its activity or shape the paths feeding into it. Reactive oxygen species and microRNAs also serve as cross points. The authors stress that these links shape how inflammation and cancer unfold together.
europmc-pmc3779219:
Johanna Gaiottino and a large group of co-authors reported a biomarker study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on neurofilament light chain, a protein from nerve fibers. When neurons are damaged, neurofilaments spill into spinal fluid, where they have shown promise as a damage marker. Blood would be far easier to sample over time.

The team built and validated a highly sensitive test for the protein in blood and spinal fluid. Patients with Alzheimer's disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome, or ALS had much higher blood levels than controls; in ALS the values were over twenty times the healthy level. Blood and spinal fluid levels tracked each other in the disease groups. For ALS, the blood test separated patients from healthy controls with about 91 percent sensitivity and specificity.
europmc-pmc3812019:
Anuradha Chowdhary, Shallu Kathuria, Jianping Xu, Jacques F. Meis, and Joseph Heitman wrote a review for PLoS Pathogens in 2013. Their subject is Aspergillus fumigatus, a common mold that causes deadly lung infections in people with weak immune systems. They ask how strains that resist azole drugs have spread so fast.

Azole sprays used on farm crops are close kin to the azole drugs used in clinics. The review links farm use to resistant strains found in soil and in patients, often with the same gene change in the mold. Resistant cases are harder to treat and fail more often. The authors warn that drug choice and farm practice now affect each other, so both fields need joint action.
europmc-pmc3840619:
Weilong Guo, Petko Fiziev, Weihong Yan, Shawn Cokus, Xueguang Sun, Michael Q. Zhang, Pao-Yang Chen, and Matteo Pellegrini present a software tool in BMC Genomics in 2013. The tool, BS-Seeker2, lines up DNA reads from bisulfite sequencing. That method maps methylation, a chemical mark that can switch genes off.

Bisulfite treatment changes the DNA code, which makes lining reads up to a reference genome tricky. The new tool uses local alignment to place more reads than rival tools. It also handles a cut-down form of the method with custom indexes, and it drops reads where the chemical change stayed incomplete. Output files give full maps of marks across the genome. Tests show the tool works fast and well on both data types.
europmc-pmc385219:
Pamela F. Colosimo, Catherine L. Peichel, Kirsten Nereng, Benjamin K. Blackman, Michael D. Shapiro, Dolph Schluter, and David M. Kingsley map armor genes in fish in PLoS Biology in 2004. Threespine sticklebacks carry bony side plates, and some wild groups have lost most of them. The team ask how many gene changes drive that loss.

Crossing fish and mapping their genes showed that a few genome regions explain plate pattern, count, and size. One major spot accounts for most of the change in pattern and number. The same major spot drives plate loss in two far-apart wild groups, a case of parallel evolution reusing one gene switch. The work shows that big body changes in nature can rest on a small set of gene changes.
europmc-pmc3867219:
Oliver J. Brady leads a large team in a mosquito survival study in Parasites & Vectors in 2013. Two Aedes mosquito species spread dengue virus, and how long adult females live sets how far the virus can travel. Heat is a main driver of that lifespan, yet lab and field results often disagree.

The team fit smooth math models to hundreds of published lab survival tests for both species across their heat range. Field test data then tuned the lab curves to real outdoor life. Age effects, which lab work often misses, were built into the field view. The result is a shared pair of survival curves by species and heat, ready for dengue spread models that need field-true mosquito lifespans.
europmc-pmc3871919:
Aurel Popa-Wagner, Smaranda Mitran, Senthilkumar Sivanesan, Edwin Chang, and Ana-Maria Buga review reactive oxygen in brain disease in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2013. The brain burns much oxygen yet keeps weak antioxidant shields. Reactive oxygen forms thus play a double role there.

At modest levels these forms help normal cell signaling. In excess they damage neurons and feed many mental and nerve diseases, from depression to schizophrenia. A shared thread is brain inflammation, lit by early-life insults or by worn cell debris in old age. A master switch protein that raises cell defenses gets close care, as do nano-carriers that ferry scavenger drugs. The authors back antioxidant therapy as a fresh path, while noting clinic proof is still thin.
europmc-pmc3934819:
Krista Fischer and a large team test whether a broad blood profile can predict who will die in the next few years, in PLoS Medicine in 2014. They profiled blood samples from 17,345 people in two population cohorts, Estonia's biobank and Finland's FINRISK study, measuring over a hundred molecules at once by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The hunt was for markers of death from any cause that beat standard risk factors.

Four markers carried the signal: alpha-1-acid glycoprotein, albumin, the size of VLDL fat particles, and citrate. Adding them to a standard risk score improved prediction of five-year death risk in the second cohort. The authors are careful: the biology behind the markers is not yet clear, and more work is needed before such profiles guide screening or prevention in the clinic.
europmc-pmc3935919:
Daniel Müllensiefen, Bruno Gingras, Jason Musil, and Lauren Stewart build a yardstick for everyday musical skill in PLoS ONE in 2014. Musical ability in the general public is not just playing an instrument: it includes listening closely, using music in daily life, and talking about it. Their concept, musical sophistication, tries to capture that whole range in one index for people who may never call themselves musicians.

The Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index asks people to rate their own skills and habits across several dimensions. It was built on an internet sample of 147,636 people, then checked in lab studies, where its scores were sound and matched performance on two listening tasks. Job, job status, age, gender, and wealth were the main social factors tied to scores.
europmc-pmc3982119:
Maged M. Costantine reviews how pregnancy changes the handling of drugs. His paper appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2014. He writes as the sole author. A pregnant body is not a standard body with a passenger. Blood volume, body water, and fat all rise. Blood proteins fall. The heart pumps more blood to the kidneys and the womb. Blood expands faster than red cell output. That gap produces the mild anemia of normal pregnancy.

Other shifts pile up as well. Breathing deepens in pregnancy. The stomach empties more slowly. Liver enzymes that process drugs change speed. Some speed up, and some slow down. Each shift alters how a drug is absorbed and spread. Each alters how fast it is broken down and cleared. Costantine argues that doses copied from non-pregnant adults can misfire. Prescribers need pregnancy-specific drug data.
europmc-pmc4015319:
Paula Dominguez-Salas and a large team of co-authors show that a mother's diet at conception can leave lasting DNA marks on her child, in Nature Communications in 2014. In lab animals, food around conception sets tags at special gene regions called metastable epialleles, with life-long effects. Human proof was lacking.

Rural Gambian women eat very unlike diets by season, giving a natural test. The team measured thirteen blood markers of food-based tag supply in mothers around conception. Levels of several markers predicted higher or lower tagging at these special regions in the infants, read from blood cells and hair roots after birth. The marks are set in the early embryo and held across body tissues, so a blood read stands for the whole body. The work shows early food can shape a child's gene settings in a lasting, body-wide way.
europmc-pmc4021419:
Antonio Gasparrini and Michela Leone extend a health risk measure to cover delayed effects, in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2014. Attributable risk states how much illness an exposure causes, a key figure for planning public action. Standard forms ignore timing, yet many exposures act with a lag or over a stretch of days.

The authors rebuild the measure inside a model family that handles delayed, curved exposure effects. The forward view counts future burden from an exposure event; the backward view counts current burden from past events. Parts tied to ranges of exposure can be split out, such as cold versus heat. They show the method on death counts and outdoor heat in London and Rome over more than a decade each. The split shows how much of the toll came from mild versus extreme heat or cold. The tools ship as free code.
europmc-pmc4106719:
Giovanni Musso and a large international team reviewed whether non-alcoholic fatty liver disease travels with chronic kidney disease. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2014. Kidney disease already affects a large share of Western adults, mostly older people, and most die of cardiovascular disease before needing dialysis.

Both conditions share drivers such as ageing, diabetes, obesity, and high blood pressure, so separating true links from shared causes is hard. Early recognition matters because treatment can slow kidney decline and cut heart complications. The review gathers the epidemiologic evidence on how strongly fatty liver and kidney disease associate, and how often they occur together. Its findings inform screening debates for patients who carry one of the two conditions.
europmc-pmc4162519:
Roger S. McIntyre, Søren Lophaven, and Christina K. Olsen ran a trial of vortioxetine, a drug for low mood, to test if it sharpens thought in sick adults. Their trial report came out in the International Journal of Neuropsychopharmacology in 2014. Faults of thought are a core part of deep low mood, not a side note.

Six hundred two adults with repeat bouts of fair to grave low mood took one of two doses of the drug or a dummy pill each day for eight weeks. No one knew who got what. The chief score mixed a test of fast symbol work with a test of word recall. Both doses beat the dummy pill by a clear gap on that score. Most side tests and the sick group's own ratings of their thought also moved the right way.
europmc-pmc4169819:
Matthew Biggerstaff, Lyn Finelli, and three co-authors gathered published estimates of influenza spread in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2014. The key measure is the reproduction number, the average count of people one case infects. Planners use it to judge how hard a flu outbreak will be to control.

The review kept 91 papers and found 20 more in their reference lists. Median values came out at 1.80 for the 1918 pandemic, 1.65 for 1957, 1.80 for 1968, and 1.46 for the 2009 pandemic. Seasonal flu sat lower, at 1.28. Most values for novel flu viruses in humans were under 1, meaning those outbreaks faded on their own. The authors call for tracking the number in each new outbreak.
europmc-pmc4181919:
Tracey J. Woodruff and Patrice Sutton set out a method for reviewing environmental health evidence in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2014. Decisions about chemical safety often rest on narrative reviews by experts, which can hide bias and cherry-picking. Medicine had fixed similar problems with systematic review rules, and the authors adapted those rules for environmental health.

Their Navigation Guide requires a written protocol before work starts, a full search of the literature, and open records of every judgment call. Reviewers grade each study for risk of bias, then rate the whole body of evidence, keeping the science separate from policy values. Unlike medical reviews, it starts human observational studies at a moderate quality rating, since controlled exposure trials in people are rarely possible. The paper argues such rigour is within reach of agencies now.
europmc-pmc4241819:
Jeffrey G. Ellis, Peter N. Dodds, and two co-authors reviewed breeding wheat that resists rust in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2014. Three rust fungi, causing stem, leaf, and stripe rust, are wheat's most damaging diseases worldwide. Breeders fight them with two classes of resistance genes carried in the plant itself.

R genes give strong, complete protection but only against matching strains of the fungus, which soon evolve around them. Adult plant resistance genes, used once the plant matures, give partial protection that often lasts for decades and sometimes covers several fungi at once. Two cloned examples work through a transporter and a kinase protein. Stacking both classes in one variety works best. The authors warn that some adult plant genes are merely weak R genes, so durability should never be assumed.
europmc-pmc4248319:
Simone Picelli, Rickard Sandberg, and three co-authors published do-it-yourself enzyme recipes for sequencing in Genome Research in 2014. Sequencers can now read thousands of samples per run, but preparing each sample's library is the bottleneck. A bacterial enzyme, Tn5 transposase, cuts DNA and pastes on sequencing tags in one step, called tagmentation, yet commercial supply is costly and fixed.

The team gives protocols to brew Tn5 in the lab and tunes the reaction for library building. Crowding agents that thicken the reaction adjust fragment lengths and let the method work on less than a picogram of starting material. Libraries from home-made enzyme matched commercial ones in gene detection and quality. Because bare Tn5 accepts any tag the user anneals to it, custom barcodes and specialized assays become easy.
europmc-pmc4339119:
Tobias Wauer and nine co-authors dissected what happens when the protein ubiquitin gains a phosphate tag at one key spot. Their study appeared in The EMBO Journal in 2015. The kinase PINK1 adds this tag, and the tagged ubiquitin switches on Parkin, a protein whose failure is tied to Parkinson's disease.

Tagging changed ubiquitin's shape, yielding two forms, one with its tail tucked into the core. Tagged ubiquitin still loaded onto carrier enzymes but blocked several of them from building chains, and most chain cutting enzymes handled it poorly. The findings explain how one small tag can reroute the cell's whole tagging system, a mechanism with direct bearing on Parkinson's biology.
europmc-pmc4384119:
Kerstin Nowotny, Tobias Jung, Annika Höhn, Daniela Weber, and Tilman Grune reviewed two intertwined harms in type 2 diabetes, in Biomolecules in 2015. The disease couples insulin resistance with failing insulin-producing cells, and high blood sugar drives most of its complications. Oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen species, appears both in the disease's early steps and in its tissue injuries. Advanced glycation end products, proteins and lipids altered by sugar, form another arm of the damage.

Each arm feeds the other: these altered products raise reactive oxygen output and weaken defenses, while oxidative conditions speed their formation. They also arrive from food, raising the question of whether diet adds real risk. The review weighs whether these products cause harm or merely mark it, and where blocking their formation or action could help prevention and care.
europmc-pmc4590619:
Phillip A. Engen and four co-authors review alcohol's effects on gut microbes, in Alcohol Research: Current Reviews in 2015. Heavy drinking is a global health burden, and its damage increasingly appears to run through the intestine. Human data are still limited, but animal and clinical studies agree that alcohol reshapes the gut's microbial community in kind and number.

That dysbiosis matters because a disturbed gut leaks. Bacterial products slip through a more permeable intestinal wall into the blood, driving body-wide inflammation and tissue damage, with alcoholic liver disease the flagship outcome. Oxidative stress sits in the same chain. The review argues for gut-directed treatments, such as probiotics and synbiotics, to be tested against alcohol-related disease.
europmc-pmc4596519:
In 2015, Tian Liu and colleagues' meta-analysis of oxidative stress markers in depression appeared. Many small studies had linked depression to an imbalance between damaging oxygen byproducts and the body's defences. The team searched seven databases for studies from 1990 to May 2015 that measured such markers in patients. The work appeared in PLOS ONE.

In total, 115 articles met the rules for inclusion. Depressed patients showed lower total antioxidant capacity during acute episodes and lower levels of several protective substances. Damage products, including malondialdehyde, were higher than in healthy controls. Some marker levels moved back toward normal after antidepressant treatment. The pooled results support a real link between depression and oxidative stress, while leaving open which markers could guide care.
europmc-pmc4686819:
Michal Kovac, Claudia Blattmann, Sebastian Ribi, and a large team sequenced osteosarcoma tumors for Nature Communications in 2015. Osteosarcoma is an aggressive bone cancer whose chaotic genetics had hidden its driver genes. The team read the protein-coding DNA of thirty-one tumors and traced how each mutation arose during tumor growth. Findings were checked against a second set of ninety-two tumors.

Fourteen genes stood out as main drivers, some new to this cancer, yet no single driver explained most tumors. Even the famous TP53 mutations often sat only in subclones. More than eighty percent of tumors, though, carried a damage pattern like that seen when BRCA repair genes fail. That shared weakness matters: cancers with BRCA-like faults can be attacked by drugs aimed at faulty DNA repair, a route the authors flag for this bone cancer.
europmc-pmc4696819:
Christian Ritz, Florent Baty, Jens C. Streibig, and two colleagues described dose-response analysis with the R package drc in PLoS ONE in 2015. Dose-response work asks how effects change as dose rises, and it appears across drug, weed, and safety science. General software can do the math, but non-standard output often demands hand programming. The drc package, built over a decade inside the free R environment, was made to remove that friction.

Users state their model of the dose-response curve through a friendly interface, then pull out summaries and derived values with ready extractor tools. The paper reviews the concepts behind modern dose-response analysis and teaches by worked examples. It also shows how the package grew from weed-science roots into a general tool, shaped by user requests. For analysts, the message is that careful curve fitting can stay flexible without becoming a programming chore.
europmc-pmc4828719:
P. Battilani leads nine authors in Scientific Reports in 2016 forecasting a toxin risk for European maize under climate change. Aflatoxins, made by fungi on crops, are the most toxic of the fungal poisons that taint food and feed, and their levels are capped by law. The team modeled Europe in a grid of over two thousand cells, pairing climate projections with crop and fungus models for the coming century.

Under a two-degree warming, the most likely path, aflatoxin B1 in maize becomes a food safety problem for Europe, spreading well beyond its current southern fringe. The five-degree path shifts the pattern again. Wheat ran far lower risk. The authors offer the maps as an early warning to ready monitoring and farm defenses.
europmc-pmc4848819:
Aaron T. L. Lun, Karsten Bach, and John C. Marioni offered a pooling method in Genome Biology in 2016 to clean up single-cell RNA data. Such data are noisy, and many genes read as zero in any one cell, which breaks standard fixes for cell-to-cell bias. Their fix adds counts across pools of cells, works out a size factor for each pool, then splits those factors back to single cells.

In simulated and real data, the split-back factors beat older methods at removing bias. Downstream results also made more sense after the fix. Sound scaling matters because false size gaps can fake gene differences between cells. The method is a practical step for a fast-growing data type.
europmc-pmc4866519:
Halit Ongen and co-authors released FastQTL in 2016, a fast mapper that links gene variants to molecular traits across the genome. Modern datasets pair DNA reads with thousands of RNA or protein measures, and testing each trait against millions of variants is slow. Standard error control by repeated shuffling adds more cost. FastQTL wraps a common nearby-variant strategy in a cluster-friendly tool.

A shortcut models shuffle results with a fitted curve, so exact corrected values come from just a few shuffles. Pilot data from the Geuvadis and GTEx projects ran about ten times faster than with older tools. The free package makes genome-scale trait mapping routine on shared computing clusters.
europmc-pmc4897919:
Ya-Qun Zhou and co-authors reviewed interleukin-6 as a rising regulator of pathological pain in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2016. Interleukin-6 is an inflammation signal with wide effects, and nerve inflammation helps drive lasting pain. In pain models, levels of the signal and its receptor climb in the spinal cord and in nerve root clusters.

Giving the signal to animals caused touch pain and heat oversensitivity. A spinal injection of an antibody that neutralizes it eased those behaviors. Clinical hints match, with higher levels in breast cancer patients who had nerve pain after chemotherapy. Blocking this signal is a live route toward pain care that skips opioid drugs.
europmc-pmc4899619:
Jean-Jacques Lebrun, writing solo, reviewed the dual role of TGF-beta in human cancer in 2012. The TGF-beta family steers growth and fate choices in all tissues, from embryo shaping to adult repair and immunity. In healthy cells and early tumors, its signals halt growth and push faulty cells to die, a tumor suppressor role. Many tumors escape by mutating the pathway's parts.

Late in disease, the same signals flip sides: cancer cells use them to loosen, spread, and seed new tumors. This switch makes drug design tricky, since blocking the path could free an early tumor while starving a late one. Timing and tumor stage decide which face the pathway shows, the review stresses.
europmc-pmc4910019:
Calum C. Bain and co-authors traced the lives of macrophages in the belly cavity in Nature Communications in 2016. These resident immune cells are among the most studied, yet their origin and upkeep were disputed. The large resident type proved long-lived and renews itself in place, keeping embryo-born cells for at least four months in mice.

Blood monocytes also slip in steadily through a CCR2-guided route and mature into a short-lived second type. Part of that stream later converts into the resident type. The cavity thus runs a mixed economy: self-kept elders plus a flow of recruits. The balance matters for infection and inflammation studies that treat the group as one kind.
europmc-pmc4915619:
John P. A. Ioannidis argued in PLoS Medicine in 2016 that most clinical research is not useful, and that reform is overdue. Blue-sky work cannot be judged by direct impact, but clinical studies should aim to change health outcomes. Eight traits mark useful work: a real problem base, fit with prior proof, fresh information, practical design, patient focus, value for money, feasibility, and openness.

Many studies, even in top journals, fail several traits at once: tiny samples, questions nobody needs, or designs no clinic could copy. Ioannidis lists fixes for funders, editors, and teams. The essay is a yardstick readers can lay against any trial report to judge whether the work can matter.
europmc-pmc4937719:
Supratim Basu, Venkategowda Ramegowda, Anuj Kumar, and Andy Pereira review how plants adapt to drought, with crops in mind. Their review appeared in F1000Research in 2016. Drought is the top environmental limit on crop yields, and climate change brings more severe dry spells. Wild plants escape drought by tricks such as early flowering. Crops, bred for yield under rich water and fertilizer, must instead keep producing grain through dry periods.

Using rice as the model crop, the review lays out the main response systems. These include water saving leaf behavior, root changes, and stress genes that guard cells. The authors stress a gap in the field. Survival tricks found in lab model plants often fail to protect yield in the field. They argue drought work should be judged by harvest under stress, not by survival alone.
europmc-pmc5010419:
Peter James, Jaime E. Hart, Rachel F. Banay, and Francine Laden studied greenness and death rates in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2016. They drew on the Nurses' Health Study, a long-running United States cohort, and used satellite images to rate the plant cover around each woman's home. The follow-up covered 108,630 women and 8,604 deaths between 2000 and 2008.

Women in the greenest fifth of home surroundings had a death rate about twelve percent lower than women in the least green fifth, after allowing for age, smoking, and wealth. The gap was largest for deaths from lung disease and cancer. Further checks pointed to cleaner air, more activity, more social contact, and better mental health as likely paths. The authors suggest that planting more vegetation could serve public health as well as climate goals.
europmc-pmc5026719:
Christopher Chibueze Azubuike, Chioma Blaise Chikere, and Gideon Chijioke Okpokwasili classify bioremediation methods in the World Journal of Microbiology & Biotechnology in 2016. Pollution from heavy metals, pesticides, waste, and hydrocarbons is rising with industry and farming. Microbes can break many pollutants down in an eco-friendly way, and this review sorts the methods by where the cleanup happens.

In situ methods treat the soil or water in place, saving digging costs but making the underground process hard to watch and steer. Ex situ methods move the material to a controlled site, costing more in digging and transport yet handling a wider range safely. Two boosters run through both: feeding the native microbes, and adding selected ones. The authors argue that site study, not price alone, should drive the choice, weighing soil type, pollutant depth, and nearness to homes.
europmc-pmc5027519:
Ana Gámez-Valero and five co-authors compare ways to isolate extracellular vesicles from blood plasma, in Scientific Reports in 2016. Vesicles are tiny parcels cells shed, prized as possible disease markers and drug carriers, but labs lack one agreed way to collect them. The team tested three routes: size-exclusion chromatography, which filters by size, and two methods that force vesicles out with added agents.

The size-based route stripped away most of the loose plasma proteins that flood blood samples. Only its vesicles showed the full set of standard vesicle markers, which suggests the forcing agents may distort or mask the parcels. Vesicles from the agent-based routes also lowered the survival of cells grown with them. The authors conclude that the isolation method shapes what a study can claim, and should be picked with the planned use in mind.
europmc-pmc5029519:
Paula Blanco and nine co-authors review bacterial efflux pumps in Microorganisms in 2016. Efflux pumps are protein machines that push substances out of bacterial cells, and they are famous for ejecting antibiotics, which makes infections hard to treat. Yet the pumps sit in the chromosomes of nearly all bacteria and long predate medical antibiotic use, so resistance is unlikely to be their first job.

The review catalogs their wider work: clearing heavy metals, pollutants, and the cell's own toxic waste, passing chemical signals between bacteria, and helping bacteria infect plants and animals. It also covers how cells switch the pumps on in answer to set signals. A final section surveys the hunt for pump blockers that could restore antibiotic power. The overall picture is of ancient, many-purpose tools that medicine happens to collide with.
europmc-pmc5037319:
Alejandra Bruna and a large co-author group build a living biobank of breast cancer explants in Cell in 2016. Breast tumors differ from patient to patient and even within one tumor, and flat cell lines capture that variety poorly. The team grew patient tumor pieces in mice, passaging them from mouse to mouse, and kept short-term cultures of cells taken from those grafts.

The grafts kept the look, molecular traits, and inner family tree of clones found in each original tumor, even after repeated passage. Cells from the grafts could be screened against drugs at high speed in dishes, and several dish results were checked and confirmed back in the mice. The bank is offered as a shared resource for finding which tumors answer which drugs, and for markers that predict response or resistance before treatment reaches patients.
europmc-pmc5056319:
The Global Burden of Disease 2015 HIV collaborators estimate the world HIV epidemic in The Lancet HIV in 2016. Their report gives new infections, people living with HIV, treatment coverage, and deaths for 195 countries and territories from 1980 to 2015. It was built with the United Nations' own projection tools, updated with fresh reviews and demographic data.

World incidence peaked in 1997 at 3.3 million new infections. After a fast fall to 2005, new infections have held near 2.6 million a year, while deaths have dropped since the mid-2000s as treatment spread. Because people on treatment live longer, the number living with HIV kept climbing, reaching 38.8 million in 2015. HIV rose over the period from the thirty-ninth to the eleventh ranked cause of death worldwide. The authors stress that country patterns differ sharply, so global averages hide local epidemics that still need targeted programs.
europmc-pmc5069819:
Aislinne Freeman and nine co-authors link social and economic status to depression across Europe in BMC Public Health in 2016. Low status tracks with more depression, but earlier studies covered single countries, split status into parts, or measured it inconsistently. Using the COURAGE ageing survey, the team analysed 10,800 adults in Finland, Poland, and Spain with one shared method, scoring status from years of education plus household income rank.

Depression odds fell with every rise in the combined status score in all three countries. Drilling down, education alone carried the effect: more years of schooling meant lower odds everywhere, while income by itself showed no link. The design cannot prove direction, so the authors ask for long-term studies. For policy, they argue that building education in low-status areas is a concrete lever, and that a shared status index makes such comparisons across countries possible.
europmc-pmc5073919:
Philip Tack, Jan Victor, Paul Gemmel, and Lieven Annemans review surgical 3D printing in BioMedical Engineering OnLine in 2016. Printing patient-specific parts from scans has spread fast in operating theatres, and the authors wanted the clinical and economic evidence, not the hype. They searched three major databases and kept case series and trials of surgical printing in humans, analysing 227 papers in an evidence table.

Printed products fall into three kinds: anatomical models for planning, guides that steer the surgeon's tools, and custom implants. Use clusters in orthopedics, jaw and face surgery, skull surgery, and spine surgery. Reported advantages repeat across papers: shorter operations, better outcomes, and less radiation exposure. Against that, printing and extra scans raise the cost of each procedure. The authors judge the benefits plausible but largely unproven and call for a formal cost-effectiveness analysis.
europmc-pmc5253119:
Kelly E. Caudle and eleven colleagues set standard terms for pharmacogenetic test results in Genetics in Medicine in 2017, writing for the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium. Pharmacogenetics reads a patient's genes to predict drug response. But labs described the same result in clashing words: one report's low function was another's null allele, and patient labels differed just as much. Sharing results between labs and health records needs one vocabulary.

The consortium collected terms in current use, then ran five survey rounds with 58 experts. They spanned clinicians, researchers, lab staff, implementers, and informatics specialists, using the Delphi method to build agreement. Consensus passed 70 percent, and 90 percent of experts backed the final term sets for allele function and for the metabolizer types that genes imply. The authors expect shared terms to cut confusion and to let records carry decision support across different systems.
europmc-pmc5256119:
Preena Tanna, Rupert W. Strauss, Kaoru Fujinami, and Michel Michaelides reviewed Stargardt disease in the British Journal of Ophthalmology in 2017. Stargardt disease is the commonest inherited macular dystrophy, affecting roughly one person in eight to ten thousand. Faults in the gene ABCA4, inherited from both parents, damage the macula, the center of the retina, causing loss of central vision, color errors, and blind spots, usually starting in childhood.

The review describes how the disease looks and progresses, with pale flecks around a wasting macula. It explains the gene's more than 900 known disease variants, which help explain why severity varies so much even within families. Animal models and disease mechanisms are covered, and so are imaging advances. No proven treatment exists yet, but three routes are in or near human trials: stem cell therapy, gene replacement, and drug approaches.
europmc-pmc5271019:
Arthur Robinson wrote the obituary of Sir William Turner for the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1916. Turner arrived in Edinburgh in 1854 as chief assistant to the anatomist Goodsir, a young surgeon lately a student at St. Bartholomew's Hospital in London. Robinson recalls that no one could have foreseen the unrivalled teacher, keen investigator, astute organizer, and strong ruler found in that hire. Turner's first year was unhappy, but persistence won him a strong position.

His duties grew from daily demonstrations in topographical and microscopic anatomy and charge of the dissecting room to summer courses on special topics. As Goodsir's health failed, Turner took over the whole department. Under him the dissecting room never held fewer than two hundred students and once passed three hundred. His voluntary demonstration class grew larger than any like it in Edinburgh, all while he kept up a stream of research.
europmc-pmc5282719:
Felice N. Jacka and a large team of colleagues ran the SMILES trial of dietary improvement for major depression, reported in BMC Medicine in 2017. Whether changing diet can treat an existing mental illness, rather than merely track with risk, was largely untested. The trial assigned adults with moderate to severe depression to seven sessions with a clinical dietitian over twelve weeks, or to a social support program with the same visit schedule.

Of 166 people assessed, 67 joined the trial, and most were already receiving therapy, drugs, or both. On the standard MADRS depression scale, the diet group improved far more than the support group by twelve weeks. Remission reached 32.3 percent in the diet group against 8.0 percent in the control group, meaning about four patients needed the program for one extra remission. Checks on dropout patterns left the result standing. The authors present dietary improvement as an effective add-on treatment.
europmc-pmc5324219:
Bram Beckers, Michiel Op De Beeck, Nele Weyens, Wout Boerjan, and Jaco Vangronsveld mapped bacteria around and inside poplar trees in Microbiome in 2017. Plant microbes help trees take up scarce food, fight disease, and bear stress. How the mixes differ between soil, root, stem, and leaf was still fuzzy. The team sampled field-grown hybrid poplars at all four sites.

Gene reads showed the soil mix at the roots varied far less from tree to tree than the mixes inside the plant. Each plant part formed its own niche with its own bacterial set. The known shift at the soil to root border was confirmed. Finer shifts then tuned the mix again in stem and leaf. A core set of bacteria ran through the whole tree. Root soil assembly looks calm and controlled; spread inside the plant is looser.
europmc-pmc5360219:
Rahul S. Desikan led a large team that built a gene risk score for Alzheimer's disease in PLoS Medicine in 2017. Spotting who will get the disease, and when, could shape both care and trials. Gene scans had found many risk variants, led by the APOE gene, but no one had woven them into an age-based risk frame for daily use.

The team pulled risk variants from a world data pool of more than fifty thousand people. They then fed those variants into a survival model built on a second set of cases and controls. The yield was a polygenic hazard score for each person. Joined with public age rates, the score gives a running risk by age. People in the top quarter fell ill far younger and at the highest yearly rate. The score held up in three more test groups.
europmc-pmc5395719:
Zachary R. Chalmers leads a large author group in a 2017 Genome Medicine study of how many changes tumors carry in their DNA. That count, called tumor mutational burden, can flag patients likely to gain from immune drugs that free the immune system to attack cancer. The team first checked that a focused gene test gives near the same count as reading all protein-coding DNA.

They then profiled a huge set of cancer cases across more than a hundred tumor types. A share of patients in nearly every type, even rare ones, carried high counts. Burden rose with age and tracked with faulty DNA repair states and certain gene changes. The authors say many patients who might gain from immune drugs are being missed by type alone.
europmc-pmc5431019:
Rillig and co-authors test whether earthworms drag microplastic down into soil. Their research article appeared in Scientific Reports. Microplastic pollution is well studied in water. Soil has drawn far less attention. Plastic bits land on the surface first. Harm to soil life depends on whether they sink. Earthworms mix soil as they burrow and feed. They were prime suspects for the transport.

The team ran a greenhouse test with one earthworm species. They spread polyethylene beads of four sizes on the soil. They then checked three layers, each 3.5 centimeters deep. Worms greatly raised the bead counts at depth. Smaller beads moved down the most. Casts, burrows, gut passage, and sticking to worm skin all play roles. Burial lengthens how long plastic stays in soil. It also exposes deeper soil life. The authors warn that groundwater could be a later stop.
europmc-pmc5653719:
Ash and co-authors model how light penetrates human skin in this technical note. The note appeared in Lasers in Medical Science. Safe laser and pulsed-light use needs penetration data. The team used Monte Carlo simulation software. Their model had multiple skin layers. They varied wavelength, beam width, and skin tone.

Penetration depth grew with longer wavelength. The deepest value reached about 5,378 micrometres. A 10-millimetre beam kept most deep fluence. It matched 73 to 88 percent of an endless beam. Wider beams added little depth. The authors say geometry shapes treatment effect. Careful modelling can guide safer light therapies. The analysis used Matlab software.
europmc-pmc5688119:
Brown and co-authors report a mouse study in Nature Communications. It shows how resident microbes protect the lungs from infection. The team challenged mice with two major lung pathogens. They were Streptococcus pneumoniae and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Mice stripped of microbes cleared both far worse. The missing link was a signal called GM-CSF. Microbes prime the lungs to make more of it. That signal boosts killing by alveolar macrophages.

Interleukin-17A carried the priming effect from microbes. Certain bacteria proved especially potent at triggering it. They live in the upper airway and the gut. Named strains include Staphylococcus and Lactobacillus species. All acted through the Nod2 sensor and GM-CSF.
europmc-pmc5689219:
O'Donnell and co-authors report overdose deaths involving fentanyl in ten states. Their report appeared in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. The period covered is July to December 2016. Illicit fentanyl drove a sharp national rise. The drug is far stronger than morphine. New analogs kept entering the supply.

Fentanyl appeared in most deaths in seven states. It was found in at least half of opioid deaths there. Many deaths also involved heroin. Analogs appeared in over ten percent in four states. Carfentanil was among the most common analogs. A drug called U-47700 was also tracked. Standard tests miss many analogs. The authors urge wider specialized testing. Better surveillance can guide the response.
europmc-pmc5701019:
Liang and co-authors show how radiation can breed its own resistance in tumors. Their study centers on STING, a host pathway that senses damaged DNA. Radiation switches STING on and boosts type I interferon. That response should help the immune system attack the tumor. Yet treated tumors often grow back.

The team found that STING also calls in suppressor myeloid cells. These cells, called MDSCs, enter tumors in part through the CCR2 pathway. Blocking CCR2 stopped that influx in their tests. An anti-CCR2 antibody eased suppression after STING activation. It also strengthened the effects of STING drugs plus radiation. The authors propose this pairing for human use.
europmc-pmc5719019:
Kinreich and co-authors study whether two brains fall into step during live social contact. They used hyperscanning EEG, which records brain waves from two people at the same time. Their groups were romantic couples and strangers, all taking part in natural male-female meetings.

The team recorded 104 adults and also tracked gaze, mood, and speech. Couples, but not strangers, showed linked brain activity in gamma rhythms. The link sat in temporal-parietal areas and was absent during rest. It grew in moments of shared gaze and warm affect. Speech itself did not explain the effect. The authors link such two-brain matching to how close the partners feel. They frame it as a brain form of the bonding first learned in early attachment.
europmc-pmc5735219:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration pools world data on body weight from 1975 to 2016. The group drew on 2,416 studies with measures on 128.9 million people. They tracked body-mass index in 200 countries. Child and teen trends get full treatment beside adult ones.

Childhood obesity rose from under 1% to about 6% in girls and 8% in boys. Severe underweight fell only a little over the same span. Gains in BMI have flattened in many rich countries, the group reports. They have sped up in parts of Asia instead. India still shows the highest rates of child underweight.
europmc-pmc5742819:
Vu and Datta review how colorectal cancer cells switch form and spread. The switch, called epithelial to mesenchymal transition, loosens cell contacts. Cells gain movement and reach distant sites more easily. The review gathers fresh work on what controls this switch.

Signals such as WNT and TGF-beta can turn the switch on. They act through factors like ZEB1 and ZEB2, which cut E-cadherin and raise other markers. Small RNAs in the miR-34 and miR-200 families hold the switch back. Tumor cells in the blood that show this switch may flag spread, the authors note.
europmc-pmc5750219:
Schubert and co-authors present PROGENy, a method that reads pathway activity from gene expression. Faulty signaling drives cancer, so its activity is a key drug target. Older methods map genes to pathways but miss later protein changes. Their signatures also tie too much to one test setup.

PROGENy draws on a large set of public perturbation experiments. Shared response genes form a common core for each pathway. The method recovers known driver mutation effects, the authors report. It also gives strong markers for drug use and patient survival. Oncogenic and tumor suppressor pathways can be told apart with it.
europmc-pmc5768719:
Zhu and co-authors present GSMR, a method that tests whether risk factors cause common diseases. The method uses summary data from genome scans and many gene variants at once. Links seen in daily life data often hide cause, effect, or confounding. This genetic approach aims to sort those cases.

The team tests body mass, cholesterol, blood pressure, height, and years of schooling against many diseases. Samples reach over four hundred thousand people. They find that schooling guards against Alzheimer disease. They also find two way links, where a factor and a disease push each other in opposed directions.
europmc-pmc5804319:
Delmont and Eren link pangenomes with metagenomes for an ocean microbe. Pangenomes list the genes of related strains. Metagenomes show which genes thrive in real waters. Joining both can reveal why microbes split into niches.

Their framework is interactive and reproducible. They apply it to Prochlorococcus, a key ocean microbe, with survey data. Near-identical strains showed sharp gaps in where they were common. Gene content tracked those gaps better than family trees did. A small core gene set tied to sugar use stood out. Readers get a method for joining gene catalogs to field data.
europmc-pmc5832819:
Manvich and co-authors challenge a core assumption behind a popular brain-control method. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. The method, DREADDs, switches chosen neurons on or off with a drug called CNO. CNO was long treated as harmless and inert.

The team gave CNO to rats and mice and measured what followed. The drug converted back into clozapine, its parent compound, in both species. Animals trained to recognize clozapine's inner effects also answered to CNO. At common working doses, some animals matched the clozapine state fully. The authors urge strict control groups in DREADD work.
europmc-pmc5917019:
Mu and co-authors review Lactobacillus reuteri in human health and disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. This probiotic bacterium lives in gut, skin, and breast milk. Its levels vary widely between people. It makes acids and reuterin that kill harmful microbes. That helps it reshape gut communities.

The bacterium can calm pro-inflammatory signals, they report. It supports regulatory T cells and strengthens the gut barrier. Fewer gut leaks may mean less body-wide inflammation. Its decline in recent decades tracks rising inflammatory disease. Adding it back may prevent or treat such illness. Readers get the evidence and the open questions.
europmc-pmc5962619:
Mohajeri and co-authors review the role of gut microbes for human health, from lab science to clinic use. Their review was published in the European Journal of Nutrition. It sums up a 2017 meeting held in Groningen. Experts from schools and firms took part. Talks took in gut-friendly foods, live germ doses, and vitamins. Early life growth and the gut-brain link also came up.

The gut mix shifts a lot in pregnancy, the authors note. Stress, diet, and drugs shape it through life. Germ-made fats can sway gut-brain signals. Stool grafts work well for one hard gut infection that keeps coming back. More proof of how they work is needed for wider use.
europmc-pmc6096619:
Eriksson and co-authors test two drugs against fatty liver in type 2 diabetes. Their EFFECT-II trial appeared in Diabetologia. Eighty-four Swedish patients took part for 12 weeks. Four arms compared dapagliflozin, omega-3 acids, both, and placebo. MRI measured liver fat at start and end.

Each active arm cut liver fat from its own baseline. The omega-3 arm fell 15 percent. Dapagliflozin alone fell 13 percent. The pair fell 21 percent. Only the pair beat placebo clearly on total liver fat. Dapagliflozin alone lowered several liver injury markers. A gene variant also shaped responses. Readers get early evidence for combined metabolic therapy.
europmc-pmc6117319:
Xing and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on sky-blue perovskite light-emitting diodes. Perovskite diodes shine well in green and near-infrared light. Blue versions have lagged behind. Their color shifts as the driving voltage rises. That shift blocks use in displays and lighting.

The team tuned the mix of cations in thin perovskite films. That made the crystal layers more even in thickness. The films hit a record light yield of 88 percent at 477 nanometers. The diodes kept a stable sky-blue color at high voltage. Peak brightness reached 2,480 candelas per square meter. That is about ten times the prior record for such blue diodes.
europmc-pmc6119719:
Taneja wrote a review in Frontiers in Immunology on how sex hormones shape immune response. Women tend to make more antibodies than men. That strength helps fight infection. It also raises the risk of autoimmune disease. Men, in turn, face higher rates of some cancers.

The review links hormones to daily rhythms, gut microbes, and gene activity. Hormones like cortisol peak at set times of day. Gut microbes can turn hormones into active signals. Genes on the X chromosome add to the sex gap in immunity. Taneja also weighs outside factors like smoking and infection. The result is a broad account of why immune illness differs by sex.
europmc-pmc6193719:
Sticht and co-authors present a resource article in PLoS ONE on miRWalk, an online tool for microRNA binding sites. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that tune gene activity by binding target messages. Knowing where they bind is key to understanding that control. miRWalk predicts and collects such sites.

The platform covers known genes from human, mouse, rat, dog, and cow. Its core predictor uses a random-forest method that scans the whole transcript, including both ends and the coding part. Results from other databases, predicted and lab-validated, are integrated too. The database updates twice a year through automated scripts. Its modular design aims at easy extension, serving researchers who study gene regulation.
europmc-pmc6258319:
Teague and co-authors reviewed how long term cohort studies keep their members. Their review and analysis appeared in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Cohort studies follow the same people for years. Members who drop out can weaken the results. The team gathered 143 studies from the past decade. Sample sizes ran from thirty people to over sixty thousand.

Ninety-five distinct retention tactics were found and sorted into four groups. Some tactics cut the burden on members. Others built community, sent reminders, or traced lost members. Studies that cut burden kept about ten percent more of their sample. Reminder heavy studies did worse by a similar share. Using more tactics overall did not help. The results favour making study life easier over chasing members harder.
europmc-pmc6279019:
Brooks and co-authors studied how gut microbe mixes differ across ethnic groups in the United States. Their study appeared in PLOS Biology. Gut communities vary a lot between people. Chronic diseases tied to those communities hit minorities hardest. Ethnic influence on gut microbes was little studied. The team combined two large American data sets with 1,673 people.

Twelve microbe groups varied by ethnicity in both data sets. Many of those groups also track with family inheritance. A family called Christensenellaceae was the most heritable of all. The varying groups formed clusters with shared feeding styles. Fermentation and methane making linked many of them. The authors argue that these microbes may mediate some health gaps. Their list gives clear targets for follow up studies. Diet, genes, and culture all remain in play.
europmc-pmc6333919:
Żylicz and co-authors order the early chromatin changes that silence one X chromosome. Their study appeared in Cell. Female cells switch off one of their two X chromosomes. The RNA Xist starts that shutdown in development. The team used female mouse stem cells. They triggered Xist and watched genes and chromatin over time.

Two changes came first in their tracking. Histone deacetylation and a ubiquitin mark appeared earliest. An enzyme, HDAC3, already sat on the X beforehand. Once Xist coated the chromosome, its action proved essential. Without it, gene silencing faltered. Marks from two Polycomb systems followed in sequence. They began in large gene-poor regions. Only with deacetylation under way did they spread into genes.
europmc-pmc6424819:
Petljak and co-authors catalog the mutational signatures written into 1,001 human cancer cell lines and 577 xenografts, then watch which signatures keep forming in culture. Each process that damages or miscopies DNA leaves a recognizable pattern of changes. Knowing which patterns stay active matters because cell lines serve as living models of real tumors.

Signatures from past tobacco smoke and ultraviolet light stopped appearing once cells grew in dishes. Repair-related signatures kept a fairly steady pace. APOBEC editing, by contrast, fired in sudden bursts separated by quiet periods, for reasons still unclear. The collection gives researchers a tested set of models for studying how cancers keep mutating.
europmc-pmc6467319:
Antcliffe and co-authors re-analyze the VANISH randomized trial of septic shock to test whether a patient's gene-expression endotype predicts who corticosteroids help or kill. Sepsis response signatures split patients into SRS1, a relatively immunosuppressed profile, and SRS2, a relatively immunocompetent one. Expression data were available for 176 patients, 83 SRS1 and 93 SRS2.

Vasopressor choice, norepinephrine or vasopressin, showed no interaction with endotype. Steroids did: hydrocortisone raised mortality sharply in SRS2 patients, with an odds ratio of 7.9 against placebo, while SRS1 patients showed no such harm. A seven-gene test at shock onset could one day steer steroid decisions.
europmc-pmc6478219:
Tran and co-authors report the first evidence that severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus circulates in Vietnam. That extends the known map of a tick-borne disease recognized in China since 2009 and later in Korea and Japan. The illness brings high fever, falling platelets and white cells, and liver enzyme rises, with death rates of 16 to 30 percent in published series.

Stored serum from 80 patients admitted with acute fever to a Hue hospital across six months was tested by PCR for the viral small segment. Two samples came back positive, both from patients who recovered. Finding even two infections in a small retrospective panel implies wider, undiagnosed transmission and argues for surveillance.
europmc-pmc6520719:
Tchesnokov and co-authors work out how remdesivir blocks the Ebola virus polymerase. Their study appeared in Viruses. Remdesivir is a prodrug of an adenosine analogue. It was in clinical development for Ebola virus disease. Its exact blocking mechanism was still unclear.

The team used purified polymerase from Ebola and RSV. The active form of remdesivir competed with ATP for a place in new RNA. Both viral enzymes took it up with like ease. Human mitochondrial polymerase rejected it about 500-fold more. Once built in, the drug did not stop the next step. Chain growth stalled mainly five positions later. The authors call this delayed chain termination.
europmc-pmc6523119:
García-Pinel and co-authors review lipid-based nanoparticles for cancer treatment. Their review appeared in Nanomaterials. Many cancer drugs dissolve poorly, break down fast, or cause harsh side effects. Lipid carriers can shield such drugs and guide them.

Types covered include liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles and nanostructured lipid carriers. These systems hold both water-loving and fat-loving drugs. They offer high loading, long stability and low cost. Loading a drug into them can cut the dose and toxicity. More drug reaches tumour tissue and less reaches healthy tissue. Drug resistance may also fall. The authors sum up lab, animal and patient trial results.
europmc-pmc6527519:
Hug and co-authors estimate neonatal mortality levels and trends worldwide. Their systematic analysis appeared in The Lancet Global Health. It covers 1990 to 2017, with projections to 2030. Data came from vital registration, sample registration and household surveys.

A Bayesian model produced country rates for deaths in the first 28 days. The global rate fell by 51% across the period. It went from 36.6 to 18.0 deaths per 1,000 live births. Annual deaths fell from 5.0 million to 2.5 million. West and central Africa and south Asia kept the highest rates. At current pace, 27.8 million more deaths are projected by 2030.
europmc-pmc6621919:
Timmermans, Souffriau, and Libert give a general tour of glucocorticoid biology. Their review appears in Frontiers in Immunology. Glucocorticoids are steroid hormones used widely against inflammation and autoimmune disease. They act through the glucocorticoid receptor, a transcription factor. Side effects and drug resistance limit their long use.

The authors trace the hormones from discovery to daily physiology. The adrenal cortex makes them under control of the HPA axis. Levels follow a daily rhythm and surge under stress. The review explains how the receptor switches genes on and off. It also covers how these drugs calm inflammation. Receptor variants and resistance get their own treatment. The authors close with the SEDIGRAM concept for gentler, selective therapy.
europmc-pmc6723519:
Smatti and co-authors review how viruses interact with autoimmune disease. Viruses have long been seen to alter conditions such as type 1 diabetes, lupus, and multiple sclerosis. Gut viruses, flu viruses, and herpesviruses are the leading suspects. Measles, mumps, and rubella viruses have also been studied.

Infection can trigger autoimmunity or protect against it. Which way it goes depends on genes, the virus strain, dose, and timing. The review lays out the main routes: viral parts that mimic body proteins, spreading targets, bystander activation, and lasting infection of B cells. Clear proof of each step is still scarce. The authors call for work that pins down exact mechanisms.
europmc-pmc6794619:
Kim and co-authors used exosomes to flip wound macrophages from attack mode to repair mode. Macrophages steer wound healing through inflammation, growth, and new vessel formation. A timely switch from the inflammatory M1 form to the healing M2 form speeds recovery. Exosomes harvested from M2 macrophages carried the instructions for that switch.

In dishes, the exosomes fully converted M1 cells into M2 cells. Marker proteins flipped as expected, and the cells behaved like genuine M2 macrophages. About 96% of M1 cells were reprogrammed in one assay. Injected at wound edges in mice, the exosomes raised M2 counts and lowered M1 counts. Healing accelerated, with more vessels, skin regrowth, and collagen laid down.
europmc-pmc6797519:
Chen and co-authors tested exosomes loaded with a small RNA to promote bone regeneration. The RNA, miR-375, was packed into exosomes from human fat-derived stem cells. The team verified the vesicles by microscopy, sizing, and protein markers. They then tuned the dose on bone marrow stem cells in culture.

At 50 micrograms per milliliter, the loaded exosomes improved bone-forming differentiation. Follow-up assays showed miR-375 works by targeting a binding protein that normally restrains a growth factor. Embedded in hydrogel, the exosomes were placed into skull defects in rats. Scans and tissue sections at eight weeks showed better bone repair than controls. The approach pairs a natural carrier with a bone-promoting signal.
europmc-pmc6886219:
Wang and co-authors report a study in Molecular Cancer on a long noncoding RNA in colorectal cancer. Such RNAs regulate cells without building proteins. Screening tumour samples against matched healthy tissue flagged one, named LINRIS, at high levels. Patients with more of it survived less well. Its very name records its job: it keeps a partner protein, IGF2BP2, stable.

LINRIS blocks the disposal route that would destroy IGF2BP2. The spared protein in turn protects messages that drive sugar burning, the aerobic glycolysis cancer cells favour. The chain runs through the growth gene MYC. Knocking LINRIS down in mice shrank tumours grown from human cells within 4 weeks. The axis is offered as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc6925219:
