Haruwaka and co-authors show a dual role for microglia at the blood-brain barrier. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Microglia patrol brain tissue for injury and infection. They also react to illness elsewhere in the body. How they affect barrier strength was unclear.

Using live imaging, the team watched microglia respond. Systemic inflammation drew them to brain blood vessels. That migration depended on the receptor CCR5. Vessel-linked microglia first helped guard the barrier. They expressed the tight-junction protein Claudin-5. They also touched endothelial cells directly. With sustained inflammation, the effect flipped. Microglia ate astrocytic end-feet and weakened the barrier. The work links body-wide immune activity to brain function.
europmc-pmc6936719:
Nickbakhsh and co-authors show that respiratory viruses influence each other's spread. Their study appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Flu and common cold viruses circulate together each season. Doctors long suspected they compete or cooperate, perhaps through short-lived broad immunity. Hard numbers, though, were scarce.

The team analysed years of diagnostic reports covering 11 respiratory viruses. Statistical tests found strong support for real interactions between them. Computer simulations then tested possible mechanisms. Even very brief interference after one infection could explain why colds dip during flu season. Knowing how these epidemics link together, the authors argue, should sharpen disease forecasts. It should also help judge control measures more fairly.
europmc-pmc6941219:
Mateo and co-authors test the drug olaparib in advanced prostate cancer with faulty DNA repair. Their trial report appeared in The Lancet Oncology. The TOPARP-B study enrolled men whose metastatic castration-resistant cancer had progressed after chemotherapy. Tumour samples were sequenced to find damage response gene defects.

Patients with such defects were assigned at random to 400 mg or 300 mg of olaparib, taken twice daily. The trial ran at 17 hospitals in the United Kingdom. Response meant tumour shrinkage, a steep fall in prostate-specific antigen, or a drop in circulating tumour cells. A dose group would count as successful if at least 19 of 44 patients responded. The design aimed to confirm that repair defects predict benefit from olaparib.
europmc-pmc6965119:
Wang and co-authors uncover a circular RNA that helps lung cancer dodge the immune system. Their study appeared in Cell Death and Disease. Circular RNAs form closed loops and often work by sponging up small regulatory RNAs. Their role in lung adenocarcinoma was largely unclear.

Profiling tumour and nearby tissue flagged three circular RNAs raised in cancer. One, circRNA-002178, stood out. It soaks up miR-34, which frees a protein called PDL1 to rise on cancer cells. PDL1 exhausts attacking T cells. The circle also travels in blood-borne vesicles, marking it as a possible early diagnosis marker. Delivered into killer T cells, it raised PD1 there too. Together, these routes help the tumour switch off immune attack, and offer targets to switch it back on.
europmc-pmc6988219:
Zhong and co-authors present a method that spots the warning point before a complex disease tips into crisis. Their study appeared in BMC Genomics. Many diseases pass through a fragile pre-disease state before sudden worsening. Clinics usually have a single sample per patient, which defeats most statistics.

Their index, called single-sample Kullback-Leibler divergence, measures how far one case sample disturbs a healthy reference background. A sharp jump in that measure flags the critical state. The method was tested on simulations and on six real data sets. These included several cancers and acute lung injury. In each, it found the pre-disease stage and marker genes that signal it. The authors aim at personal early warning, where treatment might still head off the crash.
europmc-pmc7019719:
Ko and Kim review lipid problems linked to menopause in the journal Nutrients. As estrogen falls, fat handling in the body changes. Blood fats shift, belly fat grows, and insulin works less well. Those changes raise the risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes after menopause.

The review first explains how hormone change disrupts fat and energy balance. It covers lipoproteins, body fat mass, and the build-up of harmful by-products. It then turns to food as a response. The authors discuss vitamin D, omega-3 fatty acids, antioxidants, and plant compounds. For each, they name food sources. The aim is practical dietary guidance for women after menopause.
europmc-pmc7022619:
Rychlik reviews the gut microbiota of chickens in the journal Animals, writing as sole author. Chickens are a special case among farm animals. Commercial chicks hatch in clean hatcheries, away from adult hens. In nature, a hen would seed her chicks with adult gut microbes from day one.

The review describes which microbes live in each part of the adult chicken gut. Lactobacilli dominate the crop and stomach, while the caecum holds a far richer mix. Rychlik warns that hatchery chicks make a poor natural baseline for studies. Chicks given hen microbes early resist infections such as Salmonella, he notes. He also weighs selected microbes as candidates for next-generation probiotics.
europmc-pmc7029019:
Liu and co-authors report a mouse study in Nature Communications on fasting, gut microbes, and the diabetic brain. Poor thinking is a known side effect of type 2 diabetes. Intermittent fasting eases some diabetes symptoms, but whether it guards the brain was unclear. The team put diabetic mice on a 28-day intermittent fasting plan and tested their behaviour.

Fasting made the mice think better. It raised energy-making activity in the hippocampus, reshaped gut microbes, and raised microbe-made products tied to good thinking. Wiping out gut microbes with antibiotics partly erased the gain. Giving single products, such as 3-indolepropionic acid, serotonin, or short chain fatty acids, copied much of the effect. The results point to a gut-brain route that new treatments might use.
europmc-pmc7045519:
Wu and co-authors review ferroptosis in cancer in the journal Molecular Cancer. Ferroptosis is a form of regulated cell death driven by iron and lipid damage. It differs from other death types in shape, genetics, and chemistry. Abnormal ferroptosis has been linked to cancer growth and other hard diseases.

The review focuses on gene-mark regulators and metabolic change. Organelle problems can each push a cell toward ferroptosis, the authors note. They cover mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum, lysosomes, and the Golgi body. Signalling routes and metabolic rewiring are traced as well. The authors argue that this fuller picture could guide new treatments. Cancers that resist other death routes are a prime target.
europmc-pmc7047419:
Yang and co-authors report a cancer biology study in Molecular Cancer. They study METTL14, a protein that adds a common chemical mark, m6A, to RNA. In colorectal cancer, loss of this protein tracks with a poor outlook for patients. The team asked what METTL14 does to tumour cells.

Lowering METTL14 made cancer cells grow and invade far more in lab tests, the authors report. It also raised tumour growth and spread in animals. Gene screening pointed to a long non-coding RNA called XIST. METTL14 normally marks XIST, which lets a reader protein trigger its breakdown. Without the mark, XIST builds up and drives the cancer. The findings give METTL14 a clear tumour-suppressing role.
europmc-pmc7100419:
Tan and co-authors show that a falling lymphocyte share in the blood predicts how severe COVID-19 will become. Their study appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. The team tracked full blood counts over time in patients who died and in patients who recovered.

In patients who died, the lymphocyte percentage often fell below 5 percent within two weeks. Severe cases that recovered saw it climb back above 10 percent. Moderate cases stayed above 20 percent. From these curves the authors built a Time-LYM% model with checks at days 10 to 12 and days 17 to 19. Readers get a cheap, common blood test turned into a guide for triage and intensive care.
europmc-pmc7110919:
Wu and co-authors report the eye findings in patients with COVID-19 in Hubei Province, China, in JAMA Ophthalmology. Their case series covers 38 patients treated at Yichang Central People's Hospital in February 2020. The team checked eye symptoms, blood tests, and swabs from both the nose and the eye surface.

Twelve patients had eye signs like conjunctivitis, such as redness, swelling, and watering. These signs were more common in patients with worse whole-body illness. Virus tests were positive in 28 nose swabs, but in only 2 eye swabs. Blood changes were also stronger in patients with eye problems. Readers get early evidence on how the new virus touches the eye, and what that means for diagnosis and safe eye care.
europmc-pmc7162819:
Schulz and co-authors reconstruct thousands of giant virus genomes from environmental DNA sampled worldwide, in Nature. Knowledge of these large DNA viruses had come mostly from the few grown in labs with their protist or algal hosts. Mining public metagenome data, the team rebuilt 2,074 genomes from sites across the globe.

The haul raised known evolutionary diversity 11-fold and functional diversity about 10-fold. Checking 58,023 major capsid proteins showed these viruses live nearly everywhere. Their genomes carry genes for photosynthesis and nutrient transport, suggesting they reprogram their hosts. Gene transfer traces linked virus lineages to many eukaryotic hosts. The authors cast giant viruses as major, overlooked players in ecosystems across Earth's biomes.
europmc-pmc7170819:
Ahir and co-authors review how glioblastoma brain tumors grow new blood vessels. Their article appeared in Molecular Neurobiology. Glioblastoma is a fast-growing, highly vascular brain tumor. Its growth depends on angiogenesis, the sprouting of new capillaries from existing vessels. The authors explain how signals from the tumor drive that sprouting.

The review sums up the growth factors and genes that push vessel growth in these tumors. It also covers the factors that hold the process back. Much of the focus falls on anti-angiogenesis therapy. Such treatment aims to slow the tumor by blocking its new blood supply. Readers get a clear picture of vessel growth as both a driver of the disease and a target for drugs.
europmc-pmc7192519:
Wallace examines how prior choices shape colocalisation analysis, a method for testing whether two traits share a genetic cause. The article appeared in PLoS Genetics. The method, called coloc, works from genome study summary data alone. It has become popular for comparing thousands of trait pairs. Its Bayesian design depends on prior values set by the user.

Wallace shows that leaving the default priors untouched can mislead. Wrongly set priors can shift the final conclusions a lot. The article suggests ways to derive sensible priors from the data itself. It also shows how sensitivity checks can test whether results hold up. A second weakness is the assumption of one causal variant per trait. Wallace relaxes that assumption so several variants can be modeled.
europmc-pmc7261819:
Zhu and co-authors introduce DEqMS, a statistical method for spotting proteins whose levels change between samples. Their methods paper appeared in Molecular and Cellular Proteomics. Mass spectrometry studies measure thousands of proteins at once, and finding real differences depends on estimating how much each measurement naturally varies.

Most methods miss one fact: a protein's variance depends on how many peptide fragments were used to measure it. DEqMS builds that dependence into its estimates. Tested against current approaches, it gave better accuracy and stronger statistical power on both labeled and label-free data. The method ships as a user-friendly R package, so proteomics groups can add it to standard workflows for biomarker hunting and basic biology.
europmc-pmc7275719:
Stadnytskyi and co-authors measure how long tiny droplets from speech hang in the air. Their study appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. People who carry SARS-CoV-2 without symptoms can still release virus in oral fluid. Loud speech emits thousands of droplets per second, but the smallest ones were easy to overlook.

Using sensitive laser light scattering in a closed box of still air, the team watched droplets vanish with time constants of 8 to 14 min. That behavior fits droplet nuclei about 4 micrometers wide, shrunk from droplets of 12 to 21 micrometers before drying. Normal speaking, they conclude, has a substantial chance of spreading virus through the air in confined spaces.
europmc-pmc7295519:
Clark and co-authors estimate how many people worldwide were at increased risk of severe COVID-19 because of underlying health conditions. Their modelling study appeared in The Lancet Global Health. Older age and existing illness were known to raise risk, but counts by country were missing, and shielding or vaccination plans need them.

The team used prevalence data from the Global Burden of Disease 2017 study and United Nations population estimates for 2020, covering 188 countries by age and sex. Conditions counted as risky were matched to those in World Health Organization and national guidelines. Adjustments accounted for people carrying several conditions at once. A second, stricter estimate flagged people likely to need hospital care if infected, using hospitalization ratios from mainland China.
europmc-pmc7316319:
Ellington and co-authors compare pregnant and nonpregnant US women of childbearing age who caught SARS-CoV-2. Their CDC report covers January 22 to June 7, 2020. In that span the CDC got word of 326,335 women aged 15 to 44 years with a positive test. Pregnancy can change the immune system in ways that make chest infections worse, so the split matters.

Pregnancy status was known for 91,412 women, and 8,207 of them were pregnant. The two groups coughed at like rates, and breathlessness was alike too. Pregnant women told of fever, headache, and muscle aches less often. But far more of them went to hospital: about a third, next to a small share of the rest. Even with age and health gaps ruled out, pregnancy stayed a clear risk sign.
europmc-pmc7322019:
Wang, Liu and Gao explain, atom by atom, why SARS-CoV-2 grips its human receptor more tightly than the earlier SARS virus. Their study appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Stronger binding to ACE2 is thought to help drive the new virus's high contagiousness. The spike proteins of the two viruses are 76% identical, so the difference hides in small details.

Using molecular dynamics and binding energy calculations, the team mapped the hydrogen bonds and water-shunning contacts at the interface. SARS-CoV-2's reported binding strength exceeds its predecessor's by a factor of 10 to 15. The new contact network balances specific and nonspecific interactions to achieve that grip. Such structural detail can guide surveillance of new variants and the design of agents that block or neutralize the binding surface.
europmc-pmc7327519:
Osimo and co-authors pool blood test data in Brain, Behavior, and Immunity to test links between depression and inflammation. Their meta-analysis covers 5,166 patients with depression and 5,083 controls. Earlier work had tied depression to infection and autoimmune illness, but marker results varied by study.

Across studies, patients showed higher average levels of several pro-inflammatory markers, the signals that promote inflammation. One calming marker, IL-4, ran lower in patients. The spread of values also differed: patients' immune measures varied less than controls'. The authors frame the pattern as immune dysregulation that may matter for new treatments. Readers get a careful summary of what blood markers can and cannot say about depression.
europmc-pmc7415419:
Wang and co-authors review autophagy in bone disorders in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. Bone health rests on balance between builder osteoblasts and resorber osteoclasts. Autophagy, the cell's self-recycling, and mitophagy, its mitochondria-only form, appear to regulate both cell types' growth and work.

When balance fails, diseases follow: bone loss, osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Pathways named PINK1/Parkin, SIRT1, Beclin-1, and mTOR all feed into the recycling control of bone cells. The review gathers current progress on how these switches behave in each disorder. Its hope is plain: recycling pathways are druggable, and bone disease needs new targets. Readers get a compact map of an emerging front in skeletal medicine.
europmc-pmc7453019:
Vuong and co-authors test a cat coronavirus drug against the main protease of SARS-CoV-2. The protease cuts the virus's long protein chain into working parts. Blocking it should stop the virus from copying itself.

The prodrug GC376 had cured a fatal coronavirus disease in cats. Its parent form is GC373. Both blocked the protease of SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 at very low doses in lab tests. Crystal images show the drugs bound to the active site of the enzyme. Nuclear magnetic checks show the block can reverse. Both drugs also stopped SARS-CoV-2 growth in cell culture. Since they already worked in animals, the authors back them as candidates for human trials.
europmc-pmc7460619:
André and Spruijt review liquid-liquid phase separation inside crowded cell fluids. Many cell bodies form as droplets without membranes. Their parts are proteins that split into liquid phases, much like oil in water.

In test tubes, this split reacts to acidity, heat, and salt levels. Crowding, the dense packing of molecules in cells, has got less study. Crowders can shift where phases form and what droplets hold. Most droplet parts are loose, disordered proteins with many weak grips. The authors compare cell and test-tube studies side by side. They propose that cell droplets act much like segregative phase splits. Crowding, they argue, must sit at the center of future models.
europmc-pmc7562819:
GBD 2019 Universal Health Coverage Collaborators measure effective health coverage in 204 countries and territories. Their index spans the years 1990 to 2019. Universal coverage means care of good quality without hardship.

The team mapped 23 effective coverage indicators. They cover promotion, prevention and treatment services. Five age groups run from newborn to older adults. Indicators were weighted by potential health gains. Gains were measured in disability-adjusted life-years. The new index beat older coverage measures in validity tests. Frontiers linked coverage levels to health spending per person. The work shows whether services match country health needs. It draws on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019.
europmc-pmc7599319:
Turner and co-authors report the plasmaMATCH trial of blood DNA testing in advanced breast cancer. Tumor DNA in blood may show a cancer current profile. That could avoid repeat tissue biopsies for patients.

The platform trial ran at 18 UK hospitals. A total of 1051 patients registered for the study. Blood DNA results were available for 1034 patients. Patients joined cohorts matched to mutations found in blood. Drugs included fulvestrant, neratinib and capivasertib by cohort. Agreement between two blood test methods was 96–99%. That figure came from 800 patients tested both ways. Each cohort had a set response goal. The trial tests whether blood testing can direct therapy well.
europmc-pmc7612819:
Suo and co-authors map the developing human immune system across organs before birth. Single-cell studies had covered single prenatal organs before. A whole-system view across tissues was still missing.

The team profiled nine prenatal tissues in the atlas. Methods combined single-cell RNA and receptor sequencing. Spatial transcriptomics added place data for cells. Immune effector roles came late to cell subsets. Monocytes and T cells matured before seeding outer tissues. Blood and immune growth reached beyond main organs. Human prenatal B1 cells were characterized in the work. Origins of unconventional T cells were also clarified. The atlas aids cell engineering and disease study.
europmc-pmc7678319:
Cupp and co-authors grade the proof linking a blood ratio to cancer outlook. The ratio compares neutrophils, a type of white blood cell, to lymphocytes. A high ratio is thought to signal worse survival. The authors pooled past systematic reviews to judge the claim.

They found 204 meta-analyses from 86 studies. Almost all linked a high ratio to higher risk of poor outcomes. Yet only 60, or 29%, had strong or highly suggestive support. Proof was solid for some cancers and for care with immunotherapy. The authors say the ratio looks promising, but more work must test cause and clinical use.
europmc-pmc7691519:
Fucikova and co-authors explain how to detect a form of cancer cell death that alerts the immune system. In this death, called immunogenic cell death, dying tumor cells emit warning signals. These signals draw in immune cells that present tumor parts and start an attack. Some chemo and radiation drugs can trigger it.

The authors list the key signals, such as surface calreticulin and released ATP. They also name cell stress signs that back up the call. Methods for use in lab dishes and in tissue samples are set out step by step. The aim is to find new drugs and craft personal treatment mixes for patients.
europmc-pmc7706019:
Amann and co-authors weigh why medical AI systems should be able to explain themselves. AI tools can beat humans at some analysis tasks. Yet doctors, patients, and courts all ask how a tool reached its call. The authors take clinical decision support as their test case.

They view the issue from tech, legal, medical, and patient angles. Legal points include consent, device approval, and liability for harm. The ethics frame rests on autonomy, benefit, safety, and justice. Skipping explainability, they argue, threatens core medical values. Careful design can protect trust while still gaining the speed AI offers.
europmc-pmc7775119:
Lin and co-authors survey vaccine demand and hesitancy in China. It ran nationwide from May 1 to May 19, 2020, before any COVID-19 vaccine existed. The frame was the health belief model, which links actions to felt risk and benefit. In all, 3,541 full responses came in.

Most people leaned toward vaccination: 54.6% said probably yes and 28.7% said definite yes. Belief that the shot cuts infection odds most raised firm intent. The median sum people would pay was 200 yuan, about 28 US dollars. Most trusted China-made vaccines, and 64.2% preferred a domestic shot over a foreign one.
europmc-pmc7795119:
Lee and Yoon examine how artificial intelligence is used in the health care industry. They reviewed the literature on AI tools in care settings. They also studied real cases from hospitals.

Major hospitals now use AI to support medical staff. The systems help with diagnosis and treatment across many diseases. AI also improves nursing work and hospital management. The authors weigh both sides of the shift. New chances for better care sit on one side. Hard problems of adoption sit on the other. They argue that gains need full planning. Care services and daily operations must change together to capture the value.
europmc-pmc7805219:
Storer and co-authors describe Dfam, an open database of repetitive DNA families. Dfam stores transposable element families, sequence models, and genome annotations. Releases 3.0 to 3.3 mark a big shift. A small proof-of-principle set became a broad community resource.

The database now serves curated and uncurated data alike. It covers many more species than before. New supports include consensus sequence models and protein alignments. A formal classification system orders the families. The latest release adds 266,740 new families built from scratch. They span 336 species and came from the EBI. The authors also flag the hard work left in cleaning such data.
europmc-pmc7839219:
Specht and co-authors present SCoPE2, a method that profiles proteins and gene activity in single cells. Macrophages vary widely in form and function. That spread was hard to study one cell at a time. Protein measures in single cells were the bottleneck.

SCoPE2 raises how much protein data each cell yields. It pairs those data with transcript measures from the same cells. The team used it to map macrophage diversity. States that bulk samples blur together stand apart here. The method opens single-cell protein study to more labs. It suits any field where rare cell states matter.
europmc-pmc7904519:
Weller and co-authors present clinical guidelines on diffuse gliomas in adults for the European Association of Neuro-Oncology. These brain tumours had seen major changes in how they are diagnosed. Large trials had also reshaped treatment. The association judged that fresh, evidence-based guidance was needed.

Diagnosis in the guidelines rests on the 2016 update of the WHO tumour classification. Later expert updates on molecular features are folded in. The authors define the roles of surgery, radiotherapy, and drug therapy. They also guide the lab and imaging checks that support each step. A theme runs through the document: avoid needless procedures and costs. The guidelines serve specialists who treat these tumours, patients and caregivers who face them, and the services that fund care.
europmc-pmc7924719:
Hao and co-authors present a software package called RIdeogram for drawing genome maps on chromosome diagrams. As sequencing speeds up, whole genomes from more species are on hand. Idiograms, the banded pictures of chromosomes, offer a clear way to map genome-wide data. Existing tools cover only a few model species or narrow uses.

RIdeogram is an R package that builds high-quality idiograms for any species a user chooses. It maps both continuous and discrete data onto the diagram. Continuous values appear as heat maps, and discrete ones as track labels. The result shows the layout of features along each chromosome at a glance. The authors argue this quick picture helps researchers spot patterns in omics data. The tool is aimed at the many non-model species now being sequenced.
europmc-pmc7931819:
Danecek and co-authors present a review marking twelve years of SAMtools and BCFtools. These programs process and analyse high-throughput sequencing data. They handle file conversion, sorting, queries, and statistics. They also call variants and judge their effects. Few labs in genomics work without them.

The first version went online 12 years before this account. Steady work since then has added many features and fixes. The packages have been built into countless other tools and pipelines. Both are free on GitHub under the MIT licence, for commercial and other use alike. They have been installed more than 1 million times through Bioconda. The authors recount the growth of the toolset and its place in daily genomics. The paper serves as both a history and a user guide.
europmc-pmc7951819:
Kompaniyets and co-authors present a CDC report on body mass index and severe COVID-19 outcomes in the United States. Obesity is a known risk factor for severe illness. It is common, affecting 42.4% of adults in the United States. The team used a large hospital database covering care from March to December 2020. They asked how weight class tracked with the worst outcomes of infection.

The analysis covered 148,494 adults diagnosed at 238 hospitals. About half of the patients had obesity, and many more had overweight. The report traces risk across four outcomes: hospital admission, intensive care, use of a ventilator, and death. Risk rose with body mass index above the healthy range. The authors present the pattern by age group as well. The findings support treating obesity as a high-risk condition when vaccines and care are rationed.
europmc-pmc7963219:
Starr and co-authors report a study mapping which mutations let SARS-CoV-2 escape antibody treatment. Several antibodies were in use or in trials against COVID-19. New variants raised the fear that they would stop working. The team built a yeast library covering every tolerable change to the virus's receptor-binding domain. They then tested how each change affected binding by three leading antibodies.

The maps flag the changes that break antibody binding. One single change escapes both antibodies in a well-known cocktail. Many escape changes for single antibodies already circulate in people. The library approach lets scientists see threats before they spread. It also shows which parts of the domain the antibodies cannot afford to lose. The work gives drug makers a forecast to design against.
europmc-pmc8201919:
Zhang and co-authors show how the ORF8 protein of SARS-CoV-2 helps the virus hide from immunity. Infected cells normally display viral pieces on MHC-I proteins. T cells read those displays and kill the cell.

The team found that ORF8 lowers MHC-I on the cell surface. With fewer displays, immune surveillance misses infected cells more often. The work adds a distinct evasion trick to the virus's known set. It sharpens the picture of how COVID-19 develops. It also informs study of T cell defence against the virus. The finding may guide vaccine and drug thinking.
europmc-pmc8255319:
Wang and co-authors review the molecular biology of pancreatic adenocarcinoma and its clinical hurdles. Pancreatic cancer kills nearly as many people as it strikes. Most cases are found late, with poor prospects.

The tumour's diversity, rewired metabolism, and dense stroma blunt standard therapy. New genetic insight now supports a molecular sorting of the disease. That sorting widens treatment options for subgroups. The review traces how tumour biology and its microenvironment drive growth. It also maps metabolic reprogramming in the cancer. Translational gaps between lab finds and clinic gains get frank treatment.
europmc-pmc8461619:
Correa and co-authors review how hydrogels move from the lab into real medical use. Hydrogels are water-rich gels that can do many jobs in the body. They can deliver drugs or cells and help regrow hard and soft tissue. They can also stick to wet tissue and stop bleeding.

The review stresses injectable hydrogels and their fresh gains. Uses reach from cancer immunotherapy to vaccination. Building such gels takes joint work across many fields. The authors cover early lab and clinical steps in that path. Design rules for scaling injectable gels get their own treatment. Less standard uses, like environmental work, appear too.
europmc-pmc8647919:
Lin and co-authors set minimum reporting standards for magnetic resonance spectroscopy studies in living tissue. This scanning method reads chemical signals in the body. Many ways exist to run scans and process the data. Details are often left out of reports, which blocks fair checks and pooled analysis.

A panel of experts agreed on what each report must state. The rules cover hardware, scan settings, data handling, and quality checks. A checklist helps authors and reviewers apply the rules. Editors can use it to see that reports are complete. The aim is work that others can repeat and trust. The standards cover both single scans and imaging forms.
europmc-pmc8866119:
Cao and co-authors test how well existing antibodies stand up to the Omicron variant. Omicron carries 15 mutations in its spike receptor-binding domain. That domain is the main target of neutralizing antibodies. The team screened 247 human antibodies against possible escape mutations. They used a high-throughput yeast display method. The antibodies fell into six epitope groups.

Single Omicron mutations knocked out whole groups of antibodies. Groups aiming at the ACE2-binding surface suffered most. A few broad antibodies, such as S309, held up better. Combined mutations escaped even antibodies that survived single ones. In all, over 85% of tested antibodies were escaped. Most antibody drugs lost much of their punch. Two retained reduced effect. The authors urge focus on conserved viral regions.
europmc-pmc8891019:
Ma and co-authors connect loss of a RNA-binding protein to a strong genetic risk factor for ALS and frontotemporal dementia. The protein is TDP-43. In disease, it drains from the nucleus of neurons. One of its jobs is blocking stray cryptic exons during RNA splicing. Variants in the gene UNC13A rank among the strongest risk hits. How they raise risk was a mystery. The team found a cryptic exon inside UNC13A itself.

When TDP-43 left the nucleus, that exon slipped into UNC13A RNA. Protein output then fell. The risk variants sit in the same intron as the exon. They worsen the faulty splicing when TDP-43 fails. The data were seen in human brain and in lab-grown neurons. The authors call this a direct functional link. It joins a top risk gene to a core disease process.
europmc-pmc9021019:
Zuin and co-authors probed how enhancers, DNA switches far from genes, control gene output through contact with promoters. The team placed one enhancer at hundreds of positions near a fixed promoter and measured the results. Gene output rose with contact chance, but in a nonlinear way. Models suggest brief contacts feed into slower bursts of gene activity in each cell.

The work also shows why boundary elements can block distant enhancers from reaching their genes. Stronger enhancers raised output and changed how well insulation worked. The authors offer general rules for how chromosome layout shapes long-range gene control.
europmc-pmc9284919:
Peiró-Mestres and co-authors track where monkeypox virus DNA shows up in patients during the 2022 outbreak. They tested 147 samples from 12 patients in Barcelona in May and June 2022. Samples came from saliva, semen, urine, feces, and nose, throat, and rectal swabs. Real-time PCR was used at several time points.

Virus DNA appeared in saliva from all 12 cases, sometimes at high levels. Rectal swabs were positive in 11 of 12 cases and nose-throat swabs in 10. Semen was positive in 7 of 9 cases tested. Urine and feces were also often positive. All patients were young adult men who have sex with men. The results widen what is known about shedding and spread.
europmc-pmc9674619:
Chen and co-authors review mutant p53 in cancer, from its molecular tricks to ways to strike it. The TP53 gene is the most often mutated gene in human cancers. Its normal job is to guard the genome as a tumor suppressor. Mutant forms lose that guard duty in full.

Many mutants gain fresh cancer aiding powers on top of the loss. About 80% of TP53 faults are single letter missense changes. They cluster in the part of the protein that grips DNA. The review sorts mutant types across cancer types. It then explains how mutants pile up inside cells. Gain of function feeds gene instability and tumor stemness. It also bends ferroptosis and the tumor setting. Clinic parts cover how mutants blunt chemo and radiation. Drug plans close the survey, from restoring normal shape to clearing the mutant.
europmc-pmc9950219:
Kaloni and co-authors review the BCL-2 protein family as a target for cancer therapy. Escape from cell death is a hallmark of cancer. BCL-2 family proteins control apoptotic death, the main self-destruct route. Tumors often raise pro-survival members or cut pro-death ones.

Both shifts block apoptosis and appear in many cancers. The review covers each family member's role in normal growth and body function. It shows how lost death control aids cancer growth and therapy resistance. Drugs called BH3-mimetics block pro-survival BCL-2 proteins. Their development as new cancer agents is discussed in detail. The authors frame the family as a rich source of drug targets. Readers get biology and therapy in one account.
faria-cause-sommeil-lucide-1819:
The Abbe Faria stated the suggestion theory in De la cause du sommeil lucide, printed in French in 1819. Lucid sleep, his name for the mesmeric trance, needs no magnetic fluid, he argues. The subject's own concentration raises the state. The operator's command guides it, but the power sits in the sleeper.

Faria had learned his method in India and tested it on Paris stages. His book studies the nature of man through this one strange door. Braid himself later cited Faria as a forerunner of true hypnosis. The French original is a precursor text of the whole field. It shifts the wonder from fluid to mind. Modern suggestion theory starts on its pages.
faria-sommeil-lucide-1819:
Abbe Faria explains lucid sleep without magnets in his treatise, Tome One, in French from 1819. Trance, he argues, springs from the subject's own mind, not from any fluid. The Goan priest, working in Paris, showed that expectation and a firm voice could induce the sleep he studied in his pupils.

His theory of suggestion came decades before the word grew famous. Braid later owned Faria as a forerunner of his own work on hypnotism. The book was cut short by its author's early death in Paris. It marks the birth of psychological hypnotism, the moment the marvel moved from the magnetizer's hands into the sleeper's mind.
fludd-utriusque-cosmi-vol-3-microcosmi-1:
The second tome of Fludd's history, from 1619, turns to the microcosm: man himself. Its long Latin title lists the supernatural, natural, and contrary sides of man's story. Fludd was a London doctor with a cosmic reach.

He traces the soul's fall, its powers, and its life in the body. Health and sickness get read as signs of inner order. Spirits and stars act on man in his scheme. The text is dense and diagram-rich in spirit. It forms the core of his claim that man sums up the whole world.
fludd-utriusque-cosmi-vol-4-microcosmi-s:
This 1619 section of Fludd's second tome treats the technical side of the microcosm. Its Latin title names it De Technica Microcosmi Historia. Fludd turns from man's soul to the arts man practices.

He covers skills from number and measure to war and craft. Each art is set inside his mirror scheme of world and man. The learning is wide, if the system strains at times. Engraved figures in the full edition aid the text. The section closes his survey of human art, and shows a Renaissance mind at full stretch.
fort-book-of-the-damned-1919:
Charles Fort spent years in newspaper files clipping wonders, and his first harvest came out in 1919. The Book of the Damned gathers rains of fish, falls of stones, strange lights, and folk who vanish. Fort calls such things damned because science shuts them out of its world.

His method is the pile: case on case, each clipped and cited, until doubt itself looks thin. His prose mocks the priests of science in a voice like no other writer's. The book founded the study of the strange that now bears his name, Forteana. It taught the world a new way to doubt its teachers.
friends-of-freedom-for-india-india-s-fre:
A New York support group issued this pamphlet in April 1919. It defends Indians and their American friends caught in wartime prosecutions. The lead cases are Sailendranath Ghose and Agnes Smedley. Both were arrested in New York in March 1918. Taraknath Das and Bhagwan Singh were already serving prison terms. Their offense was work for Indian freedom.

The pamphlet prints the charges under the Espionage Act. It says the defendants wrote letters to officials and ambassadors. Those letters asked that India's claim to freedom be heard. It also attacks warrantless raids and harsh questioning. The closing argument appeals to America's tradition of political asylum. Deportation, it warns, would make America serve foreign rulers.
frus-1861-d119:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton on 22 April 1861. Dayton was the new American minister to France, based in Paris. The letter is document 119 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Paris stood second only to London in the war's foreign stakes. The Emperor Napoleon III watched for a chance to favor the South. Seward's April letter set Dayton, a former senator, to guard that gate from the war's first days. Dayton had run for Vice President in 1856, which gave him rank in Paris talk. Rank in Paris talk opened doors that a plain envoy would have found barred.
frus-1861-d19:
On 21 October 1861, William H. Seward directed a fresh letter to Norman Judd in Berlin. The dispatch is document 19 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late October 1861 found Seward juggling crises on many fronts at once. His letters to Berlin formed one thread of a much wider web. In this one he directs his minister in Prussia, keeping the northern German court inside the Union's steady campaign against foreign aid to the South. The letter reached Berlin as the leaves fell, into a court deep in its own affairs. His brief from Washington was the same that month as in the spring: hold fast.
frus-1861-d219:
Another report crossed the ocean to Seward, this one from Mr. Marsh on 2 September 1861. It stands as Document 219 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d119:
On 4 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 119 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d19:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 14 February 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 19 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d219:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William Stuart a letter on 24 June 1862, printed as Document 219 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart led the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was absent that year.

Three letters in five days show the pace Seward set when business pressed. The matters at hand in such notes were often narrow: a seized ship, a detained man, a point of form. Yet each small case, handled badly, could feed the larger quarrel over Britain's part in the war. The Stuart letters repay reading as a set. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d319:
A Dayton report dated 8 August 1862 stands out of order as Document 319 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

This report duplicates the date of Document 301, and the pair shows how the legation's output could scatter in the printed volume. Both letters belong to the week Cedar Mountain was fought in Virginia. For the reader, matching the two restores the Paris post's full account of that week in the summer of 1862. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d419:
Horace J. Perry sent this report from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 May 1862. It is Document 419 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

In May 1862 the fall of New Orleans strengthened the Union's hand abroad, and agents like Perry used such news at court. Spain's stake was direct: Cuba's trade, the Gulf blockade, and the unraveling allied campaign in Mexico. A report from Madrid told Washington whether Spanish ministers leaned toward the Union, the Confederacy, or simple caution. Perry's letters are the raw feed behind Seward's answers to Madrid that season.
frus-1862-d519:
James Shepherd Pike reported from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 September 1862, the day of Antietam in far-off Maryland. The dispatch is Document 519 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Pike could know nothing of the battle as he wrote; his letter reflects the Netherlands as it stood on Dutch news alone. That innocence is part of the record's value. It shows what a friendly small power thought of the war at the very hinge of its fortunes. Victory claims and the emancipation order had not yet reset every calculation. Seward read the letter weeks later, in a changed world, as one more fixed point in his map of European opinion.
frus-1862-d619:
Bradford R. Wood, the American minister at Copenhagen, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 4 November 1862. It is Document 619 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Danish file's only printed report.

Wood's November letter gave Washington the Danish reading of the war in its second autumn. It covered the court's temper and the press. It also covered the maritime business between the two countries. A single report in a file of instructions is itself informative; Copenhagen needed little reporting because little there was in doubt. The dispatch completes the small Danish record for 1862. The record is a study in what much of the Union's diplomacy really was. It was the steady care of friendly, uncomplicated relationships.
frus-1862-d719:
Friedrich Hassaurek wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 October 1862. Hassaurek was the American minister in Ecuador, a German-born Ohio lawyer and writer. The letter is document 719 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Ecuador sat far down the Pacific coast, and its envoy's mail reached Washington slowly. Hassaurek reported on the land's politics and on the trade of its ports, where American ships called for goods. His letters were the State Department's main word from that coast. This dispatch is part of that thin but steady line, kept up by one man writing from Quito while his country fought at home.
frus-1863p1-d119:
On 16 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the first of four letters to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 119 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Four sheets in a day is another desk-clearing, smaller than the dozen of 2 March but of the same kind. Seward took the London file head by head, one point per page. This letter opens the set. The batch habit shows how the brief was run. It ran not by long essays, but by short, sharp notes an envoy could act on one at a time.
frus-1863p1-d19:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 December 1862. Adams was the American minister in London, writing on Christmas Eve. The letter is document 19 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A holiday date did not slow the legation's mail. Adams wrote through the season on the state of British feeling and the work of the South's friends in Europe. His calm, exact tone is part of why his file still reads well. This dispatch is a late-year piece of the London watch. It was sent while Washington waited for word of the new year and the freedom edict soon to come.
frus-1863p1-d219:
From his London post on 19 June 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 219 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d319:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 11 November 1862. The note is document 319 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Stuart served at the British legation in Washington and handled business with the State Department when the minister himself was away or occupied. His notes form part of the same Anglo-American exchange. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d419:
The American answer to London on 20 March 1863 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 419 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

The two men met and wrote constantly, and both knew a quarrel between their countries could hand the South its independence. That shared fear kept the tone correct even when the words were sharp. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d519:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 18 May 1863 letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid.
frus-1863p1-d619:
A dispatch dated 15 September 1863 went from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State to Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d119: On November 12, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, as both parties began their journeys east. His message is Document 119 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister traveled by way of Gibraltar and Malta, collecting talks as he went. The record supplies the date and the names and no subject. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the papers of the twin journeys.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d19: On July 15, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Stalin again, and the letter is Document 19 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Mid-July found the Red Army fighting the great tank battle at Kursk and the Western allies newly ashore in Sicily, though the record assigns this letter no subject. It belongs to the steady correspondence through which the two leaders, still strangers in person, arranged to meet at Tehran before the year ended.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d219:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt sent a second most-secret telegram from Ankara on 14 November 1943, number 1870, sent at six in the evening. It reports how Turkish foreign minister Numan Menemencioğlu handled questions from the German ambassador, Franz von Papen, about his Cairo talks with Eden.

Numan told von Papen that Eden had merely described the Moscow conference as a great success. Pressed, he denied any request for air bases but admitted Eden had sought Turkey's entry into the war, and he hid behind Turkey's unprepared state. Steinhardt adds that Ankara now feared a preventive Axis move, since the talks could not stay secret. German firms in Turkey, he adds, had been ordered to stop buying Turkish goods and ship out their stocks.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d319:
Soviet foreign commissar Vyacheslav Molotov sent Ambassador Averell Harriman an urgent, personal and secret telegram from Moscow on 25 November 1943. Delivered at Moscow the next day and forwarded to Harriman at Cairo by Navy channels, it answers Harriman's message about preparing the Tehran conference.

Molotov thanks Harriman for his message from Cairo. On the practical questions Harriman had raised, he gives one direction. General Connolly, the American commander in Tehran, may address himself to General Arkadiev. He may do so through the Soviet chargé d'affaires there, about coordinating the measures that interest him. Molotov closes with the hope of meeting soon and sends his most cordial greetings.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d419:
The Declaration on Iran, is dated 1 December 1943. It was signed at Tehran by Churchill, Stalin, and Roosevelt in that order. It is the three powers' formal statement on the country that hosted their conference. An editorial headnote traces the signed original's later path to the State Department.

The three governments recognize the help Iran has given against the common enemy, above all by carrying supplies from overseas to the Soviet Union. They admit the war has caused Iran special economic hardship, and promise such economic help as worldwide shortages of transport and goods allow. After the war, Iran's economic problems will receive full consideration alongside those of other United Nations members. The declaration closes with the three powers at one with Iran's government in desiring the maintenance of her independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, under the Atlantic Charter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d519:
Charles E. Bohlen of the Moscow embassy wrote this second memorandum on December 15, 1943. Bohlen had served as Roosevelt's Russian interpreter at Tehran a fortnight earlier and was one of the State Department's few true Soviet experts. The memorandum appears in the Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Bohlen's memoranda often preserved conversations and judgments that reached print nowhere else, because he was present where other Americans were not. A paper from mid-December belongs to the stocktaking after the summit, when officials wrote down what the new relationship with Moscow seemed to mean. Readers get a young diplomat's careful record, made before hindsight could tidy it.
frus-1944-quebec-d119:
Winston Churchill sent this personal, top-secret telegram, numbered 779, to President Roosevelt on September 4, 1944. Britain's War Cabinet was deeply disturbed by events in Warsaw. Stalin had refused to let Allied aircraft use Soviet airfields to supply the Polish fighters, and Churchill feared the wider damage to relations with Russia.

Churchill begged Roosevelt to let American aircraft drop supplies and land on Russian airfields without formal Soviet consent. The Russians, he argued, could hardly reject a finished act and might even welcome it. Britain would share full responsibility. He also warned that Warsaw's fall would destroy Premier Mikołajczyk's standing and his talks with the Lublin Committee.
frus-1944-quebec-d19:
Churchill sent another message to President Roosevelt on August 5, 1944. It came a day after his previous message. The State Department printed both letters. They sit in the pre-conference correspondence of the Quebec 1944 volume.

The first week of August 1944 moved faster than any plan. American armor was racing across France. The Red Army stood before Warsaw. Churchill wrote daily because the map changed daily. For readers, a second message in two days shows something clear. The Prime Minister was working hard to keep diplomacy level. He tried to match events that his own strategy had helped unleash.
frus-1944-quebec-d219:
An editors' note closes the zones story at Quebec. The Combined Chiefs' memorandum of September 16, 1944, was agreed by Roosevelt and Churchill later that day and folded into the final summary of conference conclusions as paragraphs 33 and 34. A map reflecting the decisions was prepared in Washington immediately afterward and sent to Ambassador Winant on September 21.

The note also marks what Quebec did not settle. The allocation of sectors inside Berlin had been left open by the London protocol of September 12, and no evidence has been found that the question was discussed at Quebec at all. Further Anglo-American negotiations led to the tripartite agreement signed in the European Advisory Commission on November 14, 1944.
frus-1945-50-intel-d119:
A draft letter from President Truman to Attorney General Clark is dated 7 August 1946. Drafts prepared for a president's signature show a decision being readied at the top. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The FBI answered to the attorney general, so a presidential letter to Clark was the heaviest paper that could enter the Latin American fight. That it survives as a draft is itself part of the story: drafts are where decisions can still be softened, delayed, or dropped. Readers should compare the draft with the authority's letter to Clark sent the next day. The two papers together show the White House and the board dividing the work of settling the dispute.
frus-1945-50-intel-d19:
Hoover wrote to Attorney General Clark on 27 September 1945, a week after the OSS order. The FBI director kept up a steady flow of paper to his chief through the autumn. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The dissolution of the OSS opened ground that Hoover meant the FBI to hold, above all in the Western Hemisphere. His letters after the order pressed the bureau's advantage while rivals regrouped. Readers can track a pattern across the Hoover papers: each one restates the bureau's claim in fresh terms for a fresh moment. This letter belongs to the first week of the new order of things, when the map of American intelligence lay open.
frus-1945-50-intel-d219: "Central Intelligence Group Memorandum" bears the date 21 July 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 219 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The bill that would create the CIA was in its last stages in Congress, and offices across Washington were getting ready. Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next.
frus-1945-50-intel-d319:
Minutes record the 10th Meeting of the National Intelligence Authority on 26 June 1947. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 319, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Congress was then debating the National Security Act, the law that would soon create the CIA and the National Security Council.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. They rarely give long speeches, but they fix the choices that later memos then carry out. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d419:
W. Park Armstrong sent a memo to Under Secretary of State James Webb on 6 March 1950. It is document 419 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950, one of several Armstrong papers in the file.

Armstrong headed the State Department's research and intelligence office under Secretary Dean Acheson. His memos to Webb brought the analysts' voice into the room where the department was run. Read with his other papers, this one shows a bureau chief pressing his office's worth, week after week. The March date places the memo in a season of fresh debate over the agency's future shape.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d119:
Military rule for a beaten Germany is spelled out in the directive enclosed with this 27 September 1944 instruction. The Secretary of State sends it to the American mission in London. It is for the ambassador's own guidance only. The covering note is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The directive goes to the supreme commander of the Allied forces in Europe. It covers the first weeks after fighting stops, before the three powers agree on a joint paper. The War and State Departments wrote it, and the Treasury agreed to it. A joint civil affairs board had not yet cleared it. The note is firm on one point: the paper is not to be laid before the European Advisory Commission.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d19: A week after winning a fourth term, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on 14 November 1944. The message stands as document 19 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. With the election settled, the president could plan openly for the winter summit, and this letter forms part of the renewed push toward fixing its date and agenda.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d219:
Stettinius laid the Soviet credit request before the President on 8 January 1945. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, gives Molotov's terms in one line and Harriman's judgment in three. Six billion dollars, thirty years, two and a half percent interest: those are the terms.

Harriman expects the subject to come up at the coming meeting. His views run as follows. It serves the United States to help the Soviet economy grow. The Russians should be given to understand that such help hangs on their conduct in world affairs. And talk of long-term credits should be kept wholly apart from the running Lend-Lease negotiations. The ambassador's full cable of comment came enclosed for the President to read.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d319:
Who sat at one conference luncheon, and what was said there, can no longer be fully known. This editorial note gathers the scraps. They come from pages of Secretary Stettinius's memoir, plus brief mentions in the books of James Byrnes and Admiral Leahy. Byrnes counted ten men at the table. Leahy and Stettinius named only eight.

The editors took the time and guest list from the official trip log, filled out by Stettinius's account. Even a lunch at Malta matters, because side talks there shaped what reached the formal table. The note shows the care taken to mark what is known and what is guessed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d419:
Unconditional surrender of Germany and Japan, at the earliest possible date, heads the Combined Chiefs' formal report of February 9, 1945. The report sums up the agreed conclusions of the Argonaut conference for Roosevelt and Churchill. Its first section states the overall objective in a single sentence.

The strategic concept follows in steps. In cooperation with Russia and other allies, Germany is to be forced to surrender first. At the same time, unremitting pressure against Japan is to be kept up and extended, with the other Pacific powers. The document is the alliance's war plan for its final year, signed off at the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d119:
Ambassador Harriman pressed his case to attend the Berlin meeting in a telegram to Charles Bohlen on July 4, 1945. The message is document 119 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. His earlier note to the Secretary of State had gone out just before Stettinius resigned, and Harriman had heard nothing back.

Harriman asks Bohlen to find that message and bring it to the new Secretary, James Byrnes. He points out that General Deane and the senior mission officers have been ordered to Berlin by the chiefs, and that the British ambassador has his instructions. He also assumes Edward Page will be needed to help with interpreting and the conference record, as at Yalta. He asks for an urgent reply.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d19:
The election will not interfere: Winant relayed Churchill's assurance to Truman from London on May 24, 1945. Talking with the Prime Minister that afternoon, Winant heard that the coming election would in no way block an early meeting with Truman and Stalin. If a meeting could be arranged by mid-June, or before July 5, Churchill would probably take Attlee with him.

Churchill added that there were no differences between him and Attlee on international relations. The short cable, sent by Army channels, cleared a political doubt from the summit's path. It also foreshadowed Potsdam, where Attlee would indeed sit beside Churchill — and then replace him mid-conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d219:
Ambassador Winant reported British alarm over an American announcement on Italy in an extract dated July 15, 1945. The extract is document 219 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full message appears later in the volume.

Winant was called to the Foreign Office that afternoon by an official named Harvey. Harvey was considerably disturbed about the Department's proposed announcement of July 17. That announcement concerned Italy and the World Security Organization. The British Embassy in Washington was being instructed to approach the Department and ask that the announcement be postponed. London wanted the question of Italy's future status discussed at the Big Three meeting first. The flare-up shows how even the timing of a press statement could open a rift between the allies.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d319:
James Dunn, Assistant Secretary of State, reported to the Secretary on July 14, 1945, after a long first talk at Potsdam with Sir Alexander Cadogan. The British Foreign Office chief had called that afternoon. For two hours the two men went over the conference agenda in a first, informal way.

The extracts printed here include the Balkans. Cadogan disagreed with Washington's reluctance to make peace with Bulgaria, Rumania, and Hungary. He repeated the British view that peace treaties would solve the allies' difficulties in those countries. The memo records the opening clash of the conference, before the heads of government had even sat down together.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d419:
Trade between Germany's zones is urged in a Joint Civil Affairs Committee memorandum on exchanging commodities. To use German resources best for German civilians, it says, inter-zonal exchange is essential. Germany as a whole is self-sufficient in vital supplies such as food and coal, but the zones themselves are lopsided.

The Russian zone, often called Germany's bread basket, grows the food. The American, British, and French zones together form a food deficit area. The British zone holds the rich Ruhr coal fields, yet lacks the pit props to work them. The American zone has no coal assets at all. The memo makes the economic case for treating Germany as one unit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d519:
The German-Polish frontier is the fourth topic in Dunn's extracts of his July 14, 1945 talk with Cadogan at Potsdam. Cadogan referred to the great economic problems raised by the Poles' territorial claims. They touched, in particular, supplying food from eastern Germany and coal from Silesia. He handed Dunn a statement of the British view on Poland's western frontier.

The British, the statement says, are willing to see several lands pass under permanent Polish administration now. They are East Prussia, Danzig, and the most eastern part of Pomerania, though not as far as the Oder River. Upper Silesia is included as well. If Russia insisted upon a larger area going to Poland, the statement adds, she should accept a proportionate adjustment to balance it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d619:
Minutes of the Combined Policy Committee, meeting at the Pentagon on July 4, 1945, are document 619 here. The top secret extracts record a 9:30 a.m. session chaired by Secretary of War Stimson. Present sat Field Marshal Wilson for Britain, C. D. Howe, and Vannevar Bush. General Groves and Sir James Chadwick sat in by invitation.

One item stands out in the extracts. Wilson stated that the British government agreed to the use of the T. A. weapon against Japan. He added that Churchill might wish to raise the matter with the President at Berlin. The committee noted that both governments had now agreed, with London's consent passed through Wilson. A further item took up what the two governments should disclose about the weapon's use. Stimson, the extracts show, had the coming meeting with Stalin in mind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1019:
Samuel Rosenman, the President's special counsel, reported to the Secretary of State on August 1, 1945, after a call from Robert Jackson. Jackson was America's chief counsel for war crimes. A London meeting on the trials had been put off a day, since the Lord Chancellor had to attend the opening of Parliament.

Jackson's views were firm on two points. The conference should refuse to name any war criminals, and should not pledge itself here to an international tribunal. He now doubts a joint court can work smoothly with the Russians. If Moscow rejects the American terms in London, he would let each nation try its own prisoners instead.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1119:
From Rome, Ambassador Kirk wrote again to the Acting Secretary of State on 18 July 1945. His reports came in a near daily rhythm during the Potsdam weeks. Each one added fresh detail from the ground in Italy.

Kirk's subject was a country in flux. Italy had a new government, a beaten army, and a future that the summit would help to fix. Washington read his cables to keep its Italian policy grounded in fact. This dispatch is one beat in that drumbeat of reporting. On its own it is routine; in sequence, the cables built the picture the talks relied on.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1219:
The Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 28 July 1945. Outgoing word from the secretary set the line for the China post. It went out in the summit's last week, while the secretary's own days were filled with the German talks.

A secretary's cable to an envoy joins two files at once: the sender's talks and the reader's post. Hurley needed the summit's drift to do his work in China. This message supplied the chief's word straight from Potsdam. It is the return half of the Hurley channel, matching the ambassador's own reports printed nearby.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1319:
Pauley wrote to the Secretary of State on 20 July 1945. His reparations reports went to both the president and the chief envoy that week. The commission's work in Moscow and Germany fed straight into the summit's central money fight.

What Germany would pay, in what form, and from which zones were the questions Pauley's facts had to answer. His note to Byrnes put that evidence in the negotiator's own hands. This message is the reparations thread at the working level of the talks. It shows the expert and the bargainer joined, one day into the hardest part of the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1419:
A second memorandum by Charles Bohlen, also dated 28 March 1960, accompanies the Yalta texts at the back of the Potsdam volume. Bohlen knew the Soviet leaders and their language as few Americans did. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Two memoranda from the same day by the same hand suggest a man clearing his desk of a subject that would not leave him. Yalta had become a political charge in America by 1960, blamed by some for the cold war itself. Bohlen, who had taken notes and translated at the talks, answered from memory and record. His pair of papers closes the volume on a note of reflection rather than decision.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-119:
Dated July 26, 1945, this memorandum came from the United States delegation as the Potsdam Conference entered its second week. Delegation memos served many masters. Some carried facts upward. Others spread a settled line sideways across the team. This one was kept in the conference files and printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

By July 26 the shape of the endgame was emerging, though much stayed contested. A staff memo from that day catches knowledge mid-stream. Readers can test it against the formal record of the plenary talks. The paper adds staff-level truth to a story often told from the top alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-19:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the July 18, 1945 plenary session give the press debate in the speakers' own words. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Cohen's record runs parallel to Thompson's minutes of the same session.

Churchill contrasts the three wartime summits on press access. At Tehran there were no journalists, at Yalta few, but here they are all about. Molotov asks where they are, and Churchill explains they stand outside the compound. He offers to address them as a newspaper man on the need for secrecy. Truman declines the offer in a few flat sentences. Each team has a press representative here, so let them handle it, and no communication will issue until the conference ends. Most of them are Americans anyway, he adds. The session then turns to business.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d719:
A second Hurley letter to the Secretary of State bears the date July 31, 1945, as document 719. Two cables from Chungking in one day mark a busy channel. The exchange sits in the second Potsdam volume, among the closing papers of the conference. Hurley's post in China kept him close to the Pacific war's endgame.

Back-to-back letters let readers follow a topic in motion. A point raised in one may be pressed in the next. The pair shows the tempo of wartime diplomacy by cable. It also shows trust: the Secretary dealt with his ambassador directly, at speed, while greater matters filled his days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d819:
Cannon wrote from Lisbon to Matthews, the director of European affairs, on July 26, 1945. Document 819 continues the Portugal thread in the Potsdam volume. The first secretary at the Lisbon embassy reported to his Department chief. The letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Reports from Lisbon carried the scent of a neutral crossroads. Spies, traders, and envoys all passed through Portugal. Cannon sorted the talk for Washington. Readers see the summit's world extending to Europe's quiet corner. The document shows that even uninvolved capitals fed the great powers' picture in the summer of decision.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d919:
The American reparations team in Moscow sent Edwin Pauley these East Prussia figures on July 24, 1945. Pauley had asked for values in his cable of July 23. The telegram gives two areas: East Prussia as a whole, and the part north of the Goldap-Braunsberg line. All sums are 1938 Reichsmarks.

Factory and mining assets came to 260 million Reichsmarks for the whole area, and 160 million for the northern part. Movable assets were 170 million and 100 million. Farm assets dwarf both figures, at about one billion for the whole area. Its farm output also ran near one billion, about 7 percent of the old Reich.
frus-1955-57v19:
National security policy fills Volume XIX of the 1955–1957 set in a single broad block. Basic policy, threat studies, posture, and weapons growth run together. Missile programs take long sections, with Atlas, Titan, Thor, and Jupiter in the mid-sample.

Home and civil defense, overseas bases, and the defense budget fill the rest. Staff papers weigh science and skill as arms in themselves. The record catches the shift to a missile age. Each program's cost and date was argued in these files before metal flew. A 1957 decision set the first test dates in these files.
frus-1961-63v19:
South Asia fills Volume XIX of the 1961–1963 set, in a single run of Documents 1–351. India leads the record, with aid on a vast scale. Pakistan follows, armed and wary, its Afghan border dispute in the files.

China's 1962 border war with India splits the volume's world. Arms rushed to Delhi strain the Pakistan tie at once. Bowles and Harriman missions thread through the cables. The papers show two clients pulling one patron apart. Each grant to one was read as a loss by the other, and priced as such. The China war's shock runs through the volume's later cables.
frus-1964-68v19:
The Arab-Israeli crisis and war of 1967 fill Volume XIX of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964-1968. The first chapter covers the prewar crisis from May 15 to June 4, 1967. The next covers the six days of war. Two long chapters follow the postwar diplomacy through the fall. They end with the adoption of UN Security Council Resolution 242 in November 1967.

The documents include cables, memos, and records of talks at the highest level. They show Washington working to stop the fighting and then to shape a settlement. Hotline exchanges with Moscow appear in the war chapters. The volume is the core U.S. record of the Six-Day War.
frus-1977-80v19:
South Asia fills Volume XIX of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1977-1980. A short regional section opens the volume. Sections then cover Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. Pakistan takes by far the largest share, with documents 230 through 471. India follows with documents 59 through 214. The Pakistan papers deal with its nuclear program, aid cutoffs, and the Soviet war next door in Afghanistan after 1979.

The India papers trace a cooler tie, with sharp press exchanges during Soviet visits noted in one cable. Food aid and development fill the Bangladesh section. The volume shows the region remade by the Afghan war.
gao-gaoreports-b-297219:
Charter Environmental protested a Forest Service award for mine clean work in GAO decision B-297219, dated December 5, 2005. The low bidder was ECI Northeast. The site was the Ore Hill Mine Site in New Hampshire. The work was to fix and clear mine waste. The call set a hard test of three like past jobs.

GAO sustained the protest in part and denied it in part. The agency counted jobs of the parent firm alone. The parent gave no pledge to back the low firm's work. That count was wrong. Past jobs of a parent need a pledge to count. Other bid flaws claimed did not hold. Forms and a sign-up step could be fixed later.
gao-gaoreports-b-305919:
