Foreign staff in money roles are the subject of this GAO decision, B-305919, dated March 27, 2006. The Defense Department uses local hires at posts abroad. A certifying officer in Europe asked if such hires could serve as Departmental Accountable Officials. Those officials answer for fiscal errors on the job. Treaties may shield local hires from U.S. law.

GAO held that the department may use funds for such hires in these roles. The law at 10 U.S.C. section 2773a allows the posts. The lack of personal liability under U.S. law does not bar the hire. But GAO urged a written policy. The policy should state when local hires may fill the roles. The ruling guides posts that staff money jobs abroad.
gao-gaoreports-b-307319:
Fees for special use of national parks are mapped in this GAO decision, B-307319, dated August 23, 2007. The National Park Service charges fees for some park uses. Two laws let it set such fees. One is the Independent Offices Appropriations Act of 1952. The other is section 3a of title 16. Users may gain goods, services, or access from the parks.

GAO held the Service may price by market value in business-like deals. It may not charge twice for the same costs. A two-part fee fails if one part tracks market value and one tracks costs. Cash past real costs goes to the Treasury. Or the Service may price to costs alone and keep that cash.
gao-gaoreports-b-310119:
HERA Constructive S.A. lost its protest — GAO decision B-310119, dated November 7, 2007. The Navy sought work on its Navy Exchange shops at Souda Bay in Crete, Greece. The award went to Michael M. Tsontos S.A. The call asked for a Greek state paper. The paper had to clear the firm for jobs of like cost, type, and size.

HERA said the winner's paper fell short of that bar. GAO denied the protest. The agency read the call term in a fair way when it took the paper. A fair read of a term binds the race. Losers must show the read was off, not just tight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-119:
Medicare Physician Fees, GAO-05-119 of March 11, 2005, tests how Medicare shifts doctor pay by place. Three cost scores raise or lower fees in each area. They track doctor work, office costs, and malpractice costs. Where scores fall below the U.S. mean, fees fall too. Rural doctors say that cut is unfair.

A 2003 law told GAO to judge the method. GAO finds the design of the scores sound. The data and the math behind them need polish, it adds. The report also weighs how the scores sway doctor pay, where doctors set up shop, and how they are hired and kept.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-219:
Adult Drug Courts, GAO-05-219 of February 28, 2005, weighs proof on a court plan born in the late 1980s. Drug courts put drug-case defendants in treatment under a judge's close eye. The aim is to cut repeat crime and drug use. Courts spread fast across the nation. Proof of their worth stayed weak and mixed for years.

Law told GAO to judge the proof. GAO sifted past studies and kept 27 sound ones, on 39 courts. It checked repeat crime, drug relapse, and how many finish the plan. It checked costs next to gains. Repeat crime fell; the rest came out mixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-719:
Federal aid to Alaska Native villages is the subject of GAO-05-719, a report dated August 2, 2005. Congress directed the review under the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2004. GAO counted aid for fiscal years 1998 through 2003. It also traced how selected funds were used. And it gathered data on homes built by villages and regional housing bodies.

GAO found that villages and regional Native nonprofits got over $3 billion in that span. About $483 million went to 216 villages. About $3 billion went to 33 regional nonprofits. The Department of Health and Human Services gave 63 percent of all funding. Funds paid for health care, housing, and water and sewer work, among other services. Readers get a full map of where the money went.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-819:
Military airlift loads are measured in GAO-05-819, dated September 29, 2005. Airlift is flexible but costly. From September 2001 to April 2005, the Defense Department spent about $9.5 billion on it for two wars. Airlift moved about 13 percent of cargo and passengers. GAO asked whether planes flew as full as they could. The study ran under the Comptroller General's own authority.

GAO found the airlift command does not track load factors in a usable way. It logs tons moved, but not the weather, runway, and other facts that shape each load. So leaders cannot tell how often planes flew near full. By GAO's math, over 97 percent of C-5 flights and over 81 percent of C-17 flights carried less than planning norms. Missing data blocks a firm verdict, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-119:
The National Flood Insurance Program and its management by the Federal Emergency Management Agency are examined in GAO-06-119, dated October 18, 2005. Private insurers sell the program's policies and adjust its claims. A private contractor helps FEMA run the program. After Hurricane Isabel hit in 2003, Congress ordered this review. GAO studied coverage limits, FEMA's monitoring, the agency's answer to complaints over Isabel claims, and its work on the 2004 reform act.

Coverage caps leave many owners short. A home worth more than $250,000 cannot be insured to full replacement cost. FEMA's checks on the 95 participating insurers lacked a sound sampling method, so results could not be projected. After Isabel, a FEMA task force reviewed 2,294 claims. Almost half of those owners won extra payments, averaging $3,300 more. Key 2004 reforms, such as a claims handbook and an appeals process, were still unfinished.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-219:
The Pentagon's business overhaul gets a progress grade in GAO-06-219, a report dated November 23, 2005. For years the Defense Department has tried to modernize its business systems. The 2005 defense law told it to build a clear business enterprise architecture and transition plan by September 30, 2005. The law also demanded sound structures for judging tech investments. GAO checked the department's compliance on each point. It made no new recommendations, since past ones still stand.

The title sums up a split result. Real progress shows in the base architecture products and in investment review habits. Much work remains before the plan hangs together. The department praised GAO's role in its transformation. It disputed two points: how complete its current-state architecture is, and where the plan fails to link up. It also pledged to fix the base causes GAO named. The report marks a milepost in a long reform.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-519:
A distant ocean disaster raised a direct question: could a tsunami hit U.S. coasts? Dated June 5, 2006, GAO-06-519 reviews U.S. tsunami preparedness. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration leads detection and warning work. It partners with federal and state agencies in a hazard mitigation program. In 2005, Congress added $17.24 million to strengthen these efforts. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami prompted the review.

GAO names coastal areas facing the greatest hazard. It judges the federal warning system's effectiveness. It describes work to reduce harm in coastal communities. It also assesses long-range planning. Partners collaborate well, GAO found, but big challenges remain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-819:
Rail and transit grants are in flux, GAO reports in GAO-06-819, a report dated August 30, 2006. A 2005 surface transportation law gave about $7.9 billion in commitment authority through fiscal year 2009 to the New Starts program. The Federal Transit Administration uses it to pick fixed guideway projects, such as rail lines, and sign full funding agreements. GAO described the program's state during this shift.

GAO found that the agency proposed five new projects for funding agreements. It requested $1.47 billion for the program in fiscal year 2007. The agency also proposed nine procedural changes and adopted four after hearing from the transit field. The new law added fresh evaluation criteria and a Small Starts program for smaller projects. GAO portrays a grant program mid-transition, with rules still settling.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1019:
Data security at the Department of Veterans Affairs is pressed again in GAO report GAO-07-1019, dated September 7, 2007. In May 2006 gear holding data on about 26.5 million veterans and active troops was stolen. Trust in the agency's care of private facts took a hard hit.

GAO asked if the agency had met past security advice, from GAO and its own inspector general. It traced agency steps since May 2006 to firm up security and guard private data. It tested coding tools at picked sites. Lasting gains, GAO said, need steady top-level drive and watch. The report is a post-theft audit with a long memory.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-119:
U.S. island territories face deep money and audit strain, GAO reports in GAO-07-119, dated December 12, 2006. The areas are American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Their economies rest on narrow bases, and shifts in tax and trade law hit them hard.

GAO named the economic hurdles each government faces. It graded each one's fiscal state. It checked their money answerability, with the Single Audit Act in view. That act covers bodies that get $500,000 or more a year in federal funds. The report gives Congress one shared picture of four small governments, and the long strain each carries.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-219:
Hurricanes Katrina and Rita drove over 1 million people from their homes. GAO studied how benefit programs coped in GAO-07-219, issued February 7, 2007. The programs cover Social Security, disability aid, food stamps, jobless benefits, and family aid. Some are run by federal staff and others by states. GAO reviewed plans and spoke with officials in five states. The question was how ready each program was for disaster.

Demand for food stamps and jobless aid rose sharply, GAO found. Social Security and disability aid saw fewer new claims. They faced heavy demand to replace lost or missed checks instead. Federal programs had disaster plans and could shift staff nationwide. State programs varied widely in readiness. Two states had required office visits to file jobless claims. Looser rules sped aid but raised the risk of improper payments. GAO urged better planning and shared lessons.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-319:
Senior health researchers must step back from decisions that touch their own interests, but the rulebook contradicts itself. GAO reviewed the recusal rules in GAO-07-319, issued April 30, 2007. The study covers the National Institutes of Health. It focuses on the cancer and allergy institutes, the two largest. GAO checked how senior staff learn the rules. It also checked guidance for outside grant reviewers.

The manual gives senior staff mixed orders, GAO found. One part says a recusal must be written. Another says it may be written. Notice to supervisors flips the same way. Staff could follow either text and reach opposite practice. Reviewer guidance is firmer. Forms spell out conflict cases before review groups meet. Staff brief reviewers aloud at first sessions. Review managers watch the meetings for fair play. GAO urged one clear written rule for senior staff.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-519:
States band together through compacts to share rivers and land, and GAO-07-519, issued April 3, 2007, maps how those pacts are run. Interstate compacts settle questions that cross state lines, such as splitting river water. Some pacts create a joint body, often called a commission, to run them. Congress must consent to pacts that shift power between states and Washington. The Tahoe Regional Planning Compact is one such case.

GAO reviewed 59 congressionally approved environment and natural resource compacts. It surveyed the 45 that have commissions. The report sets out their structures, powers, and ways to settle fights. It also covers how each body answers to the public. Worries raised about some commissions get a hearing. Tahoe's agency is then weighed against its peers. The study serves lawmakers who must bless the next pact.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-919:
Trade aid for laid-off workers is studied in GAO-07-919, dated June 29, 2007. Trade Adjustment Assistance trains workers hurt by foreign trade. The Labor Department must certify each layoff group first. From fiscal years 2004 to 2006, it approved 4,700 of 7,100 petitions. That is a 66 percent approval rate. Decisions averaged 32 days against a 40-day limit. Most denials involve workers who made no product. Congress weighs certifying whole industries at once. GAO tested two industry-based designs.

Broader eligibility would follow, GAO found, but design hurdles are real. One design needs three certified petitions in 180 days. Another ties relief to trade remedy findings. Each would sweep in workers the current test misses. Each raises questions about proof and fairness. Petition approvals fell 17 percent over the three years. Appeals reversed about a third of appealed denials. GAO made no recommendations this time. The report hands Congress the trade-offs with data attached.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-219:
Traveler inspections at entry ports are examined in full in GAO report GAO-08-219 (November 5, 2007). Customs officers guard 326 air, sea, and land ports. In 2006, they turned away over 200,000 people who sought entry illegally. They seized over 600,000 pounds of illegal drugs and more than 40,000 fake documents. Still, GAO found weak spots in the work.

Inspection steps and site layouts leave gaps that dangerous people could use. Staffing and training strain the corps as well. GAO set out four actions to tighten controls. This public version drops material the security department classed as sensitive. A testimony twin presents the same findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-319:
Federal reporting of advisory and assistance services is examined in GAO report GAO-08-319, issued March 31, 2008. Since 1994, the Office of Management and Budget has had to collect and report these costs in the President's budget. GAO reviewed 334 contract files across 10 agencies to test whether the figures were sound and how the contracts were used.

GAO found the reported figures so flawed as to be meaningless, and neither agencies nor OMB used them to manage. Nearly 20 percent of the contract actions reviewed were wrongly coded as advisory and assistance services. Causes included a broad legal definition, uneven reporting methods, and budget and buying systems that did not share data. GAO suggested Congress re-evaluate the need for separate reporting and, if more insight is wanted, clarify the definition.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-519:
Enterprise architecture programs in the military departments are graded in GAO report GAO-08-519, dated May 12, 2008. The Defense Department has been a high-risk area for business systems modernization since 1995. Congress ordered a corporate business enterprise architecture to guide its system spending.

None of the three departments has reached maturity. Air Force, Navy, and Army programs all sit at Stage 1 of GAO's five-stage maturity framework. They have not fully built the management foundation of Stage 2, let alone the later stages of building and using an architecture. The Air Force leads by a wide margin, nearly satisfying Stages 2 and 3 in full. The Navy outranks the Army. GAO repeated its old advice and urged the Navy and Army to learn from the Air Force. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-619:
Big weapons cost more and arrive later than promised, year after year. GAO-08-619, dated July 2, 2008, looks at one root cause: how the Department of Defense funds new weapon programs. The current set of major weapons is set to cost $1.6 trillion to build and buy.

GAO found most programs start without the full funds their plans call for. Costs then outrun the budget plan, and the department shifts money between programs, delays bills, or cuts the number of weapons bought. GAO said funding should rest on solid knowledge of cost and design before a program starts. That way, budgets match real needs and fewer programs fail.
gems-of-chinese-verse-1919:
Tang dynasty verse fills Gems of Chinese Verse, Englished by W. J. B. Fletcher in 1919. Du Fu and Li Bai stand among its poets, the twin peaks of China's golden age. Moonlit rivers, frontier posts, and dawn farewells supply its scenes.

Fletcher, an early English voice for Chinese poetry, prized clarity and music in his versions. Brief lyrics carry vast feeling in a few exact images. Soldiers, exiles, wives, and wanderers all speak in turn. The anthology gives new readers a fine first path into a refined art, one that shaped verse across East Asia for a thousand years and more.
georgian-poetry-1918-19:
Peace had come when Edward Marsh made this fourth volume of Georgian Poetry, dated September 1919 and dedicated to Thomas Hardy. Marsh hopes the book shows that peace has not hurt the writing of good poems. The contents lead off with Lascelles Abercrombie, Gordon Bottomley, and Francis Brett Young, among many others.

Poems are drawn from a wide range of journals, from the Athenaeum to the Westminster Gazette. The mood shifts from war grief toward fields, seasons, and quiet rooms, though the war is never far off. By this point the Georgian manner was well known and much debated. The volume lets a reader judge the school at its settled height, in the first year after the guns stopped.
hesse-demian-1919:
Hermann Hesse published Demian in 1919, his novel of awakening, first issued under the name Emil Sinclair. Emil Sinclair's journey from bourgeois innocence to selfhood under Demian's spell made the book the voice of German youth. Hesse, broken by war and analysis, wrote it in three weeks of 1917 as a confession.

Sinclair, a schoolboy, is blackmailed by Kromer over a lie and rescued by the uncanny Max Demian. Demian teaches him to read Cain's mark as a sign of the elect, not a brand of shame. War takes both to the front, where Demian dies, promising to live on inside the friend he shaped. Abraxas, the god who is both good and evil, names the wholeness Sinclair must grow toward in Hesse's creed of selfhood. The novel's influence on young readers, from 1919 to the counterculture, is hard to overstate.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle titled book nineteen of his Frederick the Great with a warning: Friedrich Like to Be Overwhelmed in the Seven Years War. Volume nineteen covers 1759 and 1760, the war's darkest stretch for Prussia. Carlyle opens by mapping five armies in winter quarters, a chain of posts from Bohemia to the Rhine holding some 300,000 men.

Eleven great battles had already been fought, from Lobositz to Hochkirch, and more were coming. Carlyle writes of a king keeping up bright hopes while enemies closed in on every side. Defeat in these years nearly ended Prussia. The volume's mood is siege-like: endurance, luck, and stubbornness against heavy odds.
hoffmann-serapion-brethren-vol1-1819:
The Serapion Brethren is E. T. A. Hoffmann's great cycle of tales, first published in German from 1819. Alexander Ewing translated volume one into English in 1886. A circle of friends meets to tell stories, debate them, and judge each tale by the vivid sight of its teller.

Inside the frame, tales of artists, madmen, automata, and ghosts unfold in turn. The Nutcracker story and tales of the singer Antonia are among the treasures here. Hoffmann blends music, dream, and terror with a craftsman's care. The frame talks give the book a second pleasure: friends arguing over what makes a story true. Volume one sets the pattern for the whole cycle.
hoffmann-serapion-brethren-vol2-1819:
Volume two of The Serapion Brethren completes Hoffmann's story cycle in Alexander Ewing's English, issued in 1892. The friends of the frame meet again, and the tales grow stranger as the evenings pass. Singers, goldsmiths, doubles, and haunted houses take their turns in the talk.

Hoffmann saves some of his richest inventions for these later nights. Music keeps its central place, as both bliss and curse for those who serve it. The arguments between tales sharpen, too, testing fancy against fact. Ewing's two volumes together give English readers the full cycle. The work remains the model for the nineteenth-century tale collection, frame and all.
i-was-there-with-the-yanks-on-the-wester:
Cyrus Leroy Baldridge served as a private in the American force in France, and this 1919 book holds his sketches from the front. Verses by Hilmar R. Baukhage, also a private, sit beside the art. Scenes are dated and placed, from Seicheprey to a Belgian town on the day the war ended.

Short poems and captions give the daily side of service. Soldiers wait in line, warm canned food over small fires, and stand guard in mud and rain. The tone mixes humor with grief for the dead. It is a plain record by men who were there.
irish-declaration-independence-1919:
Ireland's Declaration of Independence was adopted by Dail Eireann, the Irish parliament that met in Dublin in January 1919. The hosted text is the short declaration in full. It builds its case in a chain of whereas clauses. The Irish people, it says, are by right a free people. English rule rests on force and fraud. The republic promised in 1916 still stands.

The declaration points to the election of December 1918 as proof of the people's will. In that vote, Irish electors gave a huge majority to Sinn Fein. It declares the Irish Republic in force and calls on every free nation to recognize it. Britain refused, and the Irish War of Independence began the same day the Dail first met.
irving-sketch-book-1819:
Washington Irving published The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon in 1819, writing under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon. Irving was an American author living in England, and his sketches move between the two countries. Two tales in the volume soon became famous across the English-speaking world.

One tale sends Rip Van Winkle to sleep in the Catskill hills for twenty years. Another follows schoolmaster Ichabod Crane on his night ride past the Headless Horseman. Gentle essays on English country life and Christmas customs fill out the rest of the book. The Sketch Book proved that an American writer could win a wide audience at home and abroad.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-19:
Open war reaches the St. Lawrence itself in Volume 19, from 1898. Thwaites turns the annual Relations toward Quebec and the Hurons under attack. The Iroquois strike at the heart of the French colony.

Sieges, raids, and captive-taking fill report after anxious report. Priests write through fear with their usual plain, direct style. Martyrs are made, and their deaths are told without flourish. The black robes serve as war reporters as much as pastors here. Their calm prose makes the terror of those years feel close and real. Duty holds firm even when safety is gone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-benja:
Aaron ben Benjamin Wolf, rabbi at Berlin and at Frankfort on the Oder, is treated in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. Born about 1670, he died at Frankfort on July 25, 1721. His uncle Jost Liebman, the court Jew, founded a Talmud school for him and supported his students. In 1697 Aaron was made rabbi of the mark, and in 1709 chief rabbi of Berlin.

King Frederick the First's death changed his fortunes, the entry reports. His wife's family fell from favor, funds failed, and faction in the Berlin congregation wore him down. He left Berlin for Frankfort, where he served until death. None of his works was printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abarim-the-part: Abarim is a term used for the edge of the Moabite plateau. From its chief headland, Mount Nebo, the western part of Judea could be plainly seen. The entry cites Jeremiah, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Ezekiel for the name. A Midrash note adds a curious point. The mountain, it says, bore four names in all: Abarim, Hor, Nebo, and the Heights of Pisgah. It stood on the borders of four kingdoms, and each one claimed it and named it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abbas-samuel-ab:
Samuel ibn Abbas, son of Judah ibn Abbas of Fez, lived in the twelfth century. He studied philosophy, mathematics, and medicine, and traveled for study in Irak, Syria, Azerbaijan, and Kohistan. At Maragha he claimed two visions in which Mohammed came to him. He then took up Islam, under the name Samau'al Yaḥya al-Maghrabi.

His attack on his old faith, "Ifham al-Yahud," argues that the Law can be set aside. It claims that Jesus and Mohammed are both foretold in Genesis, and that the Jews hold the Torah of Ezra, not of Moses. The work had no sway on Jewish writing, the entry says. A later tract was still built on it in the fifteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abel-cheramim-s: Abel-cheramim is named only in Judges, chapter 11, verse 33. It was the place where Jephthah halted in his chase and slaughter of the Ammonites. Eusebius and Jerome place it six or seven Roman miles from Philadelphia, that is, Rabbath-Ammon. The entry is plain about the limit of that clue. The exact modern site can not be fixed from it. One point of color is added. In the time of Eusebius the place was still noted for its vineyards.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abin-ben-tanhum: Abin ben Tanḥum bar Terifon was a Palestinian scholar known for one curious piece of counting. He tries to prove a set point from a verse of Genesis. The verse says that a soul shall be cut off from his people. By his reckoning, that phrase means an early death. The death, he holds, comes before the end of the fiftieth year of a man's age. The entry cites the Jerusalem Talmud, on Bikkurim, as the source for this single teaching under his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-dav: Abraham ben David of Ostrog, in Volhynia, was a commentator who flourished about 1500. He wrote a work called Furnace for Gold, a commentary on the Targumim to the Pentateuch. Some writers also credit him with a treatise on the thirteen rules of Rabbi Ishmael for reading Scripture. That treatise was published at Canterbury in 1597 by Philip Ferdinand, a converted Jew. The entry gives no life dates beyond his time of activity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abrahams-nicola:
Nicolai Christian Levin Abrahams was a Danish scholar and professor of French language and literature at the University of Copenhagen. He was born at Copenhagen on Sept. 6, 1798 and died there on Jan. 25, 1870. He entered the university in 1815 and took a law degree in 1818.

He was one of twelve Danes who sent a literary challenge to the author Baggesen over his attack on Oehlenschläger. After four years of travel he wrote a thesis on Wace's Roman de Brut. He became lector of French in 1829 and professor in 1832, after baptism. He retired in 1857 to become a notary public. His books include a study of French manuscripts at Copenhagen, from 1844.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acceptance-719:
Acceptance, in law, is the yes one side gives to an offer from the other. In trade the hard case is the time bargain. Two sides agree to buy goods by kind or amount at a set time to come. The goods are not yet picked out. Talmudic law holds such deals void. No man may sell what he does not yet own.

A fisher may not sell his next haul. A son may not sell his share in a dying father's goods. The sages still warn that God will punish a man who breaks his word. The entry then turns to change of title in a sale. It asks when buyer and seller are both bound. Last, it takes up a wife's receipt of a writ of divorce. It weighs when that writ takes full effect, with or without an agent's hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-helene-81: Helene Adler was a German teacher and writer. She was born at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1849. Her birth house was the house where Ludwig Börne was born. She finished at the Wiesbaden Women's College in 1867. For fifteen years she taught in the school of the Frankfort Orphan Asylum. From 1882 she gave her time to books alone. Her works take in poems of 1882 and a treatise on training that same year. An essay on the training of orphans came in 1885, and more poems in 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aix-la-chapelle:
Aix-la-Chapelle, or Aachen, is a city in Rhenish Prussia. A Jewish settlement flourished there under the Roman empire. In Carolingian times a colony of Jews lived near the royal palace. In 802 Isaac entered the city in state. He had gone with Charlemagne's envoys to the calif Harun-al-Raschid.

In 1227 the emperor gave the Jews as a fief to Count Wilhelm of Julich. Converts from Judaism appear in church records of the next century. The expulsion of 1629 cost the city 136 gold guilders in yearly taxes. Six Jews were let back in 1667, against the council's protest. A cemetery was bought in 1851 and a new synagogue built in 1860. In 1900 the city held 2,100 Jewish residents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-al-tabib-abraha: Abraham al-Tabib was a Spanish physician who lived in Castile. His years fall in the first half of the fourteenth century. He was a contemporary of Abraham ibn Zarzal. Zarzal was physician to Don Pedro the Cruel, king of Castile. Al-Tabib wrote a supercommentary on Abraham ibn Ezra's work on the Pentateuch. In it he often takes issue with Solomon Franco and Franco's own supercommentary. His work has never been printed, and it survives only in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexa-or-lexa-1:
Alexa, or Lexa, is the name of two figures in this entry. The first was a foreign jurist of the third century. He debated a point of law with the Palestinian amora Mana II. The question was how to collect a disputed debt when the debtor is away. His own courts, he said, gave judgment at once. If the debtor later disproved the claim, the judgment fell.

Mana answered that Palestine did much the same, with safeguards. A crier gave thirty days' notice, on Mondays and Thursdays. If the man was far off, three more notices went out, each thirty days apart. Scholars divide on who Alexa was: a Babylonian amora, says one; a Gentile judge, says another. The second Alexa was an amora of the third generation. A Halakah is reported in his name, and he may be the same man as Alexandri II.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-algazi-yom-tob-: Yom-Tob ben Israel Jacob Algazi was a commentator who lived at Jerusalem. He worked in the eighteenth century. He wrote notes on a work by Nahmanides. That work deals with laws on the first-born. His notes came out at Leghorn in 1794. The entry adds one point of doubt. Some readers credit him with a second book. Most assign that book to his father.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amon-1419: Amon is a name borne by two men in the Bible books. The first Amon ruled Samaria under King Ahab. Ahab gave the prophet Micaiah into his hands. Micaiah had foretold ill luck for the king in war. The second use is not one man at all. It names the children of Amon in a long list. That list counts those who came back from Babylon. They came back under Zerubbabel, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-angel-shemaiah-: Shemaiah Angel was a banker and philanthropist of Damascus who died in 1874. The entry calls him a great helper of his fellow Jews in Syria and of Damascus folk at large. After the Druse outbreak of 1860 was put down, he gave 3,000 Turkish pounds to the poor of all faiths in the city. He also fed the imperial troops there for a time at his own cost. Sultan Abd-ul-Aziz gave him the Order of the Medjidie, first class, for these services. His son Eleazar, at Constantinople, followed his example.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anthropology-12:
Anthropology is the science of man, above all in his bodily traits, and of the climates and societies that shape them. The entry says Jewish anthropology holds special interest for the science. Jews form a set-apart part of mankind, by race or by social life.

That fact bears on the science's central problem, the entry argues. Are likenesses among human groups due to shared descent, or to shared conditions? If Jews are one race, their spread across lands tests what setting can change. If they are not, their strong likeness needs explaining. The entry then weighs the case for and against the purity of the Jewish race, from Bible-era intermarriage to converts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antonio-diogo-1: Diogo Antonio was a physician who lived in Lisbon in the first half of the sixteenth century. In 1539 he followed Duarte de Paz as agent of the Portuguese Maranos at Rome. His charge was to stop, or at least delay, the setting up of the Inquisition in Portugal. Money for that mission was trusted to him. The entry says he spent it instead on papal briefs that protected himself and his family. His brother Hector took over the post after him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arras-1819:
Arras, chief city of Pas-de-Calais and capital of the old Artois in France, enters Jewish history through one Hebrew document. It tells how Jacob ben Jekuthiel, facing a decree of Robert the Pious, who reigned from 996 to 1031, went to Rome to seek the pope's protection for Jews who refused baptism. The pope sent a dignitary to halt the persecution. Jacob died on his way back, about 1023, at a place on a river, probably the Scarpe, read as Arras.

Caution fills the rest of the entry. The Hebrew place name may not be Arras at all. No Jewish community there is proven for that date. Jews likely lived at Arras in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, as they did across the region, yet of their history, the entry says plainly, nothing whatever is known.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-anshel-be:
Asher Anshel ben Isaac was a preacher at Prenzlau in Prussia. He also taught in the school his father had founded there. In 1701 he published a collection of sermons at Dessau. Its title, Shemenah Lahmo, plays on his name Asher and on the blessing in Genesis chapter 49, which speaks of Asher's rich bread.

Two parts make up the book. The first holds sermons for the Sabbath and the holy days, including Hanukkah and Purim. The second treats seven solemn moments in a man's life. They are circumcision, redemption of the firstborn, bar mitzvah, marriage, ordination, burial, and resurrection. The entry rests on Michael's Or ha-Hayyim and on Steinschneider's catalogue, and it gives no dates for the preacher's birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auerbach-jacob-:
Jacob Auerbach was an educator and author. He was born at Emmendingen, Baden, on Nov. 14, 1810, and died on Oct. 31, 1887. At Carlsruhe in 1827 he met his cousin Berthold Auerbach, the novelist. The two formed a close, lasting friendship. When money trouble cut short Jacob's studies at Heidelberg, Berthold helped him.

From 1842 Jacob taught religion in the Jewish community of Frankfort-on-the-Main. After 1848 he also taught at the gymnasium there, a span of nearly forty years in all. The government pensioned him in 1879 and gave him the Order of the Red Eagle. His lasting work was the printing of Berthold's letters to him, in two volumes in 1884. The letters run from 1830 to the novelist's death and read, the entry says, like an unconscious life story. His "Schul- und Hausbibel" of 1858 also spread widely in German Jewish homes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azores-2219: The Azores are a group of islands in the Atlantic Ocean, northwest of Africa. They belong to Portugal. The islands became a refuge for Jews driven out of Portugal. When the entry was written, Jews lived at Ponta Delgada, the capital of São Miguel, and on Fayal, Terceira, and other islands. They worked in the export trade. They kept the Jewish observances, the entry says. Yet they also married into Catholic families, and Christian women who married Jews often entered the Jewish faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baltic-province:
Baltic Provinces are the three Russian governments on the Baltic Sea: Courland, Livonia, and Esthonia. They once belonged to Sweden, except Courland, a Polish dependency. Their Jewish population in 1897 was about 100,000 out of 2,386,998 people. The entry stresses how unlike other Russian Jews these Jews are. Their habits, dress, and speech run German, and they are less crowded and better off.

Legal standing shifted under many rulers, and settlement rights turn on old census dates: 1835 in Courland, 1841 for Riga. The communal councils called ḳahals were ended June 5, 1893. Many Baltic Jews work as artisans, teachers, clerks, and small traders, and many emigrate. About 25,000 are said to live in the United States alone. Church statutes from Riga in 1428 show Jews trading there early, but lasting settlement waited until 1561.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barefoot-2519:
Grief, in the Bible, is shown by walking unshod. David fled before Absalom in that state, and Micah makes it a sign of mourning. Isaiah's unshod feet may picture the neglected condition of captives. Sandals served on long journeys over stony roads, yet in and around the house they were uncommon.

Oriental custom keeps feet uncovered at home, on holy ground, and in times of mourning. Temple priests served unshod, and Moses and Joshua each heard the command to remove his shoes on sacred soil. Dusty feet were barred from the Temple ground altogether. Islam likewise admits no one into a mosque shod. In synagogue the priests still step up in stockings to bless the congregation. The Day of Atonement and the Ninth of Ab are also kept without shoes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belkind-israel-:
Israel Belkind was a Russian Hebraist and teacher born in 1861 at Logoisk, in the government of Minsk. He studied at Mohilev and at the University of Kharkov. After attacks on Jews in Russia in 1881, he backed settlement in Palestine over America.

Belkind founded a student society called Bilu at Kharkov and helped plant a farm colony near Ekron. That venture failed, and after hardship he taught Hebrew at Jaffa and Jerusalem. To fill a want of Hebrew textbooks he wrote books on arithmetic, geography, and general history in the 1890s. His father served as rabbi at the very colony his son had helped to plant near Ekron.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernays-jacob-3:
Jacob Bernays, a German philologist, was born at Hamburg on Sept. 18, 1824. He died at Bonn on May 26, 1881. The eldest son of Ḥakam Isaac Bernays, he went to Bonn in 1844 to study under Welcker and Ritschl. A prize essay on Lucretius won him gold and his teacher's strong push toward a scholar's career.

In 1853 he helped plan the new Jewish Theological Seminary at Breslau, a pioneer task. When it opened in 1854 he taught Greek and Latin there, plus Hebrew poetry and the philosophy of religion. His deep classical learning joined a thorough Hebrew schooling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-zur-3219: Beth-Zur was a city in southern Judea. Joshua and Chronicles both name it. Nehemiah mentions it as well. Rehoboam fortified the town. It was a strongly walled place. It stood on Judea's eastern boundary line. During the Maccabean wars it was besieged repeatedly. First Maccabees returns to it again and again. Its site is marked by ruins near Bêt-sur. Those ruins sit by a hill.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-birmingham-ala-: Birmingham is the capital of Jefferson county, Alabama. It was founded in 1871. Its first congregation, Emanu-El, organized in 1882. Its building was dedicated in 1889. A second congregation, Knesses Israel, followed in 1899. The entry lists the city's Jewish societies. A B'nai B'rith lodge dates from 1884. Relief and aid associations are named too. Samuel Ullman served as alderman and school-board president. About 1,400 Jews lived there among 38,415 people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blum-ernest-341: Ernest Blum was a French dramatist. He was born in Paris on August 15, 1836. His father was an actor. At eighteen he wrote for the Variétés. His first piece was "Femme Qui Mord." Dozens of theater works followed for decades. He wrote for the Gaité, Ambigu, and Châtelet. "Rocambole" in 1864 shows his Ambigu work. Collaborators like Clairville shared many bills. He also published books of vaudeville life. "Journal d'un Vaudevilliste" came in 1891. Since 1869 he has served "Le Rappel."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonet-jacob-ben: Jacob ben David ben Yom-Tob Bonet, called Bonjorn, was a Spanish astronomer. He lived probably at Perpignan in the fourteenth century. In 1361 he prepared astronomical tables at Perpignan. Those tables won a great reputation and still survive in manuscript at Paris and Oxford. They were turned into Latin in the fifteenth century. Many Hebrew commentaries were written on them. Some copies were later turned back from Latin into Hebrew again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calebites-3919: Calebites were a branch of the Edomite clan of Kenaz that moved into southern Judah before the Israelite conquest. They settled near Hebron and seem to have come from the south. Their friendliness to the Hebrews may lie behind the story of Caleb's good report as a spy. In time they were absorbed into Judah. That union was not complete in David's outlaw days. Their old lands held towns such as Ziph and Mareshah. After the Exile, the clan was pushed farther north as Edomites took the south.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caravan-4019: Caravan names a convoy of travelers or goods. Israel's trade was inland, so goods from far regions moved by caravan along the great roads. Those roads were beaten paths, poor trails unfit for wagons. The camel did the work, marching twelve to fourteen hours a day under three or four hundred pounds. Israelites themselves took little part in that trade. Phoenicians, Canaanites, and desert tribes ran it. A Midianite caravan carried Joseph down to Egypt. Israel's kings at times taxed caravans that crossed their lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castel-d-ajano-: Samuel di Castel d'Ajano was an Italian physician and philosopher who lived at Mantua in the sixteenth century. His philosophical work on the articles of belief, Meor ha-Golah, survives in manuscript. He is thought to have written a liturgical poem for the comfort of a poor captive. A note by him on a passage in Rabbi Nissim's commentary also survives. The entry suggests he was the same man as Samuel Castiglione, a Mantua physician and liturgist of the same age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chiarini-luigi-:
Luigi Chiarini, an Italian abbé, was born near Montepulciano on April 26, 1789. He died at Warsaw on Feb. 28, 1832. From 1826 he taught history and Oriental languages at the University of Warsaw. He sat on a Jewish Committee formed by decree on May 22, 1825, made up only of Christians.

That body set Chiarini to translate the Babylonian Talmud, with a state grant of 12,000 thalers. His two-volume work of 1830 set out his plan. He argued that the harms charged to Judaism spring from the Talmud's teachings. The state, he held, should help Jews free themselves from that sway and return to the simple Mosaic faith. Schools in Bible and Hebrew, plus a French Talmud with notes and refutations, were his tools. The entry grants his sincere concern for Jewish welfare, while noting old prejudices in his book. Only two volumes of his Talmud version appeared.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-circumcision-in:
Circumcision, the cutting away of the foreskin, is set out as a rite done on Jewish male children on the eighth day after birth, and on slaves of the house as well. Genesis ties it to Abraham as a token of the covenant for all generations. The penalty for skipping it was karet, being cut off from the people, the entry states.

Aliens needed the rite before sharing the Passover feast or marrying into a Jewish family. To be uncircumcised counted as a reproach, and the word for it became a slur for Philistines and other outsiders. This very long entry then ranges far beyond the Bible, tracing the rite's meaning and its wide spread across Africa and other lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cochin-10319:
Cochin, a state of India within the Madras Presidency, held 1,142 Jews in 1891, split into two classes. The White Jews, about fifty families, trace their lines to Cranganore in 1219, to Spanish exiles who arrived in 1511, to Germans, and to families from Aleppo about 1680. The Black Jews number some three hundred families.

The oldest trace is the Sasanam, two bronze tablets holding a charter from King Cheramal Perumal to Joseph Rabban. Dated about 750, it grants seventy-two free houses and feudal rights near Cranganore. Later sections follow trade under the Portuguese and Dutch, losses, and slow recovery about 1860. White Jews worked as merchants and farmers; Black Jews as fishermen, fruit sellers, and oil pressers, the entry reports.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-naphtali-:
Naphtali Cohen, a Russo-German rabbi and cabalist, was born in 1649 at Ostrowo in the Ukraine and died at Constantinople on Dec. 20, 1718. Tatars seized him in 1663 and held him for years before he escaped home. He followed his father as rabbi of Ostrowo, then led Posen from 1690 to 1704, gathering a large cabalistic library.

At Frankfort a fire that began in his house on Jan. 14, 1711, burned the whole Jewish quarter. Accused of trusting charms over firefighting, he was jailed and freed only by giving up his post. At Prague he backed the Shabbethaian Nehemiah Hayyun, then turned and banned him once he learned the man's tenets in 1713. He died on the road to the Holy Land in 1718.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-georg-ludw:
Georg Ludwig Cohn, a German jurist, was born on Sept. 19, 1845, at Breslau. He held an honorary professorship in German civil and commercial law at Heidelberg from 1888. With other scholars he helped build Endemann's handbook of trade, maritime, and exchange law, issued from 1881 to 1885. In 1877 he founded a journal of comparative law and edited it from the start.

His chair at the time stood at the University of Zurich. There he lectured on German civil and commercial law and on German and Swiss legal history. The entry lists a dozen works in Latin and German. They treat the denial of justice in old German law, the history of the check, and drafts for German check and exchange statutes. A book of German law in proverbs reached a second edition in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cowen-frederic-:
Frederic Hymen Cowen was an English conductor and composer. He was born at Kingston, Jamaica, on Jan. 29, 1852. At age four he was taken to England. His father worked for two London theaters, so great artists filled his childhood. At eight he wrote the music for an operetta called Garibaldi. By twelve he was at home in Beethoven's sonatas. Study followed at Leipsic and Berlin.

His posts trace a full career. He conducted the Covent Garden promenade concerts in 1880 and the Philharmonic concerts from 1888 to 1892. Melbourne summoned him for its Centennial Exhibition in 1888-89. In 1896 he succeeded Sir Charles Hallé at Manchester, Liverpool, and Bradford. His works include the Scandinavian Symphony and the opera Pauline.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cuttings-4819:
Cuttings, in Bible usage, are incisions or gashes made in the flesh. The Law forbids Israelites to make them. Two Hebrew terms cover the act. From the context, the ban ties to customs of mourning. In Jeremiah's days gashing oneself was the common way to show grief for dead kin. The prophet does not scold the practice. He counts the loss of that mourning as a punishment in itself.

Philistines, Moabites, and Arabs shared the custom. Persian mourners kept it for their martyrs. Sorrow alone does not explain it, the entry argues. A still older aim lay behind it: winning the god's favor, and, earlier yet, worship of the departed spirit. The torn garment of mourning is a softened form of the same rite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-da-ud-effendi-m: Da'ud Effendi Molko was chief of translation in the Turkish Foreign Office. He was born at Salonica in 1845. His family, of humble parentage, settled in Constantinople while he was a boy. He was schooled at the Camondo Institution. He joined the Foreign Office at the age of eighteen. Under Sultan 'Abd al-'Aziz he rose to translator-in-chief. He kept the post when 'Abd al-Ḥamid the Second took the throne. Honors from Turkey, Persia, France, and Prussia are listed at the close.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-death-views-and:
Views and customs concerning death changed across the ages covered by this long article. The ancient Hebrews expected to be gathered to their fathers and to sleep with them. Dying in a good old age counted as a blessing. Being cut off in midlife was feared as a misfortune. Death itself was not yet seen as a plain evil.

Later books darken the picture. Kohelet and Ben Sira saw only the dreary life of shades in Sheol ahead, which made earthly life more precious. The Book of Wisdom taught that God made man for immortality and that death entered through the devil's envy. Apocalyptic writing then raised the hope that death would one day be destroyed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dessauer-josef-:
Josef Dessauer was a German composer born at Prague on May 28, 1798. He studied piano and composition there, then followed his parents' wish and went into trade. On a business trip to Italy at twenty-three, his musical bent took over. At Naples in 1821 his songs met a warm welcome, and he chose music for life.

Dessauer settled in Vienna and toured Europe with his songs, which won him wide fame for their melodic beauty. A catalogue of 1844 lists nearly seventy of them. His five operas failed and are no longer played. A few songs still live, above all the air "Scheiden and Meiden." He died at Mödling on July 8, 1876.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dreyfus-ferdina: Ferdinand Dreyfus was a French politician and deputy born at Paris on May 5, 1849. He edited the Siècle newspaper. The Republican party elected him district deputy of Rambouillet in March 1880. He was reelected in August 1881. He then lost his seat in 1885 and was beaten again in 1889. His one book named here is a popular manual for town councillors, the Manuel Populaire du Conseiller Municipal, printed at Paris in 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-drucker-hayyim-:
Hayyim ben Jacob Drucker, also called Arbich, was an Amsterdam printer of the late seventeenth century. His work as typesetter, publisher, author, and translator runs from 1680 to 1724. He worked in the shops of David Tartas, Moses Mendez, and Asher Anshel and Company.

In 1690 Drucker edited a Judæo-German version of Manasseh ben Israel's Mikweh Yisrael. He also edited Benjamin of Tudela's Itinerary in that tongue. His own Leb Hakamim, a book on morals, came out in 1706. He issued a fresh Ze'enah u-Re'enah in 1711 and a calendar in 1718. His two sons also became printers of Judæo-German books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elead-5519: Elead was a descendant of Ephraim named in a family list in First Chronicles. The entry gives only a short record for him. He joined a band of raiders on a drive against Gath. Their aim was to carry off the flocks of that town. The men of Gath killed Elead during the raid. The entry notes one point about his name. It stands in the list in Chronicles, but it does not appear in the family list given in the Book of Numbers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-ben-mei: Eliezer ben Meir ha-Levi was rabbi of Pinsk in Russia. He lived in the second half of the eighteenth century. The entry gives only his two books. Both are homilies on the Pentateuch. They follow the order of the weekly portions. The first book came out at Sklow in 1786. The second book continues the first on the same plan. It gives two homilies for each portion of the Law. That volume came out at the same town in 1795.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-emanu-el-5719: Emanu-El was a weekly journal for Jews on the Pacific coast. It was published at San Francisco in California. The first number came out in May of 1895. Jacob Voorsanger served as its editor from the start. Its pages served the Jews of that far coast. Judaism in that region was its special field. The entry is only four lines in length. It gives no press runs, staff, or end date for the paper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-epiphanius-5819:
Epiphanius was bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, born near Eleutheropolis, Palestine, between 310 and 320. He died at sea in 403. The entry says he was likely born to Jewish parents and turned to Christianity at sixteen. A legend tells of a rich Jew, Tryphon, adopting him and leaving him a fortune. After four years in an Egyptian monastery, he founded one in his home village. He became bishop in 367.

His Panarion, written in 374-376, describes eighty heretical sects. It sorts pre-Christian systems and lists groups that grew from Judaism and Samaritanism. For the Ebionites, he is the sole source for their gospel. His work on Bible weights and measures also covers translations and places. He knew much Jewish tradition and probably knew Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-farhi-isaac-601:
Isaac Farhi was a judge and almoner of Jerusalem, born at Safed and dead at Jerusalem on May 11, 1853. About 1840 the Jerusalem rabbinate sent him to Europe to gather funds for the poor. His books are mostly on morals and sermons. Marpe la-Ezem appeared in 1830, and Matok mi-Debash in 1842, with a praise of the Holy City attached.

Later works include Mine Metikah, three sermons printed at Leghorn in 1848, and Zuf Debash in 1849. His Ma'aseh Abot, a comment on Pirke Abot, came out at Leghorn in 1864, after his death. He also left unpublished notes on the Talmud and on Maimonides. The entry's sources include Fuenn's Keneset Yisrael.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankl-otto-631:
Otto Frankl was an Austrian jurist born at Prague on October 4, 1855. He studied law at Prague, Göttingen, and Leipsic. In 1883 he began to teach law at Prague as a junior lecturer. In 1891 he became a professor there. His chief fields were mining law and bankruptcy law. His first book treats the form needed for a gift under Austrian law, printed in 1883.

Later books treat free digging claims and the bankruptcy of open trading firms. A work of 1892 covers who must pay for damage done by mines. A call to revise the Austrian bankruptcy law followed in 1896. He also helped edit two legal journals and surveys.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fulda-ludwig-64:
Ludwig Fulda, a German author born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on July 15, 1862, studied German philology and philosophy at Berlin, Leipsic, and Heidelberg. He took his doctorate in 1883. After a brief stay in Frankfort he moved to Munich in 1884. There Paul Heyse shaped his writing strongly. From 1888 he lived in Berlin.

His output spans poems, tales, comedies, and social dramas. The dramatic fable Der Talisman, from 1893, won wide fame and reached a sixteenth edition by 1900. Other plays treat lost paradise, slavery, and twin sisters. He also rendered Moliere, Beaumarchais, and Rostand Cyrano into German with much success.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gans-david-ben-:
David Gans, a German historian and star scholar born at Lippstadt in 1541, died at Prague on August 25, 1613. He learned rabbinic books at Bonn and Frankfort, then studied under Moses Isserles at Cracow. At Prague he worked with Kepler and Tycho Brahe. He joined star watch at the Prague observatory for three days in a row.

His best known book is Zemah Dawid, printed at Prague in 1592. One part gives Jewish annals, the other world annals. It was the first work of its kind among German Jews. Gans also wrote on the shape of the earth and on astronomy. Though he knew Copernicus work, he kept to the older Ptolemaic scheme.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-garmu-bet-6519: The house of Garmu was a family of skilled bakers who made the showbread for the Temple at Jerusalem. They kept their baking method secret. Temple chiefs once replaced them with experts from Alexandria, fearing the secret might die with the family. The new bakers could not match them. The Garmu men came back only when their pay was doubled. Asked why they hid the art, they said pupils might one day use it for an idol temple.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gershon-ben-hez: Gershon ben Hezekiah, a Provencal physician, star scholar, and grammarian, lived at Beaumes near the turn of the fifteenth century. His works include a tract on grammar and the Masorah and a verse tract on astronomy. A third tract treats the deathless soul. His last work, and the only one kept, is a medical book in seven parts. He says he wrote it in prison during a lockup of 119 days, at the wish of old masters seen in a dream.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-glusker-maggid-:
Glusker Maggid is the heading under which the entry defends the real existence of Abba Glusk Leczeka. Kayserling had held that Abba was only a poetical presentation of Solomon Maimon. Against that, an anonymous writer in "Ha-Karmel" (1872) reported more. Abba had lived in Glusk, near Lublin, and old people there still remembered him.

Letteris quoted a parody Abba reportedly improvised on the spot. Jacob Emden had just thrown him down a flight of stairs in Altona. A later study in the "Vossische Zeitung" (1885) retold anecdotes of his troubles in Berlin. After wandering in Western countries, Abba returned to Poland in old age. Then all trace of him was lost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-greece-11419:
Greece held no more than 9,000 Jews, the entry opens. Corfu alone had 3,500 of them. Larissa had 2,500 and Volo 1,100. Another 4,000 Jews lived in Epirus at Janina and Prevesa. Jews settled in Greek lands early on. Acts places synagogues at Corinth and Athens. Greek Jews honored Greek culture. Philo and Josephus wrote within it.

Under Byzantine emperors their state worsened. Free worship was barred in 723, and many converted or left. By 840 Greek Jews prospered in silk work. Later Spanish exiles swelled the communities after 1492. The old Greek-speaking stock was absorbed into the Spanish one. The entry ends by sorting the living communities into five groups. Arta's, it says, is the oldest in Greece.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ha-zefirah-in-m: Ha-Ẓefirah, a Hebrew newspaper, was founded by Ḥayyim Selig Slonimski at Warsaw on Jan. 25, 1862. Polish troubles forced its suspension in 1863, and Slonimski revived it in 1874. It stayed a weekly until March 1886, when a daily edition began. Alongside general news it once carried many science articles, chiefly by Slonimski and Solomon Jacob Abramowitsch. As a daily it turned wholly to political and Jewish news.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hagab-7019: Hagab names a family of Nethinim in this two-line entry. The family came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel. The entry rests on Ezra ii. 46 alone. In I Esdras v. 30 the name is given as Agaba. Nothing else is told here: no head of the family is named, and no deeds or later history are recorded for the Hagab family.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halukkah-lit-di:
Ḥaluḳḳah, meaning division or distribution, is the organized gathering of funds for poor Jews in the Holy Land. It also aids those who long to travel there for religious reasons. Nearly every congregation abroad keeps a standing committee under a gabbai or paḳid. Collections go twice a year to leaders in Jerusalem, who share the money out, with learned old men, the destitute, and widows and orphans first.

The entry traces the system from the old support of Holy Land academies to the charity-box of R. Meïr Ba'al ha-Nes, of which more than 250,000 stand in homes and synagogues. It follows the messengers, or meshullaḥim, the split of Jerusalem's Ashkenazim into some twenty-five kolelim, and the central Wa'ad ha-Kelali. Tables close the article, showing American receipts for 1890-99 near ten thousand dollars a year for Sephardim and twenty-six thousand for Ashkenazim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hama-b-hanina-7:
Ḥama b. Ḥanina was a Palestinian amora of the third century, a fellow of R. Johanan. Like his father, Ḥanina b. Ḥama, he directed a school at Sepphoris. He was well known among the halakists. His greater fame, though, was as a haggadist of high rank, often quoted by men like Levi.

His homilies aim at practice. On "Ye shall walk after the Lord your God," he asks how a man can walk after a God who is a consuming fire. His answer: copy God's ways, and clothe the naked as God did. At Lydda, Hoshaiah once rebuked his pride in the synagogues his rich ancestors built: how many scholars, he asked, might that treasure have freed for study? The entry tells that clash in full and lists his teachers as unknown.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hasmoneans-7319:
The Hasmoneans were the priestly family that ruled Judea after the Maccabean revolt. Their rule became firm in September 141 before the common era. An assembly of priests, people, and elders made Simon leader and high priest for good. Rome gave its nod to the new house soon after.

A line of rulers follows Simon, who reigned from 142 to 135 and was murdered by his son-in-law. John Hyrcanus, Aristobulus, and Alexander Jannaeus held power in turn. Queen Alexandra ruled from 76 to 67. Civil war between her sons then cost the Jews their freedom, and Rome took control. Herod ended the line in 37.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hekscher-ephrai: Ephraim ben Samuel Sanvel Hekscher headed the Jewish congregation at Altona at the start of the eighteenth century. He wrote three books, all printed at Altona. One gives sources and readings for many rabbinic laws. A second holds his answers on the Shulhan Aruk, above all on the Orah Hayyim. A third offers new readings on the Talmud, in two parts. His son Issachar edited the second part of that work in 1743. The entry names no birth or death dates for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hertzveld-estel: Estella Dorothea Salomea Hertzveld, born at The Hague on July 14, 1837, was a Dutch poetess and granddaughter of a chief rabbi of Zwolle. Sincerely religious, she drew most poem subjects from the Bible. Her first major poem appeared in 1852. Later pieces treated the Red Sea crossing, Elijah, and Paul. She also wrote a flood relief poem in 1856 and pieces for a new synagogue and school. She arranged her poems for her children in Oct. 1881 and died at Arnhem on Nov. 4, 1881.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirah-7719: Hirah was an Adullamite and the friend of Judah, in Genesis. Judah stopped at his house after the sale of Joseph, the entry notes. Hirah went with Judah to Timnah when Judah oversaw the shearing of his sheep. He was also the messenger who carried a kid from Judah to Tamar. The entry is only a few lines long. It rests on three verses of one Genesis chapter and gives no family, dates, or further acts for Hirah beyond those errands and visits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hollander-jacob:
Jacob H. Hollander, born in Baltimore on July 23, 1871, was a professor of political economy at Johns Hopkins University. He took both his degrees there, in 1891 and 1894. Before graduating he taught a term at Amherst College. Johns Hopkins then recalled him to its faculty.

Hollander rose to head his department in 1902. In 1897 he served as secretary of a United States mission on a money pact with Europe. In 1900 the government made him special commissioner on Porto Rico tax laws, then its treasurer until 1901. His books treat Baltimore's finances, state taxation, and letters of Ricardo. He also wrote on Maryland Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-huesca-ancientl:
Huesca is a city in Aragon with a long Jewish past. By the late thirteenth century it held a privileged Jewish community of 160 members and its own rabbinical college. Hard times forced the town to remit part of a tax on bread, meat, and wine in 1257.

War subsidies in 1288 were so heavy that the king cut the community's taxes. Attack came in 1391, and many Jews were baptized. By 1437 the congregation paid only 300 sueldos in tax. Huesca bred scholars and translators of Maimonides. Petrus Alfonsi was baptized there in 1106. Abraham Almosnino was burned at the stake in 1489. Weaving was a main Jewish trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-migas-abrah: Abraham ben Isaac ha-Levi ibn Migas was a Spanish physician and rabbinical scholar who lived at Constantinople in the sixteenth century. He served as court physician to Sulaiman the Great and marched with that ruler's army into Syria. Years after his return, the Jews of Damascus asked him to settle in their city. He consulted Joseph Caro on points of law, and one responsum of his stands in Caro's collection. His printed book of 1585 tells of his travels and of Kurd and Druse customs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-shem-tob-jo:
Joseph ben Shem-Tob ibn Shem-Tob was one of the most prolific Spanish Jewish writers of the fifteenth century. Born in Castile, he died in 1480. He lived at Medina del Campo, Alcala, and Segovia and held some court post that put him among Christian scholars. Public debates with them fed his anti-Christian writings.

In 1452 the Prince of Asturias sent him to Segovia to head off Easter rage against the Jews. His works run from a handbook on preaching to a study of the highest good, written in 1442. He commented on Duran's famous letter and on Crescas against Christian dogma. His largest labor was on Aristotle's Ethics in Hebrew dress, finished at Segovia in 1455 after one hundred straight days of work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-shu-aib-bis: Bishr ben Phinehas ibn Shu'aib was an Oriental mathematician of the end of the tenth century. Arabic writers often quote his Arabic works, Hottinger reports. In 997 the Jacobite Abu Ali Isa ibn Zara'ah sent him a pamphlet against Judaism. That piece seems to answer a pro-Jewish work by Ibn Shu'aib himself. The entry is brief. It names no book title of his and gives no dates beyond the century and the one exchange of 997.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-innocent-iii-lo:
Innocent III, pope from 1198 to 1216, was born at Anagni in 1161 and died July 17, 1216. A Roman writer's line fits his record toward the Jews: "Thy words are the words of God; thy deeds are the deeds of the devil." He was the first pope who did not protect the Jews but persecuted them. His opening bull "Sicut Judæis" renewed the old prohibitions on oppressing them.

His own practice broke that maxim. The Lateran Council under him passed the humiliating laws that made Jews pariahs, above all the badge. He blamed Jewish influence for heresy in southern France, invented fresh charges beside ritual murder, and pressed kings and counts to strip Jews of land, servants and protection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ibn-sid-z: Isaac ibn Sid, also called Zag or Cag, was a Spanish astronomer who worked at Toledo in the second half of the thirteenth century. His surname haHazzan suggests he was precentor at the synagogue. He took a leading part in compiling the Alfonsine Tables. Isaac Israeli reports seeing, in Isaac's own hand, records of three moon-eclipses he observed at King Alfonso's order. Alfonso called him "our learned Rabbi Çag" in official documents. In 1277 Isaac translated an Arabic work on the quadrant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-jerem: Jacob ben Jeremiah Mattithiah ha-Levi was a German translator of the seventeenth century. He turned two Hebrew works into Judaeo-German. One was Abraham Jagel's "Lekah Tob," printed at Amsterdam in 1675 and twice reissued. The other was the "Sefer ha-Yashar," which he called "Tam we-Yashar" (Frankfort, 1674, and often reprinted). It tells Bible history from Adam to the Judges, with haggadic filling-out. After each section his version adds a short summary and the story's moral lesson for the reader.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jerusalem-11519:
Jerusalem was the capital first of all Israel and later of the kingdom of Judah, and the chief city of Palestine. The entry opens with its ground: a plateau spur ringed by valleys, with the Kidron on the east and the Valley of Hinnom on the west and south. Easy approach came only from the north and northwest, it notes.

From that base the long article builds out the city's name, site, and history in depth. Hills, gates, and water all get close treatment, and the past is followed across the ages that made the city holy to Jews. Readers should expect a full city study, not a short notice, with maps and views named along the way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jesus-ben-zapph: Jesus ben Zappha was a general of Idumaea in the first century. After the Roman commander Cestius Gallus had been driven off, the rebel government at Jerusalem put him in charge, with Eleazar ben Neos beside him. Both men came from high-priestly families. Niger of Peraea, who had governed Idumaea until then, was ordered to serve under the two new generals. The entry adds a guess: he may be the former high priest who later fled Jerusalem to the Romans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-johanan-b-nappa:
Johanan ben Nappaha was a Palestinian scholar born at Sepphoris late in the second century. He never knew his parents: his father died before his birth and his mother at it. His grandfather raised him. His teachers were the last of the older masters, and for a short time he sat under Judah the Prince himself, seventeen rows behind another pupil.

Kind to stranger and brother alike, he was loved by teachers and honored by all. To pay for his learning he sold off his land, vineyard, and olive grove one by one. In his own words, he traded what God made in six days for what took forty days to give. When his means ran out he worked for bread, then fought his way back to the school. He died at Tiberias in 279.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-john-sobieski-1:
John Sobieski was king of Poland from 1674 to 1696. In his reign Poland had lost its old high place among the peoples of Europe, and Jewish wealth and weight in the land sank with it. Many poor Jews went to Prussia to hire out as field hands. In those years Sobieski also ordered the Karaite Jews to leave their biggest towns and scatter into small ones.

Yet the entry calls him a firm friend of the Jews as a whole. He gave them many rights in Lithuania and Poland, fought priestly stirring against them, and worked to undo false charges. About twenty decrees of his aided the Jews of Lemberg alone. Church power often blocked his help, but under him Jewish bodies, and their Council of the Four Lands, grew stronger again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-baru:
Joseph ben Baruch was a tosafist of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, likely the same man as Joseph of Clisson. He spent time in Paris, where he worked with Judah Sir Leon and taught Samuel of Falaise. In 1211 he moved with his brother Meir to Palestine by way of Egypt. In Jerusalem the brothers led the new congregation there.

Later writers cite him as Joseph of Jerusalem or R. Joseph of Palestine. His comments appear in the Tosafot and in works by Bezaleel Ashkenazi and others. Rulings and answers on ritual law are credited to him as well. He also wrote liturgical poems, and a confession of his for the Day of Atonement survives in the ritual.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joshua-b-levi-8:
Joshua b. Levi was a Palestinian amora of the first half of the third century. He headed the school of Lydda in southern Palestine. With Johanan bar Nappaha of Tiberias he often debated points of haggadah. His teachers included Bar Kappara and Judah b. Pedaiah, from whom he learned many legal rulings.

Gentleness marked his character. He was known for modesty and piety, and fasts he called were said to be answered. He would not curse even a Jewish Christian who vexed him, quoting God's mercy over all creatures. Haggadah held a large place in his teaching, and many tales are told in his name. Later books even gather legends of his talks with Elijah and the Angel of Death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kahana-abraham-: Abraham Aryeh Löb Kahana was a Russian rabbi of the eighteenth century. He is known as the author of "Or ha-Ne'erab," a commentary on the Talmud. His son Solomon Zalman Kahana added notes to it, and the book was printed at Ostrog in 1804. The entry adds that Kahana left two works in manuscript: "Dibre Ḥemed," a set of sermons and other pieces, and "Zer Zahab," a commentary on the Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kohler-kaufmann:
Kaufmann Kohler, a rabbi and theologian born in Fürth, Bavaria, on May 10, 1843, came from a family of rabbis. He trained for the rabbinate in several German towns and took his Ph.D. at Erlangen in 1868. His thesis on the blessing of Jacob was an early Jewish essay in higher biblical criticism. Its radical tone closed the German pulpit to him.

America gave Kohler his career. He served pulpits in Detroit from 1869, Chicago from 1871, and New York from 1879, then became president of Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati on Feb. 26, 1903. The entry stresses his Reform leadership, including the Pittsburg Conference of 1885 and its platform, plus his many books, lectures, and journal articles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-krimchaks-9519:
Krimchaks are the so-called Turkish Jews of the Crimea, centered at Kara-Su-Bazar in Taurida. In daily life they closely match their Tatar neighbors, yet they hold strictly to Talmudic Judaism. Dress, houses, and food customs follow the Tatar pattern. Their speech is pure Tatar, written in Hebrew letters.

Origins stay unsure in the entry. Krimchaks themselves place their arrival about the sixth century, while one writer puts a move from Constantinople in the fourteenth century. Wedding customs get close detail, from moving the bride's wardrobe days ahead to a week spent indoors after the rite. A report dated April 27, 1841, calls them peaceful, honest, and well-to-do workers who kept apart from other Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lehmann-joseph-:
Joseph Lehmann, a French chief rabbi, was born at Belfort on Nov. 1, 1843. His father served as rabbi at Belfort for fifty years and taught him first. Lehmann then studied at the rabbinical seminary of Paris and was ordained in September 1867. Two years later he succeeded Zadoc Kahn at a Paris temple.

During the Franco-Prussian war of 1870-71 Lehmann served as an army almoner in Paris. He taught Talmud at the Paris Talmud Torah from 1874 to 1890. In 1890 he became director of the Paris seminary and its professor of Talmud. His books treat Herod's trial, Jewish sects in the Mishnah, and public aid in old Jewish law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-jedidiah-b: Jedidiah ben Raphael Solomon Levi was a rabbi at Alessandria and at Sienna. He died in 1790. The short entry gives no birth date and no other post. It records one work of his: hymns for the reconsecration of the synagogue at Sienna in 1786. Those hymns were printed in "Seder Zemirot we-Limmud" at Leghorn in 1786. The entry lists a Bodleian catalogue page and an index as its sources, and says nothing further about his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lewin-georg-ric:
Georg Richard Lewin, a German dermatologist, was born at Sondershausen on April 25, 1820. He died at Berlin on Nov. 1, 1896. He took his medical degree in 1845 after study at Halle and Berlin. He trained further at Vienna, Würzburg, and Paris, then settled in Berlin.

Lewin worked first on the ear, then on skin diseases and syphilis. In 1865 he headed that department at the Charité Hospital, and in 1868 he became assistant professor. In 1884 Bismarck split his clinic in two and gave the skin half to Bismarck's own doctor. The move drew wide protest from medical faculties. Lewin brought in new treatments, among them mercury shots under the skin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lipschutz-lupsc:
Lipschütz is the name of a family of Polish and German rabbis. The name came from Liebeschitz, a town in Bohemia. The entry gives lives of many members across several centuries, most of them rabbis, teachers, and authors of legal replies and Talmud notes.

One member, Baruch Mordecai, born about 1810, served as rabbi for forty-three years in several towns and died at Siedlce on March 30, 1885. Another, Eliezer ben Solomon, taught many pupils and wrote replies printed at Neuwied in 1749. Aryeh Löb wrote notes on several Talmud tracts and replies on the Shulhan Aruk. The long list shows the family's wide reach.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lysimachus-1021:
Lysimachus, an anti-Jewish writer of Alexandria, is treated in a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. He lived before Apion, the better known critic of the Jews. The article says he outdid even Manetho in hostility. His subject was the exodus of the Jews from Egypt.

In Lysimachus's version, 110,000 Jews left Egypt under King Bokchoris. Led through the desert on the advice of a certain Moyses, they reached Judea after great hardship. There they founded a city he named Hierosyla, meaning temple robbery, later softened to Hierosolyma. The entry notes that his work survives only in fragments, chiefly in Josephus's Against Apion. Scholars collected those fragments in a standard edition of Greek historians. For readers, the piece preserves one of the harshest ancient attacks on Jewish origins, kept so it can be answered.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marix-adolph-10:
Adolph Marix, an American naval commander, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Saxony on April 24, 1848, he came to America as a boy. In 1864 he entered the Naval Academy at Annapolis. He graduated in 1868 and rose steadily through the officer ranks.

The article follows a career of varied stations. Marix served on ships in the North Atlantic and on the Asiatic station. He also worked in the Hydrographic Office and the judge-advocate-general's office, which sent him to Australia. In 1895 he joined the battleship Maine, leaving her only weeks before she blew up in Havana harbor. He then served as recorder of the Maine court of inquiry. Congress advanced him two numbers for conspicuous conduct in two battles at Manzanillo in 1898. Commander followed in March 1899. The entry honors a Jewish officer of the Spanish-American war.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-10619:
Menahem, king of Israel from 748 to 738 B.C., is treated in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price. Son of Gadi, he marched from Tirzah, killed the usurper Shallum, who had murdered his predecessor after six months, and seized the throne. The biblical account, which the article follows closely, shows his brutality at once: the town of Tiphsah refused him, and he punished its women with infamous cruelty.

His reign is defined by Assyria. Tiglath-pileser III, the Bible's Pul, advanced, and Menahem bought him off with a thousand talents of silver, taxed at fifty shekels from each of Israel's sixty thousand men of wealth. The king's own inscriptions, quoted here, list "Menahem of Samaria" among his tributaries, fixing the dates. The article's closing note is dry: in that anarchic age of the northern kingdom, Menahem alone died a natural death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-phoeb:
Meshullam Phoebus ben Israel Samuel, born about 1547, rose to become chief rabbi of Cracow, where he died on October 17, 1617. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He first appears as head of a flourishing yeshivah at Brest-Litovsk, where Joel Sirḳes was among his pupils.

By 1605 he was in Cracow, and leading rabbis such as Meïr Lublin consulted him on hard questions. One of his responsa shows a thorough knowledge of anatomy and some Latin, the article notes. He also wrote a treatise on the proper names used in a bill of divorce and edited the responsa of Moses Minz, printed at Cracow in 1617.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metz-10119:
Metz, a fortified city in Lorraine, held one of the oldest Jewish communities in Europe, chronicled by Gotthard Deutsch and A. Ury for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Chronicles place Jews there as early as the year 221, living on good terms with Christians. When the article appeared, the city counted 1,451 Jews among 58,462 residents.

Early centuries brought protection from bishops and dukes and a circle of scholars called the sages of Lorraine, though Crusade-era persecution and a 1365 expulsion scattered the community.
