The team asked if the gene form a person carries sets how much TL1A they make. They found that forms linked to bowel disease do raise TL1A levels. That tie helps explain why some people face stronger gut inflammation. It also names a path that new drugs could calm.
plos-pone-0004819:
Sean Kim and colleagues took a computational approach to understand in vitro alveolar morphogenesis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Primary human alveolar type II lining cells in Matrigel form alveolar like cysts using a step different from other studied lining types. Neither growth nor death is involved during cyst formation, making it a pure rearrangement process suitable for modeling cell movement and adhesion changes.

Models reproduce lumen formation dynamics from cell properties. Knowledge alveolar formation informs lung repair research. Computational tests can predict perturbations before tests. The system isolates morphogenesis steps. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004919:
Copper is a metal that every cell needs in tiny amounts. Its balance inside cells shifts as they grow old. Christian Scheckhuber and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on that shift. They tracked copper in ageing cells of the fungus Podospora anserina, a classic ageing model. They also tracked it in ageing human skin cells called fibroblasts.

Their measurements pointed to mitochondria as major players in the change. Mitochondria are the cell's energy producers. The same kind of shift appeared in the human cells, not just the fungus. That parallel suggests some features of cellular ageing are shared across very different forms of life.
plos-pone-0005019:
Lead in city air has fallen for decades. Even so, children need still lower exposure. This potent neurotoxin harms the developing brain. Nicholas Pingitore and colleagues hunted its remaining source. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used X-ray absorption spectroscopy on urban airborne lead.

The analysis fingered urban soil as the dominant source. Factories and traffic were not the main culprits anymore. Old lead settled in soil keeps rising into the air as dust. The finding points cleanup at the ground beneath cities. It also explains why air lead resists further decline. Soil is a long memory for past pollution.
plos-pone-0005119:
Viruses engineered to kill cancer are called oncolytic viruses. Some replicate only in tumor cells. Their clinical efficacy is still limited by poor infection of the tumor mass. Verónica Lopez and colleagues studied a missing factor in PLOS ONE in 2009. The factor is the tumor's stromal cells. These support cells talk constantly with malignant cells.

Tumor-associated stromal cells play a critical role in the outcome. They can shield the tumor from the viral attack. Beating cancer with viruses means beating its neighborhood too. The study used conditionally replicative adenoviruses. It shows efficacy depends on more than the virus and the cancer cell. Trial designers should measure the stroma's role. Patients might be chosen by stromal features.
plos-pone-0005219:
Melanoma that has spread is hard to treat and lacks reliable blood markers to track it. Tumors shed tiny vesicles called exosomes, which carry proteins from the cells that made them. Logozzi and colleagues measured those vesicles in melanoma patients in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Patients carried high levels of exosomes marked with the proteins CD63 and caveolin-1 in their plasma. Healthy tumor-derived vesicles also play roles in cancer growth, so the signal is biologically plausible. A blood test based on vesicles could track disease without repeated tissue samples. A test built on these tiny packets would be easy to repeat, which is just what doctors need when they track a fast-moving cancer.
plos-pone-0005319:
Human attention is not spread evenly across space, and that bias shows up in both patients and healthy people. Turriziani and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether the same spatial biases shape language processing. Their study explores the relationship between semantics and space.

Meaning and space may share mental machinery, so a skew in one could tilt the other. The work investigates how representations of space affect aspects of processing words. Links like these matter for understanding language disorders that follow brain injury to one side. Ward care for stroke cases with one-sided neglect may gain from this link, since drills that join words and space could train both at once in the same task.
plos-pone-0005419:
Caroline Kulangara and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE study on the search for a malaria vaccine. The genome of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum had opened new ways to hunt for vaccine parts. One new method picked out short repeating patterns that form coiled shapes in parasite proteins.

The authors checked how much those coiled parts stay the same across parasite strains. A part that does not change much makes a better vaccine target, since the parasite cannot easily escape it. Their checks help narrow the list of parts worth testing in future vaccine work.
plos-pone-0005519:
Renee Tsolis and co-authors read the genome of a sheep pathogen in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Brucella ovis causes a disease of the breeding organs in sheep. Unlike its close kin, it does not infect people.

The team's genome study found many broken and missing genes compared with its kin. That decay matches the germ's narrow life: one host and a narrow range of tissues. Reading which genes were lost helps explain why this Brucella stayed a farm problem while others became a threat to people as well. Its broken genes read like a record of a germ settling into a narrower and safer niche.
plos-pone-0005619:
Yosuke Kumamoto and co-authors studied skin immune cells and allergy in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Dendritic cells are the immune system's strongest teachers, showing T cells what to attack. In skin, two groups share that job: cells in the top layer and cells in the layer below.

The team showed that one group of the deeper cells, marked MGL2, is enough on its own to start contact allergy in mice. Knowing which teacher cell starts the reaction helps target allergy treatments to the right place in the skin. Skin allergy to metals and chemicals is common, so the cells that start it are a natural drug target.
plos-pone-0005719:
Akito Kawahara and colleagues built a family tree for hawkmoths in 2009 using five nuclear genes. Hawkmoths number about fourteen hundred species and serve as test cases across biology. Yet their family links, built mostly on body form, were shaky.

Gene data gave the team a firmer tree and a view of how the moths spread across the globe. A solid tree lets other work, from flight studies to pest control, rest on real kinship. The study replaces guesswork about hawkmoth history with evidence from the moths' own DNA. It covers one of the most watched moth families in science.
plos-pone-0005819:
Nishaki Mehta and co-authors made HIV testing cheaper in 2009 by validating diagnosis from dried blood spots. A spot of blood dried on paper is easy to collect, store, and ship where labs are scarce. Real-time PCR can then measure the virus from that spot.

Their method both detects HIV and counts its load at low cost. Early treatment of infected infants is now advised, which needs exactly this kind of test. The approach fits clinics that lack freezers, couriers, or big budgets. The team shows performance data to back its use in limited-resource settings.
plos-pone-0005919:
Food sharing keeps an ant colony alive, yet who hands food to whom is hard to watch. In 2009, Aurélie Buffin, Damien Denis, Gaetan Van Simaeys and their co-authors took up that puzzle in PLOS ONE. They fed ants food marked with a mild radio label so that each meal could be traced through the colony.

By tracking the label, the team could see how food moved from ant to ant and where it ended up stored. The maps point to set exchange patterns rather than random sharing among nest mates. Work of this kind helps explain how a colony feeds queens, larvae and workers with no central control at all.
plos-pone-0006019:
Learning needs the right proteins in the right neurons at the right time. Attila Stetak, Frederic Hörndli, Andres Maricq and colleagues pinned one such protein down in the worm C. elegans in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies MAGI-1, a scaffold protein at synapses, and its neuron-specific role in associative learning and memory.

A scaffold holds signaling parts in place so a synapse can change with experience. Finding that MAGI-1 acts only in certain neurons sharpens the map of the worm's learning circuit. The worm's small nervous system lets each cell be named, so a cell-specific result like this gives memory research unusually firm ground.
plos-pone-0006119:
A signal that fights tumors elsewhere in the body may reach lung tumors too. Irma Airoldi, Emma Di Carlo, Claudia Cocco and colleagues studied interleukin-12 in lung cancer in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper builds on mice lacking the IL-12 receptor part rb2, which develop lung adenocarcinomas on their own, and examines the receptor in human primary lung tumors.

IL-12 can target both the cancer cells and the normal bronchial cells around the lesions, the title reports. Non-small-cell lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer death, so a signal with that reach earns attention. The receptor's pattern in human tissue helps judge where IL-12 therapy might act.
plos-pone-0006219:
Cells talk through signals and direct touch, but passing whole genetic messages between cells was thought rare. Amy Skinner, Lee O'Neill, and Peter Kurre studied tiny bubbles called microvesicles in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Similar RNA transfer by small vesicles had been reported in immune cells.

The team shows these pathways can be aimed to carry genetic information between non-immune cells. Deliberate targeting turns a natural parcel service into a delivery tool. That opens ideas for moving therapeutic genes without viruses. It also suggests cell messages in the body may travel further than textbooks assumed.
plos-pone-0006319:
Naming a plant pathogen wrong can misdirect quarantine and crop protection. Markus Goeker and colleagues used Peronospora, a genus of downy mildew fungi, as a case study in molecular taxonomy in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Sensible species limits are crucial for plant protection and biological control.

DNA-based analysis redraws species boundaries in the genus more sensibly. Poorly drawn taxa have severe consequences across research and farming. Model organisms chosen for comparison also depend on correct names. The case study shows molecular data settling disputes that appearance alone could not.
plos-pone-0006419:
Steroid treatment can starve bone of blood until the bone dies, a condition called osteonecrosis. Ge Zhang and colleagues tested flavonoids from the herb Epimedium in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Two events interrupt bone blood supply: clotting inside vessels and fat deposits outside them. No clinical agent targets both at once.

The Epimedium flavonoids reduced the incidence of steroid-associated osteonecrosis in a dose-dependent way. The effect did not come via direct action on the expected cellular targets, the title notes. The compounds may act through circulation rather than bone cells. A plant-derived candidate for an untreatable side effect deserves the attention.
plos-pone-0006519:
Hridayesh Prakash and co-authors studied a protein that helps infected lung cells stay alive, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The germ Chlamydophila pneumoniae infects the lung and lives inside its cells. Cells it infects resist apoptosis, the built-in death program of cells. That stand has been tied to a protein called cIAP-1, which blocks cell death.

The team asked how cIAP-1 shapes the first immune response to this lung germ. A germ that keeps its host cell alive gains a safe home. If that shield could be lifted, the body might clear the germ more fast. The work shows the push and pull between the germ and the cell it lives in.
plos-pone-0006619:
Isabel Calvo and co-authors ran a genome-wide screen for caffeine tolerance in fission yeast in PLOS ONE in 2009. An excess of caffeine is cytotoxic to all eukaryotic cell types. The team aim to study how cells become tolerant to a toxic dose of this drug. They also study the relationship between caffeine tolerance and other stresses.

A genome-wide screen of genes required for caffeine tolerance tests every gene for its contribution. Yeast screens are fast and complete, giving a parts list for drug defense. Many tolerance genes will have human counterparts. The work also illuminates how caffeine affects cells beyond its stimulant fame.
plos-pone-0006719:
Enas R. Yassin and colleagues dissected how a fusion gene transforms blood cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene is NUP98-HOXA9, a hallmark of acute myeloid leukemia. It joins part of NUP98 to the DNA-binding part of HOXA9. The fused protein likely acts as a faulty transcription factor. It binds DNA and switches the wrong genes on or off.

The team introduced the fusion into primary human blood-forming cells. They then took its transforming action apart step by step. Watching healthy human cells turn cancerous shows which parts are essential. That knowledge can point to drug targets in this leukemia. It also clarifies how one fusion protein can drive a whole cancer.
plos-pone-0006819:
Lavinia Nardinocchi and colleagues targeted low-oxygen survival in cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Solid tumors often contain hypoxic, oxygen-starved zones. A factor called HIF-1α helps cancer cells survive there. It also restrains blood vessel growth and drug response in tumors. A kinase called HIPK2 normally opposes HIF-1α and supports the guardian p53.

Restoring HIPK2 and p53 activity suppressed HIF-1α in their experiments. That suppression attacks the hypoxia program cancer cells depend on. The combination offers a strategy against resistant tumor cores. Hypoxic zones often survive chemotherapy, so targeting them addresses relapse at its source.
plos-pone-0006919:
Nassima Temime-Smaali and her team used a plant-made drug to strike cancer cells that stretch their gene caps in an odd way in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some cancers stretch caps by a path called ALT, in place of the stock path. Their caps crowd in odd hubs in the cell core, with tools for gene swaps. One tool, topoisomerase III alpha, is a must for that path. The drug telomestatin grips four-strand knots in DNA, called G-quadruplexes.

The drug kept the tool from gripping those knots. It also stripped the caps bare in ALT cells. Bare caps read as harm, and harm can kill the cell. The strike is a made-to-fit blow at ALT cancers.
plos-pone-0007019:
He-Ge Chen, Wen-Jun Han, Mi Deng, and colleagues mapped control of a widespread enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protein phosphatase 2A removes phosphate tags from proteins. It supplies more than half of that activity in many cells. The enzyme is built from scaffold, catalytic, and regulatory parts.

The team studied how the scaffold part's gene, PP2A-A alpha, is switched on. Several transcription factors shared the job, including AP-2α, CREB, ETS-1, and SP-1. Knowing its controls helps explain how cells tune this master regulator. Faulty tuning is linked to cancer and other diseases.
plos-pone-0007119:
Liwen Chen, Edward Tredget, and Chenxiong Liu tested donated stem cells in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mesenchymal stem cells from bone marrow can aid tissue repair. Donor, or allogeneic, cells would be easier to stock than a patient's own. Yet immune rejection might destroy them and cut engraftment. The team compared donor and matched cells directly.

They measured engraftment and wound healing in mice for each type. The comparison tests whether off-the-shelf cell therapy is realistic. If donor cells survive long enough to help, banks of ready cells become practical for wound care.
plos-pone-0007219:
Lucia Colombo and Jason Zevin investigated how readers assign word stress in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They ran four experiments using priming methods. Their language focus is Italian, where word stress is unpredictable and often needs lookup in memory rather than simple rules.

Readers can use lexical routes based on whole words, or sub-lexical routes based on parts. The authors study how stress priming changes each route during reading aloud. Their findings show selective effects on the two pathways. Psychologists of language can use the work to model how pronunciation is planned.
plos-pone-0007319:
Melissa Garren, Laurie Raymundo, James Guest, and colleagues tested coral microbes under fish farm pollution in PLOS ONE in 2009. A coral holobiont includes the coral animal, its algal symbionts, and its microbes. Those microbes help keep the whole system balanced, so robust microbial communities support long-term reef survival.

Coastal pollution threatens that balance. The authors expose coral-associated bacterial communities to fish farm effluent. They measure how resilient the communities are to that exposure. Their results show whether farm waste can destabilize the microbes corals depend on in reef ecosystems.
plos-pone-0007419:
Ole Hartvig Mortensen, Anders Rinnov Nielsen, Christian Erikstrup, and colleagues proposed an inflammation protein as an obesity marker in 2009. Two inflammatory molecules, S100A8 and S100A9, form a combined protein called calprotectin. Plasma calprotectin levels are elevated in various inflammatory disorders, from arthritis to inflammatory bowel disease in clinical practice.

The authors hypothesize levels would rise in low-grade systemic inflammation as well. That state accompanies obesity. They test calprotectin as a novel marker of obesity. Their PLOS ONE paper evaluates whether a simple blood measure can capture the hidden inflammation that links obesity to disease.
plos-pone-0007519:
Lars Schwabe and Oliver Wolf published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the fragility of personal memories. A new memory starts out labile, then settles into stable storage. Recalling a settled memory makes it fragile again until it re-stabilizes, a step called reconsolidation. The team asked whether learning something new during that window interferes. Their test used autobiographical memories, the stories of a person's own life.

Fresh episodic learning did interfere with the reconsolidation of the recalled personal memories. The old memories came back altered by what was learned in between. That finding carries real stakes for therapy and for eyewitness accounts. It shows that remembering is not replaying a fixed record. Each recall opens a brief chance for the record to be edited, for better or worse.
plos-pone-0007619:
John Lukens and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the liver's unusual immune character. The liver is constantly exposed to bacterial products and food antigens from the gut. To avoid constant inflammation, it leans toward tolerance. The mediators that shape immune responses in that environment were not fully known. The team tested whether the liver itself can activate naive killer T cells in mice.

The liver can activate those CD8 T cells. The cells it produces, though, show dysfunctional antiviral activity. That is the tolerance trade-off made visible: response without full fighting power. Such a compromise protects the organ from friendly fire. It may also explain why some viruses persist in the liver. The study pinpoints the liver as an active teacher of T cells, not a passive bystander.
plos-pone-0007719:
Masaaki Adachi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks at what happens when cells face heat and oxidative stress at once. Pollution and ozone loss raise oxidative stress, while warming raises heat exposure. People now risk meeting both at the same time.

Cells defend themselves with a heat stress response that rescues folded proteins. The authors found that oxidative stress weakens that defense. It also slows the recovery of proteins after heat damage. The result helps explain why combined stresses can harm health more than either one alone.
plos-pone-0007819:
David Gallego-Ortega and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It compares two sister enzymes that start a key fat-building path in human cells. Choline kinase is the first enzyme of the Kennedy pathway branch. That branch makes phosphocholine, a main part of cell membranes.

Humans carry two forms, alpha and beta, with different jobs. The authors map their differential roles in lipid metabolism. The split matters for cancer, where choline use runs high. It also matters for treatment, since blocking the wrong form could cause harm. The study guides which enzyme drug makers should target.
plos-pone-0007919:
Murugesan Rajaram and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It follows a dangerous bacterium's escape from the cell compartment meant to kill it. Francisella tularensis infects macrophages, the immune cells that eat germs. It breaks out of the phagosome and multiplies in the cell body.

Infected cells then die through the Fas-mediated death pathway. The authors show that pathway switches on as the bacterium escapes. Two cell proteins, Akt and SHIP, modulate the escape. The tug-of-war between germ and host decides the infection's course. Each control point is a possible therapy target.
plos-pone-0008019:
David Lambert and colleagues read DNA from museum skins of an extinct New Zealand bird in PLOS ONE in 2009. The huia was famed for its beak: the male's was short and stout, the female's long and curved, the widest such gap known in birds. The last birds died out a century ago.

Gene tests, sex checks, and careful measures of the old specimens let the team rebuild parts of the bird's family life and variety. Museum skins thus still speak. What they say can guide care for the huia's living kin and sharpen how we read other lost species.
plos-pone-0008119:
Aimee Shen and colleagues simplified protein cleaning with a tag that cuts itself off in PLOS ONE in 2009. Labs grow useful proteins in bacteria, then must fish them out pure. Tags help the fishing, but cutting the tag off usually adds steps and cost.

Their tag borrows a cutting enzyme from the cholera germ that snips only at one exact spot, its own joint. A trigger makes it cut on command, freeing the clean protein. Fewer steps mean less loss and fewer chances to spoil delicate proteins, a gain for labs large and small.
plos-pone-0008219:
Sean Myles and colleagues presented fast genome methods for grapes in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. The genus Vitis includes the grapes used for wine and table fruit. New sequencing tools promise to speed the use of genetic data in crop improvement. Mapping genes for useful traits is a key step in breeding. Good study design comes before that mapping work.

The team showed how rapid genomic characterization can be done across the genus. A broad genetic picture helps breeders plan crosses and mapping studies. It can reveal diversity that breeding programs might otherwise miss. The work supports faster, smarter improvement of grape varieties.
plos-pone-0008319:
Carney D. Matheson and colleagues investigated an ancient tomb in Jerusalem in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Tomb of the Shroud dates to the first century of the common era. It was discovered in Akeldama, Jerusalem, and had been looted before study. An interdisciplinary team began investigating it in 2000. More than twenty stone ossuaries held human remains there.

Molecular methods were used to explore the tomb's contents. Ossuaries are boxes for collecting bones after burial. DNA and other traces can reveal kinship and disease among the dead. The work connects archaeology with laboratory science.
plos-pone-0008419:
Zhe Ji and Bin Tian studied messenger RNA endings in stem cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The 3 prime untranslated regions of mRNAs contain elements that regulate gene expression after transcription. Over half of mammalian genes have multiple polyadenylation sites. Alternative choices produce different 3 prime regions for the same gene. The team examined this during generation of pluripotent stem cells.

Reprogramming cells from different types reshaped their mRNA endings. Shorter or longer tails change how messages are controlled. Such reprogramming may be part of how stem cells reset identity. The work links RNA processing to cell fate.
plos-pone-0008519:
Otto Erlwein and co-authors test a claimed virus link in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. In October 2009, a study reported a new retrovirus in chronic fatigue syndrome. The virus, called XMRV, had also been linked to prostate cancer. It was reported in most US patients in that study. If confirmed, the claim would reshape understanding of the syndrome. Erlwein's team try to detect XMRV in their own patient group.

They fail to detect the novel retrovirus in chronic fatigue cases. Their methods were able to find the virus if present at reported levels. A negative result of this kind tempers a high-profile claim. It shows why independent replication is essential in science.
plos-pone-0008619:
Khatira Anwari and co-authors describe a membrane machine in a germ in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mitochondria, the power units of our cells, came from a free germ long ago. They still build their outer membrane much as that germ did. The germ studied here is Caulobacter crescentus, a model species. The team study its BAM complex. That machine inserts barrel-shaped proteins into the outer membrane.

They find the germ BAM complex is built from modules. Its modules echo the machine still used in mitochondria. Study of the germ version clarifies how mitochondria arose. It also reveals weak points in germ membranes that drugs could target.
plos-pone-0008719:
Soumyajit Banerjee Mustafi, Prabir Chakraborty, and Sanghamitra Raha traced how a grape compound attacks leukemia cells. Their work ran in PLOS ONE in 2010. Resveratrol is found in grape skins and red wine. It lowers levels of Hsp70, a protective protein, in chronic myelogenous leukemia cells. Lower Hsp70 helps push those cells to die. The route from compound to protein drop was unclear.

The team followed two signaling paths, Akt and ERK1/2, inside K562 leukemia cells. Resveratrol shifted both paths, and Hsp70 fell as a result. Mapping the route shows where similar drugs might strike leukemia cells.
plos-pone-0008819:
Koichi Matsumura, Maryanne Opiekun, Hiroaki Oka, and colleagues sniffed out lung cancer through urine odor. Their proof-of-principle study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lung cancer is the top cancer killer worldwide. It often grows silently until late stages. The body releases volatile compounds that change with disease. Breath studies had hinted such odor signatures exist.

Mouse models of lung cancer carried distinct urinary odor profiles. Trained detection could separate cancer urine from healthy urine. A urine test would be painless and cheap to repeat. Much work remains before human screening, but the principle held in mice.
plos-pone-0008919:
Martin Peifer, Jonathan Weiss, Martin Sos, and colleagues built a math method for judging drug pairs in fast cell screens. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Single cancer drugs often shrink tumors only briefly. Pairs of drugs can control tumors longer and better. Finding pairs that truly synergize, though, is slow. High-throughput screens test thousands of combinations on cells. Scoring synergy fairly across a whole population is the hard part.

Their lifetime modeling scores synergy from how cell populations fare over time. Population-level scoring resists the noise of single snapshots. Combination hunting for cancer drugs gets a sharper tool. Better pairs can reach animal testing sooner.
plos-pone-0009019:
Thomas Ray charted where psychedelic drugs attach across the whole human receptor set, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Psychedelics are thought to work mainly through two serotonin receptors, 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C. Drugs like the phenylalkylamines seem fairly choosy for those two. But a full census of their binding had not been assembled.

Ray mapped the drugs against the human receptorome, the full set of receptors. The chart shows which receptors each compound touches beyond the famous two. Some side targets may help explain differences between these drugs. A complete map warns against assuming one receptor explains the whole experience.
plos-pone-0009119:
Adriane Martin Hilber and co-authors pooled dozens of studies on vaginal practices and HIV risk, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many women use intravaginal practices to manage their health and sexual life. Cleansing the vagina and inserting substances are common in many regions. Such practices could harm the vaginal lining and invite infection, though.

The systematic review and meta-analysis asked two linked questions. Do these practices raise the rate of vaginal infections among women? And do they raise the chance of acquiring HIV during sex? Pooling the studies gives guidance that respects women's habits while cutting real risk.
plos-pone-0009219:
Santosh Kumar Patnaik, Eric Kannisto, and Sai Yendamuri published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces that fine-tune how genes are used. Some microRNAs show up at odd levels in cancer tissue. Two of them, miR-30a and miR-191, had been flagged that way in lung samples.

The team forced lung cells to make extra amounts of each microRNA. They used a lung cancer line, A549, and a normal lung line, BEAS-2B. Despite the extra microRNA, the cells' behavior and appearance did not change. That negative result matters: a microRNA can mark cancer tissue without driving the cancer itself.
plos-pone-0009319:
Alain Dejean and co-authors published this ant survey in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tropical rainforest canopies are often ruled by a patchwork of dominant ant species. Each holds its own trees and fights off the others, forming an ant mosaic. The team checked whether such a mosaic exists on Madagascar's Masoala Peninsula.

They surveyed tree-dwelling ants along three transects set farther and farther from the coast. They mapped which dominant species held which areas and where gaps appeared. An invasive ant species was also present in the forest. The survey gives a baseline for a coastline where native and invader ants now meet.
plos-pone-0009419:
Michael Hofreiter and co-authors published this ape diet study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bonobos and gorillas are hard to watch in dense forest. Their droppings, though, carry DNA that can betray what they ate. Earlier work had found vertebrate DNA in ape feces, which hinted at meat eating.

The team asked whether that DNA means real meat consumption or a lab artefact. They examined fecal samples from bonobos and gorillas for animal DNA. Sorting true diet from contamination matters because meat eating in apes bears on human evolution. The study tests how much trust to place in this detective method.
plos-pone-0009519:
Nicolas Maunoury and co-authors followed gene activity in root nodules in PLOS ONE in 2010. The plant Medicago truncatula hosts bacteria that turn air nitrogen into plant food. They meet in nodules, small organs on the roots. Inside, both plant cells and bacteria change into working partners. The team tracked gene switches across that change.

They found two big switch points in gene activity. Those switches keep plant cell growth and bacterial change in step. The picture shows how a partnership is choreographed at the gene level. Understanding it could help bring nitrogen fixing to more crops, cutting the need for fertilizer.
plos-pone-0009619:
Anna Divoli, Michael Wooldridge, and Marti Hearst tested a new way to search science papers in PLOS ONE in 2010. Biologists often judge a paper by its figures and captions. Standard search tools index mainly words in the text. The team built BioText, a search engine that also indexes full text with figures. They asked users to try real search tasks with each approach.

Showing full text and figures improved how well people found what they needed. Readers could judge relevance at a glance from images. The study gives evidence for a simple idea: search should match how scientists actually read. It points to richer displays as more than a cosmetic upgrade.
plos-pone-0009719:
An enzyme called IDE breaks down insulin and helps control its levels. Eun Suk Song, David Rodgers, and Louis Hersh studied a single-unit form of that enzyme. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Regulatory properties are the built-in controls that keep an enzyme from overworking.

The normal enzyme works as a pair of linked units. The single-unit, or monomeric, variant lost the regulatory properties the pair normally shows. Losing those controls reveals how much the paired shape matters. The finding explains how the enzyme keeps its activity in check.
plos-pone-0009819:
Brain cells under stress can digest parts of themselves to survive, a cleanup called autophagy. Belen Tizon and colleagues showed that a protein called cystatin C can switch that cleanup on. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The team worked with mouse primary cortical neurons and with neuronal cell lines. In both, cystatin C induced autophagy, and the cleanup protected the cells. Protection matters because neuron loss drives many brain diseases. A natural protein that triggers safe cleanup could inspire new treatments. Cortical neurons sit in the brain's outer layer, where thinking happens.
plos-pone-0009919:
Deep brain stimulation can ease Parkinson's movement problems, but it may also shift social thinking. Julie Péron and colleagues scanned patients to see how stimulation touches the theory of mind network. Their PET study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The target was the subthalamic nucleus, a small relay deep in the brain. Theory of mind is the skill of guessing what others think and feel. PET scans show which brain areas are active during tasks. The results warn that tuning movement circuits can ripple into social ones. The patients all had Parkinson's disease.
plos-pone-0010019:
Ram Gal and Frederic Libersat wrote in 2010 about a remarkable wasp. It turns a cockroach into live food for its young. The jewel wasp stings the cockroach in the head, sending venom into its brain. The prey is not paralyzed, yet it loses the will to walk away and can be led by its antenna.

The authors traced that effect to a brain region called the sub-esophageal ganglion, which helps drive walking. Venom changes nerve activity there, lowering the drive to move. The work shows, in fine detail, how a parasite can steer another animal's behavior from inside its nervous system.
plos-pone-0010119:
The authors were Oliver Weth, Christine Weth, Marek Bartkuhn, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study searched the genome for paired control sites. A protein called CTCF can insulate genes, blocking enhancers from switching on the wrong targets. Earlier work found CTCF paired with thyroid hormone receptor sites at two genes.

The team searched genome-wide for more of these composite elements. Finding them widely would suggest a modular system for organizing gene control. Such modules could explain how the same hormone signal affects some genes while leaving nearby genes untouched.
plos-pone-0010219:
The authors were Riviane da Hora, Jacques Delabie, Carolina dos Santos, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined queen fertility signals in an ant species. A wax layer on an insect's outer shell guards against water loss. In some social insects, wax also serves nest building, and ant queens handle wax in curious ways after mating.

In the ant Ectatomma tuberculatum, fertile queens show a distinctive wax pattern. The team raised glandular epithelium, a tissue layer under the shell, as a possible source. A chemical fertility signal from that layer would help workers recognize and care for their queen.
plos-pone-0010319:
Antonio V Borderia and colleagues track how weakened HIV viruses regain strength in a 2010 PLOS ONE lab study. Virus clones passed through single-cell bottlenecks lose fitness, meaning growth power. Passing them then through large populations lets fitness recover, a model of virus evolution.

After ten large passages, average fitness rose, though clones varied widely. Recovery was not matched by more viral protein output, and the shared genome text barely changed. Five populations fixed no mutation at all, yet some still gained fitness. What rose in step with fitness was variety within each virus swarm. Early recovery, the authors conclude, runs on swarm diversity, not a new master sequence.
plos-pone-0010419:
Laura Morelli and colleagues compared Y-chromosome data from Sardinia and Anatolia in PLOS ONE in 2010. Farming spread across Europe in the Neolithic age, transforming life. Two stories explain how: farmers themselves moved in, or local hunters adopted the new ways. The stories are called demic and cultural diffusion. Male-line DNA can help tell them apart, since it tracks men's movements.

Patterns in the two regions fit cultural spread better than mass migration. That suggests ideas traveled more than whole peoples did, at least on these routes. Sardinians and Anatolians thus inform a Europe-wide debate. Genes, here, act as travel records for ancient men. The verdict favors teaching and trade over invasion as farming's engine.
plos-pone-0010519:
Thomas Hofmann and colleagues showed a channel protein is vital for controlling magnesium in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Channels in the TRPM family do many jobs, from sensing to mineral balance. Most animals carry several members of this family; humans have eight. Flies are odd: they carry essentially one. That made the fly a clean test of what that single channel does.

Removing it disrupted the flies' control of magnesium outside their cells. Magnesium is a mineral every cell needs in tight amounts. A single-channel animal shows the channel's core job without backup systems hiding it. The work may clarify human mineral disorders linked to related channels. Simplicity, here, is the experiment's strength.
plos-pone-0010619:
Bo Hu and colleagues built a small artificial ecosystem in PLOS ONE in 2010. Natural microbe communities are too tangled to study piece by piece. The team instead assembled a simple synthetic community whose members react to their surroundings.

Each microbe strain played a defined role in the group. When conditions changed, the whole community shifted its behavior in response. That made the system a clean and useful test bed for basic ecology questions. Controlled communities like this could also serve industry, where mixed microbes already make fuels and chemicals. Its members were chosen, not found.
plos-pone-0010719:
Takashi Irie and colleagues dissected how Sendai virus dodges early immune defenses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sendai virus infects mice and is a close model for human respiratory viruses. Its C protein works at several steps of infection and blunts the interferon warning system.

A small set of charged building blocks in the C protein did much of that work. Changing them weakened the virus's ability to hide in cells and in mice. One protein thus juggles several tricks with the same toolkit. Mapping the toolkit shows where a weakened virus for vaccine study could be made more safely.
plos-pone-0010819:
Qian Wu and colleagues linked failed cell division to cancer signaling, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When a cell divides its body but fails to split in two, it ends with double chromosomes. Such cells appear in early cancers. A platelet protein called glycoprotein 1b alpha, targeted by the cancer gene c-Myc, was the team's focus in cultured human cells.

The protein connected division failure to known cancer-driving pathways. Cells with division errors switched those pathways on through it. A mechanical accident thus becomes a chemical growth signal. The link helps explain why chromosome-doubled cells so often turn malignant, and it names a protein where the chain might be cut.
plos-pone-0010919:
Glen Spraggon, Eric Koesema, Maria Scarselli and co-authors published this structural biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus pneumoniae, a major cause of pneumonia and meningitis, grips host cells with hair-like pili built from repeating protein units. The team reconstructed how the backbone protein, RrgB, locks together in those chains.

They combined electron microscope images of pilus pieces with an atomic crystal structure of most of RrgB, then fitted the two together. The fit shows neighboring units arranged in a single defined pattern, rather than a loose tangle. Spraggon and colleagues give the first clear picture of how this bacterial grappling hook is assembled. Such blueprints help vaccine designers, since pilus proteins are promising targets for preventing pneumococcal disease.
plos-pone-0011019:
Carla Palma, Silvia Vendetti and Antonio Cassone published this tuberculosis immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The CD4 T cells that secrete interferon-gamma protect against TB, yet uncontrolled amounts of the same response damage lungs and spoil vaccine protection. The authors found, in mice, a natural brake on that response operated by a different T cell class.

Two vaccination regimens against a TB antigen produced either a modest, protective response or a massive, non-protective one, and both generated CD8 T cells that suppressed the CD4 cells' interferon output. The receptor 4-1BB on those CD8 cells was central to their controlling role. Palma and colleagues identify a built-in thermostat for vaccine responses. Harnessing it could help TB vaccines stay protective instead of tipping into harm.
plos-pone-0011119:
Nakamura, Kinoshita, Yokoi and colleagues proposed a new cause of dry eye in PLOS ONE in 2010. People who work at screens all day often report dry, sore eyes. Blinking drops during screen use, but the authors pointed to another factor: weak tear glands.

They argued that the tear making glands underperform in many screen users, a state they call lacrimal hypofunction. Naming this mechanism widens dry eye care beyond drops and blink breaks. Treatments that restore gland function could help a growing group of patients. The study links a modern work habit to a specific, testable fault in the eye.
plos-pone-0011219:
Chambrion and Le Naour studied cell surface proteins in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells crawl using groups of surface proteins that work together. Two of these proteins, from the tetraspanin family, were tested for how they control the effects of a partner protein on cell migration.

Both proteins regulated how strongly the partner drove cells to move. That circuit matters because uncontrolled migration lets cancers spread through the body. A control circuit offers points where movement might be restrained by drugs. The finding informs metastasis research with specific, named members of the circuit.
plos-pone-0011419:
Lucy Parker and co-authors audited in 2010 the quality of studies that claim to diagnose disease from molecular fingerprints. Tests built on genomics and similar high-throughput methods promise much, but weak study design can make a test look far better than it is. A checklist tool called QUADOMICS was built to grade such studies, and the team put both the tool and recent papers to the test.

Their review of published diagnostic studies found common methodological holes, such as unclear patient selection and weak validation. The audit also judged how well the checklist itself catches those holes. The message is practical: journals and funders should require the checklist before a fingerprint test is celebrated. Patients are the ones harmed when a flawed test reaches the clinic, so quality control at the study stage is a form of patient protection.
plos-pone-0011519:
Rainer Lehmann and co-authors read the blood chemistry of exercising people in 2010 and found one molecule family in the lead. At a steady, moderate pace, the body shifts toward burning fat, and carrier molecules called acylcarnitines shuttle fat fuel into the cell's power stations. The team profiled these metabolites in people under moderate intensity exercise.

Medium-chain acylcarnitines dominated the metabolite pattern during exercise and supported continued lipid oxidation, the burning of fat. That lead pattern shows muscles switching fuel gears in an orderly way, not at random. The signature could serve as a marker of healthy fuel switching, which falters in diabetes and obesity. For fitness and metabolic medicine alike, the study turns the vague idea of fat burning into named molecules that rise on cue.
plos-pone-0011619:
Janine Quijano and co-authors studied gene signals that pattern the fruit fly wing, in PLOS ONE in 2010. One signal, called Wingless, helps lay out the wing as it grows. Another player, Sno, was already known to oppose a different growth signal in lab tests, but its true role in living animals was puzzling.

Working in developing fly wings, the team showed that Sno also pushes back against Wingless signalling. That opposition helps keep wing growth properly balanced. The finding adds a brake to a well-studied patterning system and may explain roles for the related genes in animal development more broadly.
plos-pone-0011719:
Victor Laguna-Torres and co-authors tracked respiratory viruses in Peru during the 2009 pandemic, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When the novel pandemic H1N1 influenza appeared, it entered a landscape already shared by other flu and flu-like viruses. The team sampled patients with influenza-like illness at health centres from January to July that year.

They describe how the mix of detected viruses changed before and after the pandemic strain arrived. The before-and-after picture shows the newcomer reshaping the viral landscape. Such tracking helps health systems anticipate which viruses will dominate once a pandemic strain takes hold.
plos-pone-0011819:
Alfredo Panebra and co-authors mapped how common gene patterns shape a drug-target receptor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The beta-2 adrenergic receptor sits on many cell types, from airway muscle to heart cells. Drugs that act on it treat asthma, lung disease and heart failure, yet how well they work shifts a lot from person to person.

The team built common patterns, called haplotypes, from twenty-six variable sites in the receptor gene and tested how each pattern steers receptor levels and control. The map helps explain why one inhaler dose can help one patient and barely touch the next, a step toward dosing by genes.
plos-pone-0011919:
Roby Greenwald and co-workers searched in 2010 for a breath signal of severe asthma in children. Children with severe asthma often keep having symptoms despite treatment, and their airways show high levels of oxidative stress. Oddly, their airways hold too little of S-nitrosothiols, natural compounds that relax airway muscle.

The team found that formate in exhaled breath marks that shortage. A breath test is painless and repeatable, unlike sampling airway fluid directly. If the marker holds up, doctors could follow a hidden part of asthma chemistry during clinic visits and judge whether treatments restore what severe airways are missing.
plos-pone-0012019:
Christopher Turbill and Thomas Ruf argued in 2010 that aging shapes the lives of long-lived mammals far more than those of short-lived ones. Senescence, the decline with age, is widely detected in mammals, but its importance for fitness in wild populations was disputed. Evolutionary theory predicts decline begins when natural selection grows weak, which tracks adult survival rates.

By that logic, long-lived species spend a large share of life in the zone where aging bites, while short-lived ones mostly die young from other causes. The argument reframes aging from a lab curiosity into a major ecological force for elephants, whales, and humans alike. It also tells field biologists where to look hardest for aging's effects.
plos-pone-0012119:
Federica Briatore, Annarita Patrizi, Laura Viltono, and colleagues mapped calming synapses in the mouse cerebellum for PLOS ONE in 2010. The cerebellum fine-tunes movement, and much of its surface layer works through inhibition, one cell quieting another. Small interneurons there send calming signals to the large output cells, to each other, and perhaps to other partners as well.

The team counted and measured these connections in fine detail, giving a firm map of where the calming contacts sit and how many there are. Counts like this are the ground truth that models of the cerebellum must match. They also help researchers spot what changes in diseases that disturb balance and coordination.
plos-pone-0012219:
Antonio Fasanella, Silvia Scasciamacchia, Giuliano Garofolo, and co-authors tested whether house flies can spread anthrax, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Anthrax spores survive for decades in soil, and past work suggested insects help carry them to animals and people during outbreaks. The common house fly feeds and walks on everything, making it a prime suspect as a living ferry for spores.

Their evaluation checks how well flies pick up, carry, and deposit the anthrax bacterium. Knowing the fly's true role decides whether outbreak response should include insect control or focus elsewhere. In farming regions where anthrax still strikes herds, that judgment protects both livelihoods and lives.
plos-pone-0012319:
Amber Carmon, Michael Guertin, Olga Grushko, and co-authors took apart mutations in one of the largest fly genes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The dumpy gene sprawls across seventy-eight coding segments and builds a huge protein of the matrix that surrounds cells, studded with repeating modules. Forty-five known mutations in this one gene offer a rare chance to connect each change in the DNA to a change in the animal.

Their molecular analysis maps where those mutations fall and what they do to the giant protein. Genes this size are hard to study whole, yet they matter: the human counterparts of such matrix proteins underlie many tissue diseases. The fly work shows how to read them.
plos-pone-0012419:
Mary Ann Comunale, Lucy Rodemich-Betesh, Julie Hafner and colleagues studied sugar tags on a blood protein as a liver cancer sign, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their earlier work showed that proteins gain extra fucose sugar tags as liver cancer develops. One tagged protein, alpha-1-antitrypsin, stood out, and the team checked one specific linkage of that sugar.

That linkage pattern marked patients with liver cirrhosis and cancer in a distinctive way. Blood tests for liver cancer are weak today, and many cases are found late. A sugar-based marker could join the short list of tools for catching liver cancer earlier, when treatment works far better.
plos-pone-0012519:
Laura Bonifacio and Michael Jarstfer profiled tiny RNAs in aging human skin cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Cells grown in the lab divide only so many times before senescence stops them, a guard against cancer that also models aging. Adding telomerase, the chromosome-end extender, lets cells bypass that stop, and extended culture alone also leaves marks.

The team compared microRNA profiles across young, senescent, long-cultured, and telomerase-rescued fibroblasts. Each state carried a distinct small-RNA fingerprint. Those fingerprints help separate true aging signals from mere time in a dish, a confusion that has misled aging research before.
plos-pone-0012619:
Quah-Smith, Sachdev, Wen and co-authors used brain scans to test laser acupuncture. In this method, a low laser beam replaces needles at set points on the body. It is used more and more for mental health problems, yet proof of a real brain effect was thin.

Their 2010 study scanned healthy volunteers while laser points linked to mood were stimulated. The scans showed patterns of brain activity that could make the treatment plausible, or fail to. Either way, imaging gives acupuncture claims a fair, measurable test. The work shows how old therapies can be checked with new tools.
plos-pone-0012719:
Wodarczyk, Distefano, Rowe and co-authors showed two kidney disease proteins working as a pair. Faults in the PKD1 gene cause the most common inherited kidney disease, in which cysts slowly wreck the kidneys. Its protein, polycystin-1, ends in a tail that earlier work linked to cell death control.

Their 2010 study found nephrocystin-1 joining polycystin-1 through a short matching motif. The pair then shapes how cells answer death signals. Two disease proteins acting together suggests their illnesses may share one pathway worth targeting.  Both genes were already tied to cystic kidney disorders in families.
plos-pone-0326719:
Hannah M Moloney and co-authors valued manta ray watching tourism in the Maldives in 2026. The island nation's rays draw divers from around the world, and putting a money figure on live rays strengthens the case against killing or degrading their habitat.

Surveys of more than one hundred tour operators, plus mined booking data, built the estimate. In 2021 manta tourism generated well over two hundred million dollars in total, split between direct trip spending and wider tourist spending. As the first national valuation, it hands policymakers a concrete counterweight when fishing or development interests press against ray protection.
plos-pone-0334819:
Parany and colleagues studied black rat genetics in a plague area of Madagascar in a 2026 paper. Rats carry the plague germ in the highlands, where the disease still returns. Nearly five hundred rats from six villages were sampled indoors and outdoors across two years and tested at many gene markers.

Village groups looked broadly similar, while outdoor rats carried more variety and mixed more freely. Overall separation between groups stayed low, meaning rats move widely and can quickly refill areas after culling. Killing rats alone is thus unlikely to hold, the authors argue. Pairing flea control inside homes with steps that cut contact between people and rats fits the biology better.
plos-pone-0336819:
Benjamin Schiek published a study on funding farm research in stages, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Agricultural research for development often proceeds step by step, from lab promise to field trials to wider release. Schiek treated each stage as an option: funders may continue, wait, or stop as evidence grows.

Using real option valuation, a tool borrowed from finance, Schiek priced that freedom to change course. The framework tells funders when early results justify doubling down and when a project should be paused or dropped. Development money is limited, so valuing the option to stop is as important as valuing success. The approach brings discipline to choices often made on hope or habit.
plos-pone-0344519:
Simon Beaufils, Lionel Cavin, and co-authors catalogued the bony fish fossils of the Vaches Noires cliffs in Normandy, a site famous in French paleontology since the seventeen hundreds. The mid-Jurassic fish remains are mostly fragments gathered over years by amateur collectors and kept in public collections. Their 2026 overview gives the first full account of the assemblage, naming each group and estimating body size and feeding level from living look-alikes.

The cliffs preserve a coelacanth, giant filter-feeding and predatory relatives of modern ray-finned fish, armored-scaled forms, and crushing-toothed pycnodonts represented by isolated jaw bones. Small backbones attest to little fish that rarely fossilize whole. The authors compare the assemblage with other Jurassic sites to trace how bony fish diversity and ecology evolved through the period.
plos-pone-0345719:
Sebastian Ruiz-Blais and colleagues separate singing from slow breathing in this brain study. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Toning means holding a sound through one long breath out. Therapists use such vocal work to calm people. No one knew if the voice itself mattered, or only the slow breath it forces.

People with no music training took part. They toned, sang slow songs they knew, and did matched breathing drills. Brain waves and heart rhythm were recorded through each task. The contrasts show which changes belong to making sound. They also show which belong to pacing the breath. If breath alone does the work, therapy can stay simple.
plos-pone-0345819:
Donna L Schuman and colleagues built and pilot-tested VET-SAVR, a virtual reality simulation. It trains people to spot suicide risk during home visits to rural veterans. This group has elevated suicide rates and thin access to specialists. Their 2026 feasibility study put thirty people through the headset scenario. They were nursing and social work students, health professionals, and rural community members. The scenario teaches risk recognition and counseling on securing lethal means.

Engagement ran high, the scene felt real, and nausea stayed low. Participants reliably recalled the loud cues, firearms and alcohol. They missed quieter ones like isolation. Most judged the simulation authentic. They asked for better navigation and interaction. The team calls it a feasible prototype needing polish before efficacy trials.
plos-pone-0346219:
Yasin Arafat and colleagues redesign a plasma jet that pulls nitrogen from air, aiming to cut the heavy energy cost of making fertilizer feedstock this way. Plasma methods could fix nitrogen locally without giant factories, but energy bills have blocked them. Their design swaps the usual water-based ground contact for a fixed grounded electrode and tunes gas mix and flow, checking the plasma's glow to confirm its state.

The fixed-ground version more than doubled output rate and cut energy cost to well under half of the water-ground version in matched runs. Output faded and costs shifted with longer treatment times in both setups. Arafat and colleagues present the electrode change as a concrete step toward plasma nitrogen fixing that farms could one day afford.
plos-pone-0346519:
Hanyu Cao and colleagues compared the muscle proteins of a prized Chinese pig breed with a common Western breed to learn why the local pork tastes better. Using advanced mass spectrometry on loin muscle, they catalogued hundreds of proteins differing between Huoshou black pigs and Yorkshire pigs, then cross-checked the standouts with two further methods.

Two hundred sixty-two proteins differed, clustering in metabolism, energy handling, and growth pathways. Five candidate genes emerged linking protein and gene activity to meat quality. The Western breed grows fast and lean; the Chinese breed's chemistry favours flavour and texture. The authors offer molecular targets for breeding programs that want both.
plos-pone-0347919:
Zeyu Zhu studies how the time people take to decide predicts their next move in a cooperation game, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Reanalyzing data from a network public goods experiment, he treats decision time as a sign of inner conflict: people torn between self-interest and the group deliberate longer.

Slow deciders were more likely to flip their choice in the next round. Among defectors, the fast ones were keener to form new social links, while fast cooperators shunned links with defectors more than slow cooperators did. Because thinking time is easy to observe, it could help design interventions that nudge networks toward cooperation without prying into motives.
plos-pone-0348019:
Lei Xie and Weiran Zhou modelled how city economies, energy use, and environmental quality push on each other over time. They upgraded a standard statistical tool, the vector autoregressive model, with an evolutionary search algorithm to track these moving relationships more faithfully. Their 2026 study draws on urban data to test which forces drive which.

The analysis found two-way influence between energy use and growth, yet energy consumption did not power growth over the long run. Energy's effect on environmental quality swung noticeably over time, while its effect on growth climbed steadily. The authors advise planners to build conservation and emissions cuts into development strategy from the start, rather than treating them as an afterthought.
plos-pone-0348119:
Anthony Train and colleagues traced inhaler prescribing for older adults in Ontario, Canada, from 2017 to 2023. Common puffers release strong warming gases, while dry powder and soft mist types pollute less when they fit the patient. Health records captured three quarters of a million new inhaler starts for people aged sixty five and older, split into before and during pandemic years.

New starts dropped sharply when the pandemic began, then recovered. Puffers stayed dominant, though their share fell from about seventy seven percent to about seventy percent. Powder types gained modest ground. Patterns barely differed by sex, income, or rural home. Greener switching, the authors note, remains slow despite clear climate guidance.
plos-pone-0348519:
Shravya Chitrapady and colleagues interviewed ten experienced physicians across India about diagnosing acute fevers in tropical settings and about artificial intelligence help. Dengue, scrub typhus, and leptospirosis can look nearly identical at first, yet need different treatment, and lab tools are often limited. The doctors described where their judgment gets stuck.

Interviews were recorded, transcribed, and sorted into themes. Physicians weighed the promise of an AI diagnostic aid against the messy reality of overlapping symptoms and scarce tests. Their views matter because a tool doctors distrust or cannot fit into ward routines will sit unused, however accurate it is. The study feeds those practical concerns into design.
plos-pone-0348719:
Luhang Yu and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One deep learning paper on lung tumors. It outlines tumors in ordinary two-dimensional CT slices. Fuzzy borders and odd shapes make that task hard. Their system adds two ideas to a standard backbone. One module treats the tumor edge as uncertain. It samples around a likely boundary. The other nudges outlines toward smooth, plausible shapes, using rules on curvature and compactness.

On two lung cancer datasets, the system beat classic models and mainstream transformer tools on overlap scores. Its boundaries sat much closer to expert outlines than the backbone's alone. The authors argue that handling doubt and shape openly makes tumor maps more trustworthy. Such maps could aid diagnosis and treatment checks. The method needs no extra annotations from experts.
plos-pone-0348819:
Qiufeng Jia and colleagues probed ten leading AI language models for hidden bias in medical decisions. Models can pass open bias tests while still carrying quiet associations between social groups and traits. The team built twenty-four medical test sets spanning gender, race, wealth, health status, religion, and health systems, then measured bias three ways, including word association and comparative decision tasks.

The evaluation covers both commercial systems and open models from several countries. Implicit bias in a tool that drafts advice or triages patients could steer real care unfairly, even when no explicit prejudice appears. A multi-method audit like this shows where the associations live and how strongly they move decisions, giving developers and hospitals concrete targets for correction.
plos-pone-0348919:
Sydney P Harned leads a team of five testing how well fish genetics can guide flounder management, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Southern flounder, a prized flatfish, is declining along the southeastern United States coast. Managers need to know whether local groups are separate stocks, and earlier snapshots may mislead. The team sequenced young flounder from estuaries in North Carolina and Texas across a decade, 2014 to 2023, using a genome sampling technique that reads many scattered markers.

Fish from the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic differed clearly and consistently, supporting management as distinct stocks. Inside each region, though, genetic differences between nearby estuaries appeared and vanished from year to year, likely as shifting larval drift and uneven recruitment reshuffled each year's youngsters. The lesson is methodological as much as biological: one season's sample can paint structure that the next season erases.
plos-pone-0349019:
Mizanur Rahaman and co-authors made a new electrode material for supercapacitors, devices that charge and discharge far faster than batteries. They grew tiny particles of manganese sulfide inside molybdenum oxide using hot water synthesis. The particles changed the oxide's shape from flat belts to rough fibres, opened wider gaps between its layers, and left a defect-rich surface with much more room for charge to gather.

Electrodes built from the mix stored clearly more charge than the plain oxide in both salt solutions tested. A full two-electrode cell kept about nine tenths of its capacity after a thousand charge cycles. The authors credit the larger surface and wider layers, and they offer the material as a practical step toward faster, longer-lasting energy storage.
plos-pone-0349219:
Bhola Teli and co-authors surveyed first-year engineering students at a Nepali university campus about blood donation, a lifeline that low-income health systems struggle to keep supplied. Their 2026 study questioned one hundred ninety-one students on knowledge, attitudes, and actual giving, then modeled what separates donors from non-donors.

Attitudes were warm: students scored favorably and knew a fair amount. Yet under seventeen percent had ever donated. Women knew more than men, but men were far more likely to have given blood, as were students aged twenty and over. Civil engineering students donated least among the programs. The commonest barriers were having no particular reason and never getting the chance. The authors name this a knowledge-practice gap and suggest campus drives that convert goodwill into appointments.
plos-pone-0349619:
Ahyoung Chang, Seung Gyu Baik, and Junfeng Jiao studied how surroundings shape electric car charging experiences in Travis County, Texas, in 2026. A charger can work perfectly yet still feel poor if the spot is bleak, hard to reach, or short on parking.

More than four thousand user reviews were sorted by language models into themes like operation, access, and parking, then matched to place data. Walkability, greenery, openness, and nearby amenities predicted happy reviews most strongly. Frustrations with access and parking clustered in dense commercial zones. Planners are urged to site chargers as places, not just power points.
plos-pone-0349819:
Jun Ho Lee led a study of kidney stones and uric acid in Korea. Uric acid is best known for gout, a joint disease. The team asked if high uric acid, with no gout signs, still tracks with stones. They used checkup records for more than thirty-one thousand adults. Stones were found by scans. The math split men and women and stripped out other risks step by step.

For men, the link held firm at each step. Men in the top uric acid group had more than three times the stone odds of the lowest group. For women, no clear link showed at all. The team calls this a sex-split pattern. They warn that one check in time cannot prove cause.
plos-pone-0350019:
Aniek E M Schouten and co-authors tested a quiet choice that can sway whether a treatment looks worth its cost. Health economists convert quality-of-life survey answers into scores using value sets, and each European country has its own. Their 2026 study re-ran cost analyses from two multinational trials, one on exercise for breast cancer patients and one on a kidney treatment, swapping value sets across countries.

The same answers produced noticeably different scores and health gains depending on which country's values were applied, and the gaps grew when patients reported poor quality of life. Odds that a treatment counted as cost-effective shifted by up to about eleven percentage points. The authors advise testing several value sets in multinational studies instead of trusting just one.
plos-pone-0350119:
Eugenio Trotta, Paola Palladino, and co-authors pooled the evidence on how memory, feelings, and the teacher relationship shape young children's learning of a second language. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathered nineteen studies of primary school pupils, covering more than five thousand children, with sixteen studies feeding the combined statistics.

Working memory correlated positively with language learning, the clearest cognitive signal. Among emotions, anxiety dragged learning down significantly while enjoyment nudged it up slightly. Evidence on the student-teacher relationship was qualitative only, but it consistently suggested that emotional closeness to a teacher buffers children against anxiety during language learning. The authors call for more research on positive emotions and classroom relationships across different school settings.
plos-pone-0350219:
Quanwei Shen, Lin Li, and Chenglong Li surveyed six hundred college students in Hubei Province, China, in 2026 about heavy smartphone use. They asked whether self-control lowers phone dependence directly, or through traits such as mental toughness and ease in social life.

Students with stronger self-control reported less phone dependence, as did tougher and more socially at ease students. Social ease carried part of the effect on its own, and toughness and social ease also worked as a chain between self-control and phone habits. The authors suggest colleges build students' confidence in facing problems, not just warn them about screen time.
plos-pone-0350419:
Mohammed Nasir, Bereket Tessema, and Sura Markos checked how often babies born with a spinal defect also have heart defects at an Ethiopian hospital in 2026. The two conditions share early development pathways, yet African data were thin.

Charts for two hundred sixty-five infants with the spinal defect, all scanned by ultrasound of the heart, were reviewed. About seven in a hundred had a heart defect too. A mother's past miscarriage, overweight, and diabetes each raised the odds. The rate is lower than many might fear, but the linked factors argue for routine heart checks in these newborns.
plos-pone-0350919:
Bacteria that shrug off antibiotics thrive where people and farm animals live close together. Amit R Nayak and colleagues lay out a three-year study plan for Nagpur, India, in this 2026 PLOS One protocol, tracking resistant germs across livestock, farm workers, and the farm environment.

Six important bacterial species will be sampled with the seasons, and their drug resistance profiles recorded. The team also plans to study bacteria-killing viruses, called phages, as possible treatments. No results are reported yet. The design follows the One Health idea that human, animal, and environmental health form one connected system.
plos-pone-0351119:
Xu and colleagues measured airway stiffness in scarred lungs with a light-based probe in a 2026 study. Lung scarring stiffens airways, but standard tests measure the whole lung at once. A thin probe passed into the airways recorded how airway area changed as pressure rose, in healthy volunteers and patients with scarring.

Deeper airway branches in patients tended to show lower stretch than in healthy people. One branch's stretch tracked closely with standard breathing test results. Local stiffness measures could one day spot scarring earlier or follow treatment branch by branch. The small group size makes this a proof of method rather than a clinical rule.
plos-pone-0351219:
A sudden loss of blood flow to the optic nerve, unrelated to artery inflammation, can permanently narrow vision. Heejin Yoon and colleagues reviewed thirty-eight patients to find which early signs predict whether the visual field recovers, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

About a quarter of the eyes regained a meaningful slice of field within three months. Those eyes started with sharper vision, milder field loss, and lower blood sugar levels. Eye drops sometimes prescribed showed no link to recovery. Starting vision also strongly predicted vision months later. The authors say the baseline picture, taken at the first visit, already carries most of the prognosis.
plos-pone-0351319:
Sowmya Pujari and colleagues interviewed twenty mothers from the Koraga tribe of southern Karnataka, India, about how they understand health and feed their young children. The Koraga face deep poverty and poor access to care, and their children carry high rates of undernutrition. Book knowledge of malnutrition rarely explains what mothers actually see and do, so the team listened at length, in the mothers' own languages.

Five themes came out of the conversations, covering changing ideas of health and well-being, beliefs and habits around food, and hygiene and care practices. The accounts show mothers reasoning with what they have, mixing older custom with newer clinic advice. For nutrition programs, the lesson is that messages land only when they fit this local logic, and that mothers here are partners to consult, not empty vessels to fill.
plos-pone-0351819: Vasilikos and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on making a brain covering tissue stronger with light. They used riboflavin, a vitamin, plus UVA light to crosslink collagen in cow dura mater taken from the body. The title reports a controlled, dose-based rise in the tissue's fine-scale strength. Stronger repair tissue could help surgeons patch the membrane that wraps the brain.
plos-pone-0352019:
Luiz Pimenta and three colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One laboratory comparison of toothbrush types on denture teeth. Bioelectric brushes use a mild current meant to loosen plaque with gentler scrubbing, but their effect on denture wear was unknown. Thirty-six acrylic denture teeth were machine-brushed for the equivalent of about two years of home cleaning, with a manual brush, the bioelectric brush switched off, or the same brush switched on.

Manual and switched-off brushing roughened the acrylic noticeably, while the switched-on brush caused a smaller, statistically insignificant change and left visibly shallower scratches. No group lost measurable weight. Within the limits of a bench model, the authors conclude the active bioelectric brush is kinder to denture surfaces, pending confirmation in real mouths.
plos-pone-0352119:
Abdi, Bayat, and Mowla studied two tiny gene regulators in the deadliest brain tumor in a 2026 paper. Across ten public data sets, one regulator ran high in tumors while the other ran low, compared with healthy brain. Cell experiments confirmed the same opposing pattern in two tumor cell lines.

Raising the low regulator lowered the high one and raised several of its known target genes. Tumor cell behavior shifted as well, including more cell death. The authors are careful: the link looks functional, not a proven direct binding. Still, restoring the low regulator could be a lever worth testing against a cancer with very few options.
plos-pone-0352319:
Brandyn Churchill, Xiaoxue Gao, and Rong Rong ran a vaccine information experiment during the 2024 election season, reported in PLOS ONE in 2026. They recruited nearly three hundred Democrats and a similar number of Republicans in the United States. Participants first estimated COVID-19 infection rates, severity, and vaccination levels, then some learned the true figures and reported whether they now intended to get vaccinated.

Both camps overestimated how common and severe infections were, and how many people were vaccinated — and neither side knew its own party's experience best. The striking result: people who learned they had underestimated the other party's vaccination rate became more willing to vaccinate themselves. Rivalry, it seems, can be turned toward health.
plos-pone-0352419:
Kyle Messick and seven co-authors surveyed users of generative artificial intelligence in 2026 about dishonest uses of the technology. The survey covered everything from cheating on schoolwork to misleading people online. Earlier research usually looked at one setting at a time. This study asked whether bad behaviour in one area of life carries into others, and what drives it.

People who used AI unethically in one domain tended to do so in others, and most knew their behaviour was wrong. Misuse was linked with pressure to get results, time pressure, and a feeling that everyone does it and nobody is punished. A wish for social media fame and narcissistic traits also played a part, while self-esteem and loneliness showed no link, which helps target future prevention efforts.
plos-pone-0353119:
Zouzoulas and colleagues laid out a trial plan in 2026 for early, mild cell changes on the cervix. Most such changes clear on their own, so standard care is watching and waiting. The trial tests whether a plant-based supplement that supports immunity helps more changes clear within six months.

Patients with newly confirmed mild changes will be assigned by chance to supplement or watchful waiting alone. Clearance rates will then be compared between the two groups. People with any past cervical changes or pelvic cancer are excluded. If the supplement helps, some patients could avoid long anxious monitoring, though results must come before any such claim is made.
plos-pone-0353219:
Yuhao Wang, Junjie Huang, and Qiang Zhang present this 2026 PLOS One paper on elevator repair. They teach a small language model to diagnose faults and guide upkeep before breakdowns. General models struggle in this niche. They invent answers, lack trade knowledge, and cannot read raw sensor numbers. The team fine-tuned a compact model with step-by-step examples written in varied user styles. They also turned sensor readings into text the model could reason over.

The tuned model gave diagnostic answers far better than a leading general model. Its inner patterns also sorted alarm types well. It predicted vibration levels with skill too. The authors argue that for narrow trade jobs, dense domain training beats raw model size. Small tuned models, they say, offer a cheaper path to automated upkeep advice.
plos-pone-0353519:
Bogale and colleagues, in a 2026 study, report lessons from an effort to strengthen primary health care across Ethiopia. The national Health Extension Program sends community health workers into remote areas, and an optimization project tested new delivery strategies in fourteen districts. Researchers were embedded with the teams, so strategies could be adapted to local conditions while keeping their core intact.

Adaptations were tracked as they happened, and fidelity to the plan's core was monitored across two and a half years. The authors report that adapting strategies to place and culture went together with better coverage of mother and child services. Referral links between clinics strengthened through networks of care, and services were reshaped for pastoralist communities that move with their herds. The paper's wider point is about balance: programs should bend to fit local life without bending so far that the active ingredient is lost.
plos-pone-0354019:
Adegboyega and colleagues, in a 2026 hospital study in Ilesa, southwestern Nigeria, look at how family life shapes the care of small children with malaria. Malaria still harms many children under five, and late or wrong first steps raise the risk of a bad outcome. Family support, income, and how well a family functions may all steer those first steps.

About three hundred fifty child and caregiver pairs took part.
