Most caregivers reported strong family support and a well-functioning family, though more than half lived below the study's poverty line. Even so, fewer than half sought care in the way the team judged appropriate. Caregivers from poorer families had about two and a half times the odds of poor care-seeking. Those from families that functioned poorly had about four times the odds. The authors argue that malaria programs should strengthen families and counsel caregivers, not just hand out medicine.
plos-pone-0354119:
Ying-Ai Cui and three colleagues surveyed unvaccinated medical students in China about the HPV vaccine, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The vaccine prevents cancers caused by human papillomavirus, yet uptake among Chinese students stays low. More than thirty-five hundred students at Guangdong Medical University answered questions on hesitancy and health beliefs in the summer of 2024.

Nearly three quarters said they intended to be vaccinated. Men were far less willing than women, while students who heard about the vaccine from doctors were more willing. Believing vaccination necessary, important, and beneficial all raised intention. The authors suggest clinician-led teaching in the curriculum and support aimed at male students, whom current services barely reach.
plos-pone-0354519:
Hanh Truong and co-authors make in 2026 a light activated material meant to fight rice blast, a fungus that devastates rice. The material joins a common white pigment with copper in two chemical states, made by a precipitation route. Under visible light from lamps, the copper cycle helps produce aggressive oxygen based particles that stress the fungus.

The version with the most copper blocked fungal growth most strongly after ten days, well above versions with less copper. Light tests confirmed the material absorbed more visible light than the plain pigment. The authors say field value and safety for nature still need checking before farm use.
plos-pone-0354619:
Zewudu Mulatie led a team of eight authors on this 2026 systematic review of warning flags from automated blood analyzers. These machines flag odd cell patterns that can signal blood cancers such as leukemia or lymphoma. The reviewers pooled accuracy studies from several databases and graded their quality with a standard tool.

Across the pooled studies, the flags worked well as a first screen for blood cancers. Results varied, though, because machines, flag types, and comparison tests differed between labs. Mulatie sees the flags as most valuable where budgets are tight and a fast, cheap early warning matters most.
plos-pone-0354719:
Xiuli Cheng and five colleagues published this 2026 mouse study asking whether glutamate, a common food and signaling chemical, worsens artery clogging. Mice bred to develop atherosclerosis ate normal or fatty diets, with or without added glutamate, for three months. Plaques were stained and measured, and protein profiles hunted for molecules that changed with the combination.

Glutamate alone caused almost no plaque, but paired with a rich fatty diet it enlarged lesions and raised three proteins. Cheng notes blood glutamate itself did not rise, so changes in blood fats may also share the blame.
plos-pone-0354819:
Minyeong Cho and colleagues compare in 2026 three forms of a receptor that guides immune cells toward lymph organs and can aid cancer spread. The forms differ at one end and arise from how the gene message is cut and rejoined. The team cloned each form and tested where it sits in the cell, how it signals, and how forms interact when present together.

One form reached the cell surface well and signalled strongly to both known guide chemicals. A second form barely reached the surface and gave weaker, narrower signals. The third never signalled, bound tightly to the first, and dragged it inside the cell, cutting its responses. Breast cancer cells carrying both forms failed to migrate toward the guides.
plos-pone-0354919:
Bahia Abdallah, Abir Abdel Rahman, Safoura Zangiabadi, and Hala Tamim studied 398 Syrian refugee parents who resettled in Ontario, Canada after 2015 and reported good physical health. Their 2026 cross-sectional study measured depression, anxiety, stress, and post-traumatic stress with standard scales, then compared the scores against how well each family functioned day to day.

Struggling family functioning tracked closely with higher anxiety, stress, and post-traumatic stress, though not with depression. Poorer parents also carried heavier depression, anxiety, and stress. Fathers showed a slight trend toward worse anxiety than mothers. The findings suggest refugee support programs should treat the family's daily functioning and finances as part of mental health care, not as separate problems.
plos-pone-0355219:
Correction notice: Zhonghan Wu and seven colleagues published this 2026 correction in PLOS One. It fixes parts of their earlier study of a wrist-assisted nail implant for hip fractures in obese patients with weak bones. It is not a new study. The notice replaces two methods sections and the first three tables, whose statistics were wrong.

The corrected text describes a backward-looking cohort at a hospital in Anhui, China, covering patients treated in 2022 and 2023, with a year of follow-up checks. Five hundred patients appear in the corrected tables, split evenly between the new implant and a comparison group. Readers should use these values, not the originals.
plos-pone-0355719:
Zhiyuan Mao and co-authors turned fine mine tailings, a powdery waste, into the main ingredient of a water-blocking barrier material. Cement-bentonite walls resist chemical attack poorly, and earlier tailing mixes used tailings only as minor filler. Their 2026 recipe blends full tailings with cement, bentonite clay, and sodium silicate, tuned by single-factor tests.

Raw tailings leaked water roughly a thousand times faster than the modified mixes. Adding cement at fixed clay content raised strength greatly, though it let slightly more water through. Adding clay at fixed cement steadily sealed the material tighter. Microscope scans tied performance to pore structure. Mao and colleagues present the mix for dam and waste-site sealing jobs.
plos-pone-0356419:
Anton Björnqvist and four colleagues test whether strategy mapping software can help healthcare staff evaluate their own crisis management, in this 2026 Swedish case study. Fifteen healthcare professionals worked through a four-step workshop series, using the software to lay out causes, effects, and priorities from their crisis experience. The process produced ten recommendations aimed at the risks the group judged most central.

About a year later, the researchers interviewed ten participants about what had stuck. The evaluation was judged impactful, and participants still valued the process, especially rating and ranking the recommendations together. One lesson was that facilitators may need a stronger hand in sharpening recommendations so they stay clear and actionable. The authors offer the approach as a workable template for organizations that want frontline staff, not just managers, to draw the lessons from a crisis.
plos-pone-0356619:
Fumitaka Yanase and colleagues published a 2026 randomized trial in PLOS ONE comparing two drip fluids given during major abdominal surgery. Anesthesiologists routinely use compound sodium lactate, but a bicarbonate-buffered fluid avoids adding lactate and might suit high-risk patients better. Fifty adults having elective major abdominal surgery were randomized to one fluid or the other; the main measure was an acid-base number at skin closure.

The trial was designed to show the bicarbonate fluid was not worse by more than a preset margin. It could not: the confidence range for the difference dipped just below that margin in both analyses, so non-inferiority went unproven. One secondary signal favored bicarbonate, with lower blood lactate at surgery's end, but acidity measures did not differ. The result is reported plainly as inconclusive on the main question, in a small trial, with the lactate finding exploratory.
plos-pone-0356719:
Vadim A Bakalin and fellow botanists revise a small genus of liverworts, tiny leafy plants of damp forests, across eastern Indochina. Their 2026 review sorts out six species in the region using both plant form and gene data gathered from many field sites. One species described as new comes from a high plateau in Vietnam's Central Highlands, while an old record from Thailand turned out to rest on a wrong identification.

Two other species were found in Cambodia for the first time, and the region's most common member proved widespread along Vietnam's mountain spine. Gene results also moved two species into a different subgroup than books had claimed. Bakalin and colleagues note the genus never showed its reproductive stage in the region, hinting at strong sensitivity to forest damage.
plos-pone-0356919:
Haoyu Wang led a team of seven authors studying bacteria-killing viruses on surfaces, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These viruses, called phages, must move across a surface to reach the bacteria they kill. The team asked how the surface's shape and texture change that movement, and with it the phages' killing power.

Wang's group showed that surface form does modulate phage mobility, and that potency shifts with it. Designers of phage therapies and antibacterial coatings can use that physics: a surface that helps phages spread may clear bacteria faster. As drug-resistant infections grow, phage tools are drawing fresh interest. This study adds a practical design rule for making them work outside a liquid test tube.
plos-pone-0357019:
Hoan Manh Vu and colleagues published a 2026 surgical study in PLOS ONE on a rare pancreatic tumor in children, the solid pseudopapillary neoplasm. Surgeons must clear the tumor while sparing as much working pancreas as they can. The team reviewed every child operated on for this tumor at a tertiary hospital over four years, tracking tumor position, operation, complications, and later function.

Just over thirty children were treated, mostly girls around eleven, usually presenting with abdominal pain. Tumors sat in the head of the pancreas in just under half, and tissue-sparing operations were used in nearly three in five cases. Early complications clustered in head tumors, including one severe leak needing reoperation, but no child died. One recurrence followed a margin-positive sparing operation and was cured by fuller surgery. No child developed lasting hormone problems, and temporary digestive trouble always resolved. A selective tissue-sparing strategy is backed.
plos-pone-0357119:
Di Tang and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for a twelve-week randomized trial. It asks whether exercise training improves performance in competitive first-person shooter gaming. It also asks which kind of training works better. The planned study will assign 195 gamers aged eighteen to twenty-nine to one of three groups. They are high-intensity interval training, steady moderate training, and a control group, with three sessions weekly.

The main measure is flicking capacity, the snap-aiming skill at the heart of shooter play. Other gaming metrics back it up. So do psychological skills, body composition, and physical fitness. All are rechecked four weeks after training ends, to see whether gains persist. Esports science has mostly tested single workouts. A three-month, three-arm trial would give players and coaches their first durable training guidance.
plos-pone-0357819:
Lauma Spriņģe and coauthors published a 2026 cross-sectional study in PLOS ONE on how well women in Latvia follow the national cervical cancer screening program, which invites screening every three years. Both screening too rarely and too often can cause harm, so the team surveyed nearly thirteen hundred women aged twenty-five to seventy about their screening history, health, habits, and program knowledge.

One pattern dominated: women who did not know the program's recommended interval were far more likely to be overscreened, underscreened, or unable to recall their screening history at all. Overscreening also clustered among women recruited through a colposcopy clinic, where follow-up care blurs into extra screening. Other health behaviors and background factors mattered less than simple awareness of the rules. Teaching women the right interval, and why more is not always better, they argue, is the cheapest fix for both kinds of non-compliance.
plos-pone-0357919:
Juan Carlos Suárez, Amara Tatiana Contreras, and Idupulapati M. Rao published a 2026 plant study in PLOS ONE on tepary bean, a hardy legume, grown under the acidic soils and heat of the Colombian Amazon. They wanted a fair score for how well different bean lines keep photosynthesizing when light, heat, and water stress damage the process. The team grew several hundred accessions in fields and screenhouses, under watered and droughted conditions, and measured their leaves at dawn and midday.

Their stress tolerance index split the collection into five adaptation groups, from highly adapted to very poorly adapted, with most lines in the weaker half. Three accessions stood out, pairing top index scores with thick, chlorophyll-rich leaves and strong photosynthetic efficiency under stress. Those three are nominated as parents for breeding climate-resilient beans for the western Amazon, pending yield trials to confirm their farm value.
plos-pone-0358219:
Tyler Weide and three colleagues compared groups of sperm by their energy organelles, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Not all sperm in a sample are alike. The team sorted sperm by how many mitochondria each carries, the tiny structures that power the cell, and then compared the nuclear genes in each group.

Weide's group found that the groups differ in their nuclear allele frequencies, the mix of gene variants they carry. That link between energy supply and nuclear makeup hints at hidden sorting in the race to fertilize. Fertility science cares because sperm quality checks now rely on crude measures. A deeper trait like this could refine how samples are judged in clinics and livestock breeding.
plos-pone-0359319: Carvelli and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on what one missing enzyme does to tissue in adult male mice. The enzyme, shortened to NAGLU, normally helps break down complex sugars. Without it, guard cells and lining cells in the epididymis, a tube in the male reproductive tract, showed damage under fine-scale viewing. The work links a rare disease enzyme to fertility-related tissue.
plos-pone-0359419: Li and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on tiny blood vessels in people with chronic kidney disease. The patients were not on dialysis. Looking at the nailfold under a microscope shows the smallest vessels clearly. The team checked which of those vessel signs track with how badly the kidneys fail. A painless peek at the nailfold could one day flag kidney decline early.
plos-pone-0359619: Abrha and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on children recovering from severe malnutrition in Tigray, Northern Ethiopia. The children, aged six to fifty-nine months, were treated in outpatient programs in Adet Woreda. The team measured how long recovery took and what predicted it. Their records-based design looked back at past cases. Knowing what slows recovery helps clinics save more children with the same supplies.
plos-pone-0359719:
Qing Cui and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on intensive care. It is a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV database of critical care records. The authors examine early arterial oxygen tension after a line is inserted, and whether it is associated with documented acute thrombosis, blood clots in the upper body or central veins.

Critically ill adults often receive deep lines in the neck or chest, and clots are a known hazard of those lines. An early oxygen reading that flags clot risk would be a cheap warning sign. Intensive care teams are the readers who would weigh this association before changing monitoring practice.
pmc-10661919:
Sanjay Shinde, Michael Wombeogo, and Milka Madhale write a letter on nursing care for HIV-positive men in Indonesia. Their letter, from twenty twenty-three, responds to a study by Kurniawan and co-authors. They praise the study's clear themes on nurse skills, talk, and continuity of care. They also say the study's frame is too narrow.

Families carry much home care for people with HIV, yet the study skips their role. The letter lists wider needs, like safety gear and transport for home visits. Pay for nurses in hospital and home care also matters, they argue. Support for family carers at community level rounds out their call.
pmc-10672219:
Natalia Carasek and colleagues reported an ear surgery case in 2023. Two growths affected the same ear of one woman. One was a skin-like growth in the middle ear. The other was a benign tumor on the hearing nerve. The pairing is rare and hard to treat. Hearing loss is the central problem in such cases. No prior study described a combined operation for both. The team removed both lesions in one surgical plan. They then fitted a cochlear implant in the same ear.

The operation cleared both lesions successfully. The hearing nerve and inner ear were preserved. The implant later improved the patient's hearing test results. Gains showed in both quiet and noisy settings. The authors present the sequence as a workable route. It joins tumor removal with hearing restoration in one path. The case may guide surgeons who face this rare pairing.
pmc-10695519:
Mingfeng Lee and co-authors checked in 2023 how the world's most common primary kidney filter disease, IgA nephropathy, changes its face with ethnicity. The disease deposits immunoglobulin An in the glomeruli and is a leading road to kidney failure, yet its rate, presentation, and outlook all vary by group. Incidence runs highest in Asia, then Europe, and lowest in Africa, a gradient the authors document beside gaps in biopsy appearance.

Asian patients more often show acute, aggressive lesions in kidney tissue and fare worse renally than Caucasian patients. While some comorbidity patterns run the other way, with gastrointestinal associations noted more in Europe. Genetics tracks the geography: a worked out genetic risk score is highest in Asians, intermediate in Europeans, and lowest in Africans. The review weighs how much of the ethnic variance is inherited background and how much is setting and practice.
pmc-10696819:
Silas Onyango and six colleagues study how mothers' play and talk with babies links to child development in Kenya and Zambia, in a twenty twenty-three paper. Many children in poor countries miss their growth potential from poor health, poor food, and too little stimulation. The team followed children at about ten, twenty-five, and thirty-six months of age. Mothers' activities were grouped into thinking, language, movement, and social kinds.

Higher overall stimulation scores linked to better development scores at each round. Certain activity types predicted growth more strongly than others. The authors say parent stimulation is one of the strongest known levers for early development, yet proof in Africa was thin before this study.
pmc-10712919:
Francisco Paulo Ponte Prado, Ivens Filizola Soares Machado, and five colleagues report results of an endoscopic treatment for achalasia in this two thousand twenty-three study. Achalasia is a gullet disorder causing hard swallowing and regurgitation, with no cure; treatments ease the lower gullet sphincter's grip. Peroral endoscopic myotomy cuts that muscle from inside the gullet, through the mouth, with no outside cuts. The team studied ninety-four patients treated at a reference center over six years under a set protocol.

Only three patients had problems after the procedure. Symptom scores on the Eckardt scale rose by roughly seven points soon after and stayed much better later. The authors conclude the method can be copied with a strong safety record, clear symptom relief, better gullet emptying, and better quality of life in the short term. The study adds real-world data from Brazil.
pmc-10729219:
Fang Yao and nine co-authors published a cardiology study in twenty twenty-three on two kinds of hidden fat and the heart's quiet decline, in over fifteen hundred adults from Danyang, China. Fat around the heart and fat deep in the belly were each measured, one by ultrasound and one by electrical impedance, alongside sensitive ultrasound tests of heart function.

Men carried more belly fat but less heart fat than women, an instructive split. Both depots correlated with measures of subclinical dysfunction, the stage before symptoms. Speckle-tracking imaging caught the subtle strain changes involved. The authors argue the two fat pools are not interchangeable risks. Screening either alone would miss part of the metabolic threat to the heart.
pmc-10736519:
William Windham and seven co-authors compare body function in Black and White older adults in two thousand twenty-three. Black older adults tend to score worse on tests of walking and balance. Heart and vessel risks are more common in Black adults and may play a part. The team used a short battery of body tests in a large heart study.

They studied thousands of adults over age sixty-five at one visit. Black adults scored more than a point lower than White adults. Adding heart risks to the model did not shrink the gap. The authors say other forces must be at play. They call for work on place, social life, and long term risk.
pmc-10736619:
Khushbu Patel, Deneisha Scott-Poe, and Megan Dolbin-MacNab study what forecasts how well grandfamilies work as a unit, where grandparents raise grandkids. Millions of US grandparents raise grandchildren, yet most past work looks at each person's health alone. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

Guided by family systems and bonding theories, the team surveyed custodial grandmothers raising teens in the US South. Models were built in steps, adding the child's sex, then the grandmother's stress and bonding, then the child's bonding, mood control, and behavior issues. Stress in parenting stood out, with lower stress tied to better family function. The child's traits were added last to test their extra weight.
pmc-10737219:
Navin Kaushal, Donya Nemati, and Thomas Best hunt for what predicts movement in older adults with bad knees. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, uses a large knee arthritis dataset. Regular activity guards against disability in this group, yet many stay inactive. The team sorts possible drivers into body, mind, and social buckets.

More than thirteen hundred adults aged sixty-five and up enter the analysis. Motion trackers follow activity over two years. Twenty-one candidate factors link to activity change at first pass. A layered model then tests which hold up together. Four stand out as the strongest signals. Knowing them could target help for inactive patients.
pmc-10738719:
George Demiris and five colleagues describe Sense4Safety, a technology-supported fall prevention program tested in 2023. The program serves older adults with mild cognitive impairment, a group where over sixty percent fall each year. Its parts include in-home assessment, education, regular coaching, and passive monitoring through depth sensors.

Ten low-income older adults used the intervention for three months, and all completed the study procedures. Sensor-based assessments of lower body function matched clinical expert scores closely. Two fall alerts triggered timely responses during the trial. Participants and families reported peace of mind, and the authors argue that passive sensing plus coaching can warn of rising fall risk early.
pmc-10748119:
Kaja Damnjanovic and colleagues studied vaccination intent psychology in two thousand twenty-three. They surveyed three groups after the pandemic. Health providers, parents, and laypeople took part. Questions covered decision styles and vaccine attitudes. Negative vaccine attitudes lowered intent in every group. That pattern held across all statistical models.

A shared attitudinal core predicted positive intent. Trust in government and health systems mattered. Belief in shared safety consensus also helped. Feeling free in the choice was protective too. Conspiracy beliefs pulled intent downward. Social role changed details, not the core. Campaigns can target trust and freedom framing. The findings span roles remarkably well.
pmc-10761319:
Doogyum Kim and six co-authors published a surgical case report in twenty twenty-three on moving the jaw nerve aside to place dental implants where bone is too shallow above it. In the back lower jaw, severe bone loss can leave no room even for short implants. Bone grafting is one answer; repositioning the nerve is another.

Two patients had the inferior alveolar nerve transposed and shifted sideways, allowing implants to anchor in the remaining bone. Both cases healed with full implant integration. The numbness that follows such surgery in lip and chin resolved completely in each patient. The authors present nerve repositioning as a valuable option for badly compromised jaws when grafting is impractical.
pmc-10774019:
Shinya Ikeda, Yuji Nishimoto, Masanao Toma, and Yukihito Sato report a fatal case of an infected aorta in a seventy-three-year-old woman. The germ, Campylobacter fetus, favors blood vessel tissue and can inflame the aorta. Such infections usually balloon into an aneurysm before they burst. In this woman, the chest aorta was inflamed but not widened, while a separate aneurysm sat in the belly aorta. Blood tests grew the germ, and antibiotics eased her pain.

Eight days into treatment the chest aorta burst anyway, and she died. There had been no sign of widening. The authors urge early repair, by open surgery or from inside the vessel, after only a short course of antibiotics in such cases.
pmc-10827919:
Valeria Isaac, Vladimir Lopez, and Maria Josefina Escobar compare two theories of ADHD. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, weighs executive dysfunction against state regulation. The first theory blames weak top-down control tied to dopamine networks. It fits many findings, yet not all people with ADHD show that flaw.

The second theory blames unstable arousal, the brain's alertness level. It explains day-to-day swings in focus and energy. Newer work adds body signals, like heart and skin measures, to that account. The review lays out what supports and what challenges each view. A merged picture may be needed for a condition this varied.
pmc-10994619:
Lamees Yousef and colleagues audit disability access across primary health centres in eastern Saudi Arabia. Their assessment from twenty twenty-three covered fifty-six centres in three cities. Disabled patients face physical, communication, and attitude barriers. Guidelines mean little without knowing the actual gaps.

Infrastructure, services, equipment, processes, and training were scored. Government-built centres averaged differently from other types. Ramps, devices, and staff preparation all entered the audit. Findings point to concrete fixes rather than vague goodwill. Equitable access needs assistive devices on site. Training gaps matter as much as building design. The audit gives regional planners a prioritised to-do list.
pmc-11534219:
Shadi Nazarizadeh, Zohreh Ghotbeddin, Samireh Ghafouri, and Alireza Sarkaki tested a compound called DMI in newborn rats harmed by low oxygen seizures. Such seizures in infants raise later risk of epilepsy and learning trouble. Forty-two rat pups were split into six groups, with some given the compound before a brief spell in low-oxygen air.

As the rats grew, treated ones moved better, showed less anxiety-like behavior, and learned better than untreated harmed rats. Brain wave power, which fell after the injury, held up with treatment. Tissue tests showed less oxidative stress and swelling in the memory center. The authors credit those drops for the gains.
pmc-11536619:
Yannik Hanusrichter and seven co-authors published an orthopedic series in twenty twenty-four on custom-made implant stems for the hardest bone reconstructions. When tumors are cut out or previous joint replacements have failed, standard stems often find too little bone to grip. Tailor-made stems promise fixation where shelves are empty.

Fourteen patients received fifteen custom implants between twenty seventeen and twenty twenty-four, for revision joint surgery or tumor bridges. Every implantation succeeded. Over an average thirty months, five implants needed revision, for loosening or infection. Function scores averaged in the good range. The authors call custom stems a joint-saving option worth considering case by case when nothing standard will hold.
pmc-11574619:
Bruno Bandiera and six co-authors show that a blend of scents, but no single scent, shields mice from stress damage, in a two thousand twenty-four neuroscience paper. Limbic brain regions that govern stress responses listen to the nose.

Mice under acute restraint stress that inhaled vanillin, limonene, and green odor together kept normal anxiety levels and intact recognition and spatial memory; each odorant alone failed. In a chronic unpredictable stress model of depression, the blend prevented depressive behaviors and lowered interleukin-1 beta in the prefrontal cortex. The authors nominate multi-odorant stimulation as a candidate tool against stress-induced cognitive and mood disorders.
pmc-11576619:
Georgios Sotiriou wrote a short view piece in 2024 on tiny bits of silver in coats for implants. Germs that grow near implants cause many faults, and the tiny silver kills germs well. Yet near no shop-bought titanium implants use it at all.

The author blames a thin grasp of what makes such coats work: bit size, coat type, what they are made of, and how long they last. Harm to host flesh is the next brake, since the coat must kill germ films but spare the sick person. He calls for better making and for tougher tests of how long coats last. Sound lab and beast proof must come first, he says, before trust in sick care. Well set, multi-use coats could at last move the silver past mere hype.
pmc-11585619:
Omid Rahmanian and others built a porous polymer for dye removal in two thousand twenty-four. Methylene blue is a common dye that fouls water. Their polymer builds on naphthalene building blocks. A linking reaction joined the network. Many tests proved the porous build and heat strength. Uptake tests then tuned the working setup.

Neutral water and half an hour of contact worked best. Uptake fit a single-layer model closely. Timing data matched a chemistry-driven rate model. Top load matched rival materials. The polymer thus suits waste water cleanup roles. Textile effluent is an obvious target stream. The team calls it a hopeful pick for cleanup.
pmc-11590219:
Haitao Mei and colleagues published a 2024 study of how colorectal cancer spreads. Colorectal cancer ranks among the deadliest cancers worldwide. A cell-surface protein drew the team's attention. Its levels were measured in paired tumor and normal tissues. Computer analysis traced the protein's partners and regulators.

A small RNA molecule normally restrains the protein. In tumors, that restraint appears lost. The protein connects to a known cancer signaling chain. Lab tests confirmed the regulatory links. Blocking this chain could slow invasion. The pathway also offers marker candidates for prognosis. More precise markers would help doctors judge which tumors threaten most.
pmc-11590319:
Tzu-Ling Chen, Li-Li Chen, and Meei-Ling Gau published a breastfeeding study in two thousand twenty-four in Taiwan. Health guidance urges only breast milk for the first six months of life. Whether mothers keep going depends partly on how friendly their surroundings are to breastfeeding.

The team followed one thousand eight hundred seventy mothers from just after birth to six months. They asked about family acceptance and public nursing rooms, alongside feeding practice. About thirty-one percent were still exclusively breastfeeding at six months. Higher education, having older children, and vaginal birth linked to continuing. The analysis also weighed hospital and home support factors. The authors aim to show which surroundings help mothers persist.
pmc-11606319:
Ian Hewson and a large team hunt for viruses in two sea animals of the Caribbean, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. One is a sea urchin hit by a mass death event that year. The other is a sea cucumber taken from a Florida reef in good health. Both play key roles on coral reefs, as grazers and as feeders on waste.

Gene reads from the urchin showed none of the viruses seen in its kin, which may reflect too much host DNA in the samples. The cucumber held virus kinds seen in other sea cucumbers. The work sets a base for study of whether viruses play a part in urchin deaths.
pmc-11607319:
Annabel Matison and a large team ask whether eating more fruit and vegetables guards against later depressive symptoms. Their twin cohort study was published in twenty twenty-four. Twin designs can strip out family background that muddies diet studies.

Nearly three thousand five hundred twins aged forty-five to ninety from four countries were followed for five to eleven years. Diet was grouped as low, medium, or high intake. Compared with low intake, high fruit and high vegetable intake both linked to fewer depressive symptoms over time. Within-pair comparisons tested whether shared genes or upbringing explained the link. The protective signal survived the checks, strengthening the case for diet as mental health support in later life.
pmc-11607919:
Irene Kinera-Kagimu and colleagues studied partner notification among Ugandan teens with HIV in 2024. Providers can help patients tell sexual partners about exposure risk. World guidance backs the service for teens and adults. Data on teen use in Uganda stayed scarce. The team enrolled sexually active teens at a Kampala clinic. All were aged fifteen to nineteen and in routine care. Just over three hundred seventy teens took part. Charts and questionnaires captured service use and partner traits.

About half agreed to use the notification service. Most chose to tell partners themselves first. Provider telling served as a last resort for a smaller share. Longer relationships raised the odds of service use. Teens who had lost both parents used it more. Avoiding pornography also linked to higher use. The authors call overall use low. Teen-friendly designs must raise uptake, they argue.
pmc-11610119:
Mark Yates and co-authors test a hospital program meant to cut complications in older patients with cognitive impairment. Such patients fare poorly in hospital and pick up new harms at high rates: urine infections, pneumonia, delirium, and pressure sores. The Dementia Care in Hospitals Program trained ward staff, screened older patients for impairment, and put a bedside alert, the Cognitive Impairment Identifier, on the charts of those affected.

The study rolled the program out ward by ward in hospitals across four Australian states. It covered 16,789 patients aged 65 and over admitted for at least a day. Of those screened, 37.8% had cognitive impairment. Complications struck 27.4% of screened patients, and were three times as likely in those with impairment. Yet the program did not significantly change the combined complication rate for patients with impairment. Spotting risk and teaching staff, alone, may not move hard outcomes.
pmc-11610319:
Lidia Cerron Tito and colleagues adapted a health self-management questionnaire into Spanish, in a 2024 study. A cancer diagnosis throws patients into emotional and social crisis. Tools exist to measure coping or growth after trauma, but none in Spanish captured how patients manage their health day to day. The team translated the short Smart Management Strategy scale and tested it in Peru.

The work followed a careful path: translation, back-translation, then field testing. A total of 271 Peruvian adults with various cancers completed the Spanish version. Statistical checks examined whether the scale kept its original three-part structure. Reliability was judged with standard consistency measures. Scores were also compared with a social support scale to check that the new tool measured something related but distinct. The study aims to give Spanish-speaking clinics a sound way to gauge self-management.
pmc-11611519:
Jing and co-authors trace how a circular RNA helps liver cancer resist the drug sorafenib. Sorafenib is a main oral therapy for advanced liver cancer, but resistance blocks its success. The team compared resistant and sensitive cancer cells with deep RNA sequencing.

They mapped a chain linking the circular RNA Circ_0001944, a small RNA, and a gene called FBLN2. Lab tests, including pull-down and reporter assays, checked each link. The chain blocks ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and fats. Downstream gene checks placed the chain inside known pathways, marking it as a target to restore drug response.
pmc-11611919:
Alejandro Marangoni and Erica Pensini report that adding glycerol to crude sunflower lecithin makes tiny liposomes on its own, with no homogenizer or filter needed. The starting mix holds large vesicles with many layers. Past about thirty percent glycerol by weight, light scattering shows those large vesicles fully turn into liposomes just one to two hundred nanometers wide.

Under the microscope, the liposome walls become stress-birefringent past that point, then relax again above eighty percent glycerol. The authors explain the change through the mixed phospholipids' own curve, which lowers bending energy, glycerol weakening the pull between layers, and shifts in how water coats the headgroups. The draw is simple means: cheap, food-grade materials build themselves into tiny carriers of use for foods, cosmetics, and drug delivery studies.
pmc-11613719:
Yukiko Yasui and colleagues report the case of a man on dialysis whose repeated stomach ulcers may have been worsened by a potassium-lowering resin drug. The drug is known to cause ulcers in the bowel after long use, but stomach ulcers linked to it are rarely reported. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team describes a patient who began dialysis and the drug in his early fifties. He later had a bleeding ulcer, then several more bleeding stomach ulcers that led to stomach surgery.

Examined tissue from surgery showed crystal-like deposits resembling the resin at the base of an ulcer. The authors note many other factors at play, including diabetes-related gut slowing, several medicines, and weight, all of which may have kept the drug sitting in the stomach. They present the drug as one added contributor among several, not the sole cause.
pmc-11616419:
Aadithreya Varman, Arulmozhi Varman, and Dinesh Balakumar compare two laser tools for fixing sight. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, comes from an eye clinic in Chennai, India. Both tools cut a thin lens of tissue from the eye to correct short sight with astigmatism. The newer tool adds aids that line up the eye's twist on their own.

The study covers two hundred twenty eyes treated over about a year. Both groups started with near the same level of short sight. Three months after surgery, ninety-eight percent of newer-tool eyes hit the target range. The older tool reached ninety-four percent. The authors weigh safety and sharpness of sight for both.
pmc-11619619:
Lanfranco Pellesi and a large group of colleagues published a review in two thousand twenty-four on combining migraine prevention treatments. Migraine arises from tangled mechanisms, so one drug often falls short. Pairing preventive therapies could hit several pathways at once.

The review weighs older oral preventives, Botox injections, antibody drugs against the CGRP pathway, and small-molecule CGRP blockers. Dual CGRP targeting and Botox-plus-antibody pairings look most promising in the cited evidence. Cheap oral drugs add practical value, especially with other conditions present. Costs of premium pairings strain feasibility, though. The authors find evidence too thin for guideline endorsement and call for large trials, above all for resistant patients.
pmc-11624219:
John Lazarus and co-authors bench-test a new system for clearing stone fragments during kidney stone surgery. In flexible ureteroscopy, the surgeon blasts stones apart through a thin scope, but the bits must come out, and stray fragments can grow back. Their Small Fragment Removal System has three parts: a siphon access sheath, a dual action pump, and an agitator. It was compared with a standard sheath in a validated phantom kidney.

The new system kept kidney pressure far lower: about 9 against 24 millimeters of mercury on standard flow. Its flow ran faster too, 31 against 25 milliliters a minute. On a fluid bolus, peak pressure hit only about 9 with the new system, against 41 with the standard one. It also cleared far more stone: about 78% of fragment weight against 43%. Lower pressure means less risk of infection-laden fluid being forced into the kidney.
pmc-11635319:
Lakshmi Kannan, Upasana Sahu, and colleagues test a game-based exercise program delivered by video to frail older adults in a 2024 clinical study. Frailty cuts physical activity and raises fall risk, speeding the very decline it springs from, yet traveling to exercise classes is hardest for exactly these patients. A tele-exercise program built around games aims to bring safe, motivating training into the home.

The randomized trial is a feasibility study: can frail participants use the system, stick with it, and improve physical function? Positive feasibility would justify a larger trial of gaming as geriatric medicine.
pmc-11641619:
Tianshu Hong and colleagues published a plant disease study in 2024. They studied a fungus that devastates sugarcane crops. The disease is called pokkah boeng and costs growers heavily. How the fungus defeats plant immunity was largely unknown. The team focused on a family of fungal proteins. These CFEM proteins sit at the fungus surface. Three such proteins were identified and tested carefully. All three suppressed plant immune responses broadly. They blocked reactions triggered by typical defense signals.

Two key building blocks enabled the immune suppression. Those sites also helped the fungus gather iron. Iron scarcity was created at the plant contact zone. Low free iron may quiet plant defenses effectively. Each protein contributed differently to full virulence. The fungus seems to starve defenses while feeding itself. Sugarcane breeding could target this iron strategy.
pmc-11641719:
Nadia Tasnim Ahmed and seven co-authors shared a study in twenty twenty-four. It is about neutrophil elastase. That is an inflammatory enzyme loose in diseased lungs. The team asked what it does to macrophages. They took blood monocytes from volunteers. They matured them into macrophages. They bathed the cells in the enzyme for two hours. Unbiased protein measurement found forty-one proteins changed.

The pattern was selective vandalism. Of twenty-six proteins cut down, twenty-one sat on the cell surface. Four proteoglycan receptors were in that set, with their partners. Immune signaling and scavenger receptors were clipped too. The authors give the first full map of elastase targets. The map covers the macrophage surface in full. In lungs that stay inflamed for a long time, the enzyme seems to edit a list. It edits which conversations a macrophage can still hear.
pmc-11641819:
Ava Boutilier and a team including Sherine Elsawa show that a gene switch is required for the helper state of macrophages that feeds a rare blood cancer. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The cancer, Waldenström macroglobulinemia, grows in the marrow among plasma cells and lymphocytes, and its surroundings matter.

In dishes, resting and helper-state macrophages both boosted cancer cell growth and survival. Cancer cells in turn pushed resting macrophages toward the helper state. The switch, GLI3, appeared only in helper-state cells. Macrophages from mice whose immune cells lack the gene failed to lift cancer growth and cut survival. The finding names a lever inside support cells that the tumor depends on.
pmc-11642619:
Robert Besaw and Carrie Fry study how state limits on the number of drugs Medicaid will cover each month affect addiction care, in a twenty twenty-four paper. Medicaid is the largest payer for opioid use disorder treatment in the United States. Some states cap how many prescriptions a person can fill per month to control costs. The authors ask whether those caps cut the use of two main drugs for this disorder.

They used national Medicaid drug data from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-two, covering ten states with caps of three to six drugs. States with caps filled far fewer of these drug prescriptions per head than states without. Smaller caps bit harder than larger ones. The authors warn that broad caps may block care and slow the fight against the opioid crisis.
pmc-11644619:
Rishitej Chaparala and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four antenna study using a wave-guiding feed inspired by surface plasmons. Dielectric rod antennas serve very high frequency wireless links. Feeding them well is key to strong, directed signals.

Their design feeds the rod through a patterned surface that mimics plasmon waves. Cheap circuit-board material forms the simple structure. Simulations showed high gain and good matching at the target frequency. Directional radiation suited future wireless systems. The authors also note sensing uses, such as finding hidden objects or reading material properties, that the feeder design could support.
pmc-11647219:
Brian Gac leads a team that reviews opioid marketing through opinion leaders. Their review from twenty twenty-four uses internal industry documents. Prescription opioid deaths rose sharply at the century's turn.

How drug firms marketed opioids was not well studied before. The team read the first public batch of archive documents. Files span court rulings, letters, testimony, and studies. Firms found, hired, and groomed key opinion leaders, they find. Those leaders were picked to reach key prescriber groups. Themes were coded across the document set.  Companies named include Janssen, Purdue, and Cephalon in files.
pmc-11648919:
Luyao Yan and colleagues watched a DNA repair protein at work in 2024. Light-activated proteins can repair ultraviolet damage. A related protein family sends light signals instead. One algae protein does both jobs. Ultrafast spectroscopy tracked its repair steps.

Site-directed mutations tested key protein parts. Two histidine residues proved essential for repair. Removing them nearly stopped repair completely. Electron and proton moves were coupled tightly. The full repair cycle is described. The active flavin form was identified. Findings work at molecular detail level. Dual-function proteins are now clearer. Blue light switches the protein on.
pmc-11650619:
Lingqian Zheng and colleagues pool animal studies to test if stem cells can ease a scarring disease of the belly lining, in this review from twenty twenty-four. The disease, peritoneal fibrosis, is a known risk of long-term dialysis through the belly, and it can force patients to stop that therapy. Mesenchymal stem cells are prized for calming inflammation and slowing scars.

The team searched four databases and found 15 animal studies that fit. Across them, stem cell treatment lowered key inflammation signals and cut collagen, the stuff of scars. The lining grew thinner toward normal, and fluid removal through it improved. A few measures did not change: one growth factor, and some salt and waste ratios. Since all the work is in animals, the authors frame the cells as a hope to test in people, not a proven cure.
pmc-11651219:
Menelaou and colleagues trace how smell signals reach central hubs of the human brain. Their neuroscience paper from twenty twenty-four maps stepwise pathways from the olfactory cortex. Other senses sit five or six relay steps from the default-mode network. How smell connects to those hubs was still unknown.

The smell pathway turns out shorter, at three to four steps. Two distinct routes emerge from the smell cortex subdivisions. One route reaches reward and multisensory areas early. It starts in the anterior olfactory nucleus and olfactory tubercle. The findings place smell closer to core brain hubs than other senses. That closeness may help explain strong links between smell, memory, and feeling.
pmc-11654419:
Selamawit Abrha and four colleagues measure how well Ethiopian university students can find and judge health information online. They surveyed 794 Jimma University undergraduates who use social networking sites, in a setting where such evidence from resource-limited contexts is scarce. Most respondents were male, averaging about twenty-three years old.

The mean electronic health literacy score was low. Later year of study, urban upbringing, using social sites and medical apps for health information, platform membership, and YouTube and Google use all predicted higher scores. The authors recommend expanding internet access and infrastructure across higher education institutions. Better connectivity, they argue, is a practical lever for raising students' ability to appraise online health claims.
pmc-11660319:
Dahai Yu and eleven colleagues followed New Zealand women for up to twenty-five years to compare two early warnings for type 2 diabetes. One group had diabetes only in pregnancy. The other had blood sugar above normal but below the diabetes line. Both raise risk, but by how much, and for whom, was less clear. Records linked clinic data with national health files, and risk models tracked who went on to full diabetes.

The pregnancy group faced the higher risk. Risk ran highest in women over thirty-five, in Māori women, and in women living with the least money. The first five years after birth stood out as the window where help matters most. The twenty twenty-four study tells clinics to aim early, close follow-up at the new mothers least able to absorb a second chronic disease.
pmc-11673119:
Xiaohan Li and fourteen co-authors gauge how phase state steers ice birth in specks born of tree gas. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Such specks can seed high ice clouds when thick or glass-like, yet no plain rule tied thickness to ice skill. A key speck part, 2-methyltetrols, was read for ice birth at split thickness states.

Ice birth leapt by two to three spans of ten as specks moved from wet to half-solid. A new math frame built on old birth law turned thickness into a birth rate and matched the lab reads. Field casts put such specks at one to tens per litre in cloud zones past the Amazon.
pmc-11673919:
Donald Plante, Keegan Unzen, and John Jungck print magnetic model pieces that assemble themselves into virus-like tubes. Their methods paper from twenty twenty-four extends earlier spherical models. Real helical virus shells self-assemble from many identical proteins. Physical models make that invisible process graspable.

Printed parts follow double-helix packing patterns. Magnets stand in for the forces between real subunits. Simplified charge simulations guided the piece designs. The parts reliably form cylinders on their own. Students can handle and rebuild the structures freely. Teachers gain a hands-on route into viral architecture. The approach also prototypes mesoscale self-assembly ideas.
pmc-11674919:
Layla Panahipour, Chiara Micucci, and Reinhard Gruber published a cell study in 2024. They compared two lab cell lines used in inflammation research. Both lines come from human blood-related cancers. Labs use them to stand in for immune cells. Their responses to triggers are not identical, though. No agreed gene panel marked inflammation in both. The team used RNA sequencing to settle this. Cells were exposed to two strong inflammatory triggers.

Strict cutoffs revealed clearly regulated gene sets. One line responded much more strongly overall. The other line changed fewer genes in total. Some classic inflammation genes rose in both lines. Others rose in only one line each time. The lists give labs a firmer reference point. Choosing the right line matters for each question. Shared genes offer the safest common readout.
pmc-11676219:
Adam Cwudziński and Alexander Churyumov model mixing in steel ladles with dams on the floor. Their study from twenty twenty-four combines water models with computer simulation. Steelmakers stir molten metal with gas from a top lance. Floor structures can steer that flow and speed mixing.

A small water model tested flow behaviour in the lab. Full-scale simulations then modelled hot metal with nitrogen stirring. Gas flow rate, lance depth, and dam shape were varied. A half-circle dam cut total mixing time sharply. Sets of dams performed even better in the tests. Those gains came without raising the gas flow rate. Foundries gain cheaper ways to homogenise liquid steel faster.
pmc-11679419:
Sara Abdelbaset and a team of co-authors present a smarter way to hunt for free airwaves in this twenty twenty-four paper. Smart radios need to spot unused bands before they can use them. Older methods pull fixed traits from signals at set points and can miss or misread bands.

The team treats the task as sorting signals into classes and trains a deep learning model on many signal and noise types. The model learns the traits on its own and adapts to new signals. In tests it beat two older methods and stayed accurate even with heavy background noise. Better sensing means less wasted airwave space for wireless systems.
pmc-11706519:
Gianluca Fadda and a large Italian team study what shapes hearing results after ear bone repair surgery for chronic middle ear disease. Their multicenter study was published in twenty twenty-four. The disease is common, and the surgery rebuilds the tiny sound-carrying bones, but the role of one growth type in outcomes was unclear.

One hundred and fifty-three patients entered, with and without cholesteatoma, a skin-like growth in the ear. After selection, one hundred and thirty-three were analyzed. Hearing improved clearly after surgery in both groups. Patients with the growth gained slightly less than those without. The results confirm the repair as a standard treatment, while flagging the growth as a drag on results that surgeons should weigh in planning.
pmc-11710719:
Sophie van der Landen and a large team ask how thinking skills map onto daily life, published in 2025, across the Alzheimer spectrum. Trials for new treatments track both thinking and daily function. The two are often treated as if they were the same thing. Yet how strongly each thinking skill drives daily function is still unclear. The team set out to measure those links directly.

The study included six hundred thirteen people from an Amsterdam memory clinic. All had amyloid in their spinal fluid. They took tests of memory, planning, and language, and a partner rated their daily function. Most had dementia, with smaller groups at milder stages. A statistical model that handles test error confirmed the three skill groups. The paper then weighs how much each skill explains daily function once the skills' overlap is counted.
pmc-11714119:
Elena Portacolone and co-authors published this interview study in two thousand twenty-five on social isolation among older adults who live alone with thinking problems. About four million such adults in the United States come from racially and ethnically diverse groups.

The team held long interviews with ten women living alone in Michigan, California, and Louisiana. They sorted the forces at play into personal, circle, and society levels. Staying inside a familiar home, deaths of loved ones, and hiding feelings all deepened isolation. Friends drifting away hurt as well. Strong family ties and faith groups pushed back the most. Set activities and even hard relationships helped some. The authors say support must fit each person's world, language, and habits, not just add more contact.
pmc-11714519:
GYeon Oh and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on gabapentin, a drug used more and more in older adults, often for uses beyond its label. The team asked whether starting the drug speeds up decline in people who already have thinking problems.

The study used a national Alzheimer's data set and matched each new user with up to nine non-users of like profile. It tracked thinking, daily function, and movement over one and two years. Starting gabapentin showed no clear link with worse thinking or daily function scores. One risk did stand out: new users had about twice the odds of a new fall by the second year. The authors urge care with falls when the drug is started in frail older adults.
pmc-11714919:
Jodi Liu and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on whether the United States health system could deliver new Alzheimer's drugs at scale. Such drugs slow early disease, but they need early detection, scans, and specialist visits that many areas lack.

The team built a county-level model of people aged fifty and older moving through disease stages and care steps. It weighed patient demand against local supply of doctors and services. Letting family doctors diagnose and clear patients for treatment cut specialist waits the most. Blood tests used for triage in primary care helped further. Waits in rural counties ran about three times longer than in cities. The authors say wide use of these drugs will need primary care at the center and fixes for rural gaps.
pmc-11716819:
Arielle Farhi and seven co-authors report a study from twenty twenty-five on soda drinking and dementia risk. They used data from the Northern Manhattan Study, a long-term study of a mixed group of people. Soda use was asked about at the start, in the years from nineteen ninety-three to two thousand one.

The team tracked nine hundred fifty-nine people for about eleven years on average. One hundred seventy-four of them went on to develop dementia. Diet soda use was linked to a higher risk of dementia, even after other health factors were taken into account. The work helps readers weigh a common drink habit against brain health in later life.
pmc-11754319:
Vera Maximilia Straetmanns examines the plant philosophy of Agnes Arber, a British botanist who lived from the late nineteenth century into the mid twentieth century. Her paper, published in twenty twenty-five, first gives an outline of Arber life and working style, then turns to how Arber thought about purpose in plants. Two ideas are separated. One concerns adaptation, where a trait is explained by what it does for the plant. The other concerns inner direction, where growing structures unfold toward forms they are set up to reach.

Arber doubted the first idea but built much of her plant theory on the second. Straetmanns shows this in Arber view of the leaf and in her account of parallel evolution. The paper closes by linking Arber to current debates in plant science and evolution, where her work is being read again.
pmc-11796619:
Beatriz León-Salas and a large team weigh mapping-guided pacemaker placement against the standard X-ray method. Their systematic review, with an economic study, was published in twenty twenty-five. The pacing targets the heart's own wiring in people with very slow heartbeat.

The team reviewed the literature on safety, benefit, and cost for the Spanish health system. Seven comparison studies with two hundred and thirty-one patients were kept. A partial cost study and a five-year budget look accompanied the clinical pooling. Mapping guidance avoids radiation and may place leads more exactly, but proof was still thin. The report gives health decision makers a balanced base for judging whether to fund the mapping route.
pmc-11897719:
Kazuteru Takagi leads a team that makes a plant growth oxylipin in E coli. Their work from twenty twenty-four deals with KODA, a stress helper. KODA is released by a duckweed species under drought and heat.

It is made from a fatty acid in a two step enzyme path. The team screened many duckweed species for the best maker. Two genes from the best strain were put into E coli. The bacteria then made far more KODA per weight. Plant culture needs more time, light, and space by far. Farm use for growth boosts is the end aim.
pmc-12661719:
Mengying Bai, Liujuan Zhang, and six co-authors compare protein maps of ovaries aged naturally and by chemotherapy. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, uses mouse models of both paths. Ovarian aging sets the pace for whole-body female aging, yet starts quietly. Two models supply tissue: young mice dosed with two chemo drugs, and mice aged eighteen months.

Hormone tests and tissue checks first confirm both models. Protein profiling then lists what changes in each. Shared and unique signatures are sorted by pathway analysis. Selected genes get a second check with a standard assay. Early markers and drug targets are the hoped-for output.
pmc-12661819:
Aubrianna Jones and five co-authors published a health records study in twenty twenty-five on teenagers with low back pain in a suburban American pediatric system. Back pain is rising among adolescents, yet how they actually use care was largely unknown. The team mined de-identified records for new cases from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-two.

Six thousand three hundred fifty adolescents, averaging just under fifteen years and mostly female, were identified. Four in five first appeared in ordinary outpatient clinics. About thirty-nine percent received non-opioid medication, twenty-nine percent got imaging, and a quarter used conservative hands-on care. Opioids reached eleven percent, while surgery stayed rare. The pattern gives pediatric systems a baseline for judging their own back pain care.
pmc-12667719:
Jinyu Xia and colleagues ran a prospective trial of a vacuum-assisted radiofrequency device for refreshing the skin around the eyes. That area ages early, with wrinkles, looseness, and under-eye bags as collagen fades. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team treated adult volunteers four times, spaced a few weeks apart, at a single center. Wrinkle grades, investigator ratings, and instrument measures of hydration, stretch, and gloss were tracked, along with volunteer satisfaction and pain scores.

Most of those who finished the trial improved their wrinkle grade by at least a quarter, with clear change visible from the second session on. Under-eye bags looked better on investigator ratings, and hydration and elasticity rose. Satisfaction was high, pain was minimal, and no side effects were reported over the roughly three-month watch. The authors present the device as safe and effective for this delicate area.
pmc-12686519:
Liwei Lu, Menghua Li, and Liang Chao combine satellite radar with computer modeling to watch slopes at a tailings pond, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Tailings ponds store mine waste behind dams, and a sliding slope can be a grave hazard. Water in the pond presses on the slope and can shift it.

The team used two years of satellite radar data to track how the ground surface moved. They also built a three-dimensional model that links water pressure to stress and movement inside the dam. The two methods agreed closely. Water level and the layers of rock and soil changed where the slope moved most. The authors offer the paired method as a firmer way to judge risk.
pmc-12698419:
Lingyu He and four colleagues mapped the accessory genome of the bacterium that causes strangles in horses. The twenty twenty-five study assembled 552 high-quality genomes of Streptococcus equi from public sequence archives. The strains came from five continents. The team catalogued virulence genes, resistance genes, and mobile genetic elements, then compared their distribution across regions.

The bacterium showed a closed pangenome with 1,661 core genes and 982 accessory genes. Of seventy-one virulence genes found, forty were shared by all strains. The remaining ones varied by geography, especially genes for nutrition and toxins. Almost no acquired antibiotic resistance genes appeared. Mobile elements had distinct jobs: phages carried toxin genes, while genomic islands carried iron-uptake genes. The results guide vaccine design and worldwide surveillance.
pmc-12703119:
Ying Fang and five co-authors ran a data-led trial of Traditional Chinese Medicine care after esophagus cancer surgery, in twenty twenty-five. One hundred patients were split by lot into two groups of fifty. One group got standard care around surgery, and the other got standard care plus Chinese medicine techniques. The team tracked blood sugar swings, comfort, service ratings, and stress, in both body and mind.

Blood sugar swings fell in both groups over the two weeks after surgery. The added-care group ran lower at every check, with a clear gap between the groups. The study also weighed comfort scores and stress hormones to round out the picture. The authors say the added techniques steadied sugar control and eased the stress of recovery, and they present the data as a base for wider use.
pmc-12735419:
Kostrakiewicz-Gieralt and Mannucci review plant oils in sport nutrition products for athletes. Plant oils can support health and performance in athletes. The team searched papers and patents from 2015 to 2024. Three databases and two patent engines were used for the search.

The search found 58 patents and 35 research papers in total. In all, 39 plant types from 27 families were logged. Most products target sport fuel, recovery, or performance gains. Forms held powders, tablets, drinks, and capsules for daily use. Olive, flax, and other seed oils led the list. The review maps which oils lack solid proof.
pmc-12739119:
Maryam Ghorbani, Rasoul Yaali, and Hassan Sadeghi published a movement science study in twenty twenty-five on exercise for female students with flexible flat feet. Flat arches disturb the whole leg chain, from ankles to hips, threatening balance and agility. The team tested whether general calisthenics, not foot-specific therapy, could close the functional gap.

Ninety-six students, twenty-five with flat feet and seventy-one with normal arches, trained for sixteen weeks. Movement screening, core strength, balance, and shuttle-run agility were measured before and after. The program improved functional movement performance in the flat-foot group. It also changed how screening scores related to other measures, differently between groups. The study argues broad strengthening deserves a place beside orthotics.
pmc-12743019:
Yerbol Baltabay and five co-authors track a fish tapeworm in a Kazakh reservoir and test how to kill it by freezing. Their twenty twenty-five article covers Dibothriocephalus species, whose larvae live in fish muscle and can infect people who eat raw fish. The site is the Shardara Reservoir on the Syr Darya River.

From twenty twenty-one to twenty twenty-four, the team examined close to a thousand fish of four species. Northern pike were the most infected, with about half carrying larvae, mostly in muscle and edible organs. Freezing trials set clear rules: minus twelve degrees for at least ninety-six hours, or minus fourteen for forty-eight, inactivates the larvae. The reservoir is a lasting focus of the disease.
pmc-12745819:
Ishita Goyal and four co-authors firm up calcium nitride to make ammonia by electric means at room state. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The calcium path to fix air gas holds bright hope. But it is blocked by a weak gas-wet face, slow fuel burn at the plus pole, and a key mid part that breaks down. Three fixes were brought in at once.

A wide-face nickel pole sped fuel burn, a new bath fluid held its form where the old one failed, and a flow cell kept gas and wet in close touch. Light and skin probes showed the mid part held firm. Yield hit near one third in short runs and held near one fifth past two days.
pmc-12751619:
Zhe Wang and seven co-authors pool clinical trials to compare liver toxicity and benefit across generations of lung cancer targeted drugs, in a two thousand twenty-five systematic review and meta-analysis. EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors are mainstays for non-small-cell lung cancer, but their liver risk ranking was unclear.

Six trials covering two thousand five hundred twenty-eight patients met the criteria. Newer drugs, afatinib, osimertinib, and dacomitinib, carried a lot lower risks of liver enzyme elevation than gefitinib and erlotinib. They also improved progression-free survival and response rates. Overall survival gains showed up for afatinib and osimertinib but not dacomitinib. The authors judge the newer making's risk-benefit profile superior overall.
pmc-12765919:
Su-Han Hsu and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five survey of medicine disposal and adherence among chronic disease patients in Taipei, Taiwan. Leftover medicines pile up when treatment adherence slips over long courses. Dumped wrongly, they threaten water supplies and public health.

Nearly three hundred long-term patients at one hospital answered a detailed questionnaire. It covered disposal knowledge, policy awareness, satisfaction with promotion efforts, and daily medication adherence. Group comparisons tested how age, sex, and clinical traits shifted the answers. The study ties two habits usually studied apart: taking medicines properly and throwing the extras away safely.
pmc-12785819:
Turkoglou and co-authors study the makeup of clots pulled from stroke patients. They treated 57 patients with clot removal between 2022 and 2024. Each clot was sorted by its main parts: red cells, fibrin, a mix, or organized fibrin. Clots were also classed as early or late stage. CD34 staining marked the organized fibrin type.

Most clots came from the M1 part of the middle cerebral artery. Red-cell-rich clots were the most common type at 49.1 percent. Early-stage clots made up 70.2 percent of the set. Red-cell-rich clots clustered in the proximal inner carotid artery. Clot makeup showed no clear link to long-term diseases the patients had.
pmc-12815819:
Fubing Yu and seven colleagues applied diversity-area relationships to the gut microbes of people with inflammatory bowel disease. Ecology's species-area rule describes how diversity grows with sampled area. The team extended that idea to metagenomic genes and functional gene clusters. They used shotgun sequencing from forty-two mucosal and twenty-two fecal samples. Both healthy participants and bowel disease patients were included in the twenty twenty-five analysis.

Mucosal communities differed more between individuals than fecal ones did at gene richness levels. Fecal communities, by contrast, were shaped more strongly by dominant, abundant genes. Healthy microbiomes also showed their own similarity patterns across people. The framework gives researchers a way to compare how completely different sampling sites capture gut diversity, which affects study design.
pmc-12817819:
Xiuhua Ma leads a large team in a multi-layer read of the rumen in grazing lambs. The paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The rumen's microbes turn grass into food the lamb can use, so their play with feed sets both lamb growth and grassland health. How grass kind, extra feed, microbes, and the gut wall interact was poorly known.

Gene reads of microbes and their active genes, single-cell reads of the rumen wall, and blood chemistry are combined. Extra feed under mild grazing lifts total intake but cuts grass intake. Wall cell kinds shift, and carry genes move the acids microbes make. Microbe and wall signals link on to blood nutrients such as B vitamins and bile acids.
pmc-12822019:
Iltaf Hussain and eleven co-authors set out a trial plan in 2025 for a sticker-based nudge to lift drug use as told in Pakistan. Wrong use of germ drugs feeds drug-proof germs, and more than half of people there have no phone, so app prompts will not work. A sticker that tells the tale in pics was made for sick people with a bladder infection.

The trial will take sick people with a sure, plain case from six sites in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, who by lot get the sticker or the usual care. The plan drew on nudge thought and talks with skilled staff, then tests of how well sick people grasped it. Strong shades make a missed dose stand out on the sticker. Scores rest on drug use as told, with the plan's counts and checks set out in full. No scores are in yet.
pmc-12828919:
Arya Hamedanchi and Fereshteh Rezaie lead a team cataloguing the everyday physical complaints of older Tehran residents and how those complaints weigh on well-being. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Many late-life aches signal no specific disease yet still cause real suffering. Clinicians can overlook them for that reason.

Over six hundred adults past sixty answered a structured questionnaire. Limb pain topped the list, reported by nine in ten. Back pain, weakness, and fatigue followed close behind. Past seventy, vision, hearing, and continence complaints climbed significantly. Younger seniors, oddly, minded hair and skin aging more. The more complaints a person listed, the lower their well-being score ran. The authors urge routine assessment to include plain complaints. Treating the list seriously is cheap and humane.
pmc-12837519:
Zihan Zhou, Jie Huang, and four co-authors test repeat doses of stem cells for scarred lungs. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, uses mice with silicosis, a lung scarring from silica dust. No good treatment exists for this slow disease. Stem cells from bone marrow can fight scarring, but the inflamed lung harms them early.

Single-cell gene maps show a harsh first phase that ages the donor cells. Mice given repeat doses kept more cells in the lung. Their scans and tissue showed less scarring, and lung function improved. The therapy also dialed down a gene that fires up immune cells. The work backs repeat dosing over a single shot.
pmc-12871019:
Shirzad and co-authors grade the track-care web for self-kill tries in Iran. Care in wards and post care runs on, yet death rates climb still. The team used a care board frame to probe the web in Shahriar. Count facts came from 992 try cases in a six-month span. The span ran from April to the fall of 2023 in the town. Talk facts came from 45 hands in the care web next.

Hands span mind staff, ward staff, pros, and care users in talks. Count reads were plain sums of the case facts in the work. Talk reads used a frame way in a named code tool. Of 992 sent to track care, just 15 took up the care. Just three of those came to all meets in the web.
pmc-12962919:
Fabiana Battista and others tested false memories about touch in two thousand twenty-six. Memory rebuilds events and takes in outside hints. Witness research calls this the misinformation effect. Touch events had rarely been studied this way. People watched a video of a professor and student scene. The scene included a real touch.

Recall and judgment tasks followed the viewing. A day later, false background details arrived. One version implied a harassment probe. False recall rose once the false tips arrived. Judgments of him also shifted over time. Effects were strongest for the male professor pairing. Courts should treat touch accounts with care.
pmc-13037619:
Wijit Sutthiprapa and colleagues published a 2025 veterinary study comparing hernia repairs in dogs. Perineal hernias weaken the muscles beside the rectum. Three surgical techniques are commonly used. Records from eighty-seven dogs were reviewed. Nearly all patients were male.

Surgery times differed clearly between techniques. The sling method was fastest on average. The muscle flap method took longest. Complications were compared across the groups. Site counts exceeded dog counts because some had both sides repaired. Owners and vets can weigh speed against complication profiles. Retrospective records cannot prove one method best, but they guide choices.
pmc-13121419:
Cao and five co-authors test insect powder in rooster diets, in work from twenty twenty-six. Black soldier fly larvae powder can replace part of soybean meal in poultry feed. Whether it helps or harms breeder male fertility needed a dose test.

Forty Luxi game breeder roosters ate diets with five powder levels, from none to a fifth of the mix, matched for energy and protein. Semen quality, antioxidant enzymes, and blood chemistry were measured. Mid to high levels improved sperm movement, survival, and cap integrity. Some motion traits also rose, while forward progression did not change. The work supports a set inclusion range.
pmc-13168719:
Martins Nweke and three colleagues published a systematic review in two thousand twenty-six on community programmes for high blood pressure. High blood pressure drives much illness in poorer countries with stretched clinics. Teaching people outside clinics to eat better, move more, and check their own pressure may help.

The reviewers gathered community, workplace, and home trials that mixed lifestyle teaching with self-monitoring. Seventeen studies with over five thousand adults qualified. Programmes ran from four weeks to a year. Pooling the results showed average drops in both pressure numbers, larger for the top number. The authors judge multi-part education a useful tool where clinic care is thin, while noting study quality varied.
pmc-13175819:
Jiajie Zhang leads a team with a rare Castleman disease case. Their case from twenty twenty-six deals with a woman of fifty-two. She came in with frequent urination for over six months.

A mass was found behind the peritoneum in her belly. Keyhole surgery removed the mass for tissue tests. Those tests proved mixed type unicentric Castleman disease. Her recovery after surgery was smooth and calm. She stays under close follow up watch since then. The report adds a review of care and outlook.  Past case reports are reviewed next to her case.
pmc-13179919:
Carolina Clares dos Anjos and colleagues describe a new malaria parasite species from a stranded seabird, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The bird was a Cory's shearwater, an Atlantic migrant that winters off South America. It came ashore alive on the São Paulo coast and entered a beach monitoring project's rehabilitation care.

Blood smears showed a Plasmodium parasite, and gene tests matched a known lineage never before found in this bird order. Under care for sixty-one days, the bird relapsed despite anti-malaria drugs and was put down on welfare grounds. Autopsy found an enlarged liver and spleen, liver inflammation, and bleeding in the lungs, marking the parasite as a real killer, not a passenger. The team named it Plasmodium borealis. The case is the first blood parasite record in this shearwater, and a call to watch seabirds more closely.
pmc-13183219:
Saima Sultana, Eraj Tanweer, and five co-authors teach robots to read medical actions in the dark. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, presents the I2I model. Camera-based action recognition fails when lighting drops. In medical settings a missed action can cost dearly.

Depth sensors sidestep light, since they measure distance, not brightness. The team takes depth clips from a large public action dataset. A depth histogram method pulls out shape features.
