A threshold keeps only the strongest features for the model. Tests show the model names medical actions well even in dark scenes. It beats prior methods in their comparisons.
pmc-13185119:
Hongyan Li, Shiyuan Song, Linlin Wang, and Qiang Liu review how signal networks inside cancer cells drive tumor growth and drug proofing. These networks do not act alone but merge outer and inner signals through linked parts. The review came out in twenty twenty-six.

The authors map the core shape of these networks and the main growth paths inside them, with focus on three named paths. Cross talk, feedback loops, and shape shifting let tumors adapt to their setting and to drugs. That is why blocking one path often helps only briefly, they argue. A network level view points to joint attacks and to marks that can guide care picks.
pmc-13195519:
Zhiyuan Zha leads a 2026 materials study on a composite electrode for aqueous, water-based, dual-ion batteries. Such batteries are safe and eco-friendly but suffer slow ion movement and structural swelling as ions enter and leave. The team combined bismuth telluride with antimony phosphate on nitrogen-doped carbon frameworks to form a heterointerface, a junction between unlike materials.

The junction creates a built-in electric field that speeds charge transport, while the carbon frame spreads material evenly and cushions swelling. Computer calculations showed stronger binding for both zinc and ammonium ions than the base material alone. Devices stored high charge for both ions and kept nearly full capacity over thousands of cycles for zinc, guiding dual-ion battery design.
pmc-13196719:
Qunqi Hu and Nisang Chen raise method concerns about a review pooling therapy and exercise trials for chronic pain. The review found small to moderate gains in pain and function from the paired approach. Mood and quality of life also improved. The letter writers praise the effort, then question how some trials were counted.

Their focus is trials with more than one treatment arm. In one chart, two treatment groups share control groups of near-equal size. Handbook rules say a shared control group should be split between comparisons. Leaving it whole counts the same people twice and inflates certainty. Two named trials raise this issue. The writers ask the review team to clarify or correct the handling. Sound pooling, they argue, is what makes the headline gains believable.
pmc-13197119:
Ekin Deniz Aksu and co-authors weigh ways to model where gene switch proteins bind DNA in live cells. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Lab proof of bind spots does not scale, so math models must fill the gap. Most models are built for one switch at a time and fail on new ones.

The team test DNA access, switch gene use, and motif traits as inputs. A cross-switch learn plan lets one model train on all switches at once. Stacks of models and DNA tongue model marks both lift scores. Data worth of the gold tests proved a key cap. Held-out switches in new cell kinds still scored fair.
pmc-13206919:
Vasileios Giannoudis and four colleagues published a narrative review in two thousand twenty-six on fractures that fail to heal without new bone growth. In atrophic non-union, the bone ends stay bare and inactive. Quoted rates of five to ten percent likely understate the problem.

The review gathers current thinking on causes: weak biology, poor blood supply, loose fixation, hidden infection, and host factors. It walks through the roles of inflammation, stem cells, growth proteins, and vessel growth. Evidence is patchy and often only hypothesis-grade, which explains the wide spread of treatments. The authors propose a stepwise plan: rule out infection, check stability, fix what can be fixed in the patient, then upgrade biology and mechanics in grades.
pmc-13207919:
Plant compounds ride inside a dissolving plastic to reach infected wounds, in a 2026 review authored by Elahe Norouzi on PLGA nanocarriers. The article surveys recent studies loading natural antimicrobial compounds into poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) particles, a biodegradable carrier approved for medical use, aimed at wounds colonized by microbes and biofilms.

Across the surveyed work, these formulations fought bacteria and biofilms while calming oxidation and inflammation at the wound site. They also encouraged new blood vessel growth, collagen laying, and skin resurfacing, the three engines of closure. The review compares how the particles are made, how they release their cargo, and how they attack biofilms specifically.
pmc-13210219:
Mental distress is widespread among Nigeria's future eye clinicians, and a 2026 survey headed by Michael Agyemang Kwarteng takes the measure across ten universities. The web-based cross-sectional study collected Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale responses from 474 optometry students between April and November 2024.

About half the students reported depressive symptoms, and severe anxiety affected more than a third of respondents in the survey. One in four carried all three burdens at once, and nearly half had at least two conditions together in the data. Women faced significantly higher odds of depression and overall distress than men, leading the authors to demand structured support inside training programs.
pmc-13212719:
Montaser Abdelsattar and colleagues propose in 2026 a neural network controller to keep frequency steady in small renewable power grids. Solar and wind units lack the spinning inertia of old generators, so sudden load changes can push an islanded microgrid toward failure.

The team compared their multilayer network against three conventional controllers across load swings, renewable swings, and a combined case. Pairing the network with a virtual inertia scheme performed best in every scenario. In the hardest case, the pairing cut the largest frequency deviation sharply compared with no control. Smarter control could help remote microgrids rely on renewables without risking blackouts.
pmc-13214219:
R. Di Franco leads a very large team reviewing in 2026 a radiation technique that deliberately delivers uneven doses to bulky tumours, sparing nearby tissue that limits ordinary treatment. Doses form peaks and valleys across the tumour, arranged as grids or lattices depending on the method.

Searching fifteen years of clinical reports, the reviewers gathered 29 studies covering 513 patients, mostly treated for sarcomas in the chest, pelvis, or abdomen, and often for symptom relief rather than cure. About four fifths of lesions shrank, symptoms eased consistently, and severe side effects stayed rare. Treatment settings varied widely between centres, so the authors call for shared protocols and prospective trials.
pmc-13214419:
Masoud Khorrami-Nejad and colleagues compare in 2026 how outward-turning eyes differ between females and males among more than four thousand surgical patients. Two forms of the condition, one constant in alternation and one intermittent, were analysed separately.

In the alternating form, females carried slightly more astigmatism, while males showed larger deviation angles and more severe lazy eye. In the intermittent form, females were younger, and males again had larger deviations plus more lazy eye overall. Sharpness of vision and the main focusing measure did not differ by sex in either form. After statistical adjustment, most gaps shrank, leaving a small deviation difference in one form and a lazy-eye link in the other.
pmc-13215619:
Jiguang Yu and Louis Shuo Wang present a 2026 mathematical study of how randomness should be built into predator-prey models. Standard models add simple diagonal noise terms, and the authors argue that this shortcut distorts the true pattern of population fluctuations.

Starting from an individual-based Markov chain version of the Rosenzweig-MacArthur model, they derive the noise structure that the biology actually implies. Coupled events, where a predator eats prey and gains from the same act, force a negative cross-covariance between the two populations. The authors also separate two model forms, one for studying survival inside the system and one that allows extinction, and they supply the proofs needed to keep each form sound.
pmc-13216319:
Matthias Hertel and co-authors present a 2026 methods paper on making time-series forecasts explain themselves quickly. Explanation tools based on Shapley values are trusted but slow, because they sample many altered copies of the input.

Their model, SHAPformer, is a Transformer forecaster that manipulates its own attention so it can compute exact Shapley explanations directly, without sampling background data. On synthetic series with known true explanations, the explanations matched the truth. Applied to electricity load and price data, the model forecast competitively while producing local and global explanations in under a second, hundreds of times faster than the standard permutation method. Among its findings, the recent past of the target itself dominated load forecasts.
pmc-13218619:
David Simons and colleagues map Lassa fever exposure village by village in Nigeria in a 2026 serology study. Lassa virus causes serious disease in West Africa, and vaccine trials need places where exposure is high, yet community-level maps barely exist. Without them, trial planners risk choosing sites where the virus is nearly absent.

The team surveyed nine villages across Benue, Ebonyi, and Cross River states, recruiting 1,874 people and testing blood for Lassa antibodies with a specific assay. Overall modelled seroprevalence was 3.2 percent, but village estimates ranged from under one percent to six and a half percent, a sharp patchiness. Age patterns differed too: some villages showed the build-up of endemic exposure, others the signature of a recent outbreak among younger people. None of twenty-one risk factors, including eating rodents or farm work, consistently predicted infection. The authors conclude village-level surveys are indispensable before siting vaccine trials.
pmc-13219819:
Murat Erem and colleagues build two scores for predicting death within ninety days of hip fracture surgery in a 2026 study. Existing prediction models stop at what is known before the operation, yet events during and after surgery, such as intensive care stays, carry risk. A two-stage approach could sharpen decisions at admission and after the operation.

Records of 387 patients aged sixty-five and over treated between 2018 and 2024 were analyzed, and sixty patients, 15.5 percent, died within ninety days. Five admission factors, poor nutrition score, age eighty-five or more, at least four illnesses, delay beyond five days, and fracture inside the joint capsule, formed the preoperative score. Adding an intensive care stay of five days or more made the score. Each model discriminated, and every extra point multiplied the odds of death by 2.68, so patients scoring four or more faced mortality above fifty percent. Calibration testing supported both scores.
pmc-13220619:
Madison E. Raposa and colleagues present results from the third FOCUS wave on safety culture in the United States fire service in a 2026 paper. The FOCUS instrument was built for fire departments, probing mental health, safety climate and leadership, safety behaviors, and organizational outcomes. Wave 3.0 added modules on leadership and mental health, reflecting where departments say the pressure sits.

The sample covered 9,078 firefighters in eighty-nine career, combination, and volunteer departments. Most respondents were male, non-officers, and non-veterans, and most departments were career services running thousands of calls. A gap appeared: supervisors scored fourteen points higher on support for safety than management scored on commitment to it. The numbers are stark, with twelve percent endorsing depression, ten percent anxiety, and nine percent reporting suicidal thoughts in the past month. Management commitment to safety tracked with leadership measures and negatively with burnout and intent to quit.
pmc-13220819:
Jiaoquan Chen and colleagues report a case of chronic spontaneous urticaria controlled by stapokibart in a 2026 case report. The condition raises itchy wheals and swelling without identifiable trigger, driven by mast cells, and it had tormented the forty-four-year-old woman with hives for over a year. Antihistamines failed her, and five doses of omalizumab, the second-line antibody, failed.

She was switched to stapokibart, an antibody against the interleukin-4 receptor that quiets inflammation, given as a dose and at widening intervals over thirty-five weeks. Control came fast: by week two her weekly urticaria activity score had fallen to zero and the control score reached the adequate range. By week twenty-two the control score hit its maximum, marking complete control. Three months of follow-up brought no relapse. The authors present the case as an option when omalizumab fails, while noting cyclosporine's risks make alternatives valuable.
pmc-13221419:
Rayan Ibrahim and Allison H. Moore present a 2026 math method for analyzing pseudoknots, the tangled folds that form in RNA molecules. Counting and sorting these structures with rigor has resisted standard approaches. Their scheme turns an RNA diagram into a graph, then applies a distance measure to that graph's crossings.

A pseudoknot is defined formally through a weighted covering problem on the graph. The resulting method, built in MATLAB, enumerates them and sorts RNA structures while sensing 3D shape features. Tests on a public database confirmed genus as a robust gauge of knot complexity. The work gives RNA modelers firmer math footing.
pmc-13222619:
Dingjie Wang and co-authors build a heat-responsive gel carrying carbon dots made from metronidazole for gum disease, in a 2026 study. Periodontitis starts with bacteria, yet standard local antibiotics wash away quickly and can irritate tissue. Carbon dots were cooked at two temperatures, compared, then loaded into a poloxamer gel that thickens at body temperature.

Dots made at the lower temperature kept more surface chemistry and killed bacteria better, so they advanced. The particles outperformed plain metronidazole against three periodontal bacteria while harming gum cells less. Rat testing covered safety in blood, inflammation markers, and tissue, plus bacterial load and bone imaging. The gel aims to keep treatment parked where the infection sits.
pmc-13223919:
Fivos Borbolis and Konstantinos Palikaras publish a protocol for counting contact sites between two cell parts in living worms, in a 2026 methods paper. Mitochondria-associated membranes, where the endoplasmic reticulum touches mitochondria, run calcium signals, fat handling, and stress responses. Their size offers a readout of cell health during aging and disease.

The method uses glowing reporters for each structure in the worm's gut cells, imaged by confocal scanning. Steps cover worm timing, microscope setup, and sample preparation. Analysis can proceed by hand on single images or in batches with Fiji software. Robust counting across conditions is the goal, building on an earlier study the authors cite for full use details.
pmc-13226219:
Miaomiao Liu and a large team demonstrate a 2026 electronic device that tells apart two causes of fluid around the lung: tuberculosis and late-stage cancer. The distinction changes treatment completely, yet no fast, efficient test exists. Their sensor is a memristor, a tiny component whose electrical resistance switches in response to what touches it.

Fluid samples from each condition nudged the device into measurably different electrical behaviour. The clearest signals were shifts in the ratio between its high and low resistance states and in peak current, which flipped with polarity depending on the fluid type. Tiny makeup differences between the effusions drive those responses, offering a possible bedside sorting tool.
pmc-13226819:
Shundai Ko and colleagues report a 2026 imported case of a tick-borne infection, human granulocytic anaplasmosis, diagnosed in Japan in a 77-year-old man recently returned from the United States. The disease is common in the north-eastern United States but almost unheard of in Japan. Five days of fever, lethargy, and appetite loss ended in confusion, with blood tests showing low platelets and raised liver and muscle enzymes.

His stay in Bemidji, Minnesota, a high tick-risk area, prompted immediate doxycycline treatment. Antibody tests were negative on arrival, but DNA testing found the Anaplasma bacterium, and sequencing matched reference strains exactly. He recovered quickly and left hospital on day five, underlining the value of molecular testing and travel history.
pmc-13232619:
Wu Chen and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six study of the body-clock gene BMAL1 protecting kidneys after blood-flow injury and reperfusion. Restored flow after blockage scars kidneys through progressive fibrosis. Immune macrophages can convert into scar-forming cells, worsening the damage over time.

Kidney-specific BMAL1 boosting in mice reduced scarring after the injury. The gene raised a small RNA shipped in tiny exosome packages from tubule cells. That cargo blocked a growth signal inside macrophages, stopping their conversion into scar cells. Cell and animal experiments confirmed each link. Clock biology thus offers a fresh anti-fibrosis lever for injured kidneys.
pmc-13232919:
Soorya Ram Shimgekar and colleagues published a 2026 exploratory study of suicidal thinking shared on Reddit. The group examined 59,607 posts from the r/SuicideWatch community through the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide. The Singapore team compared scores from written transcripts of 40 recorded sessions with video scores, and also let two versions of ChatGPT score the transcripts.

Scoring a transcript took about 12 minutes on average, versus 73 minutes of video. Transcript scores agreed well with video scores. The language models agreed only moderately with the human scorer and were inconsistent, giving the same score on all repeats in few cases. The authors back transcripts for teaching, but say the models need work first.
pmc-13263719:
Ming-Yi Zhang and colleagues describe three new fungi from Chinese city soils, an overlooked hunting ground. Urban soil fungi keep soil healthy and cycle nutrients, yet taxonomy there lags far behind forests. Their 2026 survey cultures eight isolates of the family Sympoventuriaceae.

Five genetic markers plus detailed morphology separated the finds from known relatives. The new species are Scolecobasidium campestre, Verruconis obovatus, and Veronaeopsis sinensis, each illustrated and compared with its nearest kin. Two belong to genera whose status has been unsettled, so the data also steady the family's family tree. City dirt, they show, still hides unnamed species.
pmc-13263819:
Michael Yan and colleagues used in 2026 Ontario health records to compare two targeted pills in lung cancer that had spread to the brain. Patients with EGFR-mutated metastatic disease received either osimertinib or the older gefitinib as first treatment, alongside brain radiation. Their database covered care from 2007 to 2024, and 481 patients met the study's rules.

Osimertinib patients stayed on first-line therapy about twice as long, a median near thirteen months against six. Control over brain disease also lasted longer, and median survival roughly doubled to about twenty-five months. Matching patients on background factors left all three advantages standing. The authors say real-world practice confirms the trial-based preference for the newer drug when the brain is involved. They note treatment duration itself as a meaningful real-world endpoint.
pmc-13264119:
Xiaokang Deng and a large team trace a pathway that drives preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy illness, in a 2026 study. Faulty placental cells that should remodel maternal arteries are central to the disease. Single-cell and genetic checks of preeclamptic placentas flagged higher levels of TET3, a regulator that changes how genes are switched on, along with altered sugar metabolism in those cells.

Lab tests showed extra TET3 slowed placental cell growth and movement by disturbing mitochondrial energy use. TET3 activated another regulator, FOS, which then suppressed PDK4, a gene controlling glucose handling. Checks in animal models and human placental samples supported the chain. Blocking this pathway is offered as a future treatment path needing further testing.
pmc-13264319:
Sara Adnane and colleagues find a long non-coding RNA that helps melanoma cells tolerate DNA damage in a 2026 study. Advanced melanoma often resists targeted drugs and immune therapy, with surviving cells seeding relapse. The RNA named DDERMMAL is found only in pigment-producing cells, the lineage melanoma comes from. Tests show it tunes damage response signaling so cells keep dividing despite genetic insults that would normally halt growth or trigger death under treatment pressure in the lab.

Tolerance of this kind lets hidden survivors hang on and gather new mutations that drive full resistance. Blocking the RNA could reopen a weak point unique to melanoma lineage cells. The work also flags it as a marker of risky staying power. Drug work would need delivery methods that reach tumor RNA selectively.
pmc-13264819:
Sally Abd-Elrahman Mohammed and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on home yoga for women after childbirth. The weeks after birth often bring pain, stress, and a drop in quality of life. Yoga mixes gentle movement, breathing, and relaxation, and doing it at home keeps costs low. The team tested a home program at a university hospital in Egypt.

Three hundred women were split evenly into a yoga group and a control group. The yoga group used a schedule card to guide and log practice, and both groups answered quality of life surveys. After the program, quality of life scores differed sharply between groups, and every woman in the yoga group reported some satisfaction, against none in the control group. The authors urge adding home yoga to routine care after birth.
pmc-13265019:
Wenshen Mo and Zhan Wang wrote a 2026 genetic study on blood proteins that may cause basal cell carcinoma, the most common skin cancer. Using protein data from the UK Biobank and an Icelandic group, they applied Mendelian randomization, a genetic method for testing cause, and traced chains where one protein acts through another.

The analysis found blood proteins affect cancer risk in one direction only, with no reverse effect, and the proteins clustered in immune and inflammation pathways. Thirteen UK proteins acted through six Icelandic-set proteins. Two hubs, STAT3 and GUCA1A, sat at the center of many chains, with the strongest single mediation reaching 15.2 percent. Sensitivity checks supported the results. The authors say the hubs could guide patient sorting and targeted treatment research.
pmc-13266019:
Hera Nirwati and colleagues test a soil bacterium's products against a key gum disease bacterium, in a 2026 study. Porphyromonas gingivalis forms biofilms and increasingly resists antibiotics. Fermentation extracts from Streptomyces strain GMR22 were split into fractions. Two fractions showed the strongest killing activity.

Microscopy confirmed sharply reduced bacterial growth after treatment. Chemical profiling named fatty acids and other compounds in the active fractions. Computer docking tested binding to two bacterial enzymes. One fatty acid bound both targets most strongly. The work supports this strain as a source of new antibacterial leads.
pmc-13266119:
Jin You Kim sums up key updates for breast MRI reporting in the 2025 BI-RADS system (2026). The standard lexicon aims to keep scan reports consistent. The new edition refines rather than rewrites core test rules. Capture and reporting guidance is now more structured.

Selected terms were aligned or removed. T2 signal brightness now helps characterise masses. Lymph node checks gained their own section. Features around tumours, such as swelling, were clarified. Medical indications for MRI assessment were also restructured. The overview helps doctors apply the updated manual in daily practice.
pmc-13266219:
Ren Liu and the team build a cell-free system that makes a nylon precursor from a bulk chemical (2026). Living-cell factories struggle with complex pathways and resource competition. The feedstock derives cheaply from caprolactam. Optimised enzyme assembly and cofactor recycling power the system.

Output rose more than five-hundred-fold to a record level, with near-total conversion. The system also produced longer related diamines at high levels. Activity survived a week of cold storage with modest loss. Avoiding living cells sidesteps their inherent limits. The authors see broad potential for efficient diamine manufacturing.
pmc-13266719:
Qian Wang and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six study predicting organ failure in intensive care patients with severe breathing failure. When several organs fail together, survival drops sharply. Early warning could guide faster action.

Patient data came from one hospital's intensive care unit over a recent period. The team combined ultrasound and laboratory measures as candidate predictors. A variable-selection method built a survival model, then checked its accuracy. Patients were split into risk groups with different outlooks. Clinicians get a structured score for spotting which respiratory failure patients head toward multi-organ trouble.
pmc-13267019:
Qing-Dong Ma and colleagues report the full chloroplast genome of a medicinal plant variety in a 2026 paper. The plant is a form of Paris polyphylla, a herb used in Chinese medicine and listed in drug standards of Gansu and Zhejiang provinces. Chloroplasts are the green parts of plant cells that carry their own small genome.

The genome is about 165,000 DNA letters long, with the usual four-part layout of plant chloroplasts. It holds 134 genes in total. Family-tree analysis placed this variety as sister to one close relative and near another well-known variety. The authors say the sequence gives a resource for future work on this herb, including checks of identity and kinship.
pmc-13267619:
Yun Zhang and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of soil quality under mangrove planting on China's coast. An invasive grass, Spartina alterniflora, has spread through coastal wetlands there. The team compared soils down to one meter under a native sedge, the invader, a restored mangrove called Kandelia obovata, and mixed stands in the Oujiang Estuary. They also compared four mangrove sites across Zhejiang Province.

Plant type and soil depth both strongly shaped soil traits. Mangrove soils held the most nitrogen and usable phosphorus, yet their ratios hinted at phosphorus shortage. A combined quality ranking put mangrove first, then the invader, mixed stands, and the sedge. Two bays ranked as the best mangrove sites. The authors say planting improves soil but will need added phosphorus over time.
pmc-13269019:
Eva Gómez-Pérez and colleagues re-examine in 2026 how drinking alcohol may raise colorectal cancer risk through the combined action of diet and gut microbes. Alcohol is a proven carcinogen with no safe intake level, and gut microbe shifts appear both in heavy drinkers and as intestinal polyps progress toward cancer. Their perspective weighs the three-way interplay among diet, microbes, and the body.

A pilot study in Asturias, northern Spain, supplies tissue, nutrition, and microbe data from people with intestinal polyps for close analysis. The authors sort what is known about how alcohol's toxicity could be amplified or softened by what people eat and which microbes they carry. They close by mapping the main unknowns that future studies must resolve.
pmc-13269519:
Vincent Leclercq published a review article in 2026 on careful use of two biomarker tests in parkinsonism, a group of movement disorders that can look alike early on. One test detects clumping activity of a brain protein, alpha-synuclein. The other measures a protein released when nerve fibers are damaged.

The first test identifies Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia with high accuracy, but misses more cases in some genetic and early forms. The second test helps separate those diseases from atypical disorders, though cut points vary with age and test platform. Leclercq proposes step-by-step paths that combine test results with scans, genes, and prior likelihood. He also stresses explaining positive and negative results clearly to patients.
pmc-13270019:
Qingling Chen, Zhaohui Liu, and Guanfeng Shi published a journal article in 2026 on moral leadership and negative workplace gossip. Moral leadership has two sides: being a moral person and actively managing ethics at work. The study asked what happens when those two sides match or mismatch in the same leader.

Using surface analysis of survey patterns, aligned leaders drew less negative gossip from staff. Leaders strong on both sides faced the least gossip of all. A leader seen as moral personally but weak on managing ethics fared better than the reverse profile. Perceived hypocrisy explained much of the effect. The authors say splitting the two sides exposes a hidden cost of virtuous leadership.
pmc-13271419:
Haoyun Zhao is lead author of a 2026 case report of a primitive neuroectodermal tumour, a rare and aggressive cancer, arising in the endometrium, the lining of the womb. Such tumours have vague symptoms and images, so they are often mistaken for harmless growths and treated late.

The patient was a 26-year-old woman with persistent abnormal womb bleeding, first diagnosed after scraping as a benign polyp. Later scans showed a large mass inside the womb, and tissue tests, including a marker called CD99 and characteristic rosette patterns, confirmed the rare tumour. She had major surgery with lymph node removal, then chemotherapy, which was stopped because of severe side effects. The authors stress early, definite diagnosis.
pmc-13272019:
Xiaotong He and coauthors measure in 2026 a blood iron-handling protein in people with ulcerative colitis and relate it to inflammation and a form of iron-driven cell death. Transferrin receptor 1 pulls iron into cells, and its role in this bowel disease was undefined. Iron balance, oxidative stress, and inflammation all shift in active colitis.

Blood from 83 patients with active disease held clearly higher receptor levels than samples from 80 healthy controls, rising further with disease severity. Levels tracked with standard inflammation markers, clotting measures, and a lipid damage marker of the cell death process. The authors propose the protein as a candidate severity marker.
pmc-13272419:
Emery M Kalondero proposes in 2026 a framework for cancer immunotherapy that demands two confirming signals before immune attack begins. Single-signal designs fail when tumors shed their target or when healthy tissue shares it, causing both missed cancers and collateral damage. The proposed system, called AABS, validates targets the way careful engineering double-checks commands.

Its simplified version runs three layers: priming that makes tumor targets more visible, a logic gate requiring two independent tumor signals at once, and effectors that fire only on dual confirmation. Cancer genome atlas data supplied supporting analysis. The author presents the design as a concept needing laboratory proof.
pmc-13272519:
Ambachew Motbaynor Wubaye and colleagues studied illness and death in camel calves in eastern Ethiopia in a 2026 cohort investigation. Camels matter greatly to herders in dry regions, and losing calves threatens herd growth. The team worked around Dire Dawa, following households over time.

They combined a survey with follow-up of calves from 385 households chosen for the study. Illness was very common in the first six months of life, and about one calf in six died in that period. Calves given free access to colostrum, the first milk after birth, faced lower risk. Older calves and those born normally also fared better. The authors urge better veterinary services and herder training on early feeding.
pmc-13272619:
Per Flodbring Larsson leads a 2026 study of a new antibody treatment for prostate cancer that has spread and no longer responds to hormone therapy. The target is a growth signal receptor called TbetaRI, which an enzyme can cut so a fragment enters the cell nucleus. That fragment helps cancer invade and spread.

The team made human antibodies that block the cut by covering the site. In mice carrying human tumors, the antibodies stopped the fragment reaching the nucleus and curbed growth, invasion, and spread. The effect matched a standard chemotherapy drug, with no clear harm to body weight, aorta, or heart in the mice tested.
pmc-13272719:
Weihua Hu leads a 2026 study of a gene called SOAT1 in glioma, an aggressive brain tumor. The team asked whether levels of this gene track with survival, immune cells in tumors, and blood test results. They used two large glioma databases and a hospital group of 195 patients who had surgery from 2016 to 2020.

SOAT1 levels rose with tumor grade, and high levels meant a worse outlook, even after other factors were counted. High levels also linked to more immune cells in tumors, especially macrophages and neutrophils, and to higher inflammation scores in blood. Salt levels in blood were lower and bilirubin higher in the high group.
pmc-13273219:
Jun Li, Weijian Li, Dan Wang, and Yulan Liu reviewed how pathogens hide from immunity by exploiting mitophagy in a 2026 article. Mitophagy is the cell's way of clearing worn out mitochondria, its energy units. Some invaders turn this cleanup to their own advantage.

The review explains how mitophagy links with mitochondrial shape change, then surveys bacteria, viruses, and parasites that use it to blunt innate immune defenses. Several pathogens adjust mitophagy up or down at different infection stages to survive. The authors list four counter strategies, including drugs that tune the pathway and engineered mitochondria. Open questions include how timing shapes evasion and how shape change connects to cleanup. New imaging tools may help answer them.
pmc-13273319:
Neeraja Vegesna and colleagues identified two chromatin reader proteins that help repair broken DNA in plants in a 2026 study. Repair happens inside chromatin, the packed form of DNA, yet plant proteins that link the two were poorly known. The team worked in Arabidopsis thaliana, a model plant.

The readers, named YAF9A and YAF9B, proved critical for fixing double strand breaks through homology directed repair, which copies information from a matching DNA stretch. Each reader connects to a distinct chromatin remodeling complex, the machines that loosen or shift DNA packaging. The reading domain of YAF9B was required for its protective role. The authors say these findings close a gap in how plants coordinate repair with chromatin state.
pmc-13273519:
Qian Shen leads a 2026 review of inherited DNA damage response gene mutations in multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow. Faults in genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, and CHEK2, which normally repair DNA, can raise myeloma risk and shape how the disease evolves and responds to treatment.

Inherited repair defects promote chromosome instability, reshape the immune setting around tumors, and aid therapy-driven progression, the authors summarize. New tools such as multiomics profiling, single-cell sequencing, and liquid biopsy improve monitoring of these changes. The faults also create vulnerabilities that precision therapies can exploit, including PARP inhibitor strategies that kill cells lacking backup repair paths.
pmc-13273719:
Faust Schotte and co-authors reviewed methods for detecting anisakid worm material in food in a 2026 systematic review. These parasites live in seafood and can infect people, and their proteins can trigger allergy even after the worms are removed. Factory checks still rely on looking by eye, which misses invisible traces.

Searching four databases, they found twenty-five articles on non-visual detection. Ten methods used DNA, fourteen used antibody chemistry, and five used mass spectrometry. Reporting of performance was too uneven for clean comparison. For routine allergen checks they recommend one glowing antibody test format. A fast DNA method called LAMP looks best for larval DNA, while mass spectrometry suits the most sensitive trace work.
pmc-13274019:
Ruth Cowlishaw and colleagues wrote a 2026 semi-systematic review of threadworm infection in baboons. The worm Strongyloides fuelleborni can infect both baboons and people, so baboon infections may matter for human health. Baboons are Africa's most widespread non-human primate, yet this risk is little studied.

The team searched three databases through December 2025, screening 1,588 articles down to forty-four for summary. Infection rates differed across the six baboon species, highest in yellow baboons at about sixty-nine percent and lowest in Guinea baboons. More than two thirds of papers never named the worm to species level. The authors urge better species identification so the true risk to people can be judged.
pmc-13274119:
Eman M Othman and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on cytokinins, chemicals long known as plant growth hormones, inside mammals. Whether these small molecules occur in animals, and where they come from, was largely undefined. The team combined chemical profiling of blood and tissues with studies of gut microbes.

Blood from five animal species consistently held several cytokinin forms, led by a storage form called zeatin-O-glucoside, at levels far below plants. In mice, fasting sharply lowered cytokinin levels in blood, gut, and urine, showing diet is a major source. Germ-free mice had much lower levels than normal mice, proving gut microbes also contribute to the supply.
pmc-13274819:
Hannah Healey, Claudia Susana Caxaj, and Elysée Nouvet present a 2026 qualitative journal article on who gets recognized as having an eating disorder. Beyond clinic wait lists, the authors argue, people face symbolic barriers: being disbelieved, misread, or ruled out by narrow ideas of what these illnesses look like. They used narrative methods informed by lived experience.

One theme ran through the accounts, summed up as 'Who Gets Seen.' Participants described struggling for legitimacy, being seen, misread, or overlooked by family, friends, and clinicians, and learning to recognize their own illness. The authors frame this as epistemic injustice, where a person's credibility is unfairly discounted. They urge reimagining who counts as deserving of care.
pmc-13275219:
Nannan Lv and co-authors linked vitamin D status with calcium, inflammation, and thyroid autoimmunity in type 2 diabetes in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Vitamin D shortage is common in diabetes and may disturb immune and metabolic health. The team split patients by their blood vitamin D level.

They enrolled 503 patients, and more than four in five fell below the deficiency cutoff. Higher vitamin D went with lower parathyroid hormone and higher calcium. An inflammation marker peaked in the moderately deficient group rather than the lowest. Thyroid hormone levels were lowest in severe deficiency. Oddly, one thyroid antibody tracked with higher vitamin D while another tracked with lower. No link appeared with blood sugar control or body mass. The authors call the thyroid pattern complex.
pmc-13275919:
Ulrike Hendgen-Cotta and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on protecting mitochondria, the tiny power stations inside cells. When mitochondria are damaged, cells can die, driving injury in the heart, brain, and liver. A protein called BNIP3 helps trigger that death, but its controls were poorly understood.

The authors worked backward from BNIP3's structure to find the short stretch that switches on cell death proteins. They then built a peptide, a small protein fragment named B-017, that blocks BNIP3 from binding those partners. In human cells the peptide stopped death signals while leaving other functions alone. In animal models it reduced tissue damage in the heart, brain, and liver. The team offers it as a candidate drug for diseases tied to failing mitochondria.
pmc-13276219:
Massrehaw Assnakew Abebe and co-authors report a 2026 computer-based study designing test proteins for epidemic typhus. This louse-spread disease, caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii, still threatens many poorer regions. Current blood tests for it are often insensitive or unreliable, delaying treatment.

Using gene and protein data, the team picked two bacterial surface proteins as the most promising targets. They then designed two engineered proteins on the computer. One strings together short immune-triggering fragments; the other uses larger chunks of the natural proteins. Checks suggested both designs would be stable, soluble, and strong at provoking immune recognition. They also barely resemble human proteins, which lowers false alarms. Computer docking tests indicated steady binding to an immune receptor. Lab validation still lies ahead.
pmc-13276319:
Salma El Aouadi and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a newborn whose breathing failed because of a rare bone disorder. Jeune syndrome narrows the chest cage so much that the lungs cannot expand. It is inherited and can also affect the pelvis and other organs.

The full-term baby boy was admitted on his first day of life in acute respiratory distress. Imaging showed a markedly narrow chest with short ribs and raised collarbones. His pelvis showed the syndrome's signature shape, with trident-like hip sockets and short iliac bones. Despite intensive support and a breathing machine, his respiratory failure worsened. He died after seven days. The authors use the case to highlight the imaging signs that let doctors recognize this rare, life-threatening condition early.
pmc-13276519:
Jacinta D Kong and colleagues argue in a 2026 article that the edible insect industry needs joined-up research. Insects offer protein for people and feed for fish, chickens, and pigs, plus fertiliser and waste processing. Production chains stretch across biology, engineering, business, and culture.

Research on edible insects has grown inside separate disciplines that rarely talk to each other. Regional industries also differ widely, from hand-harvested wild insects to automated farms. The authors say shared industry goals can pull fields together and speed practical progress. They urge durable partnerships among universities, companies, and governments so findings on farming, processing, and markets reinforce one another.
pmc-13276819:
Jackline A Odhiambo leads a 2026 survey of widowed women in Siaya County, Kenya, an area with high HIV rates. The team asked when women living with HIV may have been exposed and what risk behaviors had occurred since widowhood. A random sample of 480 widows took part, grouped by age.

About thirty-seven percent of the women had HIV, and many infections may have come after widowhood began. At least half reported sex without a condom since becoming widows. Becoming widowed before age thirty was strongly tied to condomless sex and to customs such as widow inheritance and sexual cleansing. The authors urge testing, preventive drugs, and safer practice within those customs.
pmc-13277019:
Jade Cartwright leads a 2026 study of a new mealtime model in one Australian residential aged care home. Older residents face high risk of malnutrition, poor nutrition that weakens health. The model, called Maggie Beer's Big Mission, aimed to improve food, access to meals, and the dining setting through work across many staff roles.

Interviews, audits, and meal observations ran over ten months at three points in time. Staff and residents welcomed the model and reported better meal quality and a calmer, more home-like dining room. Shared vision, training, and leadership helped the changes stick in daily routines. The authors say longer studies should test whether the gains last and what they cost.
pmc-13277319:
Aurelio Mollo and colleagues examine a chemical link inside calprotectin, a human defence protein, in a 2026 study. Calprotectin starves bacteria by locking away metals they need, a strategy called nutritional immunity. Each of its two subunits holds one sulfur-bearing residue that can pair into a disulfide bond.

The team built a clean supply of the bonded form and tested how it behaves. With calcium present it grouped into four-unit assemblies and stripped several metals from bacterial growth media. Bacteria exposed to it showed signs of iron starvation. The bond also made the protein easier for digestive enzymes to cut, which suggests oxidation helps set the protein's working lifetime.
pmc-13278019:
Soledad Gómez-Escalonilla Lorenzo leads a 2026 pre-post study of how COVID-19 lockdowns affected patients with high blood pressure and diabetes in central Spain. Restrictions cut activity and disrupted daily disease management. The team measured 152 patients from March 2019 to June 2021, before and after lockdown, tracking blood pressure, weight, blood sugar, activity, drug adherence, and quality of life.

A year after lockdown began, systolic blood pressure had risen, while activity, adherence, and mental quality of life had fallen. Patients in the least active group fared worst on adherence and mental quality of life. The most active patients actually improved their adherence. The authors caution that the design cannot prove lockdown caused each change.
pmc-13278419:
Sei-Woong Choi leads a 2026 genetic study comparing mainland and island moth populations in southern South Korea. Island populations are often expected to lose genetic diversity. The team sampled two moth species along mountain slopes on mainland Mount Jirisan and island Mount Hallasan, analyzing 155 individuals and their mitochondrial DNA.

One species kept similarly high diversity in both places, with strong gene flow across regions. The other showed lower overall diversity but, against expectation, higher diversity on the island, plus strong geographic structuring and little migration. Both species split clearly between mainland and island, but not within each mountain. Island diversity loss is not universal; species traits and setting decide the pattern, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278719:
Tetsuro Tachibana and colleagues measure a brain growth factor in patients checked for coronary artery disease, in a 2026 study. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, circulates in blood and has been linked to heart disease inconsistently. Platelets store much of it, which can distort readings.

Four hundred two patients at Fukuoka University Hospital had CT angiography of their coronary arteries. Those with significant narrowing showed lower plasma BDNF than those without. Platelet count proved the strongest driver of BDNF levels in the analysis. Once platelet count was accounted for, the link between BDNF and disease faded to non-significance. The authors warn that platelet effects must be handled in future BDNF studies.
pmc-13278919:
Leah Klingel and colleagues describe a child's blood disorder that unfolded after a common virus infection, in a 2026 case report. A healthy seven-year-old girl arrived with low counts across all blood cell lines during acute parvovirus B19 infection. The virus usually suppresses marrow briefly, so her deeper changes raised concern.

Marrow examination showed sparse tissue with abnormal development across several cell lines, short of full myelodysplastic syndrome. Extensive testing excluded immune disease, inherited marrow failure, and known predisposition genes. Repeat checks showed the abnormal pattern evolving until the syndrome diagnosis was confirmed. A donor stem cell transplant restored her blood fully. The virus lingered at low levels long after transplant without clear harm.
pmc-13279019:
Ke Cheng and co-authors report a 2026 study of colon and rectum cancer spread under low oxygen. Low oxygen zones are common in fast growing tumours. A master switch called HIF-1 turns on genes that help tumours grow new blood vessels and spread. The team asks how a protein called TDP-43 fits in that chain.

Lab and animal work showed HIF-1 turns on the gene for TDP-43. TDP-43 then holds steady a message for a second protein, TRIP6, which helps vessel growth. Cutting TDP-43 slowed spread and vessel growth. Restoring TRIP6 brought the harmful traits back. The chain gives drug makers a clear new target to test.
pmc-13279519:
Li Liu and colleagues published a 2026 article on using learning psychology to make mobile medical resources actually get used. Learning by phone and tablet now spans online courses, virtual labs, remote internships, and digital testing. It expanded quickly during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Medical schools have invested heavily, yet the authors name a stubborn gap: many students drop out, and some excellent materials draw very few clicks.

Their proposals draw on how motivation, attention, and self-regulation work, aiming to convert available content into completed learning. Strategies address course construction, learner engagement, and how medical students actually study on portable devices. The piece is practical rather than experimental, offering advice for teachers and program designers. Its point is that access alone does not educate; psychology-informed design decides whether resources fulfill their promise.
pmc-13280619:
Luca Persani and Leonidas H. Duntas present a 2026 article on diet as a supportive yet critical factor in managing thyroid disorders. The thyroid is framed as a metabolic engine converting nutrients in energy for the entire body. Macronutrients build and repair muscles and support cellular structure, while micronutrients serve growth, immune function and disease prevention. Thyroid health depends on adequate, synergistic intake of iodine, selenium and iron, termed the critical bodyguards of thyroid function.

Iodine enters the circulation as iodide and is taken up in the thyrocyte by a sodium iodide symporter. Thyroid peroxidase oxidizes it, and iodinated residues in thyroglobulin drive formation and release of thyroxine and triiodothyronine, the T4 and T3 hormones. Daily iodine sources include seafood, seaweed, dairy, eggs and iodized salt. Balance is needed: low intake promotes goiter and possibly thyroid nodules, while high regular amounts can be toxic to the thyroid.
pmc-13280919:
Mohammed Mansour Quradha and colleagues published a 2026 study testing natural deep eutectic solvents, green liquids, for extracting compounds from clary sage. Three solvent recipes mixed choline chloride with citric acid, glucose, or glycerol. Extracts were profiled by liquid chromatography, and the team ran five antioxidant assays plus tests against two cholinesterase enzymes targeted by Alzheimer's drugs and against urease.

The glucose-based solvent pulled out the most rosmarinic acid, about 44.56 micrograms per gram, and each solvent captured a distinct set of compounds, with some acids appearing in only one extract. That glucose formulation also beat the reference antioxidants BHA and alpha-tocopherol in the battery. It inhibited both, with half-blocking concentrations near 100 micrograms per milliliter, while all extracts barely touched urease, under 21 percent inhibition. The authors pitch the glucose solvent as a candidate processing ingredient.
pmc-13281919:
Mathilde Boussac and colleagues scanned the brains of people with Tourette syndrome in a 2026 study. Tourette brings tics, sudden movements or sounds the person cannot fully control. Its brain roots stay murky, with dopamine long blamed. The team used a scan tracer that lights up active NMDA receptors, doors for the signal chemical glutamate. Twelve patients and twelve healthy peers were scanned. Patients also took scales for tic severity, urges, and mood.

Patients showed higher receptor activity in five brain spots. They included a mood-and-conflict hub at the front and a movement hub deep inside. The front hub's activity rose in step with tic severity scores. The authors read this as a glutamate system running hot. A hot signal may overdrive the direct movement path and loose tics. The finding points to glutamate-calming drugs as a route worth testing.
pmc-13283219:
Salmon farms in a Chilean fjord nudge coral microbes toward drug resistance, Anna Berezkina's sampling team reports for 2026. Heavy antibiotic use in salmon farming may affect nearby sea life. Cold-water coral banks grow in fjords close to many farm sites.

Coral samples came from sites near and far from farms in Comau Fjord. Cultured coral bacteria near farms resisted slightly more drugs on average. Dominant bacteria shifted near farms in both culture and gene tests. Common farm drugs still cut growth of most isolates in lab tests. One drug, tilmicosin, was the main exception in the results. The authors call for wider checks across space and time.
pmc-13283519:
Ram Prabhoo and five fellow specialists review the evidence for a collagen supplement in osteoarthritis. They focus on the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, where the disease strikes earlier and harder than in Western populations. Standard drugs mostly mask symptoms and carry side effects, so adjuncts attract interest.

The panel concludes that undenatured type II collagen at forty milligrams daily improves pain, stiffness, function, and quality of life in early-to-moderate disease. Benefits appear inside eight weeks, with an anti-inflammatory-sparing effect. Evidence favored one branded source over others. Their consensus recommends the supplement alongside physiotherapy for long-term use in responders. They also call for larger trials and imaging studies to test any disease-modifying claim.
pmc-13283619:
Faking on personality questionnaires is the problem at the heart of a 2026 simulation study by Julius David Kleinbub and Timo Seitz. Their model tries to split true trait scores from answers warped to look good. One key premise says all test takers judge what looks good in much the same way.

Computer runs broke that premise in three distinct ways to test model strength. Recovery of true scores held up well when faking matched each persons own view of what looks good. Trouble grew when people faked toward views they did not hold themselves. Test users can trust the model within limits, but those limits depend on honest alignment.
pmc-13283719:
Josh Riesenberg and co-authors measured thigh muscle activity in 2026 in teenagers with kneecap instability, before surgery and again at return to sport. One thigh muscle, the vastus medialis obliquus, pulls the kneecap inward and steadies it. Injury and surgery can switch muscles off through a reflex called arthrogenic inhibition. Surface sensors recorded muscle signals while patients did an overhead squat in a motion lab.

Before surgery, twenty-five patients showed the front thigh muscle firing forty percent less on the treated side, while the inner muscle looked even. At clearance, in a second group of twenty, the pattern had flipped: the inner muscle fired sixty-one percent less on the treated side, while the front muscle matched. The authors flag shifting muscle deficits across recovery.
pmc-13283919:
Lasting tumor shrinkage on a targeted drug conjugate is reported for bladder cancer in a 2026 case by Zhi-ruo Jin and colleagues. The drug, disitamab vedotin, links an antibody to a cell-killing payload. It aims at HER2, a growth signal found on some bladder tumors.

The patient had advanced disease that grew after first-line chemo plus immune therapy. Tumor tests showed mid-level HER2 with a negative gene amplification test. Response held as a partial shrinkage for more than eight months. Bladder cancer struck over six hundred thousand people worldwide in 2022 by cited counts. Wider HER2 testing could open this option to more patients.
pmc-13284019:
Three bowel control scores disagree often enough to mislead follow-up in a 2026 study by Galib Bairamovi and colleagues. Children born with anorectal malformations need lifelong checks on continence after repair. Kelly, Holschneider, and Templeton scores each grade control differently.

Records covered 110 surgically treated patients seen from 2007 to 2017. All three scores were applied at the latest follow-up visit for each child. Score links were moderate, and category agreement ranged from moderate to substantial. Poor control rates shifted noticeably depending on which score was used. Predictors of poor control also changed by scoring system. Combined scoring is advised.
pmc-13284419:
Franziska Richter and colleagues report a 2026 study of diabetes risk in young cancer survivors who had radiation to the brain and spine. Such survivors face higher risk of metabolic problems, but brain tumor groups have been studied less than leukemia groups. The team drew on a survey cohort and a late-effects clinic cohort.

In the survey group of 197 respondents, diabetes was reported by about 3 percent of survivors, a rate close to the matched general public. In the clinic group that had craniospinal radiation, about one third showed poor glucose control, split between diabetes and prediabetes levels. The authors call for planned, risk-based long-term checks of blood sugar in this survivor group.
pmc-13284719:
Takayuki Katoh and Hiraku Takada boosted in 2026 the factory that builds proteins so it can insert unusual building blocks into peptides. Genetic code reprogramming lets ribosomes use backbone-altering amino acids, variants with shifted or methylated backbones that make peptides tougher and more drug-like. Their insertion lags far behind normal amino acids. The authors tested two helper factors, YebC and YeeN, that may prime the ribosome's entry site.

Across eleven test blocks, the helpers raised repeated insertion about two to threefold on average, and up to more than sixfold in the best case. Pairing YebC with two known helpers gave an eightfold rise for one hard double insertion. The factors also enabled drug-like ring-shaped peptides rich in unusual blocks. The authors see a path to large peptide libraries for screening.
pmc-13285219:
Angelo Federico recounts, in a 2026 historical article, how surgeon Archibald McIndoe treated badly burned airmen during the Second World War and how his patients formed the Guinea Pig Club in 1941. The men called themselves guinea pigs because the operations they received were new and experimental. Reconstructive surgery was still young, and options for severe burns were few.

McIndoe dropped harmful tannic acid treatments in favor of salt-water soaking, early movement, and staged skin grafts and flap surgery. Care extended beyond the operating room to mental recovery and a return to ordinary life. The town of East Grinstead, where the hospital stood, became known for accepting the men without staring. Modern burn care still follows much of this model.
pmc-13285419:
Breathing tiny plastic bits into rat lungs leaves clear marks, a 2026 toxicity study by Hyoung-Yun Han and co-authors finds. Micro and nano polyethylene bits are rising as a lung risk worry, yet safety proof is thin. Rats got weekly doses into the windpipe for thirteen weeks at four dose levels, then a four-week rest phase checked if harm faded.

Swelling cells ringed vessels and airways in both sexes at even the lowest dose for both bit sizes. Thick airway walls and lining overgrowth showed at higher doses, sooner in females for some signs. Harm signals split by sex, with some proteins surging more in females and one more in males. The authors set the lowest harm dose from these signs.
pmc-13285919:
Mingrong Cheng and colleagues review nanotechnology for liver cancer care in a 2026 survey of metabolism and immunity. Liver tumors rewire how they burn sugar, fat, and amino acids, and that rewiring also muffles immune attack. Drugs alone rarely break the loop, since targeted agents meet resistance and immune drugs answer in few patients.

Tiny carriers can land in tumors, sense acid or stress cues there, and release several drugs at once where they matter most. By tuning sugar, fat, and amino acid paths together, such platforms may lift the immune brake and boost checkpoint drugs or local care. Matching carrier design to a tumor's metabolic type offers a path to truly personal treatment. Carrier quality, shared test standards, and proof in patients remain the hurdles the authors flag for the field.
pmc-13286219: A short 2026 retraction notice from the editors of PLOS One withdraws a study of silicon carbide thin films for quantum spacecraft uses. The editors cite many references that could not be found or retrieved, plus repeated entries padding the reference list. They also cite breaches of journal rules on authorship and on declared use of artificial intelligence tools. Five named authors disagreed with the withdrawal, and two others gave no answer or could not be reached. The notice stands as the full record here.
pmc-13286819:
Yanyan Li and co-authors tell the story of a 39-year-old man whose breathing test looked like COPD but actually reflected Fabry disease, a rare inherited storage disorder. The 2026 case report follows his diagnosis through family screening after relatives were found to carry the condition. His twenty-year smoking history made the COPD label tempting.

Testing showed reduced enzyme activity and a disease-causing gene variant, plus heart wall thickening, protein in the urine, and eye changes typical of Fabry disease. Scans showed no emphysema. Doctors briefly gave inhaled bronchodilators, then stopped them and started enzyme replacement therapy as the real treatment. Reflex prescribing habits, the authors warn, can outlast the findings that should overturn them.
pmc-13286919:
Anna Meinecke and colleagues check whether an antibody called anti-Ro52 marks dryness problems in patients with inflammatory muscle diseases. The 2026 study reviews ninety-seven patients tested at Hannover Medical School between 2018 and 2024. The antibody is known from Sjögren's disease and has been tied to lung involvement in myopathy patients.

Nearly half the patients carried the antibody. Carriers had more than triple the odds of interstitial lung disease. Objective dryness, measured by standard tear and saliva tests, was also far more common among carriers. The authors conclude that the antibody flags an overlap with Sjögren's disease inside this muscle disease group, which may matter for monitoring lungs and glands.
pmc-13287219:
Tobias Dust and co-authors asked in 2026 whether mixed reality headsets help surgeons agree when planning operations for broken knee plateaus. Twelve trauma surgeons, half junior and half senior, reviewed 22 fractures in stages, using standard scans, three-dimensional reconstructions, printed models, and finally a headset view.

Agreement on treatment plan stayed high under every method. Agreement improved most with the headset for choosing the surgical route and for deciding how to position the patient, and juniors gained the most. Matching reached 57% for positioning under mixed reality. The authors present headset review as a planning and teaching aid, while noting that patient outcome studies are still needed.
pmc-13287419:
Pedram Rajabifard and co-authors followed older patients in 2026 at two Victorian units who had lower leg and ankle fractures fixed through the skin with nails and screws, rather than open surgery. All had fragile skin around the injury, a common problem after age 65.

Thirteen ankles in 11 patients, average age 82, were treated. Surgery happened at a median of three days, without waiting for swelling to settle. Six patients could bear weight right away, and the median hospital stay was five days. One deep infection needed device removal, and two small skin breaks healed with dressings. The authors see the method as workable for this group.
pmc-13287919:
Shangyuan Liu and co-authors introduce a way to create new immune targets in tumors by editing RNA, reported in 2026. Tumor-specific targets usually come from random mutations, so each patient needs a custom vaccine. Cancers with few mutations may offer almost no targets at all. The new method rewrites a chosen letter in RNA copies of shared tumor proteins instead. That small edit changes the protein piece shown to immune cells.

The team aimed the editor at contact points that T cells use to recognize their target. Edited pieces woke up matching T cells in lab tests. A vaccine built from circular RNA in fat particles then triggered strong killer T cell responses in mice. Tumors carrying the edited target grew more slowly after vaccination. The authors present the work as proof of concept for widening immune therapy to low-mutation cancers.
pmc-13288219:
Darren Hargrave and colleagues published this 2026 correction to a phase I/II study of two immune drugs in children with advanced solid tumors. The drugs, durvalumab and tremelimumab, were tested first in a dose-finding phase and then in an expansion phase. The correction fixes Table 1, the study's baseline table, where values under the tumor types heading were misaligned. A missing footnote about unrecorded histology was also restored.

The corrected table covers 50 patients in total, 29 in dose finding and 21 in expansion. Median age across the study was about eleven and a half years, with patients as young as one. Sarcomas formed the largest tumor group, and two thirds of patients had metastatic disease. Most had already received chemotherapy, and many had prior surgery or radiation. Readers can now match each tumor type count to the right phase column.
pmc-13288719:
Sung Woo Joo and Jungsun Lee map brain wiring in schizophrenia to gene activity in 2026. Their study uses MRI scans. It holds 1,216 people. Networks were built from cortex shape likeness. Patient and control maps were compared. Gene data came from the Allen atlas.

Whole-network scores barely split by group. Hub strength fell in key zones. Temporal, insular, and occipital zones were hit. Cingulate zones were hit too. Cross-module links dropped widely. Gene sets pointed to metal ion transport. Other sets pointed to nerve growth and learning. Timing sat in teen and young adult years. Synapse and growth paths look central.
pmc-13288919:
Xi Cheng and co-authors issued an author correction in 2026 for their study of a recombinant pig rotavirus vaccine. The original work built a rotavirus that expresses three versions of the VP7 surface protein. That design aimed to protect pigs against several rotavirus types at once. The correction addresses errors found in figure 6 and in a supplement figure after publication.

First, the y-axis label on three graphs in figure 6 should read RNA copies per milliliter. Second, the corrected figure 6G replaces image panels that had been duplicated by accident. A single control image now stands in, and the wrong challenge and vaccine group panels show the proper images. The supplement's figure S1B is also replaced with its correct version. The correction keeps the paper's data presentation aligned with the underlying experiments. It does not change the vaccine's reported protective claims.
pmc-13289119:
Shigeki Yamada and colleagues build an AI tool for brain scans in 2026. The tool reads plain CT scans. It seeks a treatable cause of walking and memory woes. That cause is called iNPH for short. Its scan sign is a skewed fluid pattern.

The model marks four fluid zones in the brain. Fake CT images from MRI were tried first. They proved too weak for training. Hand-marked real CT scans worked better. Test scores were high for most zones. One index split sick from well perfectly. That test held 115 patients in a row. Cut points were set from that group.
pmc-13289219:
Anil Paudel led a 2026 community survey on why households join Nepal's National Health Insurance Program. Fieldwork covered 360 randomly chosen households in Panini Rural Municipality, Arghakhanchi district, in July and August 2022. Interviews used questions shaped by the Health Belief Model, a framework about how people weigh risk and benefit.

Knowledge about the program proved a strong predictor of joining, as did feeling that premiums were affordable for the household. Recent illness and worry about poor family health also raised the odds of joining. Encouragement from neighbors, peers already enrolled, and agreement within the family mattered a great deal as well. Perceived benefits alone did not predict joining, which points planners toward outreach and trust building.
pmc-13289719:
Chunyan Guo and colleagues compare bacteria living on leaves and roots under added nitrogen, in a 2026 grassland study. Extra nitrogen in the air reshapes grassland life, yet plant microbes are rarely tracked as it comes and goes. The team ran a long test in a grass steppe, adding nitrogen for years and then halting it. They checked how each group held up and how fast it bounced back.

Leaf bacteria held up less well than root bacteria when nitrogen was added. Leaf sugar and leaf shape drove that weak hold through shifts in key bacterial groups. Root bacteria bounced back faster once inputs stopped, helped by stored nitrogen in roots and root form. Leaf microbes that aid nitrogen cycling stayed suppressed long after inputs ended. Root microbes tied to carbon cycling came back fast. The contrast shows leaf and root microbes need separate forecasts.
pmc-13290019:
Hannah M Cranford led a 2026 implementation report on modernizing disease surveillance in the United States Virgin Islands. In January 2024 the health department needed to sustain its cloud surveillance system while advancing local data modernization. Leaders chose to move the national surveillance platform to Amazon Web Services under local control and upgrade to the newest version, called NBS 7, with federal partner advice.

Phased work covered planning, cost review, deployment, database transfer, validation, and staged reconnection of reporting sites. The system went live on May 6, 2025, making the territory the first jurisdiction on that cloud host for this platform. Cost savings neared 90 percent, with faster data flow and stronger local informatics skill.
pmc-13290519:
Advanced clot-removal care leaves the heart's right side working better months later, Hammad Sheikh and colleagues report in 2026. The study covers survivors of acute pulmonary embolism treated at the Mount Sinai Health System in New York between 2021 and 2023.

Of 122 patients with scans at the start and at follow-up, some had clot removal by catheter or surgery, and the rest had blood thinners alone. In matched, adjusted comparisons, the treated group pumped more blood from the right ventricle and had triple the odds of a better tricuspid valve grade. Follow-up came at a median of 26 weeks. Sheikh and colleagues say the results back aggressive treatment for higher-risk embolism, at least among survivors.
pmc-13291119:
A hyaluronate nose spray is compared with saline by Weizheng Zhao and colleagues in a 2026 mouse study. Saline rinses are a staple for nasal disease. Plain salt water cannot copy the airway surface liquid. That gap may cap long-term rinse gains.

Mice breathed mugwort allergen through the nose. They then got saline or the test spray for days. Scratching, crusting, and tissue state were scored. Spray mice scratched less and crusted less. Allergy signals fell in tissue and blood. Mucus depth and clearance speed held up better. Cell barrier proteins stayed the same in both groups.
pmc-13291219:
High pastures on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau get strong sun. Ting-xu Feng leads a 2026 field study on using that light well. Mixed oat and pea sowing makes valued feed. Added fertilizer may lift both yield and feed quality.

Four feeding plans were compared in the trial. One gave nitrogen alone, one gave phosphorus alone. A third gave both, and a fourth gave none. Leaf color, shape, and light use were tracked. Both nutrients together raised leaf green and light scores most. Leaf size also grew under the combined plan. Feed protein and nutrient levels rose with it. Mixed feeding thus looks best for quality grass here.
pmc-13292019:
Mehrgan Shahryari and co-authors tell a 2026 diagnostic case story about a brain mass that looked like glioblastoma but was not. A 65-year-old man arrived with tingling, slowed thinking, and slurred speech, and MRI showed a lone enhancing mass in the right caudate head with wide swelling around it. Before surgery, he also received multifrequency magnetic resonance elastography, which maps tissue stiffness and viscosity.

The scan showed unusually high stiffness and viscosity, a signature tied to metastases or meningioma rather than soft glioblastoma tissue. Tissue testing then confirmed a metastasis from squamous cell carcinoma, and PET-CT located the primary tumor in the right lung hilus. The authors suggest elastography could serve as an easy extra contrast that rules glioma out when a lesion feels stiff.
pmc-13292319:
Jingyang Zhang, Qin Zheng, and Mulin Liu write a 2026 letter commenting on a single-cell study of DUSP9 in liver cancer by Xu and colleagues. That study mapped DUSP9-positive, stem-like tumor cells sitting beside cancer-associated fibroblasts and floated an inhibitor, AKOS000434153, as a candidate drug. The letter writers praise the spatial finding but question how the follow-up experiments were run.

Their core point: knockdown and drug tests happened in flat monocultures of HepG2 and Huh7 cells, cut off from the fibroblast niche the authors say sustains the stem-like state. Stromal signals often shield tumors from therapy, they argue. They propose testing the inhibitor in co-culture, 3D spheroids, or fibroblast-conditioned media instead. Those designs, they say, would show whether blocking DUSP9 survives contact with its protective soil.
pmc-13292519:
Mohammed Yousef Almulhim and Samah Faisal Fakhry interview a 2026 group of intensive care nurses in Al-Ahsa, Saudi Arabia, about learning to run continuous dialysis machines without formal training. Twenty nurses with direct responsibility for continuous renal replacement therapy described their experience in depth interviews, analyzed thematically.

Four themes structure the findings. Nurses figured things out on the floor, learning by watching and doing at the bedside. Colleagues served as the real textbook, passing know-how through demonstration and stories. Fear of making an error shadowed the machines until repetition slowly built competence. Finally, nurses named the invisible gap: no structured program exists, and they want simulation training, written protocols, and competency checks. The authors urge leaders to lift this hidden teaching burden from frontline staff.
pmc-13293119:
Mia J. Biondi and colleagues describe women and trans people receiving hepatitis C care in Canada, drawing on a national clinic cohort followed from 2015 to 2023. Their 2026 analysis covers seventeen publicly funded clinics in the Canadian Network Undertaking Against Hepatitis C. Gender shapes both the risk of catching the virus and the ability to reach treatment, yet combined data for these groups have rarely been reported.

Most people in the cohort had low liver scarring scores, though some groups were more likely to arrive with cirrhosis already present. Uptake of opioid agonist therapy, a treatment for opioid dependence, was poor among those who might benefit. The authors call for earlier case finding and for placing hepatitis C treatment alongside addiction services so fewer people are missed.
pmc-13293419:
Ellen A. M. Kuipers and co-authors sort, in a 2026 study, people awaiting weight-loss surgery into groups by behavior and mental well-being. Knowing how patients differ before surgery could help clinics tailor support to each person's needs.

Surveys from 272 patients covered health, quality of life, social support, eating habits, and low mood before surgery. Four groups emerged: one strong on all fronts, one with weaker body health, one with weaker mood yet stable body health, and one weak on both fronts. The largest group held 122 people with no deficits, based on counts the authors give. Follow-up work should test how groups fare later.
pmc-13293719:
Beatriz Mendes and colleagues map a food safety hazard in fish sold from Portuguese waters, in a 2026 epidemiological study. Larvae of Anisakis worms live in marine fish and can infect people who eat them raw or undercooked. The team examined 538 fish of five commercial species from six coastal localities, comparing winter and summer catches in 2024 to find where and when the risk runs highest.

Every species carried larvae, mostly in the guts, with a smaller share in the flesh people eat. Horse mackerel showed the heaviest infections. Genetic testing named Anisakis pegreffii as the dominant species, and a northern, winter-leaning pattern appeared for its close relative in muscle tissue. The authors stress strict freezing, cooking, and handling after capture to protect consumers.
pmc-13293819:
Qiujian Liang and co-authors link, in a 2026 study, a skeleton protein called CORO1A to inflamed cartilage cell groups and immune shifts in osteoarthritis. Joint cartilage holds varied cell types, and what ties some groups to immune change was unclear.

Gene data from many sources, plus single-cell reads, placed CORO1A mainly in inflamed and growing cartilage cells. High levels went with more immune cells in tissue and with active inflammatory signaling paths. Human and mouse diseased cartilage both showed raised levels, and cutting the protein in lab cartilage cells lowered a damaging enzyme and cell movement. CORO1A may drive part of joint inflammation.
pmc-13293919:
Huiping Tian, Yue Wang, and Song Guo follow resilience over time in a 2026 longitudinal study of 223 breast cancer patients. Resilience and meaning in life were measured right after surgery and again 3 months later. Latent profile and transition methods sorted patients into low and high resilience groups and tracked who moved between them.

Two groups appeared at both times. About 38.63% moved from low to high resilience, while 5.64% slipped the other way. Others stayed put, split between lasting high and lasting low groups. Meaning in life related closely to which path patients took. The pattern shows recovery is uneven and support needs change after surgery.
pmc-13294219:
Stephanie Casey and coauthors build a fungal bioreactor for DDT-tainted soil in a 2026 study. DDT and its breakdown products, called DDX, still linger in Swedish soils over 50 years after the ban and cling to organic matter. Their bench system washes soil with surfactant, then passes the freed chemicals over woodchips colonized by the white-rot fungus Ganoderma lucidum.

In liquid tests the fungus broke down 73% of total DDX within 10 days, give or take 6 points. Over 28 days in the reactor, soil totals fell far more with fungus than in the control run, about 45% lower in relative terms. Coupling washing with fungal breakdown scales the cleanup idea.
pmc-13294419:
Katie L. Boncella joins Micah Brown, Jonathan P. Beausejour, and Michael O. Harris-Love to introduce a 2026 research topic editorial on muscle health. Muscle does far more than move limbs: it regulates metabolism, sends hormone signals, steadies posture, and shapes immunity. Decline feeds frailty, falls, and lost independence, yet studies measure health with clashing tools and cutoffs.
