A framework grounded in the World Health Organization functioning classification links body systems to daily activity and participation. Shared language could help therapists and doctors compare studies and adopt measures in clinic. The editorial synthesizes where models agree, where they split, and how to use the common base.
pmc-13294919:
Devy F. Garna and colleagues refine a recipe for gathering the scaffold that fibroblast cells build around themselves, in a 2026 study. That scaffold, the extracellular matrix, steers how cells act and is prized for tissue repair, yet stripping cells away without wrecking it varies from lab to lab. The team tuned a detergent wash and grew human bone-forming cells on what it left.

The tuned wash cleared up to ninety-eight percent of DNA while keeping the scaffold's proteins, and the DNA scraps left were mostly tiny. Bone cells answered by dose: a mid-range amount raised an early bone enzyme and a master bone gene. By two weeks, the cells laid down more calcium and phosphate mineral than controls. The scaffold, the authors say, is an active base that nudges bone cells to build.
pmc-13295119:
Yilin Wang, Wenbing Wu, and Fuli Yao review ball-shaped nucleic acid particles for precise cancer care in a 2026 article. Each particle wears a dense shell of short genetic strands pointing outward, a shape cells absorb without extra carriers. The shell also resists breakdown, aiding stable delivery.

Design choices add antibodies, aptamers, or gene-silencing strands aimed at targets such as HER2 and PD-L1. Responsive, self-built, and peptide based carriers release cargo on cue and reshape the tumour surroundings. Uses span sensing of cancer markers, combined drug and immune delivery, and vaccine support. Early human work looks safe, though delivery strength, targeting, scale-up, and long-term safety still need work.
pmc-13295919:
Add-on blood treatments are tested in 2026 by Neusvaldo de Medeiros Caldas Júnior and co-authors in dogs with a contagious tumour spread mainly by mating. Standard chemotherapy works but can need many sessions and cause side effects, so the team try reinfusing the dog's own blood, with or without ozone.

Dogs receiving these add-ons alongside chemotherapy reached full remission in fewer sessions, without extra side effects appearing. The authors suggest the approach may make treatment quicker and easier on the animals. They stress that larger studies must confirm the benefit before wider use.
pmc-13296919:
Zarrin Moghaddam and a large materials team craft, in 2026, porous glass fibres loaded with gallium and coated in clove oil as a wound dressing candidate. The fibres were spun with a template leaving fine pores, then tested for antioxidant power, germ killing and skin cell friendliness.

One recipe, with a small gallium share and the stronger clove coating, scavenged harmful radicals best and held the most plant phenolics. Its breakdown products lowered stress chemistry inside skin cells while keeping them alive for three days, and it cut E. coli growth clearly. Gallium ions likely drive the antibacterial side, clove the antioxidant side.
pmc-13297919:
Family doctors now have a step-by-step pathway for finding dangerous fatty liver disease, summarized by Mitchell P Wilson and colleagues in a 2026 primer. The guidance distills recent Canadian consensus recommendations on metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease for front-line practice.

Screening starts with the FIB-4 blood score. Patients landing in the middle zone, between 1.3 and 2.67, move on to a stiffness scan by transient elastography, ultrasound shear wave, or magnetic resonance elastography, which perform about equally. The primer supplies thresholds, an algorithm, and notes on the practical hurdles of running this pathway in community clinics, where most patients with the condition are actually seen.
pmc-13298019:
Simulated years in the mouth roughen and soften dental fillings, especially when acid joins the wear, shows a 2026 laboratory study by Alexandru Mihai Tănasă and co-authors. They aged 120 specimens from three bulk-fill composites and one nanofilled reference material under combinations of mechanical wear, pH cycling, and heat cycling.

Roughness climbed and hardness fell as aging accumulated. The harshest changes came from wear plus acid cycling, while wear alone did least damage. Two materials, Filtek One Bulk Fill and the nanofilled Filtek Supreme Ultra, held up best, and Venus Bulk Fill fared worst. Roughness and hardness did not correlate. The authors advise matching material choice to patients facing acidic challenges.
pmc-13298419:
Nahid Sultana and co-authors link DNA methylation at birth to childhood allergy status, in a 2026 prospective study from the Isle of Wight birth cohorts. Skin prick tests for common allergens took place at ages one, three, and six. Methylation was measured at hundreds of thousands of sites in cord or newborn blood samples.

Hundreds of sites showed associations whose strength depended on the child's age. A subset pointed the same way in the parental generation, and fourteen reached significance there. For most confirmed sites, the link weakened as children grew older. The authors read the pattern as early epigenetic marks whose influence fades with age.
pmc-13298519:
Printed living gels for rebuilding teeth and gums vary enormously in strength and behavior, map Nur Haziqah Junaidi and co-authors in a 2026 scoping review. They gathered twenty-one studies that measured physical, mechanical, and flow properties of 3D-bioprinted hydrogels aimed at dental tissue engineering.

Gelatin gels reinforced with β-tricalcium phosphate reached compressive strength in the range of spongy bone, while GelMA and PEGDA blends offered adjustable softness for soft tissue work. Extrusion printing dominated, with light-based and ionic setting as the main hardening routes. Breakdown rates shifted with recipe and purpose. The authors flag missing standardization as the chief barrier to clinical translation.
pmc-13299119:
Paulina Świętoń and others test a chemokine called CXCL12 as a testing marker for brain and meningeal infections, in a 2026 study. Spinal fluid from 214 patients with confirmed meningitis or encephalitis, grouped by cause, was set against samples from a small control group. Tick-borne encephalitis received particular attention.

Levels ran clearly higher in infected patients than controls and separated the overall group reasonably well. Performance within single causes was more middling, and purulent meningitis showed no clear effect, possibly from small numbers. Pairing the marker with cell counts improved separation between tick-borne encephalitis and aseptic meningitis. Standalone value stays limited, the authors conclude.
pmc-13299719:
Luiz Gonzaga Ribeiro Silva-Neto and a team link neighbourhood food supply to overweight and anaemia in children from Brazilian favelas, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Data covered 665 children across forty communities in Maceió, plus audits of hundreds of food outlets. Both excess weight and anaemia burden low-income children at once.

About one fifth of children were overweight and half were anaemic. Greater fruit and vegetable availability nearby meant lower odds of overweight. Heavy availability of ultra-processed drinks meant higher odds of both overweight and anaemia. The authors urge policies that expand fresh food access and curb sugary drink exposure in vulnerable areas.
pmc-13300019:
Dentists who coach patients, not just treat them, sit at the center of a 2026 survey study led by Lucian Josan in Romania. Josan and colleagues asked dental practitioners and patients how much they favor the Trainer–Doctor Model, where the clinician also acts as mentor and teacher. They also gave the model's questionnaire an early psychometric check.

Both groups scored high on preference, with practitioners averaging 43.93 and patients 44.77 on the scale. Roughly seven in ten answers rated the model strongly. Factor analysis found three underlying dimensions, and internal consistency looked acceptable. Patients scored higher than dentists on three items. The authors call for fuller validation before wider use of the questionnaire.
pmc-13300119:
F Tuijnenburg and colleagues measure how often carriers of harmful variants in a heart sodium channel gene show dilated cardiomyopathy, in a 2026 retrospective study. The gene-disease link is classified as definitive, yet carrier prevalence stayed unknown. Records and heart scans covered 182 carriers at one centre, excluding severe valve or artery disease.

About one in five carriers showed signs of the enlarged, weakened heart pattern. Affected carriers were older, with larger chambers, more heart mass, and weaker pumping, while ordinary risk factors were uncommon and unconnected. Both loss and gain of channel function appeared among cases. The authors suggest a distinct gene-driven heart phenotype shaped partly by age.
pmc-13300619:
J Navarro Manchon and colleagues compare deep sedation with general anaesthesia for pulsed field ablation of the pulmonary veins, in a 2026 study. Access to general anaesthesia can bottleneck these procedures, so the team checked whether sedation managed by lab staff performed just as well. The consecutive series covered 244 patients treated with a penta-spline catheter, 202 under deep sedation and forty-two under general anaesthesia given by cardiac anaesthesiologists.

Baseline features were closely matched between the groups. At one year, freedom from atrial arrhythmias was nearly the same, about eighty-two percent under sedation and eighty-one percent under general anaesthesia, with similar splits for paroxysmal and persistent disease. Complications were also alike: one embolic event and two minor vascular problems under sedation, against one minor vascular problem in the other group. The authors recommend the deep sedation approach as a sound option when such access is limited.
pmc-13300819:
W F Hoeksema and colleagues report interim results from the STARNL-2 trial of stereotactic radiotherapy for treatment resistant ventricular tachycardia, published in 2026. The approach aims a single twenty-five gray radiation dose at the heart tissue driving the rhythm, offering a non-invasive option after drugs and ablations fail. This planned early look covers nine treated patients at one Dutch center, most with non-ischemic disease and a median of three earlier ablations.

One treatment related serious event occurred, a defibrillator malfunction that lengthened a hospital stay without lasting harm. Two deaths during follow-up were judged unrelated to treatment. Among the seven patients far enough along to judge, the median change in treated tachycardia episodes was a ninety-seven percent drop, though individual results varied widely and one patient needed another ablation. The authors call the early safety and effect encouraging for future trials.
pmc-13300919:
Plant oils may help beekeepers fight hive disease with fewer synthetic chemicals, Yordan V. Hristov and colleagues conclude in a 2026 review of essential oils for honey bees. The survey weighs laboratory and colony evidence against the major threats: foulbrood bacteria, fungi, gut parasites, and the Varroa mite.

Thymol-based products carry the firmest practical support, aimed at Varroa destructor, while results for bacterial, fungal, and intestinal diseases swing widely between studies. Success in real hives hinges on oil makeup, dose, delivery method, temperature, and colony strength. The authors cast essential oils as useful partners to standard controls, not stand-alone cures, in a more sustainable apiculture.
pmc-13301519:
In a 2026 retrospective study, Qiheng Wan and colleagues test whether a ratio built from two routine blood tests can forecast trouble after opening a fully blocked heart artery. They followed 1,513 patients who had successful stenting for chronic total occlusion at one center between 2011 and 2023, sorting them by their uric acid-to-albumin ratio.

Over a median of 810 days, the highest third of the ratio suffered major cardiovascular events at 18.5 percent, against 7.5 percent in the lowest third. Death rates split even wider, 10.7 against 2.0 percent in the same comparison. Adjusted models kept the link, and the authors offer the cheap ratio as a risk flag, not a treatment target.
pmc-13302019:
Iulia Raluca Munteanu and colleagues present a 2026 case where several imaging methods agreed on a heart diagnosis that surgery then failed to confirm. A 66-year-old man with severe blocked coronary arteries appeared to have a pouch bursting through the lower chamber wall, held in only by surrounding tissue. Such a pseudoaneurysm is dangerous and usually demands repair.

Ultrasound, CT, dye studies, and MRI all pointed the same way before his bypass operation. During surgery, no such cavity was found; instead, surgeons saw two hard, calcium-rich formations in a difficult spot. Judging removal too risky, they completed only the bypass, and recovery went well. The authors urge cautious wording for these grey-zone lesions rather than forced labels.
pmc-13302319:
Slowing childhood shortsightedness now has a toolbox worth comparing, Zofia Pniakowska and colleagues survey in a 2026 review of myopia control in children. Drawing on seventeen years of PubMed literature plus newer digital work, they weigh orthokeratology, low-dose atropine, and specialized lenses against lifestyle levers such as outdoor time and screen limits.

Defocus spectacle lenses cut progression by roughly half to two-thirds in the studies reviewed. Night-worn orthokeratology lenses trimmed eye elongation by about forty-six percent, a key driver of later eye disease. Atropine drops and combined approaches fill out the options. With myopia climbing worldwide, the authors press for fresh methods that protect sight into adulthood.
pmc-13302419:
Coffee waste becomes a battery anode in a 2026 materials study by Xinjie Sun and Hui Yang on sodium-ion storage. Spent grounds were pre-oxidized, carbonized, then sealed with an acetylene vapor coating, a pairing designed to close open pores that waste electrolyte. The finished hard carbon showed a very low surface area of 2.1 square meters per gram and widened carbon layer spacing.

The anode delivered 298 milliamp-hours per gram of reversible capacity with a seventy percent first-cycle efficiency. After five hundred cycles at a 1C rate it still held ninety-seven percent of its capacity. The authors credit the two-step pore engineering and offer it as a recipe for biomass-derived anodes.
pmc-13302819:
Stirring ceramic grit into a high-entropy alloy nearly triples its yield strength, Ning Li and colleagues show in a 2026 composites study. CoCrFeNi alloy powder was blended with silicon carbide at zero to five weight percent and fused by spark plasma sintering. Some particles broke down during sintering, seeding chromium carbides along grain boundaries; the rest pinned those boundaries and refined the grains.

Hardness climbed from about 199 to 322 Vickers across the range. Yield strength nearly tripled to 673.4 megapascals, while tensile strength reached 755.7 megapascals. The authors trace the gains to several strengthening routes acting together and pitch the mix for high-load, wear-heavy service.
pmc-13303919:
Eman Darweish leads a 2026 study of simple ultraviolet methods for measuring two diabetes drugs, dapagliflozin and vildagliptin, in the same tablet. Their light absorption bands overlap heavily, which normally forces costly separation steps first.

Four math-based approaches were built and checked, each untangling the mixed signal without prior separation. Both drugs responded in straight lines across useful dose ranges, and detection limits stayed low. Greenness and practicality scores from several rating tools were reported for each method. No meaningful gaps appeared between methods, giving quality labs cheap, greener options for routine checks.
pmc-13304819:
Lauren Brooks leads a 2026 systematic review of polyphenol supplements in multiple sclerosis. The immune disease damages nerves in 2.9 million people worldwide, and current immune drugs protect nerves only partly while causing side effects.

Three databases and a trial registry were searched in June 2025, yielding 13 eligible trials with 785 patients in total. A nano form of curcumin improved disability scores across three small trials, while green tea extract, milk thistle, cranberry, and another curcumin form showed no clear gains. Harms stayed mild overall. Mixed study quality left proof at a moderate certainty level for most outcomes assessed.
pmc-13306119:
Nathan C Bahr argued in a 2026 discussion piece that brain toxoplasmosis is missed too often in Uganda. The authors revisit fifteen possible cases of Toxoplasma meningoencephalitis found by gene sequencing of spinal fluid from patients with suspected meningitis.

Symptoms alone separate this infection poorly from other brain illnesses, and local tests lack accuracy in the authors' account. Cases often overlapped with other infections of advanced HIV, where parasite exposure is common across the region. The piece calls for faster, sharper diagnostics and wider recognition that toxoplasmosis may sit behind many hospital deaths.
pmc-13307719:
Khadiga M Kelani and co-authors build in 2026 a greener lab method that measures five overlapping drugs at once with ultraviolet light, without a split step first. The mix spans three blood pressure drugs plus a nitrosamine impurity and toluene, tested in drug products and in spiked human plasma.

A firefly tuned model picked the best light bands, and a five factor design set the calibration for the method. Recovery stayed near full in drug products, and plasma results also held close to the true values added there. Six green scoring tools rated the method well on waste, energy, and safety, which suits labs that must cut solvent use.
pmc-13307819:
Charlotte Sriruttan-Nel and co-authors analyse South African laboratory records in 2026 for schistosomiasis cases confirmed between 2019 and 2024. Public sector testing found over seventy-three thousand microscopic diagnoses across the period. Nearly every infection was Schistosoma haematobium, the urinary form of the parasite.

Test positivity sat lower than older reports suggested, hinting at early improvement possibly tied to control efforts. Burden concentrated in boys aged five to nineteen, especially in KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, and Mpumalanga provinces. Mass drug administration is expanding, yet true prevalence data remain absent, so laboratory records carry extra weight. The authors offer their analysis to guide programme scale-up. Targeting school-age boys in the three hotspot provinces, they argue, would reach the group carrying most detected disease.
pmc-13308319:
Sumon Ghosh and co-authors study in 2026 how fully patients finish rabies care after animal exposure in Bangladesh, which aims to end dog linked human rabies by 2030. Records for 457 patients who began care at the national centre in Dhaka, from February to July 2023, were checked for full course completion.

Only 17.1 percent of patients finished the full course, even though the care itself was free at the centre. Women, older patients, poorer patients, and those who lived within 10 kilometres finished more often than others in the data. Dog bites, many wounds, and prompt wound care also tracked with completion. Spread out sites and stronger follow up could lift those rates.
pmc-13308919:
Carolin Schröder and co-authors pilot in 2026 non invasive physical plasma as an add on for vulvar lichen sclerosus that defies strong steroid creams, in five women. Each woman had at least three one minute plasma rounds over a small patch, spaced four to six weeks apart, while cream care went on.

Median age was 46 years, and median illness span was three years at the start of the pilot work. No steady gain in symptoms or in looks of the skin showed after the plasma rounds in this tiny set. No grave harm arose, yet one woman quit over discomfort from the care. Three women said they would try it again, so larger controlled trials must judge its worth.
pmc-13309419:
İskender İnce led a 2026 lab study building tiny drug carriers for mouth biofilms, the sticky germ layers behind gum disease and tooth decay. Two agents were loaded together: quercetin, a plant compound, and chlorhexidine, a common germ killer. The carriers were made from a plastic-like material that breaks down in the body.

Particles were made at three drug strengths and checked for size, charge, shape, and heat behavior. They stayed stable and round, and drug release in fake saliva lasted up to 168 hours for one agent in the single-drug version. Germ tests used two common bacteria. The authors present the paired system as a candidate for slow, local mouth treatment.
pmc-13309619:
Laurence J. Kirmayer writes on diversity, equity, and inclusion in cultural psychiatry in a 2026 article. Those values sit at the core of the field, which studies how culture shapes mental illness and care. Current moves against such programs in the United States and elsewhere form the backdrop for the argument.

Each of the three values is traced through its history, evidence base, and moral weight in health care. Fair critiques of current programs are weighed beside the scope and effects of the backlash, with Canada and the United Kingdom used as contrasts. Rather than dropping the framework, the author urges renewed commitment joined with dignity and empathy. The piece addresses clinicians, researchers, and policy readers.
pmc-13310819:
Seo-Ho Cho and colleagues compare add on health questions for a standard life quality scale in China and the Netherlands in a 2026 study. The core scale has five items, and eight extra items cover sight, hearing, breathing, sleep, tiredness, ties, confidence, and memory. Whether extras work alike across cultures was unclear.

Online surveys in 2024 used quota samples that matched adult groups in each country. Most people scored at the top of the core scale, more so in China. Sight, tiredness, and sleep extras cut that top pile most. Tiredness and confidence added the most new insight in both lands, while other extras depended more on setting.
pmc-13310919:
Paula Helena Gomes de Moraes Ruiz and colleagues draft a group program to boost diabetes self care in a 2026 concept paper. Daily care for type 2 diabetes stays poor for many people despite known methods. A therapy that builds flexible thinking, called Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, helps in other long illnesses but lacks a clear build path for diabetes.

Steps from a planning frame sort barriers in glucose checks, diet, exercise, and drug taking. Core skills such as acceptance, thought loosening, and values sorting are matched to each barrier. Culture fit stories and hands on drills carry the methods. Trials must test whether the plan works across groups.
pmc-13311219:
Xiaoying Ma and co-authors, in 2026, offer a review of salidroside, a plant compound from Rhodiola rosea, packed into tiny carriers for triple-negative breast cancer care. This cancer type lacks the usual drug targets and spreads fast.

The review pulls together how the compound attacks cancer cells, in part by driving a form of cell death tied to iron, while sparing normal tissue. It then weighs carrier designs such as polymer and fat-based particles that fix the compound's poor uptake and short life in the body. A marker-guided plan and a three-step path toward clinic use close the review.
pmc-13311319:
Yusuke Fujioka and colleagues describe their 2026 surgical case of aneurysm repair where a small artery called for an unusual graft choice. Oversizing a graft limb can block it later, so fit matters.

The patient, a 76-year-old man, had a 55 mm aneurysm of the right common iliac artery found by chance on CT. His right external iliac artery had shrunk to 5 mm after a past spinal injury left his lower body paralyzed. A Gore Excluder device carried the main repair, with a slim 6 mm VBX graft as the limb. One year on, the limb stayed open and the course was smooth.
pmc-13311619:
Jensen Abascal and co-authors detail a 2026 mouse study of an in-body vaccine made from engineered dendritic cells for lung cancer. The cells were altered to release FLT3L, a signal that boosts the cell type that starts killer T-cell attacks.

Several mouse lung cancer models with differing mutation loads received the cell vaccine, alone and with PD-1 blockade. Flow tests and tissue imaging traced the immune response inside tumors. Human tumor data were also mined for related immune and lymphoid-structure signatures. The approach aims to wake up tumors that shrug off checkpoint drugs by fixing faulty antigen display.
pmc-13311719:
Anika Krishna and co-authors present a 2026 modeling study on how depression, anxiety, and body symptoms hang together in dialysis patients. Body complaints are common on dialysis, while mood problems often go unseen.

The team surveyed 1085 dialysis patients at 17 sites in northeast Ohio from 2018 to 2023 with standard mood, anxiety, and body symptom scales. About 14.3 percent screened positive for depression in this group. Models that kept the three problems apart fit slightly better than one merged distress score. The three still correlated strongly, which supports screening for all three together in dialysis care.
pmc-13311819:
Haodong Wang and co-authors detail a 2026 feeding study on whether lycopene, the red pigment in tomatoes, can guard broiler chickens' kidneys against cadmium poisoning. The metal builds up in the body and attacks kidneys through oxidative stress.

Arbor Acres broilers ate cadmium-laced feed with or without lycopene for 42 days. Lycopene reversed the growth drag and kidney tissue damage the metal caused. Deeper checks tied the protection to steadier mitochondria, the cell power units, across their birth, movement, and cleanup systems. The work suggests a feed additive route to safer poultry production on polluted land.
pmc-13311919:
Rosa Amalia and co-authors map Indonesian social media talk about oral health in a 2026 content analysis. Posts from Quora and Threads over eighteen months supply the material.

The team coded 858 posts from July 2023 to January 2025 into 19 topic classes and ran topic modeling on the text. Mouth ulcers and toothache drew the most talk. Ten themes emerged, from hygiene habits to children's dental visits and post-surgery recovery. Quora posts leaned toward symptom questions, while Threads posts read more personal and emotional. Set against national survey data, the chatter shows what worries the public most.
pmc-13312019:
Mohammad Amin Khalilzad and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how fine air particles known as PM2.5 may drive disease by switching on controlled forms of cell death. These particles, breathed in from traffic, industry, fires, and other sources, are tied to illness and death worldwide.

The review links PM2.5 exposure to several death pathways, among them apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis, and ties them to oxidative stress, damaged mitochondria, and inflammation. The same pathways appear across heart, brain, lung, kidney, liver, and eye disease in the studies surveyed. The authors map where the evidence is thin and name candidate treatments, aiming to guide later work that moves lab findings toward clinical trials.
pmc-13312419:
Yuanzhou Mao and colleagues introduce, in a 2026 study, a transformer-based artificial intelligence system built to support anesthesia decisions during orthopedic surgery. Keeping patients stable means fusing fast-changing body signals, drug and event records, and written notes in real time to head off blood pressure drops, nausea, and uncontrolled pain.

Their system, Ortho PeriFT, predicts risks, suggests fluid, vasopressor, and anesthetic adjustments through a decision module fenced by guideline rules. It monitors patients continuously, attaching calibrated uncertainty ranges so it can hold back when unsure. In internal and outside patient groups it beat classical and neural comparison models on accuracy and calibration. Off-policy estimates suggested its suggestions would have outperformed actual clinician behavior without breaking safety guardrails. The authors also report earlier warnings at the same false alarm rate.
pmc-13313019:
Yui Sasaki and co-authors offer a 2026 perspective on designing chemical sensor arrays that run from molecules floating in water all the way to paper test strips. Watching metal ions in lakes and rivers matters for ecosystems and water safety. Sensor molecules that answer binding with a color or glow change can detect several ions at once when their overlapping responses are read as a pattern.

The perspective highlights sensors that build themselves: catechol and phenylboronic acid partners link through reversible bonds. Sensing elements assemble spontaneously in water without laborious synthesis, and mixing variants tunes the array's palate. Printing these self-assembled sensors onto paper then yields portable kits for field testing with no bench instruments. The authors call this bridging of scales, from self-assembly to a pocket device, a promising route to routine multi-ion monitoring.
pmc-13314119:
Engki Zelpina and co-authors investigate, in a 2026 One Health study, resistant E. coli in chicken meat sold at local markets in West Sumatra, Indonesia. Such markets are the main meat channel locally, and the bacterium doubles as a marker of fecal contamination and antibiotic misuse on farms. Between July and September 2025 the team bought 65 chicken thigh samples from five markets. They cultured them under the national standard and tested isolates against seven drugs.

Nine samples, 13.8 percent of those tested, carried E. coli. Among the isolates, resistance peaked against streptomycin and erythromycin at 66.7 percent each, with ampicillin close behind. An amoxicillin combination kept working best. Resistance to gentamicin, streptomycin, and ampicillin moved together strongly, hinting at co-resistance carried on shared genetic elements. The authors urge local authorities to build monitoring of pathogens and resistance across the food chain before multidrug resistance becomes entrenched.
pmc-13314519:
Bingqing Lu and co-workers map why exercise rehab after heart ablation lags in practice in a 2026 study. Patients with atrial fibrillation often face relapse and low exercise tolerance after radiofrequency ablation, yet guidelines that urge exercise rehab are poorly followed.

The team summed the best proof on post-ablation exercise care, built a set of quality measures, and audited current practice against them. They then sorted the barriers that hold practice back and drafted plans to beat them, guided by an evidence-based care model from the Joanna Briggs Institute, as named in the report. An evidence team framed the core question and ran each step. The work gives hospitals a concrete path to close the gap between what guidelines say and what patients get.
pmc-13315519:
Nagham Amer Mohammed Ali and Rana Kadhim Mohammed studied in 2026 how zinc oxide nanoparticles affect gene control in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ known for biofilms and drug resistance. They asked whether the particles change small regulatory RNAs and biofilm genes at doses below those that kill the germ.

Fifty clinical isolates were tested for drug response and biofilm strength, and the lab-made particles were checked with several imaging and light tools. Killing and biofilm tests used standard dilution and staining methods. Three resistant isolates then had gene tests for ErsA, SrbA, amrZ, and algD after exposure to two set particle doses.
pmc-13316019:
Anisha R Kumar and co-authors review in 2026 how AI models for judging facial beauty can carry and deepen bias, and they propose a framework to reduce it. Such models now predict attractiveness and simulate surgery outcomes, yet training on narrow datasets misjudges underrepresented groups and pushes faces toward one look.

Benchmark sets underrepresent older adults and non-White and ethnically diverse people, methods rarely use fairness-aware training, and scoring seldom splits accuracy by demographic group. Fixes exist, from balanced data to adversarial debiasing, but no plan covered the whole build cycle until this proposal.
pmc-13316619:
Shruti Kawthekar M and co-authors tested, in a 2026 chick study, whether bacteria-eating viruses can cut Salmonella gut colonization in broiler chickens. With antibiotic resistance rising, virus therapy offers a drug-free route to safer poultry.

Sixty Cobb chicks split into six groups, receiving the viruses by mouth or into the egg at two dose levels, plus challenged and clean controls. Treated birds shed far less Salmonella in droppings across the trial, and gut counts fell in every treated group. Mouth dosing at the lower level cut shedding most, while egg dosing at the higher level gave lasting suppression. Gut tissue damage also eased. The team presents viruses as a strong stand-in for antibiotics.
pmc-13317019:
Jun Cao and colleagues distilled, in a 2026 evidence summary, the best guidance on managing swallowing problems in Parkinson's disease without drugs. Swallowing failure is common and dangerous in this illness, yet care varies, so the team hunted top-tier sources.

Following a layered evidence model, they screened guidelines, expert agreements, decision tools, and reviews up to the end of 2024, keeping 18 documents. From them came 53 best-practice points in seven areas, spanning screening, testing, rehab training, nutrition, airway protection, and outcome checks. Two reviewers extracted each point under a standard grading system. Clinicians are urged to fit the points to each patient's setting rather than copy them blindly.
pmc-13318819:
Mihai Nadaş and colleagues present a 2026 framework for literary translation from English into Romanian using open models. Romanian is a low-resource language for creative text. Their process builds data, fine-tunes a model, and tests results. It starts from a large pool of synthetic English fables.

A strong large model made 15,000 high-quality Romanian sample translations. A 12-billion-parameter open model was then fine-tuned in two stages. First-stage tuning taught fable style, and adapter shrinking eased rollout. Judging used a five-part rubric scoring accuracy, fluency, flow, style, and cultural fit. The tuned model nearly matched top commercial systems on fluency and adequacy. The team put the model, two datasets, and all scripts online for anyone to use.
pmc-13319719:
Guiyuan Ma and co-authors study views of time among mothers with cancers of the female organs in a 2026 survey from Changsha, China. A cancer call in young or mid life can wreck life plans and hopes for what lies ahead. How these women weigh past, present, and future, and what shapes that balance while they raise young children, had barely been studied.

A total of 266 women who were married or living with a partner and had at least one young child filled in a standard time view scale. Warm views of the past and focus on the future scored highest, while dark views of the past scored lower. Home place, schooling, work, inner strength, support, and worry about parenting each tied to parts of the pattern.
pmc-13320319:
Jojo Hoi-Ching Lai and co-authors test ankle taping in dancers with wobbly ankles in a 2026 trial where each dancer tried both paths. Side ankle sprains are rife among dancers and often leave lasting wobble, and dancers tend to have looser joints than other athletes, which may change how tape helps. Four balance and hop tests were run with and without tape in random order.

Eighty nine dancers from local schools joined the study and also filled in a standard ankle steadiness form and shared views on taping. Dancers with a past sprain and low steadiness scores formed the wobbly group, set next to steady peers. One leg stand results led the outcome list, with hop and reach tests and form scores as support. Same day tape effects in this art form need data of their own, the team notes.
pmc-13320419:
Maclean Vokhiwa and co-authors review how brain growth is measured in iron short young children in sub Saharan Africa in a 2026 article. Lack of iron and blood in early life can scar brain growth, and the region carries a heavy share of both. Yet studies use a sprawl of tools and scores, which makes their results hard to line up or trust side by side.

Six databases were swept for studies from 2013 to April 2024 on children under five with iron or blood lack. From 2254 records screened in total, the rules were met by 19 studies drawn from nine lands. Most weighed broad growth or thinking skills, and only three used brain scans of any kind. Tool choice, local tuning, and score rules clashed so widely that a pooled count was ruled out.
pmc-13321819:
Camila Moraes Garollo Piran and colleagues study treatment failure among young people with HIV in a 2026 cohort study from northwestern Paraná, Brazil. The study followed 512 adolescents and young people at a specialist service and used regression models to find factors tied to poor adherence and loss to follow-up.

Having a sexual partner, delay before starting therapy, and missed appointments went with worse adherence, while ages 20 to 24 went with better adherence. Drug use, one common drug combination, and unsuppressed virus results were tied to loss to follow-up, as were missed appointments. Alcohol use and some virus test patterns also raised follow-up loss, which underlines how social the roots of treatment failure can be.
pmc-13323819:
Jing Miao and co-authors test a tryptanthrin derivative named g2 against tongue cancer, in a 2026 laboratory and animal study. Tongue squamous cell carcinoma is common, aggressive and short on treatment options, and tryptanthrin compounds have shown anti-cancer promise in other settings.

Screening 36 derivatives in two tongue cancer cell lines, the team found g2 the strongest killer, with potency near two micromolar in their assays. The compound slowed migration and invasion, pushed cells into programmed death and halted the cycle in S phase, in step with dose. Gene and protein checks pointed to PI3K/AKT/P53 pathway shifts. In mouse tumours, direct injection at two dose levels slowed growth for tissue testing.
pmc-13326019:
Amarnath Pal, Milan Patra, Rianita Mondal, and Shubhasis Haldar review chromosomal instability as an engine of glioblastoma diversity in a 2026 article. The brain cancer is the most lethal of its kind, and scrambled chromosomes sit near its core.

Faulty division, extra centrosomes, weak checkpoints, and broken DNA repair all feed the instability. The chaos spawns varied tumor cells, including stem-like ones that resist therapy and spread. Shattering events called chromothripsis rearrange whole chromosomes at once. Immune effects run through the cGAS and STING pathway, which can help or hinder defense. The authors survey drugs aimed at these weak points plus cell and nanoparticle therapies.
pmc-13326519:
Licheng Liu and team mapped how Salvia miltiorrhiza roots shape their tough periderm and make tanshinones. Their 2026 study notes that perennial roots undergo repeat secondary growth, with that layer serving as both barrier and major site of special metabolite buildup. Yet the cellular programs running outer-layer growth and special chemistry were poorly known. Single-cell RNA reading and spatial chemistry checks resolved cell types and gene changes across growth stages.

Tracing the trajectory from skin to outer-layer lines revealed distinct programs tied to resin making. Spatial checks confirmed that they accumulate mainly in cork cells of mature roots, and combined analysis pointed to SmCYP76AK5 in tanshinone making. The authors present the cell guide as a tool for guessing metabolic activity by cell type, matching young and mature roots, and building models of special chemistry in long-lived plants.
pmc-13328419:
ZhiYu Zhang and co-authors propose a ferroptosis domino chain across spinal diseases in a 2026 mini review. Disc degeneration, spinal deformity, and cord injury are usually treated as separate problems, yet the authors link them through iron-driven cell death. The cascade starts inside the blood-starved disc.

Faulty force sensing there sparks oxidative stress and ferroptosis, rotting the disc matrix until structure collapses, and the resulting deformity squeezes cord blood vessels, leaking iron into a primed cord. A later injury then floods the cord with blood iron, igniting an unstoppable death storm beside inflammation. Smart gels and particles that answer oxidative cues may halt the chain while surgeons restore alignment, a dual strategy the authors champion.
pmc-13329219:
Stoye and colleagues test ways to pool studies of how well a medical test works. Each study reports hits and misses at one or more cut points. Older methods use one cut point per study. Newer methods use all of them. The team ran large computer trials of five older and six newer methods. They varied eight traits of the fake data. Those traits spanned test type and the number of cut points per study.

All methods were close on bias and on how often they held true. One newer method, a logit model, did best in most settings. Test type swayed results most. The number of cut points mattered least. Two real cases show how picks can shift answers.
pmc-13329519:
Nur Sakinah Mohd Yasin and colleagues translate and test a back pain disability questionnaire in Malay in a 2026 study. The Roland-Morris questionnaire was adapted through forward and backward translation, expert review, and checks with patients. Content and face checks involved eight rehab professionals and nine people with low back pain.

Testing then ran with 102 participants. Scores held together well and stayed steady on repeat testing among 31 people in the reported checks. Agreement with the Malay Oswestry index was moderate. Scores also differed between people with and without back pain, as expected. The authors judge the Malay version fit for use in Malaysia, while urging further tests of how it tracks change over time.
pmc-13332119:
Shengmei Wang and colleagues built a combined nanoparticle treatment for liver cancer in 2026 laboratory work. Liver cancer is usually found late, and immunotherapy often fails because the tumor surroundings suppress immune attack.

Their one-pot platform loads cantharidin, a chemotherapy drug, together with manganese ions into albumin particles. Inside tumor cells the pair raises reactive oxygen sharply, driving an iron-dependent cell death called ferroptosis and releasing alarm signals that mature dendritic cells. Manganese also sharpens the cGAS-STING alarm pathway, which the drug's DNA damage triggers, boosting type I interferon output. In mice the treatment curbed tumor growth and spread, lengthened survival, and worked even better alongside an anti-PD-L1 antibody. The design also avoids the kidney and liver harm of free cantharidin and the poor tumor reach of free manganese.
pmc-13333719:
Lars Schmidli and co-authors synthesized the evidence on biomarkers for cognitive impairment after stroke in a 2026 systematic review. Thinking problems after stroke harm quality of life and outlook, yet dependable tests to predict or track them are still lacking.

The team screened 834 studies and included 154, covering more than 114,000 patients across cohort, case-control, cross-sectional, and interventional designs. Biomarkers came from blood and other fluids as well as brain imaging, and imaging markers such as infarct size, brain shrinkage, and white matter changes were studied most often. Grouping markers by type let the authors map where evidence is strong and where it is thin. The synthesis sets priorities for building tools clinicians can trust.
pmc-13334319:
Rodrigo Yáñez-Sepúlveda and co-authors compared body mass index against bioelectrical impedance for detecting excess body fat in a 2026 cross-sectional study. BMI is cheap and universal, but it never measures fat directly, so it can mislabel people's nutritional status.

Pooling three body-composition databases gave 12,604 adults from Chile and Mexico. Obesity by fat percentage used age- and sex-specific Gallagher thresholds, while BMI obesity followed the World Health Organization cutoff of 30. Participants fell into four groups, from agreement at both ends to normal-weight obesity, where BMI looks fine but fat is high. Agreement statistics and ten machine learning models tested how badly the simple index misclassifies. The work gives Latin American clinics a clearer sense of when to distrust BMI alone.
pmc-13334519:
Mitchell Allen, Isaac Woods, and Jarrett Murphy interviewed Black male sports coaches about their role in young people's lives in a 2026 qualitative study. Black male educators make up under 2 percent of US teachers, leaving many Black boys without such mentors in school.

Five coaches serving youth in different US regions gave semi-structured interviews, interpreted through intersectionality and PVEST, a framework formally called the Phenomenological Variant of Ecological Systems Theory. Five themes emerged, covering coaches as community pillars, limitless commitment, relationship fundamentals, power dynamics, and struggles. The coaches acted as advocates, social fathers, and informal mental health supports, spotting distress and steadying boys through it. The authors argue such community roles deserve recognition in youth development and suicide prevention planning.
pmc-13334819:
K. Ishimoto and co-authors pitted two androgen receptor drugs head-to-head in nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer in a 2026 many-center look-back study. pmc-13420319:

pmc-13421519:

pmc-13422119:

pmc-13424019:

pmc-13424419:

pmc-13434419:

pmc-13437419:
