Their method first runs a genetic algorithm, which breeds and selects good task assignments like evolving organisms, to map tasks across fog nodes. A deep Q-learning agent then refines those assignments in real time, learning from feedback as conditions change on the network.

In experiments, the hybrid beat the baseline methods it was tested against on both makespan, the time to finish the whole task set, and operating cost. The genetic stage searched widely and converged toward strong scheduling patterns, while the learning stage adapted those patterns to shifting loads without starting over. The authors argue the pairing suits latency-sensitive, resource-tight fog systems, where utilization must stay high while response times stay low for connected devices.
pmc-13478519:
Mingyang Hu and colleagues report a 2026 study of NAT10, an enzyme that adds a chemical mark to RNA, in diabetic kidney disease. Cell aging in the kidney's tubules helps drive this common diabetes complication. Patient kidney tissue showed markedly higher NAT10 levels, and higher levels tracked with worse clinical outcomes.

The enzyme attached its ac4C mark to the RNA of PAPP-A, a growth-related protein, making that RNA last longer and produce more protein. Through a pathway involving p53, this pushed tubule cells into senescence. Deleting or silencing NAT10 in two mouse diabetes models eased tubule aging, and a drug blocker called Remodelin protected cells in animals and dishes alike. The authors nominate this axis as a treatment target.
pmc-13478719:
He and a team in China pinned in 2026 a blood factor that seems to drive fat tissue to age fast, and the body with it. The factor, ANGPTL8, was known for its hand in fat and sugar traffic. In a large group of adults, high blood levels of it tracked with faster body ageing and a higher risk of death. It even sharpened machine built age and death forecasts. The team then bred mice that lacked the factor's gene.

Those mice lived longer, kept their strength and skill with age, and showed fewer worn out cells in their fat. In fat cells, the factor had risen with age and switched on age linked gene sets. Tests showed it grips a cell switch called AKT2 and fires a growth path that pushes cells into worn out rest. Drugs or gene cuts that blocked that path wiped out the push.
pmc-13479419:
Yi Xu and colleagues present a 2026 design study of a targeted nanobubble platform against ovarian cancer, built largely through computer modeling with laboratory binding checks. Ovarian cancer often hides across the abdomen, defeating complete surgery and image guidance. The protein claudin-4 is enriched on these tumor cells, making it a homing address, though it also appears in some normal tissue.

A structure-guided search produced peptide P15, which bound claudin-4 tightly at nanomolar strength. Linking the peptide to the dye indocyanine green created a combined agent for the nanobubbles. The platform is designed to support ultrasound and fluorescence imaging, ultrasound-assisted delivery, and heat-based tumor killing from a single construct. The authors stress that rational design must weigh tumor enrichment and surface access because the target is not tumor-exclusive.
pmc-13479919:
Sarah Moreheart and colleagues tracked naloxone kit ownership in 2026 among sex workers who use drugs in metro Vancouver. This group faces a heavy overdose burden, driven by a toxic drug supply and the conditions of sex work and drug use environments. The data come from a community-based cohort followed from 2017 to 2024, with check-ins every six months.

Among just over five hundred participants, more than nine in ten had owned a take-home naloxone kit at some point, and ownership stayed high across the study years. Statistical modeling linked ownership to injection drug use and to other structural factors the authors examined. The findings show a harm-reduction tool reaching deep into a marginalized community over seven years. They also point to the structural conditions that help or hinder people keeping a kit on hand.
pmc-13480119:
Mohd Nur Aizat Mohd Yasim and co-authors report a 2026 case of severe stroke in a toddler after a heart procedure. An 18-month-old girl had a hole between the lower heart chambers plus a slipping aortic valve, and doctors tried to close the hole with a catheter device. Two placement tries failed as valve leakage grew and the device sat unsteadily, so the team stopped.

Two hours later the child worsened sharply. A brain scan showed a large stroke across the right side of the brain with bleeding under the skull lining and dangerous swelling. Surgeons removed part of the skull and cleared the blood collection in an emergency operation. Tests for clotting disorders came back clear. The team points to clot travel, thin blood thinning cover, dye effects, and the strain of a hard procedure as likely factors, and they stress tight dosing checks in small children.
pmc-13480919:
Courtney L Labrecque and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six study of liver stellate cell subgroups in fatty-liver-related cancer and their response to statins. Stellate cells drive scarring and support tumours. Statins lower cancer risk by unclear routes, possibly through these cells.

Single-nucleus sequencing and spatial imaging profiled matched human tumour samples. One stellate subgroup mixed activation and deactivation markers near cancer. A growth pathway switched on by a cholesterol-pathway molecule proved statin-sensitive in cell tests. Blocking or restoring pathway steps confirmed the mechanism. The work nominates a targetable circuit behind statin protection.
pmc-13481919:
Alaa Senjab and co-authors describe a 2026 case of a jaw-type tumour growing in the cheekbone of a 63-year-old man. His right midface swelled over two to three months. Scans showed a destructive mass in the cheekbone reaching toward the eye socket and a deep facial space, while the upper jaw stayed fairly spared. A small biopsy pointed to ameloblastoma, a slow but invasive tooth-forming tumour that usually sits in the lower jaw.

Surgeons removed the mass in one block through a wide facial approach chosen for full access, then rebuilt the cheek-eye contour with titanium mesh and a cheek fat flap. Final checks confirmed the diagnosis with clean margins. Scans a month later showed no leftover disease, and at six months no return had appeared, with sight and speech intact. Rare sites demand the same wide margins as jaw cases.
pmc-13482619:
Singh and colleagues comb district records in 2026 for how a century of weather drift has treated sesame farming in Bundelkhand, India's semi-arid belt where the oilseed is a cash lifeline. They charted monthly temperature and rainfall trends with standard climate statistics, then correlated both with sesame yields district by district. The region's climate signal proved double-edged for the crop.

Warming ran consistently between 0.9 and a high of 2.2 degrees Celsius per century, strongest late in and after the monsoon, while monsoon and yearly rainfall slid downward by roughly 1.03 millimeters to 1.51 millimeters per year. Sesame liked the warmth, with yields rising alongside temperature measures at correlations of 0.28 rising to 0.48, especially in August and September growth weeks. Rain hurt instead, with wet measures correlating at minus 0.26 to minus 0.47 against yield, and the authors advise planning around excess, poorly timed rain rather than drought alone.
pmc-13483119:
Calderon-Cortez and co-authors measured how much heat builds inside bone while dentists drill to collect bone graft material. Their 2026 laboratory study used 40 fragments of cow rib, split between two collector systems, with two drill sizes and two cooling-water temperatures. Excess heat can kill bone cells, so keeping drilling cool protects later healing. A thermal camera recorded temperatures during each perforation.

One collector system ran hotter than the other, adding roughly a degree of extra heat on average across the trials. Smaller drills also trended slightly hotter than larger ones. Cooling the irrigation water to 10 degrees Celsius reduced the heat buildup compared with room-temperature water. Calderon-Cortez concludes that equipment choice, drill size, and chilled irrigation together decide how much thermal stress graft harvesting puts on bone.
pmc-13483419:
Nina Higson-Sweeney and co-authors explore fatigue among depressed teenagers in a 2026 re-analysis of a large therapy trial. The trial had assigned 465 young people aged eleven to seventeen with major depression to one of three talking therapies. The new work asked how common fatigue was, what travelled with it, and whether it shifted during care.

Nearly three quarters reported strong fatigue at the start. Fatigue tied most steadily to older age and heavier depression, and by self-report also to minority background, extra health problems, and worse daily functioning. Rates fell across treatment in every arm and kept falling after therapy ended. Starting fatigue did not blunt overall gains in mood or functioning. Still, up to a third stayed tired at the last check, eighty-six weeks in, marking a leftover symptom future care should target.
pmc-13485019:
Susan L Hills and co-authors take stock of Japanese encephalitis control, a mosquito-spread brain infection vaccine that prevents yet cannot be wiped out. Published in 2026, the review covers Asia and Oceania, where the illness kills 20 to 30 percent of encephalitis cases and leaves lasting damage in up to half of survivors. Two decades of program growth form the backdrop.

Many countries have added the vaccine to national schedules, cutting illness and death markedly where coverage holds. Fresh worries include spread into wide parts of Australia and a shift toward adult cases in some long-affected areas. Because animal reservoirs keep the virus circulating, long-term high-quality vaccination must continue indefinitely. Sustaining programs, not a one-time push, is the central challenge the authors stress.
pmc-13486419:
Rongchuang Lu and others examine a calcium-signaling gene called CALML6 across many cancer types. In 2026, the study draws on public RNA reading data, checking gene action, mutations, copy number changes, methyl tagging, and drug sensitivity, then validates findings in lab cell lines. The question is whether this gene could serve as a marker of prognosis.

CALML6 ran high in some cancers, including lymph cancer and blood cancer, and low in others, including breast and colon cancer. Its action tracked lives tests in adrenal, colon, and kidney cancers and correlated with immune cell patterns and drug responses. Lab tests showed higher action in bladder, colon, and stomach cancer cells. The authors present CALML6 as a candidate prognostic marker needing test confirmation.
pmc-13487719:
Dimitrios Daskalou shows that silencing one inner-ear enzyme can protect hearing from the collateral damage of focused radiation therapy. Published in 2026, the mouse work models hearing loss after stereotactic radiosurgery for a benign nerve-sheath tumor, a treatment that often trades tumor control for progressive deafness. The enzyme NOX3, found mainly in the inner ear, generates oxidative stress there.

Mice lacking the enzyme kept their hearing and their cochlear hardware, including hair cells, synaptic ribbons, and auditory neurons, after radiation. A short local dose of silencing RNA copied the protection against scrambled controls. Fat oxidation damage and macrophage invasion inside the cochlea both fell with inhibition. Radiation timing is known in advance for scheduled patients, which makes a preventive ear treatment unusually practical.
pmc-13487919:
Hajar Ouahid and colleagues survey maternal care in the Marrakech-Safi region of Morocco in a 2026 cross-sectional study. They asked 632 adults about gender norms, using a scale adapted into Moroccan Arabic, and about use of care during pregnancy, birth in a facility, and care after birth. Detailed outcome analysis focused on 207 people who had been pregnant or whose partners had been pregnant.

People holding less equal gender views were much less likely to report antenatal care or facility birth. Living in a rural area and lacking paid work also lowered facility birth. No clear link appeared for care after birth. The authors call for action on both social norms and practical barriers like distance and cost.
pmc-13488019:
Ali Shan Hafeez and a large team analyze meningitis deaths across the United States between 1999 and 2020 in a 2026 study using national death records. Meningitis is inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, often from infection. Rates were adjusted for age and split by sex, race and ethnicity, region, state, and rural or urban residence, with trend methods marking years where the direction changed.

Age-adjusted mortality fell by more than half over the period, with the steepest drop before 2012 and a flatter pattern afterward. Men died at higher rates than women, and Black Americans carried the highest burden among the groups compared. Western and southern states showed the greatest load, which the authors say should guide targeted prevention.
pmc-13490719:
Wang and co-workers in China and Finland reported in 2026 on Pectobacterium parvum, a bacterium that rots potato stems and also harms Chinese cabbage. Gene studies of the germ at work inside plants turned up a new gene family, named PSMB for plant secondary metabolite binding. The family seems to have arrived by gene transfer from other germs and grown into a four gene island in this species.

Lab tests showed the lead protein, PSMB1a, grabs plant defence chemicals and holds them tight. It bound solanidine, a potato toxin, about a hundred times more strongly than it bound salicylic acid, a key defence signal. Deleting the whole island made the germ weaker on potato, cabbage, and radish, yet faster growing in plain lab culture. Adding the gene to a close sister species made that germ tougher and more harmful on cabbage.
pmc-13490919:
Mehta and colleagues in the United States looked in 2026 at arachnoid granulations, small pouches of the brain's middle cover that help drain fluid from the head. They checked these pouches by eye on the top surface of 882 donated brains from older adults. The team then matched pouch counts, sizes, and shapes with lab signs of Alzheimer's disease and with records of dementia.

Brains with more amyloid and more tau tangles, the two hallmark proteins of Alzheimer's, tended to have fewer of these pouches. One shape stood out in the other direction: long, linear pouches in the front and side regions went with higher odds of dementia. The findings hint that the brain's fluid drain routes may shift as Alzheimer's pathology builds up with age.
pmc-13491719:
Yoshitaka Nagashima leads a thirteen-author team describing in 2026 two spinal cord tumors that defied tidy classification. Both growths were low-grade ependymal tumors in elderly patients, with tidy borders typical of a gentler subtype called subependymoma. Yet under the microscope they lacked that subtype's signature cell clusters, showed an unexpected marker protein, and had growth rates a little higher than expected.

Chemical profiling of DNA methylation placed both tumors at the edge of the subependymoma class, with only modest confidence scores. Each tumor also carried a mutation in the promoter of the telomerase gene TERT and an extra copy of chromosome 7. Current rules therefore label them grade 2 ependymal tumors wearing a subependymoma-like profile. The authors say such mismatches, increasingly noticed, will force classification systems to adapt.
pmc-13492319:
Rahul Jain and others report the first human use of a method that makes heart rhythm ablation safer near a coronary artery. In 2026, the case concerns a seventy-one-year-old woman with frequent premature ventricular beats, including runs of ventricular tachycardia, and a genetic mutation for left-dominant arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. Detailed switching on mapping located the earliest beats in the great cardiac vein.

Because the target sat only a few mm from a major artery, the team delivered diluted iodinated contrast directly into the artery during radiofrequency ablation. The contrast cooled and protected the vessel while preserving ablation effect. The method offers a way to treat arrhythmias whose best ablation site would otherwise be too close to a coronary artery to use safely.
pmc-13493319:
Birch-Price and colleagues reported in 2026 a new family of engineered enzymes that build carbon bonds through a charged intermediate held inside the protein. Making precise carbon-carbon and carbon-nitrogen bonds is a core task in drug and chemical work, and enzymes that do it cleanly are prized. The team reshaped the code of a natural enzyme and then evolved it in the lab.

Their enzymes form a reactive imidazolium species, a short-lived charged structure, from a starting material fitted with a leaving group that made screening fast. That species can be caught by many carbon or nitrogen partners, yielding prized products such as ring-shaped esters, chiral amines, and crowded carbon centers with set handedness. X-ray structures hinted at a surprise: the leaving group stays in the pocket and helps the reaction.
pmc-13493419:
Emrah Işıktekin and three colleagues grade in 2026 two famous chatbots answering the questions breast augmentation patients ask most. The twelve questions came from a popular cosmetic surgery website ranked by user engagement. Ten board-certified plastic surgeons, blinded to which chatbot wrote which answer, scored every response on a standard quality scale after agreeing on how to apply it.

ChatGPT-4.5 averaged well above Google Gemini, roughly 3.9 against 2.8 on the five-point scale, a statistically clear win. The surgeons' verdict suggests patients researching implants will currently get more complete and reliable guidance from one system than the other. Even so, the authors insist chatbots should support rather than replace consultation, citing ethical concerns and the risk of confident errors.
pmc-13494019:
Yangtan Xiao, Chaoyi Zhang, Zhaoli Shen, and Chenggang Gao slim down in 2026 a real-time ship detector meant to watch the oceans from satellites and drones. Small vessels vanish easily in large maritime images, and heavy models cannot run on the modest hardware aboard remote platforms. Their redesign swaps in an efficient backbone network, adds grouped attention to fuse features across scales, and finishes with a module that sharpens representations cheaply.

Accuracy reached eighty-seven and a half percent on one maritime dataset and about forty-nine on a harder aerial one. Compared with the parent model, parameters fell by nearly half and arithmetic by almost half again, while speed held near eighty-seven frames per second. Traffic safety, rescue coordination, and port management all need exactly this kind of tireless, lightweight watch.
pmc-13494519:
Ni and colleagues traced a route by which chronic stress helps colorectal cancer grow, in a 2026 study. Stressed brains release parcels that reprogram immune cells inside tumors. Using mice under restraint stress with two tumor models, the team harvested brain-derived vesicles from blood. These membrane bubbles can cross from brain to body, and the team analyzed their cargo and effects.

Tumor-infiltrating helper T cells swallowed those vesicles and converted into regulatory T cells, the immune system's brakes, which then shielded the tumor. The mechanism ran through three microRNAs raising a protein, NOXA, which jammed a mitochondrial chaperone and leaked mitochondrial DNA into the cell interior. That tripped an alarm pathway that drove the conversion. In patients, tumors rich in the NOXA and regulatory markers tracked with higher anxiety scores and worse survival, marking the chain as a drug target and biomarker.
pmc-13495219:
Qian Cheng and co-authors trace, in a 2026 study, how the buckwheat family evolved its anthraquinones, compounds behind many of its herbal uses and defenses. The family spans the globe with crops and dye plants among its ranks, yet the history and control of the genes that build these compounds was unexplored. The team joined family-tree building with gene and activity mapping across species.

They date the family's split from its sister group to about sixty-six million years ago. One gene class that starts compound building grew to over two hundred copies, mostly by genes copying in place. Clusters of these genes packed tight in three species. Activity data from roots of one herb across growth years revealed layered control webs, with master switches ranked by learning tools. The authors offer the candidate genes and webs as a toolkit for breeding or engineering richer medicinal yields.
pmc-13495319:
Hao Zhou and colleagues hunt, in a 2026 study, for factors that speed bone growth in cervical ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament after surgery. In this condition a neck ligament hardens into bone and squeezes the spinal cord. Laminoplasty, which hinges the back of the neck bones open, relieves the squeeze, yet the bone can keep growing. The team rebuilt 3D models from scans of 37 patients covering 172 segments.

Segments were classed by yearly growth rate, with about two thirds classed as progressing. Two segment traits stood out as independent risks: uneven facet joint angles between the sides, and wider motion at the segment. Smoking, drinking, and longer surgery tracked with faster growth in simple checks, while age and diabetes tracked with slower growth. The authors say joint shape and looseness mark the segments to watch after surgery.
pmc-13495419:
Njoud Aldusary and colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, how ready Saudi radiologic technologists feel to scan patients with autism. MRI is loud, tight, and still, a hard mix for people with sensory sensitivity, and technologists carry the front line of that challenge. The team sent a questionnaire to 335 technologists and interviewed eight more.

Knowledge scores came out fairly high, yet only about one in eight had formal training in autism care. Practice and training scores were weak, with about half the group in the low range. Training and practice scores moved together slightly. Interviews named three themes: gaps in knowledge, wide swings in day-to-day practice, and a hunger for clear rules. The authors urge tailored training and standard protocols so that what technologists know becomes what patients experience.
pmc-13495519:
Selemon Gebrezgabiher Asgedom and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a pregnancy-related cancer that first showed itself as bleeding inside the skull. A 40-year-old Ethiopian woman arrived with a sudden severe headache, seizures, vomiting, and growing weakness on her right side, five months after a miscarriage. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, a rare cancer of placental tissue, spreads through blood and bleeds easily.

Scans showed a bleeding mass deep in the left brain plus a broad blood layer pressing on it. A pregnancy hormone blood test was raised, though lower than textbook values for the spread form. Surgeons removed the blood layer and the bleeding tumor at once, and tissue study confirmed choriocarcinoma, with lung and womb spread marking the highest stage. Multi-drug chemotherapy followed, her strength returned step by step, and the hormone level settled to normal.
pmc-13499519:
BAM Snoeker and a multinational team ask in 2026 whether knee surgeons would actually agree to randomise young patients with meniscus tears between repair and removal of the torn tissue. A trial is badly needed, yet strong surgeon preferences could sink it. Twenty-seven experienced knee surgeons in the Netherlands and Sweden each watched arthroscopy videos of 19 patients aged 19 to 46. Each surgeon judged willingness to randomise, their own surgical choice, and whether they favoured non-surgical care.

Agreement on willingness to randomise was slight, with a kappa value near zero on a scale where one means perfect agreement, and agreement on preferred treatment was only fair. Surgeons often disagreed both about entering a patient into a trial and about which operation to perform. The authors read the discord as proof that a trial is justified, while proposing a parallel observational study to capture what happens when opinion splits.
pmc-13499619:
Ritu Raj Gupta and colleagues study in 2026 a drilling method called osseodensification for placing dental implants in the soft upper jaw bone at the back of the mouth. That region often has thin ridges and low-density bone, which threatens implant stability, and standard drilling removes bone rather than preserving it. Special burs instead compact the patient's own bone along the hole walls, and the team tracked bone density and ridge width in 20 implant patients classed by bone softness.

Scans before surgery, right after, and at four months showed bone density rising significantly in both the firmer and softer bone groups across the follow-up window. Ridge width also grew, more at middle and tip levels than at the crest, with the firmer group gaining more in the reported averages. Age and gender showed no link to the changes, supporting the method for weak-bone sites.
pmc-13500119:
Kotaro Obayashi and colleagues report in 2026 an early comparison of two surgical robots for removing adrenal glands at Nippon Medical School Hospital. One platform, hinotori, is Japan's first home-developed surgical robot, and proof of its feasibility remains thin. Adrenalectomy, a standardised keyhole operation with well-defined outcomes, served as the test case. Records covered patients treated between September 2023 and May 2025, with costs drawn from the national case-payment database.

Only twelve patients qualified, five with the new robot and seven with the established da Vinci system, and starting profiles were broadly similar. Operating, anaesthesia, and console times overlapped between groups in the reported medians, and total reimbursed cost per case was nearly identical. Every new-robot case finished safely without conversion or major complications, though the authors stress the tiny sample and excluded purchase and maintenance costs, keeping conclusions exploratory.
pmc-13500419:
Zhangjie Yang and colleagues investigate in 2026 a DNA repair enzyme that appears to double as a metabolic driver in bladder cancer. The enzyme, ALKBH2, normally reverses chemical damage to DNA, yet tumours often rewire energy use toward sugar fermentation even under low oxygen, a pattern called the Warburg effect. Comparing cancer tissue with matched normal tissue and engineering cell lines to raise or silence the enzyme let the team test its role in growth and metabolism.

Extra enzyme made cancer cells proliferate, migrate, invade, and form colonies more strongly, while silencing it reversed those behaviours and shrank tumours in mouse graft models. Mechanistic work showed the enzyme strips a chemical mark from the RNA of a tumour suppressor gene, destabilising it and releasing a major growth signalling pathway under low-oxygen conditions. The authors propose the enzyme as a therapeutic target worth pursuing.
pmc-13500619:
Victor Alulema and co-authors argue in 2026 that designing delivery drones for high mountains fails when engineers treat stakeholder demands as fixed numbers. Doctors impose cold-chain rules, regulators impose safety systems, and planners impose speed targets, each adding weight and energy penalties. Their chance-based framework packages each requirement as a module with uncertain design coefficients and separates three layers of uncertainty. The method is then applied to electric vertical takeoff aircraft serving the Quito district of Ecuador at high altitude.

Three designs were compared, and demanding urgent delivery cut success odds far more sharply than adding cold-chain equipment in their simulations. Stakeholder choices dominated the design space. Nearly all design uncertainty could be cut through rotor testing, while battery energy density added surprisingly little variance. One design, lift plus cruise, was most robust, and a feasibility map relating altitude and cruise speed gives planners a negotiating tool.
pmc-13501319:
Park and colleagues presented PreFold-dG, a model that predicts how strongly two proteins bind by reusing the signals of a protein folding predictor, in a 2026 paper. Binding strength sits behind most cell processes, but experimental data are scarce. Most tools estimate how a mutation changes binding rather than the absolute value, a shortcut that risks overfitting data.

Park fed middle-layer embeddings from Boltz-2, an structure prediction foundation model, into a model, pooling detail from each residue, weighted by the distances between residues. They trained it to output the binding free energy itself. The model reached state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and held up on separate test sets, and ablation tests showed every layer of the folding model added something. The team tested it on real broadly neutralizing antibody data of evolutionary interest, suggesting such models carry untapped signal for binding energy.
pmc-13501619:
Yue Wang leads a three-author team reporting a 2026 case series of cataracts caused by electrical injury, a clouding of the eye's lens. One patient, a 30-year-old woman, developed a cataract two years after a lightning strike. A 64-year-old man injured by low voltage had a cataract that began at age 50. A 54-year-old man's high-voltage injury produced one within three months. All three showed opacities under the lens capsule, in snowflake, sunflower, or moss-like patterns, plus loose lens-supporting fibres at surgery.

Treatment was cataract extraction with a lens matched to each patient. The young woman received an extended depth-of-focus lens and the middle-aged man a toric lens. The bilateral case received a monofocal lens in one eye, while the other eye progressed to a mature cataract. Distance vision improved to 0.8 in two patients and 0.4 in the third. No complications followed.
pmc-13501719:
Faiza Ikram leads a three-author team with a 2026 scoping review of how learners regulate their studying, alone and together, inside adaptive collaborative learning settings. Self-regulated learning covers the solitary side, while socially shared regulation covers the group's joint control of goals and strategies. Following the Arksey and O'Malley framework, the team searched five sources for work published between 2004 and 2024 in higher and health professions education, then charted the results thematically.

Thirty-one studies qualified: fourteen data-based, twelve idea papers, four reviews, and one bibliometric study. Regulation proved dynamic, shifting between individual and shared modes across thinking, feeling, and drive. Recurring troubles included emotional strain, mismatched goals, hidden reasoning, uneven input, and coordination breakdowns. Adaptive systems helped with feedback, scaffolds, dashboards, and prompts, yet they usually targeted one level at a time. Evidence from health professions education was notably thin.
pmc-13501819:
Jeong Yun Jang leads an eleven-author team reporting a 2026 fifteen-year review of rectal cancer care at a high-volume Korean hospital. The team followed 6,314 patients with non-metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma treated with curative intent between 2008 and 2022, slicing the period into five three-year blocks. Mean diagnosis age was 59.4 years, and 62.0 percent of patients were men. The case mix grew harder over time: clinical T4 tumours rose from 7.0 percent to 28.0 percent of diagnoses across the blocks.

Practice transformed meanwhile. Minimally invasive surgery climbed from 44.5 percent to 91.0 percent of operations, powered by robotic adoption, and radiotherapy moved from after surgery to before it, with capecitabine the favoured partner drug. Five-year survival for the whole cohort reached 87.6 percent and improved steadily by period. Excess mortality against the general population shrank, the standardized ratio falling from 5.57 to 3.33 between the first and last periods.
pmc-13503419:
Paulina Flis and others investigate why many monitored edoxaban samples fall below trial concentrations. In 2026, the single-center look-back study at Karolinska University Hospital studies fifty samples from thirty-four individuals between 2017 and 2023, defining low levels by dose-specific thresholds. Over a third of roughly 350 lab samples had first fallen below twelve nanograms per millilitre.

Low concentrations appeared in forty-two percent of included samples, with no clear difference between dose groups. Higher kidney filtration tracked with low levels, though correlation was weak, and off-label dose cut and drug interactions each appeared in four low cases. The authors suggest healing tracking may help selected patients, while noting small, selected samples.
pmc-13503919:
Alaa M Momani leads a team designing how self-driving cars can share roadside computing without leaking private data, in a 2026 paper. Cars have weak onboard computers, so they pass heavy tasks to roadside units. Pooling all trip and task data in one learner would expose raw records and add traffic.

Their plan lets each roadside unit train its own decision policy and share only model settings, never raw logs. Four parts work together: joint choices on offloading and resource shares, tailored merging for uneven data, penalties for missed task deadlines, and handover costs when cars move between units. Simulations beat local running and several rival schemes on cost, delay, and energy. The authors note the privacy gain is practical, not a formal proof.
pmc-13505019:
Li Pu leads a team testing rapid magnetic brain stimulation for depressed patients with suicidal thoughts, in a 2026 trial. Standard drugs act slowly, a grave gap in a crisis. The method, intermittent theta burst stimulation, delivers quick pulse trains to the scalp and can be added to drug care.

Seventy-eight patients were split two-to-one between real and sham stimulation over ten days, with drug care held steady. Depression scores fell further in the real group, and suicidal thought scores fell more as well. A healthy thinking skill, reframing hard events in a kinder light, improved and tracked the mood gains. Anxiety and sleep also improved more with real treatment. Thinking speed tests did not differ. The authors note the follow-up was only immediate.
pmc-13506219:
Katy Flannery, Maryam Salik, and Hilal Arnouk tested whether a stress-response protein called heat shock protein 27 can help diagnose and grade oral squamous cell carcinoma. Earlier studies disagreed about how this protein behaves in mouth cancer. Using antibody staining plus computer-assisted image measurement, they compared tumour samples across stages and grades with healthy mouth lining.

Staining for the protein was clearly stronger in cancer tissue than in normal samples. Higher levels also tracked with the features doctors use to judge danger: spread to lymph nodes, overall clinical stage, and how abnormal the cells looked under the microscope. Because those links tie the protein to disease progression, the authors propose it as a supporting marker beside standard biopsy reading. Such a marker could sharpen diagnosis and help flag patients whose cancer is more likely to advance.
pmc-13506519:
Zdeněk Hlávka and others present a working data analysis plan for the light-adapted electroretinogram in children and teens. In 2026, the technical note reanalyzes waveforms from seventy-one people with autism spectrum disorder and ninety-eight controls, averaging about thirteen years old. It treats time-series recordings as functions rather than reducing them to peak times and amplitudes. Retinal responses encode contributions from photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and amacrine cells.

Nonparametric permutation tests found clear mean gaps between a-wave lows and b-wave highs at two flash strengths, and oscillatory ripple gaps across multiple strengths. Merged mean and covariance tests differed by age and group but not sex. The plan captures mean structure, covariance, and waveform shifts, revealing subtle group gaps traditional methods miss.
pmc-13507119:
Tatsuki Nishioka and colleagues test, in 2026 mouse work, an immune treatment for lung cancer that arises with lung scarring disease. Their model combined drug-induced lung fibrosis with injected lung tumor cells. Tumors grew more and larger in scarred lungs, killer CD8 T cells fell, and calming regulatory T cells rose in lungs and lymph nodes.

Treatment with an antibody against CD4 raised CD8 counts and their tumor-fighting gene activity. Tumor growth in scarred lungs slowed, regulatory cells fell, and survival improved. Removing CD4 cells, which include many regulatory cells, freed killer cells to act. The approach may offer an option where standard care is risky and scarce.
pmc-13507219:
Yuanyuan Jiang leads a 2026 team that hunts bacterial genes able to break down auxin herbicides by copying how those herbicides anchor to proteins. Auxin weed killers grip targets through a terminal acid group, and the team reasoned that degrading enzymes grip the same handle. Screening found bacterial P450 enzymes, a large family of oxidation catalysts, that degrade such herbicides.

An engineered variant degraded diverse auxin herbicides and other acid-bearing weed killers efficiently. Chemistry studies traced a two-step path that first cuts a key bond, then modifies the ring. Rice plants carrying the tuned gene plus its partner resisted a newly sold auxin herbicide. Mechanism-guided hunting could speed trait discovery for future crops.
pmc-13508319:
Yimeng Gao and Yongbin Li publish a data set mapping where a gene-control protein binds in worm muscle cells, in 2026 work. Gene switches can bind different DNA sites in different tissues, yet most worm binding maps come from whole animals, blending every tissue together. The protein studied, UNC-130, appears in several tissues, and muscle-specific data were missing. The team used a genetic trick to tag the protein only in muscle. A profiling method then mapped its binding across the genome in embryo cells.

The release includes raw reading data, processed files, peak lists, and normalized coverage tracks, plus details of the editing tools used. Everything sits in repositories for reuse. Beyond the biology, the set serves as a reference for refining this profiling method in worms. Other teams can use it to study how one switch runs different programs in different tissues, a core question in development.
pmc-13510819:
Mak and colleagues surveyed in 2026 how people in Hong Kong feel about screening newborn babies for X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, a rare inherited disorder that damages nerves and hormone glands. Screening boys is less disputed, since the disease hits them early and hard. Testing girls raises harder questions, because most female carriers stay well until middle age.

The online survey drew 259 replies from health workers and the public. Nearly all backed screening for boys, and most also backed it for girls, citing help with later care, family planning, and testing relatives. Others worried about anxiety from uncertain results, unfair treatment by insurers, and the high cost of new gene therapies. The authors propose an opt-in scheme with clear facts for parents, plus a three-step testing plan that sorts results by urgency.
pmc-13511519:
Maria-Anna Kyrgiafini, Georgios Stamatellos, Costas Stamatis and Zissis Mamuris published this 2026 genomics study of the Eghoria goat, Greece's main native goat breed. The team sequenced the genomes of six goats, hunting for variants that change protein sequences, and annotated what those variants might do. They then checked selected variants in 54 more animals from the breed.

Sequencing found over 10.7 million single-letter variants and about a million insertions or deletions. Filtering for likely functional impact kept 15,949 protein-changing variants and 861 coding indels. The affected genes clustered in pathways for metabolism, ion transport, calcium signalling, immune function, gene regulation and adaptation. Smell receptor genes were among the most variant-dense. Validation confirmed the chosen variants genuinely circulate in the breed. The authors present the catalogue as a resource for conserving the breed and for future breeding programmes that respect its local adaptation.
pmc-13512319:
Yin, Li, and Zhou studied in 2026 how seedlings of a prized medicinal herb, Astragalus membranaceus, respond in the first day after spraying with imidacloprid, a common insecticide. The herb yields a traditional root drug, and the spray is routine pest control, yet its early effects on the plant were barely known. Seedlings aged 80 days got plain spray, the standard dose, or a very high dose, and leaves were sampled after 24 hours.

Yin found both doses changed over a thousand small molecules and around seven thousand genes in the leaves. The standard dose mainly switched on defensive chemistry, boosting flavonoids, saponins, and related pathways. The heavy dose drove broader rewiring, including DNA copying and cell wall genes. A network analysis named five candidate hub genes linking stress signals, defensive chemistry, and transport. The authors offer these as markers for safer, standardised pesticide use on medicinal crops.
pmc-13514819:
Mihai and colleagues proposed in 2026 a practice framework using ultrasound to manage stiffness after stroke. Post-stroke spasticity mixes nerve overactivity with muscle changes such as scarring and stiffening. The framework pairs standard assessment with repeated muscle ultrasound. It guides botulinum toxin injections, electrical stimulation, shock wave therapy, and task-based rehab as one programme.

In the example case, spasticity, movement, walking, and self-care scores all improved over the programme. The authors stress the case is proof of concept, not proof of effect. Serial ultrasound, they argue, can reveal the non-nerve part of stiffness that bedside scales miss. That fuller picture supports more individual rehab plans. They call for studies to test and standardise this approach.
pmc-13515519:
Kairat Saparkhanovich Zhakipbekov and fourteen colleagues review, in a 2026 article, ways to wrap a helpful bacterium in protective packaging. The bacterium, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum, is a star probiotic, yet heat, storage, and stomach acid kill many cells before they can work. Pairing it with prebiotic fibres that feed it makes a synbiotic. The review surveys how capsules and coatings keep such pairings alive until they reach the gut.

Classical methods come first: spray drying, freeze drying, extrusion, and emulsion systems. Newer options include nano-scale capsules and water-based gels that release their cargo at a chosen site. The authors also catalogue the wall materials in common use and the food, supplement, and drug products that result. Gains in stability and delivery are weighed against cost and scale-up trouble. The closing outlook favours smarter coatings that protect cells through processing and the stomach alike.
pmc-13515919:
Chen and colleagues tackle a positioning problem in piezoelectric actuators, devices that move by tiny amounts when voltage is applied, in 2026 work on precision machinery. Such devices drive micro-assembly and atomic force microscopes, yet they suffer hysteresis: the movement lags behind the voltage, so the same signal gives different positions with the direction of travel. Older correction models are set up offline and cannot adapt when conditions change during use.

The team built a single-axis positioning stage with a two-stage flexure amplifier, and simulations confirmed a maximum output stroke of 95.95 micrometers from the mechanism. Their control method updates a mathematical hysteresis model online using only live position feedback, with no extra equations or heavy math. Tracking tests used sine waves between 0.1 and 2 hertz, plus variable signals of 3 to 7 volts. The adaptive scheme kept positioning accurate under those changing inputs.
pmc-13517319:
Mary-Elizabeth Zipparo and Rebecca T Veenhuis review how HIV rewires immune-cell metabolism in a 2026 article. Even on effective therapy, the virus hides in resting defender cells, and that hidden reservoir blocks any cure. The authors focus on the two cell families that host it: CD4 T cells and the monocyte-macrophage line. Each carries a distinct fuel-use profile during first infection, active copying, and quiet latency.

The virus favours metabolically busy cells, then rides their settling into rest to establish hiding places. Those same metabolic shifts may explain why treated people face more diabetes, heart disease, cancer, and cognitive trouble. Zipparo and Veenhuis argue that metabolism is no background noise but a lever. Targeting the fuel pathways that shelter the reservoir could support cure strategies and soften the chronic inflammation that ages patients early.
pmc-13517419:
Battal and Zamora wrote a 2026 imaging review on variant neck arteries present from birth. The carotid and vertebral arteries feed the brain through the neck. Their paths vary more than textbooks suggest, thanks to tangled fetal development. Modern scans now catch these variants often, planned or by chance.

The review walks through development first, then shows variants on scan types. Some variants are harmless quirks; others raise stroke or aneurysm risk. A few change how surgeons and intervention teams must plan their approach. Misreading a variant as disease can trigger needless treatment or harm. The authors supply a case-based visual tour for practicing radiologists. Origins, caliber, and branching can each differ from the standard map.
pmc-13518819:
Justine Creff and colleagues show in 2026 that mucus-making goblet cells in the gut lining physically crack the seals between neighboring cells. The intestinal lining must stay tight against harsh gut contents, even though plump goblet cells sit among tall, neat absorptive cells. Shape differences raised the question of how the barrier holds.

Using living tissue, organoids, drugs, genetic changes, mechanical tests, and modeling, the team found goblet cells press on neighbors until tight junctions fracture. Enlarged goblet cells made matters worse, and gut leakiness rose. Whether a junction broke depended on tissue stiffness set by the motor protein myosin II. Cell variety itself, they conclude, shapes barrier strength.
pmc-13519019:
Annalisa Giosuè leads an eleven-author study in 2026 on whether glucose spikes after meals, captured by continuous monitors, reliably describe a person with type 2 diabetes. Targeting after-meal rises protects the heart better than chasing fasting levels alone, yet fancy curve features are useless if they wobble day to day. A total of 102 patients wore monitors for 7 days and ate a standard breakfast twice.

Mean glucose, peak, and lowest-after-peak values reproduced moderately to well between repeats. Mean after-meal glucose best predicted time in range, weekly average glucose, and HbA1c, while peak height best predicted short-term variability. A plain 2-hour reading missed those signals, supporting richer monitor-derived features for clinic use.
pmc-13519219:
Dured Dardari published a short review in 2026 on diabetes drugs and bowel inflammation. The drugs are GLP-1 receptor agonists, widely used for type two diabetes and obesity. Many patients now live with both diabetes and inflammatory bowel disease. Clinicians need to know how these drugs affect the inflamed gut.

The review notes benefits beyond blood sugar and weight control. The drugs cut major heart events and lower inflammation markers in the blood. Observational data in bowel disease suggest acceptable safety. Those data also hint at fewer hospital stays and surgeries. Dardari argues the signals justify careful prospective trials. Until then, use in these patients rests on limited evidence.
pmc-13519419:
Deepak Hindal and colleagues measured how common dengue infection was among patients tested at a hospital in central India during 2024. Published in 2026, the retrospective study reviewed 1,898 samples tested with an early-detection blood test for the dengue NS1 protein at a tertiary hospital in Ratlam, Madhya Pradesh. The team also gathered age, sex, symptom, and district details for each case.

About one sample in eleven tested positive, giving a rate near nine percent among those tested. Patients averaged twenty-eight years old, nearly two thirds were male, and the twenty-one to thirty age band held the largest share of cases. The pattern points to young adult men as a key group for prevention work in the region. Readers get a compact local snapshot that can guide mosquito control and clinic readiness through the seasons.
pmc-13520419:
Rongguo Sun and colleagues investigate in 2026 a tiny RNA molecule called miR-4443 as both a warning marker and an active driver in coronary heart disease. The molecule influences muscle cells in artery walls, whose behaviour helps decide whether plaques grow or rupture.

Blood levels were higher in 200 heart patients than in healthy controls, while high levels tracked with more major heart events over time. In lab cells stressed with oxidised cholesterol, the molecule rose and pushed cell growth and movement, while blocking it slowed both. A partner protein called TIMP2 was confirmed as a direct target. Combined, the results nominate miR-4443 for prognosis testing.
pmc-13522319:
Xiaoyang Wang and Christopher C Yang introduced MediHive, a decentralized team of AI agents for medical reasoning. Published in 2026, the framework answers medical questions with language-model agents that pick their own roles, analyze first, debate where evidence diverges, and fuse peer insights over rounds toward agreement. Single agents often stumble on tangled, cross-disciplinary problems, while centrally run teams bottleneck and fail at one point.

MediHive beat single-model and centralized baselines on two medical question sets, scoring about 84 percent on MedQA and about 78 percent on PubMedQA. A shared memory pool plus iterative fusion gives the system scale and fault tolerance without a boss agent. The authors pitch it for reasoning-heavy medical tasks where uncertainty and conflicting evidence are the norm. Readers get a design that trades central control for resilient collaboration.
pmc-13522619:
Viviana Paulon and co-authors test whether spore formation can diversify an industrial yeast without gene editing in a 2026 study. The yeast strain Ethanol Red is widely used for bioethanol and was assumed to be stable. Thirty single-spore cultures were grown and profiled under three stressors common in factory feedstocks: furfural, formic acid, and salt.

Spore-derived lines differed reproducibly in growth and survival, with the widest spread under furfural stress. Salt caused mid-sized differences, while formic acid reduced survival across lines. Infrared fingerprints confirmed stress-specific chemical changes inside the cells. The authors argue that this classical, non-engineered route can reveal hidden adaptive variation and help improve workhorse strains for bioethanol and related plant-based fuel uses.
pmc-13522719:
Qian Liufu and co-authors show that ultraviolet light sets off the release of a nuclear protein. That protein drives skin inflammation and photoaging. Their 2026 study looks at human skin, at cells grown in the lab, and at mouse skin.

Human skin that had been hit by ultraviolet light in a sharp dose showed release of the protein, called HMGB1. So did skin that was photoaged over long time. Its release was tied to rises in inflammatory cytokines linked to photoaging. In cells, ultraviolet light cut the protein in the cells, but did not change its messenger RNA. That hints at active secretion, not a plain leak. When the protein or its receptor was blocked, cytokine expression fell after the light. In mice, when that path was broken up, fewer immune cells moved in, and harm to the dermis fell. The team hints at it as a target for therapy.
pmc-13522819:
Sergejs Lobanovs and five colleagues argue that fatty liver disease tied to body metabolism should be seen as a whole-body disorder, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. The disease, called MASLD, fattens the liver but also harms the heart, kidneys, brain, and pancreas. Patients differ widely in symptoms and course, so one label hides many forms. Sorting by liver traits alone misses this spread.

The authors back a data-driven way to group patients: let computer clustering find hidden subgroups from full health records, then model risks for each group. Such groups could guide who gets watched closely and which treatment fits. They note past grouping tries used unlike data, so their groups cannot be compared directly.
pmc-13523519:
Pedemonte Villablanca and colleagues report ten-year outcomes from Chile's first heart pump programme, a landmark for a country where donor hearts are scarce. Between 2013 and 2015, nine patients with heart failure received HeartWare left ventricular assist devices, which take over the failing chamber's work. Their average age was in the early forties, and their hearts pumped at barely a fifth of normal strength. Their 2026 case series follows the whole group.

Survival beat expectations: roughly three quarters were alive at one year. Among those using the pump as permanent therapy rather than a bridge, close to two thirds survived the full ten years. Four patients were still on support, and no pump ever needed replacement for failure. The burden was real, though: every patient suffered at least one infection, usually where the power cable exits the skin. Bleeding struck most of the group, and a third had neurological complications.
pmc-13524919:
Zhengwei Zhu and colleagues built a noise-tolerant way for learning agents to infer reward structure from messy signals. Published in 2026, the framework, called PI-GLS, joins Bayesian guessing for shaky labels, sampling-based symbol building, and genetic tuning of machine structures. Reward machines encode task rules as state diagrams, but older induction methods break when sensors mislabel events.

A belief-aware reward shaping step steers learning using distributions over machine states, keeping policy training steady under uncertainty. Benchmark tests showed faster convergence, stronger robustness to sensor noise, and clearer learned reward models, matching hand-built machines even under severe noise. The authors pitch the method for robots and other agents facing partial views and stochastic feedback. Readers get a principled fix for a common real-world fragility.
pmc-13526219:
Zechariah Kandathil, Arif Raihan, and Thivian Mathanaruban present a narrative review, published in 2026. It covers new treatments and biomarkers for inflammatory bowel disease. This term covers long-term gut inflammation disorders. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are the main ones. The authors survey limits of current tests and drugs. They also survey the search for better options for adult patients.

Biomarker research has already improved care, the review reports. Detection comes earlier. Treatment choices are more precise. Targeted drugs have shifted care as well. Biologics and small-molecule inhibitors are the key classes. Therapy is now better tolerated and more effective. Progress is real but incomplete, the authors conclude. Genetic, environmental, and immune factors still limit current biomarkers. They capture only part of the disease picture.
pmc-13526819:
Jun Allard tackled a classic modeling trade-off: how to keep a model simple enough to read while fitting data well. Published in 2026, the single-author work defines interpretability through arrow diagrams, where each arrow marks a positive or negative effect of one part on a process, and fewer arrows mean easier reading. Flexibility came from loosening shape assumptions while holding the same diagram fixed.

The method was applied to T cells exposed to pulsing signals, whose frequency responses cover all four filter shapes, from band-stop and band-pass to low-pass and high-pass. A simple signaling model matched the activation marker CD69 response within experimental error. Band-pass behavior traced to a desensitizing circuit, band-stop to removal-inhibition, and apparent low-pass to fixed total stimulation time. Independent lab datasets backed the approach. Readers learn simple models, flexed modestly, can explain complex cell behavior.
pmc-13527619:
Boyang Yu and colleagues hunted for shared molecular roots of COVID-19 and venous blood clots. Published in 2026, the systems biology study mined five public gene-expression datasets, comparing patients with COVID-19 and clotting disorders against controls. Clots complicate many COVID-19 cases and raise death risk, yet common pathways were poorly mapped.

Two genes stood out: SELP and CLEC4D, both tied to immune control and clot formation, with higher expression in certain immune cells confirmed by lab tests and animal models. Network analyses mapped their regulators, and drug-sensitivity checks linked them to specific chemotherapy agents. The authors propose both genes as markers and treatment targets for the two conditions jointly. Readers get a data-driven bridge between infection, immunity, and clotting.
pmc-13527919:
Shuai Xie and eight colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial of virtual reality headsets for children receiving an intravenous cannula. The trial ran at Mianyang Central Hospital in China and enrolled 188 children. Ninety-two wore VR headsets during the procedure. The other 96 received ordinary verbal comfort.

Nurses and the children rated fear and pain at five points around the needle insertion. Heart rate and blood oxygen were tracked throughout. VR lowered fear scores before the needle went in. Pain ratings, though, did not differ clearly between groups. Nurse ratings also ran lower than children's own ratings in both arms. Family satisfaction was recorded too. Together the measures show how distraction performs moment by moment.
pmc-13528019:
Ceren Gursen and nine colleagues compare women with obesity who do or do not have lipedema in a 2026 study. Lipedema is a painful, symmetric buildup of fat in the legs. It is often mistaken for plain obesity. The study enrolled 30 patients with both conditions and 29 with obesity alone. Both groups took body measures, strength tests, and questionnaires.

Body makeup looked similar between groups. Even so, the lipedema group had larger limb volume and lower waist ratios. They reported worse quality of life and more pain. Their skin was more tender to pressure, and pain interfered more with daily life. Leg strength, exercise capacity, and mobility were also lower. Grip strength and activity levels matched. The authors say lipedema adds real burden beyond weight alone.
pmc-13528219:
Matsumoto and coauthors compare two CT scan types for artery tears in neck and brain. Torn artery walls need fast, sure diagnosis to guide care. A new photon-counting scanner gives sharper vessel images. The team weighed it against the standard scanner type.

Records held 22 cases, split evenly by scanner type. All cases had MRI or vessel X-ray proof as contrast. The new scanner found tears in nine of eleven cases. The standard scanner found tears in four of eleven. Late-phase images helped in two new-scanner cases. Dose levels were like those of standard scans.
pmc-13528319:
Jacob Bahnsen Schmidt and eight colleagues train machine learning to guess where a hospital patient's bacterial infection sits in a 2026 study. Standard lab work often cannot name the focus quickly. Records came from over ten thousand patients at Rigshospitalet in Denmark. Data spanned late 2019 to mid-2023. Inputs mixed microbe results, blood tests, and vital signs.

A boosted tree model called XGBoost performed best. Its ranking score reached about 0.93, with low prediction error. A calibration step tuned its probabilities to match real odds. A conformal method then attached honest uncertainty ranges to each call. The authors say such wrapped models could aid early decisions. Knowing when the model is unsure matters as much as the guess. They present the work as support for, not a swap of, lab diagnosis.
pmc-13528419:
Agnieszka Alicja Kowalczyk, Mateusz Wilk, and Mariusz Korkosz review exercise and bone change in spondyloarthritis in a 2026 paper. The disease family inflames joints and tendon anchors, thinning bone and fusing the spine. Four databases were searched across 2024 and 2025. Only six papers fit the question. None measured exercise effects on bone density directly.

Short exercise bouts left ultrasound and MRI findings unchanged. Repeated strain, like certain physical jobs, may worsen structural damage. Beyond that, the record is thin and split. Bone loss in these patients is well proven, but the exercise side is guesswork. The authors call for studies on mechanical stress and bone rebuilding. Clinicians meanwhile must advise activity with little hard data. The review maps exactly where the blanks sit.
pmc-13529619:
Abdirashid S. Yusuf and Abdihakim Mohamed H. Ali give the first cancer snapshot for a hospital in Boorama, Somaliland, in a 2026 study. No cancer registry covers the region. The team read record books at Al-Hayat Hospital from 2018 to 2020. They found 130 suspected cancer cases with confirmed types logged.

Men made up about sixty-five percent of patients. Most were between forty-one and eighty years old. Case counts jumped from eighteen in 2018 to eighty-two in 2020. Prostate cancer led at about twenty-six percent. Esophageal cancer followed at about twelve percent. Breast and skin cancers came next. The authors say the rise may reflect better detection, not only more disease. They urge a proper registry and targeted control plans. Hospital data alone cannot give true population rates.
pmc-13530119:
A Arunkumar and co-authors test in 2026 a greener composite that mixes banana fiber with shell-derived powder inside epoxy resin. Calcium carbonate came from shells of the marine snail Turbinella pyrum, turning waste into filler. Treated banana fibers made up 30 percent of each panel.

Panels carried filler loads from zero to 20 percent and went through strength, heat, and water tests. A 10 percent load gave the best balance, reaching top tensile strength with better bending and impact results. Microscopy showed even filler spread and firm bonding. The winning mix also took up less water and broke down more slowly.
pmc-13530519:
Milewski and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 28, a prediction model for sorting mobile knee osteochondritis dissecans lesions into trap door and locked door types before surgery. These lesions are flaps of bone and cartilage in teenagers' knees. The type guides the operation, but it is normally confirmed only once the surgeon looks inside.

The multicenter study drew 407 patients under nineteen from a national prospective cohort whose lesion mobility was verified during arthroscopy. The strongest model combined three imaging signs while accounting for lost knee motion. The signs were a lesion wider than fifteen millimeters on the front X-ray view, at least moderate joint fluid on MRI, and a cartilage breach on a specific MRI sequence. On held-out patients the model reached seventy percent sensitivity and seventy-eight percent specificity for the distinction.
pmc-13530719:
Lawrence and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 196, a study of fractures of the medial epicondyle, the inner elbow bump in children. It sorts 682 cases into five recently described fracture patterns and asks whether each pattern carries its own typical injury mechanism.

The retrospective review covered patients under nineteen treated from 2012 to 2022 with a mean age of eleven and a half. The classic growth-plate fracture, type three, dominated at about sixty-nine percent of cases. Throwing caused over half of the type one and two injuries, the patterns tied to the ligament's pull. It caused under five percent of the other three types, which were nearly always traumatic. The youngest children clustered in type four, and elbow dislocation accompanied type five far more often than the rest.
pmc-13531519:
Ladds and colleagues weigh a fashionable technology in this 2026 discussion article: ambient AI scribes that listen to medical consultations and draft the notes automatically. England's ten-year health plan bets heavily on such tools to free clinicians from paperwork, and the authors, writing about general practice, ask whether the promise survives contact with reality.

They credit scribes with real potential to cut workload and restore eye contact, but they catalogue the risks with equal care. Auto-generated notes can entrench errors, flatten the reasoning that makes a record clinically useful, and shift doctors into unpaid proofreading. Consent, confidentiality of recorded conversations, and accountability when a scribe hallucinates all remain unsettled. Their verdict is conditional: scribes help only inside strong clinical oversight and honest evaluation, and hinder when deployed as a cheap substitute for thinking.
pmc-13531619:
Philipp von Stein and the REPAIR investigators ask in 2026 whether a small mitral valve opening blocks a catheter clipping treatment for leakage. Clipping narrows the opening further, raising fear of creating a tight valve. Registry data covered 1,189 patients whose opening size was measured in three dimensions before treatment.

About 28 percent started below the small-opening threshold. Their technical success ran slightly lower, yet leakage reduction, symptom gains at 30 days, and one-year survival matched the larger-opening group. Careful selection at experienced centers made the treatment feasible despite the smaller starting space.
pmc-13531919:
Zihan Lei and colleagues test in 2026 a plant alkaloid called karacoline against sepsis-driven lung injury in mice and lung cells. Sepsis can flood and scar the lungs with few good treatments. Computer target mapping plus docking pointed to a metabolic receptor, PPARγ, as the compound likely partner.

Treated mice showed less lung damage, less fluid buildup, lower inflammatory signals, and fewer dying cells. Cell tests echoed the protection, preserving power-station function against a bacterial toxin. Blocking the receptor weakened the benefit and restored harmful signaling, confirming the route. The compound merits further validation work.
pmc-13533419:
Gabrielle Halim, Andrew T Ainsworth, and Yolanda Vasquez-Salgado study in 2026 first-generation college students who feel torn between family duties and school demands. Such tension can raise distress and harm grades during the first year. Participants were 561 students from historically marginalised groups at Hispanic-serving colleges in California.

Greater tension linked to more inner distress, which linked to more academic problems. Students who balanced both worlds well showed no clear indirect path and reported less distress and fewer problems. Readers see a skill colleges can support through mentoring and flexible policies for family needs.
pmc-13534419:
Ran Zhang and colleagues create in 2026 a mouse model of X-linked Alport syndrome carrying the K229X change in the COL4A5 gene. The syndrome harms kidney filters and leads to kidney failure, yet its course is not fully clear and treatments are few. Gene editing placed the patient change into mice for close study.

Male mice showed blood and protein in urine, rising waste in blood, and falling COL4A5 levels in kidneys. Tissue checks found scarring, swelling, and irregular thickening of the filter layer that worsened with age. The model mirrors patient disease and supports tests of new therapies.
pmc-13534719:
Sofia O Breeze and colleagues study in 2026 whether waiting longer for sentinel node biopsy harms melanoma patients in the modern treatment era. The biopsy stages disease and guides referral for added drug therapy, yet delay effects were disputed. A UK centre cohort held 1,625 patients listed from 2010 to 2023.

Late surgery beyond 90 days linked to more spread before surgery and larger hidden tumour deposits. After 2016, longer waits also linked to worse disease-specific survival. Threshold analysis favoured biopsy within 68 days of diagnosis and 82 days of removal surgery. Service leaders can use the thresholds to audit local waiting lists and protect timely access.
pmc-13535719:
Yaniv Dotan and colleagues compare in 2026 two bronchoscopy sampling methods for suspected lymph node disorders in the chest. Needle aspiration is standard, yet its small samples often miss disorders that need larger tissue. In a multicentre study, 50 patients had both needle sampling and freezing-based biopsy from the same node.

Overall diagnostic yield was far higher for the freezing biopsy than for needle sampling. Among cases the needle missed, the freezing method diagnosed most, and its yield for confirmed lymph disorders more than doubled the needle yield. No major complications followed the freezing procedure in this study.
pmc-13536619:
Dai and colleagues published a 2026 study on a fat-cell switch that restrains a deep belly tumor. Retroperitoneal liposarcoma grows behind the belly organs and often returns after surgery. The switch, PPARγ, normally guides fat cell growth and maturity. The team tested 80 patient samples and lab models to trace its role.

The switch ran low in tumor tissue and foretold worse outcomes when lowest. Raising it in lab cells slowed growth and pushed cells to die. Cutting it did the opposite, freeing a key growth pathway to fire. A diabetes drug that boosts the switch shrank tumors in animal models. Safety checks in those models looked favorable for future trials. An existing drug thus gains a possible second life against RLPS.
pmc-13538519:
Yuzhengheng Zhang and colleagues test ear vagus nerve pulses in diabetic mice with low mood in a 2026 study. Diabetes and low mood feed each other, while paired drug care brings side effects and poor tolerance. Diabetic mice stressed into a combined model got daily pulses through the skin for three weeks. Mood tests, weight, fasting sugar, brain maps, and serotonin signals in a control hub were tracked.

The pulses lowered weight and fasting sugar, eased low-mood behavior, and lifted movement. Brain maps showed broad calming of stress-driven overdrive. Serotonin release in the hypothalamus surged during pulsing, with lasting levels and receptor counts also rising. Stronger serotonin signals tracked with better sugar control and mood. The authors propose the pathway as a shared lever for paired metabolic and mood care.
pmc-13538819:
Hang Su and colleagues link glucose time in range to advanced multi-organ syndrome in older adults living with type 2 diabetes in a 2026 study. The syndrome framework joins heart, kidney, and metabolic disease into stages, with the top stages classed advanced. Among 2,497 adults aged 60 years or older wearing glucose monitors, syndrome stage was set against time spent in the target glucose band.

Patients with advanced syndrome spent clearly less time in range than peers with earlier stages. Each standard drop in time in range raised advanced syndrome odds by roughly a quarter after adjustment, in a straight-line pattern leveling near the seventy percent mark. Even mid-range time above the older-adult target carried higher odds than top-range time. Extra time in range brought no added low glucose exposure.
pmc-13540819:
Yuling Liu and eight colleagues trace, in a 2026 UK Biobank study, when dementia risk begins to climb around a new diabetes diagnosis. Evidence on risk before diagnosis was thin, so the team ran matched case-control and cohort analyses together.

Records covered 44,166 people who developed diabetes and three times as many matched controls. Dementia risk was already higher a full decade before diagnosis and rose as diagnosis approached, peaking in the final two years. Risk stayed elevated after diagnosis, especially for vascular dementia, where it ran more than sixfold. The authors suggest the two years before diagnosis deserve close attention to memory and thinking.
pmc-13540919:
Li Yingxing and colleagues chart infections at one Chinese hospital in 2026. The hospital is a secondary hospital in Shandong Province. The records span twelve years, from 2014 to 2025. They also track drug resistance over that time. National checks lean on big tertiary hospitals, so smaller ones stay poorly mapped. Doctors in such hospitals need local data of their own. Good local data helps them pick the right first drug for a sick patient.

Lab records held 2,661 bacterial isolates. Gram-negative bacteria dominated the set. Two species led the list. One was Escherichia coli, the other Klebsiella pneumoniae. Each favoured distinct patient groups and sample types. Klebsiella finds crept upward over the years. Staphylococcus aureus finds declined. Resistance was fiercest in Acinetobacter baumannii.
pmc-13542019:
Sadikshya Ghimire and seven colleagues test, in a 2026 laboratory study, how vitamin B12 supply shapes the growth and nutritional richness of the freshwater alga Euglena gracilis. Most such algae need B12 yet cannot make it, depending on bacteria that synthesise this vitamin.

pmc-13542119:

pmc-13543419:

pmc-13543719:

pmc-13545519:
Lausten-Thomsen and seven co-authors track congenital syphilis in Denmark, in work from twenty twenty-six. Congenital syphilis passes from mother to baby and can seriously harm the newborn, yet it is preventable with screening and treatment. Several European countries report rising trends.

Incidence and time trends of congenital cases were assessed, along with how many pregnancies had active syphilis. Register data capture every case, not a sample, so the national picture is exact. The study tests whether Denmark is on track for elimination.
pmc-13546719:

pmc-13547419:

pmc-13547919:
Meera Thangarajah and Lucinda J. Such faults can surface as repeated infections, autoimmunity, runaway lymph tissue, allergy, or cancer, and first signs often appear long before anyone suspects the underlying cause. pmc-13548519:

pmc-13548619:
Yusuke Watanabe and colleagues compare how long Japanese men and women stay on peritoneal dialysis, in a 2026 nationwide registry analysis. This home-based dialysis method ends early for many patients because of infection or fluid trouble, and sex differences in Japan were uncharted. pmc-13548719:
Qingxiang Zheng and colleagues measure how skilled Chinese obstetric nurses are at advising mothers on breastfeeding, in a 2026 survey. pmc-13550319:
A. Martorell-Múgica and colleagues ferment farm and food industry waste into lactic acid using only the microbes already living in it, in a 2026 process study. Lactic acid feeds food, cosmetic, and bioplastic production, and pure laboratory cultures are among its biggest costs because everything must stay sterile. The culture settled into stability, accumulating lactic acid at a concentration above thirty grams per liter and converting nearly half the organic matter. Lactic acid made up almost eighty-eight percent of the products, a high selectivity explained by the community itself: over half belonged to the lactobacillus family. The authors argue open mixed cultures can slash production costs for waste-based chemicals.
pmc-13551319:

pmc-13551719:

pmc-13551819:

pmc-13551919:

pmc-13552019:

pmc-13553519:

pmc-13554019:

pmc-13554119:

pmc-13554219:
Jing Wang leads a six-author team testing whether daily LED light harms the young rat brain in a 2026 study. Rats sat under LED light each evening for a month, mimicking common human lighting. pmc-13554519:

pmc-13556019:

pmc-13556519:

pmc-13558319:

pmc-13558619:

pmc-13559319:

pmc-13562619:

pmc-13563919:

pmc-13569319:

pmc-13573419:

pmc-13574919:

pmc-13575019:

pmc-13575319:

pmc-13576019:

pmc-13576119:

pmc-13578019:

pmc-13578319:

pmc-13579119:

pmc-13579719:

pmc-13580319:

Tags are the switches and labels across that program. The review follows them through three arenas: the rescue program itself, quality checks at the ribosome door, and the shredding route for failed proteins. Tags also reach into the wider stress response and into the contact points where cell compartments touch. The authors sort a sprawling cast of tagging enzymes by job.
pmc-13581319:
Abdullah Saad, Aisha Imran, Fatima Siddiqui, and Laiba Abbas write to the editor questioning a study that tied hearts from suicide donors to worse transplant results, in a letter. The original work reported higher thirty day deaths for such hearts. The letter writers grant the topic's weight but press three soft spots in the math and the logic.

First, only six suicide donor hearts sat in the study, too few for firm claims, and no spread ranges were given. Second, no adjusted analysis sorted out rival factors like clamp time or receiver sickness. Third, lumping all suicides together skips the mechanism: livers and lungs from hanging donors do fine elsewhere, so hanging strain or overdose may drive heart results instead. Eight dropped cases add one more caution.
pmc-13581719:
Xiaohui Zhu and six colleagues pinned a gene called SYTL5 as a driver of spread in the most common form of thyroid cancer. They checked the gene in 107 pairs of tumor and healthy tissue from the same patients. The gene was switched on far more in tumors, and high levels tracked with spread to neck lymph nodes. Cell lines with the gene dimmed or boosted let the team test cause, not just correlation.

Cells with extra SYTL5 grew, moved, and invaded more; cells with it dimmed slowed and died more. Tumors grown in mice told the same story. A second factor, ZNF384, was shown to switch the gene on at its promoter. The twenty twenty-six study marks SYTL5 as both a warning sign and a drug target in thyroid cancer, and names the switch that turns it up.
pmc-13582719:
Mi Zou, Guangda Zheng, and Yanju Bao build a twelve gene risk score for lung adenocarcinoma from zinc finger protein genes, in a 2026 study. These genes carry zinc gripping parts that steer cell growth and spread. Public tumor data sets were mined for shifted family members, and a survival model kept the dozen with the sharpest signal.

The score split patients into high and low risk groups with sturdy survival separation. Low risk tumors drew more immune cells and answered immune therapy better in the data. Four candidate drugs surfaced from sensitivity screens. One risk gene was pushed in lab cells and drove more malignant behavior, backing its place in the score. The authors offer the panel as a guide for sorting patients and picking treatments.
pmc-13584219:
Kai Leong Chong and colleagues review the flow physics behind high-power extreme ultraviolet light sources for advanced chip lithography. These sources fire a high-power laser at tiny tin droplets, creating plasma that emits light at 13.5 nanometers for printing sub-10-nanometer circuits. The process spans laser absorption, plasma evolution, and debris transport across many scales.

The review covers computer models of laser-droplet interaction, droplet behavior under femtosecond to nanosecond pulses, and debris control with buffer gas jets and magnetic fields. Low energy-conversion efficiency and debris fouling of collector mirrors remain the central obstacles.
