Linking basic flow physics to source engineering should yield cleaner, more efficient light sources.
pmc-13587419:
Hüseyin Günizi and colleagues test a simple nose swab in children whose rhinitis is not driven by allergy. Non-allergic rhinitis brings the same sneezing, blockage, and drip as the allergic kind, yet allergy tests come back clean, and its subtypes are often missed. Their 2026 study enrolled 103 children aged 5 to 18, half with the condition and half healthy, and counted eosinophils, a white cell type, in nose mucus under the microscope.

Children with rhinitis carried far more of those cells in the nose than healthy children, and a cutoff value split the groups cleanly. The cell counts, though, did not track with scores on a quality-of-life questionnaire, so the swab names the subtype better than it grades how bad a child feels. The authors still back nose cytology as a cheap, gentle tool for sorting these children in clinic.
pmc-13587619:
Tippy Rolink and colleagues survey epilepsy across nine Dutch pedigree dog breeds. Each breed keeps a small, fairly inbred population, which makes inherited epilepsy a standing worry. An online questionnaire gathered case details from owners, while breed clubs and clinic records supplied the counts behind prevalence estimates for each breed line, including three coats of Dutch Shepherd.

Estimated rates ran from well under one percent in the Schapendoes to nearly three percent in the Wetterhoun and Dutch Partridge dog. Whole-body convulsions were the most common seizure form everywhere, and warning or after-effects showed in about half the dogs. Most epileptic dogs received anti-seizure medicine, most often phenobarbital, and most of those had side effects. Breeding advice has already cut rates in several breeds, with the Dutch Smoushound and Kooiker dog showing the clearest gains.
pmc-13589819:
Pourfarzad and colleagues test in 2026 whether combined exercise training calms the inflammasome, an inflammatory alarm complex inside cells, in the hearts of rats with type 2 diabetes. Diabetic cardiomyopathy, heart damage from diabetes, is fed by this chronic inflammation.

Twenty-four male Wistar rats were split into three groups of eight. The groups were healthy controls, diabetic controls, and diabetic rats trained five times a week for eight weeks with combined endurance and resistance work. After training, heart tissue from the trained diabetics showed clearly lower levels of the alarm complex's three measured components than tissue from untrained diabetic rats. The components were the sensor protein, its activating enzyme, and the inflammatory messenger interleukin-1 beta. Training also lowered final body weight and improved the insulin resistance index by reducing blood sugar and insulin.
pmc-13591219:
Matteo Carpi and Conny De Vincenzo test whether a large language model can stand in for human respondents in personality research. Fake respondents would let scholars trial short questionnaires cheaply before paying for real data. The team compared 111 Italian students with two sets of answers made by GPT, one posing as a generic student and one as a detailed made up person. All took a ten item Big Five questionnaire.

Model answers bunched tightly and skewed toward pleasant, outgoing profiles, unlike the wider human spread. Links between traits also warped: some vanished, others flipped sign. Adding a persona helped a bit yet fell short of human patterns. Carpi and De Vincenzo urge caution before treating model output as a lab for human personality.
pmc-13592319:
Fidel Lozano-Elena and three colleagues pin, in 2026, short protein chains onto silica beads in a way that locks them into helix shapes. Helices steer how proteins grip partners, yet lone peptides flop loose and lose the shape, above all when heated. Their method uses a changeable covalent link that lets attached peptides settle into their lowest energy form. Alanine rich chains dotted with lysine anchors were the test case.

Attachment point mattered: end on links sparked helices, while links spaced every second turn gave the best heat endurance. One face of each helix still points outward, free to bind. A streptavidin binding peptide kept its grip after mounting and shrugged off heat far better than free copies, the team shows.
pmc-13593619:
Nanapol Ongworawut and colleagues tried to trim stool germ tests at a big hospital in Bangkok. Stool tests eat cash and staff time, and each choice growth plate is oft debated. The team ran 597 loose-stool samples for Salmonella, Shigella, Vibrio, Aeromonas, and Plesiomonas, plus extra tests for Campylobacter and Yersinia germs.

Germs grew from just 12.7 percent of samples, mostly Salmonella at 10.4 percent and Campylobacter at 2.2 percent, with no Yersinia at all. Gram-negative broth and MSRV plates proved best for Salmonella. Plain Yersinia plates were judged poor value, and Campylobacter choice plates should swap in for filters so low-shed cases are not missed.
pmc-13596419:
Yunchen Meng and colleagues study links between exercise, emotional skill, and resilience in college students, in a 2026 survey. Resilience, the ability to bounce back, matters for students under pressure. The team asked whether physical activity supports resilience partly by building emotional intelligence. They also checked whether the paths differ by fitness level.

Nearly two thousand freshmen and sophomores at four Beijing universities took part. Students were split into three groups by fitness: general, fitness-building, and sports rehabilitation. Standard scales measured activity, emotional intelligence, and resilience. In the whole group, more activity went with stronger emotional intelligence and with greater resilience. Part of the activity link ran through emotional intelligence, as the team suspected. Group comparisons showed the routes are not identical for every fitness level. The results support campus programs that pair exercise with emotional skill building.
pmc-13596919:
Silva-Magana and four co-authors present a simulation model of antibiotic resistance in microbial communities, in work from twenty twenty-six. Resistance grows out of ecology and evolution inside complex groups of microbes. How species act on each other shapes how resistance traits spread and how long they last.

Many theory models treat such groups as uniform boxes and skip those links. This network dynamical model instead maps each group as an ecological association network. Each species is a node, and the links carry how they act on each other. Running resistance on such a network can show why the same drug pressure gives unlike outcomes in unlike groups. That is a step toward predicting resistance before it emerges.
pmc-13598019:
Nilgün Öksel and co-authors grew rat testicular tissue in the laboratory for eight weeks. The tissue sat on scaffolds of platelet-rich plasma gel. The team hunted for ways to preserve fertility. Their focus was boys whose cancer treatment will sterilize them. Immature tissue was cultured at an air-liquid interface, with the plasma given either as the supporting gel or dissolved in the medium, in their 2026 study.

The gel-supported cultures kept the developing sperm precursor cells alive best. Cells entering meiosis persisted to week eight only in that group. The stem-like spermatogonia pool also remained detectable at the end. Development in every setup stalled at the spermatocyte stage without producing round spermatids, so full sperm production in a dish remains out of reach. The authors present the plasma gel as a promising scaffold step toward future fertility restoration from banked tissue.
pmc-13599319:
Yue Li and four colleagues report a 2026 single-center study of body temperature dropping too low during trauma surgery. Such drops, called inadvertent intraoperative hypothermia, mean a core temperature below 36 degrees and are tied to worse recovery after injury. The team looked back at adults who had trauma surgery under general anesthesia at one large hospital between January 2023 and May 2025, hunting for factors that raised the risk.

Among 885 patients, 23.3 percent became too cold during surgery. Risk rose with low body mass index, a low starting temperature, longer operations, larger fluid volumes, and combined body positions. Starting temperature alone predicted the problem fairly well, and all five factors together predicted it better still. The authors present the combined model as a practical way to flag patients who need extra warming before and during surgery.
pmc-13600419:
He and colleagues commented in 2026 on a new single-cell method, wellDR-seq, that reads both the genome and the gene activity of the same breast cancer cell. Knowing which normal cell type a tumor began in, its cell of origin, could explain subtype behavior. Squeezing clean DNA and RNA from one cell is hard, and guessing DNA changes from RNA alone is coarse. The method sorts single cells into thousands of tiny wells and barcodes both layers for joint sequencing.

Applied to samples from twelve patients with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, the approach traced ancestral tumor subclones and epithelial lineages, found normal cells carrying cancer-like DNA changes. Measured how gene copy changes dose gene activity across subclones. He and colleagues present the technology as a way to join genotype and phenotype cell by cell, opening a sharper view of how breast cancers begin and diversify.
pmc-13607219:
Fahri Malkoç, Muhammed Afacan, and Oğuzhan Yüksel lead a team study of which rehabilitation patients break a bone when they fall inside the hospital. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Inpatient falls are a standing safety worry in rehab wards. Yet what turns a fall into a fracture was poorly mapped.

The team reviewed ninety-one fall events at one tertiary rehab hospital. More than half of the falls caused a fracture. Patients with fractures had weaker lumbar spine bone scores and more incontinence. Age, sex, mobility, and fall mechanics did not separate the groups. Two standard fall-risk scores were tested for how well they flag fracture risk. The resulting orthopedic burden is described in detail. The work aims prevention at bone health, not just fall counts.
pmc-13609319:
Xiaoxuan Zhu and colleagues pulsed water flow like a heartbeat for distillation in 2026. Membrane distillation desalinates salty water efficiently. Steady flow causes flux decline and fouling. Standard pulse waves help only limitedly. A heartbeat-like pulse was introduced here. Heat and mass transfer were characterised.

One parameter explained half the variance. Pulse shape dominated system performance overall. Acceleration and rest phases alternated uniquely. That rhythm mimics natural heart flow. Complex feed waters suit this mode. Fouling eased under biomimetic pulsing. Sine and square waves performed worse. Industrial desalination could adopt the approach.
pmc-13610819:
Ivana Varga leads a nine-author team comparing two famous crops with opposite reputations: industrial hemp and tobacco. Both plants have centuries of human use, but their chemistry pushed them down diverging roads. The review ranges over traditional applications, bioactive compounds, health implications, and the social, economic, and environmental sides of each crop, finishing with their governing rules.

Hemp's traditional fiber, textile, and paper roles have widened into food, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and building materials. Tobacco stayed a leaf crop defined by nicotine and its relatives, so its research centers on addiction and toxic harm. Regulation mirrors the split: tobacco is tightly controlled worldwide, while hemp restrictions keep loosening, though hemp products still need strict quality control. The authors frame hemp as an emerging sustainable resource for the bioeconomy, and tobacco as a continuing public health and environmental challenge.
pmc-13612319:
Kejun Ye leads a six-author team testing whether a simple cholesterol leftover predicts diabetes in twin pregnancies. Remnant cholesterol, computed from an ordinary lipid panel as total cholesterol minus LDL and HDL cholesterol, tracks with glucose disorders. Nobody had checked it in twins, who develop gestational diabetes at high rates. The retrospective cohort followed 347 women with twin pregnancies at a Chinese tertiary hospital between 2020 and 2025, using first-trimester blood values.

Higher remnant cholesterol was associated with later gestational diabetes after adjustment, with a smooth linear relationship. A cut-off of 1.145 mmol/L split the cohort: women above it carried 2.56 times the adjusted odds of diabetes. As a screening test alone it was modest, with an area under the curve of 0.649 and poor specificity. The association looked stronger in monochorionic twins, but that subgroup held only ten diabetes cases. The authors label both findings exploratory, needing prospective validation.
pmc-13615219:
Seoyoung Hwang, Hee Soo Jeong, and Sang Beom Jun review in 2026 a puzzle about retinal prostheses. These devices give some sight back to people with severe damage to the eye's light-sensing cells. Yet the vision they deliver is far blurrier than their design suggests. Chips placed on, under, or behind the retina have restored light sense, object finding, and motion reading in clinics. Yet sharpness in real patients lags far behind the spacing of the device's electrodes or pixels.

The authors sort the causes of this resolution gap. They include current spreading in tissue and the distance between chip and target cells. They also include nerve wiring that scrambles the signal, plus the brain's own reading of a crude code. Their message is that tighter pixel grids alone will not close the gap. Future devices must be designed around the living eye's limits, not just the engineer's drawing board.
pmc-13616419:
Tiran Bercovici, Mike Bismuth, Meir Goldsmith, Dan Peer, and Tali Ilovitsh engineer drug-carrying nanodroplets that stay quiet in the body until a two-tone ultrasound pulse pops them inside a solid tumour. Most smart medicines release passively and cannot be triggered with precision. Their droplets, each under 200 nanometres and built by microfluidic assembly, carry a fluorinated core that holds the payload and keeps the particle stable in the bloodstream.

A first ultrasound tone vaporises the droplets. A second, lower tone then makes the bubbles collapse. The collapse tears a confined pocket open and frees the drug on demand. All of this stays within safe clinical sound limits. Dense tumour tissue and poor penetration are the barriers this design attacks. Programmable release inside the tumour alone could raise the dose where it counts while sparing the rest of the body.
pmc-13617219:
Batel Hazan-Liran and Ofra Walter compare inner resources among adults who grew up with a sibling with developmental disabilities and adults whose siblings have none. They measured psychological capital, a bundle of hope, confidence, optimism, and resilience, alongside social support and self-compassion. One hundred fifty-four adults aged eighteen to seventy-one answered the survey, forty-two of them from disability families.

The three resources rose together across the whole group and within the comparison group, and psychological capital carried the link between social support and self-compassion in both groups. Contrary to the authors' expectation, siblings of people with disabilities scored no differently from other siblings on any measure. The team concludes that building psychological capital could be a practical target for programs that support siblings' well-being, whatever the family situation.
pmc-13619119:
Christine Esposito and colleagues report a 2026 follow-up study of bone-anchored maxillary protraction, a treatment that uses small anchors in the bone to pull the upper jaw forward in teenagers. The patients had Class III malocclusion, where the lower jaw sits too far ahead. Forty-five treated patients were compared with thirty-nine similar teenagers who were observed during growth instead.

X-ray measures taken at three time points showed modest gains in upper jaw position after the first treatment phase. Some of that advantage faded as growth continued, and the treatment did not change how many patients later needed jaw surgery. Among patients finished with braces alone, controls needed tooth extractions far more often than treated patients. The authors conclude the method may spare extractions while barely affecting surgery rates.
pmc-13620119:
Yang Liu and ten colleagues present the first chromosome-level genome of the greasyback shrimp, an Indo-Pacific species prized in fisheries and farming, in a 2026 paper. Shrimp genomes are hard to assemble because they are large, repetitive, and variable. The team combined long-read and short-read sequencing with a chromosome-contact method to scaffold the pieces.

The finished assembly spans close to two billion DNA letters, with most of the sequence anchored onto thirty-nine chromosomes. About fifty-seven percent of the genome proved to be repetitive sequence, and the shrimp's two genome copies differ noticeably from each other. Annotation found more than twenty-one thousand protein-coding genes, and a standard completeness check recovered nearly all core arthropod genes. The authors offer the resource as a base for work on shrimp evolution, coastal adaptation, and breeding.
pmc-13620419:
Sanyukta Padmanabhan and three colleagues review how nicotine helps cancers grow along the digestive tract without being a classic cancer-causing chemical itself. Nicotine is not classed as directly gene-damaging, yet it switches on cell receptors that feed growth signals. The team searched two databases for work since the early nineties, mixing human population studies, animal models, and lab research.

Across organs, nicotine lit up shared growth and survival pathways and encouraged blood vessel growth and inflammation. Local twists mattered too: tobacco-specific chemicals damaged DNA in mouth and pancreas, one growth pathway dominated in the food pipe, and a prostaglandin route fed tumors in stomach and liver. Immune changes may also help virus-linked cancers. The authors call nicotine a context-dependent tumor promoter and map where more proof is still needed.
pmc-13621519:
Silvia Krumm and seven colleagues interviewed employers in southern Germany about hiring and keeping people with mental health problems. Awareness of workplace mental health keeps rising, yet participation barriers persist, and the authors wanted the view from the manager's chair rather than the stigma literature. Twenty-nine employers across sectors gave semi-structured interviews during 2022 and 2023, later coded for themes.

Employers came across as genuinely torn. Many accepted mental illness as increasingly normal, valued work's health-giving structure, and cited social responsibility, labor shortages, and good past experiences as reasons to include. Worry ran alongside: unpredictable absences, team strain, and fairness questions. Support, they said, usually hinged on the employee disclosing limitations and taking personal responsibility for managing their health. The authors conclude that inclusion turns less on attitudes than on these everyday workplace negotiations.
pmc-13621719:
Nicola Pelizzari and colleagues surveyed whether species-rich city green spaces improve adult health. Green spaces seem to lift urban life quality, yet mixed yardsticks and results blocked matching across studies. Their planned review, under PRISMA rules and a public plan, screened studies from January 2014 to July 2025 and kept 147.

Most studies used tree cover or plant-cover indices, while few used combined nature or animal-richness measures. Gains ruled: 70 to 90 percent of general, mental, and wellbeing studies found gains, every drug-script study linked green contact to fewer antidepressant or anti-anxiety scripts, and chronic-disease evidence pointed shielding. Birth results varied, and poorer groups gained most. Pelizzari and colleagues tie richer green spaces to better health.
pmc-13621819:
Rafaela Souto e Souza de Melo and colleagues present a case report where two rare muscle conditions met in one family, with fatal results. One condition, mitochondrial myopathy, weakens muscles because the cell's energy producers fail. The other, malignant hyperthermia, is a dangerous reaction to certain anaesthetic drugs that sends the body into overdrive.

The report describes a deadly, unusual reaction to anaesthesia in the patient. Testing then found mitochondrial dysfunction in the mother. A variant in the RYR1 gene turned up in the father, who had no symptoms, and in a cousin with muscle breakdown after exercise. Two separate inherited problems can hide in one family, the authors stress. Care teams may face clashing priorities, so broad genetic and family checks matter before surgery.
pmc-13623119:
Saharu Magona Nerima leads a mixed-methods study of underweight among breastfeeding mothers in the slums of Kampala, Uganda. Poor nutrition while nursing can shrink both the amount and quality of breast milk, harming mother and baby. Data from city slums were scarce, so the team combined a survey with interviews of health workers.

The survey covered 285 mothers aged twenty to forty-nine, and about fourteen percent were underweight. Mothers in food-insecure homes were more likely to be underweight. Eating at least three meals a day, eating a varied diet, and living in smaller households each went with lower risk. Health workers named the same patterns, adding that mothers who work outside the home face extra strain. The authors recommend community outreach that joins family planning advice with support for household food security and varied meals.
pmc-13623219:
Abi Abdallah and co-authors report gut-first staged care for a torn aorta with blocked gut blood flow. A type A aortic tear plus gut starvation is among the deadliest heart emergencies. Guidelines urge instant repair of the aorta, yet that may be risky once gut damage is advanced.

Their patient was a 54-year-old woman whose tear ran from above the heart to the hip vessels. The team first built a bypass to the gut artery and placed a stent graft the same day. Worsening gut damage over two days forced more surgery, including removal of part of the colon.
pmc-13623919:
Friedrich C Jassil leads a real-world study of night shift work and metabolism in hospital staff in Switzerland. Lab experiments have linked night work to blood sugar problems, but evidence from actual workplaces is thin. The team followed workers through three straight night shifts and three straight day shifts with wearable sensors and phone apps.

Seventy-two workers took part, mostly women around thirty-one years old and of healthy weight. During nights they ate fewer calories, less protein, and less fat than during days. Even so, their blood sugar swung more widely and spiked higher after meals on nights. After the night block, the stress hormone cortisol ran lower, and heart rate patterns across the day shifted. Workers who ate more protein had steadier sugar, while eating at night itself tracked with wilder swings. The authors suggest meal timing trials as the next step.
pmc-13624219:
Patrick Jason Toppin leads a study asking which patients in septic shock actually gain from corticosteroid treatment, a cheap drug whose overall benefit has stayed murky for decades. Rather than run a new trial, the team emulated one inside a large intensive care database, comparing similar patients who did or did not receive the drugs.

The analysis covered 5,533 septic shock stays, about eighteen percent of them steroid-treated, and those patients were clearly sicker at the start. After statistical adjustment for that imbalance, simple blood-count patterns flagged who benefited. Patients starting with few infection-fighting lymphocytes, or with high ratios of other white cells to lymphocytes, showed lower intensive care deaths when given steroids. The signals were modest, roughly matching the power of a standard severity score. Because the tests cost almost nothing and exist everywhere, the authors suggest they could help target treatment where resources are scarce.
pmc-13624319:
Jie Miao leads a study attacking Alzheimer's disease at the brain's border, where a clogged clearance system lets toxic amyloid-beta pile up. Brain blood vessel cells ferry it out through a transporter, but the team found two blocks: a regulatory protein that disables the transporter. A stress protein jams the cell's recycling so it cannot be broken down.

Silencing the first blocker restored the transporter and improved export; silencing the second reopened the recycling pathway and let cells digest their load. Researchers packaged gene-silencing strands against both targets into tea-based nanoparticles with a homing coat, which crossed into the brain and concentrated in vessel cells and immune cells. In Alzheimer's-model mice, six weeks of treatment sharpened cognition, cut amyloid and vessel deposits, and calmed inflammation without short-term harm. The paired approach, export plus digestion, is offered as a clearance therapy template.
pmc-13625019:
Wansu Chen and colleagues question a common belief in medical prediction software, that more patient data always helps. Working with health records of adults with mild asthma, they trained transformer models to forecast sudden asthma attacks. They then trimmed the input two ways, cutting the feature list by several selection methods and shortening each patient's history, and weighed accuracy against computing cost.

Leaner models forecast nearly as well as the full eighty-feature model, and they flagged much the same high-risk patients. Shortening histories cut training time by more than seventy percent with little loss of sharpness. The catch sits at the top end, where lean models softened the highest risk estimates, a trade-off builders of hospital prediction tools should weigh.
pmc-13625719:
Yuanyuan Ma and colleagues review how bacteria coordinate two injection weapons against fungal rivals. One system, type VI, fires toxins straight into fungal cells, wrecking walls and metabolism, while type III trades signals and goods, sometimes helping fungi and sometimes fighting them, chiefly among plant-linked microbes. The conductor is quorum sensing, the chemical headcount that lets bacteria switch tactics as their numbers and fungal cues change.

Knowing when bacteria choose attack, trade, or restraint could sharpen farm biocontrol, sparing crops without blanket chemicals. The same logic may guide new antifungal ideas for clinics and the environment, where drug resistance keeps climbing. The review gathers scattered findings into a single map of who senses what, and which weapon answers.
pmc-13626319:
Chih-Hsiung Chang, Jie Chi Yang, and Dmitriy Muzylyov study how television political journalists in Taiwan think together inside a chat group. The closed LINE group links reporters across rival organizations who must pool knowledge under deadline pressure. Interviews with twelve members, split by experience, let the team rebuild the habits that turn scattered tips into shared, usable understanding.

Three mechanisms stood out. Authority floated to whoever knew the story best at that moment, private hunches were posted as readable cues others could judge, and the group assembled backing for interpretations piece by piece. Veterans said years inside the flow had retuned how they read politics altogether. The case shows a chat group acting as real infrastructure for fast, collective judgment.
pmc-13626919:
Pamela Graney leads a team on sex gaps in immune cell response. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses stem cell grown macrophages. Male and female folks often differ in swell response and outcomes.

Cells from male and female donors were grown in the lab. A bacterial part was used to spark a swell response. Gene reads showed small sex gaps at rest in the cells. Those gaps grew large once the spark was added. Spilled proteins also split by sex in matched ways. More checks in a larger group are still needed.
pmc-13628419:
Michael Sarfo and two colleagues asked 622 adults in Ghana what would make them accept a malaria vaccine. The adults lived in two towns, one with heavy malaria spread and one with light spread. Their 2026 study joined two classic models of health behaviour in a single test.

All the belief measures held up well in testing. Together they explained just over two-thirds of the spread in plans to take the vaccine. Warm views of the vaccine and its gains drove acceptance most. Feeling at risk, oddly, went with weaker plans to take it. The authors urge drives that stress the vaccine's gains. They also urge fixing false beliefs among people who feel most at risk.
pmc-13628819:
Luisa S. Welter and sixteen colleagues modelled what schizophrenia costs the world, country by country. Their prevalence-based study covered 204 countries for the year 2019, drawing per-patient costs from the published literature, standardising them, filling gaps by income group, and scaling them with global disease estimates.

About twenty-two million adults lived with schizophrenia that year. Across the income regions with full data, the combined bill reached roughly 243 billion dollars in comparable purchasing terms, split among direct care, lost productivity, and unpaid informal care. Upper-middle-income countries carried the heaviest load relative to their economies, while rich countries spent most per patient. The authors urge policymakers to fund care that improves daily functioning and participation, since per-patient costs drive the total.
pmc-13630219:
Pooja Yerramilli and two colleagues argue, in an essay, that rebuilding global health will fail on one condition. It fails unless health equity becomes its clear guiding aim. Donor shocks have disrupted the field. Recent reform schemes, they contend, tinker with how the system is arranged. They leave unasked what the system is for, and who holds power in it.

Centring equity brings shared struggles into view. Marginalised communities face them everywhere. Diseases of poverty appear in rich lands too, from hookworm in Alabama to tuberculosis in London. Four shifts follow. Move from substitution to mutual aid. Move from technical help to knowledge sharing. Move from global public goods to common goods. Move from coordination machinery to tools that also share out power and resources.
pmc-13631819:
Yongquan Wang and sixteen colleagues tested a new way to repair cut peripheral nerves in rats. The standard repair sews the nerve ends together, yet recovery is often poor. Their method wraps the join in a collagen cover that imitates the nerve's outer layer. The cover should spread tension along the nerve and let surgeons use fewer stitches, or none, at the join itself.

Computer modeling showed the cover spread stress evenly, while plain stitching concentrated tension at the join. Strength tests in rats matched that picture, since covered repairs held as well as stitched ones. Covered nerves also showed much better alignment of regrowing fibers and better blood vessel growth. Later tests tracked feeling and movement recovery along with fiber regrowth. The results support the cover as a gentler way to hold a repaired nerve together.
pmc-13632419:
Zihao Kuang and six colleagues test whether a long-run average of a simple insulin-resistance score can forecast who will develop high blood pressure. The score mixes blood fats, blood sugar, and waist size. A national study of older Chinese adults gave repeat measures years apart.

Of 2,571 adults free of high blood pressure at the start, about nine in a hundred developed it by the last check. Those with higher long-run scores were more prone to new disease. Averages over time beat single readings, the logic runs, because they smooth out daily noise. The authors say the cheap score, built from routine labs and a tape measure, could help flag risk early in community care.
pmc-13636119:
Tian Zhao and colleagues published this 2026 study of how one amino acid steers cancer-fighting T cells. Methionine, a building block the body cannot make, is essential for T cell activation. Starving tumors of it can help some immune therapies, yet cell therapies, where T cells are grown and returned, might suffer. The team tested both brief and sustained methionine restriction in lab-grown T cells and a mouse therapy model.

Brief restriction made killer T cells produce more key attack signal. The effect ran through a drop in polyamines, small molecules cells build from methionine. Adding polyamines back erased the gain, and deleting the polyamine enzyme copied it. Real tumors told a harsher story. Cells treated briefly before transfer gained no advantage, and mice on a restricted diet grew tumors faster as donated cells slid into exhaustion. The authors advise enriching, not starving, the tumor setting.
pmc-13639419:
Yue Feng and seven colleagues present a systematic review and meta-analysis of deep learning for spotting cerebral microbleeds, tiny brain bleeds seen on MRI scans. Counting these bleeds by hand is accurate but slow and costly, so automated help could change practice.

The reviewers searched five databases for original studies and graded their quality with a standard tool. At the level of individual patients, the pooled models caught most cases while keeping false alarms modest. At the level of single bleeds, accuracy was higher still. The authors offer the pooled figures as a base for building practical detection tools.
pmc-13641519:
Priya Arora and two colleagues present a 2026 narrative review of emergency care for people who arrive with acute muscle or joint pain while also living with mental health disorders. Pain care in emergency departments still centers on the body, even though anxiety, depression, and stress strongly shape recovery.

The review gathers evidence on current care pathways and finds mental health screening and support largely missing, leaving care fragmented for this group. Two to three of every ten patients with acute pain go on to chronic pain. The authors argue for integrated pathways that treat body and mind together from the first visit.
pmc-13644019:
Mona Kuroiwa and four colleagues present a 2026 analysis of whether home-area carbon monoxide exposure relates to children's movement in the United Kingdom Millennium Cohort Study. Air pollution and inactivity are both global concerns, yet child-level evidence using measured activity was scarce.

The sample held 6,281 children whose weekly steps were counted by accelerometers. Surprisingly, children in higher carbon monoxide areas recorded a few hundred more steps on average and slightly higher odds of preferring outdoor sports. The authors warn the result explains little variation and likely reflects neighborhood, school travel, and built surroundings, urging caution and richer context in future work.
pmc-13644519:
Abdelrahman Samy Ismail and five colleagues present a 2026 review of acoustic telemetry, the sound-based tracking of marine animals. Tagged fish and other sea life report movement, habitat use, and body responses to networks of listening receivers over months or years.

The review explains tag design, sensing, positioning, and data handling, then surveys uses from pollution studies to protected area design and fighting illegal fishing. Long deployments still strain power, size, and detection in noisy habitats. Emerging fixes include energy harvesting from waves and flexible, self-healing, even biodegradable power materials. The authors link those advances to tougher, greener observation platforms.
pmc-13645519:
Ziheng Zhu and four colleagues present a study of a mixed cell-death program, PANoptosis, in dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease that scars skin and weakens muscle. Excess interferon signaling is a known feature, but its link to this blended death pathway was unexplored.

Merging skin and muscle datasets with a death-gene list produced eleven candidates, and machine learning elevated four, led by ZBP1. A four-gene risk score separated patients sharply and tracked with inflammatory signatures. In human muscle cells, interferon-beta triggered the death program, while lowering ZBP1 blunted the damage. A plant compound, baicalin, bound ZBP1 directly and eased the injury.
pmc-13645719:
Published in 2026, a study by Shuwan Liu and sixteen colleagues builds an artificial intelligence system to warn of and diagnose chronic eye damage from graft-versus-host disease. This complication can follow donor stem cell transplants and may end in vision loss. The team trained their multimodal language model on records from hundreds of transplant patients, covering more than fifteen hundred eyes for the diagnosis task. Four kinds of clinical information were fused into one network.

In internal tests the system scored very high on early warning, diagnosis, and severity grading. Outside hospitals confirmed strong diagnosis scores, though early warning accuracy dropped there. Patients who came in after an early warning showed milder disease, and junior eye doctors improved when they used the tool as an aid. The authors expect the system to help clinics catch this complication sooner, when damage can still be limited.
pmc-13647119:
Mansour Alharbi reports the case of a thirteen-year-old boy whose near-constant honking cough had no physical cause. The dry cough struck every two seconds while he was awake, vanished in sleep, and left him unable to eat for three days or attend school. Exams, labs, lung tests, and a chest X-ray came back normal, and inhalers plus nasal sprays did nothing.

Psychiatric review found family stress but no psychosis, depression, or tic disorder, and the sleep pattern sealed the diagnosis of somatic cough syndrome. Behavioral therapy is the usual first treatment, yet the family could not reach it, so Alharbi tried a calming drug, bromazepam. The cough stopped within about a day and a half. Three months later he stayed symptom-free off the medicine, back at school and eating normally. The report offers the drug as a backup when therapy is out of reach.
pmc-13648419:
Rupert D. Smit and twelve colleagues test if brain drive in youth can steer healing after a spinal cord cut. Young rats got gene tools that let a drug raise or lower drive in the movement zone of the brain. All groups then played rough-and-tumble games each night as rehab. Play time was the same in all groups.

In hurt rats left alone, brain drive swung in a bad way, pulling toward the sound limb. Raised drive kept the drive aimed at the hurt limb and woke three detour paths round the cut. Reach moves and a spinal reflex both got better. Lowered drive gave the worst scores of all. The team says drive in a youth window acts like a switch for good or bad rewiring.
pmc-13649719:
Hyun-Il Gil and five colleagues linked a sugar-and-fat blood score to a lung pattern called PRISm in a huge Korean health check group. In this pattern, total breath volume falls while the share blown out fast stays normal. The group held 89,809 adults with no self-reported major illness, all checked in 2019.

The lung pattern showed in about one in thirty adults. Its share rose step by step across four bands of the blood score, and adjusted odds climbed in the same neat order. A stiff, restrictive pattern rose in step too, while the blocked-airway pattern did not. Two ways of drawing the lung cut-offs agreed. The authors call for follow-up over time to test the link.
pmc-13650719:
Takashi Iizumi and thirteen colleagues, publishing in 2026, report five-year results from a phase II trial of proton beam therapy for localized prostate cancer using fewer, larger doses than usual. Protons deposit their energy precisely, and the schedule compressed treatment into twenty-one sessions, which is more convenient if long-term safety holds.

One hundred twenty-five men were treated and followed for a median of close to six years. Serious late bowel side effects stayed rare, and late urinary effects were also uncommon. Only three men showed a biochemical sign of returning cancer, none developed clinical recurrence, and survival at five years was high. The trial met its main safety goal. The authors conclude that this moderate shortening of proton treatment looks safe and feasible, with disease control strong enough to support the schedule.
pmc-13651419:
Tingting Luo and eight co-authors, in 2026, refine brain-based prediction of autism symptoms by letting each person's distinctive connectivity pattern speak, and by respecting age. Autism varies hugely from person to person, and group-average brain maps wash out the traits that track behavior, most of all across childhood and adolescence.

Brain imaging data from 437 people in a public exchange were run through a method that pulls out a shared basis and each person's own departures from it, split by age band. Such traits tracked behavior better than plain connectivity scores. The largest gain appeared for social behavior in adolescents, where accuracy more than doubled at its peak and rose a lot on average. A fresh sample confirmed the gain. The authors argue that autism biomarker work must build in both personal variation and growth stage, to guide treatment choices.
pmc-13651519:
Matteo Ceppatelli and nine colleagues squeeze arsenic in a diamond anvil cell and watch its layered crystal rebuild itself, using single-crystal synchrotron X-ray diffraction up to extreme pressures. Gray arsenic starts as stacked layers, and earlier work disagreed about exactly how and when it collapses into a simple cubic form.

Their measurements of lattice shape and neighbor distances reveal a two-step bonding story: layers first stitch together into an intermediate pseudo-cubic structure across a defined pressure window, then complete the transition. Within that window, the spacing between layers shrinks while bonds inside the layers stretch, a trans-influence effect that converts each atom's pyramidal surroundings into octahedral ones. The persistence of lone pair electron activity explains the halfway state. The authors say the finding settles a long-standing structural argument and sharpens bond theory for the whole pnictogen family.
pmc-13651819:
Greta Gallo and eleven colleagues design short synthetic RNA hunters, called gapmers, against the coronavirus that caused COVID-19, aiming for a drug platform that can answer future variants quickly. Twenty-four antisense molecules were aimed at stretches of the viral genome that barely change between strains and sit exposed in single-stranded regions.

Screening in cells found gapmers that sharply cut viral RNA and virus production across four variants. Their power tracked how accessible the target stretch was, measured by a chemical probing method. The effect came from cleaving the viral RNA rather than from provoking the cell's own antiviral alarms. Delivered through the nose without any carrier, the naked gapmers reached lung tissue and were swallowed preferentially by alveolar macrophages, where they also reshaped the inflammatory response to viral exposure. The authors present the approach as a scalable antiviral strategy held in reserve for emerging outbreaks.
pmc-3750319:
Hoesel and Schmid review the complexity of NF-kB signalling in inflammation and cancer. NF-kB is a family of transcription factors, proteins that switch genes on. It has an essential role in inflammation and in the innate immune system, the body's first defence line.

NF-kB is also increasingly recognised as a key player across many steps, from cancer initiation to progression. During those processes it cooperates with multiple other pathways, making its effects context-dependent. The review explains why a promising drug target has proven so hard to tame safely.  Combination therapy ideas in the review stem directly from those pathway interactions described.
pmc-4696819:
Ritz, Baty, Streibig, and their colleagues wrote in 2015 on dose-response analysis using R. Dose-response work asks how an effect grows with dose, a core question in drug and toxicology studies. General commercial software can do it, but non-standard output often needs awkward manual programming.

The authors present the drc extension package for the R environment. It supplies ready models and outputs tailored to dose-response data. That saves time and cuts errors for routine and special cases alike. Free, focused tools help smaller labs run the same quality of analysis as large institutes.
pmc-5395719:
Chalmers, Connelly, Fabrizio, and their colleagues analyzed tumor mutational burden in 2017 across a huge set of human cancer genomes. Tumors that carry many mutations tend to respond better to immune checkpoint drugs, so that mutation load serves as a biomarker. It predicted response to such immunotherapy better than some standard measures.

By studying a very large collection of cancer genomes, the team revealed the landscape of mutational burden across cancer types. Some cancers carry many mutations, others very few, and burden varies within types too. Mutations create new antigens that the immune system can recognize, which explains the link to drug response. The landscape helps oncologists judge who may benefit from checkpoint blockade.
pmc-5735219:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration published this pooled analysis of body weight trends in 2017. Being underweight or obese in youth harms health across the whole life course. The team combined thousands of surveys that measured height and weight directly.

The data cover children, teens, and adults in most countries from the mid nineteen seventies to 2016. Results show obesity rising in nearly every region while underweight fell more slowly. The sheer scale makes this a standard source for global weight trends. Governments and health agencies use it to set targets and judge whether policies are working.
pmc-6193719:
Christian Sticht, Carolina De La Torre, Asma Parveen, and coauthors described the miRWalk resource in 2018. MicroRNAs control genes by binding to matching sites on their messages. Guessing those sites well is key to understanding microRNA action.

miRWalk predicts binding sites for genes of humans and several animals and also lists sites proven in experiments. Its core predictor learns from known pairs using a random forest method. A simple web interface serves users who do not code. Researchers start here when a gene change hints that a microRNA might be involved.
pmc-7904519:
Michael Weller and colleagues issued updated guidelines in 2020 on diagnosing and treating diffuse gliomas, a group of brain tumors that grow into surrounding tissue. The European Association for Neuro-Oncology produced the guidance after major changes in how these tumors are classified. Large clinical trials had also recently reported mature results that changed what good care looks like.

The guidelines walk through modern diagnosis, which now leans heavily on molecular features of the tumor, not just its look under a microscope. They then lay out treatment paths for adult patients at each stage. Doctors across Europe and beyond use this document to keep care consistent with the best current evidence.
pmc-7931819:
Petr Danecek and colleagues looked back in 2021 on twelve years of SAMtools and BCFtools, two program suites used to handle DNA sequencing data. The tools manage the standard file formats of the field, converting, sorting, and querying the huge files that sequencing machines produce. They also call genetic variants and analyze their effects.

The article describes what the suites do, how they grew from their first versions, and the standards they helped establish. Almost every genome study of the past decade has passed its data through these programs at some point. The retrospective doubles as a short history of how high throughput sequencing became routine science.
pmc-8866119:
Yunlong Cao and co-authors reported in 2021 that the Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2 could escape most of the neutralizing antibodies then known. Omicron carried an unusual cluster of changes in its receptor binding domain, the spike region that antibodies target most. The team set out at once to learn how those changes affected antibody defenses.

Using a high throughput screening method that tests many antibody interactions at speed, they mapped which antibodies kept working and which failed. Most existing antibodies lost their grip on the variant, while a few broader ones held. Coming within weeks of Omicron's emergence, the results warned that many antibody medicines would need replacing, and that vaccine strategies had to account for this escape.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-156:
With the war over, Punch for April 16, 1919, volume 156, still leads with Charivaria, its column of short jokes on the news. Peace brings new targets: American Prohibition, crowded London housing, jazz, and the cost of living in a city short of rooms.

A mock rescue party would save Scotsmen from America's dry law. The Times is rumored to deny blame for its own views. A trombone player in a tiny flat must step onto the landing for his lowest note. A Shoreditch street packs hundreds into a few houses. Parliament, the column hints, packs in its own crowd.

April 2, 1919 brings volume 156 of Punch and a Charivaria column that finds postwar Britain still short of food, space, and sense. The London humor weekly jokes about grocers, lost bones, bands home from the army, and hints for young housekeepers.

A Liverpool grocer fined for overcharging on eight foods is called fit for the Peace Conference. A proposed strike of wives fails, a Reigate man advertises for a lost human jawbone, and a hint on marble beef is left firmly to the butcher. Demobilized bandsmen, grown too large for their old uniforms, close the page.

Punch for April 23, 1919, volume 156, starts with Charivaria, brief jokes on elections, ration coupons, and the fallen German royal house. Five months after the Armistice, the London weekly still writes about war controls, now with the peace talks and old enemies in view.

Hull voters deal the Coalition a rebuke that stops short of a finishing blow. A Woking butcher is thirty-two thousand coupons short, a man with a latchkey seeks a house to fit it, and a food inspector cannot tell two grades of tinned beef apart. The ex-Crown Prince and Ludendorff trade insults in the closing items.

Dated April 30, 1919, this Punch, volume 156, opens with Charivaria, short jokes drawn from peace talks, food supply, and odd news items. The tone is dry and quick, with each item lasting only a line or two before the next target appears.

Printing House Square is rumored to deny blame for the Peace Conference, just as The Times might. Fifty London fish shops change hands under a cloud of mystery. Germany, a food report says, holds more sheep than in 1914, which prompts a jab at a German leader's noise. A health writer's claim that members of Parliament could live to one hundred meets doubt.

Punch, volume 156, for April 9, 1919, leads with Charivaria, where postwar Britain is mocked in short, neat jokes. Ministries, prisons, old tanks, and spring weather pass in review as the country adjusts to peace after four years of war.

An Air Ministry officer asks for lower pay since work has dried up, and is watched for other odd signs. A woman tries to buy Daylight Saving Certificates at a post office. War Office staff numbers fall only slowly after the Armistice, old tanks are tested as mouse traps with cheese, and Irish police pursue inquiries rather than escaped prisoners.

For February 12, 1919, Punch in volume 156 opens with Charivaria, its chain of short jokes on army orders, flu, and the housing shortage. Britain had left the war months before, yet daily life still ran on rules, rumors, and crowded rooms.

Officers may now ride their army horses for private use, a blow to taxi drivers. A man meets a badger on Hampstead Heath and calls it a thrill. An American bill would let grandfathers join settled aliens, flu experts urge masks and goggles, and the new housing chief, the column reports, has not yet found a single house.

Volume 156 of Punch for February 19, 1919, begins with Charivaria, quick jokes on demobilization, German royalty, golf, and strikes. The war had ended the autumn before, and the London weekly tracks how slowly normal life was coming back.

Word that soldiers would all be home by March 31 is denied, and the staff in charge are accused of hoping to die in harness. Woolwich Arsenal turns to making ice-cream freezers. The German ex-Crown Prince vows to die before facing trial. Soldier golfers import a new way to address the ball from Mesopotamia. A man who will not strike turns out to have no job.

Punch dated February 26, 1919, volume 156, leads with Charivaria, short jokes on the peace talks, Ireland, and George Bernard Shaw. Each item takes a headline or a public remark and twists it with a straight face.

Count Rantzau says Germany must not be treated as a second-rate nation, and the column blames its tenth-rate nobles. A general wins fame for vowing not to write a war book. Seven men attack a Dublin policeman on a Sunday. An American team comes to study British industry. Shaw's claim that Britons forget anything older than a fortnight is turned neatly back on Shaw himself.

Opening Punch for February 5, 1919, volume 156, readers find Charivaria, a page of brief jokes on the Armistice, food stores, and soldiers coming home. The German word for the truce talks is itself the first joke, for its sheer length.

A rumored Hamlet staged to cheer the clergy, with a gloomy dean as the Dane, is denied. An American senator's modest remark is answered through bacon. Stored marmalade is at last set free, to public wonder at the Food Ministry's wit. A soldier offered cash or a standard suit on discharge says he would rather pay the fine.

New Year's Day 1919 in Punch, volume 156, opens not with the usual joke column but with a poem, "To an Unknown Colleague," drawn from the swapping of minutes inside government offices. The verse honors a fellow clerk the writer worked beside for eight months yet never once met.

The two men pass on the stair without knowing each other, yet trade notes in full accord. Each asks the other's view with care, each agrees with the other in nine cases out of ten, and their friendship flows on paper alone. The poem turns office routine into a gentle joke about modern work.

Punch for January 15, 1919, volume 156, opens with Charivaria, short jokes on the first weeks of peace. A memorial at Evesham, a planned silence room, small concrete houses from America, and the recent general election give the London weekly its material.

Simon de Montfort, dead since 1265, is asked whether he has been demobilized yet. A club plans to revive its Silence Room. American one-piece concrete houses are said to pinch under the arms. A stage revival after the election hints at a beaten candidate's revenge. Some papers flirting with Bolshevism earn a French pun in reply.

January 8, 1919 in Punch, volume 156, brings Charivaria, brief jokes on the peace talks in Paris and the changed cast of public life after the election. Every item is a few lines, built on a headline, a rumor, or a new book of reference.

The one Foreign Office man who stayed home from Paris turns out to be the caretaker. Romania's king and queen plan a trip west. The German navy's command moves to Wilhelmshaven. The new Who's Who grows by eighty-six pages. Many losers of the election are, as the column puts it, not Who at all.

Volume 156 of Punch for January 22, 1919 leads with Charivaria, a run of short jokes on flu, peace talks, and slow officials. A waterspout, a sea captain's lost pocket-book, and a Bavarian uprising that cost almost nothing all pass through the column.

The waterspout seen off Guernsey is bound, in jest, for the Peace Conference. A torpedoed captain ate his pocket-book to keep his orders from the Germans. Flu control, a health chief says, needs more study, so readers will catch it at their own risk. A civil servant seen running was simply going off duty.

Punch dated January 29, 1919, volume 156, starts with Charivaria, quick jokes on the peace, the ex-Kaiser, and crowded London trains. Ireland's place at the peace talks and a coming eclipse sit beside jokes about beards left at ticket offices.

Peace, says Mr. Hughes, is a matter of time, and the ex-Kaiser wonders who will serve that time. Talk of trying him for murder ends, the column finds, at yes or no. De Valera is named a delegate for an Irish republic while still in prison, and men with beards may be asked to check them before boarding packed Tube trains.

June 11, 1919 finds Punch, volume 156, leading with Charivaria, short jokes on pay, heat, marriage, and women drivers. Summer in London and the long peace talks give the weekly a fresh set of small targets.

A Labour paper says every working man has the same right as a member of Parliament to four hundred pounds a year, and the column agrees at once. A trade paper calls women a grave danger to drivers and may, in jest, have to be rid of. Heat at Euston makes a taxi driver offer a ride to a walker, an act so odd that fellow drivers pin him down for his own good.

For June 18, 1919, Punch in volume 156 opens with Charivaria, brief jokes on President Wilson, jazz, yacht races, and the peace terms. The items are short and dry, each built from a scrap of the week's news.

A New York professor ranks Wilson among the five greatest men alive, and Sir Eric Geddes wants the full list. The jazz boom fades as an eastern one nears. No arrest follows a safe robbery at Plaistow, since the thieves wished to stay nameless. Sir Thomas Lipton vows to win the America Cup in 1920, and Philadelphia orders bright lights for ballroom sitting-out spots.

Punch for June 25, 1919, volume 156, begins with Charivaria, a page of short jokes on whisky, flying, smoking, and Serbia's arms buying. The long peace was about to be signed, yet the column keeps its eyes on small absurd things.

A man offers to buy five thousand pounds of Joy Loan if the state finds him a case of whisky, not seeing that a state with whisky would need no loan. The first flight across the Atlantic and Galway's many pubs mock American dry law. Boys smoke more, a Dublin fair restocks the zoo, and two German machine guns guard a town library.

Dated June 4, 1919, this issue of Punch, volume 156, leads with Charivaria, quick jokes on Germany's choice, jazz reaching far islands, and the many small wars still burning. Peace at Paris dominates the news while the column hunts for lighter angles.

Germany will sign, a paper says, since the Allies hold all the trumps, and all the tinned beef too. A Welsh man fined for shooting an owl blames the bird for not sounding a horn. Jazz cases appear in the Hebrides, twenty-three wars are said to run on, and Channel swimmers grow so many that a tunnel may not be needed.

March 12, 1919 brings Punch, volume 156, and a Charivaria column on flu, jazz, and whisky. Whitehall dancing, a drunk who blamed the flu, and a silent motor car show how peace was changing daily life in London that spring.

Germs, the column says, should walk rather than be carried. A young American claims he invented jazz, a claim set beside a murder confession in the same week's press. A man charged with drunkenness blames flu and whisky, and readers who saw a headline offering whisky for flu write in at once, keen to make the trade.

Punch for March 19, 1919, volume 156, opens with Charivaria, short jokes on Wilson's sea games, spring flowers, and war guilt. The peace talks in Paris run on in the background while the column picks at small stories from home.

Wilson plays shuffle-board on his ship while Lord Robert Cecil brushes up on shove-halfpenny in Paris. Lambs and primroses appear, and the column asks if the Poet Laureate waits for sunstroke before writing of spring. A war crimes panel has not yet found the ex-Kaiser guilty, though it thinks he knew something about the war.

Volume 156 of Punch, dated March 26, 1919, leads with Charivaria, brief jokes on the ex-Kaiser at work, Dublin water rates, and flu in packed trains. Each item takes one news scrap and turns it in a line or two.

William Hohenzollern saws trees in exile, which some read as spite at his own generals. Dublin raises water charges and urges citizens to try the stuff. A man in a crowded tube blows the nose of the man beside him by mistake. A beggar claims a wound from a sea battle he could not have fought. A court witness reports twenty years spent on the telephone.

Punch for March 5, 1919, volume 156, starts with Charivaria, a set of short jokes on whisky, German defeat, and a lost army mule. Ireland, Dublin's new lord mayor, and a prison escape share the page with a stray animal at Walton-on-Thames.

An evening paper asks what whisky is, and the column half recalls the name. A German paper calls defeat bitter, which the column links to tons of American bacon sold to Germany. The owner of a wandering mule is sought, and a soldier in Mesopotamia thinks the beast may be his own lost mount from six months before.

Punch for May 14, 1919, volume 156, leads with Charivaria, short jokes on the peace terms, Russia's new calendar, and late spring birds. A German delegate's manners at Paris and a Balham man bitten by a jazz player set the tone for the page.

A headline asks where Germany stands, and the column notes that Count Brockdorff-Rantzau stayed seated while speaking. Russia starts its year on October 25, which the column links, in jest, to dislike of New Year customs. Birds late in reaching Britain are said to be racing the planned flight across the Atlantic, on foot.

Volume 156 of Punch for May 21, 1919 opens with Charivaria, brief jokes on the peace talks, Friday weddings, and gifts before an engagement. Each short item turns a news scrap or a court remark into a dry punch line.

A Berlin paper mourns that the Peace Conference feels like a Diet of Worms. Readers ask if Friday weddings bring bad luck, and the column answers from hard use. A hushed-up flight from Newfoundland is blamed on an American pilot. A dish of crab is never in season at smart tables. A judge rules that gifts before an engagement are bait that cannot be claimed back.

Punch dated May 28, 1919, volume 156, puts a cartoon of Austria's fallen empire before its Charivaria column of short jokes. Cheese, peace parties, miners, and rabbits give the London weekly a set of small postwar targets.

A Danish expert blames a pig for Germany losing the war, yet fails to name which pig, which may stir the German high command. Returning cheeses merit a public welcome and a march-past, in jest. Hackney cuts power rates for the peace parties, miners in the North vote against starting a paper, and rabbits at Hassocks are said to clear five-foot fences.

For May 7, 1919, Punch in volume 156 leads with Charivaria, quick jokes on May Day snow, muzzled dogs, hotel fleas, and the secret inside a sausage. Spring weather and new dog rules frame a page of small, sharp items.

Dancing round a snow man draws no crowd on May Day. Fewer West End postmen are bitten since dogs were muzzled, though the dogs blame a rich supply of milkmen instead. A flea hops onto a hotel visitors' book as an American officer signs in, and food experts confess they cannot tell what animal, or which part, fills a sausage.
routledge-mystery-easter-island-1919:
Katherine Routledge led the Mana trip to Easter Island in 1914. Her book The Mystery of Easter Island came out in 1919. The trip made the first full study of the isle and its great stone heads, the moai. Routledge writes as both sailor and field worker.

She tells how the heads were cut, moved, and raised, and what the isle folk said of them. Strange carved birds, caves, and old rites fill the tale. The ship's tale frames the work: storms, waits, and war news from far off. The book stands as the base study of the isle.
royce-lectures-modern-idealism-1919:
Lectures on Modern Idealism, published in 1919, three years after Royce's death, prints the last lecture course he built on the idealist tradition. Kant, Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel are his subjects, the four Germans who made modern idealism.

Royce treats each thinker as a stage in one argument about selfhood and the absolute. His sympathy is with Hegel, but his exposition stays fair to all four, in the clear style of a practiced lecturer. The course sums up the tradition he had spent his life extending. It is his last word on idealism, and a graceful one.
russell-intro-mathematical-philosophy-19:
Introduction to Mathematical Philosophy, published in 1919, is Russell's plain-language account of the ideas behind Principia Mathematica. He wrote much of it in Brixton prison, where he was held for an anti-war article, working without a library.

Russell explains number, infinity, series, and the theory of descriptions for readers with no training in symbols. The paradox that shook the foundations of logic gets a clear, almost cheerful hearing. His aim was to show that the great work's ideas could live outside its notation. The book remains the friendliest door into mathematical logic ever written by one of its makers.
russia-in-1919: Russia in 1919 is named in its front pages as a work by Arthur Ransome. The pages shown here are chiefly Project Gutenberg header matter, dated May 1998, with notes on copyright law in many lands. Other notes cover keeping the file for the next readers, and release dates at the end of the stated month. The header also names Joseph Gallanar as the person who prepared the electronic text. No chapter, preface, or narrative passage appears in the portion shown here.
say-traite-economie-politique-vol1-1819:
Say's Treatise on Political Economy reached its fourth French edition in 1819, and the first volume opens the work. Say was Adam Smith's great French interpreter, who recast the master's teaching into a clearer system. His Treatise became the most influential economics textbook of its age across Europe and America.

Volume 1 treats production: how wealth is created by industry, capital, and natural agents working together. Say gives the entrepreneur, the organizer who joins the factors and bears the risk, a central place that Smith had left vague. His famous law of markets, that supply creates its own demand, is stated in these chapters. The book taught Europe economics after Smith, in prose students could actually follow. The 1819 edition shows the system in its mature, author-revised form.
say-traite-economie-politique-vol2-1819:
Volume 2 of Say's Treatise, from the same 1819 fourth French edition, completes his system of political economy. The Treatise as a whole had already passed through many printings and translations, an honor no economics book of the age could match. Say revised each edition, and the fourth was his definitive statement.

The second volume carries the argument from production into distribution and consumption: how income is shared, and how wealth is used or wasted. Say treats public spending and taxation with the same wish for clarity that marks the first volume. The applied chapters show the doctrine meeting the facts of French economic life. Read with volume 1, the book gives the French master's full doctrine in its final form. It is the textbook that taught a generation, closed and complete.
shackleton-south-1919:
Ernest Shackleton published South in 1919, the story of his last great expedition of 1914 to 1917. His ship Endurance sailed to cross Antarctica from sea to sea. Instead, the ice caught the ship, crushed it, and sank it, leaving 28 men on the floes.

Shackleton tells how the crew camped on drifting ice for months, then sailed lifeboats to Elephant Island. From there he made the famous open-boat run to South Georgia and crossed its peaks to find help. Every man lived. The book is the leader's own record of endurance and command.
shelley-cenci-1819:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote The Cenci in Italy in 1819, basing it on a true Roman story from 1599. Shelley hoped the play could be staged in London, but its subject made that impossible in his lifetime. He modeled its plain, forceful style on Jacobean tragedy.

Count Francesco Cenci is a monster of cruelty who rejoices in tormenting his family. His daughter Beatrice, driven past endurance, arranges his murder with her mother and brother. The law then punishes the victims more harshly than it ever punished the tyrant. Shelley explores how violence corrupts even the innocent. The play is his most stage-worthy drama.
sinclair-brass-check-1919:
Upton Sinclair published The Brass Check in 1919, at his own expense, after no commercial house would take it. Sinclair had spent twenty years fighting editors who trimmed his socialism, and this book names names. Its title comes from the brass checks men once bought in brothels, his metaphor for bought journalism.

The book documents, case by case, how American newspapers served their owners and advertisers: suppressed stories, planted lies, and crusades steered by business interests. Sinclair draws on his own clashes with the press over The Jungle and his later campaigns. He proposes reforms, from public ownership to reader-funded papers. The Brass Check is the first systematic American critique of the press, and its charges still start arguments.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5019:
James Polk gives four yearly addresses in one set. Their dates run from December 2, 1845, to December 5, 1848. Three stars part each address from the next. The first voices plain joy at the meeting. Polk meets the people's house for the first time as president. The Constitution lays a clear duty on him. He must give word of the state of the Union. He must urge such steps as he judges needful.

He is glad to cheer Congress on the country's thriving. Kind heaven and free forms bless that thriving. The nation stands before the world a show of happiness. Growth past match marks all the seeds of greatness. The people's love for the Union stands firm. Love for popular freedom at its base stands firm as well. He then turns to ties with foreign powers. He is glad to report their state in fair terms.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Volume 19 of The Tales and Novels of J. de La Fontaine contains The Psalter and King Candaules and the Doctor of Laws. The first is a convent tale; the second reaches back to Herodotus for one of the oldest stories of a king's folly.

The Psalter opens with a confession. The poet cannot resist the nuns once more. Their tales of convent pranks are seldom cold. They carry a grace found nowhere else. So one more must be told. It makes three, or by his count four. The gardener stands first among them. Candaules, by contrast, is the Lydian king of Herodotus. Pride in his wife's beauty ruined him. He forced his servant Gyges to view her unseen. He lost throne and life for the vanity. A doctor of laws shares the volume with him.
the-crime-against-europe-a-possible-outc:
Sir Roger Casement subtitled his book A Possible Outcome of the War of 1914, under a 1915 copyright. An unsigned introduction warns readers that the articles were written before the war began. It calls them in a sense prophetic, and credits Casement with a sharp grasp of the conditions that brought the great war about.

The introduction sketches his career in the English consular service: consul at Lorenzo Marques in 1889. Then came posts covering the Gaboon and the Congo Free State from 1898 to 1905, Santos, and Para. He was consul-general at Rio de Janeiro in 1909. A knighthood came in 1911. It also notes that he helped organize the Irish Volunteers at Dublin in November 1913 He is now in Berlin. The German chancellor has stated that German forces reaching Ireland would come as friends, not conquerors.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Dated March 18, 1897, No. 19 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and an offer headed School Books Wanted. The same offer stands in an earlier number of the paper. Used school books will be taken in exchange for subscriptions, at named prices. The list prices readers by Barnes, Appleton, and Cyr. It prices the New Franklin readers and McGuffey's Revised. A year's subscription costs $2.50.
the-hermetic-art-an-introduction-to-the-: The Hermetic Art, an introduction to the art of alchemy, 1919. The introduction. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part: Volume II, Part 19 of Don Quixote comes from Cervantes, in Ormsby's English rendering. The contents list the Part II chapters in order. Chapter one treats the visit of the curate and the barber. They come to speak with Don Quixote about his malady. Chapter two treats Sancho Panza's dispute at home. Chapter three treats the talk with Samson Carrasco. The same contents opening stands in the complete Volume II record. No text past the front matter is present here.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, July 28, 1827, No. 266, illustrates Croydon Palace. For centuries the palace housed the archbishops of Canterbury in magnificence. Lanfranc resided there at the Conquest, and his successors issued decrees from its rooms. Archbishop Parker entertained Queen Elizabeth and her court there with great splendour, and Whitgift did the same. Courtney received his pall there before the chief nobility of the realm.

The surviving fabric, mostly brick, spreads across the south-west side of Croydon church behind garden walls. Its grand hall is a lofty structure of some eight hundred square yards. A moulding runs round each wall at about fifteen feet, resting on angels bearing shields. Chichley, Stafford, Laud, Juxon, Wake, and Herring all resided there and added to its beauties. Readers meet a palace of church politics reduced to picturesque remains.

Number 349 of the Mirror, dated Saturday, December 6, 1828, still harps on the fine arts with the Arch of Constantine at Rome. A footnote promises a supplement of poetical gems from the annuals, with an engraving after Turner. The article traces triumphal arches from simple brick to marble monuments with three gates. Winged victories hung in the central vault, ready to lower crowns onto a passing victor's head.

The Arch of Constantine, noblest of them, subsists almost entire near the Appian Way. The senate and people raised it after Constantine's victory over Maxentius. It stands between the Coelian and Palatine hills as the last monument of Roman triumph. Four columns of giallo antico marble adorn each front. Readers receive Roman ceremony explained through one surviving gate, at the moment the magazine turns to Christmas gift books.

Number 383 of the Mirror, dated Saturday, August 1, 1829, illustrates Tunbridge Wells in 1748 with sketches of its famous visitors. A keyed list names twenty-three figures in the engraving. Dr. Johnson stands first, with Colley Cibber, Garrick, Lord Chatham as Mr. Pitt, and Samuel Richardson among them. Beau Nash, Miss Chudleigh, Lord Lyttelton, and Mrs. Johnson fill out the fashionable crowd.

Tunbridge, second only to Bath in its best days, was a gay, anecdotal resort of the last century. Its belles and beaux never dreamed Brighthelmstone would spread into Brighton and steal the Wells's glory. The drawing belonged to Richardson himself and was found among his papers at his death in 1761. Sir Richard Phillips now holds the original. Readers receive a spa town's golden age as a group portrait, every celebrity numbered like specimens.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, January 29, 1831, No. 473, pairs two engravings of the Strand, ancient and modern. One shows the Strand in 1547 with the Strand Cross, Convent Garden, and Edward VI's procession. The other looks from Arundel House northwards in 1700, with the maypole and garland. The editors point regular subscribers to earlier notices: old Covent Garden in Volume 12, a second notice and the original Somerset House in Volume 13.

Quoted matter begins the history: in 1222 most of the parish was an extensive garden of the Abbot and Convent of Westminster. That Convent Garden, corrupted to Covent Garden, gives the district its name. Neighbouring lands were the Elms, then Seven Acres, then Long Acre. Readers are sent back through the magazine's own back numbers as an index to London's growth. A street is treated as a palimpsest, its garden still legible under the pavement.

Volume 19, No. 532, dated February 4, 1832, opens with Robert the Devil. Every London theatre, the writers note, was preparing its own version of the French opera Robert le Diable after its Paris success. Two engravings show the castle and the cavern linked with the story.

Rather than judge an opera unseen, the magazine prints a correspondent's historical notes on the Norman sites. The castle stands on the left bank of the Seine in Normandy, defended so well by nature that only trickery could take it. Vast underground caverns run, by tradition, toward the river. Carved fragments bearing the stamp of 912 support its great age, and the forest of Bourgtheroulde spreads below.
the-seventh-manchesters-july-1916-to-mar: Captain S. J. Wilson, M.C., wrote The Seventh Manchesters, covering July 1916 to March 1919. The University Press at Manchester published the battalion history. Longmans, Green and Company handled London and other cities. A preface by Brigadier-General Anthony M. Henley is listed. Gerald B. Hurst, who commanded the seventh battalion, supplied an introduction. The pages shown give the title and publishing matter only, plus Henley's portrait caption. No preface, introduction, or narrative text follows, so the battalion's war record itself is not shown.
the-works-of-thomas-vaughan-eugenius-phi: Arthur Edward Waite edited, annotated, and introduced The Works of Thomas Vaughan, who wrote as Eugenius Philalethes. The Theosophical Publishing House in London issued the edition in 1919. It was prepared for the Theosophical Society's library committee in England and Wales. A quotation from Vaughan's Aula Lucis stands on the title page. A foreword begins by calling the book the first volume of a series of transactions. The works themselves start beyond the pages shown.
tob-0019:
Peter leads a tour of the world to come in the Apocalypse of Peter, one of the earliest Christian visions of the afterlife. This entry rests on a verified pre-1930 public-domain edition. Some early churches read the work nearly as Scripture before later ages set it aside.

Heaven shows its brightness, and hell shows punishments fitted closely to each sin: liars, murderers, and the cruel each meet a matching torment. Later ages borrowed the pattern freely, down to the great infernos of medieval poetry. The vision is stern, vivid, and oddly hopeful, since mercy keeps breaking in. Few short texts cast so long a shadow.
tob-0119:
Laurence Dermott wrote the Ahiman Rezon for the Antient Grand Lodge, the rowdy rival of Anderson's Masons. First issued in the 1750s, his constitution defends older customs against what he saw as modern tampering. Waite's scholars and traditionalists alike still argue over its claims.
